status: All 418 passages of the Meditations, in the 38 sections of the Stoic Constitution. Every passage was translated from the Greek alone by a language model and checked against the Greek in a second reading; each point raised was settled in writing in a third. The owner read the first six on 23 November 2026 and said “looks good”; the other 412 have not been read by the owner. None has been checked by a person who reads Greek.

sections.title: What I learned, and from whom
Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time
Good whatever others say, and open to being set right
Training, and the use of reason
The morning, and the question before each action
My judgment is up to me
What happens can be borne and does not harm me
Keeping the few names I have given myself
Living now as one about to die
Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready
Whether anything is better than virtue
Blaming no one for what is not up to me
Happiness and unhappiness are my own doing
The length of a life and the use of its time
The work that belongs to me
The reason that governs the whole
What the whole sends in its season
The sameness and meanness of things

edition.citation: M. Antoninus Imperator ad se ipsum, edited by Jan Hendrik Leopold, 1908.
edition.publisher_note: Library catalogues and the Classical Review give Oxford, Clarendon Press (Oxford Classical Texts). The header of the Perseus file says “Leipzig: Teubner, 1908”. Both are recorded; the text used is the Perseus file.

method: A first translator was given the Greek of a section’s passages and nothing else: no earlier translation, no article. It was asked for plain modern English that keeps the speaker, the person addressed, every “all” and “not”, and each image. Wherever the Greek can be read two ways, it was asked to translate one reading and note the other.

A second reader was given only the Greek and that English, without the first translator’s notes, and asked to list every place where the English says more, less or other than the Greek. Across the book it raised 1,458 points; it called 132 passages sound, 275 open to minor fixes, and 5 wrong in a way that changed what Marcus says.

Each point was then settled in writing: accepted (969), partly accepted (465) or declined (189), with the reason. For the first six passages the editor of this project settled the points; for the rest a third reader did, given the Greek, the draft and the points. The third reader also fixed 137 faults that neither earlier reader had caught (marked “Found while settling”). The result is the English shown here. Under each passage you can open both lists: what the Greek leaves open (3,201 notes), and what the second reader questioned.

All three readers were the same model, Claude Fable 5.2, each starting afresh and seeing only what its brief allowed. Most sections were read in Claude Code; in eleven sections at least one reading was made through the Anthropic API with the same briefs. The briefs are kept in the project (translation-translator.md, translation-checker.md, translation-settler.md).

So that a Greek word does not become a different English word from one passage to the next, the settled renderings of the first six passages were given to every reader as preferences (for example “the universe” for κόσμος, “the nature of the whole”, “the ruling part”); where a passage’s own argument needed another word, a note says so.

The 1634 translation numbers and cuts its sections differently from modern editions. Each of its passages was matched to the Greek by reading the openings and endings side by side, after a whole-book alignment had proposed the matches; together the 418 passages cover every chapter of the Greek exactly once. Where a passage joins two or more modern chapters (58 passages), they are shown as one, with the chapter breaks kept (as in 6.9–10). Where a passage covers only part of a chapter (63 passages), it carries a letter (11.8a is the first part, 3.11b a later part) and says which Greek it leaves out.

Before a section was stored, its files were checked by a script: every quoted Greek word is an exact part of the passage, every point has its decision, the typography is plain and there are no archaic forms. Where a reader had typed a Latin letter inside a quoted Greek word, or another Unicode form of the same accented letter, the quotation was corrected to the exact characters of the source; no wording was changed that way.

On 24 Nov 2026 the owner asked for a literary review of every article and every passage, so that each would “sound clear and tasteful”. Every passage was read again for clarity and taste by a reviewer, with the Greek beside the English; an independent second reader judged each proposed edit and listed what had been missed, and every objection was settled in writing, the Greek deciding the meaning. 221 edits changed the English of 161 passages. Each changed passage has a new revision, the old one kept under “superseded”, and the spelling is now British throughout. Both readers were Claude Opus 5.5.
limits: All three readers are language models. A model’s Greek can be confidently wrong; the Greek is shown beside the English so that anyone who reads Greek can object.

The Greek is a digitised copy of Leopold’s edition and has slips of its own (an accent, a breathing mark, a misprinted letter). Where the English follows the intended word despite such a slip, a note says so. Where the Greek itself does not make grammatical sense (for example 8.35, 9.28a, 7.31b), the English marks the place and does not smooth it over.

Notes that rely on a model’s memory of the manuscripts or of an editor’s conjecture say “from memory, unchecked” (205 notes). None was checked against a critical edition. In 5.8 the source prints ἐκεῖ σε (“you there”) where the text may be the one word ἐκεῖσε (“to that place”); the printed edition was not consulted. Two scraps of the source belong to no passage: the note at the end of Book 1 (Τὰ ἐν Κουάδοις πρὸς τῷ Γρανούᾳ, “among the Quadi, at the Granua”) and a stray chapter numeral inside 12.17.

The passage numbers are those of modern editions; the 1634 number is given beside each. The passages were grouped into sections by the similarity of their 1634 English, not of this translation. Measured on the new English, 352 of the 418 passages are still closest to their own section; the table above lists the rest by section. No passage was moved.
A translated passage is never edited in place. A correction is a new revision with a new id; the old one is kept in the record.
footer: Greek: M. Antoninus Imperator ad se ipsum, ed. J. H. Leopold (1908), from the Perseus Digital Library, CC BY-SA. 1634 English: Meric Casaubon (Project Gutenberg 2680). The new English is this project’s own translation.

vectors.note: The sections were grouped on the 1634 English, and each centre is the mean of its own passages in that English, so a passage in 1634 English has a head start toward its own centre. Read the new numbers as: does the passage still belong here when said in today’s words?

russian.status: Russian of the project’s own English: all 418 passages of the Meditations and the 304 quoted sections of Seneca’s letters. Made from the English, not from the Greek or Latin, at the owner’s request. Not yet read in full by the owner, nor checked against the English by a native speaker.
method: Claude Opus 5.5 translated each unit from the settled English, with a short glossary for the Stoic terms, and used no published Russian translation.
A second reader on another model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) compared the Russian with the English, passage by passage, and listed every place where it says more, less or other than the English.

The translator settled each point in writing: 148 accepted, 57 partly accepted, 7 declined. Two more points, raised by the article translators (8.3 and 3.11a), were accepted on 24 Nov 2026; 150 were accepted in all. On 24 Nov 2026 the owner asked for «части тела» in place of «члены» for the limbs of a body; five passages were changed (7.13, 7.19–22, 7.68, Ep. 90.29, Ep. 95.52).
Scripts checked that every passage is present and in order and that its paragraphs match the English; they also checked length, script and typography.

On 24 Nov 2026, in the same literary review, every passage was read again as Russian prose by a reviewer and an independent second reader (both Claude Opus 5.5), with the English deciding the meaning; each objection was settled in writing. 613 edits changed the Russian of 387 passages, among them every passage whose English the review had changed, and recurring words were made uniform (for example «маленькая душа» for “little soul” and «самообладание» for “self-control”).
limits: A translation of a translation: where the English had to choose between readings of the Greek or Latin, the Russian follows the English choice.
The translators’ notes on the Greek and Latin stay in English.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Ἀπολλωνίου τὸ ἐλεύθερον καὶ ἀναμφιβόλως ἀκύβευτον καὶ πρὸς μηδὲν ἄλλο ἀποβλέπειν μηδὲ ἐπ’ ὀλίγον ἢ πρὸς τὸν λόγον· καὶ τὸ ἀεὶ ὅμοιον, ἐν ἀλγηδόσιν ὀξείαις, ἐν ἀποβολῇ τέκνου, ἐν μακραῖς νόσοις· καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ παραδείγματος ζῶντος ἰδεῖν ἐναργῶς ὅτι δύναται ὁ αὐτὸς σφοδρότατος εἶναι καὶ ἀνειμένος· καὶ τὸ ἐν ταῖς ἐξηγήσεσι μὴ δυσχεραντικόν· καὶ τὸ ἰδεῖν ἄνθρωπον σαφῶς ἐλάχιστον τῶν ἑαυτοῦ καλῶν ἡγούμενον τὴν ἐμπειρίαν καὶ τὴν ἐντρέχειαν τὴν περὶ τὸ παραδιδόναι τὰ θεωρήματα· καὶ τὸ μαθεῖν πῶς δεῖ λαμβάνειν τὰς δοκούσας χάριτας παρὰ φίλων, μήτε ἐξηττώμενον διὰ ταῦτα μήτε ἀναισθήτως παραπέμποντα.
passages.english: From Apollonius: freedom, and unmistakably leaving nothing to the dice, and looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while; and being always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, in long illnesses; and seeing clearly, in a living example, that the same man can be most intense and can be relaxed; and not being irritable when explaining; and seeing a man who plainly counted his experience and skill in passing on the doctrines as the least of his good qualities; and learning how one should take from friends what are counted as favours, neither being lowered because of them nor letting them go by without feeling.

notes.note: The word covers freedom of mind and the bearing of a free man. The bare word is kept.
notes.other_reading: independence of spirit

notes.note: ἀκύβευτον is literally “not dicing”: not leaving a decision to chance. ἀναμφιβόλως stands directly before it and is taken with it alone, as “unmistakably”, plain to anyone watching. It can also mean “without wavering”, his own steadiness in it.
notes.other_reading: and without any wavering leaving nothing to the dice

notes.note: λόγος here is the guide a person looks to, so “reason”, the word this translation keeps for it.
notes.other_reading: to the argument

notes.note: The second word is used of a string let slack, so the pair is tight and loose. Only the first is a superlative, and “can be” is said twice so that “most” is not heard over both. The Greek has only “and” between them, and no “yet” is added.
notes.other_reading: can be at full stretch and slack

notes.note: The word is used of expounding a text or a doctrine to pupils. The plainer “explaining” is kept.
notes.other_reading: in his expositions

notes.note: “Plainly” can go with “counted”, as here, since it stands inside that phrase beside “least”, or with “seeing”, like “seeing clearly” in the clause before.
notes.other_reading: and seeing plainly a man who counted

notes.greek: τὴν ἐμπειρίαν καὶ τὴν ἐντρέχειαν τὴν περὶ τὸ παραδιδόναι τὰ θεωρήματα
notes.note: “In passing on the doctrines” is attached in the Greek to the skill and probably covers the experience too; the English leaves that as open as the Greek. τὰ θεωρήματα are the propositions of philosophy, the things taught: “doctrines” here and in 1.7, since “principles” is kept for δόγματα.
notes.other_reading: his experience, and his skill in passing on the theory

notes.note: Literally “the seeming favours”: favours as people count them, without saying that they are not real ones. The same turn is used of honours in 1.16.
notes.other_reading: the so-called favours

notes.note: Literally “being worsted, made the lesser”: losing one’s standing or independence to the giver. “Lowered” is used because “overcome” would be heard as overcome by feeling.
notes.other_reading: neither being made beholden by them

notes.note: Either letting the favour pass unnoticed or brushing it aside tactlessly.
notes.other_reading: nor dismissing them tactlessly

check.note: The adverb stands directly before “leaving nothing to the dice” and belongs to it alone; trailing after a comma it can be heard over “freedom” too. It can mean “without wavering” as well as “unmistakably”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “unmistakably leaving nothing to the dice”, with the adverb in front of the one phrase it qualifies. “Unmistakably” is kept because the plain sense of the word is “without ambiguity”, and “without wavering” is recorded in the note.

check.note: “Looking to nothing else, not even for a little while, but to reason” is dated, and the long insertion makes “but” hard to tie back to “nothing else”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while”. Nothing is dropped: the two halves of “nothing else than” are brought together so that the sentence can be followed.

check.note: The superlative belongs only to the first adjective, but in “most intense and relaxed” the “most” can be heard over both.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “can be most intense and can be relaxed”, so that “most” stays with the first word only. “Both” and “extremely” are not used: the Greek has a bare “and”, and “extremely intense and relaxed” would leave the same doubt.

check.note: “Plainly” can go with “seeing”, like “seeing clearly” just before, or with “counted”. The English takes the second without a note.
check.decided: Declined: “who plainly counted” stands, because the word sits inside the phrase about what he counted, next to “least”, and not beside the verb of seeing as “clearly” does in the clause before. A note now records the other reading.

check.greek: τὴν ἐμπειρίαν καὶ τὴν ἐντρέχειαν τὴν περὶ τὸ παραδιδόναι τὰ θεωρήματα
check.note: “In passing on” most likely covers both the experience and the skill, and repeating “his” cuts the experience loose. The plural word for what is taught is “the theory” here and “points of theory” in 1.7.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “his experience and skill in passing on the doctrines”, with one “his” so that the phrase can cover both nouns as in the Greek. “Doctrines” is used here and in 1.7 and not “principles”, which this translation keeps for δόγματα, a different word that comes in 1.9.

check.note: The verb is to be worsted, put in the weaker position, made beholden by the favour. “Overcome” reads as overwhelmed by feeling.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “neither being lowered because of them”, which keeps the sense of being made the lesser without the emotional ring of “overcome”. It says the same as “put in a lower place” in one word.

check.note: The Greek word is neutral, “what are regarded as favours”, and “what pass for” leans towards “are not really favours”. The same wording is used of honours in 1.16.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what are counted as favours”, and “what are counted as honours” in 1.16.

passages.casaubon: From Apollonius, true liberty, and unvariable steadfastness, and not to regard anything at all, though never so little, but right and reason: and always, whether in the sharpest pains, or after the loss of a child, or in long diseases, to be still the same man; who also was a present and visible example unto me, that it was possible for the same man to be both vehement and remiss: a man not subject to be vexed, and offended with the incapacity of his scholars and auditors in his lectures and expositions; and a true pattern of a man who of all his good gifts and faculties, least esteemed in himself, that his excellent skill and ability to teach and persuade others the common theorems and maxims of the Stoic philosophy. Of him also I learned how to receive favours and kindnesses (as commonly they are accounted:) from friends, so that I might not become obnoxious unto them, for them, nor more yielding upon occasion, than in right I ought; and yet so that I should not pass them neither, as an unsensible and unthankful man.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.russian: От Аполлония — свобода, и явно ничего не оставлять на волю игральных костей, и ни на что не смотреть, кроме разума, даже ненадолго; и всегда оставаться одним и тем же — при острых болях, при потере ребёнка, в долгих болезнях; и ясно увидеть на живом примере, что один и тот же человек может быть и предельно напряжённым, и расслабленным; и не раздражаться, объясняя; и видеть человека, который явно считал свой опыт и умение передавать учения наименьшим из своих достоинств; и усвоить, как нужно принимать от друзей то, что считается одолжениями, не роняя себя из-за них и не пропуская их мимо без всякого чувства.

passages.greek: Παρὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ μου Σεουήρου τὸ φιλοίκειον καὶ φιλάληθες καὶ φιλοδίκαιον· καὶ τὸ δι’ αὐτοῦ γνῶναι Θρασέαν, Ἑλβίδιον, Κάτωνα, Δίωνα, Βροῦτον, καὶ φαντασίαν λαβεῖν πολιτείας ἰσονόμου, κατ’ ἰσότητα καὶ ἰσηγορίαν διοικουμένης, καὶ βασιλείας τιμώσης πάντων μάλιστα τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῶν ἀρχομένων· καὶ ἔτι παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ τὸ ὁμαλὲς καὶ ὁμότονον ἐν τῇ τιμῇ τῆς · καὶ τὸ εὐποιητικὸν καὶ τὸ εὐμετάδοτον ἐκτενῶς καὶ τὸ εὔελπι καὶ τὸ πιστευτικὸν περὶ τοῦ ὑπὸ τῶν φίλων φιλεῖσθαι· καὶ τὸ ἀνεπίκρυπτον πρὸς τοὺς καταγνώσεως ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνοντας· καὶ τὸ μὴ δεῖσθαι στοχασμοῦ τοὺς φίλους αὐτοῦ περὶ τοῦ τί θέλει ἢ τί οὐ θέλει, ἀλλὰ δῆλον εἶναι.
passages.english: From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth and love of justice; and through him coming to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, Brutus, and getting an impression of a state with equal laws, governed by equality and an equal right to speak, and of a kingship that honours above all things the freedom of those it rules; and also from the same man: evenness and steadiness in the honour paid to […]; and doing good and sharing readily, unsparingly; and hopefulness, and trust that he was loved by his friends; and being open with those who met with his censure; and that his friends had no need to guess what he wanted or did not want, but that it was plain.

notes.note: The Greek says “brother”, and that is what is translated. From memory, unchecked: Severus was not his brother by birth and editors have doubted the word.
notes.other_reading: my kinsman

notes.note: Love of one’s own: family, household, those close to one. English has to choose.
notes.other_reading: love of his own people

notes.note: Men remembered for standing against rulers. Which Dio is meant is not certain (from memory, unchecked). The names are left bare as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, Brutus

notes.note: The same phrase as in 1.7, with “impression” for φαντασία as throughout this translation. Here it is the mental picture of such a state, a conception of it, not a passing glimpse. One article governs this and “coming to know”, so “through him” covers both.
notes.other_reading: forming the idea of a state with equal laws

notes.note: A constitution in which the law is equal for all. πολιτεία can be “state”, “constitution” or “republic”.
notes.other_reading: a constitution of equal law

notes.note: The equal right of every citizen to speak in public.
notes.other_reading: equal freedom of speech

notes.note: Kingship, rule by one man. The bare word is kept, not “monarchy” or “empire”.
notes.other_reading: a monarchy

notes.note: The Greek as given breaks off: the article τῆς has no noun before the stop. The gap is marked in the English and nothing is supplied. From memory, unchecked: printed texts have φιλοσοφίας, “philosophy”, here.
notes.other_reading: in the honour paid to philosophy

notes.note: Literally “the level and the evenly strung”: no ups and downs, the same pitch throughout.
notes.other_reading: being level and of one pitch

notes.note: “Unsparingly” stands last in the Greek, after “sharing readily”, and may go with the sharing alone or with the doing good as well. The English leaves it at the end in the same way. The same word is used of spending in 1.4.
notes.other_reading: doing good, and sharing readily and unsparingly

notes.note: Literally “the unconcealing”: he did not hide his censure from the people he censured. The Greek noun is an adverse judgment, stronger than disapproval.
notes.other_reading: hiding nothing from those he condemned

notes.note: δῆλον can be neuter, “it was plain”, as here, or masculine, with him as the subject.
notes.other_reading: but that he was plain to read

check.note: The Greek as given breaks off after the article and the noun is missing. The English marks the gap; it has to be decided whether to supply the word with a mark.
check.decided: Accepted: the gap stays marked as “[…]” and nothing is supplied, because the Greek as given has no noun there. The note names “philosophy” as the word printed texts have, from memory and unchecked.

check.note: One article governs both “coming to know” and “getting”, so “through him” covers the picture of the state as well as the five men. The semicolon cuts the second loose.
check.decided: Accepted: a comma now stands after “Brutus”, so that “through him” runs on to “getting an impression of a state”.

check.note: The same Greek phrase is “getting the impression” in 1.7 and “getting the idea” here, while “the idea” is also used for another Greek word in 1.9.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “getting an impression of a state”, the same word as in 1.7 and the one this translation keeps for φαντασία, and “idea” is left to the other word in 1.9. “Forming a picture” is not used, since it would be a third English word for the same Greek.

check.note: “Unsparingly” may qualify both the doing good and the sharing. The English ties it to the sharing only.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “doing good and sharing readily, unsparingly”, with the adverb last as in the Greek, so that it can be heard with both or with the sharing alone. “Both without stint” is not used because it would settle what the Greek leaves open.

check.note: The point is that he did not conceal his censure from the people he censured. “Hiding nothing from” suggests keeping back no information at all, and “disapproval” is weaker than the Greek word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “being open with those who met with his censure”. “Met with” is kept because the Greek says they met with condemnation from him, and “censure” gives the stronger word.

check.note: The word for “plain” can be neuter, “it was plain”, or masculine with him as subject, “he was plain to read”. The English takes the neuter.
check.decided: Declined: “but that it was plain” stands, since the clause before is about what he wanted or did not want and the neuter picks that up directly. The form is open, and a note now gives the other reading.

passages.casaubon: From my brother Severus, to be kind and loving to all them of my house and family; by whom also I came to the knowledge of Thrasea and Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus. He it was also that did put me in the first conceit and desire of an equal commonwealth, administered by justice and equality; and of a kingdom wherein should be regarded nothing more than the good and welfare of the subjects. Of him also, to observe a constant tenor, (not interrupted, with any other cares and distractions,) in the study and esteem of philosophy: to be bountiful and liberal in the largest measure; always to hope the best; and to be confident that my friends love me. In whom I moreover observed open dealing towards those whom he reproved at any time, and that his friends might without all doubt or much observation know what he would, or would not, so open and plain was he.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.russian: От брата моего Севера — любовь к родным, любовь к истине и любовь к справедливости; и то, что через него я узнал Тразею, Гельвидия, Катона, Диона, Брута и получил представление о государстве с равными законами, где правят равенство и равное право на слово, и о царской власти, которая превыше всего чтит свободу тех, кем правит; и ещё от него же — ровность и постоянство в почитании […]; и делать добро и охотно делиться, не скупясь; и надежда, и уверенность в том, что друзья его любят; и открытость с теми, кому доставалось его порицание; и то, что его друзьям не нужно было гадать, чего он хочет или не хочет, — это было ясно.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Ῥουστίκου τὸ λαβεῖν φαντασίαν τοῦ χρῄζειν διορθώσεως καὶ θεραπείας τοῦ ἤθους· καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐκτραπῆναι εἰς ζῆλον σοφιστικόν, μηδὲ τὸ συγγράφειν περὶ τῶν θεωρημάτων, ἢ προτρεπτικὰ λογάρια διαλέγεσθαι, ἢ φαντασιοπλήκτως τὸν ἀσκητικὸν ἢ τὸν ἐνεργητικὸν ἄνδρα ἐπιδείκνυσθαι· καὶ τὸ ἀποστῆναι ῥητορικῆς καὶ ποιητικῆς καὶ ἀστειολογίας· καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐν στολῇ κατ’ οἶκον περιπατεῖν μηδὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα ποιεῖν· καὶ τὸ τὰ ἐπιστόλια ἀφελῶς γράφειν, οἷον τὸ ὑπʼ αὐτοῦ τούτου ἀπὸ Σινοέσσης τῇ μητρί μου γραφέν· καὶ τὸ πρὸς τοὺς χαλεπήναντας καὶ πλημμελήσαντας εὐανακλήτως καὶ εὐδιαλλάκτως, ἐπειδὰν τάχιστα αὐτοὶ ἐπανελθεῖν ἐθελήσωσι, διακεῖσθαι· καὶ τὸ ἀκριβῶς ἀναγινώσκειν καὶ μὴ ἀρκεῖσθαι περινοοῦντα ὁλοσχερῶς μηδὲ τοῖς περιλαλοῦσι ταχέως συγκατατίθεσθαι· καὶ τὸ ἐντυχεῖν τοῖς Ἐπικτητείοις ὑπομνήμασιν, ὧν οἴκοθεν μετέδωκεν.
passages.english: From Rusticus: getting the impression that my character needed correcting and treatment; and not being turned aside into emulating the sophists, nor writing about the doctrines, or delivering little speeches of exhortation, or, to strike the imagination, making a show of being the man of discipline or the man of action; and keeping away from rhetoric and poetry and clever talk; and not walking about at home in formal dress, nor doing things of that kind; and writing short letters plainly, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; and, towards those who have been angry and have done wrong, being easy to win back and easy to reconcile, as soon as they themselves are willing to come back; and reading with care, and not being content with a rough grasp of the whole, nor quickly assenting to glib talkers; and getting to read the notes of Epictetus’s teaching, which he shared with me from his own copy.

notes.note: “Impression” for φαντασία, as throughout this translation and in the same phrase in 1.14. The Greek does not say whose character: the possessive is supplied, as the run of the chapter implies.
notes.other_reading: getting the impression of needing correction and treatment of character

notes.note: The word is medical treatment and also care or tending. The medical sense is taken, beside “correcting”.
notes.other_reading: care

notes.note: ζῆλος is eager emulation or rivalry, and the adjective says only “of the sophist’s kind”: the showy competition of professional speakers. The English takes it as striving to be like them.
notes.other_reading: into a sophist’s spirit of rivalry

notes.note: The propositions of philosophy treated as subjects for essays. “Doctrines” as in 1.8.
notes.other_reading: about speculative questions

notes.note: A diminutive with a sneer in it: little pieces urging people to philosophy.
notes.other_reading: little sermons

notes.note: A very rare word, built on φαντασία, the “impression” of the opening. It can mean “so as to strike people’s imagination”, as taken here beside the verb of showing off, or “as one struck by his own imaginings”.
notes.other_reading: carried away by a fancy, making a show of

notes.greek: τὸν ἀσκητικὸν ἢ τὸν ἐνεργητικὸν ἄνδρα
notes.note: The first is the man who practises a discipline, the second the active man. From memory, unchecked: some editors read a word meaning “benefactor” for the second.
notes.other_reading: the ascetic or the public benefactor

notes.note: Urbane, witty or polished talk.
notes.other_reading: witty conversation

notes.note: στολή is a full outfit, dress for show or for going out. The Greek does not say which garment: the fault is dressing up at home. The same word comes in 1.16.
notes.other_reading: in outdoor dress

notes.note: A diminutive, like the “little speeches” above: short letters, notes. It may be no more than a familiar way of saying “letters”.
notes.other_reading: letters

notes.note: The Greek does not say against whom. The writer himself is implied and is left out, as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: those who have been angry with me and wronged me

notes.note: Literally “easy to call back”. The passive sense is the natural one: he himself is easily won back.
notes.other_reading: ready to call them back

notes.note: Thinking round a thing in the gross, without the detail.
notes.other_reading: a general idea of it

notes.note: The verb is the Stoic term for assent. The people are those who chatter, who talk freely and at length; by the parts of the word it could also be those who talk round a subject.
notes.other_reading: nor quickly assenting to those who talk around a thing

notes.note: The verb is to meet with a thing and, of a writing, to read it.
notes.other_reading: coming upon

notes.note: Literally “the Epictetean notes”: a written record of what Epictetus taught, not notes of his own writing, so “teaching” unpacks the adjective. Presumably what Arrian took down (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the records of Epictetus’s talks

notes.note: Literally “from home”: from his own store, so from his own copy. “With me” is added. The verb is “gave a share of”, so the copy was shared, not given away.
notes.other_reading: of which he gave me a share from his own house

check.note: The word is formal or outdoor dress, and the fault is dressing up at home. “In a robe” reads today as a dressing gown, the opposite.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not walking about at home in formal dress”, and the same word is “formal dress” in 1.16.

check.note: The noun is eager pursuit or emulation, an enthusiasm for the sophists’ kind of display. “A sophist’s rivalry” suggests competing against others and is not clear English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “into emulating the sophists”, which gives the eager striving that the noun names. “A passion for sophistry” is not used: “passion” is kept for πάθος in 1.9, and “sophistry” today means false argument, not the trade of the display speaker.

check.greek: τοῦ χρῄζειν διορθώσεως καὶ θεραπείας τοῦ ἤθους
check.note: The possessive is supplied: the Greek says only “of needing correction and care of character”. The second noun is also care or tending, not only medical treatment.
check.decided: Declined: “that my character needed correcting and treatment” stands. The Greek infinitive has no subject, and in a list of what Marcus got from Rusticus the one in need is the writer, so a general “character needs” would be supplied just as much. The notes record that the possessive is added and that the second noun is also “care”.

check.note: “The man in training” reads as an athlete. The word is the man of strict discipline or austere practice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the man of discipline”, which also pairs with “the man of action”. “Strict” is left out because the Greek word does not have it.

check.note: The word is witty, clever, urbane talk. “Fine talk” is vague and overlaps with “rhetoric” just before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “clever talk”.

check.note: The diminutive is dropped here, though the diminutive a line earlier is kept as “little speeches”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “writing short letters plainly”.

check.note: “Ready to be called back” is literal but obscure: the sense is “easily won back”. With “come back” at the end of the clause the English has two different “backs” for two different people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “being easy to win back and easy to reconcile”.

check.note: The verb ordinarily means to chatter, to talk glibly and at length. “Talk around a thing”, that is, dodge the point, is a reading from the parts of the word and names a different fault.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor quickly assenting to glib talkers”. “Assenting” is kept, not “agreeing”, because the verb is the Stoic term for assent.

check.note: With a writing the verb is to meet with it, to read it. “Coming upon” suggests a chance find, which the next clause contradicts, since Rusticus gave him the notes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “getting to read”.

check.note: The Greek has an adjective, “the Epictetean notes”: the written record of his teaching. “The notes of Epictetus” can be read as notes that Epictetus himself wrote.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the notes of Epictetus’s teaching”, and the note says that “teaching” unpacks the adjective.

check.note: The adverb is idiomatically “from his own store”, that is, his own copy. “From his own house” is literal and puzzling, and “with me” is supplied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “which he shared with me from his own copy”. “Shared” is kept because the verb is “gave a share of” and does not say that he gave the copy away. The note records that “with me” is added.

passages.casaubon: To Rusticus I am beholding, that I first entered into the conceit that my life wanted some redress and cure. And then, that I did not fall into the ambition of ordinary sophists, either to write tracts concerning the common theorems, or to exhort men unto virtue and the study of philosophy by public orations; as also that I never by way of ostentation did affect to show myself an active able man, for any kind of bodily exercises. And that I gave over the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of elegant neat language. That I did not use to walk about the house in my long robe, nor to do any such things. Moreover I learned of him to write letters without any affectation, or curiosity; such as that was, which by him was written to my mother from Sinuessa: and to be easy and ready to be reconciled, and well pleased again with them that had offended me, as soon as any of them would be content to seek unto me again. To read with diligence; not to rest satisfied with a light and superficial knowledge, nor quickly to assent to things commonly spoken of: whom also I must thank that ever I lighted upon Epictetus his _Hypomnemata_, or moral commentaries and common-factions: which also he gave me of his own.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.russian: От Рустика — прийти к представлению, что мой нрав нуждается в исправлении и лечении; и не сбиться на подражание софистам, не писать об учениях, не произносить небольших увещевательных речей и не выставлять себя человеком строгой выучки или человеком дела, чтобы поразить воображение; и держаться подальше от риторики, поэзии и ловких речей; и не расхаживать дома в парадной одежде и не делать ничего подобного; и писать короткие письма просто, как то письмо, которое он сам написал моей матери из Синуэссы; и к тем, кто гневался и поступил дурно, быть отходчивым и легко мириться, как только они сами захотят вернуться; и читать внимательно, не довольствуясь приблизительным пониманием целого и не спеша соглашаться с краснобаями; и то, что мне довелось прочесть записи учения Эпиктета, которыми он поделился со мной из собственного списка.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Σέξτου τὸ εὐμενές· καὶ τὸ παράδειγμα τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρονομουμένου· καὶ τὴν ἔννοιαν τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν· καὶ τὸ σεμνὸν ἀπλάστως· καὶ τὸ στοχαστικὸν τῶν φίλων κηδεμονικῶς· καὶ τὸ ἀνεκτικὸν τῶν ἰδιωτῶν καὶ τὸ ἀθεώρητον οἰομένων· καὶ τὸ πρὸς πάντας εὐάρμοστον, ὥστε κολακείας μὲν πάσης προσηνεστέραν εἶναι τὴν ὁμιλίαν αὐτοῦ, αἰδεσιμώτατον δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐκείνοις παρ’ αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν καιρὸν εἶναι· καὶ τὸ καταληπτικῶς καὶ ὁδῷ ἐξευρετικόν τε καὶ τακτικὸν τῶν εἰς βίον ἀναγκαίων δογμάτων· καὶ τὸ μηδὲ ἔμφασίν ποτε ὀργῆς ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς πάθους παρασχεῖν, ἀλλὰ ἅμα μὲν ἀπαθέστατον εἶναι, ἅμα δὲ φιλοστοργότατον· καὶ τὸ εὔφημον ἀψοφητὶ καὶ τὸ πολυμαθὲς ἀνεπιφάντως.
passages.english: From Sextus: kindness; and the example of a household governed by its father; and the idea of living according to nature; and dignity without pretence; and skill in reading his friends, with care for them; and patience with lay people and with those who hold unexamined opinions; and adapting himself readily to everyone, so that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet at that very moment those same people held him in the greatest respect; and finding out and setting in order, with a sure grasp and by method, the principles necessary for life; and never giving so much as a sign of anger or of any other passion, but being at once most free of passion and most affectionate; and praise given quietly, and wide learning without display.

notes.note: A household under a father’s rule. It can also mean one run in a fatherly way.
notes.other_reading: a household run in a fatherly way

notes.note: The accusative breaks the run of the list, as if a verb such as “got” were understood. ἔννοια is a notion or conception, and “idea” is kept for it.
notes.other_reading: the conception

notes.note: Literally “aiming at his friends, caringly”: good at guessing them, at seeing what they feel or need before they say it. The Greek does not say what he guessed. The related noun in 1.14 is “guess”.
notes.other_reading: thoughtful attention to his friends

notes.note: Laymen: people without philosophical training.
notes.other_reading: ordinary people

notes.note: The Greek as given is rough: literally “and the unexamined of those who suppose”, with no article of its own for “those who suppose”. It is read with the article of “lay people” serving both groups and “the unexamined” as what they suppose. From memory, unchecked: the text is doubted here and editors correct it.
notes.other_reading: and with the unreasoned notions of people who merely suppose

notes.note: Literally “well fitted”: fitting himself to every kind of person.
notes.other_reading: getting on well with everyone

notes.note: A superlative: most revered. The grammar has him as the one revered “to those very people”, and sets this against the pleasantness of his company, which “yet” gives.
notes.other_reading: and yet he was at that very time most venerable to them

notes.note: The first is a Stoic term for grasping a thing securely; the second is “by a road”, by method.
notes.other_reading: with understanding and systematically

notes.note: Free of the passions in the Stoic sense, with “passion” for πάθος just before. It does not mean unfeeling, as the next word shows.
notes.other_reading: wholly unmoved by passion

notes.note: εὔφημον is speaking well, praise, the word given as “speaking well of” in 1.13. It could also be fair or seemly speech in general. The adverb is literally “without noise”.
notes.other_reading: fair speech without noise

check.note: The Greek as given does not construe: “the unexamined” stands like a new item and “those who suppose” has no article or object. The English gives the likely sense without marking the difficulty.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sense is kept, now as “those who hold unexamined opinions”, and the note says outright that the Greek as given is rough and doubted. It is read as it stands, with one article serving both groups and “the unexamined” as what they suppose, so no corrected text is translated.

check.note: “What his friends wanted” is supplied: the Greek says only that he was good at aiming at, reading, his friends, in a caring way. “Careful” and “out of concern for them” double the one adverb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “skill in reading his friends, with care for them”. Nothing is said about what he read in them, and the one adverb is given once; “real” is not added.

check.note: The Greek sets pleasantness against respect: more agreeable than flattery, yet deeply respected. “And” flattens the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and yet at that very moment those same people held him in the greatest respect”.

check.note: The word is the quality of fitting oneself readily to each person. “Getting on well” gives the result and loses the image.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “adapting himself readily to everyone”.

check.note: In a philosopher’s mouth these are laymen, people without philosophical training, which is narrower than “ordinary people”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “patience with lay people”, in a form that does not single out men.

check.note: “Of people” is supplied, and “without noise” is odd English for “quietly”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “praise given quietly”.

passages.casaubon: Of Sextus, mildness and the pattern of a family governed with paternal affection; and a purpose to live according to nature: to be grave without affectation: to observe carefully the several dispositions of my friends, not to be offended with idiots, nor unseasonably to set upon those that are carried with the vulgar opinions, with the theorems, and tenets of philosophers: his conversation being an example how a man might accommodate himself to all men and companies; so that though his company were sweeter and more pleasing than any flatterer's cogging and fawning; yet was it at the same time most respected and reverenced: who also had a proper happiness and faculty, rationally and methodically to find out, and set in order all necessary determinations and instructions for a man's life. A man without ever the least appearance of anger, or any other passion; able at the same time most exactly to observe the Stoic _Apathia_, or unpassionateness, and yet to be most tender-hearted: ever of good credit; and yet almost without any noise, or rumour: very learned, and yet making little show.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.russian: От Секста — доброта; и пример дома, которым правит отец; и мысль о жизни согласно природе; и достоинство без притворства; и умение понимать друзей, заботясь о них; и терпение к непосвящённым и к тем, кто держится непроверенных мнений; и способность легко приноравливаться ко всем, так что общение с ним было приятнее всякой лести, и всё же в ту же самую минуту эти же люди относились к нему с величайшим почтением; и умение находить и приводить в порядок, уверенно и методично, принципы, необходимые для жизни; и никогда не подавать даже признака гнева или какой-либо иной страсти, но быть одновременно и в высшей степени свободным от страстей, и в высшей степени сердечным; и похвала негромкая, и обширная учёность, не выставляемая напоказ.

passages.greek: Παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ ἥμερον καὶ μενετικὸν ἀσαλεύτως ἐπὶ τῶν ἐξητασμένως κριθέντων· καὶ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον περὶ τὰς δοκούσας τιμάς· καὶ τὸ φιλόπονον καὶ ἐνδελεχές· καὶ τὸ ἀκουστικὸν τῶν ἐχόντων τι κοινωφελὲς εἰσφέρειν· καὶ τὸ ἀπαρατρέπτως τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπονεμητικὸν ἑκάστῳ· καὶ τὸ ἔμπειρον ποῦ μὲν χρεία ἐντάσεως, ποῦ δὲ ἀνέσεως· καὶ τὸ παῦσαι τὰ περὶ τοὺς ἔρωτας τῶν· μειρακίων· καὶ ἡ κοινονοημοσύνη καὶ τὸ ἐφεῖσθαι τοῖς φίλοις μήτε συνδειπνεῖν αὐτῷ πάντως μήτε συναποδημεῖν ἐπάναγκες, ἀεὶ δὲ ὅμοιον αὐτὸν καταλαμβάνεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν διὰ χρείας τινὰς ἀπολειφθέντων· καὶ τὸ ζητητικὸν ἀκριβῶς ἐν τοῖς συμβουλίοις καὶ ἐπίμονον, ἀλλ’ οὐ τὸ προαπέστη τῆς ἐρεύνης, ἀρκεσθεὶς ταῖς προχείροις φαντασίαις· καὶ τὸ διατηρητικὸν τῶν φίλων καὶ μηδαμοῦ ἁψίκορον μηδὲ ἐπιμανές· καὶ τὸ αὔταρκες ἐν παντὶ καὶ τὸ φαιδρόν· καὶ τὸ πόρρωθεν προνοητικὸν καὶ τῶν ἐλαχίστων προδιοικητικὸν ἀτραγῴδως· καὶ τὸ τὰς ἐπιβοήσεις καὶ πᾶσαν κολακείαν ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ συσταλῆναν καὶ τὸ φυλακτικὸν ἀεὶ τῶν ἀναγκαίων τῇ ἀρχῇ καὶ ταμιευτικὸν τῆς χορηγίας καὶ ὑπομενετικὸν τῆς ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων τινῶν καταιτιάσεως· καὶ τὸ μήτε περὶ θεοὺς δεισίδαιμον μήτε περὶ ἀνθρώπους δημοκοπικὸν ἢ ἀρεσκευτικὸν ἢ ὀχλοχαρές, ἀλλὰ νῆφον ἐν πᾶσι καὶ βέβαιον καὶ μηδαμοῦ ἀπειρόκαλον μηδὲ καινοτόμον· καὶ τὸ τοῖς εἰς εὐμάρειαν βίου φέρουσί τι, ὧν ἡ τύχη παρεῖχε δαψίλειαν, χρηστικὸν ἀτύφως ἅμα καὶ ἀπροφασίστως, ὥστε παρόντων μὲν ἀνεπιτηδεύτως ἅπτεσθαι, ἀπόντων δὲ μὴ δεῖσθαι· καὶ τὸ μηδὲ ἄν τινα εἰπεῖν μήτε ὅτι σοφιστὴς μήτε ὅτι οὐερνάκλος μήτε ὅτι σχολαστικός, ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἀνὴρ πέπειρος, τέλειος, ἀκολάκευτος, προεστάναι δυνάμενος καὶ τῶν ἑαυτοῦ καὶ ἄλλων. πρὸς τούτοις δὲ καὶ τὸ τιμητικὸν τῶν ἀληθῶς φιλοσοφούντων, τοῖς δὲ ἄλλοις οὐκ ἐξονειδιστικὸν οὐδὲ μὴν εὐπαράγωγον ὑπ’ αὐτῶν· ἔτι δὲ τὸ εὐόμιλον καὶ εὔχαρι οὐ κατακόρως· καὶ τὸ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος ἐπιμελητικὸν ἐμμέτρως, οὔτε ὡς ἄν τις φιλόζωος οὔτε πρὸς καλλωπισμὸν οὔτε μὴν ὀλιγώρως, ἀλλ’ ὥστε διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν προσοχὴν εἰς ὀλίγιστα ἰατρικῆς χρῄζειν ἢ φαρμάκων καὶ ἐπιθεμάτων ἐκτός· μάλιστα δὲ τὸ παραχωρητικὸν ἀβασκάνως τοῖς δύναμίν τινα κεκτημένοις, οἷον τὴν φραστικὴν ἢ τὴν ἐξ ἱστορίας νόμων ἢ ἐθῶν ἢ ἄλλων τινῶν πραγμάτων, καὶ συσπουδαστικὸν αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ἕκαστοι κατὰ τὰ ἴδια προτερήματα εὐδοκιμῶσι· πάντα δὲ κατὰ τὰ πάτρια πράσσων, οὐδὲ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐπιτηδεύων φαίνεσθαι, τὸ τὰ πάτρια φυλάσσειν. ἔτι δὲ τὸ μὴ εὐμετακίνητον καὶ ῥιπταστικόν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τόποις καὶ πράγμασι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐνδιατριπτικόν· καὶ τὸ μετὰ τοὺς παροξυσμοὺς τῆς κεφαλαλγίας νεαρὸν εὐθὺς καὶ ἀκμαῖον πρὸς τὰ συνήθη ἔργα· καὶ τὸ μὴ εἶναι αὐτῷ πολλὰ τὰ ἀπόρρητα, ἀλλ’ ὀλίγιστα καὶ σπανιώτατα καὶ ταῦτα ὑπὲρ τῶν κοινῶν μόνων· καὶ τὸ ἔμφρον καὶ μεμετρημένον ἔν τε θεωριῶν ἐπιτελέσει καὶ ἔργων κατασκευαῖς καὶ διανομαῖς καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις, ὅ ἐστιν ἀνθρώπου πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ δέον πραχθῆναι δεδορκότος, οὐ πρὸς τὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς πραχθεῖσιν εὐδοξίαν. οὐκ ἀωρὶ λούστης, οὐχὶ φιλοικοδόμος, οὐ περὶ τὰς ἐδωδὰς ἐπινοητής, οὐ περὶ ἐσθήτων ὑφὰς καὶ χρόας, οὐ περὶ σωμάτων ὥρας. ἡ ἀπὸ Λωρίου στολὴ ἀνάγουσα ἀπὸ τῆς κάτω ἐπαύλεως· χιτὼν ἐν Λανουβίῳ τὰ πολλά· τῷ φελώνῃ ἐν Τούσκλοις παραιτουμένῳ ὡς ἐχρήσατο καὶ πᾶς ὁ τοιοῦτος τρόπος. οὐδὲν ἀπηνὲς οὐδὲ μὴν ἀδυσώπητον οὐδὲ λάβρον οὐδὲ ὥστ’ ἄν τινα εἰπεῖν ποτε· ἕως ἱδρῶτος· ἀλλὰ πάντα διειλημμένα λελογίσθαι ὡς ἐπὶ σχολῆς, ἀταράχως, τεταγμένως, ἐρρωμένως, συμφώνως ἑαυτοῖς. ἐφαρμόσειε δ’ ἂν αὐτῷ τὸ περὶ τοῦ Σωκράτους μνημονευόμενον, ὅτι καὶ ἀπέχεσθαι καὶ ἀπολαύειν ἐδύνατο τούτων, ὧν οἱ πολλοὶ πρός τε τὰς ἀποχὰς ἀσθενῶς καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἀπολαύσεις ἐνδοτικῶς ἔχουσι. τὸ δὲ ἰσχύειν καὶ ἐγκαρτερεῖν καὶ ἐννήφειν ἑκατέρῳ ἀνδρός ἐστιν ἄρτιον καὶ ἀήττητον ψυχὴν ἔχοντος, οἷον ἐν τῇ νόσῳ τῇ Μαξίμου.
passages.english: From my father: gentleness, and holding firm, unshaken, to what had been decided after examination; and no empty pride in what are counted as honours; and love of work, and perseverance; and listening to those who had something to bring to the common good; and giving each person what they deserved, without being turned aside; and knowing from experience where there is need to tighten and where to slacken; and putting a stop to love affairs with youths; and his sense of being one among others, and that his friends were not bound to dine with him every time, nor obliged to travel with him, and that those who had been kept away by some need always found him the same; and careful inquiry in council, and persistence, and not “he gave up the search too soon, content with the impressions that lay to hand”; and keeping his friends, never tiring of them quickly nor being infatuated with them; and self-sufficiency in everything, and cheerfulness; and foresight from far off, and arranging the smallest things in advance without making a drama of it; and that acclamations and all flattery were held in check under him; and always watching over what the empire needed, and managing its spending thriftily, and putting up with the blame that came for some things of this kind; and being neither superstitious about the gods, nor, with people, courting the public or eager to please or fond of the crowd, but sober in everything and firm, and never lacking in taste, and no lover of novelty; and using the things that add to the ease of life, of which fortune gave him plenty, without conceit and at the same time without apology, so that when they were there he took them without affectation, and when they were not he did not need them; and that no one could have said he was a sophist, or a home-bred buffoon, or a pedant, but a ripe man, complete, beyond flattery, able to take charge of his own affairs and other people’s. Besides these: honouring those who truly practise philosophy, and not reproaching the others, nor yet being easily led by them; and again, being good company and gracious, but not to excess; and taking care of his own body in due measure, not as someone in love with life would, nor for the sake of looks, nor yet carelessly, but so that through his own attention he needed very little from medicine, or from drugs and external dressings; and above all, giving way without envy to those who had some ability, such as ability in speaking, or the ability that comes from the study of laws or customs or some other matters, and joining eagerly in their efforts, so that each should be well thought of according to their own strengths; and doing everything by the ancestral ways, without setting out to be seen doing even this: keeping the ancestral ways. And again: not being easily shifted and restless, but staying long in the same places and at the same business; and after his attacks of headache, coming straight back fresh and at full strength to his usual work; and that he did not have many secrets, but very few and very rarely, and those only about public matters; and good sense and measure in putting on shows, in building works, in handouts and things of that kind, which is the way of a person who looks to the thing itself that has to be done, not to the good name that comes of having done it. Not one to bathe at odd hours, not fond of building, not one to be inventive about food, nor about the weave and colours of clothes, nor about the beauty of bodies. The formal dress from Lorium, coming up from the villa below; a tunic at Lanuvium for the most part; how he dealt with the cloak at Tusculum that was asking to be excused; and all that way of behaving. Nothing harsh, nor yet relentless, nor violent, nor such that one could ever have said “to the point of sweat”; but everything reasoned out, each part taken separately, as if at leisure, without disturbance, in order, with strength, in agreement with itself. What is recorded of Socrates would fit him: that he was able both to go without and to enjoy those things which most people are weak at going without and give way in enjoying. To be strong, and to hold out and stay sober in each of the two, is the mark of a man who has a soul that is sound and unbeaten, as in the illness of Maximus.

notes.note: The father by adoption, the emperor Antoninus Pius. The father by birth is named differently in 1.2.
notes.other_reading: From my adoptive father

notes.note: Literally “on the things judged in an examined way”: decisions, or judgments, reached after scrutiny.
notes.other_reading: to judgments reached after scrutiny

notes.note: Literally “the seeming honours”: honours as people count them, the same turn as with favours in 1.8.
notes.other_reading: the so-called honours

notes.greek: ποῦ μὲν χρεία ἐντάσεως, ποῦ δὲ ἀνέσεως
notes.note: The image is a string tightened and let go, the same pair as in 1.8. The image is kept, and what is tightened is left unsaid, as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: where to press and where to ease off

notes.greek: τὸ παῦσαι τὰ περὶ τοὺς ἔρωτας τῶν· μειρακίων
notes.note: The stop after τῶν in the Greek as given is a slip and is read through. The last word means adolescents and young men, older than boys. It is open whether he ended such affairs of his own or put a stop to the practice around him, and the English leaves it open too.
notes.other_reading: and having brought his own passion for youths to an end

notes.note: A very rare word, perhaps Marcus’s own, and in the nominative, which breaks the run of the list. Built from “common” and “minded”, it seems to mean not setting himself above others, which the examples that follow bear out. The sense is not certain: it could also be consideration for others, or public spirit.
notes.other_reading: his consideration for others

notes.note: Literally “that it was left to his friends” not to dine and not to travel with him: they were let off the obligation, not kept from doing so.
notes.other_reading: leaving his friends free not to dine with him and not to travel with him

notes.note: “In every case”, taken here as “every time”. It can also be “necessarily”, which would make it a twin of “obliged” in the next phrase.
notes.other_reading: were not bound to dine with him as a matter of course

notes.note: To be away from home together with him: on his journeys, not necessarily in foreign countries.
notes.other_reading: to go away with him

notes.note: The text is doubtful here: the article stands before a finite verb, “he left off the search too soon”, which does not construe as ordinary Greek. The English takes the article as quoting the phrase, a thing that could not be said of him; the other course is to suppose the words damaged. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the text here.
notes.other_reading: and he never left off the search too soon

notes.note: “Impressions” for φαντασίαι, as throughout: the first appearances of a matter, the ones nearest to hand.
notes.other_reading: with first appearances

notes.note: The first word is literally “nowhere”, that is, in no case: “never” here and at “never lacking in taste” further on.
notes.other_reading: in no case tiring of them quickly

notes.note: Mad about a person: excessive or infatuated attachment, set against quickly tiring of them.
notes.other_reading: nor doting on them

notes.note: Literally “the bright”: a beaming, cheerful look or temper. The Greek names no face.
notes.other_reading: a bright face

notes.note: Literally “untragically”: without stage manner, without fuss.
notes.other_reading: without fuss

notes.note: A slip in the Greek as given for the infinitive συσταλῆναι, which is read. The phrase before it, “in his time” or “in his own case”, is taken as “under him”.
notes.other_reading: were cut short where he was concerned

notes.note: The supply of means: here the public outlay or the treasury’s resources.
notes.other_reading: a careful steward of the public funds

notes.greek: τῆς ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων τινῶν καταιτιάσεως
notes.note: Either blame over some matters of this kind, as taken here, or blame from certain people in such matters.
notes.other_reading: the blame some people laid on him in such matters

notes.note: By its parts, “delighting in the crowd”, which the English keeps. After the two words before it, it may rather mean playing to the crowd.
notes.other_reading: or playing to the crowd

notes.note: One who cuts new ground: an innovator, or a chaser of novelty.
notes.other_reading: no innovator

notes.note: Literally “without pretexts”: without making excuses for using them. It can also mean without hesitation.
notes.other_reading: and without hesitation

notes.note: The Latin word vernaculus in Greek letters: a slave born in the house, a type known for pert, low joking. “Home-bred buffoon” gives the word and the type together. The sense is not certain.
notes.other_reading: a home-born slave

notes.note: A man of the schools, bookish and unpractical.
notes.other_reading: a bookish man

notes.note: Literally “those who philosophise”: who live as philosophers, not only study.
notes.other_reading: true philosophers

notes.note: Easily led aside, taken in.
notes.other_reading: nor yet being taken in by them

notes.note: The last word is taken with the dressings alone: things laid on the outside of the body. It could instead mean “apart from”, governing both nouns, which would turn the phrase.
notes.other_reading: or went without drugs and dressings

notes.greek: τὴν ἐξ ἱστορίας νόμων ἢ ἐθῶν
notes.note: ἱστορία is inquiry and the knowledge it gives. The feminine article picks up “ability”, which the English repeats.
notes.other_reading: the knowledge that comes from research into laws or customs

notes.note: Literally “being eager together with them”: he threw his own effort in behind theirs.
notes.other_reading: and actively backing them

notes.greek: πάντα δὲ κατὰ τὰ πάτρια πράσσων
notes.note: The construction changes here to a participle in the nominative, “he, doing everything”. It is kept in the run of the list. τὰ πάτρια are the customs handed down from the fathers, “the ancestral ways” both times.
notes.other_reading: He did everything by the customs of his fathers

notes.note: Literally “not practising to be seen even at this very thing”. He kept the ancestral ways and made no show of keeping them.
notes.other_reading: without even seeming to make a point of it

notes.note: θεωρίαι here are public spectacles, the games and shows an emperor gives.
notes.other_reading: in the giving of public spectacles

notes.note: Distributions: handouts of money or food to the people.
notes.other_reading: in largesses

notes.note: The Greek has no verb in this sentence or the next ones. “At odd hours” is “out of season”, at the wrong time of day.
notes.other_reading: no bather at unseasonable hours

notes.note: A deviser or inventor: one who thinks up refinements. The word governs the food, the clothes and the bodies alike, so “inventive about” is used for all three.
notes.other_reading: not one to think up dishes

notes.note: “Bodies” very likely means slaves, whose looks a rich man would choose for. The bare word is kept.
notes.other_reading: nor about the good looks of his slaves

notes.greek: ἡ ἀπὸ Λωρίου στολὴ ἀνάγουσα ἀπὸ τῆς κάτω ἐπαύλεως
notes.note: A jotting without a verb, and doubtful: the participle is active, “bringing up”, and has no object, so the Greek as given does not construe securely. “Coming up” is the nearest sense, and the point of the remark is not known. The noun is the “formal dress” of 1.7; Lorium was a country house of his (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the robe he wore coming up from his villa at Lorium, down below

notes.greek: τῷ φελώνῃ ἐν Τούσκλοις παραιτουμένῳ ὡς ἐχρήσατο
notes.note: The word as given is “cloak”, which fits the list of clothes, but the participle “asking to be excused” is in the dative and agrees with it, and a cloak cannot ask. The English gives what stands, and the word is suspect. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts read a word meaning “tax collector”, which construes.
notes.other_reading: how he treated the tax collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon

notes.note: Not to be moved by entreaty, implacable. It can also mean not to be put out of countenance, shameless.
notes.other_reading: nor yet shameless

notes.note: Given as a thing people say: driving a matter until one sweats. It is kept word for word.
notes.other_reading: at fever heat

notes.note: The infinitive has nothing to hang on, like much in this chapter. Literally “everything, divided up, to have been reasoned out”.
notes.other_reading: but he had thought everything through, point by point

notes.note: Marcus does not say where the saying comes from, and it is not traced here.
notes.other_reading: the saying about Socrates

notes.note: “In each of the two”: in going without and in enjoying. Holding out answers to the first and staying sober to the second, but the Greek joins the verbs to both.
notes.other_reading: to hold out in the one case and stay sober in the other

notes.note: Sound, well fitted, whole of its kind. “Complete” is kept for another word, τέλειος, earlier in the passage.
notes.other_reading: a soul that is complete and unbeaten

notes.greek: οἷον ἐν τῇ νόσῳ τῇ Μαξίμου
notes.note: A clipped ending. It is open whether this is how Antoninus bore himself while Maximus was ill, or how Maximus was in his own illness, which 1.15 speaks of. The English is left as bare as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: as he showed during the illness of Maximus

check.greek: τῷ φελώνῃ ἐν Τούσκλοις παραιτουμένῳ ὡς ἐχρήσατο
check.note: The participle “asking to be excused” is dative and agrees with the cloak, so the one asking is whoever he dealt with, not Antoninus as in the English. A cloak cannot ask, so the word itself is suspect and the doubt should be marked.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “how he dealt with the cloak at Tusculum that was asking to be excused”, which gives the participle back to the word it agrees with. The Greek as given says “cloak” and no other word is put in its place. The note marks the word as suspect and gives the reading with “tax collector”, from memory and unchecked.

check.greek: τὸ ἐφεῖσθαι τοῖς φίλοις μήτε συνδειπνεῖν αὐτῷ πάντως μήτε συναποδημεῖν ἐπάναγκες
check.note: “Free neither to dine nor to travel” reads as if they were not free to do these things, where the Greek says they were let off any obligation to. The adverb with “dine” may be “necessarily” and not “every time”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that his friends were not bound to dine with him every time, nor obliged to travel with him”. Each adverb keeps its own verb as in the Greek, and the note records “necessarily” as the other sense of the first.

check.note: The verb is to be away from home with him. “Abroad” today means foreign countries, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to travel with him”, without “abroad”.

check.greek: ἡ ἀπὸ Λωρίου στολὴ ἀνάγουσα ἀπὸ τῆς κάτω ἐπαύλεως
check.note: The clause has no verb and the participle is active, “bringing up”, with no object, so the Greek as given does not construe securely. “Coming up” smooths this over, and “robe” again reads as a dressing gown.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “The formal dress from Lorium, coming up from the villa below”, with the same word as in 1.7. “Coming up” is kept as the nearest sense, and the note now says that the participle is active and without an object and that the phrase is doubtful.

check.note: A finite verb after the article does not construe as ordinary Greek. Taking it as a quoted remark is possible but is a decision about a doubtful text, and the prefix of the verb means “before the time”.
check.decided: Accepted: the quoted remark is kept, since the nominative participle that follows fits a quoted sentence, and it now reads “he gave up the search too soon”. The note says that the text is doubtful and that this is one way of reading it. “The charge” is not added.

check.note: A rare word turned into an explanatory clause. It could equally be consideration for the feelings of others or public-mindedness, and the choice should be shorter and flagged as uncertain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “his sense of being one among others”, which is shorter, and the note says the sense is not certain and gives the other two. “Fellow-feeling” is not used because it means sympathy, which is not in the parts of the word, “common” and “minded”.

check.note: The word means adolescents and young men, older than children. “Boys” suggests children.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “love affairs with youths”.

check.note: “Nowhere” is word for word: English says “never” or “in no case”, here and at “nowhere lacking in taste”. “Mad about them” is colloquial and can be heard as “angry about”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “never tiring of them quickly nor being infatuated with them”, and “never lacking in taste” further on.

check.note: “Face” is supplied: the word is cheerfulness, brightness of manner generally.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and cheerfulness”, and the note keeps the literal “the bright”.

check.note: The word can mean taking pleasure in the mob or, as the two words before it suggest, playing to the mob. The English takes the first.
check.decided: Declined: “fond of the crowd” stands, because the word is built from “crowd” and “delight in” and that is what its parts say. A note now gives “playing to the crowd” as the other reading.

check.note: “Without excuses” is unclear: the sense is that he used good things without apologising for having them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “without apology”.

check.note: The Latin word is a home-bred slave and, by extension, someone with a slave’s pert, coarse wit. “Household jester” fuses the two into something the word does not quite say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a home-bred buffoon”, which keeps the home-bred slave of the word and the type meant by it. The note flags the sense as uncertain.

check.note: “External” belongs with the applications, not with the drugs, but the English makes the drugs too “applied from outside”. The word could also be “apart from”, governing both nouns.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or from drugs and external dressings”, so that “external” goes with the dressings alone. The note keeps “apart from” as the other reading.

check.note: The word carries eagerness on their behalf: he backed them so that each would get credit. “Working alongside” loses the zeal.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “joining eagerly in their efforts”, which keeps both parts of the word, “with” and “be eager”.

check.greek: οὐδὲ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐπιτηδεύων φαίνεσθαι, τὸ τὰ πάτρια φυλάσσειν
check.note: The trailing infinitive is not English, and “our” is supplied twice for the word that means ancestral ways, tradition.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “doing everything by the ancestral ways, without setting out to be seen doing even this, keeping the ancestral ways”. “Our” and “yet” are gone, and one English phrase stands for the repeated Greek word. “Setting out to be seen” is closer than “making a show” to the Greek, which is “practising to be seen”.

check.note: A reader of today will not know what “distributions” are: public handouts of money or grain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in handouts”. “To the people” is left to the note, since the Greek has the one word.

check.note: The word is a deviser, an inventor: someone who thinks up refinements for the table. “Give thought to” is weaker.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not one to be inventive about food”. “Think up dishes” is not used because the same word also governs the clothes and the bodies that follow, and “inventive about” can carry all three.

check.note: “Bodies” can mean slaves, which fits a list about household display. The English takes the general sense.
check.decided: Declined: “the beauty of bodies” stands, because the Greek has the bare word “bodies” and does not say slaves. The note already gives “the good looks of his slaves” as the other reading.

check.note: “Complete” has already been used for a different Greek word in this passage, in “a ripe man, complete”. This word is sound, well knit, fully fitted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a soul that is sound and unbeaten”, and “complete” is left to the earlier word.

check.note: The infinitives may be distributed: holding out in going without, staying sober in enjoying. The English applies them all to both.
check.decided: Declined: “in each of the two” stands, because the Greek word is a single “in each” set after the verbs and does not divide them. The note gives the distributed reading.

check.note: Found while settling: “even the smallest things” had an “even” that the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “arranging the smallest things in advance”.

check.greek: οἷον τὴν φραστικὴν ἢ τὴν ἐξ ἱστορίας
check.note: Found while settling: the feminine article twice picks up “ability”, but the English put “skill” and “knowledge” in its place.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “such as ability in speaking, or the ability that comes from the study of laws or customs or some other matters”.

passages.casaubon: In my father, I observed his meekness; his constancy without wavering in those things, which after a due examination and deliberation, he had determined. How free from all vanity he carried himself in matter of honour and dignity, (as they are esteemed:) his laboriousness and assiduity, his readiness to hear any man, that had aught to say tending to any common good: how generally and impartially he would give every man his due; his skill and knowledge, when rigour or extremity, or when remissness or moderation was in season; how he did abstain from all unchaste love of youths; his moderate condescending to other men's occasions as an ordinary man, neither absolutely requiring of his friends, that they should wait upon him at his ordinary meals, nor that they should of necessity accompany him in his journeys; and that whensoever any business upon some necessary occasions was to be put off and omitted before it could be ended, he was ever found when he went about it again, the same man that he was before. His accurate examination of things in consultations, and patient hearing of others. He would not hastily give over the search of the matter, as one easy to be satisfied with sudden notions and apprehensions. His care to preserve his friends; how neither at any time he would carry himself towards them with disdainful neglect, and grow weary of them; nor yet at any time be madly fond of them. His contented mind in all things, his cheerful countenance, his care to foresee things afar off, and to take order for the least, without any noise or clamour. Moreover how all acclamations and flattery were repressed by him: how carefully he observed all things necessary to the government, and kept an account of the common expenses, and how patiently he did abide that he was reprehended by some for this his strict and rigid kind of dealing. How he was neither a superstitious worshipper of the gods, nor an ambitious pleaser of men, or studious of popular applause; but sober in all things, and everywhere observant of that which was fitting; no affecter of novelties: in those things which conduced to his ease and convenience, (plenty whereof his fortune did afford him,) without pride and bragging, yet with all freedom and liberty: so that as he did freely enjoy them without any anxiety or affectation when they were present; so when absent, he found no want of them. Moreover, that he was never commended by any man, as either a learned acute man, or an obsequious officious man, or a fine orator; but as a ripe mature man, a perfect sound man; one that could not endure to be flattered; able to govern both himself and others. Moreover, how much he did honour all true philosophers, without upbraiding those that were not so; his sociableness, his gracious and delightful conversation, but never unto satiety; his care of his body within bounds and measure, not as one that desired to live long, or over-studious of neatness, and elegancy; and yet not as one that did not regard it: so that through his own care and providence, he seldom needed any inward physic, or outward applications: but especially how ingeniously he would yield to any that had obtained any peculiar faculty, as either eloquence, or the knowledge of the laws, or of ancient customs, or the like; and how he concurred with them, in his best care and endeavour that every one of them might in his kind, for that wherein he excelled, be regarded and esteemed: and although he did all things carefully after the ancient customs of his forefathers, yet even of this was he not desirous that men should take notice, that he did imitate ancient customs. Again, how he was not easily moved and tossed up and down, but loved to be constant, both in the same places and businesses; and how after his great fits of headache he would return fresh and vigorous to his wonted affairs. Again, that secrets he neither had many, nor often, and such only as concerned public matters: his discretion and moderation, in exhibiting of the public sights and shows for the pleasure and pastime of the people: in public buildings. congiaries, and the like. In all these things, having a respect unto men only as men, and to the equity of the things themselves, and not unto the glory that might follow. Never wont to use the baths at unseasonable hours; no builder; never curious, or solicitous, either about his meat, or about the workmanship, or colour of his clothes, or about anything that belonged to external beauty. In all his conversation, far from all inhumanity, all boldness, and incivility, all greediness and impetuosity; never doing anything with such earnestness, and intention, that a man could say of him, that he did sweat about it: but contrariwise, all things distinctly, as at leisure; without trouble; orderly, soundly, and agreeably. A man might have applied that to him, which is recorded of Socrates, that he knew how to want, and to enjoy those things, in the want whereof, most men show themselves weak; and in the fruition, intemperate: but to hold out firm and constant, and to keep within the compass of true moderation and sobriety in either estate, is proper to a man, who hath a perfect and invincible soul; such as he showed himself in the sickness of Maximus.

nearest.title: What I learned, and from whom

passages.russian: От отца — мягкость и твёрдая, непоколебимая верность тому, что было решено после рассмотрения; и отсутствие пустого тщеславия в том, что считается почестями; и любовь к труду, и упорство; и готовность выслушивать тех, кто мог что-то принести для общей пользы; и умение воздавать каждому по заслугам, не уклоняясь; и знание по опыту, где нужно натянуть, а где ослабить; и то, что он положил конец любовным увлечениям юношами; и его сознание, что он один из многих, и то, что друзья не обязаны были ни каждый раз обедать с ним, ни сопровождать его в поездках, а те, кого задержала какая-нибудь нужда, всегда находили его прежним; и тщательное разбирательство на советах, и настойчивость, и никак не «он прекратил поиск слишком рано, довольствуясь представлениями, что были под рукой»; и умение сохранять друзей, никогда быстро не пресыщаясь ими и не теряя от них головы; и самодостаточность во всём, и бодрость; и предусмотрительность издалека, и заблаговременное устройство самых мелких дел без лишнего шума; и то, что при нём приветственные возгласы и всякая лесть были обузданы; и постоянная забота о том, в чём нуждалась держава, и бережливое управление её расходами, и терпение к упрёкам, которые за подобное доставались; и то, что он не был ни суеверен в отношении богов, ни, в отношении людей, искателем народной милости, угодником или любителем толпы, но во всём был трезв и твёрд, никогда не впадал в безвкусицу и не гнался за новизной; и то, что вещами, облегчающими жизнь, которых судьба дала ему вдоволь, он пользовался без кичливости и вместе с тем без оправданий, так что, когда они были, брал их без жеманства, а когда их не было, в них не нуждался; и то, что никто не мог бы сказать о нём, что он софист, или доморощенный шут, или педант, — но зрелый муж, совершенный, недоступный лести, способный управлять и своими, и чужими делами. Кроме того: он почитал тех, кто истинно занимается философией, а остальных не корил, но и не шёл легко у них на поводу; и ещё — был приятен в общении и любезен, но не сверх меры; и в меру заботился о своём теле — не как тот, кто влюблён в жизнь, и не ради красоты, но и не небрежно, а так, что благодаря собственному вниманию очень мало нуждался во врачебном искусстве, в лекарствах и наружных припарках; и, главное, без зависти уступал тем, кто обладал какой-либо способностью, например способностью к красноречию или способностью, что даётся изучением законов, обычаев или чего-то иного, и ревностно присоединялся к их стараниям, чтобы каждый пользовался доброй славой по собственным достоинствам; и делал всё по обычаям предков, не стараясь, чтобы видели даже это — что он хранит обычаи предков. И ещё: его нелегко было сдвинуть, он не был беспокоен, а подолгу оставался в одних и тех же местах и при одних и тех же делах; и после приступов головной боли сразу же возвращался, свежий и полный сил, к привычной работе; и то, что тайн у него было не много, а совсем мало и очень редко, и только касающиеся государственных дел; и благоразумие и мера в устройстве зрелищ, в постройках, в раздачах и прочем подобном — как у человека, который смотрит на само дело, что нужно сделать, а не на добрую славу, которая приходит за сделанное. Не из тех, кто моется в неурочное время; не любитель строиться; не выдумщик ни в еде, ни в выделке и цвете одежды, ни в красоте тел. Парадная одежда из Лория, по дороге наверх с виллы внизу; в Ланувии — по большей части туника; как он обошёлся в Тускуле с плащом, который просил, чтобы его извинили; и вся эта манера держаться. Ничего грубого, но и ничего неумолимого, ничего неистового, ничего такого, о чём можно было бы сказать: «до пота»; но всё обдумано, каждая часть взята по отдельности, словно на досуге, без смятения, в порядке, с силой, в согласии с самим собой. К нему подошло бы то, что записано о Сократе: он умел и обходиться без того, и наслаждаться тем, без чего большинство по слабости не может обойтись и чему, наслаждаясь, поддаётся. Быть сильным, и выдерживать, и хранить трезвость и в том и в другом — признак человека, у которого душа здоровая и непобеждённая, как в болезни Максима.

passages.greek: Παρὰ Μαξίμου τὸ κρατεῖν ἑαυτοῦ καὶ κατὰ μηδὲν περίφορον εἶναι· καὶ τὸ εὔθυμον ἔν τε ταῖς ἄλλαις περιστάσεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς νόσοις· καὶ τὸ εὔκρατον τοῦ ἤθους καὶ μειλίχιον καὶ γεραρόν· καὶ τὸ οὐ σχετλίως κατεργαστικὸν τῶν προκειμένων· καὶ τὸ πάντας αὐτῷ πιστεύειν περὶ ὧν λέγοι ὅτι οὕτως φρονεῖ, καὶ περὶ ὧν πράττοι ὅτι οὐ κακῶς πράττει. καὶ τὸ ἀθαύμαστον καὶ ἀνέκπληκτον καὶ μηδαμοῦ ἐπειγόμενον ἢ ὀκνοῦν ἢ ἀμηχανοῦν ἢ κατηφὲς ἢ προσσεσηρός, ἢ πάλιν θυμούμενον ἢ ὑφορώμενον· καὶ τὸ εὐεργετικὸν καὶ τὸ συγγνωμονικὸν καὶ τὸ ἀψευδές· καὶ τὸ ἀδιαστρόφου μᾶλλον ἢ διορθουμένου φαντασίαν παρέχειν· καὶ ὅτι οὔτε ᾠήθη ἄν ποτέ τις ὑπερορᾶσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ οὔτε ὑπέμεινεν ἂν κρείττονα αὐτοῦ αὑτὸν ὑπολαβεῖν· καὶ τὸ εὐχαριεντίζεσθαι.
passages.english: From Maximus: self-mastery and being carried off course in nothing; and good spirits in illness as in other hard circumstances; and a character well blended, mild and dignified; and getting through what lay before him without complaining; and that everyone believed of him that whatever he said was what he thought, and that in whatever he did he was not acting badly. And not being amazed, and not being startled, and never hurrying or hanging back or at a loss or downcast or putting on a grin, or again angry or suspicious; and doing good, and forgiving, and not lying; and giving the impression of one not bent rather than of one being straightened; and that no one would ever have thought they were looked down on by him, nor have gone so far as to suppose themselves better than him; and being pleasantly witty.

notes.note: Literally “carried round”: swung about, unsteady in purpose.
notes.other_reading: and not wavering in anything

notes.greek: ἔν τε ταῖς ἄλλαις περιστάσεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς νόσοις
notes.note: Literally “both in the other circumstances and in illnesses”. The order is turned for English. The noun often means hard circumstances, which is why illness is counted among them, and “hard” is written; it can also be plain “circumstances”.
notes.other_reading: in illness as in other circumstances
