check.decided: Declined: “well-tuned” stays. ἐμμελής, “in tune”, answers ἀπηχές, “out of tune”, earlier in the same sentence, and the English keeps that image with “jarring” and “well-tuned”; “tactful” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
passages.russian: От грамматика Александра — не придираться и не набрасываться с упрёками на тех, кто произнёс неправильную форму слова, допустил грамматическую ошибку или режущий слух звук, но ловко произнести самому как раз то, что следовало сказать, — в виде ответа, или поддержки, или совместного обсуждения самого предмета, а не выражения, или с помощью другого такого же тонко настроенного напоминания мимоходом.

passages.greek: ὅρα γοῦν ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει.
passages.english: See, at any rate, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

notes.note: “At any rate”, “for instance”: it brings in a case that supports what came just before. This passage is one sentence from the end of a chapter, and what it supports is not in the Greek given; nothing was supplied.
notes.other_reading: See, for instance

notes.greek: ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει
notes.note: Marcus does not give the saying. From memory, unchecked: Crates is most likely the Cynic philosopher, Xenocrates was a head of Plato’s school known for his gravity, and the remark itself is lost. αὐτοῦ is “himself”, with the force of “even Xenocrates”.
notes.other_reading: what Crates says even about Xenocrates

part.left_out: Οἷον δὴ τὸ φαντασίαν λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄψων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἐδωδίμων, ὅτι νεκρὸς οὗτος ἰχθύος, οὗτος δὲ νεκρὸς ὄρνιθος ἢ χοίρου· καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι ὁ Φάλερνος χυλάριόν ἐστι σταφυλίου καὶ ἡ περιπόρφυρος τριχία προβατίου αἱματίῳ κόγχης δεδευμένα· καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν συνουσίαν ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις· οἷαι δὴ αὗταί εἰσιν αἱ φαντασίαι καθικνούμεναι αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ διεξιοῦσαι δι’ αὐτῶν, ὥστε ὁρᾶν οἷά τινά ποτέ ἐστιν· οὕτως δεῖ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ποιεῖν καὶ ὅπου λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται, ἀπογυμνοῦν αὐτὰ καὶ τὴν εὐτέλειαν αὐτῶν καθορᾶν καὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνεται περιαιρεῖν. δεινὸς γὰρ ὁ τῦφος παραλογιστὴς καὶ ὅτε δοκεῖς μάλιστα περὶ τὰ σπουδαῖα καταγίνεσθαι, τότε μάλιστα καταγοητεύῃ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts all of the chapter but its last sentence in its section 6.11 and makes that last sentence, on Crates and Xenocrates, a section of its own, 6.12.

passages.casaubon: See what Crates pronounceth concerning Xenocrates himself.
passages.russian: Посмотри, во всяком случае, что Кратет говорит о самом Ксенократе.

passages.greek: Λακεδαιμόνιοι τοῖς μὲν ξένοις ἐν ταῖς θεωρίαις ὑπὸ τῇ σκιᾷ τὰ βάθρα ἐτίθεσαν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὗ ἔτυχεν, ἐκαθέζοντο.
passages.english: At their public shows the Spartans used to set the benches for foreign visitors in the shade, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to.

notes.note: “Lacedaemonians”, the formal name of the Spartans. The English uses the name a reader of today knows.
notes.other_reading: The Lacedaemonians

notes.note: ξένος is both “foreigner” and “guest”: visitors from other cities. μέν and δέ set them against the Spartans themselves, which the English gives with “while”.
notes.other_reading: for their guests

notes.note: “At the viewings”: public spectacles or festivals where people sat to watch.
notes.other_reading: at their festivals

notes.note: Literally “where it chanced”: anywhere, with no care for comfort.
notes.other_reading: and sat themselves anywhere

check.note: ξένοι here are visitors from other cities, guests. “Strangers” is weaker and can mean any unknown person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “foreign visitors”. The Greek word here means people from other cities who have come to watch, which “strangers” did not say.

check.note: μὲν and δὲ set the visitors against the Spartans themselves, and “and” flattens the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “while they themselves sat wherever they happened to”, so the contrast of μέν and δέ is heard.

passages.casaubon: The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were content to sit anywhere.
passages.russian: На своих зрелищах спартанцы ставили скамьи для чужеземных гостей в тени, а сами садились где придётся.

passages.greek: Ὅταν τινὸς ἀναισχυντίᾳ προσκόπτῃς, εὐθὺς πυνθάνου σεαυτοῦ· δύνανται οὖν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀναίσχυντοι μὴ εἶναι; οὐ δύνανται· μὴ οὖν ἀπαίτει τὸ ἀδύνατον· εἷς γὰρ καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ἐκείνων τῶν ἀναισχύντων, οὓς ἀνάγκη ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ εἶναι. τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ πανούργου καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀπίστου καὶ παντὸς τοῦ ὁτιοῦν ἁμαρτάνοντος ἔστω σοι πρόχειρον· ἅμα γὰρ τῷ ὑπομνησθῆναι ὅτι τὸ γένος τῶν τοιούτων ἀδύνατόν ἐστι μὴ ὑπάρχειν, εὐμενέστερος ἔσῃ πρὸς τοὺς καθ’ ἕνα. εὔχρηστον δὲ κἀκεῖνο εὐθὺς ἐννοεῖν, τίνα ἔδωκεν ἡ φύσις τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἀρετὴν πρὸς τοῦτο τὸ ἁμάρτημα· ἔδωκε γὰρ ὡς ἀντιφάρμακον πρὸς μὲν τὸν ἀγνώμονα τὴν πρᾳότητα, πρὸς δὲ ἄλλον ἄλλην τινὰ δύναμιν, ὅλως δὲ ἔξεστί σοι μεταδιδάσκειν τὸν πεπλανημένον· πᾶς γὰρ ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἀφαμαρτάνει τοῦ προκειμένου καὶ πεπλάνηται. τί δὲ καὶ βέβλαψαι; εὑρήσεις γὰρ μηδένα τούτων, πρὸς οὓς παροξύνῃ, πεποιηκότα τι τοιοῦτον, ἐξ οὗ ἡ διάνοιά σου χείρων ἔμελλε γενήσεσθαι· τὸ δὲ κακόν σου καὶ τὸ βλαβερὸν ἐνταῦθα πᾶσαν τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχει. τί δὲ καινὸν ἢ ξένον γέγονεν, εἰ ὁ ἀπαίδευτος τὰ τοῦ ἀπαιδεύτου πράσσει; ὅρα μὴ σεαυτῷ μᾶλλον ἐγκαλεῖν ὀφείλῃς, ὅτι οὐ προσεδόκησας τοῦτον τοῦτο ἁμαρτήσεσθαι· σὺ γὰρ καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου εἶχες πρὸς τὸ ἐνθυμηθῆναι ὅτι εἰκός ἐστι τοῦτον τοῦτο ἁμαρτήσεσθαι, καὶ ὅμως ἐπιλαθόμενος θαυμάζεις εἰ ἡμάρτηκε. μάλιστα δέ, ὅταν ὡς ἀπίστῳ ἢ ἀχαρίστῳ μέμφῃ, εἰς σεαυτὸν ἐπιστρέφου· προδήλως γὰρ σὸν τὸ ἁμάρτημα, εἴτε περὶ τοῦ τοιαύτην τὴν διάθεσιν ἔχοντος ἐπίστευσας ὅτι τὴν πίστιν φυλάξει, εἴτε τὴν χάριν διδοὺς μὴ καταληκτικῶς ἔδωκας μηδὲ ὥστε ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς πράξεως εὐθὺς ἀπειληφέναι πάντα τὸν καρπόν. τί γὰρ πλέον θέλεις εὖ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπον; οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῦτο, ὅτι κατὰ φύσιν τὴν σήν τι ἔπραξας, ἀλλὰ τούτου μισθὸν ζητεῖς; ὡσεὶ ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς ἀμοιβὴν ἀπῄτει, ὅτι βλέπει, ἢ οἱ πόδες, ὅτι βαδίζουσιν. ὥσπερ γὰρ ταῦτα πρὸς τόδε τι γέγονεν, ὅπερ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν ἐνεργοῦντα ἀπέχει τὸ ἴδιον, οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος εὐεργετικὸς πεφυκώς, ὁπόταν τι εὐεργετικὸν ἢ ἄλλως εἰς τὰ μέσα συνεργητικὸν πράξῃ, πεποίηκε, πρὸς ὃ κατεσκεύασται, καὶ ἔχει τὸ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Whenever you take offence at someone’s shamelessness, ask yourself at once: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible. For this person too is one of those shameless people who must exist in the universe. Have the same thought ready to hand for the scoundrel, and for the faithless person, and for everyone who does wrong in any way whatever. For as soon as you are reminded that it is impossible for people of this kind not to exist, you will be kinder towards each one of them. It is useful too to think at once of this: what virtue nature has given to a human being to meet this wrong. For it has given, as an antidote, gentleness against the unfeeling person, and against another some other power. And in general you are free to teach the one who has gone astray to think otherwise; for everyone who does wrong misses what they were aiming at and has gone astray. And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence. And what new or strange thing has happened, if the untaught person does what an untaught person does? See whether you ought not rather to blame yourself, because you did not expect that this person would do this wrong. For you did have from reason the means to reflect that this person was likely to do this wrong, and yet you forgot it and are surprised that they have done wrong. Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something that ended there, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done good to a person? Is it not enough that you have done something in accord with your own nature, but you look for a wage for it? As if the eye demanded a return because it sees, or the feet because they walk. For just as these have come into being for one particular thing, and in doing it according to their own build they receive in full what is their own, so too a human being, who is by nature a doer of good, whenever they do some good, or in some other way work together towards things of the middle kind, has done what they were built for, and has what is their own.

notes.note: Literally to strike or stumble against something. The English takes the settled figurative sense, “take offence”, and keeps it for this verb in 10.30 and 6.20.
notes.other_reading: Whenever you stumble against someone’s shamelessness

notes.greek: ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀναίσχυντοι μὴ εἶναι
notes.note: “The universe” is the settled rendering of ὁ κόσμος and is kept here because the argument is about what the order of things must contain. “In the world” would be the more natural English.
notes.other_reading: for there to be no shameless people in the world

notes.note: ἀγνώμων has a wide range: without consideration, unfeeling, unfair, senseless, also ungrateful. The English reads “unfeeling”, the sense that gentleness best answers, and keeps “ungrateful” for ἀχάριστος later in the passage.
notes.other_reading: against the inconsiderate person (or: the ungrateful person)

notes.note: The verb means to teach someone so that they change their view. It is rendered “teach … to think otherwise” here and “teach otherwise” where it recurs in this section.
notes.other_reading: you are free to re-educate the one who has gone astray

notes.greek: πᾶς γὰρ ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἀφαμαρτάνει τοῦ προκειμένου
notes.note: A play on words: ἁμαρτάνω (to do wrong) originally means to miss a mark, and ἀφαμαρτάνω is to miss it altogether. τὸ προκείμενον is what is set in front of a person, their target. The English cannot repeat the one root.
notes.other_reading: for everyone who errs errs from the mark set before them

notes.note: The settled rendering of διάνοια is “thought”, with “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that could be made worse, so “mind”.
notes.other_reading: that was going to make your thought worse

notes.note: “There” points back to the mind: what is bad and harmful for you exists only in it. The Greek says only “there”; the English adds no noun but puts “it is there that” first, so that the word is heard to point back to the mind.
notes.other_reading: has its whole existence here, in the mind

notes.note: ἀφορμαί are starting points or resources. λόγος is taken as the faculty of reason, as in the settled list; it could also be “the argument”, meaning the reasoning just given.
notes.other_reading: you did have starting points from the argument

notes.note: The Greek repeats one root three times: ἄπιστος (faithless), ἐπίστευσας (you trusted), πίστιν (faith, trust). English needs “trusted” for the verb, so the chain is only partly visible.
notes.other_reading: you had faith that such a person would keep faith

notes.greek: τὴν χάριν διδοὺς μὴ καταληκτικῶς ἔδωκας
notes.note: χάρις (a favour) is the root of ἀχάριστος (ungrateful: one who returns no favour). καταληκτικῶς is a rare adverb, from the verb “to come to an end”; it is taken as giving in a way that ends with the giving and looks for nothing further.
notes.other_reading: in bestowing the kindness you did not bestow it once and for all

notes.note: ἀπέχω is the word used on receipts: to have received payment in full. It answers the “wage” and “return” just before, so the English reads “receive in full what is their own”.
notes.other_reading: they have their own payment in full

notes.note: εὐεργετικός, apt to do good to others, comes twice in the sentence. The English has “a doer of good” and “do some good”, so that the one word is heard both times.
notes.other_reading: who is by nature beneficent, whenever they do something beneficent

notes.note: τὰ μέσα, “the middle things”, is taken as the Stoic name for things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health and wealth, towards which people can work together. It could instead mean what lies in the middle between people, the common interest.
notes.other_reading: or in some other way contribute to the common good

notes.note: κατασκευή (how a thing is constructed) and κατεσκεύασται at the end are the same word; the English has “build” and “built”. The usual philosophical English is “constitution”.
notes.other_reading: acting according to their own constitution … what they were constituted for

check.note: “Help with the things in between” does not tell a reader of today what lies between what, and “help with” is weaker than the Greek, which is working together toward something.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “or in some other way work together toward things of the middle kind”. The gloss “those neither good nor bad” is not in the Greek, so it is given in the note and not in the text.

check.note: “Their own” is dropped from “according to the way they are built”, though it answers “what is their own” in the same clause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in doing it according to their own build they receive in full what is their own”, so that “own” is heard twice as in the Greek.

check.note: “To another” is not in the Greek, and the same Greek word was given just before in different English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who is by nature a doer of good, whenever they do some good”. “To another” is gone and the one Greek word has one English wording in both places.

check.note: The Greek word can mean unfeeling, ungrateful or senseless. “Inconsiderate” picks a mild sense, and “unfeeling” is the likelier stronger reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “against the unfeeling person”, the stronger sense that gentleness answers. “Inconsiderate” is kept in the note as the other reading.

check.note: A small Greek word of emphasis is dropped: “you did in fact have”. It sharpens the reproach.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For you did have from reason the means”, which gives the stress that had been dropped.

check.note: The Greek “there” points back to the mind of the clause before, but in the English it can be taken to point at what the other people did.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence”, so that “there” is heard to point back to the mind. No noun is added, because the Greek has only “there”; the note says what it points to.

passages.casaubon: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What? Is it then possible, that there should not be any impudent men in the world! Certainly it is not possible.' Desire not then that which is impossible. For this one, (thou must think) whosoever he be, is one of those impudent ones, that the world cannot be without. So of the subtile and crafty, so of the perfidious, so of every one that offendeth, must thou ever be ready to reason with thyself. For whilst in general thou dost thus reason with thyself, that the kind of them must needs be in the world, thou wilt be the better able to use meekness towards every particular. This also thou shalt find of very good use, upon every such occasion, presently to consider with thyself, what proper virtue nature hath furnished man with, against such a vice, or to encounter with a disposition vicious in this kind. As for example, against the unthankful, it hath given goodness and meekness, as an antidote, and so against another vicious in another kind some other peculiar faculty. And generally, is it not in thy power to instruct him better, that is in an error? For whosoever sinneth, doth in that decline from his purposed end, and is certainly deceived, And again, what art thou the worse for his sin? For thou shalt not find that any one of these, against whom thou art incensed, hath in very deed done anything whereby thy mind (the only true subject of thy hurt and evil) can be made worse than it was. And what a matter of either grief or wonder is this, if he that is unlearned, do the deeds of one that is unlearned? Should not thou rather blame thyself, who, when upon very good grounds of reason, thou mightst have thought it very probable, that such a thing would by such a one be committed, didst not only not foresee it, but moreover dost wonder at it, that such a thing should be. But then especially, when thou dost find fault with either an unthankful, or a false man, must thou reflect upon thyself. For without all question, thou thyself art much in fault, if either of one that were of such a disposition, thou didst expect that he should be true unto thee: or when unto any thou didst a good turn, thou didst not there bound thy thoughts, as one that had obtained his end; nor didst not think that from the action itself thou hadst received a full reward of the good that thou hadst done. For what wouldst thou have more? Unto him that is a man, thou hast done a good turn: doth not that suffice thee? What thy nature required, that hast thou done. Must thou be rewarded for it? As if either the eye for that it seeth, or the feet that they go, should require satisfaction. For as these being by nature appointed for such an use, can challenge no more, than that they may work according to their natural constitution: so man being born to do good unto others whensoever he doth a real good unto any by helping them out of error; or though but in middle things, as in matter of wealth, life, preferment, and the like, doth help to further their desires he doth that for which he was made, and therefore can require no more.
passages.russian: Всякий раз, когда тебя задевает чьё-то бесстыдство, тотчас спроси себя: «Разве возможно, чтобы в мироздании не было бесстыдных людей?» Невозможно. Так не требуй невозможного. И этот человек — один из тех бесстыдных, которые неизбежно есть в мироздании. Держи ту же мысль наготове и для негодяя, и для вероломного, и для всякого, кто каким бы то ни было образом поступает дурно. Ведь как только ты напомнишь себе, что невозможно, чтобы людей такого рода не было, ты станешь мягче к каждому из них. Полезно и тотчас подумать вот о чём: какую добродетель дала природа человеку против этого дурного поступка. Ведь против бесчувственного она дала как противоядие кротость, а против другого — какую-то другую силу. И вообще, ты волен научить заблудившегося думать иначе: всякий, кто поступает дурно, промахивается мимо того, к чему стремился, и сбился с пути. И какой, собственно, вред ты потерпел? Ведь ты обнаружишь, что ни один из тех, на кого ты раздражён, не сделал ничего такого, от чего твой ум должен был бы стать хуже; а именно там целиком и существует то, что для тебя дурно и что тебе вредит. И что нового или странного случилось, если невежда делает то, что делает невежда? Смотри, не лучше ли тебе винить самого себя за то, что ты не ожидал от этого человека такого дурного поступка. Ведь у тебя было от разума средство сообразить, что он, вероятно, совершит этот дурной поступок, а ты забыл и удивляешься, что он поступил дурно. Прежде всего, когда винишь кого-то в вероломстве или неблагодарности, обратись к себе. Ведь ясно, что дурно поступил ты сам — поверил ли ты, что человек такого склада будет верен, или же, оказывая услугу, оказывал её не как нечто, что на этом и кончается, и не так, чтобы сразу получить весь плод от самого действия. Чего же ещё ты хочешь, сделав человеку добро? Неужели мало того, что ты сделал нечто согласное с собственной природой, а ты ищешь за это платы? Как если бы глаз требовал вознаграждения за то, что видит, или ноги — за то, что ходят. Как они возникли ради чего-то одного определённого и, делая это согласно своему устройству, сполна получают своё, так и человек, по природе творящий добро, всякий раз, когда сделает какое-нибудь добро или иным образом посодействует в вещах промежуточного рода, сделал то, для чего он устроен, и имеет своё.

passages.greek:
Συνεχῶς ἐφιστάναι, τίνες εἰσὶν οὗτοι, ὑφ’ ὧν μαρτυρεῖσθαι θέλεις, καὶ τίνα ἡγεμονικὰ ἔχουσιν· οὔτε γὰρ μέμψῃ τοῖς ἀκουσίως πταίουσιν οὔτε ἐπιμαρτυρήσεως δεήσῃ, ἐμβλέπων εἰς τὰς πηγὰς τῆς ὑπολήψεως καὶ ὁρμῆς αὐτῶν.

ʽΠᾶσα ψυχή, φησίν, ἄκουσα στέρεται ἀληθείας·ʼ οὕτως οὖν καὶ δικαιοσύνης καὶ σωφροσύνης καὶ εὐμενείας καὶ παντὸς τοῦ τοιούτου. ἀναγκαιότατον δὲ τὸ διηνεκῶς τούτου μεμνῆσθαι· ἔσῃ γὰρ πρὸς πάντας πρᾳότερος.
passages.english:
Keep turning your attention to who these people are whose testimony in your favour you want, and what ruling parts they have. For you will neither blame those who stumble against their will nor need their testimony, if you look into the springs of their judgment and impulse.

“Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler towards everyone.

notes.note: An infinitive used as a command, with no person; the next clause has “you want”, so the English uses an imperative. The verb is to fix attention on something, often by halting to do so; with “constantly” the English gives the attention and not the halt.
notes.other_reading: Constantly to stop and consider

notes.note: Literally “to be witnessed to”, that is, to be spoken well of. The witness word is kept because ἐπιμαρτυρήσεως (testimony) picks it up in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: whose approval you want … nor will you need their approval

notes.note: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, the ruling part of the soul, the mind that directs a person, stands here in the plural: what kind of ruling part each of them has.
notes.other_reading: what sort of governing minds they have

notes.note: ἀκουσίως (not willingly) is the same word as ἄκουσα in the saying that follows; the English has “against their will” and “against its will” so that the link shows.
notes.other_reading: those who stumble involuntarily

notes.note: “He says”, with no name. The saying is Plato’s, and Marcus seems to have it in the form in which Epictetus quotes it (from memory, unchecked). The speaker is left unnamed as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: “Every soul,” Plato says

notes.note: σωφροσύνη covers self-control, moderation and soundness of mind. The English reads “self-control”.
notes.other_reading: moderation

check.note: “Stop constantly” reads as a contradiction in English. The Greek verb is to turn one’s attention to something, and the idea of halting is not needed here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Keep turning your attention to who these people are”. The Greek verb is to fix attention on something, and “constantly” goes with it.

check.note: “Ruling parts” is a technical term that a reader of today may not place as the mind that directs a person; “governing minds” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “what ruling parts they have” stands. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is “the ruling part” in the settled list of this translation, the Greek plural gives each person one, and the note explains the term.

passages.casaubon: Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire. For then neither wilt thou see cause to complain of them that offend against their wills; or find any want of their applause, if once thou dost but penetrate into the true force and ground both of their opinions, and of their desires. 'No soul (saith he) is willingly bereft of the truth,' and by consequent, neither of justice, or temperance, or kindness, and mildness; nor of anything that is of the same kind. It is most needful that thou shouldst always remember this. For so shalt thou be far more gentle and moderate towards all men.
passages.russian:
Постоянно обращай внимание на то, кто такие эти люди, чьего свидетельства в свою пользу ты хочешь, и каковы их ведущие начала. Ведь ты не станешь ни винить тех, кто оступается невольно, ни нуждаться в их свидетельстве, если вглядишься в источники их суждения и побуждения.

«Всякая душа, — говорит он, — лишается истины против воли». Значит, так же — и справедливости, и самообладания, и доброты, и всего подобного. Необходимее всего постоянно помнить об этом: ведь ты будешь мягче ко всем.

passages.greek:
Πόθεν ἐλήλυθεν ἕκαστον καὶ ἐκ τίνων ἕκαστον ὑποκειμένων καὶ εἰς τί μεταβάλλει καὶ οἷον ἔσται μεταβαλὸν καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν κακὸν πείσεται.

Καὶ Πρῶτον, τίς ἡ πρὸς αὐτούς μοι σχέσις καὶ ὅτι ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν γεγόναμεν καὶ καθ’ ἕτερον λόγον προστησόμενος αὐτῶν γέγονα ὡς κριὸς ποίμνης ἢ ταῦρος ἀγέλης. ἄνωθεν δὲ ἔπιθι ἀπὸ τοῦ· εἰ μὴ ἄτομοι, φύσις ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα· εἰ τοῦτο, τὰ χείρονα τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, ταῦτα δὲ ἀλλήλων. Δεύτερον δέ, ὁποῖοί τινές εἰσιν ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης, ὲν τῷ κλιναρίῳ, τἄλλα· μάλιστα δέ, οἵας ἀνάγκας δογμάτων κειμένας ἔχουσι· καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα, μεθ’ οἵου τύφου ποιοῦσιν. Τρίτον, ὅτι, εἰ μὲν ὀρθῶς ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν, οὐ δεῖ δυσχεραίνειν· εἰ ὀ οὐκ ὀρθῶς, δηλονότι ἄκοντες καὶ ἀγνοοῦντες. πᾶσα γὰρ ψυχὴ ἄκουσα στέρεται, ὥσπερ τοῦ ἀληθοῦς, οὕτως καὶ τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἑκάστῳ προσφέρεσθαι. ἄχθονται γοῦν ἀκούοντες ἄδικοι καὶ ἀγνώμονες καὶ πλεονέκται καὶ καθάπαξ ἁμαρτητικοὶ περὶ τοὺς πλησίον. Τέταρτον, ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς πολλὰ ἁμαρτάνεις καὶ ἄλλος τοιοῦτος εἷ· καὶ εἴ τινων δὲ ἁμαρτημάτων ἀπέχῃ, ἀλλὰ τήν γε ἕξιν ἐποιστικὴν ἔχεις, εἰ καὶ διὰ δειλίαν ἢ δοξοκοπίαν ἢ τοιοῦτό τι κακὸν ἀπέχῃ τῶν ὁμοίων ἁμαρτημάτων. Πέμπτον, ὅτι οὐδὲ εἰ ἁμαρτάνουσι κατείληφας· πολλὰ γὰρ κατ’ οἰκονομίαν γίνεται καὶ ὅλως πολλὰ δεῖ πρότερον μαθεῖν, ἵνα τις περὶ ἀλλοτρίας πράξεως καταληπτικῶς τι ἀποφήνηται. Ἕκτον, ὅτι, ὅταν λίαν ἀγανακτῇς ἢ καὶ δυσπαθῇς, ἀκαριαῖος ὁ ἀνθρώπειος βίος καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον πάντες ἐξετάθημεν. Ἕβδομον, ὅτι οὐχ αἱ πράξεις αὐτῶν ἐνοχλοῦσιν ἡμῖν· ἐκεῖναι γάρ εἰσιν ἐν τοῖς ἐκείνων ἡγεμονικοῖς· ἀλλὰ αἱ ἡμέτεραι ὑπολήψεις. ἆρον γοῦν καὶ θέλησον ἀφεῖναι τὴν ὡς περὶ δεινοῦ κρίσιν καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ἡ ὀργή. πῶς οὖν ἀρεῖς; λογισάμενος ὅτι οὐκ αἰσχρόν· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ μόνον ᾖ τὸ αἰσχρὸν κακόν, ἀνάγκη καὶ σὲ πολλὰ ἁμαρτάνειν καὶ λῃστὴν καὶ παντοῖον γενέσθαι. Ὄγδοον, ὅσῳ χαλεπώτερα ἐπιφέρουσιν αἱ ὀργαὶ καὶ λῦπαι αἱ ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις, ἤπερ αὐτά ἐστιν ἐφ’ οἷς ὀργιζόμεθα καὶ λυπούμεθα. Ἔνατον, ὅτι τὸ εὐμενὲς ἀνίκητον, ἐὰν γνήσιον ᾖ καὶ μὴ σεσηρὸς μηδὲ ὑπόκρισις. τί γάρ σοι ποιήσει ὁ ὑβριστικώτατος, ἐὰν διατελῇς εὐμενὴς αὐτῷ καί, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε, πρᾴως παραινῇς καὶ μεταδιδάσκῃς εὐσχολῶν παρ’ αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν καιρὸν ὅτε κακοποιεῖν σε ἐπιχειρεῖ· ʽμή, τέκνον· πρὸς ἄλλο πεφύκαμεν. ἐγὼ μὲν οὐ μὴ βλαβῶ, σὺ δὲ βλάπτῃ, τέκνον.ʼ καὶ δεικνύναι εὐαφῶς καὶ ὁλικῶς ὅτι τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, ὅτι οὐδὲ μέλισσαι αὐτὸ ποιοῦσιν οὐδ’ ὅσα συναγελαστικὰ πέφυκε. δεῖ δὲ μήτε εἰρωνικῶς αὐτὸ ποιεῖν μήτε ὀνειδιστικῶς, ἀλλὰ φιλοστόργως καὶ ἀδήκτως τῇ ψυχῇ καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐν σχολῇ μηδὲ ἵνα ἄλλος παραστὰς θαυμάσῃ, ἀλλ’ ἤτοι πρὸς μόνον καὶ ἐὰν ἄλλοι τινὲς περιεστήκωσι. Τούτων τῶν ἐννέα κεφαλαίων μέμνησο ὡς παρὰ τῶν Μουσῶν δῶρα εἰληφὼς καὶ ἄρξαι ποτὲ ἄνθρωπος εἶναι, ἕως ζῇς. φυλακτέον δὲ ἐπίσης τῷ ὀργίζεσθαι αὐτοῖς τὸ κολακεύειν αὐτούς· ἀμφότερα γὰρ ἀκοινώνητα καὶ πρὸς βλάβην φέρει. πρόχειρον δὲ ἐν ταῖς ὀργαῖς ὅτι οὐχὶ τὸ θυμοῦσθαι ἀνδρικόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πρᾷον καὶ ἥμερον ὥσπερ ἀνθρωπικώτερον, οὕτως καὶ ἀρρενικώτερον καὶ ἰσχύος καὶ νεύρων καὶ ἀνδρείας τούτῳ μέτεστιν, οὐχὶ τῷ ἀγανακτοῦντι καὶ δυσαρεστοῦντι· ὅσῳ γὰρ ἀπαθείᾳ τοῦτο οἰκειότερον, τοσούτῳ καὶ δυνάμει. ὥσπερ τε ἡ λύπη ἀσθενοῦς, οὕτως καὶ ἡ ὀργή· ἀμφότεροι γὰρ τέτρωνται καὶ ἐνδεδώκασιν. Εἰ δὲ βούλει, καὶ δέκατον παρὰ τοῦ Μουσηγέτου δῶρον λάβε, ὅτι τὸ μὴ ἀξιοῦν ἁμαρτάνειν τοὺς φαύλους μανικόν· ἀδυνάτου γὰρ ἐφίεται. τὸ δὲ συγχωρεῖν ἄλλοις μὲν εἶναι τοιούτους, ἀξιοῦν δὲ μὴ εἰς σὲ ἁμαρτάνειν, ἄγνωμον καὶ τυραννικόν.
passages.english:
Where each thing has come from, and what underlying materials each is made of, and what it is changing into, and what it will be like when it has changed, and that it will suffer nothing bad.

And first: what my relation to them is, and that we have come into being for one another’s sake; and that, on another account, I have come into being to stand at their head, as a ram stands at the head of a flock or a bull of a herd. But go back further and start from this: if not atoms, then nature is what governs the whole; if that is so, the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another. Second: what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their principles have laid on them; and these very things, with what conceit they do them. Third: that if they do these things rightly, one should not be annoyed; and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance. For every soul is deprived against its will, as of the truth, so too of dealing with each person as they deserve. At any rate they are aggrieved to hear themselves called unjust and unfeeling and greedy and, in a word, prone to do wrong to their neighbours. Fourth: that you yourself also do many wrongs and are another of the same kind; and if you do hold back from certain wrongs, you still have the disposition that brings them on, even if it is through cowardice or hunger for reputation or some such bad thing that you hold back from wrongs like theirs. Fifth: that you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong; for many things are done with some further purpose in view, and in general one must first learn many things in order to pronounce on another’s action with a sure grasp. Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out. Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone. How, then, will you take it away? By reasoning that it is not shameful. For if what is shameful is not the only bad thing, you too must do many wrongs and become a robber and anything at all. Eighth: how much harder are the things that our fits of anger and distress over such matters bring on than the very things that anger and distress us. Ninth: that kindness is unbeatable, if it is genuine and not a grin or play-acting. For what will the most insolent person do to you, if you go on being kind to them and, if the chance comes, gently advise them and teach them otherwise, at your ease, at the very moment when they are trying to do you harm: “No, child. We are made by nature for something else. I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.” And show, with a light touch and in general terms, that this is so: that not even bees do it, nor any of the creatures that are by nature herd animals. And it must be done neither with irony nor with reproach, but with affection and with no bite in your soul; and not as in a lecture room, nor so that someone else standing by may admire, but to that person alone, even if some others are standing around. Remember these nine headings as gifts you have received from the Muses, and begin at last to be a human being, while you live. One must guard against flattering them just as much as against being angry with them, for both are unsocial and lead to harm. And in your fits of anger have this ready to hand: that it is not flying into a rage that is manly, but that what is gentle and mild, as it is more human, is also more masculine; and that it is this that has a share of strength and sinew and manly courage, not the one who is indignant and discontented. For the closer this is to freedom from passion, the closer it is to power. And just as distress belongs to a weak person, so does anger; for both have been wounded and have given in. And if you like, take a tenth gift too, from the Leader of the Muses: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible. And to allow them to be such to others, but to require that they not do wrong to you, is unfeeling and tyrannical.

notes.note: The chapter is a list of headings with no main verb. Here the Greek has only “and out of what underlying things each”; the English supplies “is made of”. ὑποκείμενα are the underlying materials a thing consists of.
notes.other_reading: and out of what underlying things each has come

notes.greek: τίς ἡ πρὸς αὐτούς μοι σχέσις
notes.note: The chapter opens with “And”, as if continuing, and “them” is never explained: it is the people who offend, as the rest shows. Both are left as they stand. The first heading speaks in the first person; from the fourth the Greek turns to the second.
notes.other_reading: First, how one stands in relation to other people

notes.note: A future participle of purpose: to stand in front of them, which covers both leading and protecting. The word λόγος just before it is here an account or way of reckoning, not reason.
notes.other_reading: and, from another point of view, born to protect them

notes.note: ἄνωθεν is “from above”, here from higher up in the argument, from an earlier starting point. It can also mean “over again”.
notes.other_reading: But go over it again from the beginning

notes.greek: εἰ μὴ ἄτομοι, φύσις ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα
notes.note: A compressed either-or with no verbs: if things are not atoms (the Epicurean view), then they are governed by nature. The English supplies “then” and “is what”. τὰ ὅλα is rendered “the whole” as settled.
notes.other_reading: if there are not just atoms, there is a nature governing all things

notes.note: κλινάριον is a small bed or couch. After “at table” it is taken as the bed; it could be the dining couch. The grave accent on ὲν is a slip in the copy for ἐν.
notes.other_reading: on the couch

notes.note: Literally “what necessities of principles they have lying on them”. The word “laid” belongs to the compulsions, and the principles are taken as their source: what these people hold forces them to act as they do.
notes.other_reading: what fixed constraints of belief they are subject to

notes.note: “These very things” may be what their principles compel or their conduct at table and in bed; the Greek does not say. τῦφος is literally smoke: conceit, a puffed-up delusion.
notes.other_reading: and how puffed up they are in doing just what they do

notes.greek: ἄχθονται γοῦν ἀκούοντες ἄδικοι καὶ ἀγνώμονες
notes.note: ἀκούω with a nominative is the idiom “to be called”. ἀγνώμων is rendered “unfeeling”, as at the end of the passage and in 9.42; it also means inconsiderate, unfair or senseless.
notes.other_reading: they are pained when they hear the words unjust, inconsiderate

notes.note: ἕξις is a settled state of character, here “disposition”. ἐποιστικός is a rare word, “apt to bring on”: the state from which such wrongs come.
notes.other_reading: you still have the habit that tends that way

notes.note: The Stoic term for a secure grasp of something as true (κατάληψις); καταληπτικῶς at the end of the sentence is the same word, so the English has “grasp” for both.
notes.other_reading: you are not even sure whether they are doing wrong

notes.note: Literally “by management”: done as part of some arrangement, for a purpose beyond the act itself that the onlooker does not know. The English has to spell this out a little.
notes.other_reading: many things are done for reasons of policy

notes.note: A past tense, “were stretched out”, the word for laying out a corpse. The past treats the near future as already done; the English uses a present.
notes.other_reading: in a little while all have been laid out

notes.note: κρίσις is the act of judging. Since “judgments” has just been used for ὑπολήψεις, the English has “verdict” here to keep the two Greek words apart. “And be willing to let it go” is moved after the object.
notes.other_reading: take away, and be willing to let go, the judgment that it is something terrible

notes.note: The Greek does not say what is “not shameful”: it is taken to be what has been done to you, which brings no shame on you. The next sentence rests on the Stoic rule that only the shameful is bad.
notes.other_reading: By reflecting that being wronged is no disgrace to you

notes.note: παντοῖον is “of every kind”: a person who will turn into anything, do anything.
notes.other_reading: become a robber and whatever else you please

notes.note: A participle of the verb for drawing back the lips and showing the teeth: a fixed or mocking grin. The image is kept as “a grin”.
notes.other_reading: not a smirk

notes.note: Literally “if it so happened”: if the occasion arises.
notes.other_reading: if it should so happen

notes.note: “Being at leisure”: unhurried, with time to spare for the other person, at the very moment of being attacked.
notes.other_reading: taking your time

notes.note: The verb is the one used two lines later of creatures that “are by nature” herd animals. The English has “made by nature” and “are by nature” so that the two are heard together.
notes.other_reading: born for something else

notes.note: εὐαφῶς is “with a good touch”, tactfully. ὁλικῶς is “in a general way”, taken as speaking of the general rule and not of this person’s fault.
notes.other_reading: tactfully and as a universal truth

notes.greek: ἤτοι πρὸς μόνον καὶ ἐὰν ἄλλοι τινὲς περιεστήκωσι
notes.note: The Greek as given does not fully construe: ἤτοι, “either”, has no “or” to answer it, and some words seem to have dropped out. The English leaves “either” untranslated and supplies “that person”; nothing is added to fill the gap.
notes.other_reading: but either to that person alone, even if some others are standing around

notes.note: The Muses are nine, like the nine headings. The Leader of the Muses below (Μουσηγέτης) is a title of Apollo.
notes.other_reading: as gifts from the nine Muses

notes.note: The sentence plays on four words: ἀνδρικόν (manly), ἀνθρωπικώτερον (more human), ἀρρενικώτερον (more male) and ἀνδρεία (courage, literally manliness). The English has “manly”, “human”, “masculine” and “manly courage”, the last so that the end of the sentence answers its beginning.
notes.other_reading: what is gentle and mild is more human and so more of a man’s part, and manliness belongs to it

notes.note: ἥμερος is the word for tamed animals and cultivated plants; of a person it means mild, civilised, and is praise. “Mild” is used because “tame” belittles a person in English.
notes.other_reading: what is gentle and tame

notes.note: “This” points back to what is gentle and mild, and the same pronoun returns in the next clause. The form could also be masculine, the person who has that quality, set against “the one who is indignant”.
notes.other_reading: strength and sinew and manly courage belong to the gentle person

notes.note: ἀπάθεια is the Stoic term for being free of the passions, not for dullness or indifference.
notes.other_reading: the nearer this is to being unmoved

notes.greek: τὸ μὴ ἀξιοῦν ἁμαρτάνειν τοὺς φαύλους
notes.note: ἀξιόω is to think something right and so to claim or require it of others; the English has “require” both times it occurs. The negative goes with the infinitive in sense.
notes.other_reading: to expect bad people not to do wrong

notes.note: The dative “to others” is taken with “be such”: to accept that they behave like this towards other people.
notes.other_reading: to grant others that such people exist

notes.note: The same word as ἀγνώμονες earlier in the passage, so “unfeeling” is kept: it is unfeeling to accept that others are wronged and claim exemption only for yourself. Beside “madness” in the sentence before it could also mean senseless.
notes.other_reading: is unreasonable and tyrannical

check.greek: ἤτοι πρὸς μόνον καὶ ἐὰν ἄλλοι τινὲς περιεστήκωσι
check.note: The Greek “either” has no answering “or”, so the Greek as given breaks off or has lost some words. The English keeps a dangling “either” that reads like a slip and not like a marked gap, and “that person” is supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but to that person alone, even if some others are standing around”, without the dangling “either”. The note says that the Greek has an “either” with no “or” and may have lost some words, and that “that person” is supplied.

check.note: In the Greek it is the compulsions that are laid on these people, by their principles. “The principles laid down in them” moves the participle to the principles and adds “in them”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what compulsions their principles have laid on them”. In the Greek the word for “laid” agrees with the compulsions, not with the principles.

check.note: “Go at it from further up” is not clear English. The Greek is to go over the matter from an earlier starting point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But go back further and start from this”.

check.note: The Greek phrase means done as a matter of management, for a purpose beyond the act itself. “With a further arrangement in view” is hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for many things are done with some further purpose in view”.

check.note: This verb, to take a thing hard, is given the same English word, “distressed”, as a different Greek word later in the passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “extremely indignant or even take it hard”, so that “distress” and “distressed” are left for the other Greek word later in the passage.

check.note: “Should it so fall out” is an archaic turn of phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if the chance comes”.

check.note: The sentence turns on the word “manly” and ends by giving the gentle person a quality named from the same root. “Courage” alone loses the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “strength and sinew and manly courage”, so that the last word answers “manly” at the start of the sentence, as ἀνδρεία answers ἀνδρικόν.

check.note: Of a person “tame” sounds belittling in English, which works against the point. The Greek word is mild, civilised.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what is gentle and mild”. The Greek word is used of tamed animals, but of a person it is praise, which “tame” is not in English; the note records the literal sense.

check.note: No person has been named, so “this person” has nothing to point to in the English. The Greek pronoun picks up what is gentle and mild, or the one who has that quality.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “this person” is gone, but the English reads “it is this that has a share of strength and sinew and manly courage” and not “the gentle one”. The Greek pronoun points back to “what is gentle and mild” and comes again in the next clause (“the closer this is”), so “this” is kept in both; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: The Greek word can also mean senseless or unreasonable, which fits beside “madness” in the sentence before. “Inconsiderate” matches the earlier use but is weak here.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “inconsiderate” is replaced, but by “unfeeling” and not “unreasonable”. The same Greek word stands earlier in the passage among the names people hate to be called, and one English word is kept for both places; “unreasonable” is recorded in the note.

check.greek: τὸ μὴ ἀξιοῦν ἁμαρτάνειν τοὺς φαύλους
check.note: The Greek verb is to think it right, to expect or claim, a milder word than “demand”, and “demand” is also the English for another Greek verb in 9.42. The same holds for the second use in the last sentence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “require” both times. “Demand” was too strong, but “expect” in English can mean merely to foresee, which is what 9.42 tells the reader to do; the Greek verb is a claim on how others should behave.

check.note: The Greek ending means prone to, given to. “People who do wrong” states the fact and not the tendency.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “prone to do wrong to their neighbours”, which gives the tendency that the Greek ending marks.

check.note: “And in the rest” is awkward English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “at table, in bed, and so on”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s “born for something else” hid the fact that the same Greek verb comes again two lines later, of the creatures that “are by nature” herd animals.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “made by nature for something else”, so that the appeal to nature in the spoken words and in the proof from bees and herd animals is heard as one.

passages.casaubon: Of everything thou must consider from whence it came, of what things it doth consist, and into what it will be changed: what will be the nature of it, or what it will be like unto when it is changed; and that it can suffer no hurt by this change. And as for other men's either foolishness or wickedness, that it may not trouble and grieve thee; first generally thus; What reference have I unto these? and that we are all born for one another's good: then more particularly after another consideration; as a ram is first in a flock of sheep, and a bull in a herd of cattle, so am I born to rule over them. Begin yet higher, even from this: if atoms be not the beginning of all things, than which to believe nothing can be more absurd, then must we needs grant that there is a nature, that doth govern the universe. If such a nature, then are all worse things made for the better's sake; and all better for one another's sake. Secondly, what manner of men they be, at board, and upon their beds, and so forth. But above all things, how they are forced by their opinions that they hold, to do what they do; and even those things that they do, with what pride and self-conceit they do them. Thirdly, that if they do these things rightly, thou hast no reason to be grieved. But if not rightly, it must needs be that they do them against their wills, and through mere ignorance. For as, according to Plato's opinion, no soul doth willingly err, so by consequent neither doth it anything otherwise than it ought, but against her will. Therefore are they grieved, whensoever they hear themselves charged, either of injustice, or unconscionableness, or covetousness, or in general, of any injurious kind of dealing towards their neighbours. Fourthly, that thou thyself doest transgress in many things, and art even such another as they are. And though perchance thou doest forbear the very act of some sins, yet hast thou in thyself an habitual disposition to them, but that either through fear, or vainglory, or some such other ambitious foolish respect, thou art restrained. Fifthly, that whether they have sinned or no, thou doest not understand perfectly. For many things are done by way of discreet policy; and generally a man must know many things first, before he be able truly and judiciously to judge of another man's action. Sixthly, that whensoever thou doest take on grievously, or makest great woe, little doest thou remember then that a man's life is but for a moment of time, and that within a while we shall all be in our graves. Seventhly, that it is not the sins and transgressions themselves that trouble us properly; for they have their existence in their minds and understandings only, that commit them; but our own opinions concerning those sins. Remove then, and be content to part with that conceit of thine, that it is a grievous thing, and thou hast removed thine anger. But how should I remove it? How? reasoning with thyself that it is not shameful. For if that which is shameful, be not the only true evil that is, thou also wilt be driven whilest thou doest follow the common instinct of nature, to avoid that which is evil, to commit many unjust things, and to become a thief, and anything, that will make to the attainment of thy intended worldly ends. Eighthly, how many things may and do oftentimes follow upon such fits of anger and grief; far more grievous in themselves, than those very things which we are so grieved or angry for. Ninthly, that meekness is a thing unconquerable, if it be true and natural, and not affected or hypocritical. For how shall even the most fierce and malicious that thou shalt conceive, be able to hold on against thee, if thou shalt still continue meek and loving unto him; and that even at that time, when he is about to do thee wrong, thou shalt be well disposed, and in good temper, with all meekness to teach him, and to instruct him better? As for example; My son, we were not born for this, to hurt and annoy one another; it will be thy hurt not mine, my son: and so to show him forcibly and fully, that it is so in very deed: and that neither bees do it one to another, nor any other creatures that are naturally sociable. But this thou must do, not scoffingly, not by way of exprobation, but tenderly without any harshness of words. Neither must thou do it by way of exercise, or ostentation, that they that are by and hear thee, may admire thee: but so always that nobody be privy to it, but himself alone: yea, though there be more present at the same time. These nine particular heads, as so many gifts from the Muses, see that thou remember well: and begin one day, whilest thou art yet alive, to be a man indeed. But on the other side thou must take heed, as much to flatter them, as to be angry with them: for both are equally uncharitable, and equally hurtful. And in thy passions, take it presently to thy consideration, that to be angry is not the part of a man, but that to be meek and gentle, as it savours of more humanity, so of more manhood. That in this, there is strength and nerves, or vigour and fortitude: whereof anger and indignation is altogether void. For the nearer everything is unto unpassionateness, the nearer it is unto power. And as grief doth proceed from weakness, so doth anger. For both, both he that is angry and that grieveth, have received a wound, and cowardly have as it were yielded themselves unto their affections. If thou wilt have a tenth also, receive this tenth gift from Hercules the guide and leader of the Muses: that is a mad man's part, to look that there should be no wicked men in the world, because it is impossible. Now for a man to brook well enough, that there should be wicked men in the world, but not to endure that any should transgress against himself, is against all equity, and indeed tyrannical.
passages.russian:
Откуда пришла каждая вещь, из каких лежащих в основе веществ она состоит, во что превращается, какой будет, превратившись, и что она не претерпит ничего дурного.

И во-первых: каково моё отношение к ним и что мы появились на свет друг ради друга; а в ином смысле — что я появился на свет, чтобы стоять во главе их, как баран стоит во главе отары или бык — во главе стада. Но вернись ещё дальше и начни вот с чего: если не атомы, то целым правит природа; а если так, то худшее существует ради лучшего, а лучшее — друг ради друга. Во-вторых: каковы они за столом, в постели и прочем; а главное — к чему принуждают их собственные принципы и с каким самомнением они делают именно это. В-третьих: если они делают это правильно, досадовать не надо; а если неправильно, то ясно, что против своей воли и по незнанию. Ведь всякая душа лишается против своей воли — как истины, так и умения обходиться с каждым по достоинству. Во всяком случае, им обидно слышать, когда их называют несправедливыми, бесчувственными, жадными и, одним словом, склонными поступать дурно с ближними. В-четвёртых: что ты и сам совершаешь много дурных поступков и такой же, как они; а если от каких-то дурных поступков и удерживаешься, то всё же в тебе есть склонность, которая к ним ведёт, пусть ты и удерживаешься от таких же дурных поступков, как у них, из трусости, или из жажды славы, или из-за чего-то ещё столь же дурного. В-пятых: что ты даже не знаешь наверняка, поступают ли они дурно; ведь многое делается ради какой-то дальнейшей цели, и вообще нужно сперва многое узнать, чтобы с твёрдым пониманием высказываться о чужом поступке. В-шестых: что, когда ты крайне негодуешь или даже просто тяготишься, человеческая жизнь длится миг и вскоре все мы будем лежать мёртвыми. В-седьмых: нас тревожат не их поступки — они в их ведущих началах, — а наши собственные суждения. Во всяком случае, убери приговор, будто это нечто ужасное, согласись его отпустить — и гнева нет. Как же ты его уберёшь? Рассудив, что это не позорно. Ведь если позорное — не единственное дурное, то и тебе неизбежно совершать много дурных поступков, стать разбойником и кем угодно. В-восьмых: насколько тяжелее то, что навлекают наши вспышки гнева и огорчения из-за подобных дел, чем то самое, что вызывает у нас гнев и огорчение. В-девятых: доброта непобедима, если она искренна, а не ухмылка и не игра. Ведь что сделает тебе самый наглый человек, если ты будешь неизменно добр к нему и, когда представится случай, станешь мягко его увещевать и не спеша переучивать — в то самое время, когда он пытается причинить тебе вред: «Не надо, дитя. Мы по природе созданы для другого. Мне-то вреда не будет, это тебе причиняется вред, дитя». И покажи ненавязчиво и в общих словах, что это так: что так не поступают даже пчёлы и никакие другие существа, по природе стадные. И делать это нужно без иронии и без упрёка, а с любовью и без жала в душе; и не как в школе, и не для того, чтобы восхитился кто-то другой, стоящий рядом, а ему одному, даже если вокруг стоят и другие. Помни эти девять пунктов как дары, полученные тобой от Муз, и начни наконец быть человеком, пока живёшь. Остерегаться нужно льстить им так же, как и гневаться на них: и то и другое противно общественному и ведёт ко вреду. А в приступах гнева держи под рукой вот что: мужественна не ярость, а то, что мягко и кротко, — как оно человечнее, так и мужественнее; и что именно оно причастно силе, крепким жилам и мужеству, а не тот, кто негодует и недоволен. Ведь чем оно ближе к бесстрастию, тем ближе к мощи. И как огорчение свойственно слабому, так и гнев: ведь оба ранены и сдались. А если хочешь, прими и десятый дар — от Предводителя Муз: требовать, чтобы дурные люди не поступали дурно, — безумие, ведь это стремление к невозможному. А позволять им быть такими с другими, но требовать, чтобы они не поступали дурно с тобой, — бесчувственно и тиранично.

passages.greek: Ὅταν τις ἁμάρτῃ τι εἰς σέ, εὐθὺς ἐνθυμοῦ τί ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακὸν ὑπολαβὼν ἥμαρτε. τοῦτο γὰρ ἰδὼν ἐλεήσεις αὐτὸν καὶ οὔτε θαυμάσεις οὔτε ὀργισθήσῃ. ἤτοι γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς τὸ αὐτὸ ἐκείνῳ ἀγαθὸν ἔτι ὑπολαμβάνεις ἢ ἄλλο ὁμοειδές· δεῖ οὖν συγγινώσκειν. εἰ δὲ μηκέτι ὑπολαμβάνεις τὰ τοιαῦτα ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά, ῥᾷον εὐμενὴς ἔσῃ τῷ παρορῶντι.
passages.english: Whenever someone does you some wrong, consider at once what they judged to be good or bad when they did the wrong. For once you have seen this you will pity them, and will be neither surprised nor angry. For either you yourself still judge the same thing to be good as they do, or another thing of the same kind; so you must forgive. But if you no longer judge such things to be good and bad, you will more easily be kind to one who fails to see.

notes.note: The verb belonging to ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the settled list. It comes three times in the passage and the English has “judge” each time.
notes.other_reading: with what notion of good or bad they did the wrong

notes.note: θαυμάζω is to wonder at; here to be surprised, as in 9.42.
notes.other_reading: you will neither wonder nor be angry

notes.note: The ordinary word for “forgive”, literally “to know or think along with”. The literal sense fits the argument, since you share the other’s judgment.
notes.other_reading: so you must make allowance, as one who thinks the same

notes.note: παροράω is to see beside the thing, to overlook or see wrongly. It is taken as failing to see what is truly good and bad; the same verb gives “what they are failing to see” in 11.13 and 10.4.
notes.other_reading: to the one who sees amiss

passages.casaubon: Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be evil, when he did trespass. For this when thou knowest, thou wilt pity him thou wilt have no occasion either to wonder, or to be angry. For either thou thyself dust yet live in that error and ignorance, as that thou dust suppose either that very thing that he doth, or some other like worldly thing, to be good; and so thou art bound to pardon him if he have done that which thou in the like case wouldst have done thyself. Or if so be that thou dost not any more suppose the same things to be good or evil, that he doth; how canst thou but be gentle unto him that is in an error?
passages.russian: Когда кто-то поступит с тобой дурно, сразу подумай, что он счёл благом или злом, совершая этот дурной поступок. Ведь, увидев это, ты пожалеешь его и не будешь ни удивляться, ни гневаться. Либо ты сам ещё считаешь благом то же, что и он, либо другое того же рода, — тогда надо простить. Если же ты уже не считаешь подобное благом и злом, тебе будет легче быть благожелательным к тому, кто не разглядел.

passages.greek: Ὅταν προσκόπτῃς ἐπί τινος ἁμαρτίᾳ, εὐθὺς μεταβὰς ἐπιλογίζου τί παρόμοιον ἁμαρτάνεις· οἷον, ἀργύριον ἀγαθὸν εἶναι κρίνων ἢ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἢ τὸ δοξάριον καὶ κατ’ εἶδος. τούτῳ γὰρ ἐπιβάλλων ταχέως ἐπιλήσῃ τῆς ὀργῆς, συμπροσπίπτοντος τοῦ ὅτι βιάζεται· τί γὰρ ποιήσει; ἤ, εἰ δύνασαι, ἄφελε αὐτοῦ τὸ βιαζόμενον.
passages.english: Whenever you take offence at someone’s wrongdoing, turn at once to yourself and reckon up what wrong of a similar kind you do: for example, judging money to be a good, or pleasure, or a scrap of reputation, and so on, kind by kind. For when you put your mind to this you will quickly forget your anger, as it strikes you at the same time that they are being forced: for what are they to do? Or, if you can, take away from them what is forcing them.

notes.note: “Having crossed over”: shifting from the other person to yourself. The Greek does not say where to; “to yourself” is supplied from the sense.
notes.other_reading: pass over at once and reckon up

notes.note: A diminutive of δόξα (reputation), said with contempt.
notes.other_reading: petty fame

notes.note: The phrase is literally “and by kind”: a short way of saying “and so on through each sort of case”.
notes.other_reading: and the like, class by class

notes.note: ἐπιβάλλω with a dative is to apply oneself, or one’s mind, to something.
notes.other_reading: for if you fix on this

notes.note: The form can be passive (“is forced”) or middle (“uses force”). It is taken as passive, with “what are they to do?” following: the person is forced by their own false judgment.
notes.other_reading: that they are acting with violence

notes.note: Read as middle, “that which forces”. It could be passive, “the part of them that is forced”.
notes.other_reading: take away from them the compulsion they are under

check.note: The Greek is to pass over, here from the other person to oneself. “Turn round” suggests a bodily movement.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “turn at once to yourself and reckon up”. The note says that “to yourself” is supplied from the sense.

passages.casaubon: When thou art offended with any man's transgression, presently reflect upon thyself; and consider what thou thyself art guilty of in the same kind. As that thou also perchance dost think it a happiness either to be rich, or to live in pleasure, or to be praised and commended, and so of the rest in particular. For this if thou shalt call to mind, thou shalt soon forget thine anger; especially when at the same time this also shall concur in thy thoughts, that he was constrained by his error and ignorance so to do: for how can he choose as long as he is of that opinion? Do thou therefore if thou canst, take away that from him, that forceth him to do as he doth.
passages.russian: Всякий раз, когда тебя задевает чей-то дурной поступок, тотчас обратись к себе и прикинь, какой подобный дурной поступок совершаешь ты сам: например, считая благом деньги, или наслаждение, или крупицу славы, и так далее, вид за видом. Ведь, вникнув в это, ты быстро забудешь свой гнев, поскольку тебе одновременно придёт на ум, что его вынуждают: а что ему делать? Или, если можешь, отними у него то, что его вынуждает.

passages.greek: Ἕωθεν προλέγειν ἑαυτῷ· συντεύξομαι περιέργῳ, ἀχαρίστῳ, ὑβριστῇ, δολερῷ, βασκάνῳ, ἀκοινωνήτῳ· πάντα ταῦτα συμβέβηκεν ἐκείνοις παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν. ἐγὼ δὲ τεθεωρηκὼς τὴν φύσιν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ὅτι καλόν, καὶ τοῦ κακοῦ ὅτι αἰσχρόν, καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντος φύσιν ὅτι μοι συγγενής, οὐχὶ αἵματος ἢ σπέρματος τοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ νοῦ καὶ θείας ἀπομοίρας μέτοχος, οὔτε βλαβῆναι ὑπό τινος αὐτῶν δύναμαι· αἰσχρῷ γάρ με οὐδεὶς περιβαλεῖ· οὔτε ὀργίζεσθαι τῷ συγγενεῖ δύναμαι οὔτε ἀπέχθεσθαι αὐτῷ. γεγόναμεν γὰρ πρὸς συνεργίαν ὡς πόδες, ὡς χεῖρες, ὡς βλέφαρα, ὡς οἱ στοῖχοι τῶν ἄνω καὶ κάτω ὀδόντων. τὸ οὖν ἀντιπράσσειν ἀλλήλοις παρὰ φύσιν· ἀντιπρακτικὸν δὲ τὸ ἀγανακτεῖν καὶ ἀποστρέφεσθαι.
passages.english: At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one. All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad. But I, who have seen the nature of the good, that it is honourable, and of the bad, that it is shameful, and the nature of the very person who does wrong, that they are akin to me, sharing not the same blood or seed but mind and a portion of the divine, can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful, nor be angry with one who is akin to me, nor hate them. For we have come into being to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is to work against one another.

notes.note: An infinitive used as a command, with the reflexive “oneself”, which in Greek of this date serves for any person. The English reads “say to yourself”; how far the speech runs is not marked, so no quotation marks are used.
notes.other_reading: One should say to oneself at dawn, in advance

notes.note: περίεργος is someone who is busy with what is not their concern.
notes.other_reading: a busybody

notes.note: βάσκανος is grudging and malicious, the word used of the evil eye.
notes.other_reading: a spiteful one

notes.note: καλόν and αἰσχρόν are both “beautiful, ugly” and “honourable, shameful”. The English takes the moral pair and keeps “shameful” for αἰσχρῷ below, so that the reason given for not being harmed can be followed.
notes.other_reading: that it is beautiful … that it is ugly

notes.note: “Akin”, picked up by τῷ συγγενεῖ below. The words “blood or seed” and “mind and a portion of the divine” all depend on μέτοχος, “sharing in”: kinship by shared mind, not by family.
notes.other_reading: a kinsman, not of the same blood or seed, but a sharer in mind

notes.note: ἀπόμοιρα is a share portioned off from something larger: a portion of what is divine.
notes.other_reading: a fragment of the divine

notes.note: The image is of throwing something around a person, as a garment or a net. It is kept as “wrap”.
notes.other_reading: involve in what is shameful

notes.note: The verb usually means to be hated by someone; with this dative it is to be at enmity with them. The English reads “hate”.
notes.other_reading: nor be at enmity with them

notes.note: The same root as ἀντιπράσσειν just before, and set against συνεργίαν (working together). “Work” is kept in all three. The adjective has no object of its own; “one another” is carried over from the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: and indignation and turning away are forms of opposition

passages.casaubon: In the country of the Quadi at Granua, these. Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have happened unto them, through ignorance of that which is truly good and truly bad. But I that understand the nature of that which is good, that it only is to be desired, and of that which is bad, that it only is truly odious and shameful: who know moreover, that this transgressor, whosoever he be, is my kinsman, not by the same blood and seed, but by participation of the same reason, and of the same divine particle; How can I either be hurt by any of those, since it is not in their power to make me incur anything that is truly reproachful? or angry, and ill affected towards him, who by nature is so near unto me? for we are all born to be fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of the upper and under teeth: for such therefore to be in opposition, is against nature; and what is it to chafe at, and to be averse from, but to be in opposition?
passages.russian: На рассвете говори себе заранее: я встречу человека, вмешивающегося в чужие дела, неблагодарного, наглого, коварного, завистливого, необщественного. Всё это постигло их от незнания того, что хорошо и что дурно. Но я, увидевший природу блага — что оно прекрасно, и природу дурного — что оно постыдно, и природу самого поступающего дурно — что он сродни мне и делит со мной не ту же кровь или семя, а ум и частицу божественного, — не могу ни потерпеть вреда от кого-либо из них, ведь никто не облечёт меня в постыдное, ни гневаться на того, кто мне сродни, ни ненавидеть его. Ведь мы появились на свет, чтобы действовать сообща, как ноги, как руки, как веки, как ряды верхних и нижних зубов. Поэтому действовать друг против друга противно природе; а негодовать и отворачиваться — значит действовать друг против друга.

passages.greek: Ἐπὶ τοῦ φαντασίαν παρασχόντος ὅτι ἥμαρτε· τί δαὶ οἶδα εἰ τοῦτο ἁμάρτημα; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἥμαρτεν, ὅτι κατέκρινεν αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν, καὶ οὕτως ὅμοιον τοῦτο τῷ καταδρύπτειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ὄψιν. Ὅτι ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν ὅμοιος τῷ μὴ θέλοντι τὴν συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν καὶ τὰ βρέφη κλαυθμυρίζεσθαι καὶ τὸν ἵππον χρεμετίζειν καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα ἀναγκαῖα. τί γὰρ πάθῃ τὴν ἕξιν ἔχων τοιαύτην; εἰ οὖν γοργὸς εἶ, ταύτην θεράπευσον.
passages.english: In the case of someone who has given the impression of having done wrong: “But how do I know whether this is a wrong?” And if they did do wrong, that they have condemned themselves, and so this is like tearing at one’s own face. That whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be. For what are they to do, having a disposition like that? So if you are vigorous, cure that disposition.

notes.note: φαντασία is “impression” as settled: the person has produced the impression that they did wrong.
notes.other_reading: someone who appears to have done wrong

notes.note: δαί is a colloquial particle that sharpens a question. It is rendered with “But”.
notes.other_reading: And how

notes.note: The Greek has only “that …”, a thought to be held ready, with no verb of saying; so too the next sentence. The bare “that” is kept in both places.
notes.other_reading: then tell yourself that they have condemned themselves

notes.note: καταδρύπτω is to tear with the nails, as mourners did. ὄψις is the face, or possibly the eyes. The Greek does not say what “this” is; it is taken to be the wrongdoing.
notes.other_reading: like tearing at one’s own eyes

notes.note: ὀπός is the sharp milky juice of the fig tree. English has no single plain word; the English reads “sap”.
notes.other_reading: to have acrid juice in its figs

notes.note: An idiom, literally “what is the person to undergo?”, used for “what else can they do?”. It is taken of the bad person, who cannot help it with such a disposition. ἕξις is rendered “disposition”, as in 11.18.
notes.other_reading: For what is to become of a person in such a condition?

notes.note: γοργός is fierce, vigorous, quick to act. The English gives the plain sense and adds no mockery; the Greek may be straight praise or a slight taunt.
notes.other_reading: So if you are fierce

notes.note: “That” is feminine in the Greek and points to the disposition just named. It is most naturally the other person’s; it could be read as a turn back to your own.
notes.other_reading: treat this condition of yours

check.note: “So” in “so keen” is added and gives a sneer the Greek does not have, and “keen” is weaker than the Greek word, which is vigorous, spirited, fierce.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “So if you are vigorous”. The added “so” and the weak “keen” are gone; “a person of energy” is longer than the one Greek adjective needs.

check.note: The Greek pronoun is feminine and refers to the disposition just named. “This” in English could be the wrong, or the whole situation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “cure that disposition”, since the Greek pronoun is feminine and points to the disposition just named.

check.note: The Greek word can be the face or the eyes, the sight. The other reading is “tearing at one’s own eyes”.
check.decided: Accepted: “face” is kept, as the finding allows, and the note records the other reading, “eyes”.

passages.casaubon: At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin indeed, as it seems to be? But if it be, what do I know but that he himself hath already condemned himself for it? And that is all one as if a man should scratch and tear his own face, an object of compassion rather than of anger. Again, that he that would not have a vicious man to sin, is like unto him that would not have moisture in the fig, nor children to welp nor a horse to neigh, nor anything else that in the course of nature is necessary. For what shall he do that hath such an habit? If thou therefore beest powerful and eloquent, remedy it if thou canst.
passages.russian: О том, кто, как показалось, поступил дурно: «А откуда я знаю, дурной ли это поступок?» А если он и поступил дурно, то он сам себя осудил, а значит, это всё равно что раздирать себе лицо. Что тот, кто не хочет, чтобы дурной человек поступал дурно, похож на того, кто не хочет, чтобы смоковница давала сок в смоквах, чтобы младенцы плакали, чтобы конь ржал, — или чего-либо ещё из того, чему необходимо быть. Ведь что ему делать при такой склонности? Так что, если ты энергичен, вылечи эту склонность.

passages.greek: Ὅταν ἄλλος ψέγῃ σε ἢ μισῇ ἢ τοιαῦτά τινα ἐκφωνῶσιν, ἔρχου ἐπὶ τὰ ψυχάρια αὐτῶν, δίελθε ἔσω καὶ ἴδε ποῖοί τινές εἰσιν. ὄψει ὅτι οὐ δεῖ σε σπᾶσθαι, ἵνα τούτοις τί ποτε περὶ σοῦ δοκῇ. εὐνοεῖν μέντοι αὐτοῖς δεῖ· φύσει γὰρ φίλοι, καὶ οἱ θεοὶ δὲ παντοίως αὐτοῖς βοηθοῦσι, δι’ ὀνείρων, διὰ μαντειῶν, πρὸς ταῦτα μέντοι, πρὸς ἃ ἐκεῖνοι διαφέρονται.
passages.english: When someone else blames you or hates you, or people voice things of that kind, go to their little souls, pass inside and see what sort of people they are. You will see that you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you. You must wish them well, however; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in every kind of way, through dreams, through oracles, yet towards the things those people care about.

notes.note: The Greek moves from the singular “another” to a plural verb, and stays in the plural. The shift is marked with “people”.
notes.other_reading: or utters things of that kind

notes.note: A diminutive of ψυχή (soul), said with pity or contempt.
notes.other_reading: their poor souls

notes.note: To be pulled, wrenched or convulsed: the torment of anxiety over their opinion. The words οὐ δεῖ before it are taken as “need not”, following “you will see”; they can also mean “must not”.
notes.other_reading: that you must not be racked

notes.note: Literally “that some particular thing may seem to them about you”: that they should hold one opinion of you or another.
notes.other_reading: so that these people may have any opinion of you whatever

notes.note: No verb and no “your”: by nature they are friends, which is taken as friends to you. φίλοι can also mean “dear”.
notes.other_reading: for by nature they are dear to you

notes.note: διαφέρομαι usually means to differ or quarrel. The English takes a sense found in later Greek, to be concerned about something, to set store by it (from memory, unchecked). The point is that the gods help them even towards things that are not truly good.
notes.other_reading: yet towards the things those people quarrel over

check.note: The Greek can be “you must not” as well as “you need not”, and the verb is passive, to be torn or racked, and not to strain oneself by choice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you need not be torn apart”, which gives the passive verb its force. “With worry” is not in the Greek and is not added; “need not” is kept because it follows “you will see”, and the note records “must not”.

check.note: The Greek verb is to utter, to voice. “Cry out” suggests shouting.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or people voice things of that kind”.

check.note: “Very” is added, and the English clause is hard to follow. The Greek is “yet toward those things which they care about”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yet toward the things those people care about”, without the added “very”.

passages.casaubon: When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee, get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them, and behold what manner of men they be. Thou shalt see, that there is no such occasion why it should trouble thee, what such as they are think of thee. Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends. And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
passages.russian: Когда кто-то другой винит тебя или ненавидит, или люди говорят что-то в этом роде, иди к их маленьким душам, войди внутрь и посмотри, каковы они. Ты увидишь, что тебе не нужно разрываться на части ради того, чтобы эти люди думали о тебе то или иное. Однако желать им добра ты должен: ведь по природе они друзья; и боги тоже всячески помогают им — снами, прорицаниями, — пусть и в том, о чём заботятся они сами.

passages.greek: Καταφρονήσει μού τις; ὄψεται. ἐγὼ δὲ ὄψομαι ἵνα μή τι καταφρονήσεως ἄξιον πράσσων ἣ λέγων εὑρίσκωμαι. μισήσει; ὄψεται. ἀλλὰ ἐγὼ εὐμενὴς καὶ εὔνους παντὶ καὶ τούτῳ αὐτῷ ἕτοιμος τὸ παρορώμενον δεῖξαι, οὐκ ὀνειδιστικῶς οὐδὲ ὡς κατεπιδεικνύμενος ὅτι ἀνέχομαι, ἀλλὰ γνησίως καὶ χρηστῶς, οἷος ὁ Φωκίων ἐκεῖνος, εἴ γε μὴ προσεποιεῖτο. τὰ ἔσω γὰρ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν βλέπεσθαι ἄνθρωπον πρὸς μηδὲν ἀγανακτικῶς διατιθέμενον μηδὲ δεινοπαθοῦντα. τί γάρ σοι κακόν, εἰ αὐτὸς νῦν ποιεῖς τὸ τῇ φύσει σου οἰκεῖον καὶ δέχῃ τὸ νῦν τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει εὔκαιρον, ἄνθρωπος τεταμένος πρὸς τὸ γίνεσθαι δι’ ὅτου δὴ τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον;
passages.english: Will someone despise me? That is for them to see to. But I will see to it that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves to be despised. Will they hate me? That is for them to see to. But I am kind and well-disposed to everyone, and ready to show this very person what they are failing to see, not with reproach, nor as if making a show of putting up with them, but genuinely and good-heartedly, like the famous Phocion, if indeed he was not pretending. For what is within must be like this, and a human being must be seen by the gods to be one who is not disposed to be indignant at anything and makes a grievance of nothing. For what is bad for you, if you yourself are now doing what is proper to your nature, and are accepting what is now in season for the nature of the whole, a human being straining towards this: that what is good for all in common should come about, by whatever means?

notes.note: Literally “that person will see”, an idiom for “that is their affair”. Marcus then uses the same verb of himself, ὄψομαι. “See to” is kept in both.
notes.other_reading: That is their concern.

notes.greek: ἐγὼ εὐμενὴς καὶ εὔνους παντὶ καὶ τούτῳ αὐτῷ ἕτοιμος
notes.note: There is no verb; the English supplies a present, and after the two futures a future is as possible. “This very person” can go with what follows (ready to show them) or with what precedes (well-disposed to everyone, and to them).
notes.other_reading: will be kind and well-disposed to everyone and to this very person, ready to show

notes.note: χρηστός is good in the sense of decent, kind and useful. Since “kind” is used for εὐμενής, the English reads “good-heartedly”.
notes.other_reading: sincerely and decently

notes.note: Phocion was an Athenian general and statesman of the fourth century BC, remembered for bearing no grudge against the city that condemned him (from memory, unchecked). ἐκεῖνος marks him as well known.
notes.other_reading: as Phocion did in the well-known story

notes.note: The “must” of the sentence governs both halves: what is within must be like this, and a human being must be seen by the gods to be of this kind. The obligation lies on the person.
notes.other_reading: and the gods must see a human being who is not disposed to be indignant at anything

notes.note: To complain loudly of what one suffers, to treat it as an outrage. “At nothing” earlier in the clause is taken with this word too.
notes.other_reading: and does not cry out at hard treatment

notes.note: The passage begins in the first person and here turns to the second; the change is kept. κακόν is “bad”, as elsewhere in this section.
notes.other_reading: For what harm is there to you

notes.note: “Stretched”, that is, pulled taut towards something; “straining” keeps the image. Some editors are believed to print a word meaning “stationed” here instead (from memory, unchecked); the text as given is translated.
notes.other_reading: a human being posted to see that the common good is brought about

notes.note: The phrase is “through whatever”, and the form can also mean “through whomever”. συμφέρον is rendered “what is good for” as settled.
notes.other_reading: that the common benefit should come about through whoever it may be

check.note: The “must” lies on the person, who must be seen by the gods to be of this kind. The English puts the obligation on the gods.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a human being must be seen by the gods to be one who is not disposed to be indignant at anything”. The “must” lies on the person, not on the gods.

check.greek: ἀλλὰ ἐγὼ εὐμενὴς καὶ εὔνους παντὶ
check.note: The Greek has no verb. After the two future verbs before it a future, “shall be kind”, is as likely as the present.
