check.decided: Declined: the present tense stands. A Greek clause with no verb is ordinarily read as a present, and it then states a settled character against the two futures before it; the note records “will be”.

check.note: The Greek verb is to complain bitterly of what one suffers, to make a grievance of it. “Cry out at hard treatment” is stiff and suggests a shout of pain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and makes a grievance of nothing”. The grievance wording is taken, but “of what happens to them” is not in the Greek, where “at nothing” governs both halves of the clause.

check.note: “Stretched toward” is literal and is not how English says that a person is bent on something; “intent on” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a human being straining toward this”. “Stretched toward” was not natural English, but the Greek word is an image of something pulled taut, which “straining” keeps and “intent” loses.

passages.casaubon: Will any contemn me? let him look to that, upon what grounds he does it: my care shall be that I may never be found either doing or speaking anything that doth truly deserve contempt. Will any hate me? let him look to that. I for my part will be kind and loving unto all, and even unto him that hates me, whom-soever he be, will I be ready to show his error, not by way of exprobation or ostentation of my patience, but ingenuously and meekly: such as was that famous Phocion, if so be that he did not dissemble. For it is inwardly that these things must be: that the Gods who look inwardly, and not upon the outward appearance, may behold a man truly free from all indignation and grief. For what hurt can it be unto thee whatsoever any man else doth, as long as thou mayest do that which is proper and suitable to thine own nature? Wilt not thou (a man wholly appointed to be both what, and as the common good shall require) accept of that which is now seasonable to the nature of the universe?
passages.russian: Кто-то будет меня презирать? Об этом пусть позаботится он сам. А я позабочусь о том, чтобы меня не застали за делом или словом, достойным презрения. Будет меня ненавидеть? Об этом пусть позаботится он сам. А я добр и доброжелателен ко всем и готов показать этому самому человеку, чего он не видит, — не с упрёком и не так, будто выставляю напоказ своё терпение, а искренне и благодушно, как знаменитый Фокион, если только он не притворялся. Ведь внутри должно быть именно так, и боги должны видеть в человеке того, кто ни на что не склонен негодовать и ничего не считает обидой. Да и что для тебя дурного, если ты сам сейчас делаешь то, что свойственно твоей природе, и принимаешь то, что сейчас своевременно для природы целого, — ты, человек, устремлённый к тому, чтобы совершилось то, что хорошо для всех сообща, каким бы то ни было путём?

passages.greek: Ἐν τοῖς γυμνασίοις καὶ ὄνυξι κατέδρυψέ τις καὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ ἐρραγεὶς πληγὴν ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ’ οὔτε ἐπισημαινόμεθα οὔτε προσκόπτομεν οὔτε ὑφορώμεθα ὕστερον ὡς ἐπίβουλον· καίτοι φυλαττόμεθα, οὐ μέντοι ὡς ἐχθρὸν οὐδὲ μεθ’ ὑποψίας, ἀλλ’ ἐκκλίσεως εὐμενοῦς. τοιοῦτόν τι γινέσθω καὶ ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς μέρεσι τοῦ βίου· πολλὰ παρενθυμώμεθα τῶν οἷον προσγυμναζομένων. ἔξεστι γάρ, ὡς ἔφην, ἐκκλίνειν καὶ μήτε ὑποπτεύειν μήτε ἀπέχθεσθαι.
passages.english: In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners. For it is possible, as I said, to step aside, and neither to suspect nor to hate.

notes.note: Plural: in the gymnasia, or in bouts of exercise. The first two verbs have no object in the Greek; the English supplies one twice so that they can stand.
notes.other_reading: In training bouts someone scratches with the nails

notes.note: ἐρραγείς is from the verb “to break, to burst”: bursting or crashing in with the head. πληγή is a blow, or the wound it leaves. The past tenses describe what typically happens.
notes.other_reading: and, crashing in with the head, has left a bruise

notes.note: To set a mark on something. It is taken as marking the person down as an offender; it could be making a sign of protest.
notes.other_reading: there is no making a point of it

notes.note: ἔκκλισις is the Stoic term for avoidance, and here also the literal dodge of a wrestler. The English has “stepping aside”, and “step aside” for the verb ἐκκλίνειν below.
notes.other_reading: but with good-natured avoidance

notes.note: The verb is “to let pass in one’s thoughts”, and the form is taken as an exhortation. προσγυμναζόμενοι are those who train against a person; οἷον, “as it were”, marks the figure.
notes.other_reading: much should be disregarded in those who are, so to speak, wrestling partners

notes.note: As in 2.1: to be at enmity. The English reads “hate”.
notes.other_reading: nor to bear ill will

check.note: The two Greek particles are “both … and”, joining the two things that happen in training. “Even” gives the first a stress the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins “In the gymnasium someone has scratched” with no “even”. The two Greek particles pair the scratching and the butting as “both … and”.

passages.casaubon: Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with his nails, and hath broken thy head. Well, thou art wounded. Yet thou dost not exclaim; thou art not offended with him. Thou dost not suspect him for it afterwards, as one that watcheth to do thee a mischief. Yea even then, though thou dost thy best to save thyself from him, yet not from him as an enemy. It is not by way of any suspicious indignation, but by way of gentle and friendly declination. Keep the same mind and disposition in other parts of thy life also. For many things there be, which we must conceit and apprehend, as though we had had to do with an antagonist at the palestra. For as I said, it is very possible for us to avoid and decline, though we neither suspect, nor hate.
passages.russian: В гимнасии кто-то расцарапал нас ногтями, боднул головой и нанёс удар; но мы не берём его на заметку, не обижаемся и не подозреваем потом, что он злоумышляет против нас. Мы, конечно, остерегаемся, но не как врага и не с подозрением, а доброжелательно уклоняясь. Пусть нечто подобное будет и в прочих частях жизни: будем многое спускать тем, кто нам как бы товарищи по упражнениям. Ведь можно, как я сказал, уклониться — и не подозревать, и не ненавидеть.

passages.greek: Πῶς ὠμόν ἐστι μὴ ἐπιτρέπειν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ὁρμᾶν ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα αὐτοῖς οἰκεῖα καὶ συμφέροντα. καίτοι τρόπον τινὰ οὐ συγχωρεῖς αὐτοῖς τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ὅταν ἀγανακτῇς, ὅτι ἁμαρτάνουσι· φέρονται γὰρ πάντως ὡς ἐπὶ οἰκεῖα καὶ συμφέροντα αὐτοῖς. —ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔχει οὕτως.— οὐκοῦν δίδασκε καὶ δείκνυε μὴ ἀγανακτῶν.
passages.english: How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong. For they are certainly being carried towards things they take to suit them and to be good for them. “But it is not so.” Then teach them and show them, without being indignant.

notes.note: The verb belonging to ὁρμή, “impulse” in the settled list: to set out after a thing. “To have impulses towards” would be stiff, so the English reads “go after”.
notes.other_reading: not to allow people their impulse towards

notes.note: οἰκεῖα are things that belong to one, are proper to one’s nature. The English reads “suit them”; συμφέροντα is “good for them” as settled.
notes.other_reading: what appears to them to be their own and to their advantage

notes.note: “In every case” or “certainly”. The second is taken.
notes.other_reading: For in every case they are carried

notes.note: The edition sets these words between dashes as an objection by another voice: the things are not really good for them. The English uses quotation marks.
notes.other_reading: “But they are mistaken.”

passages.casaubon: Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most to their own proper good and behoof? But thou after a sort deniest them this liberty, as often as thou art angry with them for their sins. For surely they are led unto those sins whatsoever they be, as to their proper good and commodity. But it is not so (thou wilt object perchance). Thou therefore teach them better, and make it appear unto them: but be not thou angry with them.
passages.russian: Как жестоко — не позволять людям стремиться к тому, что кажется им подходящим и хорошим для них. А ведь ты в некотором смысле не позволяешь им этого всякий раз, когда негодуешь, что они поступают дурно. Ведь они, конечно, влекутся к тому, что считают подходящим и хорошим для себя. «Но это не так». Тогда учи их и показывай, не негодуя.

passages.greek:
Τὸ ἐπίκοτον τοῦ προσώπου λίαν παρὰ φύσιν, ὅταν πολλάκις ἐναποθνῄσκειν ᾖ πρόσχημα ἢ τὸ τελευταῖον ἀπεσβέσθη, ὥστε ὅλως ἐξαφθῆναι μὴ δύνασθαι. αὐτῷ γε τούτῳ παρακολουθεῖν πειρῶ, ὅτι παρὰ τὸν λόγον. εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ συναίσθησις τοῦ ἁμαρτάνειν οἰχήσεται, τίς ἔτι τοῦ ζῆν αἰτία;

Πάντα ὅσα ὁρᾷς ὅσον οὔπω μεταβαλεῖ ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα φύσις καὶ ἄλλα ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ποιήσει καὶ πάλιν ἄλλα ἐκ τῆς ἐκείνων οὐσίας, ἵνα ἀεὶ νεαρὸς ᾖ ὁ κόσμος.
passages.english:
A scowl on the face is very much against nature. When it is often there, the look of the face dies in it, or in the end has been put out, so that it cannot be kindled at all. Try to grasp at least this very point, that it is against reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is going to go, what cause is there still for living?

Everything you see, the nature that governs the whole will change in almost no time, and will make other things out of their substance, and again others out of the substance of those, so that the universe may always be young.

notes.note: ἐπίκοτος is “bearing a grudge, wrathful”: the angry cast of a face.
notes.other_reading: A look of rancour on the face

notes.greek: ὅταν πολλάκις ἐναποθνῄσκειν ᾖ πρόσχημα ἢ τὸ τελευταῖον ἀπεσβέσθη
notes.note: The Greek as given does not construe: word for word, “whenever often to-die-in-it be outward show, or in the end it was quenched”. The English is a reconstruction: πρόσχημα (the outward appearance) is taken as what dies and is put out, “often” is taken with the scowl, “of the face” is supplied, and a new sentence is begun where the Greek clause hangs on “against nature”. Editors are believed to treat the text as damaged here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: when it is often put on, its comeliness begins to die, and at last is extinguished

notes.note: The image is of a lamp or fire: put out, and unable to be lit. It is kept.
notes.other_reading: so that it can never be rekindled

notes.note: παρακολουθέω with a dative is to follow with the mind, to stay aware of. The dative is taken as its object, explained by the “that” clause, and the next sentence, on losing awareness, continues the thought. It could be a dative of means.
notes.other_reading: Try to conclude from this very fact that it is against reason

notes.note: συναίσθησις is the awareness a person has of their own state. The link of thought with the scowl is not spelled out in the Greek, and none is supplied.
notes.other_reading: if even the consciousness of doing wrong is lost

notes.note: αἰτία is a cause or ground. “Cause” is used so that “reason” stays with λόγος in the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: what reason is left for living?

notes.note: An idiom, literally “as much as not yet”: all but now, at any moment.
notes.other_reading: in a moment

notes.note: The same phrase as in 11.18. τὰ ὅλα is rendered “the whole” as settled, and ὁ κόσμος at the end “the universe”.
notes.other_reading: the nature that governs all things

check.note: The Greek as given does not construe, and the English reads smoothly with no sign of the difficulty; “of the face” is supplied. A rendering of this kind can stay, but the clause should be marked as uncertain.
check.decided: Accepted: the rendering is kept, and the note now says plainly that the Greek as given does not construe, that the English sentence is a reconstruction, and that “of the face” and the break into a new sentence are supplied.

check.note: The Greek tense is a finished state, “has been put out”, and the English “it” could be the scowl or the look. In the Greek what is quenched is the look.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the look of the face dies in it, or in the end has been put out”, a finished state with the look as its one subject. “Altogether” is not added, since the Greek word for it belongs to the next clause, “cannot be kindled at all”.

check.note: The Greek case here can also give “follow out from this very fact”: try to conclude from this that it is against reason. The English takes it as the thing to be grasped.
check.decided: Declined: “Try to grasp at least this very point” stands. The Greek verb with this case regularly means to follow a thing with the mind, and the next sentence, on losing awareness, continues that thought; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: “what reason is left for living” used “reason” for αἰτία one sentence after “against reason”, where it stands for λόγος, so two Greek words shared one English word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what cause is there still for living?”, which keeps “reason” for λόγος alone in this passage.

passages.casaubon: An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death. But were it so, that all anger and passion were so thoroughly quenched in thee, that it were altogether impossible to kindle it any more, yet herein must not thou rest satisfied, but further endeavour by good consequence of true ratiocination, perfectly to conceive and understand, that all anger and passion is against reason. For if thou shalt not be sensible of thine innocence; if that also shall be gone from thee, the comfort of a good conscience, that thou doest all things according to reason: what shouldest thou live any longer for? All things that now thou seest, are but for a moment. That nature, by which all things in the world are administered, will soon bring change and alteration upon them, and then of their substances make other things like unto them: and then soon after others again of the matter and substance of these: that so by these means, the world may still appear fresh and new.
passages.russian:
Хмурость на лице весьма противна природе. Когда она бывает часто, облик лица в ней умирает или в конце концов гаснет, так что его уже вовсе не разжечь. Постарайся понять хотя бы вот что: это противно разуму. Ведь если уйдёт даже сознание того, что поступаешь дурно, какая ещё остаётся причина жить?

Всё, что ты видишь, природа, управляющая целым, почти мгновенно изменит и из его вещества сделает другое, а из вещества того — снова другое, чтобы мироздание всегда было молодым.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν δύνασαι, μεταδίδασκε· εἰ δὲ μή, μέμνησο ὅτι πρὸς τοῦτο ἡ εὐμένειά σοι δέδοται. καὶ οἱ θεοὶ δὲ εὐμενεῖς τοῖς τοιούτοις εἰσίν, εἰς ἔνια δὲ καὶ συνεργοῦσιν, εἰς ὑγίειαν, εἰς πλοῦτον, εἰς δόξαν· οὕτως εἰσὶ χρηστοί. ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ σοί· ἢ εἰπέ, τίς ὁ κωλύων;
passages.english: If you can, teach them otherwise; and if not, remember that kindness has been given to you for this. The gods too are kind to such people, and towards some things they even work with them, towards health, towards wealth, towards reputation: so good are they. You may be so too; or tell me, who is stopping you?

notes.note: The Greek has no object; the English adds “them”. The verb is to teach someone into a different view, as in 9.42.
notes.other_reading: If you can, show the better way

notes.note: “Such people” are not named: those who go wrong and cannot be taught.
notes.other_reading: to people of that kind

notes.note: χρηστός is good in the sense of kind and helpful. Since “kind” is used for εὐμενής, the English reads “good”.
notes.other_reading: so generous are they

notes.note: Literally “it is open to you also”. The Greek does not say to do what; it is taken as to be kind as the gods are.
notes.other_reading: It is in your power too

passages.casaubon: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee. The Gods themselves are good unto such; yea and in some things, (as in matter of health, of wealth, of honour,) are content often to further their endeavours: so good and gracious are they. And mightest thou not be so too? or, tell me, what doth hinder thee?
passages.russian: Если можешь, переучи их; а если нет, помни, что для этого тебе и дана доброта. И боги добры к таким людям и кое в чём даже содействуют им — ради здоровья, ради богатства, ради славы: вот насколько они хороши. Можно и тебе быть таким; или скажи, кто тебе мешает?

passages.greek:
Ὁμοθαμνεῖν μέν, μὴ ὁμοδογματεῖν δέ.

Οἱ ἐνιστάμενοι προιόντι σοι κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὥσπερ ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγιοῦς πράξεως ἀποτρέψαι σε οὐ δυνήσονται, οὕτως μηδὲ τῆς πρὸς αὐτοὺς εὐμενείας ἐκκρουέτωσαν, ἀλλὰ φύλασσε σεαυτὸν ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέρων ὁμοίως, μὴ μόνον ἐπὶ τῆς εὐσταθοῦς κρίσεως καὶ πράξεως, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς πρὸς τοὺς κωλύειν ἐπιχειροῦντας ἢ ἄλλως δυσχεραίνοντας πρᾳότητος. καὶ γὰρ τοῦτο ἀσθενές, τὸ χαλεπαίνειν αὐτοῖς, ὥσπερ τὸ ἀποστῆναι τῆς πράξεως καὶ ἐνδοῦναι καταπλαγέντα· ἀμφότεροι γὰρ ἐπίσης λειποτάκται, ὁ μὲν ὑποτρέσας, ὁ δὲ ἀλλοτριωθεὶς πρὸς τὸν φύσει συγγενῆ καὶ φίλον.
passages.english:
To grow on the same stem, but not to hold the same principles.

Just as those who stand in your way as you go forward in accord with right reason will not be able to turn you aside from sound action, so let them not knock you out of your kindness towards them either; but keep watch over yourself on both counts alike: not only in steady judgment and action, but also in gentleness towards those who try to hinder you or are otherwise annoyed. For this too is weakness, to be harsh with them, just as it is to abandon the action and give in from fright. For both are equally deserters from their post: the one who has flinched, and the one who has become estranged from a person who is by nature kin and friend.

notes.note: A rare verb from θάμνος (a bush or shrub): to belong to the same plant. This is the closing maxim of a chapter about a branch cut from its tree and grafted back; the earlier part is not given here, so who is to do this is not said, and only the words that stand are translated.
notes.other_reading: To share one trunk

notes.note: To hold the same δόγματα, “principles” in the settled list. The two verbs are built alike in Greek (same bush, same principles); English cannot match the pair in one word each.
notes.other_reading: but not to share one mind

notes.greek: προιόντι σοι κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον
notes.note: ὀρθὸς λόγος, “right reason”, is a fixed Stoic phrase. “In accord with right reason” is taken with “go forward”.
notes.other_reading: those who, in accord with right reason, cannot turn you as you advance

notes.note: To knock out or drive off, as from a position. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: let them not shake you out of

notes.note: κρίσις is the act of judging. The settled list keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, which does not occur in this passage, so “judgment” is used here.
notes.other_reading: steady decision

notes.note: To be annoyed, or to make difficulties. “Annoyed” is kept, as for the same verb in 11.18.
notes.other_reading: or are otherwise troublesome

notes.note: A military word: those who leave their place in the line.
notes.other_reading: deserters from the ranks

check.note: “Show” is added in “show their annoyance”. The Greek verb is to be annoyed, and can also be to make difficulties.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “show” is gone and the English now reads “or are otherwise annoyed”. “Annoyed” is the word used for the same verb in 11.18; “ill-disposed” would name a standing attitude, which the Greek verb does not.

part.left_out: Κλάδος τοῦ προσεχοῦς κλάδου ἀποκοπεὶς οὐ δύναται μὴ καὶ τοῦ ὅλου φυτοῦ ἀποκεκόφθαι. οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἄνθρωπος ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀποσχισθεὶς ὅλης τῆς κοινωνίας ἀποπέπτωκε. κλάδον μὲν οὖν ἄλλος ἀποκόπτει· ἄνθρωπος δὲ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν τοῦ πλησίον χωρίζει μισήσας καὶ ἀποστραφείς, ἀγνοεῖ δὲ ὅτι καὶ τοῦ ὅλου πολιτεύματος ἅμα ἀποτέτμηκεν ἑαυτόν. πλὴν ἐκεῖνό γε δῶρον τοῦ συστησαμένου τὴν κοινωνίαν Διός· ἔξεστι γὰρ ἡμῖν πάλιν συμφῦναι τῷ προσεχεῖ καὶ πάλιν τοῦ ὅλου συμπληρωτικοῖς γενέσθαι. πλεονάκις μέντοι γινόμενον τὸ κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην διαίρεσιν δυσένωτον καὶ δυσαποκατάστατον τὸ ἀποχωροῦν ποιεῖ. ὅλως τε οὐχ ὅμοιος ὁ κλάδος ὁ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς συμβλαστήσας καὶ σύμπνους συμμείνας τῷ μετὰ τὴν ἀποκοπὴν αὖθις ἐγκεντρισθέντι, ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 11.7 with the gardeners' saying about the grafted branch and begins its 11.8 with the closing maxim of chapter 11.8, then runs on through chapter 11.9.

passages.casaubon: To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions. They that shall oppose thee in thy right courses, as it is not in their power to divert thee from thy good action, so neither let it be to divert thee from thy good affection towards them. But be it thy care to keep thyself constant in both; both in a right judgment and action, and in true meekness towards them, that either shall do their endeavour to hinder thee, or at least will be displeased with thee for what thou hast done. For to fail in either (either in the one to give over for fear, or in the other to forsake thy natural affection towards him, who by nature is both thy friend and thy kinsman) is equally base, and much savouring of the disposition of a cowardly fugitive soldier.
passages.russian:
Расти на одном стебле, но не держаться одних принципов.

Как те, кто встаёт у тебя на пути, когда ты идёшь вперёд согласно правому разуму, не смогут отвратить тебя от здравого действия, так пусть они не выбьют тебя и из доброты к ним; но следи за собой в обоих отношениях равно: не только в твёрдом суждении и действии, но и в мягкости к тем, кто пытается тебе помешать или как-то иначе на тебя досадует. Ведь и это слабость — ожесточаться на них, так же как отказаться от действия и уступить от испуга. Оба одинаково дезертируют со своего поста: и тот, кто дрогнул, и тот, кто отдалился от человека, по природе ему родного и дружественного.

passages.greek: Τῷ γράσωνι μήτι ὀργίζῃ, μήτι τῷ ὀζοστόμῳ ὀργίζῃ; τί σοι ποιήσει; τοιοῦτον στόμα ἔχει, τοιαύτας μάλας ἔχει, ἀνάγκη τοιαύτην ἀποφορὰν ἀπὸ τοιούτων γίνεσθαι. —ἀλλ’ ὁ ἄνθρωπος λόγον ἔχει, φησί, καὶ δύναται συννοεῖν ἐφιστάνων τί πλημμελεῖ.—εὖ σοι γένοιτο· τοιγαροῦν καὶ σὺ λόγον ἔχεις, κίνησον λογικῇ διαθέσει λογικὴν διάθεσιν, δεῖξον, ὑπόμνησον· εἰ γὰρ ἐπαίει, θεραπεύσεις καὶ οὐ χρεία ὀργῆς.
passages.english: Surely you are not angry with the person who reeks of goat? Surely you are not angry with the one whose breath smells? What do you want them to do? The person has that kind of mouth, has that kind of armpits; from such things such a smell must come. “But a human being has reason,” someone says, “and can work out, by stopping to think, where they are at fault.” Good for you! Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.

notes.note: γράσων is someone who smells like a goat, said of rank armpits, as “armpits” below shows. The goat is kept, and the same words are used for γράσωνα in 11.15.
notes.other_reading: the person whose armpits smell

notes.note: μήτι opens a question that expects the answer no. The Greek repeats the verb in both questions and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: Are you angry with

notes.note: Literally “what will he do for you?”. The person is taken as the subject and “for you” loosely, because the next sentence explains that they cannot help the smell. The words can also have the anger as subject, or mean what they mean in 11.18, where they are “what will that person do to you?”.
notes.other_reading: What good will it do you? (or: What will they do to you?)

notes.note: The Greek has no pronoun, only “has”. To avoid “he” where no man is singled out the English has “the person” and then “they”, although the Greek is singular throughout.
notes.other_reading: He has that kind of mouth, he has that kind of armpits

notes.note: The words can mean a human being in general or this particular person. The general sense is taken: a human being, unlike a mouth or an armpit, has reason.
notes.other_reading: But this person has reason

notes.note: “He says”: an unnamed objector. The edition sets the objection between dashes; the English uses quotation marks.
notes.other_reading: it is said

notes.note: Literally to strike a false note in music; so to offend, to be at fault.
notes.other_reading: where they are out of tune

notes.note: A wish, “may it go well with you”, used as approval of the objection, perhaps with some irony.
notes.other_reading: Bless you

notes.note: ἐπαΐω is to give ear and to understand. The English reads “listen”.
notes.other_reading: for if they understand

check.note: The English silently picks one of three readings. The words can also mean “What good will it do you?”, with the anger as subject, or “What will he do to you?”, as the same words are rendered in 11.18; either change the wording or keep it and note the other reading.
check.decided: Accepted: “What do you want them to do?” is kept, as the finding allows, because the next sentence explains that the person cannot help the smell. The note now gives both other readings and points to the same words in 11.18.

check.note: The Greek can be this person or “a human being” in general, which gives the objection more weight: a human being, unlike an armpit, has reason.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But a human being has reason”. The note records that the words can also mean this particular person.

part.left_out: Οὔτε τραγῳδὸς οὔτε πόρνη.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 5.22 at 'no more occasion of anger' and begins its 5.23 with the chapter's last words, 'neither roarer nor harlot'.

passages.casaubon: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive. What can he do? such is his breath naturally, and such are his arm holes; and from such, such an effect, and such a smell must of necessity proceed. 'O, but the man (sayest thou) hath understanding in him, and might of himself know, that he by standing near, cannot choose but offend.' And thou also (God bless thee!) hast understanding. Let thy reasonable faculty, work upon his reasonable faculty; show him his fault, admonish him. If he hearken unto thee, thou hast cured him, and there will be no more occasion of anger.
passages.russian: Неужели ты гневаешься на того, кто воняет козлом? Неужели гневаешься на того, у кого пахнет изо рта? Что ему, по-твоему, делать? Такой у него рот, такие у него подмышки; от такого неизбежно исходит такой запах. «Но у человека есть разум, — говорят, — и он может, остановившись и подумав, сообразить, в чём он неправ». Молодец! Что ж, и у тебя есть разум: разумным расположением расшевели разумное расположение; покажи ему, напомни. Ведь если он послушает, ты его вылечишь, и гнев не нужен.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν σφάλλεται, διδάσκειν εὐμενῶς καὶ τὸ παρορώμενον δεικνύναι. εἰ δὲ ἀδυνατεῖς, σεαυτὸν αἰτιᾶσθαι ἢ μηδὲ σεαυτόν.
passages.english: If someone is mistaken, teach them kindly and show them what they are failing to see. But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.

notes.note: Literally “is tripped up”, so “is mistaken”. The Greek names no subject; the English supplies “someone”.
notes.other_reading: If someone trips

notes.note: The commands are infinitives with no person; “you cannot” in the next sentence shows who is addressed, so the English uses imperatives.
notes.other_reading: the thing is to teach kindly

notes.note: “What is being overlooked”: what the person is failing to see, as in 11.13.
notes.other_reading: point out what has been overlooked

check.note: The Greek verb is to trip, to be mistaken. “Is slipping” in English of today suggests someone getting worse over time; “is going wrong” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “If someone is mistaken”. “Is slipping” suggested a decline over time; “going wrong” is avoided because “wrong” stands for another Greek verb throughout this section.

passages.casaubon: Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
passages.russian: Если кто-то ошибается, учи его по-доброму и покажи, чего он не видит. А если не можешь, вини себя — или даже не себя.

passages.greek: Ὅρα μήποτέ τι τοιοῦτον πάθῃς πρὸς τοὺς ἀπανθρώπους, οἷον οἱ ἀπάνθρωποι πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους.
passages.english: See that you never come to feel towards the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel towards human beings.

notes.note: πάσχω is to undergo or be affected: here, to come to be in a certain state of feeling towards someone.
notes.other_reading: See that you are never affected towards the inhuman as

notes.greek: οἷον οἱ ἀπάνθρωποι πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους
notes.note: The text is translated as given. Some editors are believed to change the second “the inhuman” to “human beings”, giving “as human beings feel towards human beings” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: what human beings feel towards human beings

passages.casaubon: Take heed lest at any time thou stand so affected, though towards unnatural evil men, as ordinary men are commonly one towards another.
passages.russian: Смотри, чтобы никогда не испытывать к бесчеловечным ничего похожего на то, что бесчеловечные испытывают к людям.

passages.greek: Ἰκτεριῶσι τὸ μέλι πικρὸν φαίνεται καὶ λυσσοδήκτοις τὸ ὕδωρ φοβερὸν καὶ παιδίοις τὸ σφαιρίον καλόν. τί οὖν ὀργίζομαι; ἢ δοκεῖ σοι ἔλασσον ἰσχύειν τὸ διεψευσμένον ἢ τὸ χόλιον τῷ ἰκτεριῶντι καὶ ὁ ἰὸς τῷ λυσσοδήκτῳ;
passages.english: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?

notes.note: σφαιρίον is a diminutive, a little ball. καλόν here is “beautiful, fine” to the child’s eye, not the moral sense.
notes.other_reading: a ball seems a fine thing

notes.note: The Greek moves from the first person to the second in one breath; both are kept.
notes.other_reading: Or does it seem to the speaker himself

notes.note: A neuter participle, “that which has been deceived” or “the state of being deceived”. The English reads “a false belief”.
notes.other_reading: that being deceived has less power

notes.note: A diminutive of χολή, bile, which was held to cause jaundice. ἰός is the poison passed on by the mad dog’s bite.
notes.other_reading: the gall

passages.casaubon: To them that are sick of the jaundice, honey seems bitter; and to them that are bitten by a mad dog, the water terrible; and to children, a little ball seems a fine thing. And why then should I be angry? or do I think that error and false opinion is less powerful to make men transgress, than either choler, being immoderate and excessive, to cause the jaundice; or poison, to cause rage?

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Больным желтухой мёд кажется горьким, укушенным бешеной собакой вода кажется страшной, а маленьким детям их мячик кажется прекрасным. Почему же тогда я сержусь? Или ты думаешь, что у ложного убеждения меньше власти, чем у желчи над больным желтухой и у яда над укушенным бешеной собакой?

passages.greek: Ὡς σαπρὸς καὶ κίβδηλος ὁ λέγων· ἐγὼ προῄρημαι ἁπλῶς σοι προσφέρεσθαι. τί ποιεῖς, ἄνθρωπε; τοῦτο οὐ δεῖ προλέγειν. αὐτὸ φανήσεται· ἐπὶ τοῦ μετώπου γεγράφθαι ὀφείλει· εὐθὺς ἡ φωνὴ τοιοῦτον ἠχεῖ, εὐθὺς ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασιν ἐξέχει, ὡς τῶν ἐραστῶν ἐν τῷ βλέμματι πάντα εὐθὺς γνωρίζει ὁ ἐρώμενος. τοιοῦτον ὅλως δεῖ τὸν ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι, οἶον γράσωνα, ἵνα ὁ παραστὰς ἅμα τῷ προσελθεῖν, θέλει οὐ θέλει, αἴσθηται. ἐπιτήδευσις δὲ ἁπλότητος σκάλμη ἐστίν. οὐδέν ἐστιν αἴσχιον λυκοφιλίας· πάντων μάλιστα τοῦτο φεῦγε. ὁ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ἁπλοῦς καὶ εὐμενὴς ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασιν ἔχουσι ταῦτα καὶ οὐ λανθάνει.
passages.english: How rotten and counterfeit is the person who says: “I have chosen to be straightforward with you.” What are you doing, man? This is not a thing to announce beforehand. It will show of itself. It ought to be written on the forehead. At once the voice has that ring, at once it stands out in the eyes, just as the one who is loved at once knows everything in the look of the lovers. In short, the straightforward and good person must be like someone who reeks of goat, so that whoever stands near notices as soon as they come up, whether they want to or not. But a studied straightforwardness is a dagger. Nothing is more shameful than a wolf’s friendship: shun this above all things. The good and straightforward and kind person has these things in their eyes, and does not escape notice.

notes.note: The word for base or adulterated coin. The image is kept as “counterfeit”.
notes.other_reading: How rotten and false

notes.note: ἁπλῶς, “simply, without folds”, belongs with ἁπλοῦν and ἁπλότητος below. “Straightforward” is used for all of them.
notes.other_reading: to deal with you in simplicity

notes.note: οὐ δεῖ can mean “one should not” or “there is no need”. The English wording leaves room for both: after “rotten and counterfeit” the first fits, and “it will show of itself” supports the second.
notes.other_reading: There is no need to announce this beforehand

notes.note: Literally “at once the voice sounds such a thing”: the voice itself carries the character, with no need to announce it.
notes.other_reading: the voice at once sounds of it

notes.greek: ὡς τῶν ἐραστῶν ἐν τῷ βλέμματι πάντα εὐθὺς γνωρίζει ὁ ἐρώμενος
notes.note: ἐραστής and ἐρώμενος are the lover and the one loved in a Greek love affair; the lovers are plural and the beloved singular. Both numbers are kept.
notes.other_reading: as the beloved reads everything at once in a lover’s glance

notes.note: The copy has οἶον, a slip for οἷον (“like”). γράσων is the goat-smelling person of 5.28: goodness should be as impossible to miss as a strong smell.
notes.other_reading: like someone with rank armpits

notes.note: ἐπιτήδευσις is the deliberate practice or cultivation of something, here a straightforwardness that is put on. σκάλμη is a rare word for a knife or short sword; its meaning is given from memory, unchecked.
notes.other_reading: A put-on simplicity is a concealed knife

notes.note: “Wolf-friendship”: the friendship of wolves, which is a pretence and ends in an attack. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: than false friendship

notes.note: The subject has one article for three adjectives, the first verb is plural and the second singular. The plural is probably a slip in the text, unless three persons are meant; the English has one person and a singular throughout.
notes.other_reading: The good, the straightforward and the kind have these things in their eyes, and they do not go unnoticed

check.note: “Straightforwardness that is practised as a pursuit” is clumsy and unclear. The Greek noun here is a studied practice, something put on.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But a studied straightforwardness is a dagger”.

check.note: The Greek has a plural verb with a singular subject, followed by a singular verb, and the English gives a singular without remark. It is probably a slip in the text, or three persons are meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the singular is kept and the note says that the Greek has a plural verb here, probably a slip in the text.

check.note: The Greek can be “one should not” as well as “there is no need”. After “rotten and counterfeit” the stronger sense is at least as likely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This is not a thing to announce beforehand”, which leaves room for both “should not” and “need not”. The note gives the two senses.

passages.casaubon: How rotten and insincere is he, that saith, I am resolved to carry myself hereafter towards you with all ingenuity and simplicity. O man, what doest thou mean! what needs this profession of thine? the thing itself will show it. It ought to be written upon thy forehead. No sooner thy voice is heard, than thy countenance must be able to show what is in thy mind: even as he that is loved knows presently by the looks of his sweetheart what is in her mind. Such must he be for all the world, that is truly simple and good, as he whose arm-holes are offensive, that whosoever stands by, as soon as ever he comes near him, may as it were smell him whether he will or no. But the affectation of simplicity is nowise laudable. There is nothing more shameful than perfidious friendship. Above all things, that must be avoided. However true goodness, simplicity, and kindness cannot so be hidden, but that as we have already said in the very eyes and countenance they will show themselves.

nearest.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

passages.russian: Как гнил и фальшив тот, кто говорит: «Я решил быть с тобой прямым». Что ты делаешь, человек? Об этом не нужно объявлять заранее. Это обнаружится само. Это должно быть написано на лбу. Сразу же так и звучит голос, сразу же это проступает в глазах — так же, как любимый сразу всё узнаёт по взгляду влюблённых. Словом, прямой и хороший человек должен быть как тот, от кого разит козлом, — чтобы стоящий рядом, едва подойдя, замечал это, желая того или нет. А нарочитая прямота — это кинжал. Нет ничего позорнее волчьей дружбы: её избегай больше всего. У хорошего, прямого и доброго человека всё это в глазах, и он не остаётся незамеченным.

passages.greek: Οἱ ἄνθρωποι γεγόνασιν ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν· ἢ δίδασκε οὖν ἢ φέρε.
passages.english: Human beings have come into being for one another’s sake. So either teach them or bear with them.

notes.note: The same thought and nearly the same wording as in 11.18, and it is rendered the same way.
notes.other_reading: People exist for the sake of one another

notes.note: The two commands have no object in the Greek; the English adds “them” and “with them”. φέρω is to carry, to endure.
notes.other_reading: So either teach or endure

passages.casaubon: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.
passages.russian: Люди возникли ради друг друга. Так что или учи их, или терпи.

passages.greek: εἰς τὸ πᾶν ἀεὶ ὁρᾶν, τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ ἐκεῖνο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν σοι ποιοῦν, καὶ ἀναπτύσσειν διαιροῦντα εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον, ἐντὸς οὗ πεπαῦσθαι αὐτὸ δεήσει.
passages.english: Always see in full what that very thing is that produces the impression in you, and open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over.

notes.note: The words can be an adverb with “see” (“altogether, in full”, or “in every case”), or what is looked at, “look to the whole”, meaning the whole of the thing or the universe. The English takes “in full” because the question “what that thing is” follows at once as what is to be seen. The passage starts in mid-chapter, and the sentence before it, not translated here, breaks off at “for let your impulse be”, so these words may once have belonged to that sentence.
notes.other_reading: Always look to the whole: what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you

notes.note: The verbs here (“see”, “open out”) are infinitives, the notebook form for an instruction to oneself, and are written as commands. “See” is kept for this verb here and in 12.10; “look” is left for the different verb of 6.3.
notes.other_reading: Always to look in full at what that thing itself is … and to open it out

notes.note: Literally “the thing making the impression for you”; the dative “for you” can also be heard as “on you”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία: how a thing presents itself to the mind.
notes.other_reading: the thing that makes the impression on you

notes.note: An image: to unfold or unroll something folded up, as one opens a scroll or a folded cloth. It is kept as “open it out”.
notes.other_reading: and unfold it

notes.note: “The cause” here is the Stoic term for the active element that shapes a thing and makes it what it is, set against its material. It is not an earlier event that brought the thing about.
notes.other_reading: the causal element, the shaping principle

notes.greek: εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον
notes.note: The Greek says “into” four times and has no “and”: four separate heads, counted off one by one. The English keeps all four.
notes.other_reading: into the cause, the material, the purpose and the time

notes.note: Literally “the reference”, “the carrying back”: what the thing is referred to. The word has a range (relation, reference, the end something is directed to), and the English narrows it to “purpose”, as also in 12.10. The sister passage 8.11 asks at this point in the same list “What does it do in the universe?”, which supports the narrower sense.
notes.other_reading: into the reference, what it relates to

notes.note: The infinitive is a perfect: not “will have to stop” but “will have to have stopped”, to be over and done, which the English gives as “will have to be over”. “It” is neuter and so is the thing, not the impression (which is feminine in Greek).
notes.other_reading: the time within which it will have to have ceased

check.note: The English takes these words as an adverb with “see”, “in full”. They can as well mean “in every case” or “look to the whole”, and at a cut edge they may belong to the sentence before; the choice should not be silent.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English still reads “in full”, since “altogether” is a settled sense of the phrase and the question “what that thing is” follows at once as the thing to be seen. The note now sets out “in every case” and “look to the whole” as well, and says that the sentence before the cut breaks off at “for let your impulse be”, so the words may have belonged to it.

check.note: With an indirect question (“what it is”) the verb is an instruction to look and examine, and “see what it is” reads a little oddly as a command; “look at” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek verb is the plain word for seeing, the same one that opens 12.10, and Marcus has a different verb for “look” in 6.3, so “see” is kept for the one and “look” for the other. “See what it is” is ordinary English for an instruction to find out.

check.note: The Greek word means “reference”, that to which the thing is referred or related. “Purpose” is one way of taking it and is narrower than the Greek.
check.decided: Declined: “purpose” stays. The word means what a thing is carried back or referred to, and in this list that is the end it serves: the sister passage 8.11 has at the same place “What does it do in the universe?”. Bare “reference” would be heard today as a citation, and the note gives the wider sense.

check.note: “Will have to have ceased” is exact to the perfect infinitive but hard to read at first pass; “must come to its end” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the time within which it will have to be over”. “Be over” keeps the finished state that the Greek perfect expresses, which “come to its end” would turn into the act of stopping, and it reads at first pass.

check.greek: εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον
check.note: The Greek repeats “into” four times with no “and”, a deliberate count of four separate heads. The English runs them into one list and adds “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time”, with “into” four times and no “and”, as in the Greek. The Greek has “the”, not “its”, so “the” is kept.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “open it out by dividing it”, but the Greek has only the participle “dividing”, with no word for “by”, and the same participle is “dividing” in 12.10.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “open it out, dividing it into”, the same word in the same form as in 12.10.

part.left_out: Εἰ μὴ καθήκει, μὴ πράξῃς· εἰ μὴ ἀληθές ἐστι, μὴ εἴπῃς. ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔστω ιη′
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 12.13 with 'Ever maintain thine own purpose' and begins its 12.14 here, where modern editions begin chapter 12.18; this Greek text prints both as chapter 12.17.

passages.casaubon: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

passages.russian: Всегда рассматривай до конца, что такое сама та вещь, которая производит в тебе представление, и раскрывай её, разделяя на причину, на материю, на цель, на срок, в пределах которого ей придётся окончиться.

passages.greek: Τοιαῦτα τὰ πράγματα ὁρᾶν, διαιροῦντα εἰς ὕλην, αἴτιον, ἀναφοράν.
passages.english: See things as being of this kind, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.

notes.note: Literally “such”, “of this kind”, said of the things. Nothing in the sentence answers “such”: it may point back to the chapter before, which is not part of this passage, or forward to the division that follows, and the English leaves it as open as the Greek. Some editions may print a fuller text in which words meaning “as they are” answer “such” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: See things in this way, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction to oneself, written as a command.
notes.other_reading: To see things as being of this kind

notes.note: Three bare nouns with no “and”. “Matter” is the noun; the related adjective in 12.17b and 8.11 is given as “material”. “Cause” is the Stoic active element that shapes the matter, not an earlier event, and the third word is literally “reference”, what the thing is referred to, narrowed to “purpose” as in 12.17b.
notes.other_reading: into matter, cause, reference

check.note: The Greek as given says only “such”. “As they are” is not in these words, and adding it makes the claim that this division shows things as they really are.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “See things as being of this kind”, which says no more than “such”. It does not read “in this way” because the Greek word describes the things, not the manner of seeing, and may point back to the chapter before as easily as forward to the division.

check.note: From memory only: “such” with nothing answering it is abrupt, and the text may have lost a following “as they are”. If the English translates a restored text, that should be said openly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps to the words given and supplies nothing. The note says that “such” has nothing to answer it and that a fuller text with “as they are” may exist, marked as from memory, unchecked.

check.note: Here the Greek is the noun “matter”; in 12.17b and 8.11 it is the adjective “material”. Both were given as “material”, and “matter” is the plainer word for the noun.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “matter” for the noun here, and “material” is kept for the adjective in 12.17b and 8.11, so the two Greek forms can be told apart.

check.note: As in 12.17b, the word is “reference”, what the thing is referred to, and “purpose” narrows it.
check.decided: Declined: “purpose” stays, as in 12.17b, so that the word is the same in both passages. In this list what a thing is referred to is the end it serves, and bare “reference” would be heard today as a citation; the note gives the literal sense.

passages.casaubon: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

passages.russian: Смотри, каковы вещи, разделяя их на материю, причину, цель.

passages.greek: Τοῦτο τί ἐστιν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ, τί μὲν τὸ οὐσιῶδες αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες, τί δὲ ποιεῖ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, πόσον δὲ χρόνον ὑφίσταται;
passages.english: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up? What in it is substance and material, and what is cause? What does it do in the universe? And how long does it last?

notes.note: A set philosophical phrase, “itself by itself”: the thing taken alone, apart from everything around it. The English reads “in itself”.
notes.other_reading: what is it, itself by itself

notes.note: The noun means how a thing is built or put together: construction, constitution. The dative is loose (“in”, “by”, “in respect of”), and the English reads “in its own make-up”.
notes.other_reading: by its own constitution

notes.note: One article covers both adjectives, so this is one element with two names, not two elements; literally “the substance-like and material of it”. In Stoic use “substance” (οὐσία) is the underlying stuff, close to “material”. The English says “what in it is”, without a word such as “part”, which the Greek does not have.
notes.other_reading: What is its substance, that is, its material

notes.note: Literally “the cause-like”: the Stoic active element that shapes the material and makes the thing what it is. The plain word “cause” is kept.
notes.other_reading: the causal element, the shaping principle

notes.note: “The universe” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation. “The world” is also possible; the Greek does not decide between the ordered whole and the world people live in.
notes.other_reading: What does it do in the world?

notes.note: The verb means “subsists”, “has existence”; with “how long a time” the English reads “last”. The tense is present, so the question is how long such a thing stands in being, not how long it has left.
notes.other_reading: and for how long a time does it exist?

check.note: One article covers both adjectives, a single element named twice. “Part” is supplied here and again with “cause”, and suggests a separable piece.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What in it is substance and material, and what is cause?”, with no “part”. “Material” is kept rather than “matter” because the Greek here is the adjective, as in 12.17b, while “matter” is used for the noun in 12.10.

passages.casaubon: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.

nearest.title: The reason that governs the whole

passages.russian: Эта вещь — что она сама по себе, в собственном устройстве? Что в ней вещество и материя, а что — причина? Что она делает в мироздании? И как долго она длится?

passages.greek: Διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας φυσιολογεῖν, παθολογεῖν, διαλεκτικεύεσθαι.
passages.english: Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.

notes.note: Three bare verbs with no “and”, infinitives used as an instruction to oneself, written as three commands. The first two are built on the word for reasoning or giving an account, hence “reason about”. The three seem to answer to the three parts of Stoic philosophy (physics, ethics, logic), each brought to bear on the impression; that is an inference, not something the Greek says.
notes.other_reading: apply the study of nature, the study of the passions, and dialectic

notes.note: A rare verb: “to give an account of the πάθη”. The noun’s range runs from “what one undergoes” and “feelings” to the Stoic sense of the passions, the feelings that disturb; the English takes the Stoic sense.
notes.other_reading: reason about feelings, about what one undergoes

notes.note: “To practise dialectic”, the Stoic name for the art of reasoning correctly: testing a statement by question and argument, and seeing what follows from what. “Logic” would be a wider and more modern label.
notes.other_reading: test it by argument

notes.greek: ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας
notes.note: Literally “in the case of every impression, if it can be done”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία. “Every” is kept, with its own limit “if possible”.
notes.other_reading: in the case of every impression, if that can be done

check.note: The Greek has three verbs and no “apply”: three things to do with each impression. The English turns them into three school subjects brought to bear, and adds “apply” and an “and”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic”, three verbs with no “apply” and no “and”, as in the Greek. It does not say “as a student of”, because the Greek names three things to do and no persons.

check.note: The word can be about the passions or more widely about what is undergone, affections of any kind. The English takes the first; the advice is to keep “passions” but be aware of the wider sense.
check.decided: Accepted: “the passions” is kept, as the point advises, now inside the verb phrase “reason about the passions”. The note sets out the wider sense, feelings or whatever one undergoes.

check.note: The verb is “to practise dialectic”, the testing of a statement by question and argument. “Logic” is a wider and more modern label.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “practise dialectic”, which is the verb the Greek has. The note explains dialectic as the testing of a statement by question and argument.

passages.casaubon: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.

nearest.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

passages.russian: Постоянно и, если можно, при каждом представлении рассуждай о природе, рассуждай о страстях, упражняйся в диалектике.

passages.greek: Ἔσω βλέπε· μηδενὸς πράγματος μήτε ἡ ἰδία ποιότης μήτε ἡ ἀξία παρατρεχέτω σε.
passages.english: Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.

notes.note: Open: “look inside” can mean inside things or inside yourself, and the Greek does not say which. Because the next clause is about the quality and worth of things, the English is left as bare as the Greek, “look inside”, which leans towards inside things.
notes.other_reading: Look within yourself.

notes.note: In Stoic use a thing’s quality is what makes it the kind of thing it is, and “its own” marks what is peculiar to this thing. The adjective is the one given as “its own” in 8.11 (“its own make-up”).
notes.other_reading: its particular quality, what it is in particular

notes.note: “Worth” or “value”, a Stoic term for how much a thing counts for. The English reads “worth”.
notes.other_reading: its value

notes.note: An image: “let it not run past you”, as something that goes by before you notice; the image is kept. The Greek is negative throughout, “of no thing let neither … nor …”, which the English gives as “with any thing, do not let either … or …”.
notes.other_reading: Let neither the quality nor the worth of anything escape you.

check.note: The adjective means “its own, proper to it” and is given as “its own” in 8.11. “Particular” can be read as “some specific quality” and loses the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you”. “Of any thing” has moved to the front as “with any thing” so that “its own” has something to refer to.

passages.casaubon: Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

passages.russian: Смотри внутрь. Ни у какой вещи не давай проскочить мимо тебя ни её собственному качеству, ни её ценности.

passages.greek: Πρόσεχε τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ.
passages.english: Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.

notes.note: Literally “what lies under” or “what lies before one”: the thing itself that one is dealing with and that an impression is of. It can also be the matter in hand, the business being done, or in Stoic physics the underlying material. The English takes the first, and “you” is supplied, since the Greek says only “what lies before”.
notes.other_reading: to the matter in hand (or: to the underlying material)

notes.note: “Principle” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation: a settled view one holds and acts from. It could also be heard as the particular belief or judgment involved in the case.
notes.other_reading: or to the belief

notes.note: “Activity”: a thing’s being at work, or the act one is engaged in. “Action” is the narrower choice.
notes.other_reading: or to the action

notes.note: “What is signified”: a Stoic term from logic for the meaning that a word or statement carries, as against the sound of the words. The English reads “what is meant”.
notes.other_reading: or to the thing signified, the meaning

notes.greek: ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ
notes.note: The Greek joins the four with “or”, not “and”, and “or” is kept. This is part of a chapter and the Greek ends here; nothing was supplied.
notes.other_reading: to the thing before you and the principle and the activity and what is meant

check.note: The Greek is “what underlies”, most naturally the object itself, the thing in front of you. “The matter in hand” reads as the task being dealt with, and “matter” collides with “material” and “matter” in the neighbouring passages.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the thing before you”. The Greek word is literally what lies under or before one, which in a list with principle, activity and meaning is most naturally the thing itself, and “matter” is now left for the different word in 12.10.

check.note: The word is a judgment or opinion held, as well as a principle or doctrine. “Principle” picks the second; the judgment being made about the object fits the list at least as well.
check.decided: Declined: “principle” stays. It is the rendering settled for this Greek word across the translation, and “judgment” is kept there for a different Greek word, so using it here would make two Greek words sound like one. The note records “belief” as the other reading.

check.note: Could be “the action” being done just as well as “activity” in general; the English is acceptable.
check.decided: Declined: “activity” stays. The Greek word names something’s being at work, which is wider than a single deed, and the point itself finds the English acceptable. The note records “action”.

part.left_out: Δικαίως ταῦτα πάσχεις· μᾶλλον δὲ θέλεις ἀγαθὸς αὔριον γενέσθαι ἢ σήμερον εἶναι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.20 after the four things to attend to and begins its 8.21 with the rest of the chapter, 'Most justly have these things happened unto thee'.

passages.casaubon: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.

nearest.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

passages.russian: Обращай внимание на то, что перед тобой, или на принцип, или на действие, или на то, что имеется в виду.

passages.greek:
Ἐξάλειψον τὴν φαντασίαν. στῆσον τὴν νευροσπαστίαν. περίγραψον τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου. γνώρισον τὸ συμβαῖνον ἢ σοὶ ἢ ἄλλῳ. δίελε καὶ μέρισον τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν. ἐννόησον τὴν ἐσχάτην ὥραν. τὸ ἐκείνῳ ἁμαρτηθὲν ἐκεῖ κατάλιπε ὅπου ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπέστη.

Συμπαρεκτείνειν τὴν νόησιν τοῖς λεγομένοις. εἰσδύεσθαι τὸν νοῦν εἰς τὰ γινόμενα καὶ ποιοῦντα.

Φαίδρυνον σεαυτὸν ἁπλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ καὶ τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας ἀδιαφορίᾳ. φίλησον τὸ ἀνθρώπινον γένος. ἀκολούθησον θεῷ.
passages.english:
Wipe out the impression. Stop the pulling of the puppet strings. Draw a line around the present time. Recognise what is happening, whether to you or to another. Take the thing before you apart and divide it into what is cause and what is material. Think of the last hour. The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.

To stretch thinking out alongside what is being said. To have the mind get inside the things that come about and the things that act.

Brighten yourself with simplicity and modesty and with indifference towards what lies between virtue and vice. Love the human race. Follow god.

notes.note: The word means the working of a puppet by its cords. The image is kept; what pulls the strings (impulses, passions) is not said here.
notes.other_reading: Stop being jerked about like a puppet.

notes.note: περιγράφω is to draw a line around, and so to mark off or to limit. The drawing of the line is kept; “the present of time” is given as “the present time”.
notes.other_reading: Limit yourself to the present moment.

notes.note: The verb covers both coming to know a thing and recognising it for what it is. The command is for a single act, so the English reads “recognise”.
notes.other_reading: Get to know what is happening

notes.greek: τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν
notes.note: τὸ ὑποκείμενον is literally “what lies under”, the object in front of one. The causal and the material are the two Stoic principles, the active cause and the matter it works on; one article covers both.
notes.other_reading: divide the underlying object into the causal and the material

notes.note: The dative is taken as the doer (“the wrong done by that one”), and the English reads “that person” since the form need not single out a man. The dative could just possibly be the one wronged.
notes.other_reading: The wrong done to that person

notes.note: Literally “took its stand” or “came into existence”. The point is that the wrong exists in the one who did it.
notes.other_reading: where the wrong has its footing

notes.note: The two sentences of this chapter are infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; they are kept impersonal. νόησις is given as “thinking” to keep it apart from νοῦς, “mind”, in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: Keep your thinking in step with what is being said.

notes.note: The verb is to get into a thing, to slip or sink inside it. The English keeps the “in” and adds no “down”.
notes.other_reading: To have the mind sink into

notes.note: Literally “the things coming about and making”, under one article, and the second has no object. ποιεῖν is the Stoic verb for what acts as a cause; the English reads “the things that act” and supplies no object, so the Greek is not tied to the causes of just those events.
notes.other_reading: into the things that come about and the things that make them

notes.note: The verb is to make bright, and so also to wash clean or to cheer. The brightness is kept.
notes.other_reading: Cleanse yourself with simplicity

notes.note: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy. “Modesty” narrows it.
notes.other_reading: a sense of shame; self-respect

notes.note: No article: “god” or “a god”. Lower case as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: Follow a god.

check.note: The verb here is to recognise what is happening for what it is, in a single act, not a gradual getting acquainted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Recognise what is happening”. The Greek command is in the form used for one act, and “get to know” describes a slow process.

check.note: One article covers both participles and the second has no object. “Them” is supplied and fixes the makers as the causes of exactly those events.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “them” is removed, but “the things that bring about” is not English without an object. The English now reads “the things that come about and the things that act”, which leaves the second word as open as the Greek, and the note gives the reading with “them”.

check.note: The verb is to get inside, to slip or sink into. The “down” is not in the word, the “in” is.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To have the mind get inside”. The Greek prefix means “into”, and nothing in the word says “down”.

part.left_out: ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν ὅτι ʽπάντα νομιστί, ἐτεῇ δὲ μόνα τὰ στοιχεῖαʼ, ἀρκεῖ δὲ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι τὰ πάντα νομιστὶ ἔχει· ἤδη λίαν ὀλίγα.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 7.21 at 'love mankind; obey God' and begins its 7.22 with the rest of chapter 7.31, 'All things (saith he) are by certain order'.

passages.casaubon: Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the last hour. That which thy neighbour hath committed, where the guilt of it lieth, there let it rest. Examine in order whatsoever is spoken. Let thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes. Rejoice thyself with true simplicity, and modesty; and that all middle things between virtue and vice are indifferent unto thee. Finally, love mankind; obey God.
passages.russian:
Сотри представление. Останови дёрганье за нитки марионетки. Очерти границу вокруг настоящего времени. Распознай, что происходит — с тобой или с другим. Разбери то, что перед тобой, и раздели на причинное и материальное. Подумай о последнем часе. Дурной поступок, который совершил тот человек, оставь там, где этот дурной поступок возник.

Протягивать мысль вдоль того, что говорится. Давать уму проникать внутрь того, что совершается, и того, что действует.

Озаряй себя простотой, скромностью и безразличием к тому, что лежит между добродетелью и пороком. Люби род человеческий. Следуй богу.

passages.greek: Τέσσαρας μάλιστα τροπὰς τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ παραφυλακτέον διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπειδὰν φωράσῃς ἀπαλειπτέον, ἐπιλέγοντα ἐφ’ ἑκάστου οὕτως· τοῦτο τὸ φάντασμα οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον· τοῦτο λυτικὸν κοινωνίας· τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λέγειν ἐν τοῖς ἀτοπωτάτοις νόμιζε. τέταρτον δέ ἐστι, καθὸ σεαυτῷ ὀνειδιεῖς, ὅτι τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ καὶ ὑποκατακλινομένου τοῦ ἐν σοὶ θειοτέρου μέρους τῇ ἀτιμοτέρᾳ καὶ θνητῇ μοίρᾳ, τῇ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ταῖς τούτου τραχείαις ἢ λείαις κινήσεσιν.
passages.english: Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This thing you are about to say is not from yourself.” For count it among the most absurd things not to speak from yourself. The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.

notes.note: Literally “turnings”: turns the ruling part (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν) takes away from its course. The English keeps “turns” and adds no “aside”, which the Greek leaves unsaid.
notes.other_reading: four lapses of the ruling part

notes.note: “Must be wiped off”, the same image of wiping a writing surface clean as ἐξαλείφω elsewhere. The form does not say by whom; the “you” comes only from the verb before it.
notes.other_reading: must be rubbed out

notes.note: Not φαντασία (“impression”) but φάντασμα, which in Stoic usage is a picture in the mind with nothing real behind it. “Imagining” keeps the two apart.
notes.other_reading: This impression is not necessary.

notes.note: Literally “apt to loosen fellowship”. κοινωνία is the noun behind κοινωνικός (“social”); the English reads “community”.
notes.other_reading: This one loosens the bond between people.

notes.greek: τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν
notes.note: Literally “this you are about to say not from yourself”. “Not from yourself” is taken as the point of the sentence, as the clause that follows shows: the words are not your own real thought.
notes.other_reading: You are not going to say this from yourself.

notes.note: ἄτοπος is literally “out of place”, and so strange or absurd. The English gives the sense, since nothing in the sentence turns on the literal one.
notes.other_reading: among the most out-of-place things

notes.note: The first three turns are each met by a sentence to say; the fourth is put differently, as the ground of a reproach you will make to yourself, and its content follows with ὅτι. The change of construction is kept.
notes.other_reading: The fourth is when you will reproach yourself that this is a case of

notes.note: Literally “this is of the more divine part being beaten”: the Greek genitive says whose sign or whose doing a thing is. The English reads “is the mark of”.
notes.other_reading: that this is the more divine part in you being beaten

notes.note: The verb is to lie down in the lower place, as on a dinner couch, and so to give way to someone. The image is kept as “lying down under”.
notes.other_reading: giving way to

notes.note: Literally “of less honour” or “of less value”, a comparative answering “more divine”.
notes.other_reading: the less honourable and mortal portion

notes.note: “Rough or smooth movements” is school language for pain and pleasure felt in the body; both this and “the portion of the body” are taken to depend on “lying down under”, so “under” is repeated. From memory, unchecked: the wording at this point has been doubted and some editions print something else (“gross pleasures”).
notes.other_reading: and its pains or pleasures

check.note: “Turnings of the ruling part” is not clear English. The Greek means turns away from the right course, lapses or deviations.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Four turns that the ruling part takes”, which is plain English and keeps the Greek image. “Aside” is not added, because the Greek word says only “turn”, and the note gives “lapses”.

check.note: The verb is to be on guard against. “Watched for” can be read as looked forward to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “guarded against”. The Greek verb is the one for keeping guard, and it cannot mean waiting in hope.

check.note: The word here means absurd or strange. “Out-of-place” gives the make-up of the word, not its sense, and reads oddly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “among the most absurd things”. Nothing in the sentence turns on the literal “out of place”, which is recorded in the note.

check.greek: τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ καὶ ὑποκατακλινομένου τοῦ ἐν σοὶ θειοτέρου μέρους
check.note: The genitive says what a thing is the sign of. “Belongs to … being beaten” does not construe as English, and the second verb is to give way, to take the lower place.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under”. “The mark of” gives the genitive in plain English; “lying down under” is kept because the Greek verb is a picture of lying in the lower place, and the note gives “giving way to”.

check.note: Found while settling: “the one by which you will reproach yourself” makes the fourth turn the tool of the reproach, where the Greek makes it the ground of it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the one for which you will reproach yourself”. The Greek word means “in respect of which”.

passages.casaubon: Four several dispositions or inclinations there be of the mind and understanding, which to be aware of, thou must carefully observe: and whensoever thou doest discover them, thou must rectify them, saying to thyself concerning every one of them, This imagination is not necessary; this is uncharitable: this thou shalt speak as another man's slave, or instrument; than which nothing can be more senseless and absurd: for the fourth, thou shalt sharply check and upbraid thyself; for that thou doest suffer that more divine part in thee, to become subject and obnoxious to that more ignoble part of thy body, and the gross lusts and concupiscences thereof.
passages.russian: Против четырёх поворотов ведущего начала нужно прежде всего быть настороже непрестанно и, всякий раз поймав их, стирать, говоря над каждым так: «Это воображаемое не нужно». «Это разлагает общность». «То, что ты собираешься сказать, — не от тебя самого». А говорить не от себя считай одной из самых нелепых вещей. Четвёртый — тот, за который ты будешь упрекать себя: это знак того, что более божественная часть в тебе побеждена и лежит, покорившись менее ценной и смертной доле — телесной — и её грубым или гладким движениям.

passages.greek: Ἐξάλειφε τὰς φαντασίας συνεχῶς σεαυτῷ λέγων· νῦν ἐπ’ ἐμοί ἐστιν ἵνα ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ψυχῇ μηδεμία πονηρία ᾖ μηδὲ ἐπιθυμία μηδὲ ὅλως ταραχή τις, ἀλλὰ βλέπων πάντα ὁποῖά ἐστι χρῶμαι ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν. μέμνησο ταύτης τῆς ἐξουσίας κατὰ φύσιν.
passages.english: Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually: “Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all, but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth.” Remember this power in accordance with nature.

notes.note: “Continually” can go with “wipe out” or with “saying”. It is put with “saying”, which it stands next to; “keep wiping out” gives the form of the command, which is the one for an action that goes on.
notes.other_reading: Keep wiping out impressions continually, saying to yourself

notes.note: ἐπ’ ἐμοί is the Stoic phrase for what is in a person’s own power; the ἵνα clause gives what is in that power, a later Greek use.
notes.other_reading: Now it lies in my power that

notes.note: ἐπιθυμία is appetite or craving, one of the passions. “Desire” is kept for ὄρεξις, which is used in other passages of this section.
notes.other_reading: no desire

notes.note: ὁποῖα is “of what kind”: seeing the sort of thing each is comes before using each according to its worth.
notes.other_reading: seeing all things as they are

notes.note: The form is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive. It is taken as subjunctive, still hanging on the words before “that”, because the “but” answers the three things the soul is to be without; as indicative it would be a new statement of what is already done.
notes.other_reading: instead, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth

notes.note: ἀξία is the worth or value a thing has. The phrase is “according to its worth”, not “as it deserves” in a moral sense.
notes.other_reading: I deal with each as it deserves

notes.note: “In accordance with nature” stands at the end with no article. It can describe the power (one you have by nature) or the remembering or using of it; the English leaves it as loose as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: Remember this power, as nature would have you.

check.note: The word stands between the command and “saying” and can go with either. The English puts it with “saying”, while the form of the command already means “keep wiping”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually”. “Keep” gives the form of the command, and “continually” stays with “saying”, the word it stands next to; the note gives the other reading. “Your” is not added, since the Greek has only “the impressions”.

check.note: The Greek is “of what kind”: seeing what sort of thing each is, which is what makes it possible to value each by its worth. “As they are” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “seeing what kind of thing everything is”. “Everything” keeps the Greek “all”, which the suggested wording left out.

check.note: The form may continue “it is up to me that”, something still to be done, where the English states it as a fact.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is”, with the using still depending on what is up to the speaker. The Greek “but” answers the “no … no … no” of the clause before, so it most naturally carries that clause on; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: The phrase stands at the end with no article and may go with “power” or with the verb. The relative clause “which is” is not in the Greek and fixes one reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Remember this power in accordance with nature.” The added “which is” is gone, and the phrase hangs as loosely in the English as in the Greek; the note sets out the two ways of taking it.

passages.casaubon: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
passages.russian: Стирай представления, постоянно говоря себе: «Сейчас от меня зависит, чтобы в этой душе не было ни порочности, ни вожделения, ни вообще никакого смятения, но чтобы я, видя, какова каждая вещь, пользовался каждой по её достоинству». Помни об этой власти, согласной с природой.

passages.greek: Πειρῶ μὲν πείθειν αὐτούς, πρᾶττε δὲ καὶ ἀκόντων, ὅταν τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁ λόγος οὕτως ἄγῃ. ἐὰν μέντοι βίᾳ τις προσχρώμενος ἐνίστηται, μετάβαινε ἐπὶ τὸ εὐάρεστον καὶ ἄλυπον καὶ συγχρῶ εἰς ἄλλην ἀρετὴν τῇ κωλύσει, καὶ μέμνησο ὅτι μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως ὥρμας καὶ ὅτι τῶν ἀδυνάτων οὐκ ὠρέγου. τίνος οὖν; τῆς τοιᾶσδέ τινος ὁρμῆς. τούτου δὲ τυγχάνεις· ἐφ’ οἷς προήχθημεν, ταῦτα γίνεται.
passages.english: Try to persuade them, but act even against their will whenever the reasoning of justice leads that way. If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue; and remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible. What were you desiring, then? An impulse of some such kind. And this you attain: the things we were led forward for, these come about.

notes.note: “Them” is not explained; the Greek does not say who they are.
notes.other_reading: Try to persuade people

notes.note: Literally “the reason of justice”: what justice, reasoned out, requires. “Reasoning” keeps λόγος close to “reason”, as in the glossary, and leaves “principle” for δόγμα.
