part.left_out: Ἀτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τοῦτό μοι συνέβη. οὐμενοῦν ἀλλʼ εὐτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τούτου μοι συμβεβηκότος ἄλυπος διατελῶ, οὔτε ὑπὸ παρόντος θραυόμενος οὔτε ἐπιὸν φοβούμενος. συμβῆναι μὲν γὰρ τὸ τοιοῦτο παντὶ ἐδύνατο, ἄλυπος δὲ οὐ πᾶς ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἂν διετέλεσε. διὰ τί οὖν ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ἀτύχημα ἢ τοῦτο εὐτύχημα; λέγεις δὲ ὅλως ἀτύχημα ἀνθρώπου, ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπότευγμα τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; ἀπότευγμα δὲ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἶναι δοκεῖ σοι, ὃ μὴ παρὰ τὸ βούλημα τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ ἐστι; τί οὖν; τὸ βούλημα μεμάθηκας· μήτι οὖν τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῦτο κωλύει σε δίκαιον εἶναι, μεγαλόψυχον, σώφρονα, ἔμφρονα, ἀπρόπτωτον, ἀδιάψευστον, αἰδήμονα, ἐλεύθερον, τἄλλα, ὧν συμπαρόντων ἡ φύσις ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀπέχει τὰ ἴδια; μέμνησο λοιπὸν ἐπὶ παντὸς τοῦ εἰς λύπην σε προαγομένου τούτῳ χρῆσθαι τῷ δόγματι· οὐχ ὅτι τοῦτο ἀτύχημα, ἀλλὰ τὸ φέρειν αὐτὸ γενναίως εὐτύχημα.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 4.40 with the image of the promontory and begins its 4.41 with the rest of the chapter, 'Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened'.

passages.casaubon: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
passages.russian: Быть подобным мысу, о который непрестанно разбиваются волны; а он стоит, и вокруг него вздыбившаяся вода убаюкивается.

passages.greek: Τὸν ὑγιαίνοντα ὀφθαλμὸν πάντα ὁρᾶν δεῖ τὰ ὁρατὰ καὶ μὴ λέγειν· τὰ χλωρὰ θέλω· τοῦτο γὰρ ὀφθαλμιῶντός ἐστι. καὶ τὴν ὑγιαίνουσαν ἀκοὴν καὶ ὄσφρησιν εἰς πάντα δεῖ τὰ ἀκουστὰ καὶ ὀσφραντὰ ἑτοίμην εἶναι, καὶ τὸν ὑγιαίνοντα στόμαχον πρὸς πάντα τὰ τρόφιμα ὁμοίως ἔχειν ὡς μύλην πρὸς πάντα ὅσα ἀλέσουσα κατεσκεύασται. καὶ τοίνυν τὴν ὑγιαίνουσαν διάνοιαν πρὸς πάντα δεῖ τὰ συμβαίνοντα ἑτοίμην εἶναι, ἡ δὲ λέγουσα· τὰ τεκνία σῳζέσθω, καί· πάντες ὅ τι ἂν πράξω ἐπαινείτωσαν, ὀφθαλμός ἐστι τὰ χλωρὰ ζητῶν ἢ ὀδόντες τὰ ἁπαλά.
passages.english: The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased. And healthy hearing and healthy smell must be ready for everything that can be heard and smelled, and the healthy stomach must be the same towards all foods, as a mill is towards everything it was built to grind. So too the healthy mind must be ready for everything that happens. But the mind that says, “Let the little ones be kept safe,” and “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things, or teeth that look for the soft things.

notes.note: The colour word runs from pale green to yellowish; here it is green as the colour that is easy on sore eyes.
notes.other_reading: pale things

notes.note: A participle: “of one who is suffering from ophthalmia”, a soreness of the eyes. The English gives it plainly.
notes.other_reading: that is what a person with sore eyes does

notes.note: The word can mean the gullet or the stomach. With food and a mill, “stomach”.
notes.other_reading: gullet

notes.note: “To be disposed alike” towards all foods, as a mill or millstone is. “Alike” can go with “all foods” (the same towards each) or with the comparison (in the same way as a mill); the English is worded so that both are heard.
notes.other_reading: must take all foods just as a millstone takes all that it was made to grind

notes.note: The faculty, set beside eye, hearing and stomach, so “mind” and not the glossary’s first choice “thought”.
notes.other_reading: thought

notes.note: A diminutive, “little children”, and a verb that is both “be kept safe” and “survive”. The Greek has “the”, not a possessive, and the English follows it.
notes.other_reading: “Let my little ones live”

notes.note: Literally “but the one that says”, feminine, picking up “mind”. The English repeats the noun.
notes.other_reading: But the one that says

check.note: The noun is a diminutive, “little ones”. The diminutive is rendered in 5.5 (“your poor body”) but dropped here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let the little ones be kept safe”. “Little ones” gives the diminutive, and “the” replaces the supplied possessive, since the Greek has only the article.

check.note: “Alike” can go with “all foods” or with the comparison, in the same way as a mill. The English takes the first; the difference is slight.
check.decided: Declined: “must be the same toward all foods, as a mill is” stands. The Greek adverb stands between “all foods” and “as a mill” and can be heard with either, and the English wording lets both be heard; the note records the choice.

passages.casaubon: A good eye must be good to see whatsoever is to be seen, and not green things only. For that is proper to sore eyes. So must a good ear, and a good smell be ready for whatsoever is either to be heard, or smelt: and a good stomach as indifferent to all kinds of food, as a millstone is, to whatsoever she was made for to grind. As ready therefore must a sound understanding be for whatsoever shall happen. But he that saith, O that my children might live! and, O that all men might commend me for whatsoever I do! is an eye that seeks after green things; or as teeth, after that which is tender.

nearest.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

passages.russian: Здоровый глаз должен видеть всё видимое, а не говорить: «Хочу зелёного»; ведь это свойственно тому, у кого больные глаза. И здоровый слух и здоровое обоняние должны быть готовы ко всему слышимому и обоняемому, и здоровый желудок должен одинаково относиться ко всякой пище, как мельница — ко всему, что она устроена молоть. Так и здоровый ум должен быть готов ко всему, что случается. А ум, который говорит: «Пусть малыши уцелеют» и «Пусть все хвалят всё, что я ни сделаю», — это глаз, который ищет зелёного, или зубы, которые ищут мягкого.

passages.greek: Μηκέθ’ ὅλως περὶ τοῦ οἷόν τινα εἶναι τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα διαλέγεσθαι, ἀλλὰ εἶναι τοιοῦτον.
passages.english: No longer to discuss at all what the good man is like, but to be one.

notes.note: To converse, discuss or argue a question, the word for philosophical talk. It is an infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person, and the English keeps it so.
notes.other_reading: Stop arguing altogether about what the good man is like, and be one

notes.note: The Greek has the word for a man, not the general word for a person, so the English keeps “man”.
notes.other_reading: the good person

notes.note: “No longer” and “at all” together: the discussing is to stop entirely.
notes.other_reading: Not any more, in any way

passages.casaubon: Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be such.

nearest.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

passages.russian: Больше вообще не рассуждать о том, каков хороший человек, а быть таким.

passages.greek: Εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἑκάστου, παρέχειν δὲ καὶ ἑτέρῳ παντὶ εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἡγεμονικόν.
passages.english: To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.

notes.note: An infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person. The reflexive later is third person, so the English stays impersonal with “one’s own”.
notes.other_reading: Enter into each person’s ruling part, and let every other person enter into yours

notes.note: To offer or to allow: either holding oneself open or simply not preventing.
notes.other_reading: to offer every other person entry

notes.note: “Of each”, with no noun: each person one deals with.
notes.other_reading: of everyone

check.note: The “also” or “in turn” of the Greek is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and also to allow every other person”, which gives the “also” of the Greek.

passages.casaubon: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
passages.russian: Входить в ведущее начало каждого человека и позволять также каждому другому входить в своё ведущее начало.

passages.greek: Εἴ τίς με ἐλέγξαι καὶ παραστῆσαί μοι, ὅτι οὐκ ὀρθῶς ὑπολαμβάνω ἢ πράσσω, δύναται, χαίρων μεταθήσομαι· ζητῶ γὰρ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὑφ’ ἧς οὐδεὶς πώποτε ἐβλάβη, βλάπτεται δὲ ὁ ἐπιμένων ἐπὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀπάτης καὶ ἀγνοίας.
passages.english: If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change. For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.

notes.note: To test by questioning and so to prove wrong. “Refute” is the nearest single word.
notes.other_reading: can prove me wrong

notes.note: Literally “to set beside me”, to bring a thing home to someone so that they see it.
notes.other_reading: and show me

notes.note: The verb of the noun the glossary gives as “judgment”: to take a thing to be so. Hence “judging”; the verb for judging in 5.3 and 8.38 is a different one.
notes.other_reading: that what I suppose or do is not right

notes.note: Literally “I will shift, rejoicing”. The verb is the one given as “change one’s mind” in 4.12 and 8.16; here it answers both judging and acting, so the English has the bare “change”.
notes.other_reading: I will gladly change my mind

notes.greek: ἐπὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀπάτης καὶ ἀγνοίας
notes.note: The first noun is deception, here the state of being deceived, whoever did the deceiving. “Delusion” says that; “their own deception” could be heard as their deceiving of others.
notes.other_reading: in their own self-deception and ignorance

check.note: “Judge” and “judgment” stand for another Greek verb and noun elsewhere in this section (5.3, 8.16, 8.38). This verb is “suppose, take a view”.
check.decided: Declined: “judging” stands. The glossary gives “judgment” for the noun of this verb, the other verb for judging does not occur in this passage, and the note at 8.16 marks where “judgment” there stands for a different word.

check.note: The verb is “change” without an object, and it answers both thinking and acting. “My mind” narrows it to the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “I will gladly change”. In this passage the verb answers both “judging” and “acting”, so the bare verb is right here, while 4.12 and 8.16, which speak of a view corrected, keep “change one’s mind”.

check.note: “Their own deception” can be read as their deceiving of others. The Greek is one’s own being deceived.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “their own delusion”. That is the state of being deceived, which is what the Greek says, without the further claim of “self-deception” that the person is the one doing the deceiving.

check.note: The verb with its preposition is “persist in”, stronger than “stay in”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the one who persists in”, the stronger verb of the Greek.

passages.casaubon: If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me, that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.

nearest.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

passages.russian: Если кто-нибудь может опровергнуть меня и ясно показать, что я неправильно сужу или поступаю, я с радостью изменюсь. Ведь я ищу истину, от которой никто никогда не потерпел вреда; вред терпит тот, кто упорствует в своём заблуждении и невежестве.

passages.greek: Οὐχ ὁρᾷς πῶς οἱ βάναυσοι τεχνῖται ἁρμόζονται μὲν μέχρι τινὸς πρὸς τοὺς ἰδιώτας, οὐδὲν ἧσσον μέντοι ἀντέχονται τοῦ λόγου τῆς τέχνης καὶ τούτου ἀποστῆναι οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν; οὐ δεινὸν εἰ ὁ ἀρχιτέκτων καὶ ὁ ἰατρὸς μᾶλλον αἰδέσονται τὸν τῆς ἰδίας τέχνης λόγον ἢ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς;
passages.english: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it? Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?

notes.note: βάναυσος is the word for people in the manual, workshop trades and usually carries some contempt. The English names the trades and leaves the slight unsaid. “Craftsmen” is kept for τεχνῖται because it is from the same root as τέχνη, “craft”, which comes twice more in the passage.
notes.other_reading: the common craftsmen; mere tradesmen

notes.greek: ἁρμόζονται μὲν μέχρι τινὸς πρὸς τοὺς ἰδιώτας
notes.note: ἁρμόζονται πρός is literally “fit themselves to”. The ἰδιῶται are those outside the craft, here most naturally the customers who have no training in it.
notes.other_reading: fit in with the untrained up to a point; go along with their customers so far

notes.note: The λόγος of a craft is its rationale, the rule or account by which the work is done. The English has “reason” because the second sentence sets this λόγος beside the human being’s own λόγος, and the argument needs one English word for both.
notes.other_reading: hold on to the principle (or rule) of their craft

notes.note: Literally “do not submit to standing away from it”. The English states a refusal, since the Greek has no word for being unable.
notes.other_reading: and cannot bear to leave it; and will not bring themselves to depart from it

notes.note: δεινόν runs from “terrible” to “strange” or “outrageous”. With εἰ it is a usual way of protesting at something absurd, so the English has “shocking”.
notes.other_reading: Is it not a terrible thing if; Is it not strange if

notes.note: The ἀρχιτέκτων is the chief builder who directs the work, not only a designer. With the doctor this may be a step up from the trades of the first sentence, or two more examples of a craft.
notes.other_reading: the architect

notes.note: A future, “will respect”, turned as “are to have more respect”. The verb αἰδεῖσθαι means to respect or revere, with a sense of feeling shame before something.
notes.other_reading: will revere the reason of their own craft more

notes.greek: τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς
notes.note: Literally “his own, which is common to him with the gods”: “reason” is supplied from earlier in the sentence. ὁ ἄνθρωπος is the human being in general, so the English does not write “he”. It has “their own reason” and then repeats “a human being”, so that the last clause cannot be taken to mean the builder and the doctor.
notes.other_reading: than man has for his own, which he has in common with the gods

check.note: οὐδὲν ἧσσον is the set phrase “none the less”, answering μέν with μέντοι, and does not measure how firmly they hold. “No less firmly” makes a comparison with nothing to compare and adds “firmly”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft”. οὐδὲν ἧσσον μέντοι is the ordinary Greek for “none the less”, and the Greek has no word for “firmly”.

check.note: οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν states a refusal as a fact, and “cannot bear” adds inability and feeling. ἀποστῆναι, to stand away from, is also stronger than “leave”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and will not agree to abandon it”. The Greek verb says that they do not submit to doing it, with no word for being unable, and ἀποστῆναι is to stand away from or desert, which “abandon” gives.

check.note: βάναυσοι marks the manual, workshop trades, not “common” in the sense of ordinary. The Greek article is generic, so “the” wrongly suggests a particular group.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “craftsmen in the manual trades”, without “the”. “Craftsmen” is kept instead of the suggested “men” because τεχνῖται is from the same root as τέχνη, “craft”, which comes twice more in the passage, and because the Greek does not single out men.

check.note: “The reason of their craft” is not clear English of today. “Reasoning” is offered for both places, or keeping “reason” and accepting the oddness, since the same word must carry through to the human being’s own λόγος.
check.decided: Declined: “the reason of their craft” stands. The Greek uses one word, λόγος, for what the craft has and for what a human being shares with the gods, and the second is the faculty of reason, which “reasoning” would weaken. The choice is recorded in a note.

check.note: δεινόν can be “terrible” or “strange, shocking”. Since the point is an absurdity, “shocking” is at least as likely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Is it not shocking if”. δεινὸν εἰ is a usual Greek way of protesting that something is absurd or outrageous, and the note keeps “terrible” as the other reading.

check.greek: ἢ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς
check.note: After the plural “the master builder and the doctor”, the singular “their” and “they” can be read as pointing to the builder and the doctor, where both Greek pronouns refer only to the human being. “His” and “he” are suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods”, so that the last clause can only be about the human being. “His” and “he” are not used because ὁ ἄνθρωπος is the human being in general and does not single out a man.

passages.casaubon: Dost thou not see, how even those that profess mechanic arts, though in some respect they be no better than mere idiots, yet they stick close to the course of their trade, neither can they find in their heart to decline from it: and is it not a grievous thing that an architect, or a physician shall respect the course and mysteries of their profession, more than a man the proper course and condition of his own nature, reason, which is common to him and to the Gods?
passages.russian: Разве ты не видишь, как мастера ручных ремёсел до известной степени приспосабливаются к непосвящённым, но всё же держатся разума своего ремесла и не соглашаются от него отступить? Разве не возмутительно, если архитектор и врач будут больше уважать разум своего ремесла, чем человек — свой собственный разум, который у него общий с богами?

passages.greek: πάσης αἱρέσεως κοινόν. πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι καὶ τῷ ὀργάνῳ, δι’ οὗ πράσσεις.
passages.english: … is common to every school. To be occupied only with what is being done now, and with the instrument through which you act.

notes.note: The passage begins in the middle of a sentence. These words are its predicate, “common to every school”, and the subject stands before the cut: not leaving philosophy whatever happens, and not joining in the chatter of the untrained. The English adds “is” and a mark of omission, so that the words are not read as a heading for the sentence that follows.
notes.other_reading: Common to every school.

notes.note: αἵρεσις is literally a “choice”, and then a school of philosophy that one chooses to follow. The English takes it in that second sense.
notes.other_reading: common to every sect; common to every choice of a way of life

notes.greek: πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι
notes.note: The verb is an infinitive with no finite verb, and the English keeps it so. It can be read as an instruction, as the infinitive often is in this notebook, or as one more thing that every school holds. πρὸς with the dative and εἶναι means to be at something, busy with it.
notes.other_reading: Be intent only on what is being done now

notes.note: ὄργανον is a tool, an instrument, or an organ of the body. The Greek does not say which instrument is meant: it could be the body, the mind, or whatever means the action uses. The English keeps the open word.
notes.other_reading: and with the tool through which you act

notes.note: The verb has no object: “through which you act”, not “with which you do it”. It is the only second person in the passage.
notes.other_reading: the instrument you are doing it with

check.note: These words are the predicate that closes a sentence whose subject lies before the cut. As a capitalised sentence at the head of the passage they read as a heading for the rule that follows, which the Greek full stop keeps apart.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “… is common to every school.”, in lower case after a mark of omission. The Greek words are the end of a sentence begun before the cut, and a note says that “is” and the mark are added.

check.greek: πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι
check.note: The Greek is an infinitive with no finite verb, which can be a command, a bare statement of the rule, or a continuation of what the schools share, and the English makes it a command. “Intent” is also slightly more than πρὸς with εἶναι, “to be at, to be occupied with”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To be occupied only with what is being done now”. Keeping the infinitive leaves both readings open as the Greek does, and “occupied with” is the plain sense of πρὸς with εἶναι. The command is recorded in a note as the other reading.

check.note: πράσσεις has no object, “through which you act”. The English supplies “it” and so ties the instrument to this one act.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the instrument through which you act”. The Greek verb stands alone, with no “it”.

part.left_out: Ὁ Ἐπίκουρος λέγει ὅτι· ʽἐν τῇ νόσῳ οὐκ ἦσάν μοι αἱ ὁμιλίαι περὶ τῶν τοῦ σωματίου παθῶν οὐδὲ πρὸς τοὺς εἰσιόντας τοιαῦτά τινα, φησίν, ἐλάλουν, ἀλλὰ τὰ προηγούμενα φυσιολογῶν διετέλουν καὶ πρὸς αὐτῷ τούτῳ ὤν, πῶς ἡ διάνοια συμμεταλαμβάνουσα τῶν ἐν τῷ σαρκιδίῳ τοιούτων κινήσεων ἀταρακτεῖ τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν τηροῦσα. οὐδὲ τοῖς ἰατροῖς ἐμπαρεῖχον, φησί, καταφρυάττεσθαι ὥς τι ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς.ʼ ταὐτὰ οὖν ἐκείνῳ, ἐν νόσῳ, ἐὰν νοσῇς καὶ ἐν ἄλλῃ τινὶ περιστάσει· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφίστασθαι φιλοσοφίας ἐν οἷς δήποτε τοῖς προσπίπτουσι μηδὲ ἰδιώτῃ καὶ ἀφυσιολόγῳ συμφλυαρεῖν,
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.41 with the words about not chattering with the ignorant and begins its 9.42 here, with 'It is common to all trades and professions'; its 9.41 holds the first part of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
passages.russian: … — общее для всякой школы. Заниматься только тем, что делается сейчас, и орудием, которым ты действуешь.

passages.greek: Εἰ κυβερνῶντα οἱ ναῦται ἢ ἰατρεύοντα οἱ κάμνοντες κακῶς ἔλεγον, ἄλλῳ τινὶ ἂν προσεῖχον ἢ πῶς αὐτὸς ἐνεργοίην τὸ τοῖς ἐμπλέουσι σωτήριον ἢ τὸ τοῖς θεραπευομένοις ὑγιεινόν;
passages.english: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?

notes.greek: κυβερνῶντα οἱ ναῦται ἢ ἰατρεύοντα οἱ κάμνοντες
notes.note: The participles are bare accusatives, “one steering”, “one doctoring”, with no article and no pronoun. The first person in the if-clause is supplied, because the verb ἐνεργοίην later in the sentence is first person. “Their” in “their doctor” is also supplied.
notes.other_reading: If the sailors were speaking ill of the one steering, or the sick of the one doctoring

notes.note: One word, “doctoring”, turned as “while I was their doctor”. “Treating” is not used here because the sentence ends with a different Greek word, θεραπευομένοις, “those under treatment”.
notes.other_reading: while I was treating them

notes.note: The imperfect with εἰ, answered by ἂν and an imperfect, makes an unreal condition, which may refer to the present or to the past. The English takes it as present.
notes.other_reading: If the sailors had been speaking ill … would I have attended

notes.note: The form is either first person singular, “would I attend”, or third person plural, “would they attend”. The English takes it as first person to agree with ἐνεργοίην.
notes.other_reading: would they be attending to anything other than

notes.note: The dative can be neuter, “anything else”, or masculine, “anyone else”. With ἢ πῶς following, “anything other than how” is the reading that construes.
notes.other_reading: would I pay attention to anyone else, or to how

notes.note: As given, the verb is first person singular, “I myself might bring about”, and the English follows it. From memory, unchecked, the text is doubted here and a third person form, “he himself”, is also read, which would make the sailors and the sick the subject of the main verb.
notes.other_reading: would they be attending to anything other than how he himself might bring about

notes.note: τὸ σωτήριον is “what saves” or “what brings safety”. οἱ ἐμπλέοντες are all who sail in the ship, a wider word than the sailors of the first clause, so the English keeps the two apart, as also “the sick” and “those under treatment”.
notes.other_reading: what saves those sailing in the ship; the safety of those on board

notes.note: ὑγιεινόν is what makes for health, as σωτήριον is what makes for safety. The English gives the two phrases the same shape.
notes.other_reading: what is healthy for those under treatment; what restores those under treatment to health

check.greek: Εἰ κυβερνῶντα οἱ ναῦται ἢ ἰατρεύοντα οἱ κάμνοντες κακῶς ἔλεγον
check.note: The Greek has no “me”: the two participles stand without article or pronoun, and the first person is supplied from ἐνεργοίην. προσεῖχον by itself could also be “they would attend”. No change is asked for, only that the choice be known.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “of me while I was steering”, as the point itself advises. The later verb ἐνεργοίην with αὐτός, “I myself might bring about”, makes the speaker the one who steers. The notes say that the first person is supplied and give the reading “would they attend”.

check.note: From memory, this verb is a place where the text is disputed, with a third person form, “how he himself might bring about”, read by some. The English follows the first person of the text as given, and no change is asked for.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “how I myself might bring about”, which is what the Greek as given says. The note records the doubt about the text, marked as from memory, unchecked.

check.note: “Them” is supplied, and “doctoring” in the English of today more often means tampering with something. “Treating them” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “while I was their doctor”. “Treating” is not used because the sentence ends with a different Greek word, θεραπευομένοις, which is already “those under treatment”. “Their” is still supplied, as a note says.

check.note: ὑγιεινόν is what makes for health, parallel to σωτήριον, what makes for safety. “What is healthy for” is flatter than “what keeps those on board safe” and loses the parallel.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what makes those under treatment healthy”, in the same shape as “what keeps those on board safe”. The suggested “restores” is not used because ὑγιεινόν says only that the thing makes for health, not that health is given back.

passages.casaubon: Will either passengers, or patients, find fault and complain, either the one if they be well carried, or the others if well cured? Do they take care for any more than this; the one, that their shipmaster may bring them safe to land, and the other, that their physician may effect their recovery?
passages.russian: Если бы моряки бранили меня, пока я стою у руля, или больные — пока я их лечу, разве занимался бы я чем-то иным, кроме того, как мне самому добиться, чтобы уцелели те, кто на борту, или выздоровели те, кого лечат?

passages.greek: Ἔθιζε καὶ ὅσα ἀπογινώσκεις. καὶ γὰρ ἡ χεὶρ ἡ ἀριστερὰ πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα διὰ τὸ ἀνέθιστον ἀργὸς οὖσα τοῦ χαλινοῦ ἐρρωμενέστερον ἢ ἡ δεξιὰ κρατεῖ· τοῦτο γὰρ εἴθισται.
passages.english: Practise even the things you have given up on. For in fact the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in.

notes.note: An active imperative, “accustom”, with no “yourself” expressed; the things given up on are its object. The same root returns in ἀνέθιστον and εἴθισται, so one English word, “practise” (“practice”), is kept for all three.
notes.other_reading: Accustom yourself even to the things you have given up on.

notes.note: The verb is to give something up as hopeless. It does not say whether these are tasks thought to be beyond one’s power or anything written off, and “have given up on” leaves that as open as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: the things you despair of

notes.note: The two particles together can be “for in fact”, or the first can be “even” (or “too”) and go with the left hand. The English reads “for in fact”; the “though” that follows already carries the surprise.
notes.other_reading: For even the left hand

notes.note: Literally “being not working”: the adjective covers idle, slow and of no use, and the participle is read as a concession, “though”. “No good at” is used so that the hand is not heard as lazy.
notes.other_reading: which is idle (or: slow) at everything else

notes.note: With its article the phrase means “the rest”, all the other things, so the English reads “anything else”.
notes.other_reading: at other things

notes.note: The word is the bridle or the bit; what the hand actually holds is the reins. The literal “bridle” is kept.
notes.other_reading: holds the reins

notes.note: With the genitive the verb means to have hold of, or to have mastery over. The English takes the physical grip.
notes.other_reading: masters the bridle more strongly than the right

notes.note: The form can be read with “this” as subject (“this has become habitual”) or with the hand as subject (“it has been accustomed to this”). The English takes the hand as subject and writes “has had practice in”, which keeps the word “practice” and the passive sense of the Greek perfect.
notes.other_reading: for this has become its habit

check.note: The sense of “despair of” is right (to give up on as hopeless), but the phrase is bookish for a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the things you have given up on”, which says what the Greek verb says, to give something up as hopeless, in words of today. “Despair of” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The two particles can be no more than “for in fact”; the English takes the first as “even” and attaches it to the left hand. That is a fair reading but a choice, and it puts a second “even” right after the first.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “For in fact the left hand”, so the two particles are taken together and “even” is not said twice. “For even the left hand” is recorded in a note as the other reading.

check.note: The participle is a concession (“although it is”), and the adjective here is “ineffective, no good for work” more than “idle”, which suggests laziness. “Everything else” is also a little more than “the other things”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else”: the participle is taken as a concession and “idle” gives way to “no good”. “Anything else” stays for τὰ ἄλλα, because with its article the phrase means “the rest”, all the other things, not merely some others.

check.note: “For want of” is dated. The link through “practice” to the first and last words of the passage is rightly kept.
check.decided: Accepted: “For lack of practice” replaces “for want of practice”, and the word “practice” still answers the first and last words of the passage.

check.note: The inverted order of “because this it has practised” is not natural English. The Greek perfect is also closer to “it has been trained to this” than to an active “has practised”, and “this” can be the subject (“this has become its habit”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “because this is what it has had practice in”, in ordinary word order. “Has had practice in” is written in place of the suggested “has been practised in” because it is plainer English and still gives the passive sense of the Greek perfect; the reading with “this” as subject is in the note.

passages.casaubon: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right, because it hath been used unto it.

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: Упражняйся даже в том, в чём ты отчаялся. Ведь и левая рука, хотя от недостатка упражнения ни на что другое не годна, держит поводья крепче правой, потому что в этом она упражнялась.

passages.greek:
Ἐν τῷ γράφειν καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν οὐ πρότερον ἄρξεις πρὶν ἀρχθῇς. τοῦτο πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῷ βίῳ.

Δοῦλος πέφυκας, οὐ μέτεστί σοι λόγου.
passages.english:
In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.

You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.

notes.note: The verb means to rule or command, and also to begin; here it is active and then passive of the same verb. In the setting of writing and reading the sense is the master and the pupil: no one gives the rules before having been given them. “Rule … been ruled” keeps the one verb and its sense of command.
notes.other_reading: you will not lead before you have been led (in sense: you will not teach before you have been taught)

notes.greek: τοῦτο πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῷ βίῳ
notes.note: The Greek has no verb: “this, much more, in life”. “Is so” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: This holds much more in life.

notes.greek: Δοῦλος πέφυκας, οὐ μέτεστί σοι λόγου
notes.note: The words scan as a line of spoken verse (an iambic trimeter) and read like a quotation from a play; from memory, unchecked, the line is counted as a fragment of an unknown dramatist. The Greek as given has no quotation marks and none are added. The two halves stand side by side with only a comma; the English uses a semicolon and adds no “because”.
notes.other_reading: “You are a born slave, you have no say.”

notes.note: The last word is open. In a stage line spoken to a slave it would mean speech: “you have no right to speak”. In this notebook the word is nearly always “reason”, and with “by nature” that sense gives a connected thought, so the English reads “reason”, the settled rendering.
notes.other_reading: you have no say

notes.note: The perfect can mean “you are by nature” or “you were born”. The English reads “by nature”, the sense that goes with “reason” in the second half; “you were born” goes with “you have no say”.
notes.other_reading: You were born a slave

check.note: The verb is “rule, be master, be in command” (and can also be “begin”). “Lead … led” keeps the active and passive pair but is softer than the Greek; in writing and reading the point is being the master only after being under one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “you will not rule before you have been ruled”. The Greek has one verb of command, first active and then passive, and “rule … been ruled” gives that with one English verb, where the suggested “be the master … been under a master” turns the verbs into nouns; the schoolroom sense is explained in the note.

check.note: The last word can equally be “speech, a say”: “you have no say”. The sentence reads like a quoted verse line, where the plain sense would be that a slave has no right to speak; the English takes “reason” without sign, and nothing marks the words as a quotation.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “you have no share in reason”. The Greek says “there is no share for you in λόγος”, the word this notebook uses for reason, and the edition prints the sentence without quotation marks. The note records that the line scans as verse and that in a play it would mean “you have no say”.

check.note: The verb can be “you were born” as well as “you are by nature”. The colon also makes the second clause an explanation of the first, where the Greek only sets the two side by side with a comma.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The colon is replaced by a semicolon, so that the second half is set beside the first and not offered as its explanation. “By nature” is kept for πέφυκας because it is the sense that goes with “reason” in the second half; “you were born” is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: In matter of writing or reading thou must needs be taught before thou can do either: much more in matter of life. 'For thou art born a mere slave, to thy senses and brutish affections;' destitute without teaching of all true knowledge and sound reason.

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian:
В письме и чтении ты не будешь править, пока сам не побудешь под правлением. В жизни это так тем более.

Ты по природе раб; ты не причастен разуму.

passages.greek: “Λόγον ἔχεις;” “ἔχω.” “τί οὖν οὐ χρᾷ; τούτου γὰρ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ποιοῦντος τί ἄλλο θέλεις;”
passages.english: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it? For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?”

notes.note: The word is taken as the faculty, “reason”, the settled rendering. The quotation marks and the division between two speakers are in the edition’s Greek.
notes.other_reading: “Are you in possession of reason?”

notes.note: The verb has no object expressed; “it” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: “Why then do you not make use of it?”

notes.note: A participle phrase (a genitive absolute), which the Greek leaves open between “when”, “if” and “since”. The English reads “when”. “Its own work” is literally “what is its own”.
notes.other_reading: For if it does what is its own to do

notes.note: Literally “what other thing do you want?”, which can be heard as “what else” or “what more”.
notes.other_reading: what more do you wish for?

check.note: The participle phrase can be a condition (“if this does its own part”) as well as a time; “work” is supplied for “what is its own”. Neither misleads.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “when it is doing its own work”. The Greek phrase has no “if” or “when” of its own, and English “when” in a general statement covers both; “to do what is one’s own” is the ordinary Greek for doing one’s own job. The conditional reading and the literal wording are recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: «Есть у тебя разум?» «Есть». «Так почему же ты им не пользуешься? Ведь если он делает своё дело, чего ещё ты хочешь?»

passages.greek: Ὁ μὲν χωρὶς χιτῶνος φιλοσοφεῖ, ὁ δὲ χωρὶς βιβλίου. ἄλλος οὗτος ἡμίγυμνος· ἄρτους οὐκ ἔχω, φησί, καὶ ἐμμένω τῷ λόγῳ.—ἐγὼ δὲ τροφὰς τὰς ἐκ τῶν μαθημάτων οὐκ ἔχω καὶ ἐμμένω.
passages.english: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.

notes.note: The chiton is the basic garment worn next to the skin. To go without it is to go in a cloak alone.
notes.other_reading: without a shirt

notes.note: One verb in Greek: to do philosophy, or to live as a philosopher.
notes.other_reading: lives as a philosopher

notes.note: There is no verb: “this other one, half naked”. The English makes it a short sentence introducing the speaker of the next words, and the quotation marks around his words are added, since the edition has none here. It is open whether this is a third figure or a closer look at one of the first two.
notes.other_reading: This other one, half naked, says: “I have no bread, and yet I hold to reason.”

notes.note: The Greek has a bare “and”, which here sets the holding against the lack. The English writes “and yet”, in this sentence and in the last.
notes.other_reading: and I hold to reason

notes.note: With the article, in a philosopher’s mouth, the word could be reason itself or the teaching (the argument) the speaker has taken up. The English keeps “reason”, the settled rendering.
notes.other_reading: and yet I stand by my teaching

notes.note: Open between the food that learning itself gives the mind and a living earned from one’s learning or lessons. The English phrase leans to the first but does not shut out the second. “Bread” above is plural in the Greek (“loaves”), answered here by a plural word for food.
notes.other_reading: I get no living from my studies

notes.note: The edition puts a dash before these words to mark a turn, perhaps a change of speaker: it may be Marcus himself or one more philosopher answering the half-naked one. The English leaves the sentence outside the quotation marks, as Marcus’s own, and begins a new sentence in place of the dash. The particle is given as “and”, because this speaker says of himself what the last one said; “but” is the other way to hear it.
notes.other_reading: “But I,” says another, “have no nourishment from learning, and yet I hold to reason.”

notes.note: As given: “I do not have … and I hold”, with no object for the second verb; “to reason” is supplied from the sentence before. From memory, unchecked, the place of the negative has been doubted, and with it moved the sentence becomes a self-reproach.
notes.other_reading: I have the nourishment of learning and I do not hold to it

check.note: The “and” after “I have no bread” is “and yet”: the point is that the speaker stays in spite of having no bread. Plain “and” loses the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and yet I hold to reason”, and the same in the last sentence. “Yet” is written and not “still”, because the Greek word marks the contrast only and the verb already says “stay”; a note records that the Greek has a bare “and”.

check.note: With the article, in the mouth of a philosopher, this may be “the doctrine, my principle, the argument” and not reason as a faculty. The English chooses “reason” without sign.
check.decided: Declined: “Reason” is kept. The Greek τῷ λόγῳ can be either reason or the speaker’s teaching and nothing in the sentence decides, so the settled rendering of the word stands; “principle” is also this translation’s word for another Greek term. The other reading is recorded in the note.

check.note: The Greek dash and particle mark a turn, possibly a new speaker. The English closes the quotation and runs on with “And”, so the last sentence is taken as Marcus’s own comment; it could be one more philosopher speaking, and the particle is “but” here more than “and”.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “And I, for my part,” as a new sentence outside the quotation marks. The speaker goes on to say of himself what the half-naked one said (he lacks, and he holds), so the particle δέ turns to a new person without setting him against the last. A dash cannot stand as a pause in the English; the possible change of speaker and the “but” are recorded in the note.

check.greek: ἐγὼ δὲ τροφὰς τὰς ἐκ τῶν μαθημάτων οὐκ ἔχω καὶ ἐμμένω
check.note: The Greek has only the verb “I hold”, with “to reason” understood from before. “To it” is added, and in the English its antecedent is unclear: “it” can be taken as the nourishment or the learning just mentioned.
check.decided: Accepted: The last words now read “and yet I hold to reason”. The Greek has only the verb, with “reason” understood from the sentence before; naming it removes the “it” that could be taken as the learning or the nourishment, and the note says that the object is supplied.

check.note: From memory, the placing of the negative in this last sentence has been doubted, and with it moved the sentence becomes a self-reproach: “I have the nourishment of learning and do not hold to it”. The English rightly follows the Greek as given and should stay.
check.decided: Accepted: The English follows the Greek as given and its sense is not changed here. The note says, from memory and unchecked, that the place of the negative has been doubted, and gives the sentence as it would read with the negative moved.

passages.casaubon: There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I depart not from reason.

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: Один занимается философией без туники, другой без книги. Вот ещё один, полуголый: «Хлеба у меня нет, — говорит он, — и всё же я держусь разума». А у меня, со своей стороны, нет пищи, которую даёт учение, и всё же я держусь разума.

passages.greek: Δικαίως ταῦτα πάσχεις· μᾶλλον δὲ θέλεις ἀγαθὸς αὔριον γενέσθαι ἢ σήμερον εἶναι.
passages.english: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.

notes.note: This is part of a chapter, and nothing in the Greek given says what “these things” are. The English keeps the bare words and supplies nothing.
notes.other_reading: what is happening to you

notes.note: Literally “justly you undergo these things”. The verb can be the neutral “have happen to one” or the stronger “suffer”; the English takes the neutral sense and puts “justly” into the verb “deserve”.
notes.other_reading: You suffer these things justly.

notes.note: The comparative goes with the “than” that follows: “you want rather … than”. The same two words can also mean “or rather”, a correction of what was just said, but then “than” has nothing to answer. The connecting particle is light: the English joins the two clauses with a semicolon and writes neither “but” nor a “because” the Greek does not have.
notes.other_reading: or rather, you choose to become good tomorrow instead of being good today

notes.note: The Greek has only “than to be today”, with “good” understood; the English repeats “good”. The contrast of “become” and “be” is in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: than be so today

check.note: “You suffer these things justly” is accurate word for word but stiff. The verb is neutral, “what happens to you”, and need not mean suffering.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “You deserve these things that are happening to you”, with the neutral sense of the verb and “deserve” for “justly”. “These things” is kept because the Greek has the word ταῦτα and the suggested wording drops it.

check.note: The connecting particle is left out. The two words are also a common way of saying “or rather”; with “than” following, the comparison is the natural reading and the English takes it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The two clauses are now joined by a semicolon, as the Greek joins them with a stop and a light particle. “But” is not written, because it would set the second clause against the first where the Greek particle only moves on; the reading “or rather” is recorded in the note.

part.left_out: Πρόσεχε τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ.
part.why: The 1634 translation makes the chapter's first sentence its section 8.20 and begins its 8.21 here, with 'Most justly have these things happened unto thee'.

passages.casaubon: Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be so to-day.

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: Ты заслуживаешь того, что с тобой происходит: ты предпочитаешь стать хорошим завтра, а не быть хорошим сегодня.

passages.greek: Καββαλικώτερος, ἀλλ’ οὐχὶ κοινωνικώτερος οὐδὲ αἰδημονέστερος οὐδ’ εὐτακτότερος ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν οὐδὲ εὐμενέστερος πρὸς τὰ τῶν πλησίον παροράματα.
passages.english: Better at throwing an opponent, but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder towards the oversights of those nearby.

notes.note: A wrestling word in a Doric (Spartan) form: “more able to throw down”; “an opponent” is supplied, because “throw” alone is heard in English of throwing a thing. From memory, unchecked, it echoes a Spartan saying reported by Plutarch, where the man who beat a wrestler is called not better but better at throwing. The sentence has no verb and no subject, so who is compared with whom is left open.
notes.other_reading: A better wrestler

notes.note: The settled rendering “social” is kept. The sense is not “fond of company” but “given to acting for the community, for the common good”.
notes.other_reading: more public-spirited

notes.note: The word covers modesty, a sense of shame, decency and respect for others. The English reads “modest”, which narrows it.
notes.other_reading: with more sense of shame

notes.note: The adjective is the soldier’s “in good order”, “disciplined”; the preposition is “at” or “over” what happens. The phrase “in the face of what happens” is read with this adjective only, not with the ones before it.
notes.other_reading: nor more orderly when things happen

notes.note: Well disposed, gracious, kind. With faults as the object it comes near “more forgiving”.
notes.other_reading: nor more forgiving of

notes.note: The noun means things overlooked: mistakes made by not seeing. “Those nearby” is literally “those near”, the people one lives among, often put as “neighbours”; no “his” is written, because the Greek does not say whose they are.
notes.other_reading: the slips of his neighbours

check.note: “An opponent” is supplied, harmlessly. The Greek is a bare comparative with no subject or verb, and the English rightly leaves it a fragment; “a better wrestler” or “better at throwing his man” are other ways.
check.decided: Declined: “Better at throwing an opponent” is kept. The Greek word is made from the wrestling verb “to throw down”, so “throwing” has to stay, and “throw” without an object is heard in English of throwing a thing; “his man” would add a “his” as well. The note now says that “an opponent” is supplied.

check.note: To a reader of today “social” means sociable, fond of company. The Greek word is about acting for the community, for the common good.
check.decided: Declined: “More social” is kept. κοινωνικός is one of the words this translation renders by one English word in every passage, and “social” is that word. The note says that the sense is acting for the community and not liking company.

check.note: The Greek word is having a sense of shame, self-respect, decency; “modest” narrows it towards humility.
check.decided: Declined: “More modest” is kept. Modesty is one of the senses of αἰδήμων, and a single comparative is needed to stand in the row of five, as in the Greek. The note records that the Greek word also covers a sense of shame and decency, and that the English narrows it.

check.note: “Better ordered” is not said of a person in English. The word is the soldier’s “in good order, disciplined”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “better disciplined in the face of what happens”.

check.note: The article is dropped: the Greek is “of his neighbours”, the people around him, and bare “of neighbours” reads oddly. “Oversights” is good.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the oversights of those nearby”, which gives the Greek article. “His” is not written, because the sentence has no subject and the Greek does not say whose neighbours they are.

passages.casaubon: He hath a stronger body, and is a better wrestler than I. What then? Is he more bountiful? is he more modest? Doth he bear all adverse chances with more equanimity: or with his neighbour's offences with more meekness and gentleness than I?

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: Искуснее в том, чтобы повалить противника, но не более общественный, не более скромный, не более собранный перед лицом того, что случается, не более снисходительный к оплошностям ближних.

passages.greek: Ἡ βιωτικὴ τῇ παλαιστικῇ ὁμοιοτέρα ἤπερ τῇ ὀρχηστικῇ κατὰ τὸ πρὸς τὰ ἐμπίπτοντα καὶ οὐ προεγνωσμενα ἕτοιμος καὶ ἀπτὼς ἑστάναι.
passages.english: The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing, in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall.

notes.note: An adjective with “art” understood, formed like the two words that follow for wrestling and dancing. “The art of” is written three times to keep the parallel.
notes.other_reading: Living is more like wrestling than dancing

notes.note: Literally “in respect of the standing …”: the phrase gives the point of likeness. The English makes it “in that it stands”.
notes.other_reading: in respect of standing ready

notes.note: Literally “the things that fall upon”, used of blows and of events; the Greek does not name what they fall on, and “it” is supplied. The word shares its root with ἀπτὼς (“not falling”) later in the sentence, so “fall” is kept in both places.
notes.other_reading: whatever comes at it

notes.note: Literally “not known beforehand”. The word has lost its accent in the copy; it is read as the ordinary participle.
notes.other_reading: and are not known in advance

notes.note: The two adjectives are nominative, which in this construction refers them to the subject of the sentence, “the art of living” (the first can serve as a feminine); they may still point loosely to the person who lives, as to a wrestler. The second means “not falling”, “not thrown”, and is given as “does not fall”; from memory, unchecked, it is a word used of wrestlers. In the Greek both adjectives go with “stand” and both face “the things that fall on it”; the English divides them to stay readable.
notes.other_reading: in that one stands ready and firm on one’s feet against what falls on one unforeseen

check.note: The English makes the art of living do the standing. The nominatives can be taken with “the art of living” by grammar, but the picture is of the person, like a wrestler, standing ready; an art that “stands unfallen” is hard to picture.
check.decided: Declined: The art of living still does the standing. The two adjectives are in the nominative, and in this Greek construction that refers them to the subject of the sentence, which is “the art of living”; the suggested “one has to” would also add an obligation the Greek does not state. The reading with a person standing is recorded in the note.

check.note: “Unfallen” is not a word of today’s English and has a religious ring. The Greek is the wrestler’s “not thrown”; “not falling” would keep the echo of “fall on”, which “not thrown” loses.
check.decided: Accepted: “Unfallen” is gone and the English now reads “and does not fall”, which keeps the echo of “fall on”. The clause is reordered to “stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall”, so that “fall” is not read with “against”.

check.note: The past tense “were not foreseen” sits oddly beside the present “fall on it”; the Greek pairs two participles, “what falls on one and is not known beforehand”. The Greek word is also printed without its accent, a slip of the copy.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the things that fall on it and are not foreseen”, with both verbs in the present and the “and” of the Greek kept. The missing accent is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's, than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing may cast him down.

nearest.title: Training, and the use of reason

passages.russian: Искусство жить больше похоже на искусство борьбы, чем на искусство танца, — тем, что оно стоит наготове к тому, что непредвиденно на него падает, и не падает.

passages.greek: Ὅταν εὐφρᾶναι σεαυτὸν θέλῃς, ἐνθυμοῦ τὰ προτερήματα τῶν συμβιούντων· οἷον τοῦ μὲν τὸ δραστήριον, τοῦ δὲ τὸ αἰδῆμον, τοῦ δὲ τὸ εὐμετάδοτον, ἄλλου δὲ ἄλλο τι. οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως εὐφραίνει ὡς τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν ἀρετῶν ἐμφαινόμενα τοῖς ἤθεσι τῶν συζώντων καὶ ἀθρόα ὡς οἷόν τε συμπίπτοντα. διὸ καὶ πρόχειρα αὐτὰ ἑκτέον.
passages.english: When you want to cheer yourself, think of the strong points of the people you live with: for example, the energy of one, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and something else in someone else. For nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in the characters of the people you live with, and coming together, as many at once as possible. And so they must be kept ready to hand.

notes.note: The same verb comes back in the second sentence (εὐφραίνει), so one English word, “cheer”, is used for both. Its range runs from “gladden” to “delight”.
notes.other_reading: When you want to gladden yourself

notes.note: Literally the points in which someone is ahead: advantages, superior qualities. The English takes the plain “strong points”.
notes.other_reading: the merits (or: the advantages) of the people you live with

notes.note: The quality of being effective in action, of getting things done. “Energy” narrows it a little.
notes.other_reading: the effectiveness of one

notes.note: The quality of having αἰδώς: a sense of shame, respect for others and for oneself. “Modesty” is one side of it.
notes.other_reading: the sense of shame (or: the self-respect) of another

notes.note: Literally readiness to give a share of what one has.
notes.other_reading: the readiness to share of a third

notes.note: The Greek says likenesses (images, copies) of the virtues, not the virtues themselves, and the English keeps that. It need not be dismissive.
notes.other_reading: the images of the virtues

notes.note: A different verb from τῶν συμβιούντων in the first sentence, with the same sense, “those who live with”. The Greek names no person in either place; the English supplies “you” in both, since the passage is addressed to “you”.
notes.other_reading: in the characters of those who share one’s life

notes.note: Literally “falling together in as dense a crowd as possible”. It is open whether the likenesses crowd together in the same people or come before the mind all at once. The English leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: and meeting the eye all together, as far as that can be

notes.note: An impersonal form (“they are to be kept”) with no “you”. The καί is taken with διό (“and so”); it could instead mark “them too”. “They” is most naturally the strong points, but could be the likenesses.
notes.other_reading: So these too must be kept at hand

check.note: The καί is dropped, and the impersonal “one must keep them” has become a passive with a loose “they”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “And so they must be kept ready to hand”, which gives the καί together with διό. The Greek form is impersonal and has no “you”, so “you should” is not taken, and “they” is as loose as the Greek αὐτά, which a note records.

check.note: The near-synonym τῶν συμβιούντων was “the people you live with”, but here the English has “the people one lives with”. The Greek has neither “you” nor “one” in either place, and the change of person jars.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the people you live with” in both sentences. The Greek names no person in either place, and the passage as a whole is addressed to “you”.

passages.casaubon: When thou wilt comfort and cheer thyself, call to mind the several gifts and virtues of them, whom thou dost daily converse with; as for example, the industry of the one; the modesty of another; the liberality of a third; of another some other thing. For nothing can so much rejoice thee, as the resemblances and parallels of several virtues, visible and eminent in the dispositions of those who live with thee; especially when, all at once, as near as may be, they represent themselves unto thee. And therefore thou must have them always in a readiness.
passages.russian: Когда хочешь себя порадовать, думай о достоинствах тех, с кем живёшь: например, об энергичности одного, скромности другого, щедрости третьего и о чём-то ещё в ком-то ещё. Ведь ничто так не радует, как подобия добродетелей, проступающие в характерах тех, с кем живёшь, и сходящиеся вместе — как можно больше сразу. Поэтому их и надо держать под рукой.

passages.greek: Ὅταν ἀναγκασθῇς ὑπὸ τῶν περιεστηκότων οἱονεὶ διαταραχθῆναι, ταχέως ἐπάνιθι εἰς σεαυτὸν καὶ μὴ ὑπὲρ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα ἐξίστασο τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ· ἔσῃ γὰρ ἐγκρατέστερος τῆς ἁρμονίας τῷ συνεχῶς εἰς αὐτὴν ἐπανέρχεσθαι.
passages.english: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to. For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.

notes.note: Literally “beyond what is necessary”. The word echoes ἀναγκασθῇς (“you are forced”) at the start, so “force” is used in both places. Whether “beyond” means longer or further is not said.
notes.other_reading: do not stay out of the rhythm longer than is necessary

notes.note: Literally “the things standing around”, the usual word for circumstances. The Greek has no “your”.
notes.other_reading: by what surrounds you

notes.note: οἱονεί (“as it were”, “in a way”) softens the strong verb, which means to be thoroughly disturbed or thrown into disorder. The English keeps both.
notes.other_reading: to be, so to speak, badly shaken

notes.note: Literally “stand out of the rhythm”, an image from music or dance. The verb is one of movement, so the English reads “step out of”. The present imperative with μή can also mean “do not keep standing out of”.
notes.other_reading: do not stay out of step

notes.note: Literally “more in command of the harmony”. ἁρμονία is the fitting-together or tuning of notes, not harmony in the modern sense of chords. The familiar word is kept so that the musical image, begun with “rhythm”, stays visible.
notes.other_reading: you will be more the master of the tuning

notes.note: The same verb as ἐπάνιθι (“go back”) earlier in the sentence, so “go back” is repeated. “It” (αὐτήν) is the harmony.
notes.other_reading: by constantly returning to it

check.note: The verb is one of movement: step out of, leave. “Be out of” makes it a state.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to”. The Greek verb is one of movement, to stand out of or leave, and does not name a state.

check.note: The Greek has no “your”: it says “by the things standing around”, by circumstances.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “When circumstances force you”. The Greek has only “the things standing around”, with no “your”.

passages.casaubon: Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out, presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
passages.russian: Когда обстоятельства вынуждают тебя как бы прийти в смятение, быстро возвращайся в себя и не выходи из ритма больше, чем вынужден. Ведь ты будешь твёрже владеть гармонией, постоянно к ней возвращаясь.

passages.greek: Τρέχε ἐπὶ τὸ σεαυτοῦ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ τὸ τοῦ ὅλου καὶ τὸ τούτου. τὸ μὲν σεαυτοῦ, ἵνα νοῦν δικαικὸν αὐτὸ ποιήσῃς· τὸ δὲ τοῦ ὅλου, ἵνα συμμνημονεύσῃς τίνος μέρος εἶ· τὸ δὲ τούτου, ἵνα ἐπιστήσῃς πότερον ἄγνοια ἢ γνώμη, καὶ ἅμα λογίσῃ ὅτι συγγενές.
passages.english: Run to your own ruling part, and to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To your own, so that you make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that you remember along with it what you are a part of. To this person’s, so that you take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that it is akin.

notes.note: The Stoic term for the governing part of the soul, here “the ruling part” as in the glossary. The whole is said to have one as well.
notes.other_reading: your own governing mind

notes.note: Literally “and that of this one”. The Greek does not say who: presumably the person in front of you, the one whose act is in question. The form could be masculine or neuter; the English reads “this person’s”.
notes.other_reading: and to that of this man

notes.note: The adjective (δικαϊκός, given here without its diaeresis) is a rare one meaning “just” or “concerned with justice”. From memory, unchecked, some editors have doubted the word. It is translated as it stands.
notes.other_reading: so that you make it a mind set on justice

notes.note: The prefix adds “together with” or “at the same time” to “remember”. The English gives it as “along with it”; the “it” is supplied, and the Greek does not state what the remembering goes together with.
notes.other_reading: so that you also remember what you are a part of

notes.note: τίνος can be “of what” or “of whom”. The English takes “what”, the whole just named.
notes.other_reading: whose part you are

notes.note: There is no verb and no subject: “whether ignorance or γνώμη”. γνώμη ranges over judgment, purpose and knowledge, and the two words echo each other in sound. The English takes the contrast as between acting in ignorance and acting on a considered purpose, and supplies “there is” and “there”.
notes.other_reading: whether it is ignorance or judgment (or: or knowledge)

notes.note: Literally “that it is akin”, neuter, so it is the other person’s ruling part that is akin. The Greek does not say to what: to your own, to that of the whole, or to both.
notes.other_reading: and at the same time reckon that it is akin to yours

check.note: “To yours” is added. The Greek says only “that it is akin” and leaves open to what: to you, to the whole, or both, since all three ruling parts have just been named.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now ends “reckon that it is akin”. The Greek says only that the other person’s ruling part is akin and does not say to what; a note gives “to yours” as the reading not taken.

check.note: γνώμη can be a considered judgment or opinion as well as a deliberate purpose, and “intent” chooses the second. The English “it” also has no clear antecedent; the Greek has no subject.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whether there is ignorance there or intent”, so that no “it” without an antecedent stands in for the missing subject. “Intent” is kept for γνώμη, since the word can mean a deliberate purpose and that makes a clear contrast with ignorance; the note gives “judgment” and “knowledge” as the other senses.

check.note: The prefix says “remember along with it, at the same time”. “Also” is a possible way to give it but reads as if a second thing were being remembered.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so that you remember along with it what you are a part of”. The prefix of the verb says “together with”; a note says that “it” is supplied.

check.note: As given the word lacks its diaeresis. It is a rare adjective, “inclined to justice, righteous”, and “just” is acceptable.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “a just mind”, as the point proposes. The word is read as δικαϊκόν, a rare adjective for “just”, and the note records the missing mark and the doubt about the word.

passages.casaubon: As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy refuge be with all speed. To thine own, that it resolve upon nothing against justice. To that of the universe, that thou mayest remember, part of whom thou art. Of his, that thou mayest consider whether in the estate of ignorance, or of knowledge. And then also must thou call to mind, that he is thy kinsman.
passages.russian: Беги к своему ведущему началу, и к ведущему началу целого, и к ведущему началу этого человека. К своему — чтобы сделать его справедливым умом. К ведущему началу целого — чтобы вместе с ним помнить, чего ты часть. К ведущему началу этого человека — чтобы заметить, невежество там или умысел, и одновременно учесть, что оно родственно.

passages.greek: Πόνει μὴ ὡς ἄθλιος μηδὲ ὡς ἐλεεῖσθαι ἢ θαυμάζεσθαι θέλων, ἀλλὰ μόνον ἓν θέλε· κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ὡς ὁ πολιτικὸς λόγος ἀξιοῖ.
passages.english: Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired, but want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.

notes.note: The verb means to labour and also to bear hardship or pain. “Toil” is used because it carries both the work and its hardness.
notes.other_reading: Bear your hardship

notes.note: “As a miserable person”: someone suffering under the labour, to be pitied. The word comes from the word for a struggle or contest, which may be felt after “toil”.
notes.other_reading: not like someone wretched

notes.note: Both forms can be middle (“to move and to check oneself”) or passive (“to be set moving and to be held back”). The English takes the middle: what is wanted is the person’s own moving and stopping, with reason setting the measure.
notes.other_reading: to be set in motion and to be held in check

notes.note: Literally “the political reason”: reason as it belongs to a πόλις, a community of fellow citizens. “Civic” keeps the adjective wide. The Greek does not say which city, and the Stoics also call the universe a city.
notes.other_reading: as the reason of a citizen (or: the reason of the community) thinks right

notes.note: The verb is “thinks fit”, “claims as right”, “demands”. The English takes the milder “thinks right”.
notes.other_reading: requires

check.note: “Hard” is added, and the verb also means to bear toil or pain, which suits “as a wretch” and “wanting to be pitied”. The English decides for plain work.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Toil”. The verb covers both hard work and bearing hardship, and “toil” carries both in one word without an added “hard”.

check.note: “Wretch” is old-fashioned and today suggests someone contemptible; the Greek means someone miserable, to be pitied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not as someone miserable”. The Greek word means a person in misery, one to be pitied, and “wretch” today suggests someone contemptible.

check.note: The “but” that sets this against the two refusals is dropped by starting a new sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the passage is now one sentence and reads “but want one thing only”, so that the “but” of the Greek sets the one wish against the two refusals.

check.note: Both forms can be passive: “to be set moving and to be checked”. The English takes them as the person’s own acts.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the forms are open, as the point says, and a note records the passive reading. The English keeps “to move and to hold back”, because κινεῖσθαι is the ordinary Greek for a living thing’s own moving and the sentence says what the person is to want to do.

check.note: πολιτικὸς is an adjective, “civic, of the community”, and “of a citizen” narrows it to one person’s standing. ἀξιοῖ is “thinks right, claims”, a shade milder than “requires”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as civic reason thinks right”. πολιτικός is an adjective for what belongs to a city or community, not to one citizen, and ἀξιοῖ is “thinks fit” before it is “demands”.

passages.casaubon: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.

nearest.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

passages.russian: Трудись не как несчастный и не как тот, кто хочет, чтобы его жалели или им восхищались, но желай лишь одного: двигаться и сдерживаться так, как считает правильным гражданский разум.

passages.greek: Ἑνὶ τέρπου καὶ προσαναπαύου, τῷ ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν σὺν μνήμῃ θεοῦ.
passages.english: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.

notes.note: “In one thing”. The Greek does not add “only”, and neither does the English.
notes.other_reading: Let one thing be your pleasure and your rest

notes.note: To rest upon something, to find one’s rest in it. The same verb is used of philosophy in 6.12 and has the same English there.
notes.other_reading: and lean on it for rest

notes.greek: ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν
notes.note: Literally “passing from a social act to a social act”. “Social” (κοινωνικός) is the glossary word: an act that serves the common life of people with one another.
notes.other_reading: passing from an act for the common good to an act for the common good

notes.note: Literally “with memory of god”. The noun has no article, so “a god” is also possible.
notes.other_reading: with remembrance of god

passages.casaubon: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.
passages.russian: Находи радость в одном и в нём отдыхай: переходить от одного общественного действия к другому общественному действию, держа в уме бога.

passages.greek: Εἰ μητρυιάν τε ἅμα εἶχες καὶ μητέρα, ἐκείνην τ̓ ἂν ἐθεράπευες καὶ ὅμως ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο. τοῦτό σοι νῦν ἐστιν ἡ αὐλὴ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὧδε πολλάκις ἐπάνιθι καὶ προσαναπαύου ταύτῃ, δι’ ἣν καὶ τὰ ἐκεῖ σοι ἀνεκτὰ φαίνεται καὶ σὺ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀνεκτός.
passages.english: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now. Go back here often and rest in philosophy. Because of it, the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.

notes.note: The verb means to attend on, serve, look after, and also to pay court to someone, the sense that prepares “the court” in the next sentence. “Wait on” is meant to carry both. The Greek says “that one” for the stepmother; the English names her.
notes.other_reading: you would pay court to the stepmother

notes.greek: ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο
notes.note: Literally “your going back to your mother would be continual”. The noun is from the same root as ἐπάνιθι (“go back”) below, so the English keeps “going back” and “go back”.
notes.other_reading: your return to your mother would be constant

notes.note: αὐλή is the court, the emperor’s palace and the life around it. By the order of the words the court answers to the stepmother and philosophy to the mother; the Greek does not spell that out and neither does the English.
notes.other_reading: the palace and philosophy

notes.note: Either “to this place” or “in this way” (as you would go back to your mother). The English takes “here”, meaning to philosophy, because the next clause sets it against “the things there”.
notes.other_reading: Go back in this way often

notes.note: “In this one”, feminine. The court and philosophy are both feminine nouns in Greek, and “this one” is the nearer of the two, philosophy. The English writes the noun so that it is clear which is meant.
notes.other_reading: and rest in her

notes.note: The preposition with this case gives a cause (“on account of which”), not a means (“by means of which”).
notes.other_reading: thanks to which

notes.note: “The things there”, that is at court, as against “here”.
notes.other_reading: what you meet at court

notes.note: The verb is carried over from the clause before, so “seem” is repeated. “Among them” is most naturally the things there (neuter), but the form could also be heard as the people there.
notes.other_reading: and you are bearable among the people there

check.note: The verb means to wait on, attend to, pay court to. “Duty” is brought in, and the courtier’s sense of the word, which prepares the court in the next sentence, is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you would wait on the stepmother”. The verb is the one for attending on someone and for paying court, and “duty” is not in it. The noun is kept because “her” would point to the mother, while the Greek “that one” points to the stepmother.

check.note: The Greek says “rest in her” or “in this one”. Naming philosophy is a gloss, made necessary only because “here” before it is unclear.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “rest in philosophy”. The Greek ταύτῃ is “this one”, the nearer of two feminine nouns, the court and philosophy; “her” or “it” would not say which, and “her” would bring in the mother, whom the Greek does not name here. A note records the choice.

check.note: ὧδε can be “here” (to philosophy) or “in this way” (as you would to your mother). The English chooses the first without sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the word is open, as the point says, and a note records “in this way”. The English keeps “here”, because the next clause sets it against “the things there” (τὰ ἐκεῖ), which gives ὧδε the sense of place.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “through which”, which can be heard as “by means of which”. The Greek preposition with this case gives a cause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “because of which”. With this case διά means “on account of”, so philosophy is the reason the things at court seem bearable, not a tool for bearing them.

passages.casaubon: If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also; nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse be continually. So let the court and thy philosophy be unto thee. Have recourse unto it often, and comfort thyself in her, by whom it is that those other things are made tolerable unto thee, and thou also in those things not intolerable unto others.
passages.russian: Если бы у тебя одновременно были мачеха и мать, ты служил бы мачехе, но всё же постоянно возвращался бы к матери. Вот что для тебя теперь двор и философия. Часто возвращайся сюда и находи отдых в философии. Благодаря ей и то, что там, кажется тебе сносным, и сам ты кажешься сносным среди этого.

passages.greek: Μηκέτι σου μηδεὶς ἀκούσῃ καταμεμφομένου τὸν ἐν αὐλῇ βίον μηδὲ σὺ σεαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Let no one hear you finding fault with life at court any more, and do not hear yourself doing it either.

notes.note: To blame, find fault with, complain of.
notes.other_reading: complaining about life at court

notes.note: “The life at court”: αὐλή is the emperor’s court, as in 6.12.
notes.other_reading: life in the palace

notes.note: Literally “nor you yourself”, with “hear” understood: you are not to hear yourself doing it, that is, not to complain even inwardly. μηδέ can be “nor” or “not even”; the English takes “nor” and supplies “hear” and “doing it”.
notes.other_reading: not even you yourself

check.note: The Greek is “nor you [hear] yourself”. The English can be misread as “not even you finding fault”, and μηδὲ may be plain “nor” and not “not even”.
