notes.other_reading: the impressions it is at every moment up to you to fan back into flame

notes.greek: δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν
notes.note: Here he turns from “you” to the first person, and the change is kept. “This” is whatever is in front of him and is not named. The verb is the glossary’s “judgment” word.
notes.other_reading: I can think what I should about this.

notes.note: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια, and “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty, which has an inside and an outside, so “mind” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: The things outside my thought are nothing at all to my thought.

notes.greek: οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν
notes.note: An idiom, “nothing at all in relation to”: they have no bearing on it, are no concern of it. The short English idiom “are nothing to” is kept.
notes.other_reading: have no bearing whatever on my mind

notes.note: A present, “you are upright”, where English might expect a future. The adjective means standing straight, on one’s feet, and also right or correct; “upright” leaves both open and adds no verb of standing.
notes.other_reading: Learn this and you are in the right.

check.greek: πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ
check.note: “Be made dead” is not natural English for the verb, and “how else … unless” is awkward, though the sense is right.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out”. “Killed” replaces “made dead” and “else” is dropped because “unless” already says it; the passive “are put out” is kept, since the Greek does not say who puts them out.

check.greek: ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι
check.note: The word for “without a break” can go with the rekindling or with “it is up to you”, and the English hung “continually” at the end without choosing openly. The relative clause was also made a new sentence beginning “And”, which the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause is joined back to its sentence and reads “the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame”, with “keep” for the adverb, which stands next to the verb of rekindling in the Greek. A note gives the other reading.

check.note: The Greek is only “you are upright”, or “you are right”. “Stand” was added and fixed the bodily picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Learn this and you are upright”, with no added “stand”. “Upright” leaves both senses of the Greek word open, and the note gives “you are in the right”.

part.left_out: Ἀναβιῶναί σοι ἔξεστιν· ἴδε πάλιν τὰ πράγματα, ὡς ἑώρας· ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ τὸ ἀναβιῶναι.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 7.2 at 'Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be right' and begins its 7.3 with the rest of the chapter, the lines on living again.

passages.casaubon: What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only, which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be right.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Как можно убить принципы, если не погаснут отвечающие им представления — те представления, которые ты волен снова и снова раздувать в пламя? Я могу составить об этом должное суждение. Если могу, отчего я в смятении? То, что вне моего ума, для моего ума — ровно ничто. Усвой это — и ты стоишь прямо.

passages.greek: Ἔξεστι περὶ τούτου μηδὲν ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ μὴ ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ· αὐτὰ γὰρ τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ἔχει φύσιν ποιητικὴν τῶν ἡμετέρων κρίσεων.
passages.english: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.

notes.note: Impersonal: “it is allowed, it is open”, a matter of freedom more than of bare possibility. “One is free” keeps it impersonal, since the Greek names no “you”.
notes.other_reading: It is possible to form no judgment about this

notes.note: “About this” with nothing named: the matter in front of him. The form could also be masculine, “about this person”.
notes.other_reading: to form no judgment about this man

notes.note: The verb is from the word for a crowd: to be bothered, pestered. “Trouble” is used for this word and its compound (ἐνοχλεῖν) throughout the section, and “disturb” for ταράσσειν, to keep the two apart. The Greek has “the soul”, where the article stands for the owner; “one’s” follows the impersonal opening.
notes.other_reading: and not to be bothered in the soul

notes.note: κρίσις is close in sense to ὑπόληψις, which the glossary renders “judgment”. Since both stand in this one sentence, κρίσις is given as “verdicts”, so that the two Greek words can be told apart.
notes.other_reading: a nature that produces our judgments

notes.note: Literally “a nature productive of”: things are not of a kind to make our verdicts for us.
notes.other_reading: things themselves are not of a nature to create our verdicts

check.note: The Greek word means “it is allowed, it is open to you”, a matter of freedom more than of mere possibility.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “One is free to form no judgment about this”, which gives the freedom. “You are free” is not used, because the Greek verb is impersonal and names no “you”.

check.note: “Troubled in the soul” is stiff for a reader of today; the article here stands for the owner.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not to be troubled in one’s soul”. The article is given as a possessive, but as “one’s” and not “your”, to match the impersonal opening.

passages.casaubon: It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to beget and force upon us any opinion at all.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Можно не составлять об этом никакого суждения и не тревожиться душой; ведь сами вещи не обладают природой, порождающей наши приговоры.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ, οἷον λέγω, οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. εἰ δέ τις ἄλλος αὐτὸ φοβῆσαι ἢ λυπῆσαι δύναται, ποιείτω· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς. τὸ σωμάτιον μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει· τὸ δὲ ψυχάριον τὸ φοβούμενον, τὸ λυπούμενον, τὸ περὶ τούτων ὅλως ὑπολαμβάνον, οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ· οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην. ἀπροσδεές ἐστιν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδειαν ποιῇ· κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτὸ ταράσσῃ καὶ ἐμποδίζῃ.
passages.english: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.

notes.note: The glossary’s “the ruling part”: the part of the soul that judges and directs.
notes.other_reading: the governing part, the directing mind

notes.note: The Greek doubles the pronoun, “itself … to itself”: the trouble would be its own doing. English carries this in “for itself”. “Trouble” is the word used for this verb throughout the section.
notes.other_reading: The ruling part does not itself trouble itself

notes.note: “Frighten itself into desire” is what the words say, and it is hard sense: fear does not lead into desire, and the next sentence speaks of frightening and distressing, not of desire. From memory, unchecked, editors have doubted the text here and suspect that words have dropped out or been altered. The English follows the Greek as given and does not smooth it.
notes.other_reading: it does not frighten itself or lead itself into desire

notes.note: Masculine, “anyone else”, a person; “them” is used for it as the glossary allows. It could loosely cover anything outside the ruling part.
notes.other_reading: But if something else can frighten or distress it

notes.greek: ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς
notes.note: The adverb is made from the glossary’s “judgment” word: “in the way of judging”. Verb and noun are the same word in Greek, “turn itself into such turns”, meaning the changes of fear and distress; the English keeps one “turn” and gives the noun as “directions”. “Its own” gives the force of the doubled αὐτὸ … ἑαυτὸ.
notes.other_reading: for it will not of itself, through its judgment, change into such states

notes.note: A diminutive, as is ψυχάριον below. It is belittling rather than fond; both are kept as “little”.
notes.other_reading: the poor body … the poor soul

notes.greek: μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει
notes.note: The verb πάσχειν (to suffer, to have something done to one) comes three times in two sentences and “suffer” is kept for all three. “Say so” fills in an object the Greek leaves out.
notes.other_reading: Let the body itself see to it, if it can, that nothing happens to it, and let it speak if anything does.

notes.note: Either “in general, in a word”, summing up the list, or “at all”, or “wholly”. It is taken as summing up, which is the usual sense where the word has no “not” beside it.
notes.other_reading: that forms any judgment at all about these things

notes.note: The two negatives with this verb form are read as the strong denial, “will certainly suffer nothing”, given as “nothing at all”.
notes.other_reading: need suffer nothing

notes.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην
notes.note: The verb is second person, “you will not lead it”, a sudden turn to “you” in a chapter otherwise about “it”; the turn is kept as the Greek gives it. From memory, unchecked, the form has been questioned. κρίσιν is “verdict” as in 6.52, to keep it apart from “judgment”.
notes.other_reading: for it will not be brought to judge so

notes.note: This word and ἔνδειαν in the next clause share the root for need, so “need” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: is self-sufficient, unless it creates a want for itself

notes.note: Each adjective is answered by its own verb in the next clause (ταράσσῃ, ἐμποδίζῃ); the pairs are kept as “undisturbed … disturbs” and “unhindered … hinders”.
notes.other_reading: untroubled and unobstructed

check.note: The English follows the Greek word for word, but “frighten itself into desire” is hard sense, and the text is probably at fault here. The reader will stumble and should be told why.
check.decided: Accepted: the literal “it does not frighten itself into desire” is kept and not smoothed, and the note now says plainly that the sense is hard and that the Greek is doubted here (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The doubled “itself” copies the Greek idiom and reads clumsily in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The ruling part does not make trouble for itself”. The Greek doubled pronoun is an idiom for “by its own doing”, which “for itself” carries, and “trouble” is kept for the verb.

check.note: A small Greek word sets “anyone else” against the ruling part itself, and the English dropped it.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “But if anyone else”, so that the contrast with the ruling part itself is heard.

check.note: “Turn itself into such turns” keeps the Greek word play at the cost of sense: it reads as if the ruling part became a turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “turn itself in such directions”. One “turn” keeps the image, and the note explains that verb and noun are the same word in Greek.

check.note: The word ὅλως can sum up the list (“in general”) or mean “at all”, and the English takes the first. “The judgments” also adds an article the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the article is dropped and the English reads “that in general forms judgments about these things”. “In general” stands, because the Greek word usually means “at all” only beside a “not”, and here it closes a list; the note gives the other reading.

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην
check.note: The sudden “you will lead” in a chapter otherwise in the third person is kept faithfully; the verb has been questioned, from memory. Nothing to change unless the Greek is judged at fault.
check.decided: Accepted: “for you will not lead it to such a verdict” stands, since that is what the Greek as given says, and the note now marks the change of person and that the form has been questioned (from memory, unchecked).

passages.casaubon: This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power. But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear. For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it. But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing. Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Ведущее начало само себя не тревожит; я имею в виду, например, что оно не доводит себя страхом до вожделения. Если же кто-то другой может его напугать или огорчить — пусть; ведь само оно, собственным суждением, не повернёт себя в такую сторону. Пусть само тельце заботится, если может, чтобы ничего не претерпеть, и пусть скажет, если что-то претерпевает. А маленькая душа — то, что боится, что огорчается, что вообще составляет суждения обо всём этом, — вовсе ничего не претерпит; ведь ты не приведёшь её к такому приговору. Ведущее начало, насколько зависит от него самого, ни в чём не нуждается, если только само не создаст себе нужды; и точно так же оно невозмутимо и беспрепятственно, если только само себя не возмущает и само себе не препятствует.

passages.greek: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ
passages.english: You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.

notes.note: περισσὰ is “more than is needed”. Three words in the sentence begin with περι- (περισσὰ, περιελεῖν, περιποιήσεις), a sound play English cannot keep.
notes.other_reading: Many of the things that trouble you are superfluous and you can remove them

notes.greek: ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα
notes.note: Literally “lying wholly upon your judgment”, with the preposition that gives “up to you” elsewhere in the section. The participle may give the reason; it is left as a plain description, since the Greek has no “since”. ὅλα is taken as “wholly”, not “all of them”.
notes.other_reading: since all of them lie in your own judgment

notes.note: Literally “wide space”, room to move. The image of space is kept.
notes.other_reading: a great deal of freedom

notes.note: “Already” or “at once”: the room comes with the stripping away, not later.
notes.other_reading: and you will already have made plenty of room for yourself

notes.note: The Greek as given stops here without a full stop: the sentence runs on in the rest of the chapter, which says by what means the room is made. Only what is given is translated, and the full stop that closes it is an addition.
notes.other_reading: and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself, …

check.greek: ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα
check.note: The participle may give the reason (“since they lie wholly in your judgment”) and not just a description. The preposition is also the one of the “up to you” idiom used elsewhere in the section, which “rest on” does not echo.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “things that rest wholly on your judgment”. The Greek has a bare participle and no word for “since”, so the reason is left for the reader to draw, as in the Greek; the note records the causal reading and the echo of “up to you”.

part.left_out: τῷ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον περιειληφέναι τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τὸν ἀίδιον αἰῶνα περινοεῖν καὶ τὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἑκάστου πράγματος ταχεῖαν μεταβολὴν ἐπινοεῖν, ὡς βραχὺ μὲν τὸ ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, ἀχανὲς δὲ τὸ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.30 at 'thou shalt have room enough' and begins its 9.31 with the rest of the chapter, from 'To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind'.

passages.casaubon: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Ты можешь отсечь многое лишнее из того, что тебя тревожит, — то, что целиком держится на твоём суждении, — и сразу освободишь для себя много простора.

passages.greek: Μηδὲν πλέον σαυτῷ λέγε ὧν αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι ἀναγγέλλουσιν. ἤγγελται ὅτι ὁ δεῖνά σε κακῶς λέγει. ἤγγελται τοῦτο· τὸ δέ, ὅτι βέβλαψαι, οὐκ ἤγγελται. βλέπω ὅτι νοσεῖ τὸ παιδίον. βλέπω· ὅτι δὲ κινδυνεύει, οὐ βλέπω. οὕτως οὖν μένε ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν καὶ μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε καὶ οὐδέν σοι γίνεται· μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων.
passages.english: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.

notes.note: The participle means “going before, leading the way”. It is most likely meant of time, the impressions that arrive first, which the later phrase “the first impressions” (τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν) supports; “lead the way” keeps it a different word from “first”, as it is in the Greek. It can also mean “leading, principal”.
notes.other_reading: than what the principal impressions report

notes.note: The image is of a messenger bringing news. The same verb returns three times (ἤγγελται) and “report” is kept for all of them.
notes.other_reading: than what the impressions that lead the way announce

notes.note: The Greek word for an unnamed person, “so-and-so”.
notes.other_reading: a certain person

notes.note: “The child”, a small child. The article may stand for “my”, which would make the example his own; the English leaves it as the Greek has it. “The child” is repeated in the next sentence, where the Greek leaves the subject unspoken.
notes.other_reading: I see that my child is sick.

notes.note: The verb is “say in addition”, to add a comment to what was reported. It is built on the “say” of the first sentence (λέγε) and returns in the last, so “say … further” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: and add nothing yourself from within

notes.note: A present, “nothing happens to you”, kept as a present. It could be heard as “nothing is the matter with you”.
notes.other_reading: and nothing comes of it for you

notes.note: The Greek has only “or rather, say further”. “Something” is supplied, and what is to be said is not spelled out.
notes.other_reading: Or rather, do add a comment

notes.greek: ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων
notes.note: The participle is “recognising, being acquainted with”, a little more than knowing: he is to speak as someone to whom each thing that happens is familiar. κόσμῳ is the glossary’s “universe”; “the world” would also fit.
notes.other_reading: as one who knows each thing that comes about in the world

check.note: The passage opens with “say” and closes twice with a compound of the same verb, “say in addition”. “Add” drops the saying, so the link between the first sentence and the last two is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “say nothing further yourself from within” and “do say something further”, so that the “say” of the first sentence is heard again at the end.

check.note: Two Greek words, “leading the way” and “first”, are both given as “first”. Marcus probably means the same impressions, but the difference is not visible.
check.decided: Accepted: the opening now reads “the impressions that lead the way”, and “first impressions” is kept for the later phrase, so that the two Greek words stay two in English. The note says that the same impressions are probably meant.

check.note: The article may stand for the possessive, “my child”, which would make the example Marcus’s own. The English leaves it neutral.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the child”. The Greek has only the article and no word for “my”, and English “the child” can be heard of one’s own child just as the Greek can; the note gives “my child”.

check.note: The Greek verb is to recognise or be acquainted with, a little more than to know.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe”.

passages.casaubon: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in the world.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Не говори себе ничего сверх того, что сообщают представления, идущие впереди. Сообщили, что такой-то говорит о тебе дурно. Это сообщили; а что тебе причинён вред — не сообщали. Я вижу, что ребёнок болен. Вижу; а что ребёнок в опасности — не вижу. Так всегда и оставайся при первых представлениях и сам изнутри ничего сверх них не говори — и с тобой ничего не случится. Или, вернее, говори и сверх них, как тот, кто узнаёт каждое событие в мироздании.

passages.greek: Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί. ἆρον οὖν ὅτε θέλεις τὴν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων.
passages.english: That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.

notes.note: The sentence opens with a bare “That”, with no verb of saying or remembering; it reads as a heading for something to keep in mind. It is kept bare, here and in 2.15, and no “remember” is added. πάντα is plural, “all things”, and returns in “all things steady”.
notes.other_reading: Remember that everything is what you judge it to be

notes.note: “And this is up to you”: the pronoun is feminine and points to the judgment, so the English reads “this judgment” to keep it from being heard as “this fact”.
notes.other_reading: and it is in your power

notes.note: The verb is to lift, and so to lift away, remove. The form is a single act, “take it away”.
notes.other_reading: So remove the judgment when you choose

notes.note: A sailing image: literally “just as to one who has bent round the cape”. The Greek has no “you” and no verb here; it may be felt as “for you, as for a sailor who …”.
notes.other_reading: and, like someone who has doubled the cape, you find calm

notes.greek: γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων
notes.note: Three items with no verb; “there is” and a colon are supplied. γαλήνη is the calm of the sea; σταθερὰ is steady, standing firm; ἀκύμων is literally “waveless”.
notes.other_reading: calm, everything still, and a waveless gulf

check.note: “As for someone” reads in English as “concerning someone”, so the comparison with a sailor who has rounded the headland can be missed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm”. “Just as” makes the comparison unmistakable; “you find” is not used, because the Greek has no verb and no “you” here.

check.note: The bare “That …” copies the Greek note form, but a reader of today may take it for a broken sentence; the same holds for 2.15. Any fix adds a word.
check.decided: Accepted: the bare “That” is kept, in the same form here and in 2.15, because the Greek has no verb of remembering and none may be added. The note explains that it reads as a heading.

check.note: The Greek has only “and this is up to you”; the English repeats the noun.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “and this judgment is up to you”. The Greek “this” is feminine and so can only point to the judgment, while a bare English “this” would be heard as “this fact”; the note says so.

check.note: Found while settling: the word for “all things” in the first sentence returns here, and the draft gave it as “everything”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all things steady”, so that the “all things” of the opening is heard again in the calm.

passages.casaubon: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Что всё — суждение, а суждение зависит от тебя. Так убери суждение, когда захочешь, — и, как для того, кто обогнул мыс, наступает тишь: всё неподвижно, и бухта без волны.

passages.greek: Μὴ τοιαῦτα ὑπολάμβανε, οἷα ὁ ὑβρίζων κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται, ἀλλὰ ἴδε αὐτά, ὁποῖα κατʼ ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν.
passages.english: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.

notes.note: The verb of the glossary’s “judgment” word, so “judge”. The Greek has no noun for what is judged (“such things as …”); “things” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: Do not take things the way the one who abuses you takes them

notes.note: The verb covers insult, outrage and high-handed ill-treatment, in word or act; “abuses” covers both word and act. “You” as its object is supplied from the σε that follows.
notes.other_reading: the person who insults you, the person who treats you with contempt

notes.greek: κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται
notes.note: κρίνειν is a different verb from ὑπολαμβάνειν, though close in sense. “Decide” is used for it so that the two can be told apart; its noun, κρίσις, is “verdict” in 6.52 and 7.16.
notes.other_reading: as the person who abuses you judges them, or wants you to judge them

notes.note: “See them”: the pronoun standing alone after its verb is the ordinary “them”. With more weight on it, it would be “look at the things themselves”.
notes.other_reading: but look at the things themselves, as they truly are

check.note: The Greek verb is wider and stronger than insulting: to treat with insolence, to abuse or wrong someone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the person who abuses you”, which covers ill-treatment in act as well as in word. The note records that “you” is supplied.

check.note: The pronoun may carry stress, “look at the things themselves”, as against the other person’s view of them; “them” gives only the weak sense.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “see them”. The pronoun stands alone after its verb, where Greek uses it as the ordinary “them”; the stressed sense would more naturally have the noun with it, as in 6.52. The note gives the stronger reading.

check.note: The verb is “decide” here, while its noun is “verdict” in 6.52 and 7.16, so the link between verb and noun is not visible.
check.decided: Declined: “decides” stays. “Judge” is already given to the other verb in this sentence, and the two Greek verbs have to be told apart; English has no plain verb made from “verdict”. The note names the noun and where it comes.

passages.casaubon: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Не суди о вещах так, как решает о них тот, кто тебя оскорбляет, или как он хочет, чтобы решил ты, но смотри, каковы они поистине.

passages.greek: Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. δῆλα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα· δῆλον δὲ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον τοῦ λεγομένου, ἐάν τις αὐτοῦ τὸ νόστιμον μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς δέχηται.
passages.english: That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.

notes.note: A bare “That …” again, as in 12.22, with no verb of remembering; none is added. From memory, unchecked: Monimus is credited with saying that everything supposed is smoke or vanity, in words built on this same root, and Marcus’s phrase echoes him.
notes.other_reading: Remember that all is opinion.

notes.greek: τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα
notes.note: The preposition can mean “to” or “in answer to, against”. It is taken as the replies made to Monimus, which gives the contrast with the next clause: the objections are plain, but so is the use. It can also be the words addressed to him, or more sharply the things said against him.
notes.other_reading: what was said to Monimus the Cynic is plain

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: Monimus of Syracuse, a Cynic philosopher of the fourth century BC, a follower of Diogenes. The Cynics were a school known for blunt speech and contempt for convention.

“What is said”, singular: it is taken as Monimus’s saying itself, that everything is judgment, set against the plural “things said” in answer to it. Both are the same Greek participle, which “said” and “saying” let the reader hear.
notes.other_reading: the usefulness of what is said

notes.note: A food word. From memory, unchecked, it is used both of what feeds well and of what tastes good, and so of the good part of a thing, the pith. “What is nourishing” keeps a food image and suits the talk of usefulness.
notes.other_reading: if one takes the savour of it

notes.note: Literally “up to the true”: the saying is to be taken so far as it is true and no further.
notes.other_reading: within the limits of what is true

check.greek: τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα
check.note: The preposition can mean “said to” or “said against, in reply to” Monimus. The English has chosen the reply, which decides what the whole remark is about.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “in answer to”, which covers replies and objections alike and gives the contrast with the next clause. The note now sets out the other readings, “said to” and “said against”.

check.note: “Enough” adds a shade of concession. The Greek balances two things and gives them the same plain word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying”, with nothing added to the first “plain”.

check.note: The Greek word is what is savoury or pleasant to taste, and so the good part of a thing. “Nourishing” moves the picture from flavour to food value.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “what is nourishing in it”. From memory, unchecked, the Greek word is used of food that feeds well as well as of food that tastes good, and “what is good in it” would drop the food image; the note gives the flavour reading.

check.note: The Greek sets a limit: take it up to the point where it is true and no further. “As far as the truth goes”, after a comma, reads as “as regards the truth”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true”, without the comma, so that the limit is heard.

check.note: The same participle is “what is said” in the plural and then “the saying” in the singular. A reader cannot tell that the two share a word or whose saying is meant.
check.decided: Declined: “the saying” stands. The Greek changes from plural to singular, one saying against the many replies, and “said” and “saying” let the shared word be heard; “what he said” would add a “he” the Greek does not have. The note says whose saying is meant.

passages.casaubon: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.
passages.russian: Что всё — суждение. Ведь то, что было сказано в ответ кинику Мониму, ясно; но ясна и польза изречения, если брать из него питательное, насколько оно истинно.

passages.greek: Σήμερον ἐξῆλθον πάσης περιστάσεως, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐξέβαλον πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλὰ ἔνδον ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν.
passages.english: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.

notes.note: Literally “what stands around”: one’s circumstances, and especially hard ones, a crisis. The picture matters, since he goes on to say it was not “outside” at all, so the English reads “all that hemmed me in”, where “me” is supplied. The Greek repeats the noun and the English repeats the phrase.
notes.other_reading: Today I got out of every difficulty, or rather I threw every difficulty out

notes.note: This verb and ἐξέβαλον both begin with ἐξ-, “out”: “went out of” against “threw out”. The pair is kept with “got out of” and “threw out”.
notes.other_reading: Today I escaped all that hemmed me in, or rather I cast it out

notes.note: No subject is expressed; “it” is supplied, meaning all that hemmed him in.
notes.other_reading: for they were not outside

notes.note: The Greek has only the article, “in the judgments”; the English reads “my”, as English does where Greek leaves the owner to be understood.
notes.other_reading: but within, in the judgments

check.note: The Greek word is literally what stands around one, the circumstances that hem one in. The play of going out, throwing out, outside and inside rests on that picture, which “difficulty” does not carry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in”. The phrase is repeated and not shortened to “it all”, because the Greek repeats the noun.

passages.casaubon: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Сегодня я выбрался из всего, что меня теснило, вернее, выбросил всё, что меня теснило: ведь оно было не снаружи, а внутри, в моих суждениях.

passages.greek:
Ἀνθρώπῳ οὐδενὶ συμβαίνειν τι δύναται ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνθρωπικὸν σύμπτωμα, οὐδὲ βοὶ ὃ οὐκ ἔστι βοικόν, οὐδὲ ἀμπέλῳ ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀμπελικόν, οὐδὲ λίθῳ ὃ οὐκ ἔστι λίθου ἴδιον. εἰ οὖν ἑκάστῳ συμβαίνει ὃ καὶ εἴωθε καὶ πέφυκε, τί ἂν δυσχεραίνοις; οὐ γὰρ ἀφόρητόν σοι ἔφερεν ἡ κοινὴ φύσις.

Εἰ μὲν διά τι τῶν ἐκτὸς λυπῇ, οὐκ ἐκεῖνό σοι ἐνοχλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν περὶ αὐτοῦ κρῖμα, τοῦτο δὲ ἤδη ἐξαλεῖψαι ἐπὶ σοί ἐστιν. εἰ δὲ λυπεῖ σέ τι τῶν ἐν τῇ σῇ διαθέσει, τίς ὁ κωλύων διορθῶσαι τὸ δόγμα; ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ εἰ λυπῇ ὅτι οὐχὶ τόδε τι ἐνεργεῖς ὑγιές σοι φαινόμενον, τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖς ἢ λυπῇ;—ἀλλὰ ἰσχυρότερόν τι ἐνίσταται.—μὴ οὖν λυποῦ· οὐ γὰρ παρὰ σὲ ἡ αἰτία τοῦ μὴ ἐνεργεῖσθαι.—ἀλλὰ οὐκ ἄξιον ζῆν μὴ ἐνεργουμένου τούτου.—ἄπιθι οὖν ἐκ τοῦ ζῆν εὐμενής, ᾗ καὶ ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἀποθνῄσκει, ἅμα ἵλεως τοῖς ἐνισταμένοις.
passages.english:
Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence, nor to an ox that is not of the ox kind, nor to a vine that is not of the vine kind, nor to a stone that is not proper to a stone. So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it? For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.

If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and it is in your power to wipe that out at once. But if what distresses you is something in your own disposition, who prevents you from putting your principle right? In the same way, if you are distressed because you are not doing some particular thing that seems sound to you, why not do it rather than be distressed? “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life kindly disposed, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.

notes.note: σύμπτωμα is a chance event, often a mishap. “Occurrence” keeps it neutral and keeps it apart from the verb “happen” (συμβαίνειν) beside it.
notes.other_reading: a mishap of the human kind

notes.note: The Greek plays on one root: the common nature “brought” (ἔφερεν) nothing that cannot be “borne” (ἀφόρητον). “Bringing” and “borne” are set close together, which is as near as English comes. The verb is imperfect, kept as “was bringing”; it can also be heard as “was never going to bring”.
notes.other_reading: For what the common nature brought you was not something unbearable.

notes.note: The nature common to all things, that is, the nature of the whole. “The common nature” is kept because the same phrase in 5.25 is set against the speaker’s own nature.
notes.other_reading: the nature that all things share

notes.note: The verb ranges from “be annoyed” to “find hard to bear”. “Resent” is used here and for the same verb in 10.3 and 7.64.
notes.other_reading: why would you be annoyed?

notes.note: κρῖμα is the finding one arrives at. The glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, so “verdict” stands for κρῖμα and κρίσις throughout this section.
notes.other_reading: your own judgment about it

notes.note: ἤδη can go with “wipe out” (“at once”) or with “is in your power” (“here and now, as things stand”). The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: and wiping that out is, here and now, in your power

notes.note: δόγμα is “principle” throughout this translation; here it is the belief a person holds, the thing in their own disposition that distresses them. “Your” renders the Greek article.
notes.other_reading: who prevents you from putting your belief right?

notes.note: The argument runs on one verb in four forms (ἐνεργεῖς, ἐνεργεῖσθαι, ἐνεργουμένου, ὁ ἐνεργῶν). “Do” and “be done” are kept for all of them. Elsewhere in this section the noun ἐνέργεια is “activity”.
notes.other_reading: you are not carrying out some particular activity

notes.note: ᾗ is “in the way that” or “just as”. ὁ ἐνεργῶν has no object: the English takes it as the person who does manage to do the thing, who also dies; it could be simply “the one who is active”.
notes.other_reading: in the same way as the active person dies too

notes.note: The form can be neuter (“the things that stand in the way”) or masculine (“the people who stand in the way”). The neuter is taken because the objection above speaks of “something stronger”.
notes.other_reading: gracious towards those who stand in your way

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀφόρητόν σοι ἔφερεν ἡ κοινὴ φύσις
check.note: The Greek plays on one root, “bring” and “not to be borne”, and the English loses the echo. “Was not bringing” is stiff and “the common nature” is hard for a reader of today to place.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “was bringing you nothing that could not be borne”, so that “bringing” and “borne” stand close together as the two Greek words do. “The common nature” is kept, because the same Greek phrase in 5.25 is set against the speaker’s own nature, and a note now explains it.

check.note: Here δόγμα is the belief one holds, and “principle” suggests a rule of conduct and makes the sentence hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “putting your principle right”. “Principle” stays for δόγμα because the glossary settles it and the same word returns in 4.49b; “your” is taken from the Greek article so that the sentence is clearly about something the person holds, and a note gives “belief”.

check.note: ἤδη can go with “wipe out” (at once) or with “is in your power” (here and now), and the English has chosen the first.
check.decided: Declined: ἤδη stands directly before “wipe out” in the Greek, so “to wipe that out at once” is a sound reading. The note gives the other, “here and now in your power”.

check.note: ὁ ἐνεργῶν has no object and can be “the one who does accomplish it” or simply “the one who is active”. “The way … dies” also suggests a manner of dying, where the Greek compares.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “just as the one who is doing it dies too”, since the Greek compares and does not describe a manner of dying. “Doing it” is kept so that one English verb runs through all four forms of the Greek verb; the note gives “the one who is active”.

check.note: The dative plural can be masculine or neuter, and “gracious” suits persons at least as well as things. The English has chosen things.
check.decided: Declined: the English has to choose one gender, and the neuter follows the “something stronger” that stands in the way two lines above. The note gives “those who stand in your way”.

passages.casaubon: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable. If therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt. But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee. Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men, thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Ни с каким человеком не может случиться ничего, что не было бы человеческим событием, ни с быком — ничего, что не было бы бычьим, ни с лозой — ничего, что не было бы свойственно лозе, ни с камнем — ничего, что не было бы присуще камню. Так если с каждым случается то, что для него и привычно, и естественно, зачем тебе негодовать? Ведь общая природа не несла тебе ничего такого, что нельзя было бы вынести.

Если ты огорчаешься из-за чего-то внешнего, то тебя тревожит не оно, а твоя собственная оценка его, и в твоей власти сразу её стереть. Если же тебя огорчает что-то в твоём собственном расположении, кто мешает тебе исправить свой принцип? Точно так же, если ты огорчаешься оттого, что не делаешь какого-то определённого дела, которое кажется тебе здравым, почему бы не сделать его, вместо того чтобы огорчаться? «Но на пути стоит что-то более сильное». Тогда не огорчайся: ведь причина того, что дело не делается, не в тебе. «Но не стоит жить, если это не сделано». Тогда уходи из жизни благожелательно — так же, как умирает и тот, кто это делает, — и при этом благосклонно к тому, что стоит на пути.

passages.greek:
Μηδενὶ ἐξέστω εἰπεῖν ἀληθεύοντι περὶ σοῦ ὅτι οὐχ ἁπλοῦς ἢ ὅτι οὐκ ἀγαθός, ἀλλὰ ψευδέσθω, ὅστις τούτων τι περὶ σοῦ ὑπολήψεται. πᾶν δὲ τοῦτο ἐπὶ σοί· τίς γὰρ ὁ κωλύων ἀγαθὸν εἶναί σε καὶ ἁπλοῦν; σὺ μόνον κρῖνον μηκέτι ζῆν, εἰ μὴ τοιοῦτος ἔσῃ· οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱρεῖ λόγος μὴ τοιοῦτον ὄντα.

Τί ἐστι τὸ ἐπὶ ταύτης τῆς ὕλης δυνάμενον κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πραχθῆναι ἢ ῥηθῆναι; ὅ τι γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο ᾖ, ἔξεστιν αὐτὸ πρᾶξαι ἢ εἰπεῖν καὶ μὴ προφασίζου ὡς κωλυόμενος. Οὐ πρότερον παύσῃ στένων πρὶν ἢ τοῦτο πάθῃς, ὅτι οἷόν ἐστι τοῖς ἡδυπαθοῦσιν ἡ τρυφή; τοιοῦτό σοι τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς ὑποβαλλομένης καὶ ὑποπιπτούσης ὕλης ποιεῖν τὰ οἰκεῖα τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῇ· ἀπόλαυσιν γὰρ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν πᾶν ὃ ἔξεστι κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν φύσιν ἐνεργεῖν. πανταχοῦ δὲ ἔξεστι. τῷ μὲν οὖν κυλίνδρῳ οὐ πανταχοῦ δίδοται φέρεσθαι τὴν ἰδίαν κίνησιν οὐδὲ τῷ ὕδατι οὐδὲ πυρὶ οὐδὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὅσα ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς ἀλόγου διοικεῖται· τὰ γὰρ διείργοντα καὶ ἐνιστάμενα πολλά· νοῦς δὲ καὶ λόγος διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ἀντιπίπτοντος οὕτως πορεύεσθαι δύναται ὡς πέφυκε καὶ ὡς θέλει. ταύτην τὴν ῥᾳστώνην πρὸ ὀμμάτων τιθέμενος, καθ’ ἣν ἐνεχθήσεται ὁ λόγος διὰ πάντων ὡς πῦρ ἄνω, ὡς λίθος κάτω, ὡς κύλινδρος κατὰ πρανοῦς, μηκέτι μηδὲν ἐπιζήτει· τὰ γὰρ λοιπὰ ἐγκόμματα ἤτοι τοῦ σωματίου ἐστὶ τοῦ νεκροῦ, ἢ χωρὶς ὑπολήψεως καὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ τοῦ λόγου ἐνδόσεως οὐ θραύει οὐδὲ ποιεῖ κακὸν οὐδ’ ὁτιοῦν. ἐπεί τοι καὶ ὁ πάσχων αὐτὸς κακὸς ἂν εὐθὺς ἐγίνετο· ἐπὶ γοῦν τῶν ἄλλων κατασκευασμάτων πάντων, ὅ τι ἂν κακόν τινι αὐτῶν συμβῇ, παρὰ τοῦτο χεῖρον γίνεται αὐτὸ τὸ πάσχον, ἐνταῦθα δέ, εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, καὶ κρείττων γίνεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἐπαινετώτερος, ὀρθῶς χρώμενος τοῖς προσπίπτουσιν. ὅλως δὲ μέμνησο ὅτι τὸν φύσει πολίτην οὐδὲν βλάπτει ὃ πόλιν οὐ βλάπτει, οὐδέ γε πόλιν βλάπτει ὃ νόμον οὐ βλάπτει· τούτων δὲ τῶν καλουμένων ἀκληρημάτων οὐδὲν βλάπτει νόμον. ὃ τοίνυν νόμον οὐ βλάπτει, οὔτε πόλιν οὔτε πολίτην.
passages.english:
Let it not be possible for anyone to say truthfully of you that you are not straightforward or that you are not good, but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be mistaken. All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward? You have only to decide not to go on living unless you are going to be such a person, for reason does not require you to live either, if you are not such a person.

With this material, what can be done or said in the soundest way? For whatever it is, it is possible to do it or say it, and do not make the excuse that you are being prevented. You will not stop groaning until this has come over you: that what luxury is to those who live for pleasure, that, for you, is doing the things that belong to the way a human being is made, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand. For one must judge to be an enjoyment everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature. And it is possible everywhere. Now a cylinder is not granted everywhere to be carried along in its own motion, nor is water, nor fire, nor the other things that are governed by nature or by a soul without reason: for the things that bar them and stand in their way are many. But mind and reason can make their way through everything that falls against them, as is their nature and as they wish. Set this ease before your eyes, the ease with which reason will be carried through all things as fire is carried up, as a stone down, as a cylinder down a slope, and look for nothing more. For the remaining obstacles either belong to the little body, the dead thing, or, without a judgment and the giving in of reason itself, they break no one and do nothing bad at all. Otherwise the one affected would themselves at once become bad. At any rate with all other made things, whatever bad thing happens to any of them, the thing affected itself becomes worse because of it. But here, if it must be said, the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them. In general, remember that nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city, and nothing harms the city that does not harm the law. And of these so-called strokes of bad luck not one harms the law. So what does not harm the law harms neither city nor citizen.

notes.note: ἁπλοῦς is literally “single, simple”: a person with no folds or double dealing. “Straightforward” is used.
notes.other_reading: that you are not simple

notes.note: The verb covers both saying what is false and being mistaken. Since the person is said to “judge”, not to speak, the English has “be mistaken”; set against “say truthfully” it could also be “be saying what is false”.
notes.other_reading: but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be saying what is false

notes.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱρεῖ λόγος μὴ τοιοῦτον ὄντα
notes.note: αἱρεῖ λόγος is a fixed phrase for what reason dictates or what the argument proves; literally reason “takes” or “chooses”. The clause is elliptical: “you to live” is supplied from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: for reason does not choose life either for one who is not such

notes.note: The text as given puts a question mark here, which would make the first clause a question. That breaks the pair οἷον … τοιοῦτο (“what … that”), so the English sets the mark aside and reads one statement running on. The capital on Οὐ is the edition’s paragraph inside chapter 33, not a new chapter.
notes.other_reading: Will you not stop groaning before you have come to feel what luxury is to those who live for pleasure? That is what it is for you to do …

notes.note: Literally “until you undergo this”: the point is to come to feel it, not merely to think it.
notes.other_reading: until you experience this

notes.note: κατασκευή is how a thing is built or constituted. “The way a human being is made” lets the link to κατασκευασμάτων further on (“made things”) be heard.
notes.other_reading: what belongs to the human constitution

notes.note: The Greek is impersonal (“one must”), so “one” is kept. ὑπολαμβάνειν is the verb of ὑπόληψις (“judgment”), so “judge” is kept, though “count as” is the more natural English.
notes.other_reading: For you should count as enjoyment everything …

notes.note: A cylinder or roller, the stock Stoic example of a thing that moves by its own shape once pushed. The Greek word is the name of the solid, so “cylinder” is kept.
notes.other_reading: a roller

notes.note: “Without reason” can go with “soul” alone or with both nouns. The English takes it with “soul” alone: in Stoic terms plants are governed by “nature” and animals by a soul that lacks reason.
notes.other_reading: by a nature or a soul that is without reason

notes.note: σωμάτιον is a diminutive of “body”, used slightingly; “little body” is written wherever it occurs. τοῦ νεκροῦ calls the body “the corpse” or “the dead thing”.
notes.other_reading: belong to this poor body, the corpse

notes.note: ἔνδοσις is a slackening or giving way, here of reason itself. “Giving in” is used.
notes.other_reading: and the surrender of reason itself

notes.note: The verb has no object in the Greek. “No one” is supplied, because the same verb is used of the person (“broken”) in 4.49b.
notes.other_reading: they do not crush

notes.note: The argument runs on κακόν, κακός, χεῖρον. “Bad”, “bad”, “worse” are kept so that the chain shows, and “harm” is kept for βλάπτει at the end of the chapter.
notes.other_reading: would at once become evil himself

notes.note: Literally “if one must say it”. The first καί is taken with the second as “both … and”; it can also be “even” or “actually”, in contrast with “becomes worse” just before.
notes.other_reading: But here, if one may say so, the human being actually becomes better and more praiseworthy

notes.note: Literally “the by-nature citizen”: the human being as a citizen, by nature, of the city that is the universe. φύσει could also be taken loosely as “the true citizen”.
notes.other_reading: the true citizen

notes.note: ἀκλήρημα is a piece of bad luck, literally a bad lot drawn. It is a different word from ἀτύχημα (“misfortune”) used in 4.49.
notes.other_reading: these so-called misfortunes

check.greek: ἀλλὰ ψευδέσθω, ὅστις τούτων τι περὶ σοῦ ὑπολήψεται
check.note: The “but” is dropped. The verb of the relative clause is future and is about thinking, not speaking, so “be saying what is false” narrows the command to speech.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now runs on with “but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be mistaken”, which restores the “but” and the future and no longer limits the verb to speech. “Judge” is kept for the verb, as the glossary keeps “judgment” for its noun.

check.greek: σὺ μόνον κρῖνον μηκέτι ζῆν, εἰ μὴ τοιοῦτος ἔσῃ
check.note: The English can be read as “decide to stop living only if”. In the Greek “only” goes with the command: “you have only to resolve”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “You have only to decide not to go on living unless you are going to be such a person”, so that “only” goes with the command. “Decide” is kept for κρίνω, as in 4.39.

check.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱρεῖ λόγος μὴ τοιοῦτον ὄντα
check.note: The Greek is elliptical and “you to live” is rightly supplied, but the verb is said to be “decides for, approves”, which is weaker than “require”.
check.decided: Declined: αἱρεῖ λόγος is a fixed phrase for what reason dictates, so “require” gives its usual force, and “approve” would be a different verb. The note now gives the literal “choose” as the other reading.

check.note: The Greek as given has a question mark in the middle of the pair “what … such”, so the sentence as punctuated does not construe. The English reads through it as one statement, and that should be recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stays one statement, and the note says that the question mark of the text as given has been set aside and gives the question as the other reading.

check.note: The inverted “such for you is doing … the things that …” is hard to follow at first reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that is what it is for you to do, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand, the things that belong to the way a human being is made”.

check.greek: ἀπόλαυσιν γὰρ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν πᾶν ὃ ἔξεστι κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν φύσιν ἐνεργεῖν
check.note: The dangling “it …, everything” is awkward English, where the Greek order is plain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For one must judge everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature to be an enjoyment”, which removes the dangling “it”. “Judge” is kept, since the verb is the one whose noun is “judgment” later in the chapter.

check.note: The word here is a thing that rolls, and “cylinder” is a geometry word in English today; “roller” is proposed.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek word is itself the name of the solid, and the image of a cylinder on a slope is the stock Stoic one, clear in English as it stands. The note gives “roller”.

check.note: The verb has no object and means that the obstacles do not crush the person. “They break nothing” turns it into a statement about objects.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they break no one and do nothing bad at all”, so that the verb is about the person. “Break” is kept because the same verb is “broken” in 4.49b, and a note says that “no one” is supplied.

check.greek: καὶ ὁ πάσχων αὐτὸς κακὸς ἂν εὐθὺς ἐγίνετο
check.note: The word for “himself” is dropped, and “as well” leaves the reader asking as well as what.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Otherwise the one affected would themselves at once become bad”, which restores the emphatic pronoun and drops “as well”. “Themselves” is used because the Greek does not single out a man.

check.note: The first καί can be “even, actually” and not “both”, in contrast with “becomes worse” just before. The parenthesis is literally “if one must say it”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “if it must be said” now gives δεῖ its force. “Both better and more praiseworthy” stays, because the two καί most naturally pair the two comparatives; a note gives “actually becomes better”.

check.note: “The citizen by nature” is unclear in English; it means the one who is a citizen by nature.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city”.

passages.casaubon: Let it not be in any man's power, to say truly of thee, that thou art not truly simple, or sincere and open, or not good. Let him be deceived whosoever he be that shall have any such opinion of thee. For all this doth depend of thee. For who is it that should hinder thee from being either truly simple or good? Do thou only resolve rather not to live, than not to be such. For indeed neither doth it stand with reason that he should live that is not such. What then is it that may upon this present occasion according to best reason and discretion, either be said or done? For whatsoever it be, it is in thy power either to do it, or to say it, and therefore seek not any pretences, as though thou wert hindered. Thou wilt never cease groaning and complaining, until such time as that, what pleasure is unto the voluptuous, be unto thee, to do in everything that presents itself, whatsoever may be done conformably and agreeably to the proper constitution of man, or, to man as he is a man. For thou must account that pleasure, whatsoever it be, that thou mayest do according to thine own nature. And to do this, every place will fit thee. Unto the _cylindrus_, or roller, it is not granted to move everywhere according to its own proper motion, as neither unto the water, nor unto the fire, nor unto any other thing, that either is merely natural, or natural and sensitive; but not rational for many things there be that can hinder their operations. But of the mind and understanding this is the proper privilege, that according to its own nature, and as it will itself, it can pass through every obstacle that it finds, and keep straight on forwards. Setting therefore before thine eyes this happiness and felicity of thy mind, whereby it is able to pass through all things, and is capable of all motions, whether as the fire, upwards; or as the stone downwards, or as the _cylindrus_ through that which is sloping: content thyself with it, and seek not after any other thing. For all other kind of hindrances that are not hindrances of thy mind either they are proper to the body, or merely proceed from the opinion, reason not making that resistance that it should, but basely, and cowardly suffering itself to be foiled; and of themselves can neither wound, nor do any hurt at all. Else must he of necessity, whosoever he be that meets with any of them, become worse than he was before. For so is it in all other subjects, that that is thought hurtful unto them, whereby they are made worse. But here contrariwise, man (if he make that good use of them that he should) is rather the better and the more praiseworthy for any of those kind of hindrances, than otherwise. But generally remember that nothing can hurt a natural citizen, that is not hurtful unto the city itself, nor anything hurt the city, that is not hurtful unto the law itself. But none of these casualties, or external hindrances, do hurt the law itself; or, are contrary to that course of justice and equity, by which public societies are maintained: neither therefore do they hurt either city or citizen.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Пусть никто не сможет правдиво сказать о тебе, что ты не прямодушен или что ты не добр; пусть всякий, кто соберётся судить о тебе что-то такое, ошибается. Всё это в твоей власти: ведь кто мешает тебе быть добрым и прямодушным? Тебе надо лишь решить не жить дальше, если ты не будешь таким, ведь и разум не требует, чтобы ты жил, если ты не таков.

Что с этим материалом можно сделать или сказать самым здравым образом? Ведь что бы это ни было, это можно сделать или сказать, и не отговаривайся тем, что тебе мешают. Ты не перестанешь стонать, пока тебя не проймёт вот что: чем для живущих ради наслаждения служит роскошь, тем для тебя — делать то, что свойственно устройству человека, с материалом, который дан и оказался под рукой. Ведь удовольствием следует считать всё, что можно делать в согласии со своей природой. А это возможно везде. Цилиндру же не везде дано нестись своим движением, и воде тоже, и огню, и прочему, что управляется природой или душой, лишённой разума: ведь много того, что их сдерживает и встаёт у них на пути. А ум и разум могут пробиться сквозь всё, что на них обрушивается, так, как свойственно их природе и как они хотят. Поставь перед глазами эту лёгкость, с которой разум будет нестись сквозь всё, как огонь вверх, камень вниз, цилиндр по склону, — и ничего больше не ищи. Ведь прочие препятствия либо относятся к маленькому телу, мёртвой вещи, либо без суждения и уступки самого разума никого не ломают и вообще ничего дурного не делают. Иначе затронутый ими сам тотчас стал бы дурным. Во всяком случае, у всех прочих устроенных вещей, что бы дурное ни случилось с любой из них, сама затронутая вещь от этого становится хуже. А здесь, если уж надо так сказать, человек становится и лучше, и достойнее похвалы, правильно пользуясь тем, что с ним случается. Вообще помни, что тому, кто по природе гражданин, не вредит ничто, что не вредит городу, а городу не вредит ничто, что не вредит закону. А из этих так называемых ударов злой судьбы ни один не вредит закону. Что же не вредит закону, не вредит ни городу, ни гражданину.

passages.greek: Ἀβιάστως διαζῆσαι ἐν πλείστῃ θυμηδίᾳ, κἂν πάντες καταβοῶσιν ἅτινα βούλονται, κἂν τὰ θηρία διασπᾷ τὰ μελύδρια τοῦ περιτεθραμμένου τούτου φυράματος. τί γὰρ κωλύει ἐν πᾶσι τούτοις τὴν διάνοιαν σῴζειν ἑαυτὴν ἐν γαλήνῃ καὶ κρίσει τῇ περὶ τῶν περιεστηκότων ἀληθεῖ καὶ χρήσει τῶν ὑποβεβλημένων ἑτοίμῃ, ὥστε τὴν μὲν κρίσιν λέγειν τῷ προσπίπτοντι· τοῦτο ὑπάρχεις κατ’ οὐσίαν, κἂν κατὰ δόξαν ἀλλοῖον φαίνῃ· τὴν δὲ χρῆσιν λέγειν τῷ ὑποπίπτοντι· σὲ ἐζήτουν· ἀεὶ γάρ μοι τὸ παρὸν ὕλη ἀρετῆς λογικῆς καὶ πολιτικῆς καὶ τὸ σύνολον τέχνης ἀνθρώπου ἢ θεοῦ· πᾶν γὰρ τὸ συμβαῖνον θεῷ ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐξοικειοῦται καὶ οὔτε καινὸν οὔτε δυσμεταχείριστον, ἀλλὰ γνώριμον καὶ εὐεργές.
passages.english: To live life through unforced and in the greatest gladness, even if everyone is shouting whatever they like against you, even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you. For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm, in a true verdict on what stands around it, and in a ready use of what is put before it, so that the verdict says to what befalls, “This is what you are in reality, even if in opinion you look like something else,” and the use says to what comes to hand, “You are what I was looking for. For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue, and in general for the craft of a human being or a god”? For everything that happens is made akin to a god or a human being, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and easy to work.

notes.note: The sentence is a bare infinitive with no main verb: it can be a command to oneself, a wish, or a statement of what is possible. The English leaves it as an infinitive. ἀβιάστως is “without being forced”, free of any constraint.
notes.other_reading: Live your life through without constraint

notes.note: The Greek has no object for “shout against”, and none for “around” in the next clause; “you” is supplied twice, since Marcus is addressing himself.
notes.other_reading: even if everyone cries out whatever they like

notes.note: φύραμα is a kneaded lump, dough or paste: the body. The participle comes from a verb used of something that sets or curdles around a thing, and can also be heard as “fed to growth around”. μελύδρια before it is a diminutive, “little limbs”.
notes.other_reading: of this paste that has been fed up around you

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary; here the faculty is meant, so “the mind”.
notes.other_reading: prevents thought from keeping itself

notes.note: κρίσις is the act of judging and its result. “Verdict” is used because the glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις; here the verdict is then made to speak.
notes.other_reading: in a true judgment about its circumstances

notes.greek: ὥστε τὴν μὲν κρίσιν λέγειν τῷ προσπίπτοντι
notes.note: The result clause is still part of the question, so the English carries the question through both speeches and puts the question mark after the second.
notes.other_reading: … what is put before it? Then the verdict says to what befalls: …

notes.note: κατ’ οὐσίαν and κατὰ δόξαν set what the thing is against what it is thought or reputed to be. “In reality” stands for the literal “in substance”; δόξα covers both “opinion” and “reputation”.
notes.other_reading: This is what you are in substance, even if by common report you look like something else

notes.note: The Greek has no quotation marks. The English ends the speech of “use” after “a human being or a god”; it could end after “looking for”, or run on to the end of the chapter.
notes.other_reading: “You are what I was looking for.” For to me what is present is always …

notes.note: Two verbs are set side by side: προσπίπτω, what falls on the mind (“befalls”), and ὑποπίπτω, what falls under its hand as stuff to work with (“comes to hand”).
notes.other_reading: to what falls under it

notes.note: “Of a citizen”, the virtue of one who lives in a community. “Political” would mislead in today’s English.
notes.other_reading: rational and social virtue

notes.note: The datives can go with “happens” (“everything that happens to a god or a human being”) or with the verb, as the English takes them. The verb means to make a thing one’s own, akin to one or at home with one.
notes.other_reading: For everything that happens to a god or a human being is made their own

notes.note: Said of material that is easy to work, which keeps up the image of “material” and “craft”.
notes.other_reading: easy to deal with

check.greek: ὥστε τὴν μὲν κρίσιν λέγειν τῷ προσπίπτοντι
check.note: The result clause is still part of the question in the Greek, but the English closes the question and starts a fragment with “So that”. “It” after “befalls” is also supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the question now runs on through “so that the verdict says …” and “the use says …”, and the question mark comes after the second speech, as the Greek construction has it. “It” after “befalls” is dropped.

check.note: “In substance … in opinion” is abstract; the Greek contrast is between what the thing really is and what it is taken to be.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “This is what you are in reality, even if in opinion you look like something else”. “Opinion” is kept for δόξα, which is wider than repute and is the word behind “add to it by opinion” in 7.64.

check.greek: πᾶν γὰρ τὸ συμβαῖνον θεῷ ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐξοικειοῦται
check.note: The English ends the speech of “use” before this sentence and takes the datives with the verb, both without a sign. “Is made to belong to” is also unclear for a verb that means “is made akin to, at home with”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is now “is made akin to”. The speech of “use” still ends before this sentence and the datives still go with the verb, and the notes on σὲ ἐζήτουν and on this clause give the other readings.

passages.casaubon: Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy pampered mass of flesh. For what in either of these or the like cases should hinder the mind to retain her own rest and tranquillity, consisting both in the right judgment of those things that happen unto her, and in the ready use of all present matters and occasions? So that her judgment may say, to that which is befallen her by way of cross: this thou art in very deed, and according to thy true nature: notwithstanding that in the judgment of opinion thou dust appear otherwise: and her discretion to the present object; thou art that, which I sought for. For whatsoever it be, that is now present, shall ever be embraced by me as a fit and seasonable object, both for my reasonable faculty, and for my sociable, or charitable inclination to work upon. And that which is principal in this matter, is that it may be referred either unto the praise of God, or to the good of men. For either unto God or man, whatsoever it is that doth happen in the world hath in the ordinary course of nature its proper reference; neither is there anything, that in regard of nature is either new, or reluctant and intractable, but all things both usual and easy.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Прожить жизнь без принуждения и в величайшей радости, даже если все кричат против тебя что им вздумается, даже если звери рвут на куски маленькие части этого комка теста, загустевшего вокруг тебя. Ведь что во всём этом мешает уму сохранять себя в покое, в верном приговоре тому, что его окружает, и в готовом использовании того, что перед ним положено, так чтобы приговор говорил тому, что выпадает: «Вот что ты есть в действительности, хотя по мнению и кажешься чем-то иным», а использование говорило тому, что попадает под руку: «Ты — то, что я искал. Ведь для меня настоящее — всегда материал для разумной и гражданской добродетели и вообще для мастерства человека или бога»? Всё, что случается, сделано родственным богу или человеку, и оно ни ново, ни трудно в обращении, но привычно и податливо в работе.

passages.greek:
Ὅπου ἔργον ἐπιτελεῖσθαι δύναται κατὰ τὸν κοινὸν θεοῖς καὶ ἀνθρώποις λόγον, ἐκεῖ οὐδὲν δεινόν· ὅπου γὰρ ὠφελείας τυχεῖν ἔξεστι διὰ τῆς εὐοδούσης καὶ κατὰ τὴν κατασκευὴν προιούσης ἐνεργείας, ἐκεῖ οὐδεμίαν βλάβην ὑφορατέον.

Πανταχοῦ καὶ διηνεκῶς ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ συμβάσει θεοσεβῶς εὐαρεστεῖν καὶ τοῖς παροῦσιν ἀνθρώποις κατὰ δικαιοσύνην προσφέρεσθαι καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ φαντασίᾳ ἐμφιλοτεχνεῖν, ἵνα μή τι ἀκατάληπτον παρεισρυῇ.
passages.english:
Where a piece of work can be completed in accordance with the reason that gods and human beings have in common, there is nothing to fear there. For where it is possible to gain benefit through an activity that travels a good road and goes forward in accordance with the way we are made, no harm is to be suspected there.

Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present, and to work with a craftsman’s care on the present impression, so that nothing slips in that has not been grasped.

notes.note: δεινόν is “terrible, to be feared”. No verb is expressed.
notes.other_reading: there nothing is terrible

notes.note: Literally “having a good road”, travelling well: a stock Stoic image for activity that flows as it should. The road is kept.
notes.other_reading: an activity that prospers

notes.note: Literally “in accordance with the constitution”, with no word for whose. The first person plural is supplied, and the wording matches the same word in 10.33.
notes.other_reading: in accordance with one’s constitution

notes.note: To look at something from under the brows: to suspect or eye with apprehension.
notes.other_reading: no harm need be feared there

notes.note: The same word, “present”, comes three times (παρούσῃ, παροῦσιν, παρούσῃ) and is kept three times. σύμβασις is what has come about, the event or turn of things.
notes.other_reading: with what is happening to you now

notes.note: An adverb, “in a god-revering way”. The plural “gods” is the usual sense of the compound; the word does not itself say singular or plural.
notes.other_reading: piously

notes.note: A rare compound: to practise one’s craft lovingly on something. The impression is treated as stuff to be worked on with care.
notes.other_reading: to apply your skill to the present impression

notes.note: A Stoic term: an impression that has not been “grasped”, that is, not tested and securely taken hold of before assent.
notes.other_reading: so that nothing unexamined slips in

check.note: The verb is “to go well, to have a clear way”. “Keeps to” adds the idea of an agent holding a course.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “an activity that travels a good road”, which drops the added idea of holding a course. The road is kept because the Greek verb has it.

check.note: The person whose constitution is meant is supplied; the Greek has only “the constitution”. The point is noted as harmless, with no change proposed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as the point itself proposes, and the note says what is supplied.

passages.casaubon: Where the matter may be effected agreeably to that reason, which both unto the Gods and men is common, there can be no just cause of grief or sorrow. For where the fruit and benefit of an action well begun and prosecuted according to the proper constitution of man may be reaped and obtained, or is sure and certain, it is against reason that any damage should there be suspected. In all places, and at all times, it is in thy power religiously to embrace whatsoever by God's appointment is happened unto thee, and justly to converse with those men, whom thou hast to do with, and accurately to examine every fancy that presents itself, that nothing may slip and steal in, before thou hast rightly apprehended the true nature of it.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian:
Где дело может быть исполнено согласно разуму, общему у богов и людей, там нечего бояться. Ведь где можно получить пользу через деятельность, которая идёт добрым путём и продвигается сообразно нашему устройству, там не следует подозревать никакого вреда.

Всюду и без перерыва в твоей власти, благоговея перед богами, быть вполне довольным настоящим стечением событий, справедливо обходиться с людьми, которые сейчас рядом, и с тщанием мастера трудиться над настоящим представлением, чтобы не вкралось ничего не постигнутого.

passages.greek: Ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ ἡγεμονικῷ κακὸν σὸν οὐχ ὑφίσταται οὐδὲ μὴν ἔν τινι τροπῇ καὶ ἑτεροιώσει τοῦ περιέχοντος. ποῦ οὖν; ὅπου τὸ περὶ κακῶν ὑπολαμβάνον σοί ἐστι. τοῦτο οὖν μὴ ὑπολαμβανέτω καὶ πάντα εὖ ἔχει. κἂν τὸ ἐγγυτάτω αὐτοῦ, τὸ σωμάτιον, τέμνηται, καίηται, διαπυίσκηται, σήπηται, ὅμως τὸ ὑπολαμβάνον περὶ τούτων μόριον ἡσυχαζέτω· τουτέστι, κρινέτω μήτε κακόν τι εἶναι μήτε ἀγαθόν, ὃ ἐπίσης δύναται κακῷ ἀνδρὶ καὶ ἀγαθῷ συμβαίνειν. ὃ γὰρ καὶ τῷ παρὰ φύσιν καὶ τῷ κατὰ φύσιν βιοῦντι ἐπίσης συμβαίνει, τοῦτο οὔτε κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν οὔτε παρὰ φύσιν.
passages.english: What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you. Where, then? In the place where you have what judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well. Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet. That is, let it decide that what can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good. For what happens equally to the one who lives against nature and to the one who lives in accordance with nature is neither in accordance with nature nor against nature.

notes.note: Literally “a bad thing of yours”, “your evil”. “Bad” is used for κακόν throughout the section so that it matches “a bad man” below.
notes.other_reading: No evil of yours has its being in another’s ruling part

notes.note: A term for having real existence or subsistence.
notes.other_reading: does not lie in

notes.note: “What surrounds” is usually the surrounding air or environment. Since the next sentence calls the body “what is nearest”, it could also mean the body as the envelope around the ruling part. “What surrounds you” leaves both open; “you” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: of the body that encloses you

notes.note: Literally “let this not judge”: no object is given. The sense is “let it not form the judgment that something is bad”.
notes.other_reading: So let it make no such judgment

notes.note: Diminutive of “body”, used slightingly; “little body” throughout this section.
notes.other_reading: this poor body

notes.note: A medical word: to suppurate, to fill with pus.
notes.other_reading: suppurates

notes.note: κρίνω stands beside ὑπολαμβάνω: “judge” is kept for the second (the verb of ὑπόληψις) and “decide” for the first.
notes.other_reading: let it judge that nothing is either bad or good

notes.note: The Greek has ἀνήρ, a man, so “man” is kept.
notes.other_reading: to a bad person and a good one

check.note: “You” is supplied. The phrase can mean the surroundings or the body that encloses the ruling part; the English allows both, so no change is proposed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as the point itself proposes. The note says that “you” is supplied and gives the reading that takes the phrase of the body.
