passages.casaubon: In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction, yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil. For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature, and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Дурное для тебя существует не в чужом ведущем начале и не в каком-либо повороте и превращении того, что тебя окружает. Где же? Там, где у тебя то, что судит о дурном. Так пусть оно не судит — и всё хорошо. Даже если ближайшее к нему, тельце, режут, жгут, если оно гноится, гниёт, всё равно пусть та часть, что судит об этом, хранит тишину. То есть пусть она решит: то, что может одинаково случиться с дурным человеком и с хорошим, — ни дурное, ни хорошее. Ведь то, что случается одинаково с живущим против природы и с живущим согласно с природой, — ни согласно с природой, ни против природы.

passages.greek: Ἀτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τοῦτό μοι συνέβη. οὐμενοῦν ἀλλʼ εὐτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τούτου μοι συμβεβηκότος ἄλυπος διατελῶ, οὔτε ὑπὸ παρόντος θραυόμενος οὔτε ἐπιὸν φοβούμενος. συμβῆναι μὲν γὰρ τὸ τοιοῦτο παντὶ ἐδύνατο, ἄλυπος δὲ οὐ πᾶς ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἂν διετέλεσε. διὰ τί οὖν ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ἀτύχημα ἢ τοῦτο εὐτύχημα; λέγεις δὲ ὅλως ἀτύχημα ἀνθρώπου, ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπότευγμα τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; ἀπότευγμα δὲ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἶναι δοκεῖ σοι, ὃ μὴ παρὰ τὸ βούλημα τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ ἐστι; τί οὖν; τὸ βούλημα μεμάθηκας· μήτι οὖν τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῦτο κωλύει σε δίκαιον εἶναι, μεγαλόψυχον, σώφρονα, ἔμφρονα, ἀπρόπτωτον, ἀδιάψευστον, αἰδήμονα, ἐλεύθερον, τἄλλα, ὧν συμπαρόντων ἡ φύσις ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀπέχει τὰ ἴδια; μέμνησο λοιπὸν ἐπὶ παντὸς τοῦ εἰς λύπην σε προαγομένου τούτῳ χρῆσθαι τῷ δόγματι· οὐχ ὅτι τοῦτο ἀτύχημα, ἀλλὰ τὸ φέρειν αὐτὸ γενναίως εὐτύχημα.
passages.english: “I am unfortunate, because this has happened to me.” No, rather: “I am fortunate, because although this has happened to me I go on undistressed, neither broken by what is present nor afraid of what is coming.” For a thing of this kind could have happened to anyone, but not everyone would have gone on undistressed at it. Why then is that a misfortune rather than this a piece of good fortune? And do you call anything at all a human being’s misfortune that is not a failure of the human being’s nature? And does anything seem to you to be a failure of the human being’s nature that is not against what that nature wills? Well then: you have learned what it wills. Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free, and the rest, the things with which, when they are present together, the human being’s nature has in full what is its own? From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”

notes.note: The passage begins part-way through the chapter. The Greek has no quotation marks; they are added for the two things said. The argument plays on ἀτυχής, εὐτυχής, ἀτύχημα, εὐτύχημα, so “unfortunate, fortunate, misfortune, good fortune” are kept.
notes.other_reading: Unlucky me, that this has happened to me.

notes.note: “Without λύπη”. λύπη is “distress” throughout the section, and “pain” is kept for πόνος.
notes.other_reading: I go on free of pain

notes.note: A “miss”, a failure to hit the mark. It shares its root with ἀτύχημα (“misfortune”), which English cannot show: a misfortune of a human being must be a missing of human nature’s mark.
notes.other_reading: a miscarriage of human nature

notes.note: Literally “the will of his nature”, that is, of the human being’s nature. “What that nature wills” avoids “his” for ἄνθρωπος.
notes.other_reading: against the purpose of his nature

notes.note: Literally “great-souled”: a person too large in spirit to be shaken by what happens.
notes.other_reading: great-souled

notes.note: A Stoic term: not “falling forward”, that is, not rushing into assent before a thing is clear.
notes.other_reading: unhurried in assent

notes.note: The word can be passive (“not deceived, not in error”) or active (“not deceiving, truthful”). After “not rash” it is taken as passive.
notes.other_reading: truthful

notes.note: Having αἰδώς: a sense of shame and of respect for others. “Modest” narrows it.
notes.other_reading: self-respecting

notes.note: ἀπέχω is the word used on receipts, “to have received in full”. Human nature, when these qualities are present, has been paid what is its own.
notes.other_reading: has received all that belongs to it

notes.note: λοιπόν can be “from now on” or a plain “so then”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: So then, remember

notes.note: “Nobly”, as befits good birth; it also covers “bravely”.
notes.other_reading: to bear it bravely

check.greek: ἀπότευγμα δὲ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἶναι δοκεῖ σοι, ὃ μὴ παρὰ τὸ βούλημα τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ ἐστι
check.note: “It … when it” has nothing to refer to. The Greek has a relative clause: does that seem a failure which is not against what the nature wills.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And does anything seem to you to be a failure of the human being’s nature that is not against what that nature wills?”, with a relative clause as in the Greek.

check.note: “Great-souled” is a translator’s word, not one in use today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “great-hearted”, and a note gives the literal “great-souled”.

check.note: The word can be passive, “not deceived, not in error”, or active, “truthful”. The English has chosen the first; “free from error” is proposed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not deceived”, which is plainer than “undeceived” and keeps the passive sense beside “not rash”. “Free from error” is not used because “free” closes the same list; the note gives “truthful”.

check.greek: ὧν συμπαρόντων ἡ φύσις ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀπέχει τὰ ἴδια
check.note: In the Greek the nature is the subject and “has in full” what is its own. The English makes the qualities the givers and loses “in full”.
check.decided: Accepted: the nature is now the subject: “the things with which, when they are present together, the human being’s nature has in full what is its own”.

check.note: The word here is “from now on” or “so then”. “For the rest” suggests “as for the remainder”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “From now on, remember”. The word is rendered once, as “from now on”, and a note gives “so then”.

part.left_out: Ὅμοιον εἶναι τῇ ἄκρᾳ, ᾗ διηνεκῶς τὰ κύματα προσρήσσεται· ἡ δὲ ἕστηκε καὶ περὶ αὐτὴν κοιμίζεται τὰ φλεγμήναντα τοῦ ὕδατος.
part.why: The 1634 translation gives the chapter's opening image of the promontory as its own section 4.40 and begins its 4.41 here, at 'Oh, wretched I'.

passages.casaubon: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself, as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great happiness.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: «Я несчастлив, потому что со мной случилось это». Нет, лучше так: «Я счастлив, потому что, хотя со мной это и случилось, я остаюсь без огорчения, не сломленный настоящим и не страшащийся грядущего». Ведь нечто подобное могло случиться с каждым, но не каждый остался бы при этом без огорчения. Почему же скорее то — несчастье, чем это — счастье? И разве ты вообще называешь несчастьем человека то, что не есть промах природы человека? И разве кажется тебе промахом природы человека то, что не идёт против того, чего эта природа хочет? Так вот: чего она хочет, ты узнал. Разве это случившееся мешает тебе быть справедливым, великодушным, владеющим собой, благоразумным, неопрометчивым, необманутым, скромным, свободным и прочим — тем, с чем, когда всё это вместе налицо, природа человека полностью обладает своим? Впредь при всём, что ведёт тебя к огорчению, не забывай пользоваться этим принципом: не «это несчастье», а «благородно перенести это — счастье».

passages.english:
What is not harmful to the city does not harm the citizen either. At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either. And if the city is harmed, one should not be angry, but should show the one who harms the city what is being overlooked.

Think often of the speed with which the things that are and the things that come to be are carried past and drawn away. For the substance of things is like a river in unbroken flow, the activities are in continual change, the causes in countless turns, and almost nothing stands still, even what is close at hand. And the boundlessness of the past and of the future is a yawning gulf in which all things vanish. How then is a person not a fool who, among these things, is puffed up, or torn about, or complains bitterly, as though at something that troubled them for a time, and a long one?

Remember the whole substance of things, of which you have the smallest share; and the whole of time, of which a brief, momentary interval has been marked off for you; and fate: how small a part of it are you?

Someone else does me some wrong? That is for them to see to: they have their own disposition, their own activity. I now have what the common nature wants me to have now, and I do what my own nature wants me to do now.

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: these words are thought to be an editor’s supplement, the manuscripts running straight from “one should not be angry” to “with the one who harms the city”. The English translates the text as given.
notes.other_reading: one should not be angry with the one who harms the city: what is it that is being overlooked?

notes.note: Literally “what the thing being overlooked is”. The Greek does not say who overlooks it; in context it is the person doing the harm.
notes.other_reading: what it is that they are failing to see

notes.note: The stuff of which things are made, “substance” or “being”. “Of things” is supplied here and in “the whole substance of things” in the next chapter, so that the word is not read as a bare term of the schools.
notes.other_reading: For all that exists is like a river

notes.note: The phrase is uncertain. As punctuated in the text given, it closes the clause: “almost nothing stands still, even what is close at hand”. With other punctuation and a small correction (from memory, unchecked) it opens the next clause, about the gulf of past and future that lies close beside one.
notes.other_reading: and almost nothing stands still. And close beside you is the boundless gulf of the past and of the future

notes.note: “Yawning, gaping”: used as a noun for an abyss. “Is” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: is an abyss

notes.note: Literally “pulled” or “convulsed”: dragged this way and that. Paired with “puffed up” it seems to mean being torn about by events.
notes.other_reading: or racked

notes.greek: ὡς ἔν τινι χρόνῳ καὶ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἐνοχλήσαντι
notes.note: The phrase is hard as given and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked; a future participle has been proposed). The English takes τινι as the “something” that troubled the person and χρόνῳ as “for a time”; τινι can also go with χρόνῳ, “in some span of time”.
notes.other_reading: as though the thing that troubled them belonged to some span of time, and a long one

notes.note: αἰών is time without limit. The English has “the whole of time” and not “eternity”.
notes.other_reading: the whole of eternity

notes.note: From a word for something too short to be cut: a hair’s breadth, an instant.
notes.other_reading: a short, hair’s-breadth interval

notes.note: πόστος asks “which in the series?”, “what fraction?”. The question mark stands in the text given, so the sentence turns into a question at its end.
notes.other_reading: of which you are what fraction of a part?

notes.note: ἁμαρτάνω is to miss, to go wrong; with the words for “against” and the speaker it is to wrong someone.
notes.other_reading: Someone else makes some mistake against me?

notes.note: Literally “he will see”: an idiom for “that is his affair, let him look to it”. The Greek subject is singular (“another”); “they” is used as the glossary allows.
notes.other_reading: He will see to that

notes.note: The nature common to all things, the nature of the whole, set here against the speaker’s own nature. The same phrase is “the common nature” in 8.46.
notes.other_reading: universal nature

check.note: The participle is present, “what is being overlooked”. The English perfect leaves it unclear that the oversight is the wrongdoer’s own and still going on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what it is that is being overlooked”, which gives the present tense. The passive is kept because the Greek does not name who overlooks, and the note gives “what it is that they are failing to see”; “should” is also repeated before “show” so that the clause is not read as a command.

check.note: “Substance” without an article is a term of philosophy, and a reader of today needs something plainer. The same word returns below and the two should stay alike.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the substance of things” here and “the whole substance of things” in the next chapter, so the two stay alike and the bare term is gone. “All that exists” is not used because “the things that are” has just rendered a different Greek phrase in the sentence before.

check.greek: καὶ σχεδὸν οὐδὲν ἑστὼς καὶ τὸ πάρεγγυς· τὸ δὲ ἄπειρον
check.note: The last words of the clause do not construe easily. The English takes them with what goes before, which the text as given allows; the other reading takes them forward and needs a correction.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the reading that the given punctuation allows, and the note now marks the phrase as uncertain and gives the other reading.

check.note: “Gap” is too small a word for the boundless past and future in which all things vanish.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a yawning gulf”.

check.greek: ὡς ἔν τινι χρόνῳ καὶ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἐνοχλήσαντι
check.note: The Greek is hard as given. The English uses τινι twice (“something” and “some length of time”) and ends in a doubling, “for some length of time, and for long”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as though at something that troubled them for a time, and a long one”, so that τινι is rendered once. The note says the phrase is doubted and gives the other construction.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “among such things” for a Greek word that is “these”, pointing back to the flowing things just listed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “among these things”.

passages.casaubon: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this, neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen that is thought to have done the wrong. Again, often meditate how swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux; and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves, subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost, that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this, and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time? Consider the whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together, of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Что не вредит городу, то не вредит и гражданину. При всяком представлении, будто тебе причинён вред, применяй это правило: если городу это не вредит, то и мне не причинено вреда. А если городу вредят, не надо гневаться, а надо показать тому, кто вредит городу, что́ упущено из виду.

Часто думай о том, с какой быстротой проносится мимо и уносится прочь всё, что есть, и всё, что возникает. Ведь вещество — как река в непрерывном течении, действия — в постоянных переменах, причины — в бесчисленных поворотах, и почти ничто не стоит на месте, даже то, что рядом. А беспредельность прошлого и будущего — зияющая бездна, в которой всё исчезает. Как же не глупец тот, кто среди всего этого надувается спесью, или мечется, или горько жалуется, будто на нечто, донимавшее его какое-то время, да ещё долгое?

Помни обо всём веществе, в котором у тебя ничтожнейшая доля; и обо всём времени, из которого тебе отмерен краткий, мгновенный промежуток; и о роке — какая же малая ты его часть?

Кто-то другой поступает со мной дурно? Это его дело: у него своё расположение, своя деятельность. У меня сейчас то, что общая природа хочет, чтобы у меня было сейчас, и я делаю то, что моя природа хочет, чтобы я делал сейчас.

passages.greek: Ἐπὶ μὲν παντὸς πόνου πρόχειρον ἔστω ὅτι οὐκ αἰσχρὸν οὐδὲ τὴν διάνοιαν τὴν κυβερνῶσαν χείρω ποιεῖ· οὔτε γὰρ καθὸ λογική ἐστιν οὔτε καθὸ κοινωνικὴ διαφθείρει αὐτήν. ἐπὶ μέντοι τῶν πλείστων πόνων καὶ τὸ τοῦ Ἐπικούρου σοι βοηθείτω, ὅτι οὔτε ἀφόρητον οὔτε αἰώνιον, ἐὰν τῶν ὅρων μνημονεύῃς καὶ μὴ προσδοξάζῃς. κἀκείνου δὲ μέμνησο, ὅτι πολλὰ πόνῳ τὰ αὐτὰ ὄντα λανθάνει, δυσχεραινόμενα· οἷον τὸ νυστάζειν καὶ τὸ καυματίζεσθαι καὶ τὸ ἀνορεκτεῖν· ὅταν οὖν τινι τούτων δυσαρεστῇς, λέγε ἑαυτῷ, ὅτι πόνῳ ἐνδίδως.
passages.english: At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse, for it does not ruin the mind either in so far as it is rational or in so far as it is social. With most pains, though, let Epicurus’s saying help you as well: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion. And remember this too: that many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”

notes.note: Literally “the thought that steers”, the image of a helmsman. διάνοια here is the faculty, so “mind”.
notes.other_reading: the understanding that steers you

notes.note: To destroy or corrupt. The subject is still the pain.
notes.other_reading: it does not corrupt it

notes.note: “The thing of Epicurus”: a saying of his. Epicurus (341 to 270 BC) founded the rival school; Marcus borrows from him here.
notes.other_reading: the remark of Epicurus

notes.note: The adjectives are neuter though “pain” is masculine: “it is a thing neither unbearable nor everlasting”.
notes.other_reading: that pain is neither past bearing nor without end

notes.note: “The limits”: Epicurus taught that pain has limits in strength and in length. The Greek does not say whose limits; “its limits” is the likely sense.
notes.other_reading: if you remember its limits

notes.note: An Epicurean word: to add an opinion on top of what is actually felt.
notes.other_reading: and do not add your own imaginings

notes.note: Literally “many things, being the same as pain, escape notice, being resented”: they are resented without its being noticed that they are pain. “As such” is supplied, and the bare participle is turned into a clause with a first-person plural subject.
notes.other_reading: many things that are found disagreeable are, unnoticed, the same as pain

notes.note: To suffer from heat: either hot weather or the heat of a fever.
notes.other_reading: being feverish

notes.note: The Greek is reported speech with a second-person verb, and has the third-person reflexive ἑαυτῷ for “yourself”. The English turns it into direct speech.
notes.other_reading: tell yourself that you are giving in to pain

check.note: The Greek is a bare participle; “though”, the subject of “resent” and “as such” are supplied. The supplement is fair and no change is proposed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as the point itself proposes, and the note lists the words supplied.

passages.casaubon: What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind, that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all, can be made worse. For neither in regard of the substance of it, nor in regard of the end of it (which is, to intend the common good) can it alter and corrupt it. This also of Epicurus mayst thou in most pains find some help of, that it is 'neither intolerable, nor eternal;' so thou keep thyself to the true bounds and limits of reason and give not way to opinion. This also thou must consider, that many things there be, which oftentimes unsensibly trouble and vex thee, as not armed against them with patience, because they go not ordinarily under the name of pains, which in very deed are of the same nature as pain; as to slumber unquietly, to suffer heat, to want appetite: when therefore any of these things make thee discontented, check thyself with these words: Now hath pain given thee the foil; thy courage hath failed thee.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: При всякой боли держи под рукой вот что: она не постыдна и не делает хуже ум, стоящий у руля, ведь она не губит его ни в том, в чём он разумен, ни в том, в чём он общественен. При большинстве же болей пусть помогает тебе и изречение Эпикура: что боль ни невыносима, ни вечна, если ты помнишь о пределах и ничего не добавляешь к ней мнением. И помни ещё вот что: многое, что тождественно боли, не замечается как боль, хотя мы им тяготимся, — например, сонливость, перегрев и отсутствие аппетита. Поэтому, когда тебе неприятно что-то из этого, говори себе: «Ты поддаёшься боли».

passages.greek: Μή σε συγχείτω ἡ τοῦ ὅλου βίου φαντασία, μὴ συμπερινόει ἐπίπονα οἷα καὶ ὅσα πιθανὸν ἐπιγεγενῆσθαι, ἀλλὰ καθ’ ἕκαστον τῶν παρόντων ἐπερώτα σεαυτόν· τί τοῦ ἔργου τὸ ἀφόρητον καὶ ἀνύποιστον; αἰσχυνθήσῃ γὰρ ὁμολογῆσαι. ἔπειτα ἀναμίμνῃσκε σεαυτὸν ὅτι οὔτε τὸ μέλλον οὔτε τὸ παρῳχηκὸς βαρεῖ σε, ἀλλ’ ἀεὶ τὸ παρόν, τοῦτο δὲ κατασμικρύνεται, ἐὰν αὐτὸ μόνον περιορίσῃς καὶ ἀπελέγχῃς τὴν διάνοιαν, εἰ πρὸς τοῦτο ψιλὸν ἀντέχειν μὴ δύναται.
passages.english: Do not let the impression of your whole life confound you. Do not take in at one sweep of thought what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you. Instead, at each of the things present, ask yourself: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it. Then remind yourself that it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and show your mind up if it cannot hold out against the present stripped bare.

notes.note: “The impression of the whole life”: the picture of one’s life taken all at once. “Your” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: the picture of your life as a whole

notes.note: Literally “pour together”: to throw into confusion.
notes.other_reading: Do not let it overwhelm you

notes.note: A compound: to go round a number of things together in thought, to take them in at once.
notes.other_reading: do not think over all together

notes.note: The form is a perfect infinitive, “to have come on (you)”, where the sense may seem to want a future, “are likely to come”. The English translates the perfect as it stands: the picture of a whole life includes what is past, and the chapter goes on to name the past beside the future. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed the future here.
notes.other_reading: what hardships and how many are likely to come on you

notes.note: “The task” or “the business in hand”; it can also be loosely “the matter”.
notes.other_reading: What is there in this that is unbearable

notes.note: The Greek does not say what would be admitted: either what the unbearable thing is, or that there is one.
notes.other_reading: For you will be ashamed to confess what it is

notes.note: “Is made small”, passive. The English has “shrinks”.
notes.other_reading: and this is cut down to size

notes.note: ἀπελέγχω is to refute or convict by cross-examination, and so to expose. “Show up” keeps both the exposure and the shame, and is the English for the same root (ἐλέγξειν) in 1.17a. διάνοια here is the faculty, “mind”.
notes.other_reading: and convict your mind; or: and put your mind to shame

notes.note: “Bare, stripped”: the present on its own, without the past and future added. It is a different word from “alone” (μόνον) just before.
notes.other_reading: against this alone

check.note: The Greek as given is a perfect infinitive and the English follows it. But the thought points to troubles still to come, and from memory editors read a future here.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek as given has the perfect and it construes, so the English follows it; the chapter itself goes on to name the past beside the future. The note gives the future reading and says that it rests on memory.

check.note: The adjective means “by itself, stripped of the rest”, and “this bare thing” is odd English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “against this, stripped bare”, which removes “this bare thing” and keeps the image. “Alone” is not used because it already renders a different Greek word in the same sentence.

passages.casaubon: Let not the general representation unto thyself of the wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee. Let not thy mind wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other. But as everything in particular doth happen, put this question unto thyself, and say: What is it that in this present matter, seems unto thee so intolerable? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess it. Then upon this presently call to mind, that neither that which is future, nor that which is past can hurt thee; but that only which is present. (And that also is much lessened, if thou dost lightly circumscribe it:) and then check thy mind if for so little a while, (a mere instant), it cannot hold out with patience.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.russian: Пусть тебя не сбивает с толку представление обо всей твоей жизни. Не охватывай одним махом мысли, какие тяготы и сколько их, вероятно, на тебя обрушилось. Вместо этого о каждом из того, что есть сейчас, спрашивай себя: «Что в этом деле невыносимого и нестерпимого?» Ведь тебе будет стыдно признаться. Затем напомни себе, что тебя тяготит не будущее и не прошлое, а всегда настоящее; а оно съёживается, если ты отграничишь его само по себе и пристыдишь свой ум, если он не может выстоять против голого настоящего.

passages.greek:
Τὸ τὰ ἀδύνατα διώκειν μανικόν· ἀδύνατον δὲ τὸ τοὺς φαύλους μὴ τοιαῦτά τινα ποιεῖν.

Οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ συμβαίνει ὃ οὐχὶ πέφυκε φέρειν. ἄλλῳ τὰ αὐτὰ συμβαίνει καὶ ἤτοι ἀγνοῶν ὅτι συμβέβηκεν, ἢ ἐπιδεικνύμενος μεγαλοφροσύνην, εὐσταθεῖ καὶ ἀκάκωτος μένει. δεινὸν οὖν ἄγνοιαν καὶ ἀρέσκειαν ἰσχυροτέρας εἶναι φρονήσεως.

Τὰ πράγματα αὐτὰ οὐδ’ ὁπωστιοῦν ψυχῆς ἅπτεται οὐδὲ ἔχει εἴσοδον πρὸς ψυχὴν οὐδὲ τρέψαι οὐδὲ κινῆσαι ψυχὴν δύναται, τρέπει δὲ καὶ κινεῖ αὐτὴ ἑαυτὴν μόνη καὶ οἵων ἂν κριμάτων καταξιώσῃ ἑαυτήν, τοιαῦτα ἑαυτῇ ποιεῖ τὰ προσυφεστῶτα.
passages.english:
To chase after impossible things is madness. And it is impossible that bad people should not do things of this kind.

Nothing happens to anyone that they are not fitted by nature to bear. The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.

Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all, nor do they have a way in to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul. But it alone turns and moves itself, and whatever kind of verdicts it thinks itself worthy to pass, of that kind it makes for itself the things that stand before it.

notes.note: φαῦλος is “of poor quality, mean”: in Stoic use, everyone who is not wise. It is not the same word as κακός, which is “bad” elsewhere in this section; κακός does not occur in this passage.
notes.other_reading: that inferior people should not do such things

notes.note: “Some such things”: the Greek does not say which. Marcus has some particular offence in mind.
notes.other_reading: should not act in some such way

notes.note: πέφυκε is “is so made by nature”. The subject is the person, not the thing. “Fitted by nature to bear” is used here and in 10.3.
notes.other_reading: that it is not in their nature to bear

notes.note: ἀρέσκεια is the wish to please or to make an impression on others. It picks up “showing off greatness of mind”.
notes.other_reading: ignorance and vanity

notes.note: “Terrible”, also “strange, shocking”.
notes.other_reading: It is a strange thing, then

notes.note: φρόνησις is practical wisdom, good sense in living.
notes.other_reading: stronger than good sense

notes.note: “Itself, itself, alone”: the soul is both what turns and what is turned, and nothing else does it.
notes.other_reading: but it turns and moves itself, by itself

notes.note: κρῖμα, a finding or verdict; “verdict” throughout the section, with “judgment” kept for ὑπόληψις.
notes.other_reading: whatever judgments it thinks itself worthy of

notes.note: Literally “of whatever verdicts it thinks itself worthy”. “To pass” is supplied; the phrase can also be heard as the verdicts the soul thinks fit for itself.
notes.other_reading: and whatever verdicts it thinks it deserves

notes.note: A rare word: the things that “stand there besides”, that is, that present themselves to the soul from outside. Its exact force is not certain.
notes.other_reading: the things that present themselves to it

check.note: The Greek is the plain word for bad or inferior people, and “worthless” adds contempt.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “bad people”. The note says that the Greek word is not the one rendered “bad” elsewhere in the section.

check.greek: τρέπει δὲ καὶ κινεῖ αὐτὴ ἑαυτὴν μόνη
check.note: The “but” is dropped, though the sentence answers the one before. “Itself, alone” reads as “in solitude”, where the Greek means “it alone”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But it alone turns and moves itself”, which restores the “but” and makes “alone” mean that nothing else does it.

check.note: The English is literal and obscure. The phrase can also mean “whatever verdicts it sees fit to pass”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whatever verdicts it thinks itself worthy to pass”. “Thinks itself worthy” is kept because the Greek verb has the soul as its own object; “to pass” is supplied to make the phrase clear, and a note says so.

check.note: “Such it makes for itself the things that stand before it” is inverted and old-fashioned in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it makes the things that stand before it to be of that kind for itself”. “Stand before it” is kept for the rare Greek word, with its note.

passages.casaubon: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things. Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true prudence? As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have any co-existence with her.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Гнаться за невозможным — безумие. А невозможно, чтобы дурные люди не делали подобного.

Ни с кем не случается ничего, что он по природе не способен вынести. С кем-то другим случается то же самое, и он — либо потому, что не знает о случившемся, либо потому, что выставляет напоказ величие духа, — стоит твёрдо и остаётся невредим. Ужасно же, что незнание и желание угодить сильнее мудрости.

Сами вещи вовсе никак не касаются души, и нет у них доступа в душу, и они не могут ни повернуть, ни сдвинуть душу. Но она одна поворачивает и движет себя сама, и какие приговоры она сочтёт себя достойной вынести, такими она и делает для себя вещи, которые перед ней предстают.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ κυριεῦον τῆς ψυχῆς σου μέρος ἄτρεπτον ἔστω ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ λείας ἢ τραχείας κινήσεως καὶ μὴ συγκρινέσθω, ἀλλὰ περιγραφέτω αὑτὸ καὶ περιοριζέτω τὰς πείσεις ἐκείνας ἐν τοῖς μορίοις. ὄταν δὲ ἀναδιδῶνται κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν συμπάθειαν εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν ὡς ἐν σώματι ἡνωμένῳ, τότε πρὸς μὲν τὴν αἴσθησιν φυσικὴν οὖσαν οὐ πειρατέον ἀντιβαίνειν, τὴν δὲ ὑπόληψιν τὴν ὡς περὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ μὴ προστιθέτω τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Let the ruling and governing part of your soul not be turned by the smooth or rough motion in the flesh, and let it not be blended in, but let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body. But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a unified body, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural; but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad.

notes.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ κυριεῦον τῆς ψυχῆς σου μέρος
notes.note: Here ἡγεμονικόν is an adjective with “part” and is paired with a second word, “being master”. At the end of the passage it stands alone as “the ruling part”.
notes.other_reading: The part of your soul that leads and is master

notes.note: “Not turned”: unmoved, unaltered. “Turn” is kept because the same verb is used of the soul in 5.19.
notes.other_reading: let it be unmoved

notes.note: “Smooth or rough motion” is the language of the pleasure schools (Cyrenaic and Epicurean) for pleasure and pain. Marcus uses their terms.
notes.other_reading: by pleasure or pain in the flesh

notes.note: To be combined or compounded with something. The Greek does not say with what, the motion or the flesh, and the English leaves it unsaid too.
notes.other_reading: and let it not be blended with that motion

notes.note: What is undergone: the states the flesh is put into. “Feelings” narrows it a little.
notes.other_reading: those affections

notes.note: “In the parts”: the parts of the body where the feelings arise. “Of the body” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: within the limbs

notes.note: The text given has a slip in the breathing; it is read as ὅταν, “when”.
notes.other_reading: whenever

notes.note: Obscure, and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked). συμπάθεια is the technical term for a feeling shared between joined parts, not pity, so “shared feeling”. What “the other” is set against is not said; it may be the shared feeling of mind with body, as distinct from that of one bodily part with another.
notes.other_reading: by that other sympathy which joins mind and body

notes.note: διάνοια as the faculty, “mind”.
notes.other_reading: into thought

notes.greek: τὴν ὡς περὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ
notes.note: Literally “the judgment as about a good or a bad thing”.
notes.other_reading: the judgment that treats it as good or evil

check.note: “Unturned by” is not English in this sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let the ruling and governing part of your soul not be turned by”.

check.note: “With it” is supplied, and the reader cannot tell whether “it” is the motion or the flesh. The Greek has no object.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and let it not be blended in, but let it draw a line around itself”. No object is supplied, since the Greek has none and “them” would choose one; the “but” of the Greek is also restored.

check.note: “The parts” alone is unclear; the parts of the body are meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “within the parts of the body”. “Where they arise” is not added, since the Greek has only “in the parts”.

check.note: No reader of today will understand “the other sympathy”. The Greek is itself obscure and has been doubted, and “sympathy” here is the technical sense of a shared feeling, not pity.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by the other shared feeling, as in a body that is one”. “Shared feeling” replaces “sympathy”, which today means pity; “the other” and “as in” stay as the Greek has them, and the note marks the phrase as uncertain.

passages.casaubon: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members. But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural. However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling, which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
passages.russian: Пусть ведущее и правящее начало твоей души не поворачивается от гладкого или шершавого движения в плоти и пусть не смешивается с ним, а очертит вокруг себя границу и замкнёт эти чувства в частях тела. Но когда они поднимаются в ум через то другое, совместное чувство, как в едином теле, тогда не надо пытаться противиться ощущению, которое естественно; но пусть ведущее начало не прибавляет от себя суждения, что это нечто хорошее или дурное.

passages.greek: Πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον ἤτοι οὕτω συμβαίνει ὡς πέφυκας αὐτὸ φέρειν ἢ ὡς οὐ πέφυκας αὐτὸ φέρειν. εἰ μὲν οὖν συμβαίνει σοι ὡς πέφυκας φέρειν. μὴ δυσχέραινε, ἀλλ’ ὡς πέφυκας φέρε. εἰ δὲ ὡς μὴ πέφυκας φέρειν, μὴ δυσχέραινε· φθαρήσεται γάρ σε ἀπαναλῶσαν. μέμνησο μέντοι ὅτι πέφυκας φέρειν πᾶν, περὶ οὗ ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει ἐστὶ τῇ σῇ φορητὸν καὶ ἀνεκτὸν αὐτὸ ποιῆσαι κατὰ φαντασίαν τοῦ συμφέρειν ἢ καθήκειν σεαυτῷ τοῦτο ποιεῖν.
passages.english: Everything that happens either happens in such a way that you are fitted by nature to bear it, or in such a way that you are not fitted by nature to bear it. So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do. And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up. Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable, through the impression that it is good for you, or is your duty, to do so.

notes.note: “You are so made by nature.” The word comes six times and one phrase is kept for it each time.
notes.other_reading: you are naturally able to bear it

notes.note: The text given has a full stop after φέρειν where the sense needs a comma; the English reads one sentence.
notes.other_reading: bear, do not be annoyed

notes.note: Literally “for it will be destroyed, having used you up”: what cannot be borne ends with the one it destroys.
notes.other_reading: for it will come to an end when it has consumed you

notes.greek: ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει ἐστὶ τῇ σῇ
notes.note: “It is up to your judgment”: the same construction as “in your power” (ἐπὶ σοί) elsewhere.
notes.other_reading: which it is in the power of your judgment to make bearable

notes.note: Two near-synonyms. The first is from the same root as “bear” (φέρειν).
notes.other_reading: bearable and tolerable

notes.greek: κατὰ φαντασίαν τοῦ συμφέρειν ἢ καθήκειν
notes.note: συμφέρειν (“to be good for”) echoes φέρειν (“to bear”), a play English cannot keep. καθήκειν is the Stoic word for what it is appropriate or due for one to do; the English has “is your duty”.
notes.other_reading: by picturing it as to your advantage, or as fitting for you

notes.note: “To do this” most naturally means to make the thing bearable, that is, to bear it.
notes.other_reading: to act so

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural constitution either able, or not able to bear. If thou beest able, be not offended, but bear it according to thy natural constitution, or as nature hath enabled thee. If thou beest not able, be not offended. For it will soon make an end of thee, and itself, (whatsoever it be) at the same time end with thee. But remember, that whatsoever by the strength of opinion, grounded upon a certain apprehension of both true profit and duty, thou canst conceive tolerable; that thou art able to bear that by thy natural constitution.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Всё, что случается, случается либо так, что ты по природе способен это вынести, либо так, что ты по природе не способен это вынести. Итак, если это случается с тобой так, что ты по природе способен вынести, не негодуй, а выноси, как ты по природе способен. А если так, что ты по природе не способен вынести, не негодуй: ведь оно погибнет, истощив тебя. Помни, однако, что ты по природе способен вынести всё, что от твоего собственного суждения зависит сделать выносимым и терпимым, через представление, что так поступать тебе во благо или что это твой долг.

passages.greek: Ὃ θέλει, ἔξωθεν προσπιπτέτω τοῖς παθεῖν ἐκ τῆς προσπτώσεως ταύτης δυναμένοις. ἐκεῖνα γάρ, ἐὰν θελήσῃ, μέμψεται τὰ παθόντα, ἐγὼ δέ, ἐὰν μὴ ὑπολάβω ὅτι κακὸν τὸ συμβεβηκός, οὔπω βέβλαμμαι· ἔξεστι δέ μοι μὴ ὑπολαβεῖν.
passages.english: Let whatever likes fall from outside on the things that can be affected by this falling. For those things, once affected, will complain if they like. But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed. And it is possible for me not to judge so.

notes.note: Literally “what wishes”: let whatever likes to, fall. The same verb returns in “if they like”.
notes.other_reading: Let anything that wants to fall from outside

notes.greek: τοῖς παθεῖν ἐκ τῆς προσπτώσεως ταύτης δυναμένοις
notes.note: A neuter plural, “the things that can be affected”: the parts of the body. προσπιπτέτω and προσπτώσεως are the same word, verb and noun, so “fall” and “falling” are kept.
notes.other_reading: on the parts that can suffer from this impact

notes.note: A singular verb with the neuter plural subject “those things”: “if they like”.
notes.other_reading: if it wishes

notes.note: To blame or find fault.
notes.other_reading: will find fault

notes.note: οὔπω is “not yet”, which is kept; it can be weaker, “not so far”, “not at all as things stand”.
notes.other_reading: I am not harmed

notes.note: ὑπολαμβάνω is the verb of ὑπόληψις (“judgment”). The Greek has no “so”; it is added.
notes.other_reading: And I am free not to suppose it

check.note: The English reads at first as “whatever is going to fall”. The Greek verb is “wants”: let whatever wishes to, fall.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let whatever likes fall from outside on the things that are able to be affected by this falling”. “This falling” is kept because the Greek has “this”.

check.note: The same verb opens the passage, where the draft had “will”, so the echo between the two places is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “likes” and “if they like”, so the one Greek verb is heard in both places.

passages.casaubon: Of things that are external, happen what will to that which can suffer by external accidents. Those things that suffer let them complain themselves, if they will; as for me, as long as I conceive no such thing, that that which is happened is evil, I have no hurt; and it is in my power not to conceive any such thing.

passages.russian: Пусть что угодно падает извне на то, что способно претерпевать от этого падения. Ведь те, претерпев, будут жаловаться, если захотят. А я, если не сужу, что случившееся — зло, ещё не потерпел вреда. А не судить так — в моей власти.

passages.greek: Ἐμποδισμὸς αἰσθήσεως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἐμποδισμὸς ὁρμῆς ὁμοίως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἔστι δέ τι ἄλλο ὁμοίως ἐμποδιστικὸν καὶ κακὸν τῆς φυτικῆς κατασκευῆς. οὕτως τοίνυν ἐμποδισμὸς νοῦ κακὸν νοερᾶς φύσεως. πάντα δὴ ταῦτα ἐπὶ σεαυτὸν μετάφερε. πόνος, ἡδονὴ ἅπτεταί σου; ὄψεται ἡ αἴσθησις. ὁρμήσαντι ἔνστημα ἐγένετο; εἰ μὲν ἀνυπεξαιρέτως ὥρμας, ἤδη ὡς λογικοῦ κακόν, εἰ δὲ τὸ κοινὸν λαμβάνεις, οὔπω βέβλαψαι οὐδὲ ἐμπεπόδισαι. τὰ μέντοι τοῦ νοῦ ἴδια οὐδεὶς ἄλλος εἴωθεν ἐμποδίζειν· τούτου γὰρ οὐ πῦρ, οὐ σίδηρος, οὐ τύραννος, οὐ βλασφημία, οὐχ ὁτιοῦν ἅπτεται,
passages.english: A hindrance to sensation is a bad thing for an animal nature. A hindrance to impulse is likewise a bad thing for an animal nature. And there is something else that likewise hinders, and is a bad thing for, the way a plant is made. In the same way, then, a hindrance to mind is a bad thing for a nature that has mind. Now carry all of this over to yourself. Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to. Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered. What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it,

notes.note: “A nature that has life”, here animal life, the level that has sensation and impulse. The genitive is “an evil of” such a nature; the English has “a bad thing for”.
notes.other_reading: an evil of the living nature

notes.note: “The plant constitution”; “the way a plant is made” matches the rendering of κατασκευή in 10.33 and 7.53.
notes.other_reading: the constitution of plants

notes.note: The glossary gives “of mind” for νοερός. “A nature that has mind” keeps “mind” so that the link with “a hindrance to mind” can be heard.
notes.other_reading: a thinking nature

notes.note: Literally “sensation will see”: the idiom for “that is its affair”, as in 5.25.
notes.other_reading: let sensation look to it

notes.note: Something that “stands in the way”: the noun of the verb so rendered in 8.47 and 10.33.
notes.other_reading: Did an obstacle meet your impulse?

notes.note: A Stoic term: without the “reservation” (ὑπεξαίρεσις), the unspoken clause “if nothing prevents” with which a wise person frames every impulse.
notes.other_reading: If you set out unconditionally

notes.note: “As of a rational one”: a bad thing for you in so far as you are rational. “Being” is supplied. The word for “already” before it answers “not yet” in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: an evil of you as rational

notes.note: Literally “but if you take the common”. What “the common” is is not clear: the lot common to all, the general rule that impulses meet obstacles, or the usual reservation. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: but if you take the usual reservation for granted

notes.note: Literally “no one else is accustomed to hinder”. The Greek does not say else than whom; the sense is no one but the mind itself, or but you.
notes.other_reading: no one other than the mind itself ever hinders

notes.note: “Iron”: the sword or the knife.
notes.other_reading: nor steel

notes.note: The passage ends here with a comma, part-way through the chapter and the sentence. The comma is kept and nothing is supplied.
notes.other_reading: nor anything at all touches it.

check.note: “A nature of mind” is not clear English; a nature that has mind, a thinking nature, is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a nature that has mind”. “Mind” is kept, as the glossary has it, so that the nature is named from the same word as the hindrance to mind just before; the note gives “a thinking nature”.

check.note: The first word is paired with “not yet” in the next clause: in that case it is already a bad thing, but otherwise you have not yet been harmed. “At once” loses the pair.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being”, so that “already” answers “not yet” in the next clause.

check.note: “What is common” is obscure in English, and the Greek can be taken as the common lot or as the general view, that is, an impulse held with the usual reservation. The reader of the English gets neither.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “But if you accept the common lot”, which chooses one reading in plain words and keeps the Greek shape of a verb with its object. The note gives the reading that takes it of the usual reservation.

check.note: “No one else” leaves the reader asking else than whom; the Greek means no one other than the mind itself.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek has only “no one else” and does not say else than whom, so the English does not say it either. The note explains that no one but the mind itself is meant.

part.left_out: ὅταν γένηται ʽσφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃʼ.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.39 at 'nor anything else that can penetrate into her' and makes the chapter's last words, on the rounded sphere, its section 8.40.

passages.casaubon: That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise, whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.

passages.russian: Помеха ощущению — это плохо для животной природы. Помеха побуждению — это точно так же плохо для животной природы. И есть ещё нечто, что точно так же мешает устройству растения и плохо для него. Таким же образом, значит, помеха уму — это плохо для природы, наделённой умом. Теперь перенеси всё это на себя. Касается ли тебя боль, касается ли наслаждение? Пусть об этом позаботится ощущение. Встало ли что-то на пути твоего побуждения? Если твоё побуждение было без оговорки, то это уже плохо для тебя как для разумного существа. Но если ты принимаешь общий удел, тебе ещё не навредили и не помешали. А тому, что принадлежит уму, никто другой обычно не мешает: ведь его не касается ни огонь, ни железо, ни тиран, ни клевета, ни что бы то ни было,

passages.greek: Ὁ Ἐπίκουρος λέγει ὅτι· ʽἐν τῇ νόσῳ οὐκ ἦσάν μοι αἱ ὁμιλίαι περὶ τῶν τοῦ σωματίου παθῶν οὐδὲ πρὸς τοὺς εἰσιόντας τοιαῦτά τινα, φησίν, ἐλάλουν, ἀλλὰ τὰ προηγούμενα φυσιολογῶν διετέλουν καὶ πρὸς αὐτῷ τούτῳ ὤν, πῶς ἡ διάνοια συμμεταλαμβάνουσα τῶν ἐν τῷ σαρκιδίῳ τοιούτων κινήσεων ἀταρακτεῖ τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν τηροῦσα. οὐδὲ τοῖς ἰατροῖς ἐμπαρεῖχον, φησί, καταφρυάττεσθαι ὥς τι ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς.ʼ ταὐτὰ οὖν ἐκείνῳ, ἐν νόσῳ, ἐὰν νοσῇς καὶ ἐν ἄλλῃ τινὶ περιστάσει· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφίστασθαι φιλοσοφίας ἐν οἷς δήποτε τοῖς προσπίπτουσι μηδὲ ἰδιώτῃ καὶ ἀφυσιολόγῳ συμφλυαρεῖν,
passages.english: Epicurus says: “In my illness my conversations were not about the sufferings of the little body, nor,” he says, “did I talk about such things to those who came in. Instead I went on inquiring into the leading questions of nature, and stayed on this very point: how the mind, though it has its share in such motions in the bit of flesh, stays untroubled, keeping its own good. Nor did I give the doctors the chance,” he says, “to put on airs as though they were doing something. Rather, life went on well and nobly.” So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls, and not to chatter along with someone who is a layman and has not studied nature,

notes.note: ὁμιλίαι are one’s dealings and talk with others; it can also mean a teacher’s lectures.
notes.other_reading: my lectures

notes.note: “He says” is put in twice inside the quotation, as Greek does; both are kept.
notes.other_reading: he goes on

notes.note: Diminutive of “body”, “little body” throughout the section. σαρκιδίῳ below is the same kind of diminutive of “flesh”.
notes.other_reading: of my poor body

notes.note: λαλεῖν is plain “talk”. “Chatter” is kept for συμφλυαρεῖν at the end of the passage, which is “talk nonsense along with”.
notes.other_reading: did I chatter

notes.note: φυσιολογέω is to give an account of nature, the Epicurean name for natural philosophy. τὰ προηγούμενα is most likely “the leading, principal matters”; it can also mean “what went before”, that is, the subjects he had been on already.
notes.other_reading: I went on with my earlier inquiries into nature

notes.note: “Being at this very thing”: occupied with this one point.
notes.other_reading: and was intent on just this

notes.note: “Taking a share along with”: the mind does share in what the flesh undergoes. The participle could be “though it shares” or simply “while it shares”.
notes.other_reading: while it shares in

notes.note: The verb of ἀταραξία, the Epicurean word for freedom from disturbance.
notes.other_reading: stays calm

notes.note: From a verb for a horse snorting and prancing: to give oneself airs over someone. The Greek does not say over whom.
notes.other_reading: to swagger over me

notes.note: “As though doing something”, that is, something that mattered.
notes.other_reading: as if they were achieving something important

notes.greek: ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς
notes.note: Literally “life was led well and finely”. The Greek does not say whose life. καλῶς is “finely, nobly”, a word of worth and not of happiness.
notes.other_reading: my life went on well and happily

notes.note: The Greek has no verb: “the same things, then, as he”. “Do” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: The same, then, as he did

notes.note: ἰδιώτης is a layman, one with no training in philosophy; the second word is “without knowledge of the study of nature”. The English keeps the “and” and takes the two as describing one person; they could be two.
notes.other_reading: with the layman and with the one ignorant of nature

notes.note: The passage ends here with a comma, part-way through the sentence: the infinitives “not to stand away … not to chatter” are left without their verb. The comma is kept and nothing is supplied.
notes.other_reading: nor to join in the nonsense of the layman … (is …)

check.note: The Greek is plain “talk”. “Chatter” is also used below for a different verb that really is “talk nonsense with”, so two Greek words get one English word and the first is coloured.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “did I talk about such things to those who came in”, and “chatter” is left for the different Greek word at the end of the passage.

check.note: The “but” is dropped. The object can be “the leading, principal questions”, as taken, or “what went before”, the earlier inquiries.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Instead I went on inquiring into the leading questions of nature”, which restores the “but”. “Leading” is kept, and the note gives the reading “what went before”.

check.note: The second verb is a participle under the first: the mind stays untroubled while, or by, keeping its own good. Two equal verbs flatten that.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “stays untroubled, keeping its own good”.

check.greek: ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς
check.note: The “but” before the clause is dropped, and “finely” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Rather, life went on well and nobly”, which restores the “but” and removes “finely”. “Nobly” is used and not “happily” because καλῶς speaks of what is fine; the Greek does not say whose life, so no possessive is added.

check.note: The Greek has no verb and “do” is supplied. The supplement is fair and no change is proposed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as the point itself proposes, and the note says that “do” is supplied.

check.note: The Greek has two descriptions joined by “and”: an ordinary person, and one who knows nothing of the study of nature. The English folds the second into the first.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “someone who is a layman and has not studied nature”, which keeps the “and” and both descriptions. They are still taken of one person, since the Greek sets the two words side by side with no article; the note gives the other reading.

part.left_out: πάσης αἱρέσεως κοινόν. πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι καὶ τῷ ὀργάνῳ, δι’ οὗ πράσσεις.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.41 at 'silly people, and mere naturalists' and begins its 9.42 with the rest of the chapter, 'It is common to all trades and professions'.

passages.casaubon: 'In my sickness' (saith Epicurus of himself:) 'my discourses were not concerning the nature of my disease, neither was that, to them that came to visit me, the subject of my talk; but in the consideration and contemplation of that, which was of especial weight and moment, was all my time bestowed and spent, and among others in this very thing, how my mind, by a natural and unavoidable sympathy partaking in some sort with the present indisposition of my body, might nevertheless keep herself free from trouble, and in present possession of her own proper happiness. Neither did I leave the ordering of my body to the physicians altogether to do with me what they would, as though I expected any great matter from them, or as though I thought it a matter of such great consequence, by their means to recover my health: for my present estate, methought, liked me very well, and gave me good content.' Whether therefore in sickness (if thou chance to sicken) or in what other kind of extremity soever, endeavour thou also to be in thy mind so affected, as he doth report of himself: not to depart from thy philosophy for anything that can befall thee, nor to give ear to the discourses of silly people, and mere naturalists.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Эпикур говорит: «Во время болезни я беседовал не о том, как страдает тельце, и не толковал, — говорит он, — о таких вещах с теми, кто ко мне заходил. Напротив, я продолжал исследовать главные вопросы природы и останавливался именно на этом: как ум, хоть он и причастен таким движениям в кусочке плоти, остаётся невозмутимым, сохраняя своё собственное благо. И не давал я врачам случая, — говорит он, — важничать, будто они что-то делают. Жизнь же шла хорошо и благородно». Так делай и ты то же, что он, — в болезни, если болеешь, и при любых других обстоятельствах. Ведь не отступать от философии, что бы ни случилось, и не пустословить вместе с человеком непосвящённым, не изучавшим природы,

passages.greek:
Εἰ μήτε κακία ἐστὶ τοῦτο ἐμὴ μήτε ἐνέργεια κατὰ κακίαν ἐμὴν μήτε τὸ κοινὸν βλάπτεται, τί ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ διαφέρομαι, τίς δὲ βλάβη τοῦ κοινοῦ;

Μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς τῇ φαντασίᾳ συναρπάζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ βοηθεῖν μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα ἐλαττῶνται, μὴ μέντοι βλάβην αὐτὸ φαντάζεσθαι· κακὸν γὰρ ἔθος. ἀλλ’ ὡς ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει, μεμνημένος ὅτι ῥόμβος, οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὧδε. ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων. ἄνθρωπε, ἐπελάθου τί ταῦτα ἦν;—ναί· ἀλλὰ τούτοις περισπούδαστα.—διὰ τοῦτ’ οὖν καὶ σὺ μωρὸς γένῃ; Ἐγενόμην ποτέ,
passages.english:
If this is neither badness of mine nor an activity that comes from badness of mine, and the community is not harmed, why am I upset over it? And what harm is there to the community?

Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if they are coming off worse in the middle things; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit. But as the old man, on leaving, asked for his foster-child’s top, remembering that it was a top, so too in this case. Otherwise you become someone calling out on the Rostra. Man, have you forgotten what these things were? “Yes, but they are much sought after by these people.” And is that a reason for you to become a fool as well? I once was,

notes.note: “Badness”, the usual word for vice. “Badness” is kept to match “bad” for κακόν elsewhere in the section.
notes.other_reading: If this is neither a vice of mine

notes.note: “The common thing”: the community, or the common good.
notes.other_reading: and the common good is not harmed

notes.note: The verb covers being at odds, being anxious and being put out about something.
notes.other_reading: why am I anxious about it?

notes.note: The question can ask what harm there is to the community in this case, or what harm to the community is at all. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: And what is harm to the community?

notes.note: The commands in this chapter are infinitives (“not to be swept off … to help … not to form the impression”); the English writes them as imperatives. φαντασίᾳ and φαντάζεσθαι below are noun and verb of one word, so “impression” and “form the impression”.
notes.other_reading: Not to be carried away wholesale by the impression

notes.note: “To help” has no object, and the English gives none. The plural “they are coming off worse” in the next clause shows that other people are meant.
notes.other_reading: but help them

notes.note: “According to worth”: either what the people deserve or what the matter is worth. “As far as is deserved” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: and as far as the matter is worth

notes.note: Literally “they are made less in respect of the middle things”: the Stoic “middle” or indifferent things, neither good nor bad, such as money or health. The school term is kept as the Greek has it.
notes.other_reading: even if their loss is in things that are neither good nor bad

notes.greek: ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει
notes.note: An allusion that is lost, probably to a scene in a play. θρεπτός is a child brought up in the house, a foster-child or a home-bred slave; ῥόμβος is a spinning top, or a bull-roarer. ἀπῄτει is “asked for as due” or “asked to have back”; the English has the plain “asked for”.
notes.other_reading: as the old man, when he went away, asked for his nursling’s top back

notes.note: “Remembering that it was a top”: the point seems to be that he humoured the child without forgetting how little the thing was. The participle may be concessive, “though he remembered”.
notes.other_reading: though he did not forget that it was only a top

notes.greek: ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων
notes.note: The Greek as given does not construe securely and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked), so the English here is a guess. It takes ἐπεί τοι as “otherwise”, καλῶν as “calling out” and τὰ ἔμβολα as the Rostra, the speakers’ platform at Rome named after ships’ beaks: a man declaiming in public over such losses.
notes.other_reading: Since there you are, crying out on the Rostra.

notes.note: “Yes” is an odd answer to “have you forgotten?”; it may mean “yes, it is known what they are”. “Yes” is kept. The dashes in the text mark a second speaker, shown here with quotation marks.
notes.other_reading: “No, but these people set great store by them.”

notes.note: “To these people, things much striven for”: the word describes how eagerly the people pursue the things, not what the things are worth.
notes.other_reading: but these people are very keen on them

notes.note: The passage ends here with a comma, at the start of a new sentence, with nothing in the passage to say what the speaker once was or became. The fragment is kept and nothing is supplied. In the full chapter the sentence goes on to its own complement; as cut, it can be heard as an answer to the question about becoming a fool.
notes.other_reading: I once became,

check.note: The object of “help” and the subject of “deserve” are supplied. The phrase is “according to worth” and may be the worth of the matter, not the desert of the people; in 8.43 the same phrase is “according to its worth”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved”, with no object and no subject supplied, so that the worth can be that of the people or of the matter. The “but” after “the impression” is also restored, and the note gives both readings.

check.note: “The middle things” is a school term for things neither good nor bad that no reader of today knows. The Greek verb is “they are coming off worse in”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “even if it is in the middle things that they are coming off worse”, which gives the verb its sense. “The middle things” is kept because it is what the Greek says and the gloss “neither good nor bad” would add words; the note explains the term.

check.note: The verb is “asked for as his due” or “asked back”. The story is not known, so “back” is a choice. The “but” before the sentence is also dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But as the old man, on leaving, asked for his foster-child’s top”, with the “but” restored and “back” left to the note.

check.greek: ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων
check.note: The Greek as given does not construe, and the English is a guess that does not say so. The opening words are “for otherwise”, as in 10.33, not “since”, and “the Rostra” is an interpretation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Otherwise you become someone calling out on the Rostra”. The note says that the Greek as given does not construe securely, that the English is a guess, and that “the Rostra” is an interpretation.

check.note: The word describes what the people do, “eagerly sought after by them”, not what the things are worth. “Worth” brings in a valuation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Yes, but they are much sought after by these people”, which says what the people do and brings in no valuation.

part.left_out: ὁπουδήποτε καταληφθείς, εὔμοιρος ἄνθρωπος· τὸ δὲ εὔμοιρος, ἀγαθὴν μοῖραν σεαυτῷ ἀπονείμας· ἀγαθαὶ δὲ μοῖραι ἀγαθαὶ τροπαὶ ψυχῆς, ἀγαθαὶ ὁρμαί, ἀγαθαὶ πράξεις.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 5.29 at 'Once I was; let that suffice' and begins its 5.30 with the rest of the chapter, 'Let death surprise me when it will'.

passages.casaubon: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly hurt thereby: for that is not right. But as that old foster-father in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise. For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.
passages.russian:
Если это не дурное во мне и не деятельность, исходящая из дурного во мне, и общности не причинён вред, отчего я этим расстроен? И какой вред общности?

Не давай представлению целиком увлечь тебя, но помогай, насколько можешь и насколько они того заслуживают, даже если они терпят урон в средних вещах; не составляй себе, однако, представления, будто это вред: это дурная привычка. Но как тот старик, уходя, просил волчок своего воспитанника, помня, что это волчок, — так и в этом случае. Иначе ты становишься тем, кто взывает с ростр. Ты забыл, человек, чем всё это было? «Да, но эти люди очень этого добиваются». И разве поэтому и тебе надо стать глупцом? Я когда-то был,

passages.greek:
Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἄξιος ἐμαυτὸν λυπεῖν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄλλον πώποτε ἑκὼν ἐλύπησα.

Εὐφραίνει ἄλλον ἄλλο, ἐμὲ δέ, ἐὰν ὑγιὲς ἔχω τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, μὴ ἀποστρεφόμενον μήτε ἄνθρωπόν τινα μήτε τι τῶν ἀνθρώποις συμβαινόντων, ἀλλὰ πᾶν εὐμενέσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρῶν τε καὶ δεχόμενον καὶ χρώμενον ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν.
passages.english:
I do not deserve to cause myself distress, for I have never yet willingly distressed anyone else.

One thing gladdens one person, another another. I am gladdened if I have my ruling part sound: not turning away from any human being or from any of the things that happen to human beings, but looking at everything with kindly eyes, accepting it, and using each thing according to its worth.

notes.note: Literally “not worthy”: the speaker has not earned it.
notes.other_reading: It is not right that I should distress myself

notes.note: “Willingly, on purpose.”
notes.other_reading: I have never intentionally distressed another

notes.note: A conditional clause, and the “if” is kept. ὑγιές is “healthy, sound”.
notes.other_reading: but me, to keep my ruling part healthy

notes.note: The participles that follow (turning away, looking, accepting, using) all describe the ruling part, not the speaker.
notes.other_reading: a ruling part that does not turn away

notes.note: “With well-meaning eyes”; the same word as “kindly disposed” in 8.47.
notes.other_reading: with friendly eyes

notes.note: “Using each according to worth”: ἑκάστῳ can be each thing or each person, and the worth is the worth of that thing or person.
notes.other_reading: and dealing with each as it deserves

passages.casaubon: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according to to true worth of the thing itself.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Я не заслуживаю того, чтобы огорчать себя: ведь я ещё никогда по своей воле не огорчал никого другого.

Одного радует одно, другого — другое. А меня радует, если моё ведущее начало здраво: не отворачивается ни от какого человека и ни от чего из того, что случается с людьми, но смотрит на всё добрыми глазами, всё принимает и каждой вещью пользуется по её достоинству.

passages.greek: Ὁ πόνος ἤτοι τῷ σώματι κακόν· οὐκοῦν ἀποφαινέσθω· ἢ τῇ ψυχῇ· ἀλλ’ ἔξεστιν αὐτῇ τὴν ἰδίαν αἰθρίαν καὶ γαλήνην διαφυλάσσειν καὶ μὴ ὑπολαμβάνειν ὅτι κακόν. πᾶσα γὰρ κρίσις καὶ ὁρμὴ καὶ ὄρεξις καὶ ἔκκλισις ἔνδον καὶ οὐδὲν ὧδε ἀναβαίνει.
passages.english: Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul. But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing. For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.

notes.note: Literally “well then, let it declare”: the subject is the body, and what it is to declare is left unsaid. “The body” and “it so” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: then let the body give its own opinion

notes.note: Two weather words: a clear sky and a calm sea.
notes.other_reading: its own serenity and stillness

notes.note: The verb of ὑπόληψις, so “judge”; κρίσις in the next sentence is “verdict”.
notes.other_reading: and not to suppose that it is bad

notes.note: The act of judging; “verdict” as elsewhere in this section, since “judgment” is kept for ὑπόληψις.
notes.other_reading: For every judgment

notes.note: The Stoic pair: reaching towards a thing and leaning away from it.
notes.other_reading: wanting and avoiding

notes.note: Literally “nothing comes up here”, that is, into the place inside where these acts happen. From memory, unchecked: some texts read “nothing bad”.
notes.other_reading: and nothing bad climbs up to here

check.note: “The body” and “it so” are supplied; the Greek is only “then let it declare”. The supplement is the natural one and no change is proposed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, as the point itself proposes, and the note says which words are supplied.

passages.casaubon: If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil. For all judgment and deliberation; all prosecution, or aversation is from within, whither the sense of evil (except it be let in by opinion) cannot penetrate.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian: Боль — это плохо либо для тела, и тогда пусть тело об этом и заявит, либо для души. Но душа может сохранять собственное ясное небо и тишь и не судить, что это плохо. Ведь всякий приговор, и побуждение, и желание, и отвращение — внутри, и ничто сюда не взбирается.

passages.greek:
Ἆρον τὴν ὑπόληψιν, ἦρται τὸ βέβλαμμαι· ἆρον τὸ βέβλαμμαι, ἦρται ἡ βλάβη.

Ὃ χείρω αὐτὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἄνθρωπον οὐ ποιεῖ, τοῦτο οὐδὲ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ χείρω ποιεῖ οὐδὲ βλάπτει οὔτε ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἔνδοθεν.

Ἠνάγκασται ἡ τοῦ συμφέροντος φύσις τοῦτο ποιεῖν.
passages.english:
Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.

What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them from outside or from within.

The nature of what is beneficial is bound by necessity to do this.

notes.note: The article turns the first-person verb into a quoted thing, so it stands in quotation marks. ἦρται is a perfect: the thing “has been taken away” at once.
notes.other_reading: and the thought “I am hurt” is gone

notes.note: Literally “worse than himself”: worse than he was. “They” is used for ἄνθρωπος.
notes.other_reading: does not make a man worse than himself

notes.note: “Neither from outside nor from inside”: the Greek gives no object for “harm”; “them” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: nor does it do harm, outwardly or inwardly

notes.note: Literally “the nature of the beneficial”. The glossary has “is good for” for συμφέρει; with no object here the English has “what is beneficial”. It may be a roundabout way of saying “what is beneficial, by its nature”.
notes.other_reading: What is good for the whole is, by its nature

notes.note: A perfect passive: “has been compelled”.
notes.other_reading: has been forced

notes.note: “To do this”: the Greek does not say what “this” is. It may look back to the chapter before or to whatever has just happened.
notes.other_reading: to bring this about

passages.casaubon: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.

nearest.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

passages.russian:
Убери суждение — и убрано «мне причинили вред». Убери «мне причинили вред» — и убран сам вред.

То, что не делает человека хуже, чем он был, не делает хуже и его жизнь и не вредит ему ни извне, ни изнутри.

Природа полезного по необходимости обязана так поступать.
