notes.note: The adverb of κοινωνικός, “social”: as a member of the community, for the common good. The glossary word is kept, in the phrase “as a social being”.
notes.other_reading: I have done something for the common good

notes.note: Perfect: “I have been benefited”, the benefit being in the act itself.
notes.other_reading: then I have my reward

notes.note: ἵνα with the subjunctive standing alone as a command: “see that this always meets you ready to hand”. The English joins the verb and the adjective in “comes to hand”.
notes.other_reading: Let this thought always be ready when you need it

notes.note: Literally “stop nowhere”. What is not to stop is not said: the doing of such acts, or the keeping of the thought at hand.
notes.other_reading: and do not leave off at any point

notes.note: A craft, skill or profession.
notes.other_reading: What is your profession?

notes.note: ὴ is a slip in the copy for ἢ, “than”: “how … other than from”, though the Greek has no “other” for it to lean on. θεωρήματα are the propositions a science or craft rests on, literally “things contemplated”; the English reads “points of theory”. The Greek ends with a full stop; the English has a question mark.
notes.other_reading: except from theorems

notes.note: κατασκευή is how a thing is built, its constitution.
notes.other_reading: the particular constitution of man

check.note: “In a social way” is unclear in English. The sense is “for the common good, as a member of the community”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “I have done something as a social being”. “Social” is the settled word for this family of Greek words and is kept; the new phrase says more plainly that the act is that of a member of the community.

check.note: Both Greek words are rendered in full, “comes to meet you ready at hand”, and the result is heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “See that this always comes to hand”, in which “comes” is the Greek verb and “to hand” the Greek adjective. “When you need it” is not added, since the Greek does not have it.

check.greek: πῶς καλῶς γίνεται ὴ ἐκ θεωρημάτων
check.note: The letter printed ὴ must be the word for “than”. Even so the Greek is harsh, since “than” has nothing to lean on; the English supplies “except”, the only sense available.
check.decided: Accepted: “except” stands, as suggested, and the note records the slip in the copy and the roughness of the Greek.

check.note: One word, “theorems” or “things contemplated”, becomes four, and “truths” asserts more than the Greek.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “points of theory”, which drops “truths” and keeps the Greek root. “Principles” was not used because it is this translation’s word for δόγμα.

passages.casaubon: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines; some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the proper and particular constitution of man?

nearest.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

passages.russian:
Я сделал что-то как общественное существо — значит, я получил пользу. Следи, чтобы это всегда было у тебя под рукой, и никогда не останавливайся.

В чём твоё ремесло? Быть хорошим. А как это может хорошо получиться, если не из теоретических положений — одних о природе целого, других о собственном устройстве человека?

passages.greek: Ὁποῖά τινά ἐστι τὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δοκοῦντα ἀγαθά, κἂν ἐντεῦθεν λάβοις. εἰ γάρ τις ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά, οἷον φρόνησιν, σωφροσύνην, δικαιοσύνην, ἀνδρείαν, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα προεπινοήσας ἐπακοῦσαι δυνηθείη τό· ʽὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶνʼ, οὐ γὰρ ἐφαρμόσει. τὰ δέ γε τοῖς πολλοῖς φαινόμενα ἀγαθὰ προεπινοήσας τις ἐπακούσεται καὶ ῥᾳδίως δέξεται ὡς οἰκείως ἐπιλεγόμενον τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ κωμικοῦ εἰρημένον. οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν· οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο, τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πλούτου καὶ τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων παρεδεχόμεθα ὡς ἱκνουμένως καὶ ἀστείως εἰρημένον. πρόιθι οὖν καὶ ἐρώτα, εἰ τιμητέον καὶ ἀγαθὰ ὑποληπτέον τὰ τοιαῦτα, ὧν προεπινοηθέντων οἰκείως ἂν ἐπιφέροιτο τὸ τὸν κεκτημένον αὐτὰ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐπορίας ʽοὐκ ἔχειν ὅποι χέσῃʼ.
passages.english: What kind of things they are that seem good to most people, you can gather from this as well. For if a person had in mind certain things that truly are good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, then, with these first in mind, they could not listen to the words “because of the good things”, for it will not fit. But a person who has first in mind the things that appear good to most people will listen, and will readily accept what the comic poet said as a fitting thing to add. So even most people have an impression of the difference. For otherwise this line would not jar and be refused in the one case, while, when it is said of wealth and of the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation, we accept it as aptly and wittily said. Go on, then, and ask whether one should honour and judge to be good the kind of things which, when they have first been brought to mind, can fittingly be followed by the line that their owner, because of the plenty, “has nowhere to shit”.

notes.note: “You could grasp even from this”: from the test that follows.
notes.other_reading: you may learn from the following too

notes.note: ὡς ἀληθῶς is “truly”. The phrase can be “certain things that truly are good” or “certain existing things as truly good”.
notes.other_reading: if someone thought of certain real things as truly good

notes.note: “Having thought of beforehand”. The verb comes three times with this prefix and once without (ἐπινοήσειεν); “in mind” and “first” are kept for it, and “brought to mind” for the passive at the end.
notes.other_reading: having first conceived of these

notes.note: The opening words of a comic line whose end is given at the close of the passage: a man has so many good things that he “has nowhere to shit”. The Greek here is only “because of the good things”.
notes.other_reading: “for all his goods”

notes.note: To give ear to. It can also be taken as “to hear in addition”, that is, to hear the line tacked on.
notes.other_reading: could not bear to hear added

notes.note: “The comic poet”, not named. The line may be Menander’s (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the writer of comedy

notes.greek: οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν
notes.note: καί is “even”: even ordinary people have an impression of the difference between the two kinds of good. φαντάζονται is the verb of “impression”.
notes.other_reading: So the many too perceive the difference

notes.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε
notes.note: The second οὐ is hard: taken strictly, the two negatives cancel and give the wrong sense. It is read as the first negative repeated, “for otherwise this would not jar”; editors may remove or bracket it (from memory, unchecked). “Otherwise”, “line” and “in the one case” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: for otherwise this would not fail to jar

notes.note: The verb is in the first person plural, where the rest of the passage speaks of “a person” and “most people”. Its tense is past, inside the “otherwise”, which is how Greek states what would be so now; the English has the present.
notes.other_reading: while we would be accepting it

notes.note: Pieces of good luck, lucky gains.
notes.other_reading: the advantages that bring luxury or fame

notes.note: From the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”.
notes.other_reading: to be supposed good

notes.note: The coarse word is in the Greek. τὸν κεκτημένον is masculine, “the man who owns them”, with no man singled out; the English has “their owner”.
notes.other_reading: that he who has them is so well off that he “has no place left to relieve himself”

check.greek: ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά
check.note: The Greek can be “conceived of certain things as being truly good”, the person’s own conception and not the writer’s statement that they are good.
check.decided: Declined: the participle “being” can equally stand with “truly good” as a description of the things, and the next sentence sets against them “the things that appear good to most people”, which is the writer’s own division. The note gives the other construction.

check.note: “Go on to” is added here, but the same verb two lines later is plain “will listen”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they could not listen to the words”, so the verb is “listen” both times. The note records the sense “hear in addition”.

check.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο
check.note: The Greek as given has two negatives and, taken strictly, says “would not fail to jar”. The English translates one, which the argument needs; from memory, editors remove or bracket the second. “Line” and “in the one case” are supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the sense stands, as suggested, and the note says that the second negative is passed over as a repetition of the first and names the words supplied.

check.note: The tense is past in Greek, inside the unreal condition. The present makes it a plain fact.
check.decided: Declined: in Greek a past tense with this particle is the ordinary way to state what would be so now, and one negative governs both halves of the sentence, so “would not jar” followed by “while we accept it” gives the same sense in English. The note records the tense.

check.greek: τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων
check.note: “That go to” is unclear. The sense is the strokes of good fortune that make for luxury or fame.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation”. “Reputation” is kept for the Greek word, as in the other passages of this section.

check.note: “This” is not in the Greek, which has “because of his abundance”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “because of the plenty”, with the Greek article and no “this”.

check.note: Found while settling: “picture the difference” is not plain English, and the verb is the verb of “impression”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have an impression of the difference”.

passages.casaubon: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore, and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
passages.russian: Каковы те вещи, что кажутся благами большинству, можно понять и отсюда. Ведь если бы человек держал в уме некоторые подлинные блага, например мудрость, самообладание, справедливость, мужество, то, заранее держа их в уме, он не смог бы выслушать слова «из-за благ»: они не подойдут. А тот, кто заранее держит в уме то, что представляется благом большинству, выслушает и легко примет сказанное комическим поэтом как уместное добавление. Так что даже у большинства есть представление о разнице. Иначе эта строка в одном случае не коробила бы и не отвергалась, а когда её говорят о богатстве и об удачах, ведущих к роскоши или славе, мы принимаем её как сказанную метко и остроумно. Так иди же и спроси, следует ли чтить и признавать благом такие вещи, вслед за которыми, если сперва вызвать их в уме, уместно звучит строка о том, что их владельцу из-за изобилия «негде посрать».

passages.greek: Πῶς ἐναργὲς προσπίπτει τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἄλλην βίου ὑπόθεσιν εἰς τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν οὕτως ἐπιτήδειον ὡς ταύτην, ἐν ᾗ νῦν ὢν τυγχάνεις.
passages.english: How plainly it comes home that there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be.

notes.note: An exclamation. προσπίπτει, “strikes, falls upon”, is the word used of impressions; it has no object, so the English reads “comes home”.
notes.other_reading: How clearly it strikes you

notes.note: ὑπόθεσις as in 8.1: the footing or position of a life. The English reads “situation in life”.
notes.other_reading: no other calling in life

notes.note: “For philosophising”: the practice, not the subject.
notes.other_reading: for the practice of philosophy

passages.casaubon: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?

nearest.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

passages.russian: Как ясно доходит до тебя, что нет в жизни другого положения, столь подходящего для философии, как то, в котором ты сейчас оказался.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ οἱ ἰατροὶ ἀεὶ τὰ ὄργανα καὶ σιδήρια πρόχειρα ἔχουσι πρὸς τὰ αἰφνίδια τῶν θεραπευμάτων, οὕτω τὰ δόγματα σὺ ἕτοιμα ἔχε πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι, καὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ μικρότατον οὕτω ποιεῖν ὡς τῆς ἀμφοτέρων πρὸς ἄλληλα συνδέσεως μεμνημένον. οὔτε γὰρ ἀνθρώπινόν τι ἄνευ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα συναναφορᾶς εὖ πράξεις οὔτ’ ἔμπαλιν.
passages.english: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready for knowing things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, as one who remembers the bond that ties the two to each other. For you will not do any human thing well without referring it at the same time to the divine, nor the other way round.

notes.note: σιδήρια is “irons”: the surgeon’s iron tools, knives and lancets.
notes.other_reading: their instruments and irons

notes.note: Literally “for the sudden ones among treatments”.
notes.other_reading: for treatments needed suddenly

notes.greek: πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι
notes.note: “For knowing” governs “things divine and human”; the same “for” is taken to run on to “doing everything”. “Knowledge of things divine and human” was a standing definition of wisdom (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: for understanding divine and human things

notes.note: “A referring together”: carrying the human act back to the divine along with it. The root is that of ἀναφοράς in 12.8, where the English has “aims”.
notes.other_reading: without relating it to the divine as well

notes.note: “Nor the reverse”: nor anything divine without reference to the human.
notes.other_reading: nor the opposite

check.note: The Greek is “for the sudden ones among their treatments”, that is, emergencies. The English is right but stiff.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for emergency treatments”, which is plainer and still keeps the Greek noun “treatments”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek is a plain command, “have ready”, with the same verb as the doctors’ “have”; “you should have” softened it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so have your principles ready”.

passages.casaubon: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.

nearest.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

passages.russian: Как у врачей всегда под рукой инструменты и ножи для срочного лечения, так и ты держи наготове свои принципы, чтобы познавать божественное и человеческое и делать всё, даже самое малое, как тот, кто помнит о связи, соединяющей одно с другим. Ведь ты не сделаешь хорошо ничего человеческого, не соотнося его одновременно с божественным, и наоборот.

passages.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι τὸ νευροσπαστοῦν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἔνδον ἐγκεκρυμμένον· ἐκεῖνο ῥητορεία, ἐκεῖνο ζωή, ἐκεῖνο, εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, ἄνθρωπος. μηδέποτε συμπεριφαντάζου τὸ περικείμενον ἀγγειῶδες καὶ τὰ ὀργάνια ταῦτα τὰ περιπεπλασμένα· ὅμοια γάρ ἐστι σκεπάρνῳ, μόνον διαφέροντα, καθότι προσφυῆ ἐστιν. ἐπεί τοι οὐ μᾶλλόν τι τούτων ὄφελός ἐστι τῶν μορίων χωρὶς τῆς κινούσης καὶ ἰσχούσης αὐτὰ αἰτίας, ἢ τῆς κερκίδος τῇ ὑφαντρίᾳ καὶ τοῦ καλάμου τῷ γράφοντι καὶ τοῦ μαστιγίου τῷ ἡνιόχῳ.
passages.english: Remember that what pulls the strings is that thing hidden inside. That is oratory, that is life, that, if one must say it, is the human being. Never picture along with it the vessel-like thing that surrounds it and these little tools moulded around it. For they are like a carpenter’s axe, differing only in being grown on. For without the cause that moves them and holds them in check, these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip.

notes.note: “What pulls the strings”, as of a puppet worked by cords.
notes.other_reading: the puppet-master

notes.note: ῥητορεία is oratory, public speaking. It sits oddly beside “life” and “the human being”, and the word may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). It is translated as it stands.
notes.other_reading: that is the power of speech

notes.note: “If one must say it”: an apology for the bold wording.
notes.other_reading: if the word may be allowed

notes.note: A compound of the verb of “impression”: do not take in, in the same picture, what lies around it.
notes.other_reading: never include in your thought of it

notes.note: “The vessel-like thing lying round it”: the body as a container.
notes.other_reading: the vessel that encloses it

notes.note: ὀργάνια is a diminutive of ὄργανον, which is both “tool” and bodily “organ”. The comparison with the carpenter’s axe turns on the first sense, so the English reads “little tools”.
notes.other_reading: these organs moulded round it

notes.note: A carpenter’s axe or adze, a tool for shaping wood.
notes.other_reading: an adze

notes.note: “In that they are grown on”: attached by growth.
notes.other_reading: in that they are part of the body’s growth

notes.note: ἴσχω is to hold, hold back or check: the cause that sets the parts moving and stops them.
notes.other_reading: the cause that moves and sustains them

notes.note: Literally “than [there is use] of the shuttle to the weaver, of the pen to the writer, of the little whip to the charioteer”. The comparison is compressed: “without the cause that moves them” has to be carried over to the three tools, and the English puts those words first so that they are heard over both halves. ὑφαντρίᾳ is a woman weaver.
notes.other_reading: than the shuttle is without the weaver, the pen without the writer, or the whip without the charioteer

check.note: “Oratory” is literal and puzzling in English. The word can be taken more widely as speech, the power of persuading.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek word is the art of the public speaker, not the general word for speech, so “oratory” is what it says, odd as it is. The note records the wider sense and that the word may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “Adze” is correct but rare; the tool is a carpenter’s axe.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “like a carpenter’s axe”.

check.note: Read by itself the English says a shuttle is of little use to a weaver. The Greek is compressed in the same way, and “without the cause that moves it” has to be carried over to the shuttle, the pen and the whip.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “without the cause that moves them and holds them in check these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip”. With “without” placed first it is heard over both halves of the comparison; “without the weaver” was not written because the Greek has “to the weaver”, and the note marks what is left unsaid.

check.note: The Greek word is feminine, “the weaving woman”.
check.decided: Declined: English “weaver” serves for a woman as for a man, and “weaving woman” would put a weight on the word that the Greek does not. The note says that the Greek word is feminine.

check.note: The verb is “holds”: either “restrains” or “holds together, sustains”. The English picks the first.
check.decided: Accepted: “holds them in check” stands, as suggested, and the note records “sustains”.

passages.casaubon: Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that (to speak true) is man himself. As for thy body, which as a vessel, or a case, compasseth thee about, and the many and curious instruments that it hath annexed unto it, let them not trouble thy thoughts. For of themselves they are but as a carpenter's axe, but that they are born with us, and naturally sticking unto us. But otherwise, without the inward cause that hath power to move them, and to restrain them, those parts are of themselves of no more use unto us, than the shuttle is of itself to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the coachman.
passages.russian: Помни: то, что дёргает за ниточки, — это то, что спрятано внутри. Это — красноречие, это — жизнь, это, если надо так сказать, — человек. Никогда не воображай вместе с ним окружающее его подобие сосуда и эти вылепленные вокруг него орудьица. Ведь они подобны топору плотника и отличаются лишь тем, что приросли. Без причины, которая их движет и сдерживает, пользы от этих частей на деле не больше, чем от челнока ткача, пера пишущего и кнутика возничего.

passages.greek: Μή, εἴ τι αὐτῷ σοὶ δυσκαταπόνητον, τοῦτο ἀνθρώπῳ ἀδύνατον ὑπολαμβάνειν, ἀλλ’ εἴ τι ἀνθρώπῳ δυνατὸν καὶ οἰκεῖον, τοῦτο καὶ σεαυτῷ ἐφικτὸν νόμιζε.
passages.english: If something is hard for you yourself to carry out, do not judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.

notes.note: “Hard to work through to the end”, hard to master by effort.
notes.other_reading: hard for you to master

notes.note: An infinitive used as a command, the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”. The second half has a plain imperative, νόμιζε, “consider”.
notes.other_reading: do not suppose

notes.note: οἰκεῖον is what belongs to a being by its nature. The English reads “proper to them” for the human being.
notes.other_reading: possible and natural to man

passages.casaubon: Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that very possible unto thee also.

nearest.title: The morning, and the question before each action

passages.russian: Если что-то тебе самому трудно исполнить, не считай это невозможным для человека; но если что-то возможно для человека и ему свойственно, считай, что и тебе это по силам.

passages.greek: Ἀναχωρήσεις αὑτοῖς ζητοῦσιν ἀγροικίας καὶ αἰγιαλοὺς καὶ ὄρη, εἴωθας δὲ καὶ σὺ τὰ τοιαῦτα μάλιστα ποθεῖν. ὅλον δὲ τοῦτο ἰδιωτικώτατόν ἐστιν ἐξόν, ἧς ἂν ὥρας ἐθελήσῃς, εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀναχωρεῖν. οὐδαμοῦ γὰρ οὔτε ἡσυχιώτερον οὔτε ἀπραγμονέστερον ἄνθρωπος ἀναχωρεῖ ἢ εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν, μάλισθʼ ὅστις ἔχει ἔνδον τοιαῦτα, εἰς ἃ ἐγκύψας ἐν πάσῃ εὐμαρείᾳ εὐθὺς γίνεται· τὴν δὲ εὐμάρειαν οὐδὲν ἄλλο λέγω ἢ εὐκοσμίαν. συνεχῶς οὖν δίδου σεαυτῷ ταύτην τὴν ἀναχώρησιν καὶ ἀνανέου σεαυτόν· βραχέα δὲ ἔστω καὶ στοιχειώδη ἃ εὐθὺς ἀπαντήσαντα ἀρκέσει εἰς τὸ πᾶσαν λύπην ἀποκλύσαι καὶ ἀποπέμψαι σε μὴ δυσχεραίνοντα ἐκείνοις ἐφʼ ἃ ἐπανέρχῃ. τίνι γὰρ δυσχερανεῖς; τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κακίᾳ; ἀναλογισάμενος τὸ κρῖμα, ὅτι τὰ λογικὰ ζῷα ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν γέγονε καὶ ὅτι τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι μέρος τῆς δικαιοσύνης καὶ ὅτι ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι καὶ πόσοι ἤδη διεχθρεύσαντες, ὑποπτεύσαντες, μισήσαντες, διαδορατισθέντες ἐκτέτανται, τετέφρωνται, παύου ποτέ. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπονεμομένοις δυσχερανεῖς; ἀνανεωσάμενος τὸ διεζευγμένον τό· ἤτοι πρόνοια ἢ ἄτομοι, καὶ ἐξ ὅσων ἀπεδείχθη ὅτι ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις. ἀλλὰ τὰ σωματικά σου ἅψεται ἔτι; ἐννοήσας ὅτι οὐκ ἐπιμίγνυται λείως ἢ τραχέως κινουμένῳ πνεύματι ἡ διάνοια, ἐπειδὰν ἅπαξ ἑαυτὴν ἀπολάβῃ καὶ γνωρίσῃ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐξουσίαν, καὶ λοιπὸν ὅσα περὶ πόνου καὶ ἡδονῆς ἀκήκοας καὶ συγκατέθου. ἀλλὰ τὸ δοξάριόν σε περισπάσει; ἀπιδὼν εἰς τὸ τάχος τῆς πάντων λήθης καὶ τὸ χάος τοῦ ἐφʼ ἑκάτερα ἀπείρου αἰῶνος καὶ τὸ κενὸν τῆς ἀπηχήσεως καὶ τὸ εὐμετάβολον καὶ ἄκριτον τῶν εὐφημεῖν δοκούντων καὶ τὸ στενὸν τοῦ τόπου, ἐν ᾧ περιγράφεται· ὅλη τε γὰρ ἡ γῆ στιγμὴ καὶ ταύτης πόστον γωνίδιον ἡ κατοίκησις αὕτη; καὶ ἐνταῦθα πόσοι καὶ οἷοί τινες οἱ ἐπαινεσόμενοι; λοιπὸν οὖν μέμνησο τῆς ὑποχωρήσεως τῆς εἰς τοῦτο τὸ ἀγρίδιον ἑαυτοῦ καὶ πρὸ παντὸς μὴ σπῶ μηδὲ κατεντείνου, ἀλλὰ ἐλεύθερος ἔσο καὶ ὅρα τὰ πράγματα ὡς ἀνήρ, ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ὡς πολίτης, ὡς θνητὸν ζῷον. ἐν δὲ τοῖς προχειροτάτοις, εἰς ἃ ἐγκύψεις, ταῦτα ἔστω τὰ δύο· ἕν μέν, ὅτι τὰ πράγματα οὐχ ἅπτεται τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀλλʼ ἔξω ἕστηκεν ἀτρεμοῦντα, αἱ δὲ ὀχλήσεις ἐκ μόνης τῆς ἔνδον ὑπολήψεως· ἕτερον δέ, ὅτι πάντα ταῦτα, ὅσα ὁρᾷς, ὅσον οὐδέπω μεταβαλεῖ καὶ οὐκ ἔτι ἔσται· καὶ ὅσων ἤδη μεταβολαῖς αὐτὸς παρατετύχηκας, συνεχῶς διανοοῦ. ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις.
passages.english: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself. For nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul, above all for someone who has such things within that, on bending to look into them, they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order. So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to. For what will you resent? The badness of people? Think over the conclusion: that rational animals have come to be for the sake of one another, and that forbearance is a part of justice, and that they go wrong against their will, and how many before now, after feuding, suspecting, hating, fighting with spears, have been laid out and turned to ash; and then stop at last. Or will you also resent what is allotted from the whole? Renew for yourself the either-or, “either providence or atoms”, and all the grounds on which it was proved that the universe is, as it were, a city. Or will the things of the body still touch you? Consider that the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power; and, for the rest, all that you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure. Or will petty fame distract you? Look at how fast everything is forgotten, and at the gulf of endless time on either side, and the emptiness of the echo, and how changeable and undiscerning those are who seem to give praise, and the narrowness of the place in which that petty fame is confined. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a corner of it is this dwelling place? And here, how many are there, and what sort of people, who will give the praise? For the rest, then, remember the withdrawal into this little country place of your own; and before everything do not be torn about and do not strain, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal animal. And among the things readiest to hand, which you will bend to look into, let there be these two. One, that things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within. The other, that all these things you see will change in almost no time and will no longer be; and keep thinking of how many things you have yourself already seen change. The universe is alteration; life is judgment.

notes.note: The word is the superlative of the adjective from ἰδιώτης, a private person with no training, here one untrained in philosophy. The English reads “someone with no training at all”, with “at all” for the superlative.
notes.other_reading: But all of this is as unphilosophical as can be

notes.note: The two comparatives can be adverbs with the verb (“retreats more quietly or with less business”) or describe the place retreated to. The English takes them of the place.
notes.other_reading: For nowhere does a person retreat more quietly or with less trouble than into their own soul

notes.note: The verb is to stoop and peer into something. It comes again near the end of the passage (ἐγκύψεις), and the English has “bend to look into” both times.
notes.other_reading: as soon as they look into them

notes.greek: τὴν δὲ εὐμάρειαν οὐδὲν ἄλλο λέγω ἢ εὐκοσμίαν
notes.note: εὐμάρεια is ease or comfort; εὐκοσμία is orderliness, good behaviour, a well-kept state. Marcus defines the first by the second, so the English keeps two plain nouns.
notes.other_reading: and by comfort I mean nothing other than being well ordered

notes.note: The English follows the text as given, “wash away all distress”. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are not agreed here and some editors print a pronoun (“wash it wholly clean”, of the soul) in place of λύπην, or a verb meaning “shut out”.
notes.other_reading: to wash the soul wholly clean

notes.note: κρῖμα is a decision reached, a ruling. The glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, which comes twice later in this passage, so the English has “conclusion” here to keep the two words apart.
notes.other_reading: Think over the judgment you have reached

notes.note: ἄκοντες is “unwilling”, “not of their own will”; it can also be heard as “without meaning to”. The English keeps the stronger, literal sense, which is the Socratic claim that nobody goes wrong willingly.
notes.other_reading: that they go wrong without meaning to

notes.note: The Greek has a participle (“having renewed”) with no main verb, as also at ἐννοήσας and ἀπιδὼν below; a verb such as “stop” or “you will not resent it” is understood from the answer before. The English turns all three into commands. τὸ διεζευγμένον is the logicians’ term for an either-or statement, and the verb repeats “renew yourself” above, so “renew” is kept.
notes.other_reading: Having called back to mind the disjunction, “either providence or atoms”

notes.note: πνεῦμα here is the breath that runs through the body and carries sensation; its smooth or rough movement is pleasure or pain. The English keeps “breath”. διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary, but here the faculty is meant (it takes itself back and knows its power), so the English has “mind”.
notes.other_reading: that thought does not mingle with the vital spirit, whether its motion is smooth or rough

notes.note: A diminutive of δόξα, reputation, with a belittling tone. The English has “petty fame”.
notes.other_reading: that little bit of reputation

notes.note: The genitive πάντων can be the things forgotten (“everything”), the people forgotten (“everyone”) or the people who forget (“how fast everyone forgets”). The English takes it of things.
notes.other_reading: how fast everyone is forgotten

notes.note: Literally “this dwelling” or “this habitation”. It can mean the inhabited part of the earth or the particular place where one lives; “this dwelling place” can be heard either way.
notes.other_reading: this inhabited part of the earth, or: this place where you live

notes.note: σπῶ is a middle or passive command from σπάω, to pull, wrench or tear: “do not be torn about”, or “do not be convulsed”. κατεντείνου is “do not strain”. The English keeps the image of being pulled apart.
notes.other_reading: do not be distracted and do not overstrain yourself

notes.note: ἀγρίδιον is a little field or small farm; it picks up the “country places” (ἀγροικίας) of the first line, so the English has “little country place”. ἑαυτοῦ is used here for the second person: the place may be one that belongs to you or one that is yourself.
notes.other_reading: this little plot that is yourself

notes.note: A different word from the μεταβολή (“change”) just before; it means becoming other. The English has “alteration” so that the two Greek words stay two English words.
notes.other_reading: The universe is change; life is opinion.

notes.note: Two bare nouns set side by side, like “the universe is alteration” before them. ὑπόληψις is what one takes things to be, the same word as “the judgment within” a few lines above; it does not mean being judged.
notes.other_reading: life is what you judge it to be

check.note: “Layman” leaves a reader asking “layman in what?”. The word means what is most typical of an ordinary person with no philosophical training.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the mark of someone with no training at all”, so “layman” is gone. “Unphilosophical” is not taken, because the Greek word names the untrained ordinary person and does not name philosophy; the note gives that rendering.

check.greek: ἐγκύψας ἐν πάσῃ εὐμαρείᾳ εὐθὺς γίνεται
check.note: The Greek says “at once” one time and the English says it twice. The verb is also more physical than “look”: stooping to peer in.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “on bending to look into them, they are at once in complete ease”, with “at once” said once. The same verb near the end of the passage is now “bend to look into” as well.

check.note: “Reckon up the verdict” is not clear English, and “verdict” suggests a court ruling on someone. The word is the settled conclusion that the following clauses spell out.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Think over the conclusion: that …”. “You have concluded” is not taken, because the Greek has only the noun and no “you”.

check.note: A reader will not know what it is to “renew an alternative”. The sense is to call up the either-or afresh in the mind.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Renew for yourself the either-or”. “Either-or” is taken; “renew” is kept because it is the same verb as “renew yourself” a few lines above, and “for yourself” gives the middle form of the Greek verb.

check.note: The three answers are participles with no finite verb; something like “stop” or “you will not” is understood from the first answer. The English makes each a new command without any sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the commands are kept as the plainest English. The note on ἀνανεωσάμενος says that all three answers are participles with no main verb and that the verb is understood from the answer before.

check.note: “To you” is not in the Greek, which speaks generally of what is allotted from the whole.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “what is dealt out from the whole”.

check.note: The genitive can be neuter (“all things are forgotten”) or masculine (“all people are forgotten”, which suits the talk of fame). The English takes it as things without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “how fast everything is forgotten”, since “all is forgotten” would still be heard as things. The note now gives both other readings, “everyone is forgotten” and “everyone forgets”.

check.note: “It” has no near antecedent in the English and may be taken as the echo. The Greek subject is the petty fame.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the place in which that petty fame is confined”, so the subject is named.

check.note: The English takes this as the inhabited part of the earth. It can also be the spot where you yourself live.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “this dwelling place”, which is the literal sense and can be heard either way. The note gives both narrower readings.

check.note: The Greek is a command with an adverb, “for the rest”. The English turns it into a statement about what is left to do.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “For the rest, then, remember the withdrawal …”, a command as in the Greek.

check.note: The word picks up the country places of the first line, and “little field” hides the echo. The genitive may also mean the plot that is yourself.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “this little country place of your own”, so the echo of “country places” can be heard. “Yourself” is not added, because the Greek genitive may be simply possessive; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: On its own “life is judgment” may be heard as “life is being judged”. The word is what one takes things to be, as in “the judgment within” above.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek is two bare nouns side by side, exactly like “the universe is alteration” before it, and “what you judge it to be” adds a “you” and a clause that are not there. “Judgment” repeats the word of “the judgment within” three sentences earlier, and a new note says that being judged is not meant.

check.greek: καὶ λοιπὸν ὅσα περὶ πόνου καὶ ἡδονῆς
check.note: Found while settling: λοιπὸν here was “and then”, while the same adverb below is now “for the rest”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “and, for the rest, all that you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure”, so the adverb has one rendering in the passage.

check.note: Found while settling: “speak well of you” and, two sentences on, “who will praise you” each add a “you” that the Greek does not have, the same small addition as in “dealt out to you”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “those who seem to give praise” and “who will give the praise”.

passages.casaubon: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end. As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee? How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
passages.russian: Люди ищут для себя мест уединения: деревенских уголков, морских берегов, гор. И ты тоже привык очень сильно тосковать о таком. Но всё это — признак человека, совсем не прошедшего выучку, когда ты волен в любой час, какой пожелаешь, уединиться в самом себе. Ведь нигде человек не уединится тише и свободнее от дел, чем в собственной душе, — особенно тот, у кого внутри есть такое, во что стоит лишь вглядеться, наклонившись, и он тотчас в полной непринуждённости; а непринуждённостью я называю не что иное, как должный порядок. Так давай себе постоянно это уединение и обновляй себя. И пусть будут краткими и простейшими те положения, которых, едва они тебе встретятся, будет достаточно, чтобы смыть всякое огорчение и отпустить тебя без досады к тому, к чему ты возвращаешься. На что же ты будешь досадовать? На людскую испорченность? Перебери в уме вывод: что разумные живые существа появились ради друг друга, что снисходительность — часть справедливости, что они ошибаются против воли, и сколько людей прежде, враждуя, подозревая, ненавидя, сражаясь копьями, легли мёртвыми и обратились в пепел; и уймись наконец. Или ты будешь досадовать и на то, что уделено от целого? Обнови в себе это «или — или»: «либо провидение, либо атомы» — и все доводы, которыми было доказано, что мироздание — как бы город. Или тебя всё ещё будет касаться телесное? Подумай, что ум не смешивается с дыханием, движется ли оно плавно или резко, как только ум вернулся к себе и познал собственную власть; и, кроме того, всё, что ты слышал о боли и наслаждении и с чем согласился. Или тебя будет отвлекать жалкая слава? Посмотри, как быстро всё забывается, на бездну бесконечного времени по обе стороны, на пустоту отзвука, на переменчивость и неразборчивость тех, кто будто бы хвалит, и на тесноту места, в котором заключена эта жалкая слава. Ведь вся земля — точка, а какой маленький её уголок — это наше обиталище? И здесь сколько их и какие это люди — те, кто будет хвалить? Итак, впредь помни об уходе в этот свой деревенский уголок; и прежде всего не мечись и не напрягайся, но будь свободен и смотри на вещи как мужчина, как человек, как гражданин, как смертное живое существо. А среди того, что у тебя всего ближе под рукой и во что ты будешь вглядываться, наклоняясь, пусть будут эти два положения. Первое: вещи не касаются души, но стоят вне её, неподвижно, и смятение происходит только от суждения внутри. Второе: всё то, что ты видишь, почти тотчас изменится и перестанет быть; и постоянно думай о том, сколько перемен ты сам уже видел. Мироздание — превращение; жизнь — суждение.

passages.greek: Μὴ κατατρίψῃς τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦ βίου μέρος ἐν ταῖς περὶ ἑτέρων φαντασίαις, ὁπόταν μὴ τὴν ἀναφορὰν ἐπί τι κοινωφελὲς ποιῇ (ἤτοι γὰρ ἄλλου ἔργου στέρῃ). τουτέστι φανταζόμενος τί ὁ δεῖνα πράσσει καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν καὶ τί λέγει καὶ τί ἐνθυμεῖται καὶ τί τεχνάζεται καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ποιεῖ ἀπορρέμβεσθαι τῆς τοῦ ἰδίου ἡγεμονικοῦ παρατηρήσεως. χρὴ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὸ εἰκῇ καὶ μάτην ἐν τῷ εἱρμῷ τῶν φαντασιῶν περιίστασθαι, πολὺ δὲ μάλιστα τὸ περίεργον καὶ κακόηθες καὶ ἐθιστέον ἑαυτὸν μόνα φαντάζεσθαι, περὶ ὧν εἴ τις ἄφνω ἐπανέροιτο· τί νῦν διανοῇ; μετὰ παρρησίας παραχρῆμα ἂν ἀποκρίναιο ὅτι τὸ καὶ τό· ὡς ἐξ αὐτῶν εὐθὺς δῆλα εἶναι, ὅτι πάντα ἁπλᾶ καὶ εὐμενῆ καὶ ζῴου κοινωνικοῦ καὶ ἀμελοῦντος ἡδονικῶν ἢ καθάπαξ ἀπολαυστικῶν φαντασμάτων ἢ φιλονεικίας τινὸς ἢ βασκανίας καὶ ὑποψίας ἢ ἄλλου τινός, ἐφ’ ᾧ ἂν ἐρυθριάσειας ἐξηγούμενος, ὅτι ἐν νῷ αὐτὸ εἶχες. ὁ γάρ τοι ἀνὴρ ὁ τοιοῦτος, οὐκέτι ὑπερτιθέμενος τὸ ὡς ἐν ἀρίστοις ἤδη εἶναι, ἱερεύς τίς ἐστι καὶ ὑπουργὸς θεῶν, χρώμενος καὶ τῷ ἔνδον ἱδρυμένῳ αὐτῷ, ὃ παρέχεται τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἄχραντον ἡδονῶν, ἄτρωτον ὑπὸ παντὸς πόνου, πάσης ὕβρεως ἀνέπαφον, πάσης ἀναίσθητον πονηρίας, ἀθλητὴν ἄθλου τοῦ μεγίστου, τοῦ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς πάθους καταβληθῆναι, δικαιοσύνῃ βεβαμμένον εἰς βάθος, ἀσπαζόμενον μὲν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ ἀπονεμόμενα πάντα, μὴ πολλάκις δὲ μηδὲ χωρὶς μεγάλης καὶ κοινωφελοῦς ἀνάγκης φανταζόμενον τί ποτε ἄλλος λέγει ἢ πράσσει ἢ διανοεῖται. μόνα γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πρὸς ἐνέργειαν † ἔχει καὶ τὰ ἑαυτῷ ἐκ τῶν ὅλων συγκλωθόμενα διηνεκῶς ἐννοεῖ κἀκεῖνα μὲν καλὰ παρέχεται, ταῦτα δὲ ἀγαθὰ εἶναι πέπεισται· ἡ γὰρ ἑκάστῳ νεμομένη μοῖρα συνεμφέρεταί τε καὶ συνεμφέρει. μέμνηται δὲ καὶ ὅτι συγγενὲς πᾶν τὸ λογικόν, καὶ ὅτι κήδεσθαι μὲν πάντων ἀνθρώπων κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσιν ἐστί, δόξης δὲ οὐχὶ τῆς παρὰ πάντων ἀνθεκτέον, ἀλλὰ τῶν ὁμολογουμένως τῇ φύσει βιούντων μόνων. οἱ δὲ μὴ οὕτως βιοῦντες ὁποῖοί τινες οἴκοι τε καὶ ἔξω τῆς οἰκίας καὶ νύκτωρ καὶ μεθʼ ἡμέραν, οἷοι μεθʼ οἵων φύρονται, μεμνημένος διατελεῖ. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ τὸν παρὰ τῶν τοιούτων ἔπαινον ἐν λόγῳ τίθεται, οἵγε οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς ἀρέσκονται.
passages.english: Do not wear away what is left of your life in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit (for in truth you are deprived of other work). That is, forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part. So you must avoid, in the chain of your impressions, even what is random and to no purpose, but far the most what is meddling and malicious. And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”; so that from them it would be plain straight away that everything is simple and kindly and belongs to a social animal, one that cares nothing for imaginings of pleasure or of enjoyment in general, or for any rivalry, or envy and suspicion, or anything else that you would blush to explain you had in your mind. For a man of this kind, who no longer puts off being, so to speak, among the best already, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods. He also uses what is enshrined within him, which makes the person unstained by pleasures, unwounded by any pain, untouched by any insult, insensible to any wickedness, an athlete in the greatest contest, the contest not to be thrown by any passion, dyed deep in justice, welcoming with his whole soul everything that happens and is allotted, and not often, nor without a great need that serves the common benefit, forming an impression of what another person is saying or doing or thinking. For it is only what is his own that he has for his activity, and what is spun for him out of the whole he thinks of without a break; and the former he makes fine, and the latter he is convinced are good. For the lot dealt to each person is carried along with them and carries them along with it. He remembers too that everything rational is kin, and that to care for all human beings is in keeping with the nature of a human being, but that the good opinion to hold on to is not that of everyone, but only of those who live in agreement with nature. As for those who do not live so, he keeps in mind all the time what sort of people they are at home and outside the house, by night and by day, and what they are like and with what kind of people they are mixed up. So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.

notes.note: The passage runs on one root: φαντασία, with its verb φαντάζομαι. The English keeps “impression” and “form an impression” throughout, though in plain speech the sense is close to picturing or imagining what others are up to.
notes.other_reading: in imaginings about other people

notes.note: ἤτοι normally opens an “either … or”, and no “or” follows, so the parenthesis does not construe as given and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked: some editors mark a gap or change the particle). The English takes the particle as an emphatic “in truth”. στέρῃ is “you are deprived of”, “you go without”.
notes.other_reading: for either you are being deprived of some other work, [or …]

notes.note: The English takes ὅσα as the relative that joins the list to the verb, “all such things as make you wander away”; “you” is supplied. The list can also be ended at “and all such things”, with “makes” said of the whole habit.
notes.other_reading: and everything of that kind: this makes you stray from watching over your own ruling part

notes.note: The Greek is impersonal here and at χρὴ just before (“one must”), and turns to the second person in the same sentence (“you would answer”). Marcus often uses ἑαυτόν for “yourself”, and the English has “you” throughout so that the sentence holds together.
notes.other_reading: And one must accustom oneself

notes.note: Literally “this and that”, standing for a definite content that could be named. In English of today “this and that” is a vague answer, so the English has “This, and this”.
notes.other_reading: “Such and such”

notes.note: φάντασμα is the thing imagined, a figment, not the φαντασία (“impression”) of the rest of the passage, so the English gives it a different word, “imaginings”.
notes.other_reading: impressions of pleasure or of enjoyment in general

notes.note: The word is love of strife or, by the spelling that became confused with it, love of winning. “Rivalry” covers both.
notes.other_reading: any love of quarrelling

notes.greek: τὸ ὡς ἐν ἀρίστοις ἤδη εἶναι
notes.note: Literally “the being already as among the best”. The ὡς softens the claim (“so to speak”); it could also be heard as “being as one of the best is”.
notes.other_reading: who no longer puts off taking his place now among the best

notes.note: ἱδρύω is the verb for setting up a statue, altar or shrine, which carries on the image of the priest: what is “set up” within him is the god in him, which Marcus elsewhere calls the δαίμων. “Enshrined” keeps the image; the Greek does not name what it is.
notes.other_reading: that which is seated within him

notes.note: ὕβρις is outrage or insolence. It can be insult done to him, which cannot reach him, or insolence of his own, which he is free of. The English takes it as what is done to him, in line with “unwounded” before it.
notes.other_reading: untouched by any arrogance

notes.note: The edition marks the text as corrupt at this point with a dagger, so the wording is uncertain. The English gives the words as they stand: only his own things he “has” “for activity”.
notes.other_reading: For he keeps only his own affairs in view for action

notes.note: The same rare verb in the passive and the active: the lot “is carried along with” and “carries along with”. Neither verb has its companion expressed; the English supplies the person, the only one the sentence names (“each”). There may also be a play on συμφέρει, “is good for”.
notes.other_reading: is borne along with the whole and bears the person along with it

notes.note: δόξα is opinion, here the opinion others hold of one, reputation. The English has “good opinion” so that the contrast (that of everyone, or only that of those who live by nature) stays clear.
notes.other_reading: but that the reputation to cling to is not the one that comes from everyone

notes.note: φύρω is to mix, knead or muddle; of people, to mix with others in a disorderly way, with a tone of dirt. The English keeps “mixed up”.
notes.other_reading: what they are like and what sort of company they wallow in

check.note: As given, the particle means “either” and has no answering “or”, so the parenthesis does not construe; the English reads it as “surely” without saying so. The verb is “you are deprived of”, not “you are robbing yourself”.
check.decided: Accepted: the parenthesis reads “(for in truth you are deprived of other work)”, with no “yourself”. The note says that the particle has no answering “or”, that the words do not construe as given, and that the text is doubted.

check.note: The English makes a restrictive clause, “all such things as make you wander away”. The list can also end at “and all such things”, with “this makes you stray” said of the whole habit.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “and all such things as make you wander away”, because ὅσα can itself be the relative that joins the list to the verb. A note now records the other reading and says that “you” is supplied.

check.note: In English of today “this and that” is a vague brush-off, the opposite of the frank and exact answer that is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the answer now reads “This, and this”, which stands for a definite content; a note gives the literal wording.

check.note: The verb is “renders, makes”, and the same verb a few lines on is given as “makes fine”. “Keeps” suggests preserving a state already there.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “which makes the person unstained by pleasures”, the same word as “makes fine” below.

check.note: The word can be outrage done to him, as in the English, or arrogance of his own, like the wickedness in the next phrase. The English chooses the first.
check.decided: Declined: the draft stands. The two phrases before it, on pleasures and pain, are about what comes at him from outside, and the Greek genitive allows “untouched by”; the note already records “untouched by any arrogance” as the other reading.

check.note: “Unfeeling of” is not current English and is hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “insensible to any wickedness”.

check.note: “To the depth” is not idiomatic English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “dyed deep in justice”, which keeps the image of dyeing.

check.note: The edition marks the text as corrupt here. The English gives a smooth sense and supplies “as matter”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “For it is only what is his own that he has for his activity”, with “as matter” removed. The note says that the edition marks the place as corrupt and that the wording is uncertain.

check.note: Neither verb has an expressed companion or object, and the English supplies the person both times. It can also be read: the lot is carried along with the whole and carries the person along.
check.decided: Declined: the draft stands. Something has to be supplied in English, and the person is the only companion the sentence itself names (“the lot dealt to each”); the note records the reading with the whole.

check.note: Found while settling: “dealt out to him” adds “to him”, which the Greek does not have, the same addition as was removed at the same verb in 4.3.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “everything that happens and is dealt out”.

passages.casaubon: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work. That is, spend not thy time in thinking, what such a man doth, and to what end: what he saith, and what he thinks, and what he is about, and such other things or curiosities, which make a man to rove and wander from the care and observation of that part of himself, which is rational, and overruling. See therefore in the whole series and connection of thy thoughts, that thou be careful to prevent whatsoever is idle and impertinent: but especially, whatsoever is curious and malicious: and thou must use thyself to think only of such things, of which if a man upon a sudden should ask thee, what it is that thou art now thinking, thou mayest answer This, and That, freely and boldly, that so by thy thoughts it may presently appear that in all thee is sincere, and peaceable; as becometh one that is made for society, and regards not pleasures, nor gives way to any voluptuous imaginations at all: free from all contentiousness, envy, and suspicion, and from whatsoever else thou wouldest blush to confess thy thoughts were set upon. He that is such, is he surely that doth not put off to lay hold on that which is best indeed, a very priest and minister of the gods, well acquainted and in good correspondence with him especially that is seated and placed within himself, as in a temple and sacrary: to whom also he keeps and preserves himself unspotted by pleasure, undaunted by pain; free from any manner of wrong, or contumely, by himself offered unto himself: not capable of any evil from others: a wrestler of the best sort, and for the highest prize, that he may not be cast down by any passion or affection of his own; deeply dyed and drenched in righteousness, embracing and accepting with his whole heart whatsoever either happeneth or is allotted unto him. One who not often, nor without some great necessity tending to some public good, mindeth what any other, either speaks, or doth, or purposeth: for those things only that are in his own power, or that are truly his own, are the objects of his employments, and his thoughts are ever taken up with those things, which of the whole universe are by the fates or Providence destinated and appropriated unto himself. Those things that are his own, and in his own power, he himself takes order, for that they be good: and as for those that happen unto him, he believes them to be so. For that lot and portion which is assigned to every one, as it is unavoidable and necessary, so is it always profitable. He remembers besides that whatsoever partakes of reason, is akin unto him, and that to care for all men generally, is agreeing to the nature of a man: but as for honour and praise, that they ought not generally to be admitted and accepted of from all, but from such only, who live according to nature. As for them that do not, what manner of men they be at home, or abroad; day or night, how conditioned themselves with what manner of conditions, or with men of what conditions they moil and pass away the time together, he knoweth, and remembers right well, he therefore regards not such praise and approbation, as proceeding from them, who cannot like and approve themselves.
passages.russian: Не изнашивай остаток жизни в представлениях о других людях, когда ты не соотносишь их с чем-то общеполезным (ведь, по правде, ты лишаешься другого дела). То есть представляя себе, что делает такой-то и зачем, что говорит, что у него на уме, что он затевает, и всё подобное, отчего ты уходишь в сторону от надзора за собственным ведущим началом. Поэтому в цепи своих представлений избегай даже случайного и бесцельного, но больше всего — вмешивающегося в чужое и злонамеренного. И приучай себя иметь лишь такие представления, о которых, если бы кто-нибудь вдруг спросил: «О чём ты сейчас думаешь?», ты тотчас откровенно ответил бы: «О том-то и о том-то»; так чтобы из них сразу было ясно, что всё просто и доброжелательно и подобает общественному животному, которому нет дела до картин наслаждения или вообще удовольствия, или до какого-либо соперничества, или зависти и подозрения, или чего-нибудь иного, о чём ты покраснел бы, объясняя, что это у тебя на уме. Ведь такой человек, который больше не откладывает того, чтобы быть, так сказать, уже среди лучших, есть своего рода жрец и служитель богов. Он пользуется и тем, что водворено в нём, как в святилище, — тем, что делает человека незапятнанным наслаждениями, неуязвимым для всякой боли, недосягаемым для всякого оскорбления, нечувствительным ко всякому злонравию, атлетом в величайшем состязании — состязании за то, чтобы не быть поверженным никакой страстью, глубоко прокрашенным справедливостью, всей душой принимающим всё происходящее и уделённое, и не часто и не без великой нужды, служащей общей пользе, составляющим себе представление о том, что другой говорит, делает или думает. Ведь только своё он имеет для своей деятельности, а о том, что спрядено ему из целого, думает непрестанно; и первое он делает прекрасным, а во втором убеждён, что оно хорошо. Доля, выпавшая каждому, несётся вместе с ним и несёт его с собой. Он помнит также, что всё разумное родственно и что заботиться обо всех людях соответствует природе человека, но дорожить надо добрым мнением не всех, а лишь тех, кто живёт согласно с природой. А о тех, кто живёт не так, он всё время помнит, каковы они дома и вне дома, ночью и днём, что они собой представляют и с какими людьми водятся. Поэтому он ни во что не ставит и похвалу таких людей, которые не нравятся даже самим себе.

passages.greek:
Ὁ θεὸς πάντα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ γυμνὰ τῶν ὑλικῶν ἀγγείων καὶ φλοιῶν καὶ καθαρμάτων ὁρᾷ· μόνῳ γὰρ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ νοερῷ μόνων ἅπτεται τῶν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ εἰς ταῦτα ἐρρυηκότων καὶ ἀπωχετευμένων. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ σὺ τοῦτο ἐθίσῃς ποιεῖν, τὸν πολὺν περισπασμὸν σεαυτοῦ περιαιρήσεις· ὁ γὰρ μὴ τὰ περικείμενα κρεᾴδια ὁρῶν, ἦ πού γε ἐσθῆτα καὶ οἰκίαν καὶ δόξαν καὶ τὴν τοιαύτην περιβολὴν καὶ σκηνὴν θεώμενος, ἀσχολήσεται.

Τρία ἐστὶν ἐξ ὧν συνέστηκας· σωμάτιον, πνευμάτιον, νοῦς. τούτων τἄλλα μέχρι τοῦ ἐπιμελεῖσθαι δεῖν σά ἐστι, τὸ δὲ τρίτον μόνον κυρίως σόν. ὃ ἐὰν χωρίσῃς ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ, τουτέστιν ἀπὸ τῆς σῆς διανοίας, ὅσα ἄλλοι ποιοῦσιν ἢ λέγουσιν ἢ ὅσα αὐτὸς ἐποίησας ἢ εἶπας καὶ ὅσα ὡς μέλλοντα ταράσσει σε καὶ ὅσα τοῦ περικειμένου σοι σωματίου ἢ τοῦ συμφύτου πνευματίου ἀπροαίρετα πρόσεστιν καὶ ὅσα ἡ ἔξωθεν περιρρέουσα δίνη ἑλίσσει, ὥστε τῶν συνειμαρμένων ἐξῃρημένην καὶ καθαρὰν τὴν νοερὰν δύναμιν ἀπόλυτον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς ζῆν, ποιοῦσαν τὰ δίκαια καὶ θέλουσαν τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ λέγουσαν τἀληθῆ· ἐὰν χωρίσῃς, φημί, τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ τούτου τὰ προσηρτημένα ἐκ προσπαθείας καὶ τοῦ χρόνου τὰ ἐπέκεινα ἢ τὰ παρῳχηκότα, ποιήσῃς τε σεαυτόν, οἷος ὁ Ἐμπεδόκλειος σφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃ περιηγέι γαίων, μόνον τε ζῆν ἐκμελετήσῃς ὃ ζῇς, τουτέστι τὸ παρόν· δυνήσῃ τό γε μέχρι τοῦ ἀποθανεῖν ὑπολειπόμενον ἀταράκτως καὶ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἵλεως τῷ σαυτοῦ δαίμονι διαβιῶναι.
passages.english:
God sees all ruling parts bare of their material vessels and husks and refuse. For with only the part of himself that is of mind he touches only what has flowed out of himself into these and been channelled off. If you too make a habit of doing this, you will strip away most of your distraction. For someone who does not look at the surrounding scraps of flesh is hardly likely to busy themselves with gazing at clothing and a house and reputation and that kind of wrapping and stage scenery.

There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours. So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that attaches to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you, and all that the whirl streaming round outside sets spinning, so that the power of mind, lifted clear of what is bound up with it by fate, and clean, lives set loose by itself, doing what is just and willing what happens and saying what is true; if, I say, you separate from this ruling part the things fastened onto it by attachment, and what of time lies ahead or has gone by, and make yourself like the sphere of Empedocles, “rounded, rejoicing in its encircling solitude”, and practise living only what you are living, that is, the present: then what is left until you die, at least, you will be able to live through untroubled, kindly, and gracious towards your own guardian spirit.

notes.note: φλοιός is bark, husk or rind, any outer covering; κάθαρμα is what is thrown away in cleaning, refuse. The three nouns (vessels, husks, refuse) are all images for the body and its coverings.
notes.other_reading: bare of their material vessels and bark and impurities

notes.note: “Into these” can point to the vessels and husks, into which the ruling parts have flowed from god, or to the ruling parts themselves. The English leaves it as “these”.
notes.other_reading: what has flowed out of himself into these ruling parts

notes.note: τὸν πολὺν with a noun is “the greater part of” or “all this great”; the English has “most of”. σεαυτοῦ can go with the verb (“strip from yourself”) or with the noun (“your distraction”). The Greek also plays on the prefix περι- (“around”) here and in the next sentence: distraction, stripping away, surrounding flesh, wrapping.
notes.other_reading: you will strip away from yourself that great distraction

notes.note: After a negative this idiom means “much less”: one who does not look at the flesh will, still less, spend time gazing at clothes. The Greek has no “not” here and puts it as a half question; the English has “is hardly likely to”.
notes.other_reading: will someone who does not look at the surrounding scraps of flesh busy themselves, do you suppose, with gazing at clothing and a house and reputation?

notes.note: σκηνή is a tent or hut and also the stage building and its scenery. With θεώμενος, the verb for watching a show, the English takes the theatre sense.
notes.other_reading: that kind of wrapping and tent

notes.note: Both are diminutives, with a belittling tone. πνευμάτιον is the breath that keeps the body alive, not “spirit” in the modern sense, so the English has “a little breath”.
notes.other_reading: a poor body, a puff of breath

notes.note: As given, the relative ὃ (“which”) has no construction with what follows, since the object of “separate” is the string of “all that” clauses. The English treats it as a loose connective, “So”; from memory, unchecked, some editors print διό (“therefore”). The long “if” clause is taken up again further down.
notes.other_reading: Which third part, if you separate from yourself

notes.note: The passage has both νοῦς and διάνοια. The English keeps “mind” for νοῦς and νοερός and “thought” for διάνοια, as the glossary prefers, though διάνοια here is the faculty.
notes.other_reading: that is, from your understanding

notes.note: σύμφυτος is inborn, grown together with something. The English takes it with “you”, carried over from the body “that surrounds you”; it can also mean grown together with the body.
notes.other_reading: the little breath that has grown with it

notes.note: A rare word built on εἱμαρμένη, fate: the things fated together with it, bound up with it by fate. The English spells the sense out.
notes.other_reading: lifted clear of the things that share its fate

notes.note: προσπάθεια is passionate attachment to something, a clinging. The English has “attachment”.
notes.other_reading: the things that hang on it through its passions

notes.note: The epic forms show these words are a line of verse quoted from Empedocles, so they are set in quotation marks, which the Greek as given does not have; the line may begin at σφαῖρος. μονίη can be “solitude” (from μόνος) or “rest”, “staying still” (from μένω), and περιηγής is “circular” or “encircling”. The English has “its encircling solitude”.
notes.other_reading: rounded, rejoicing in its circular stillness

notes.note: ἵλεως is “gracious”, the word for a god who is well disposed; here it is you who are so towards your δαίμων, the divine being assigned to each person, which Marcus identifies with the mind. “Guardian” is supplied in the English so that “spirit” is not heard as your own soul or mood. The dative may go with all three words or only with the last.
notes.other_reading: untroubled, and kindly and gracious towards the god within you

check.note: The word is plural and here means outer coverings; “bark” is odd of a human being.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “vessels and husks and refuse”. The plural is kept and the image of an outer covering stays.

check.note: With the article the adjective means “the greater part of” or “all this great amount of”. “The great distraction” reads as one particular distraction.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “you will strip away most of your distraction”. “Most of” is taken; “strip away” is kept instead of “rid yourself”, because the verb is taking off something that lies around one, the image that runs through the passage.

check.note: The Greek has no “not”; the idiom is an ironic half question, “will they, do you suppose, spend time gazing at clothing?”. “A person” after “wrapped round” is also supplied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “is hardly likely to busy themselves with gazing at”, so the flat “not” is gone and the tone of supposing is kept without a first-person aside. “A person” is dropped: the flesh is now “the surrounding scraps of flesh”.

check.note: As given, “which” has no construction, since the object of “separate” is the string of “all that” clauses. “So” answers to a corrected text, not to the Greek as given.
check.decided: Accepted: “So if” is kept, and the note now says that the relative does not construe as given and that “So” treats it as a connective, in line with a correction that some editors print (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The adjective normally means inborn, grown together with you. The English makes it grown with the body, which is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the little breath born with you”, the usual sense of the word. A note records “grown with the body” as the other reading.

check.note: The noun can be “solitude” or “stillness”, and the word with it is an adjective, “circular” or “encircling”. The English chooses “solitude” and turns the adjective into “all around it”; it is also unsure where the quotation begins.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “rejoicing in its encircling solitude”, with the adjective kept as an adjective. “Solitude” stays, since the sentence is about the mind living set loose by itself; the note gives “circular stillness” and says the quotation may begin one word earlier.

check.greek: τό γε μέχρι τοῦ ἀποθανεῖν ὑπολειπόμενον
check.note: The particle “at least” is dropped: whatever of the past is gone, you can at least live the remainder well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “then what is left until you die, at least, you will be able to live through …”. The order is changed so that “untroubled” is not read with “die”.

check.note: “Guardian” is not in the Greek word. The adjective is “gracious, kindly toward”, a little other than “at peace with”, and the adverb before it may go with the same dative.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “untroubled, kindly, and gracious toward your own guardian spirit”, with “gracious toward” for ἵλεως and “kindly” for εὐμενῶς as in 3.4. “Guardian spirit” is kept, because “your own spirit” alone would be heard as your own soul or mood; the note says that “guardian” is supplied.

check.note: Found while settling: “into them” reads in English as “into the ruling parts”, but the Greek “into these” more naturally points to the vessels and husks, since the ruling parts are themselves what has flowed from god.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “into these”, which leaves the reference as open as the Greek, and the note gives both ways of taking it.

check.note: Found while settling: this is the same participle as in “the surrounding scraps of flesh” in the chapter before, and “wrapped round you” made it a different English word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the little body that surrounds you”, so the repeated Greek word is one English word in both chapters.

passages.casaubon: God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross. For with His simple and pure understanding, He pierceth into our inmost and purest parts, which from His, as it were by a water pipe and channel, first flowed and issued. This if thou also shalt use to do, thou shalt rid thyself of that manifold luggage, wherewith thou art round about encumbered. For he that does regard neither his body, nor his clothing, nor his dwelling, nor any such external furniture, must needs gain unto himself great rest and ease. Three things there be in all, which thou doest consist of; thy body, thy life, and thy mind. Of these the two former, are so far forth thine, as that thou art bound to take care for them. But the third alone is that which is properly thine. If then thou shalt separate from thyself, that is from thy mind, whatsoever other men either do or say, or whatsoever thou thyself hast heretofore either done or said; and all troublesome thoughts concerning the future, and whatsoever, (as either belonging to thy body or life:) is without the jurisdiction of thine own will, and whatsoever in the ordinary course of human chances and accidents doth happen unto thee; so that thy mind (keeping herself loose and free from all outward coincidental entanglements; always in a readiness to depart:) shall live by herself, and to herself, doing that which is just, accepting whatsoever doth happen, and speaking the truth always; if, I say, thou shalt separate from thy mind, whatsoever by sympathy might adhere unto it, and all time both past and future, and shalt make thyself in all points and respects, like unto Empedocles his allegorical sphere, 'all round and circular,' &c., and shalt think of no longer life than that which is now present: then shalt thou be truly able to pass the remainder of thy days without troubles and distractions; nobly and generously disposed, and in good favour and correspondency, with that spirit which is within thee.
passages.russian:
Бог видит все ведущие начала обнажёнными от вещественных сосудов, шелухи и отбросов. Ведь лишь той частью себя, которая есть ум, он касается лишь того, что истекло из него самого в них и было туда отведено. Если и ты привыкнешь так делать, то сбросишь с себя большую часть того, что тебя отвлекает. Ведь кто не смотрит на окружающие его клочки плоти, тот вряд ли станет хлопотать, разглядывая одежду, дом, славу и тому подобную обёртку и театральные декорации.

Есть три вещи, из которых ты состоишь: тельце, дыханьице, ум. Из них два других твои постольку, поскольку ты должен о них заботиться, но лишь третье — по-настоящему твоё. Итак, если ты отделишь от себя, то есть от своей мысли, всё, что другие делают или говорят, или всё, что ты сам сделал или сказал, и всё, что тревожит тебя как грядущее, и всё, что помимо твоего выбора пристаёт к тебе от облекающего тебя тельца или от врождённого дыханьица, и всё, что раскручивает вихрь, текущий кругом снаружи, — так, чтобы сила ума, поднятая над тем, что сплетено с ней роком, и чистая, жила сама по себе, отпущенная на волю, делая справедливое, желая происходящего и говоря истинное; если, говорю я, ты отделишь от этого ведущего начала то, что прикреплено к нему привязанностью, и то из времени, что впереди или миновало, и сделаешь себя подобным сфере Эмпедокла, «округлой, радующейся объемлющему её одиночеству», и будешь упражняться в том, чтобы проживать только то, что проживаешь, то есть настоящее, — тогда остаток жизни до смерти ты, по крайней мере, сможешь прожить невозмутимо, доброжелательно и благосклонно к собственному духу-хранителю.

passages.greek:
πῶς ἅπτεται θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος καὶ κατὰ τί ἑαυτοῦ μέρος καὶ ὅταν πῶς ἔχῃ διακέηται τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦτο μόριον.

Οὐδὲν ἀθλιώτερον τοῦ πάντα κύκλῳ ἐκπεριερχομένου καὶ ʽτὰ νέρθεν γᾶς (φησὶν) ἐρευνῶντοςʼ καὶ τὰ ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν πλησίον διὰ τεκμάρσεως ζητοῦντος, μὴ αἰσθομένου δέ, ὅτι ἀρκεῖ πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ ἔνδον ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονι εἶναι καὶ τοῦτον γνησίως θεραπεύειν. θεραπεία δὲ αὐτοῦ, καθαρὸν πάθους διατηρεῖν καὶ εἰκαιότητος καὶ δυσαρεστήσεως τῆς πρὸς τὰ ἐκ θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων γινόμενα. τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ θεῶν αἰδέσιμα δι’ ἀρετήν· τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων φίλα διὰ συγγένειαν, ἔστι δὲ ὅτε καὶ τρόπον τινὰ ἐλεεινὰ δι’ ἄγνοιαν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν· οὐκ ἐλάττων ἡ πήρωσις αὕτη τῆς στερισκούσης τοῦ διακρίνειν τὰ λευκὰ καὶ μέλανα.
passages.english:
How a human being touches god, and with what part of themselves, and in what state this part of the human being is when that happens.

Nothing is more wretched than a person who goes round everything in a circle and, as it is said, “searches into the things beneath the earth”, and looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly. To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of their excellence; and what comes from people is dear because of kinship, and sometimes also, in a way, pitiable because of their ignorance of what is good and bad. This disability is no less than the one that takes away the power to tell white from black.

notes.note: The Greek given begins in the middle of a list: these are indirect questions that hang on a verb in the part of the chapter not given. Nothing is added; they are left as a list of questions, with a capital letter at the start.
notes.other_reading: [to consider] how a human being lays hold of god

notes.note: The Greek has two verbs side by side that both mean “is in a certain state”, with nothing joining them, so the clause does not construe as given; one looks like a gloss on the other (from memory, unchecked: editors bracket ἔχῃ). διακέηται is itself an odd form. The English translates the sense once.
