notes.other_reading: and when this part of the human being is in what state, how disposed

notes.note: “He says” marks the words in quotation marks as a quotation from an author who is not named; the Doric form γᾶς shows it is verse. The English has “as it is said” so that “he” is not taken for the wretched person. From memory, unchecked: the line is Pindar’s, quoted by Plato in the Theaetetus.
notes.other_reading: and, as the poet says, “searches into what lies under the earth”

notes.note: τέκμαρσις is inference from signs, conjecture. The English has “by guesswork”.
notes.other_reading: and tries to work out from signs what is in the souls of their neighbours

notes.greek: πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ ἔνδον ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονι εἶναι
notes.note: πρός with εἶναι is to be occupied with something, and μόνῳ says with this and nothing else: “keep only to”. δαίμων is the divine being within each person, not “demon” in the later sense; the English has “guardian spirit”, as in 12.3, with “guardian” supplied.
notes.other_reading: to be with the god within them, and with that alone

notes.note: θεραπεύω is to serve or attend on a god, and also to tend or care for. The English keeps “serve” for the verb and for the noun θεραπεία after it.
notes.other_reading: and to tend it sincerely. Tending it means

notes.note: The noun from εἰκῇ, “at random”: acting or thinking without purpose. The English has “aimlessness”.
notes.other_reading: clean of passion and thoughtlessness

notes.note: ἀρετή is excellence or virtue; the Greek does not say whose. The English takes it as that of the gods and has “their excellence”.
notes.other_reading: deserves reverence because of its goodness

notes.note: πήρωσις is a maiming or disabling, often used of blindness. The English keeps the general word, since the comparison with not telling white from black supplies the blindness.
notes.other_reading: This blindness is no less than the one that robs a person of telling white from black

check.note: Two verbs stand side by side with no connective, so the clause does not construe as given; it looks like a doublet, one verb a variant or gloss of the other. The English renders both and is hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “and in what state this part of the human being is when that happens”. Both verbs mean “is in a certain state”, so one English phrase covers them; the note says that the clause does not construe as given and gives the wording with both verbs.

check.note: A reader will take “he” in “as he says” to be the wretched person just described. The word marks a quotation from an unnamed author.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “as it is said”, so no “he” can be mistaken for the wretched person. “The poet” is not put into the text, because the Greek names no one; the note gives it.

check.greek: πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ ἔνδον ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονι εἶναι
check.note: The trailing “alone” is ambiguous in English. The Greek means attending to this spirit and nothing else, and “guardian” is added to the noun.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “to keep only to the guardian spirit within them”, so “only” plainly goes with the spirit. “Guardian spirit” is kept, as in 12.3, because “spirit” alone would be heard as the person’s own soul or mood; the note says that “guardian” is supplied.

check.note: Found while settling: the same Greek phrase was “from gods” here and “from the gods” in the next sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “from the gods and from people”, so the phrase is the same in both sentences and follows the glossary.

part.left_out: Πῶς πάντα ταχέως ἐναφανίζεται, τῷ μὲν κόσμῳ αὐτὰ τὰ σώματα, τῷ δὲ αἰῶνι αἱ μνῆμαι αὐτῶν. οἶά ἐστι τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα καὶ μάλιστα τὰ ἡδονῇ δελεάζοντα ἢ τῷ πόνῳ φοβοῦντα ἢ τῷ τύφῳ διαβεβοημένα· πῶς εὐτελῆ καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητα καὶ ῥυπαρὰ καὶ εὔφθαρτα καὶ νεκρά, νοερᾶς δυνάμεως ἐφιστάναι. τί εἰσιν οὗτοι, ὧν αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι. τί ἐστι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ ὅτι, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ μόνον ἴδῃ καὶ τῷ μερισμῷ τῆς ἐννοίας διαλύσῃ τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ, οὐκέτι ἄλλο τι ὑπολήψεται αὐτὸ εἶναι ἢ φύσεως ἔργον· φύσεως δὲ ἔργον εἴ τις φοβεῖται, παιδίον ἐστί· τοῦτο μέντοι οὐ μόνον φύσεως ἔργον ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφέρον αὐτῇ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the earlier parts of chapter 2.12 in its sections 2.9 and 2.10 and opens its 2.11 with that chapter's last sentence, on how man touches God, before going on through chapter 2.13.

passages.casaubon: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible, that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is within him, and truly and really to serve him. His service doth consist in this, that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, either in regard of the gods or men. For indeed whatsoever proceeds from the gods, deserves respect for their worth and excellency; and whatsoever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be entertained, with love, always; sometimes, as proceeding from their ignorance, of that which is truly good and bad, (a blindness no less, than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black:) with a kind of pity and compassion also.
passages.russian:
Как человек касается бога, и какой своей частью, и в каком состоянии бывает эта часть человека, когда это происходит.

Нет ничего жалче человека, который обходит всё по кругу и, как говорится, «исследует то, что под землёй», и по догадкам ищет, что в душах у ближних, но не замечает, что довольно держаться одного лишь духа-хранителя внутри себя и по-настоящему служить ему. Служить ему — значит хранить его чистым от страсти, бесцельности и недовольства тем, что исходит от богов и от людей. Ведь то, что от богов, достойно благоговения за их совершенство; а то, что от людей, дорого по родству, а иногда и в каком-то смысле достойно жалости из-за их незнания того, что хорошо и что дурно. Это увечье не меньше того, что лишает способности отличать белое от чёрного.

passages.greek:
Μὴ τὰ ἀπόντα ἐννοεῖν ὡς ἤδη ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τῶν παρόντων τὰ δεξιώτατα ἐκλογίζεσθαι καὶ τούτων χάριν ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι πῶς ἂν ἐπεζητεῖτο, εἰ μὴ παρῆν. ἅμα μέντοι φυλάσσου, μὴ διὰ τοῦ οὕτως ἀσμενίζειν αὐτοῖς ἐθίσῃς ἐκτιμᾶν αὐτά, ὥστε, ἐάν ποτε μὴ παρῇ, ταραχθήσεσθαι.

Εἰς σαυτὸν συνειλοῦ· φύσιν ἔχει τὸ λογικὸν ἡγεμονικὸν ἑαυτῷ ἀρκεῖσθαι δικαιοπραγοῦντι καὶ παρ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο γαλήνην ἔχοντι.
passages.english:
Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present, and on their account to remind yourself how they would be sought after if they were not present. At the same time, though, be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.

Draw in upon yourself. It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.

notes.note: The first sentence is in infinitives used as instructions, with no person; the second turns to “you”. The English keeps the impersonal form for the first (“Not to think …”), adding “yourself” only where English needs an object for “remind”.
notes.other_reading: Do not think of absent things as already there

notes.note: Literally “as already being”: as if they already existed or were already yours.
notes.other_reading: as if they were already yours

notes.note: δεξιός is “on the right hand”, so lucky, favourable, and also fine or choice. The English has “the best”.
notes.other_reading: the most fortunate of the things that are present

notes.note: χάριν with the genitive is “for the sake of” or “on account of”. The English takes it as giving the occasion for the reminder. ἐπεζητεῖτο is “would be sought after”, so “missed”.
notes.other_reading: and, for their sake, to remind yourself how much you would miss them if they were not there

notes.note: The verb “accustom” has no object in the Greek; “yourself” is understood. ἐκτιμάω is to value highly, to overvalue.
notes.other_reading: that you do not get into the habit of overvaluing them

notes.note: Literally “roll yourself up” or “coil yourself up” into yourself, as a thing is wound tight. The English has “draw in”, which keeps the movement.
notes.other_reading: Coil yourself up into yourself.

notes.note: γαλήνη is the calm of a still sea. The English keeps “calm”.
notes.other_reading: and by that very fact is at peace

check.note: A small point: “on their account” reads as “because of them”, while the Greek is closer to “with regard to these” or “for their sake”. Nothing here misleads.
check.decided: Declined: the draft stands. The Greek word with a genitive means “for the sake of” or “on account of”, and “on their account” can be heard in both ways, while “as to these” is weaker than the Greek; the note gives “for their sake”.

passages.casaubon: Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou wouldst want them, if they were not present. But take heed withal, lest that whilst thou dust settle thy contentment in things present, thou grow in time so to overprize them, as that the want of them (whensoever it shall so fall out) should be a trouble and a vexation unto thee. Wind up thyself into thyself. Such is the nature of thy reasonable commanding part, as that if it exercise justice, and have by that means tranquillity within itself, it doth rest fully satisfied with itself without any other thing.
passages.russian:
Не думать об отсутствующем так, будто оно уже есть, но перебрать лучшее из того, что есть, и по этому поводу напоминать себе, как бы ты его искал, если бы его не было. Но вместе с тем остерегайся, как бы, так радуясь ему, не приучить себя ценить его настолько, что, если его когда-нибудь не будет, ты встревожишься.

Удались в себя. Природа разумного ведущего начала такова, что оно довольно собой, когда поступает справедливо и тем самым пребывает в покое.

passages.greek:
Ἐναργὲς ἔστω ἀεὶ τὸ ὅτι τοιοῦτο ἐκεῖνο ὁ ἀγρός ἐστι καὶ πῶς πάντα ἐστὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ἐνθάδε τοῖς ἐν ἄκρῳ τῷ ὄρει ἢ ἐπὶ τοῦ αἰγιαλοῦ ἢ ὅπου θέλεις. ἄντικρυς γὰρ εὑρήσεις τὰ τοῦ Πλάτωνος· ʽσηκὸν ἐν ὄρει, φησί, περιβαλλόμενος καὶ βδάλλων βληχήματα.ʼ

Τί ἐστί μοι τὸ ἡγεμονικόν μου καὶ ποῖόν τι αὐτὸ ἐγὼ ποιῶ νῦν καὶ πρὸς τί ποτε αὐτῷ νῦν χρῶμαι; μήτι κενὸν νοῦ ἐστι; μήτι ἀπόλυτον καὶ ἀπεσπασμένον κοινωνίας; μήτι προστετηκὸς καὶ ἀνακεκραμένον τῷ σαρκιδίῳ, ὥστε τούτῳ συντρέπεσθαι;
passages.english:
Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like. For you will find exactly what Plato says: “putting a sheepfold round himself on a mountain,” he says, “and milking the bleaters.”

What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now? Can it be empty of mind? Can it be cut loose and torn away from community? Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?

notes.note: The wording does not construe cleanly: literally “that, the country place, is such”, with a neuter “that” beside the masculine noun and no “this” expressed. The English takes ἐκεῖνο as pointing to the country place one longs for (“over there”) and supplies “this” for the place where one is; ἀγρός is “country place” to match 4.3. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the text.
notes.other_reading: that this place is just what that country retreat is

notes.note: “Outright”, “exactly”. The Greek says only “you will find outright the words of Plato”, that is, find them borne out.
notes.other_reading: For you will find Plato’s saying plainly true

notes.note: A σηκός is a pen or fold for animals; the English has “sheepfold” so that “pen” is not misread. From memory, unchecked: the words come from the Theaetetus of Plato, where a ruler shut inside his city wall is compared to a herdsman in a mountain fold; Marcus quotes loosely.
notes.other_reading: “putting a pen round himself in the hills”

notes.note: Literally “milking bleatings”, the sound standing for the animals that make it. The English has “the bleaters” so that it can be read; the text here has also been doubted (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: “and milking bleatings”

notes.note: μήτι opens a question asked with misgiving: “can it be that …?”, “it is not …, is it?”. The English has “Can it be” for all three questions.
notes.other_reading: It is not empty of mind, is it?

notes.note: κοινωνία is sharing, fellowship, the common life of rational beings; the adjective is “social” in the glossary. The English has “community”.
notes.other_reading: cut loose and torn away from society

notes.note: “To turn together with it”: to be swayed whichever way the flesh is swayed. From memory, unchecked: another reading gives a verb meaning “to be nourished with it”.
notes.other_reading: so that it is moved by every movement of the flesh

check.note: The Greek does not construe cleanly: the pronouns are neuter, the noun masculine, and no “this” is expressed. The English joins “that” to the noun and supplies “this”; it can also be read “this place is just what that country retreat is”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the reading is kept and the English now has “the country place over there is just like this”, with “country place” to match 4.3. The note says that the words do not construe cleanly, that “this” is supplied, and gives the other reading.

check.greek: ἄντικρυς γὰρ εὑρήσεις τὰ τοῦ Πλάτωνος
check.note: “Fit” is supplied. The Greek says only “you will find exactly what Plato says”, that is, find it to be so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “For you will find exactly what Plato says”, so “fit” is gone. The suggested “it … as” is not taken, because that too is more than the Greek has.

check.note: “Pen” can be misread as a writing pen.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “putting a sheepfold round himself”, and the note keeps “pen” as the more general word.

check.note: The Greek says, harshly, “milking bleatings”. “Flock” is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “milking the bleaters”, which keeps the sound standing for the animals and adds no “flock”. The note gives the literal “milking bleatings”.

check.note: The particle, three times, gives an anxious question, “can it be that …?”. The plain “Is it” drops that tone each time.
check.decided: Accepted: all three questions now begin “Can it be”.

passages.casaubon: Let it always appear and be manifest unto thee that solitariness, and desert places, by many philosophers so much esteemed of and affected, are of themselves but thus and thus; and that all things are them to them that live in towns, and converse with others as they are the same nature everywhere to be seen and observed: to them that have retired themselves to the top of mountains, and to desert havens, or what other desert and inhabited places soever. For anywhere it thou wilt mayest thou quickly find and apply that to thyself; which Plato saith of his philosopher, in a place: as private and retired, saith he, as if he were shut up and enclosed about in some shepherd's lodge, on the top of a hill. There by thyself to put these questions to thyself or to enter in these considerations: What is my chief and principal part, which hath power over the rest? What is now the present estate of it, as I use it; and what is it, that I employ it about? Is it now void of reason ir no? Is it free, and separated; or so affixed, so congealed and grown together as it were with the flesh, that it is swayed by the motions and inclinations of it?
passages.russian:
Пусть тебе всегда будет ясно, что вон та загородная местность — точно такая же, как здесь, и что всё здесь то же самое, что на вершине горы, на морском берегу или где угодно. Ведь ты найдёшь в точности то, что говорит Платон: «обнеся себя, — говорит он, — овечьим загоном на горе и доя блеющих».

Что для меня моё ведущее начало, и каким я его делаю теперь, и для чего я теперь им пользуюсь? Неужели оно пусто, лишено ума? Неужели отрезано и оторвано от общности? Неужели расплавлено в кусочке плоти и смешано с ним, так что поворачивается, как поворачивается плоть?

passages.greek: Οὔτε τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι ὡς τὰ φυτὰ τίμιον οὔτε τὸ ἀναπνεῖν ὡς τὰ βοσκήματα καὶ τὰ θηρία οὔτε τὸ τυποῦσθαι κατὰ φαντασίαν οὔτε τὸ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι καθ’ ὁρμὴν οὔτε τὸ συναγελάζεσθαι οὔτε τὸ τρέφεσθαι· τοῦτο γὰρ ὅμοιον τῷ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα τῆς τροφῆς. τί οὖν τίμιον; τὸ κροτεῖσθαι; οὐχί. οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ τὸ ὑπὸ γλωσσῶν κροτεῖσθαι· αἱ γὰρ παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν εὐφημίαι κρότος γλωσσῶν. ἀφῆκας οὖν καὶ τὸ δοξάριον· τί καταλείπεται τίμιον; δοκῶ μὲν τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ἐφ’ ὅ καὶ αἱ ἐπιμέλειαι ἄγουσι καὶ αἱ τέχναι. ἥ τε γὰρ τέχνη πᾶσα τούτου στοχάζεται, ἵνα τὸ κατασκευασθὲν ἐπιτηδείως ἔχῃ πρὸς τὸ ἔργον πρὸς ὅ κατεσκεύασται· ὅ τε φυτουργὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπιμελούμενος τῆς ἀμπέλου, καὶ ὁ πωλοδάμνης καὶ ὁ τοῦ κυνὸς ἐπιμελούμενος τοῦτο ζητεῖ. αἱ δὲ παιδαγωγίαι, αἱ δὲ διδασκαλίαι ἐπὶ τί σπεύδουσιν; ὧδε οὖν τὸ τίμιον καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ἂν εὖ ἔχῃ, οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιποιήσεις σεαυτῷ. οὐ παύσῃ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τιμῶν; οὔτ’ οὖν ἐλεύθερος ἔσῃ οὔτε αὐτάρκης οὔτε ἀπαθής· ἀνάγκη γὰρ φθονεῖν, ζηλοτυπεῖν, ὑφορᾶσθαι τοὺς ἀφελέσθαι ἐκεῖνα δυναμένους, ἐπιβουλεύειν τοῖς ἔχουσι τὸ τιμώμενον ὑπὸ σοῦ. ὅλως πεφύρθαι ἀνάγκη τὸν ἐκείνων τινὸς ἐνδεῆ, προσέτι δὲ πολλὰ καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς μέμφεσθαι. ἡ δὲ τῆς ἰδίας διανοίας αἰδὼς καὶ τιμὴ σεαυτῷ τε ἀρεστόν σε ποιήσει καὶ τοῖς κοινωνοῖς εὐάρμοστον καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς σύμφωνον, τουτέστιν ἐπαινοῦντα ὅσα ἐκεῖνοι διανέμουσι καὶ διατετάχασιν.
passages.english: It is not breathing through the surface as plants do that is of value, nor breathing as cattle and wild beasts do, nor being stamped by an impression, nor being pulled on strings by impulse, nor herding together, nor taking in food; for this last is like passing out the waste from the food. What then is of value? Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well. What is left that is of value? I think it is this: to move and to hold back in keeping with the way one is oneself made, which is also where tending and the crafts lead. For every craft aims at this, that the thing made should be fit for the work it was made for. The planter and the one who tends the vine, the breaker of colts and the one who tends the dog are after this. And the upbringing of children, and teaching: what are they pressing towards? Here, then, is what is of value. And if this is in a good state, you will not be acquiring any of the other things for yourself. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and, what is more, to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself, well fitted to your fellows and in tune with the gods, that is, praising all that they deal out and have arranged.

notes.note: The argument turns on one root: τίμιον (“worth valuing”, “precious”), τιμῶν, τὸ τιμώμενον, τιμή. “Value” is kept for all of them, including the last, where “honour” would be the usual word.
notes.other_reading: is nothing to prize

notes.note: Literally “to breathe through”: to give off vapour through the surface, as plants do, set against ἀναπνεῖν, the breathing of animals. “Breathing” is used for both so that the pair can be heard; the technical word for the plant is “transpire”.
notes.other_reading: It is not transpiring as plants do

notes.note: The verb is from the puppet moved by strings. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: nor being jerked about like a puppet by impulse

notes.note: κροτέω is to strike together, to clap, so to applaud. Marcus moves from clapping with hands to praise as “clapping of tongues”; “clap” is kept so the step can be seen.
notes.other_reading: Then not being applauded by tongues either

notes.greek: κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι
notes.note: κατασκευή is the way a thing is built or made up, and the same root returns twice in the next sentence (“the thing made”, “was made for”), so “made” is kept; ἰδίαν, “one’s own”, is given by “oneself”. ἴσχεσθαι is to be held or to hold oneself in check; the Greek is impersonal here.
notes.other_reading: to act and to refrain according to one’s own constitution

notes.note: ἐπιμέλεια is care given to something; the Greek is plural, the different forms of such care. The same root comes twice below for the one who “tends” the vine and the dog, and “tending” keeps the link.
notes.other_reading: which is also where training and the crafts lead

notes.greek: ὅ τε φυτουργὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπιμελούμενος τῆς ἀμπέλου
notes.note: This can be two people (the planter, and the one who tends the vine) or one person named twice. Two are kept, as the Greek has two articles.
notes.other_reading: The gardener who tends the vine

notes.note: A plain future: “you will acquire”, “you will secure”. The thought is probably that a person whose own working is in good order will not go after the other things; the English keeps the plain future.
notes.other_reading: you will not care to get any of the other things for yourself

notes.greek: οὐ παύσῃ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τιμῶν
notes.note: As punctuated this is a question, “Will you not stop …?”, which in Greek is a way of urging. The next sentence then gives the result if you do not stop; the Greek does not spell out that “if”.
notes.other_reading: You will not stop valuing many other things too? Then you will not be free

notes.note: φύρω is to mix or muddle; in the perfect passive, to be in a muddle or turmoil.
notes.other_reading: is bound to be in turmoil

notes.note: αἰδώς is respect or reverence; τιμή is honour, and here it closes the chain on “value”. διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary; the faculty is meant here, so the English has “mind”.
notes.other_reading: But reverence and honour for your own understanding

notes.note: κοινωνοί are those who share something with you, partners, here those who share the common life. The English has “your fellows”.
notes.other_reading: well fitted to those who share society with you

check.note: “Transpiring” is a technical word of botany that most readers will not know, and it loses the pairing with “breathing” in the next phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “breathing through the surface as plants do”, so that the plant’s breathing and the animal’s “breathing” in the next phrase are heard as a pair, as the two Greek verbs on one root are. “Transpire” moves to the note as the technical word.

check.note: “Leftovers” suggests uneaten food on the plate. The Greek means the waste the body passes out.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “passing out the waste from the food”. The Greek word means what the body has left over and expels, so “waste” is right, but the Greek has “the food”, not “our food”.

check.note: “Try” is added. The Greek is a plain future: you will not acquire, or secure, any of the other things for yourself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you will not be acquiring any of the other things for yourself”. The Greek verb is a plain future with no idea of trying, and a note records the looser sense.

check.note: “The kinds of tending” is stiff and unclear on first reading. The link with “tends” (the vine, the dog) is good and should be kept.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “where tending and the crafts lead”. The Greek has the plural with the article and no “every”, which English gives best by the bare word; the link with “tends” below is kept.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “on a level with” for a word that says only “like”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for this last is like passing out the waste from the food”, since the Greek states a likeness and does not rank the two.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s “the way one is made” left out ἰδίαν, “one’s own”, which carries the contrast with what is shared with plants and animals.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in keeping with the way one is oneself made”.

check.greek: προσέτι δὲ πολλὰ καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς μέμφεσθαι
check.note: Found while settling: the draft passed over καί before “the gods”, which here means “even” or “too”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and what is more to find much fault even with the gods”.

passages.casaubon: Not vegetative spiration, it is not surely (which plants have) that in this life should be so dear unto us; nor sensitive respiration, the proper life of beasts, both tame and wild; nor this our imaginative faculty; nor that we are subject to be led and carried up and down by the strength of our sensual appetites; or that we can gather, and live together; or that we can feed: for that in effect is no better, than that we can void the excrements of our food. What is it then that should be dear unto us? to hear a clattering noise? if not that, then neither to be applauded by the tongues of men. For the praises of many tongues, is in effect no better than the clattering of so many tongues. If then neither applause, what is there remaining that should be dear unto thee? This I think: that in all thy motions and actions thou be moved, and restrained according to thine own true natural constitution and Construction only. And to this even ordinary arts and professions do lead us. For it is that which every art doth aim at, that whatsoever it is, that is by art effected and prepared, may be fit for that work that it is prepared for. This is the end that he that dresseth the vine, and he that takes upon him either to tame colts, or to train up dogs, doth aim at. What else doth the education of children, and all learned professions tend unto? Certainly then it is that, which should be dear unto us also. If in this particular it go well with thee, care not for the obtaining of other things. But is it so, that thou canst not but respect other things also? Then canst not thou truly be free? then canst thou not have self-content: then wilt thou ever be subject to passions. For it is not possible, but that thou must be envious, and jealous, and suspicious of them whom thou knowest can bereave thee of such things; and again, a secret underminer of them, whom thou seest in present possession of that which is dear unto thee. To be short, he must of necessity be full of confusion within himself, and often accuse the Gods, whosoever stands in need of these things. But if thou shalt honour and respect thy mind only, that will make thee acceptable towards thyself, towards thy friends very tractable; and conformable and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
passages.russian: Ценно не дыхание через поверхность, как у растений, и не дыхание, как у скота и зверей, и не то, что на тебе отпечатывается представление, и не то, что побуждение дёргает тебя за нити, и не сбивание в стада, и не приём пищи: ведь это последнее сродни выведению отходов пищи. Что же тогда ценно? Чтобы тебе рукоплескали? Нет. Значит, и не чтобы рукоплескали языками: ведь похвалы многих — это рукоплескание языков. Итак, ты отпустил и мелкую славу. Что остаётся ценного? Думаю, вот что: двигаться и сдерживаться сообразно тому, как ты сам устроен, — к этому ведут и уход, и ремёсла. Ведь всякое ремесло стремится к тому, чтобы сделанное было пригодно для дела, ради которого его сделали. К этому стремятся и тот, кто сажает, и тот, кто ухаживает за лозой, и объездчик жеребят, и тот, кто ухаживает за собакой. А воспитание детей, обучение — к чему они устремлены? Вот это, значит, и ценно. И если с этим всё хорошо, ты не станешь приобретать себе ничего другого. Не перестанешь ли ты ценить и многое другое? Тогда ты не будешь ни свободным, ни самодостаточным, ни бесстрастным. Ведь неизбежно будешь завидовать, ревновать, подозрительно смотреть на тех, кто может это отнять, строить козни тем, у кого есть то, что ценишь ты. Короче, тот, кто нуждается в чём-нибудь из этого, неизбежно пребывает в смятении и вдобавок много пеняет даже на богов. А уважение к собственному уму и ценность, которую ты ему придаёшь, сделают тебя приятным самому себе, хорошо прилаженным к собратьям и созвучным богам, то есть хвалящим всё, что они уделяют и что установили.

passages.greek: Ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα, ὦ ψυχή, ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἁπλῆ καὶ μία καὶ γυμνή, φανερωτέρα τοῦ περικειμένου σοι σώματος; γεύσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τῆς φιλητικῆς καὶ στερκτικῆς διαθέσεως; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα πλήρης καὶ ἀνενδεὴς καὶ οὐδὲν ἐπιποθοῦσα οὐδὲ ἐπιθυμοῦσα οὐδενὸς οὔτε ἐμψύχου οὔτε ἀψύχου πρὸς ἡδονῶν ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ χρόνου, ἐν ᾧ ἐπὶ μακρότερον ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ τόπου ἢ χώρας ἢ ἀέρων εὐκρασίας; οὐδὲ ἀνθρώπων εὐαρμοστίας; ἀλλὰ ἀρκεσθήσῃ τῇ παρούσῃ καταστάσει καὶ ἡσθήσῃ τοῖς παροῦσι πᾶσι καὶ συμπείσεις σεαυτὴν ὅτι πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι, πάντα σοι εὖ ἔχει καὶ εὖ ἕξει, ὅσα φίλον αὐτοῖς καὶ ὅσα μέλλουσι δώσειν ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τοῦ τελείου ζῴου, τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ δικαίου καὶ καλοῦ καὶ γεννῶντος πάντα καὶ συνέχοντος καὶ περιέχοντος καὶ περιλαμβάνοντος διαλυόμενα εἰς γένεσιν ἑτέρων ὁμοίων; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τοιαύτη, οἵα θεοῖς τε καὶ ἀνθρώποις οὕτως συμπολιτεύεσθαι ὡς μήτε μέμφεσθαί τι αὐτοῖς μήτε καταγινώσκεσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν;
passages.english: Will you ever, soul, be good and simple and one and bare, plainer to see than the body wrapped round you? Will you ever taste the loving and affectionate disposition? Will you ever be full and in need of nothing, longing for nothing and desiring nothing, whether living or lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor time in which to enjoy them longer? Nor a place or a country or a mild climate? Nor people who suit you well? But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you, from the gods, that all things are well with you and will be well, all that pleases them and all that they are going to give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the good and just and beautiful one, which begets all things and holds them together and surrounds them and takes them into itself as they are dissolved for the birth of others like them? Will you ever be such as to live as a fellow citizen with gods and human beings in such a way that you neither find any fault with them nor are condemned by them?

notes.note: Marcus addresses his soul directly, and every “you” in the passage is the soul (the Greek forms are feminine). The Greek has no “my”.
notes.other_reading: Will you ever, my soul, be good

notes.note: “More visible”, “more manifest” than the body around it: the soul is to show more plainly than its covering.
notes.other_reading: more in the open than the body that surrounds you

notes.note: Two near synonyms for a state inclined to love: φιλέω is the general word, στέργω the affection of family. The English has “loving and affectionate”.
notes.other_reading: the state of one who loves and cherishes

notes.note: ἀπολαύσεις here can be the verb “you will enjoy” or again the noun “enjoyments” of the line before. It is taken as the verb.
notes.other_reading: Nor time for longer enjoyments?

notes.note: Literally “a good blending of airs”, the Greek way of saying a temperate climate.
notes.other_reading: or a good mixture of airs

notes.note: Literally “a good fitting together of people”. It can be people who fit well with you, or harmony among people. The same root is “well fitted” in 6.16.
notes.other_reading: Nor harmony among the people around you?

notes.note: The Greek punctuation carries the question through to the end of this long sentence, so “but will you be content …?” is still asked, not asserted.
notes.other_reading: but you will be content with your present state

notes.greek: πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι
notes.note: Literally “all things are present to you from the gods”. The main verb is “are present”, repeating the word used twice just before, so the English says that the soul has everything, and has it from the gods. The words can also be heard as a statement only about where its present things come from.
notes.other_reading: that all you have comes from the gods

notes.note: φίλον with the dative is the idiom “it pleases them”; the adjective is singular beside the plural “all that”. A verb such as “to give” can be supplied from the next clause.
notes.other_reading: all that is dear to them

notes.note: σωτηρία is keeping a thing safe and whole. “Preservation” is used because “safety” suggests rescue from a danger.
notes.other_reading: for the safety of the perfect living being

notes.note: “The perfect living being” is the universe, thought of as one living thing. ζῷον is the ordinary word for an animal; here “living being” reads better.
notes.other_reading: the perfect animal

notes.note: “To live as a fellow citizen with”: the universe as a city shared by gods and people.
notes.other_reading: to share one community with gods and human beings

check.greek: ὅτι πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι
check.note: The Greek says “that everything is present to you, from the gods”: you have everything, and have it from them. The draft made “comes from” the main statement, so the claim of having everything disappeared.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that all things are present to you, from the gods”. In the Greek “are present” is the main verb, so the soul is to be persuaded that it has everything, and the word still answers “present state” and “all that is present” just before.

check.note: The neuter singular with the dative means “whatever it pleases them”, parallel to “all that they are going to give”. “Dear to them” suggests things the gods cherish.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all that pleases them”. The Greek adjective is singular beside a plural “all that”, which is the idiom “it pleases them” and not a description of things the gods hold dear; “all that” is kept to match the clause that follows.

check.note: “Safety” suggests protection from a danger. The sense is keeping the whole living being in being.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for the preservation of the perfect living being”. The Greek word covers both safety and keeping a thing whole, and the second is the sense here.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “longing for nothing more”, but the Greek has no “more”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “longing for nothing and desiring nothing”, with the “and” the Greek has between the two.

passages.casaubon: O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple, single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed. Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full, and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything, either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity, nor the favour either of the weather or of men. When thou shalt have content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things; all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of them he may beget others again like unto them. Such one day shall be thy disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
passages.russian: Будешь ли ты когда-нибудь, душа, доброй, простой, единой и обнажённой, виднее облекающего тебя тела? Вкусишь ли когда-нибудь любящего и нежного расположения? Будешь ли когда-нибудь полной и ни в чём не нуждающейся, ни о чём не тоскующей и ничего не желающей — ни живого, ни неживого, — чтобы пользоваться наслаждениями? Ни времени, чтобы дольше ими пользоваться? Ни места, ни страны, ни мягкого климата? Ни людей, которые тебе подходят? Но будешь ли ты довольна своим нынешним состоянием, и будешь ли радоваться всему, что налицо, и убедишь ли себя, что всё у тебя налицо — от богов, что всё у тебя хорошо и будет хорошо, — всё, что им угодно, и всё, что они намерены дать ради сохранения совершенного живого существа, доброго, справедливого и прекрасного, которое всё порождает, всё скрепляет, всё объемлет и всё распадающееся принимает в себя ради рождения других, подобных ему? Будешь ли ты когда-нибудь такой, чтобы жить согражданкой богов и людей так, чтобы и самой ни в чём их не упрекать, и не быть ими осуждённой?

passages.greek: Περισπᾷ τί σε τὰ ἔξωθεν ἐμπίπτοντα; καὶ σχολὴν πάρεχε σεαυτῷ τοῦ προσμανθάνειν ἀγαθόν τι καὶ παῦσαι ῥεμβόμενος. ἤδη δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν περιφορὰν φυλακτέον· ληροῦσι γὰρ καὶ διὰ πράξεων οἱ κεκμηκότες τῷ βίῳ καὶ μὴ ἔχοντες σκοπόν, ἐφ’ ὃν πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν καὶ καθάπαξ φαντασίαν ἀπευθύνουσιν.
passages.english: Do the things that fall on you from outside distract you at all? Then give yourself leisure to learn some further good thing, and stop wandering. But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too: those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.

notes.note: The accent on τί may only be thrown back from the following σε, giving the indefinite “somewhat”, “at all”, or it may be the question word “why”. The English takes “at all”, since the word stands second in its clause, and gives the Greek “and” that follows as “Then”. From memory, unchecked: editors differ on whether this is a question or a statement.
notes.other_reading: Why do the things that fall on you from outside distract you?

notes.note: προσ- adds “in addition”: to learn something good on top of what you know.
notes.other_reading: to learn something good

notes.note: περιφορά is a being carried round. The first kind is being pulled about by outside things; “the other” is busy action without an aim. The English has “drifting”.
notes.other_reading: the other way of going round in circles

notes.note: ληρέω is to talk nonsense, to be silly. With “through their actions too” the point is that one can babble in deeds as well as words.
notes.other_reading: For they are talking nonsense in their actions as well

notes.note: The participle says that they have grown weary; “life” can be what has wearied them or the field in which they have toiled. “Worn out by life” is meant in the sense of exhausted, not of wishing to die.
notes.other_reading: those who have worn themselves out in living

notes.note: As accented this is a present, “at which they direct”; a future (“will direct”) is one accent away. English needs “at which to direct”.
notes.other_reading: no target at which they will direct every impulse

notes.note: καθάπαξ is “once for all”, “altogether”, “in general”: it widens the claim from every impulse to every impression. φαντασία is “impression” as elsewhere, though here it comes close to “thought”.
notes.other_reading: every impulse and every thought whatever

check.note: The accent on τί may be only that of an unstressed word before another (“somewhat”, as the draft takes it), or it may be the question word: “Why do the things that fall on you from outside distract you?”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “distract you at all”. The word stands second in its clause, after the verb, which is the usual place for the unstressed “somewhat” and an unusual one for the question word “why”; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: “Worn out by life” reads as weary of living. The Greek can equally mean those who have tired themselves out in their living, by busy toil, which suits “through their actions”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “worn out by life”, because the Greek participle says that they have grown weary and does not say that they wore themselves out. A note now records that “life” may be the cause of the weariness or the field in which they have toiled.

check.note: The word means “altogether, in general”: it widens from every impulse to every impression as well. “In a word” signals a summing up, which this is not.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “every impulse and, in general, every impression”. The Greek word widens the claim to all impressions; it does not sum up.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek form is impersonal, “must be guarded against”, and the draft had “you must guard”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well”, which names no person, as the Greek does not.

passages.casaubon: Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another kind of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and labour in this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all their motions, and desires.
passages.russian: Отвлекает ли тебя хоть сколько-нибудь то, что сваливается на тебя извне? Тогда дай себе досуг научиться ещё чему-нибудь хорошему и перестань блуждать. Но теперь надо остерегаться и другого рода метаний. Ведь и в поступках глупят те, кто устал от жизни и не имеет мишени, на которую направлять всякое побуждение и вообще всякое представление.

passages.greek: Τίς ὑπονοίας χρεία παρὸν σκοπεῖν τί δεῖ πραχθῆναι, κἂν μὲν συνορᾷς, εὐμενῶς, ἀμεταστρεπτὶ ταύτῃ χωρεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ συνορᾷς, ἐπέχειν καὶ συμβούλοις τοῖς ἀρίστοις χρῆσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἕτερά τινα πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιβαίνῃ, προιέναι κατὰ τὰς παρούσας ἀφορμὰς λελογισμένως, ἐχόμενον τοῦ φαινομένου δικαίου; ἄριστον γὰρ κατατυγχάνειν τούτου, ἐπεί τοι ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν.
passages.english: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back; and if you do not see it clearly, to hold off and use the best advisers; and if some other things stand in the way of this, to go forward as present means allow, in a considered way, holding to what appears just? For to reach this is best, since failure, at any rate, is falling away from this.

notes.note: ὑπόνοια is a surmise, a suspicion, a guess at what lies under the surface. It could be suspicion of other people or anxious conjecture about how things will turn out. The English has “guessing”, since the word is set against looking at what has to be done.
notes.other_reading: What need is there of suspicion

notes.note: “See it all together”, take it in at a glance. The English has “see it clearly”.
notes.other_reading: if you can see the whole of it

notes.note: To hold back, to suspend action or judgment.
notes.other_reading: to suspend judgment

notes.note: ἀφορμή is a starting point, and so the means or opening one has to act from. The English has “as present means allow”.
notes.other_reading: to go forward from the openings that are there

notes.note: An adverb from the verb “to reckon, to reason”: in a reasoned or considered way. It describes how one goes forward.
notes.other_reading: with reasoning

notes.greek: ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν
notes.note: Literally “since the falling away, at least, is from this”, which is obscure as given. It is taken to mean that the only failure there is, is failing to hit what is just. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the verb and some read a command.
notes.other_reading: since if you are to fail, let it be in aiming at this

check.note: The word is either conjecture (so the draft) or suspicion, misgiving. The second reading gives “What need is there of suspicion”, an uneasy mistrust about the outcome or about others.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “guessing”. The word is set against being able to look at what has to be done, a contrast of conjecture with inspection, and the note records “suspicion” as the other reading.

check.greek: ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν
check.note: The Greek says only “the failure, at least, is from this”, which is obscure as given. The draft added “any” and a second “falling short” to make sense of it; the verb is recalled, from memory only, as having been doubted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “since failure, at any rate, is falling away from this”, without the added “any”. The note says that the Greek is obscure as given and that the verb has been doubted.

check.note: “With reasoning” is stiff. The sense is “in a considered way”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in a considered way”. The Greek adverb describes the manner of going forward, not a step taken beforehand, so “after thinking it through” is not used.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “your present means”, and the Greek has no “your”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as present means allow”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “other things” for a phrase that says “some other things”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if some other things stand in the way of this”.

part.left_out: σχολαῖόν τι καὶ ἅμα εὐκίνητόν ἐστι καὶ φαιδρὸν ἅμα καὶ συνεστηκὸς ὁ τῷ λόγῳ κατὰ πᾶν ἑπόμενος.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 10.13 here and makes the chapter's closing sentence its section 10.14.

passages.casaubon: What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy mind at all? What now is to be done, if thou mayest search and inquiry into that, what needs thou care for more? And if thou art well able to perceive it alone, let no man divert thee from it. But if alone thou doest not so well perceive it, suspend thine action, and take advice from the best. And if there be anything else that doth hinder thee, go on with prudence and discretion, according to the present occasion and opportunity, still proposing that unto thyself, which thou doest conceive most right and just. For to hit that aright, and to speed in the prosecution of it, must needs be happiness, since it is that only which we can truly and properly be said to miss of, or miscarry in.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Зачем гадать, когда ты волен рассмотреть, что надо делать, и, если видишь это ясно, идти туда с доброй волей и не поворачивая назад; а если не видишь ясно — повременить и воспользоваться лучшими советчиками; а если этому мешает что-то другое — продвигаться, насколько позволяют наличные средства, обдуманно, держась того, что представляется справедливым? Ведь достичь этого — лучше всего, поскольку неудача, во всяком случае, есть отпадение именно от этого.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν Οὐκ ἔρχεται ἐπὶ σὲ τὰ πράγματα ὧν αἱ διώξεις καὶ φυγαὶ θορυβοῦσί σε, ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ αὐτὸς ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνα ἔρχῃ· τὸ γοῦν κρῖμα τὸ περὶ αὐτῶν ἡσυχαζέτω κἀκεῖνα μενεῖ ἀτρεμοῦντα καὶ οὔτε διώκων οὔτε φεύγων ὀφθήσῃ.
passages.english: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them. At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay still, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.

notes.note: As given, the passage opens with Εἰ μὲν (“If, on the one hand”) and then a word with a capital letter, as though the sentence began there; nothing answers “on the one hand”, and the negative is the one used in statements. The English begins at the capital and leaves the first two words untranslated. Probably the edition bracketed them and the brackets were lost in copying (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: If the things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them, then at least let your judgment about them be quiet

notes.note: Literally “pursuits and flights”: chasing some things and running from others. The same pair returns as verbs at the end, so “pursue” and “avoid” are kept in both places.
notes.other_reading: the things you are thrown into turmoil chasing and running from

notes.note: The verb is from θόρυβος, the noise of a crowd, and is also used of one person being disturbed or confused. “Let your judgment be quiet” answers it.
notes.other_reading: raise a clamour in you

notes.note: κρῖμα is a ruling or decision, a different word from ὑπόληψις, which is “judgment” in the glossary. “Judgment” is used here as the plainer word, and nothing in the passage depends on the difference.
notes.other_reading: at least let your verdict on them keep still

notes.note: “Not trembling”, at rest.
notes.other_reading: and they will not tremble

check.note: The capital on Οὐκ after Εἰ μὲν, the lack of any answering particle, and the negative of statements in a condition all suggest that Εἰ μὲν does not belong and the chapter begins with a flat statement. The draft built the whole chapter as a condition, which makes the assertion hypothetical.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now opens with a statement, “The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you”, because the capital letter on the third word shows that the edition begins its sentence there. “So” is not added before “at least”, since the Greek particle limits and does not draw a conclusion; the note says which two words are left untranslated.

check.note: “Uproar” is the noise of a crowd; of one person it reads oddly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “throw you into turmoil”. The Greek verb is used of one person being disturbed as well as of a noisy crowd, and a note keeps its root sense of noise, which “be quiet” answers.

passages.casaubon: The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all pursuing and flying cease.
passages.russian: Вещи, погоня за которыми и бегство от которых приводят тебя в смятение, не приходят к тебе — это ты сам в некотором роде идёшь к ним. Пусть хотя бы твоё суждение о них затихнет, и они останутся на месте, и тебя не увидят ни гонящимся за ними, ни бегущим от них.

passages.greek: Ὅσην εὐσχολίαν κερδαίνει ὁ μὴ βλέπων τί ὁ πλησίον εἶπεν ἢ ἔπραξεν ἢ διενοήθη, ἀλλὰ μόνον τί αὐτὸς ποιεῖ, ἵνα αὐτὸ τοῦτο δίκαιον ᾖ καὶ ὅσιον ἢ † κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν· μὴ μέλαν ἦθος περιβλέπεσθαι, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς τρέχειν ὀρθόν, μὴ διερριμμένον.
passages.english: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing, so that this very thing may be just and holy, or in keeping with the good man: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that.

notes.note: “Good leisure”: free time, freedom from being busy.
notes.other_reading: How much time and ease a person gains

notes.note: The edition marks the text as corrupt here with a dagger, and “or in keeping with the good man” does not join to what goes before or after. The words are translated as they stand. From memory, unchecked: some editors read a proper name here and take what follows as a quotation.
notes.other_reading: or, as the good man would have it:

notes.note: The construction changes to infinitives with no stated subject. μέλαν is “black”, “dark”; the phrase has no article and can be the dark character of some other person that one looks round at, bad character in general, or, less likely, a manner of looking. The first is taken.
notes.other_reading: do not glance about at the dark characters around you

notes.note: The image is of a runner keeping to the line marked on the track. ὀρθόν can go with the runner (“upright”, “straight”) or be an adverb with “run”.
notes.other_reading: but to run on the line, upright

notes.note: “Not flung about”: not thrown from side to side, or not scattered in many directions.
notes.other_reading: not darting from side to side

check.note: The edition marks the text as corrupt here, and “or in keeping with the good man” sits oddly after “just and holy”, yet the draft gives it smoothly. A proposed correction, recalled from memory only, makes this a poet’s name introducing the words that follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the bare rendering “or in keeping with the good man” stands, since nothing surer can be put in its place from the Greek as given. The note now says plainly that the edition marks the place as corrupt and that the words do not join to what comes before or after.

check.note: “A black character” can be misread today as a remark about a person’s colour. The sense is dark, bad character, and the Greek has no article, so it may be general.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not to look round at a dark character”. “Dark” keeps the image without the possible misreading; the article stays because English needs one with the singular, and the note says the Greek may be general.

passages.casaubon: Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.
passages.russian: Сколько досуга выигрывает тот, кто не смотрит, что сказал, сделал или подумал сосед, а смотрит только на то, что делает он сам, чтобы именно это было справедливым и святым, или подобающим хорошему человеку: не оглядываться на тёмный нрав, а бежать прямо по линии, не мечась из стороны в сторону.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν κρεῖττον εὑρίσκεις ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ δικαιοσύνης, ἀληθείας, σωφροσύνης, ἀνδρείας καὶ καθάπαξ τοῦ ἀρκεῖσθαι ἑαυτῇ τὴν διάνοιάν σου, ἐν οἷς κατὰ τὸν λόγον τὸν ὀρθὸν πράσσοντά σε παρέχεται, καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις· εἰ τούτου, φημί, κρεῖττόν τι ὁρᾷς, ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνο ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τραπόμενος τοῦ ἀρίστου εὑρισκομένου ἀπόλαυε. εἰ δὲ μηδὲν κρεῖττον φαίνεται αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος, τάς τε ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτῷ καὶ τὰς φαντασίας ἐξετάζοντος καὶ τῶν αἰσθητικῶν πείσεων, ὡς ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγεν, ἑαυτὸν ἀφειλκυκότος καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτὸν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προκηδομένου· εἰ τούτου πάντα τὰ ἄλλα μικρότερα καὶ εὐτελέστερα εὑρίσκεις, μηδενὶ χώραν δίδου ἑτέρῳ, πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας οὐκέτι ἀπερισπάστως τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐκεῖνο, τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ σόν, προτιμᾶν δυνήσῃ. ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις οὐδʼ ὁτιοῦν ἑτερογενές, οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν· πάντα ταῦτα, κἂν πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐναρμόζειν δόξῃ, κατεκράτησεν ἄφνω καὶ παρήνεγκεν. σὺ δέ, φημί, ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως ἑλοῦ τὸ κρεῖττον καὶ τούτου ἀντέχου· “κρεῖττον δὲ τὸ συμφέρον.” εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι, καὶ ἀτύφως φύλασσε τὴν κρίσιν· μόνον ὅπως ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιήσῃ.
passages.english: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your thought being content with itself in the things where it has you acting according to right reason, and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you, which has put its own impulses under itself, which examines the impressions, which has pulled itself away, as Socrates used to say, from the feelings of the senses, and has put itself under the gods, and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else. Once you have tipped and turned aside towards anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honour above all else that good which is proper to you and is yours. For it is not permitted that anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures, should take up a position against the rational and civic good. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so, and guard your verdict without conceit. Only see that you make the examination without slipping.

notes.note: διάνοια is the thinking faculty here. The glossary’s “thought” is kept so that the word matches 3.7, where it stands beside νοῦς (“mind”).
notes.other_reading: your mind being content with itself

notes.greek: καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις
notes.note: The Greek as given has ἐν, “in”, before “fate”, and the English follows it: the thought is content with itself in two fields, where it acts by right reason and, in fate, where things are allotted without choice. Without that ἐν the words mean “content with fate”, with fate as the partner of “itself”. From memory, unchecked: editors print the text without it.
notes.other_reading: and content with fate in the things that are allotted without your choosing

notes.note: εὑρισκομένου is a present participle, “being found”, and answers “if you find” at the start, so the English keeps the finding open. It can also be heard as a finished event.
notes.other_reading: enjoy the best thing, now that it is found

notes.greek: αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος
notes.note: δαίμων is a divine being; here it is the divine part housed in each person, which Marcus elsewhere equates with mind and reason. “Spirit” is used for it throughout this section. ἐνιδρυμένου is the word for a god’s statue or shrine set up in a place, so “seated” is weaker than the Greek.
notes.other_reading: the god itself that has its shrine in you

notes.note: πεῖσις here is from πάσχω, “what is undergone”, not from πείθω, “persuasion”: what the senses are made to feel. From memory, unchecked: the saying of Socrates is a loose recollection of Plato’s Phaedo, where the soul is told to withdraw from the senses, and not an exact quotation.
notes.other_reading: from the affections of the senses; or, on the other derivation, from the persuasions of the senses

notes.greek: πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας
notes.note: ῥέπω is the tipping of a scale pan and ἀποκλίνω a leaning off to one side; the image is a balance, and both verbs go with “towards which”. The Greek is a relative clause on “nothing else”; the English begins a new sentence and writes “anything else” for the relative.
notes.other_reading: towards which, once you have inclined and turned aside, you will no longer be able

notes.note: Literally “without being dragged around”, that is, without distraction. It can go with “be able” or with “honour above all”; the sense is the same.
notes.other_reading: to honour undistracted

notes.note: Two words for one thought: ἴδιον is what belongs to a being as its own and no other’s, σόν is simply “yours”. The English reads “proper to you” for the first so that the pair does not say the same thing twice.
notes.other_reading: that good which is your own and yours

notes.greek: ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις
notes.note: ἀντικαθῆσθαι is to sit over against, used of an army encamped opposite another. θέμις is what divine law allows, so “not permitted” is still weaker than the Greek.
notes.other_reading: For it is not lawful that anything of another kind should sit encamped against the good of a rational being and a citizen

notes.note: πολιτικός means “of a citizen, made for life in a city”. “Civic” is used for it throughout this section to keep it apart from κοινωνικός, “social”.
notes.other_reading: the good of a rational being and a citizen

notes.note: In the Greek the examples follow “of a different kind” at the end of the clause. The English moves the whole phrase before the verb so that the examples are not read as examples of the good.
notes.other_reading: For it is not permitted that there should take up a position against the rational and civic good anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many

notes.note: Two aorists of what regularly happens, with no object in the Greek. The English puts them in the present and supplies “you” with the second verb.
notes.other_reading: have suddenly prevailed and carried away

notes.note: An objection from an imagined speaker, as the edition’s quotation marks show. The Greek names no one who is benefited and the English leaves that open too; “you” in the reply is supplied from the commands that follow. “Benefits” is used and not the glossary’s “is good for”, because this passage also speaks of “the good” (ἀγαθόν) and the two would run together.
notes.other_reading: “But the better is what is good for a person.”

notes.greek: εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι
notes.note: Very compressed: “if the [benefit] as to a rational [being], keep this; if the one as to an animal, declare”. What is to be declared is not said; the English takes it as an admission that this is the kind of benefit meant. ζῷον is “animal” here because the contrast is with the rational being; in other passages of this section, where no such contrast is drawn, the word is “living being”.
notes.other_reading: If it is your benefit as a rational being, watch over it; but if as a living being, declare it

notes.note: τῦφος is smoke, and so puffed-up delusion or conceit. κρίσις is the deciding or its result; “verdict” keeps it apart from ὑπόληψις, “judgment”, as in 11.16. The clause can also be heard as “keep your judgment free of delusion”.
notes.other_reading: and keep your decision without self-deception

notes.note: ἀσφαλῶς is literally “without tripping”: securely, on firm footing. ἐξέτασις, “examination”, is the noun of the verb used above of the spirit that “examines the impressions”.
notes.other_reading: Only see that you make the examination securely.

check.greek: καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις
check.note: The Greek as given has ἐν before “fate”, so fate is not the thing the thought is content with. The English translated a bare dative, “content with fate”, and the departure should be a decision and not silent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now follows the Greek as given and reads “and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing”, so that the thought is content with itself in both fields. “Content with fate”, the sense without the ἐν, is recorded in the note.

check.note: The participle is present. “Now that it is found” makes the finding a finished event, where the Greek can as well mean “what is found to be best”, matching “if you find” at the start.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “enjoy what is found to be best”. The participle is present and passive, so the finding stays open and no “you” is added; the finished-event reading is kept in the note.

check.note: The Greek says “the impressions”; “its own” is said only of the impulses in the clause before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “which examines the impressions”. “Its own” belongs only to the impulses.

check.greek: πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας
check.note: Both participles hang on “toward which”. “Leaned away” with nothing after it reads as leaning away from something unnamed, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else”, with both verbs governing “toward”. “Anything else” stands for the Greek relative and picks up “nothing else” from the sentence before.

check.note: “Your own and yours” reads as saying the same thing twice. The first word is “proper, peculiar to you”, the second “yours”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “that good which is proper to you and is yours”. The second “is” is added so that “you and yours” is not heard as one phrase.

check.note: θέμις is what sacred law or the established order allows; “not right” is the weaker, everyday word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “it is not permitted”. The Greek word is about what divine law allows, which “not right” did not reach.

check.greek: οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν
check.note: The examples belong to “anything of a different kind”. In the English they stood directly after “the rational and civic good” and read as examples of that good, the opposite of what is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the list now stands directly after “anything whatever of a different kind”, and “the rational and civic good” closes the sentence. In the Greek the examples follow “of a different kind”, so this is their place.

check.note: There is no “me” in the Greek. Adding it settles in advance the question the next sentence asks: benefits you as rational, or as an animal.
check.decided: Accepted: the objection reads “But the better is what benefits.” The Greek names no one, and it is the reply that asks whose benefit is meant.

check.note: The contrast is rational being against mere animal. A rational being is also a living being, so “living being” does not make the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “But if as an animal”. The contrast is with the rational being, which “living being” would include; the note says that the word is “living being” in other passages of the section.

check.note: “Safely” is unclear here; the Greek word is “securely, without slipping”, that is, a test that cannot go wrong.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Only see that you make the examination without slipping.” That is the literal sense of the Greek word and is clearer than “safely”; “soundly” is left for the word “soundest” in 4.51.

check.note: Found while settling: “hold your verdict” can be heard as “hold it back”, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “guard your verdict without conceit”. φύλασσε is the word for keeping watch over something.

passages.casaubon: If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better than a mind contented both with those things which according to right and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart, and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Если ты найдёшь в человеческой жизни что-нибудь лучше справедливости, истины, самообладания, мужества и, одним словом, лучше того, чтобы твоя мысль была довольна собой там, где благодаря ей ты действуешь согласно правому разуму, и довольна роком в том, что уделено без твоего выбора; если, говорю, ты видишь что-то лучше этого, обратись к нему всей душой и наслаждайся тем, что нашёл лучшим. Если же ничто не оказывается лучше самого духа, водворённого в тебе, который подчинил себе собственные побуждения, который проверяет представления, который оторвал себя, как говорил Сократ, от чувственных ощущений, и подчинил себя богам, и заботится о людях; если ты находишь всё прочее меньше и дешевле его, не давай места ничему другому. Стоит тебе склониться и свернуть к чему-нибудь другому, ты уже не сможешь без того, чтобы тебя дёргало туда и сюда, чтить превыше всего то благо, которое тебе свойственно и есть твоё. Ведь не дозволено, чтобы хоть что-нибудь иного рода — похвала многих, или должности, или богатство, или вкушение наслаждений — занимало позицию против разумного и гражданского блага. Всё это, даже если ненадолго кажется подходящим, вдруг берёт верх и сбивает тебя с курса. А ты, говорю я, просто и свободно выбери лучшее и держись его. «Но лучшее — то, что полезно». Если полезно тебе как разумному существу — держись этого. Если же как животному — так и скажи и охраняй своё решение без спеси. Только смотри не оступись, проводя проверку.

passages.greek: Ἐὰν τὸ παρὸν ἐνεργῇς ἑπόμενος τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ, ἐσπουδασμένως, ἐρρωμένως, εὐμενῶς, καὶ μηδὲν παρεμπόρευμα, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς, ὡσεὶ καὶ ἤδη ἀποδοῦναι δέοι· ἐὰν τοῦτο συνάπτῃς μηδὲν περιμένων μηδὲ Φεύγων, ἀλλὰ τῇ παρούσῃ κατὰ Φύσιν ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ τῇ ὧν λέγεις καὶ Φθέγγῃ ἡρωικῇ ἀληθείᾳ ἀρκούμενος, εὐζωήσεις. ἔστι δὲ οὐδεὶς ὁ τοῦτο κωλῦσαι δυνάμενος.
passages.english: If you do the work that is present, following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, with good will, and with nothing as a side business, but keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment; if you join this together, waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing, but content with the present work that is according to nature and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.

notes.note: ἐνεργῇς here and ἐνεργείᾳ below are the same word, verb and noun, and “present” is repeated with them. The English reads “do the work that is present” and “the present work” so that the close is heard picking up the opening. The word is strictly “be active” and “activity”.
notes.other_reading: If you are active in what is present

notes.note: There is no verb in the Greek: literally “and nothing a side-trade”. παρεμπόρευμα is goods dealt in on the side of one’s main trade. The English supplies “with” and “as” and takes the phrase with the doing of the present work; it can also be heard as a first object of “keep”.
notes.other_reading: and admit nothing as a sideline

notes.greek: τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς
notes.note: ἑαυτοῦ stands for “your own”, a common late use. δαίμων is “spirit” as in 3.6. ἑστῶτα is “standing”, with no “and” between it and “pure”; it may also be a quality of its own, standing firm or steady.
notes.other_reading: keep your own spirit pure and standing firm

notes.note: “To give back” what was lent or entrusted. The Greek does not say to whom.
notes.other_reading: as if you had to return it at once

notes.note: συνάπτω is to fasten or join together, the verb of “joining one good to another” in 12.29. The Greek does not say what is joined to what: it may be the present work and the pure spirit joined to each other, or the practice kept unbroken from one moment to the next.
notes.other_reading: if you keep this joined up without a break

notes.note: “Heroic truth” is a strange phrase and is translated as it stands: truthfulness of the kind the heroes of old had. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the adjective.
notes.other_reading: the truthfulness of a hero

notes.note: One word, “you will live well”, in the sense of a good and happy life.
notes.other_reading: you will have a happy life

check.note: “Carry out what is present” is not clear English; the Greek means the thing in hand.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “do the work that is present”. “In front of you” is not used, because the Greek word is “present” and it returns at the close, where the English has to be able to repeat it.

check.note: The Greek has no verb here: “and nothing a by-work”. The English supplies “with” and “as” smoothly, which is a fair repair but a repair.
check.decided: Accepted: “and with nothing as a side business” stays, and the note now says outright that the Greek has no verb and that “with” and “as” are supplied.

check.note: ἑστῶτα can be a second quality of its own, “standing firm, steady”, and not only the posture of the pure spirit.
check.decided: Declined: “standing pure” stays. The Greek has no “and” between the two words, so the closest English keeps them as one phrase; “pure and standing firm” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The verb in the active with an object is “join, fasten together”, as in 12.29, not “hold fast to”, which would need another form and case. The participles say how the joining is done: waiting for nothing, fleeing nothing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “if you join this together”. The verb is active with an object and means to join or fasten, as in 12.29; the note says that the Greek leaves open what is joined to what.

check.note: The close picks up the opening word for word, but the English had “carry out what is present” and then “present activity”. The article was also dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “content with the present work that is according to nature”, with the article, and the opening reads “do the work that is present”, so the same two words open and close the passage.

passages.casaubon: If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak, contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Если ты делаешь дело, которое перед тобой, следуя правому разуму, усердно, энергично, доброжелательно и без всяких побочных занятий, но сохраняешь свой дух стоящим в чистоте, как если бы тебе пришлось вернуть его сию же минуту; если ты соединишь это, ничего не ожидая и ни от чего не убегая, но довольствуясь нынешним делом, согласным с природой, и героической правдой в том, что говоришь и произносишь, — ты будешь жить хорошо. И нет никого, кто мог бы этому помешать.

passages.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, ἐὰν πρὸς τὰ ἀδιάφορά τις ἀδιαφορῇ. ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ διῃρημένως καὶ ὁλικῶς καὶ μεμνημένος ὅτι οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ὑπόληψιν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν ἐμποιεῖ οὐδὲ ἔρχεται ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀτρεμεῖ, ἡμεῖς δέ ἐσμεν οἱ τὰς περὶ αὐτῶν κρίσεις γεννῶντες καὶ οἷον γράφοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐξὸν μὲν μὴ γράφειν, ἐξὸν δέ, κἄν που λάθῃ, εὐθὺς ἐξαλεῖψαι· ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ καὶ λοιπὸν πεπαύσεται ὁ βίος. τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα; εἰ μὲν γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστί, χαῖρε αὐτοῖς καὶ ῥᾴδια ἔστω σοι· εἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν, ζήτει τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦτο σπεῦδε, κἂν ἄδοξον ᾖ· παντὶ γὰρ συγγνώμη τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ζητοῦντι.
passages.english: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul, if a person is indifferent towards the things that are indifferent. And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things taken apart and as a whole, and remember that none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once; and remember that this kind of attention will be for a short time, and after that life will be over. But what is hard about these things being otherwise? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them and let them be easy for you. And if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation. For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.

notes.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ
notes.note: The opening is loose: an infinitive phrase, then “this power [is] in the soul”. The English keeps the looseness with a colon. κάλλιστα is “most finely, most nobly”.
notes.other_reading: The power to live life through in the noblest way is in the soul

notes.note: A play on one word. τὰ ἀδιάφορα is the Stoic term for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health, wealth, reputation and death; the verb says to be towards them as they are.
notes.other_reading: if one makes no difference of the things that make no difference

notes.note: Two adverbs: “dividedly and wholly”, that is, looking at the thing split into its parts and also as one whole.
notes.other_reading: by analysis and as a whole
