notes.note: ὑπόληψις is “judgment” by the glossary; κρίσεις in the next clause is “verdicts” to keep the two words apart, though Marcus seems to mean much the same by both.
notes.other_reading: none of them produces in us an opinion about itself

notes.note: No subject is given: “even if perhaps it escapes notice”. The English takes the subject to be a verdict that got written without being noticed. που is “somehow, perhaps” and need not mean a place.
notes.other_reading: and, even if one has been written unawares

notes.greek: ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ
notes.note: A bare “that” in the Greek, with no “and remember”; the English supplies the two words, taking the clause as a second thing to remember. The same Greek word can mean “because”, giving a reason for what goes before.
notes.other_reading: because this kind of attention will be for a short time

notes.greek: τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα;
notes.note: Word for word: “What, however, [is] hard [in] these things being otherwise?” The English keeps “hard”, which “easy” in the next sentence answers, and leaves “otherwise” as bare as the Greek, where the likeliest sense is “other than you would wish”. From memory, unchecked: some editors change ἄλλως to καλῶς, giving “what is hard about getting these things right?”
notes.other_reading: Yet what is so hard to bear if these things are other than you would wish?

notes.note: ἄδοξον is “without reputation”: either bringing no fame or held in low regard.
notes.other_reading: even if it is looked down on

notes.note: συγγνώμη is pardon or allowance that is available, not a forgiveness already given. The Greek has no verb: “for to everyone [there is] pardon who seeks their own good”.
notes.other_reading: for anyone may be excused for seeking their own good

check.greek: ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ
check.note: Coming straight after “the things that are indifferent”, “they will be indifferent” reads first as said of the things. The subject is the person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things”, so that the sentence cannot be heard as said of the things.

check.note: The Greek is “even if”, and the small word after it is more likely “somehow, at some point” than a place. “Slipped in” brings an image of its own; the Greek only says that it escaped notice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “even if one somehow escapes notice”. “Even” is restored and “slipped in somewhere” goes, since the Greek speaks only of escaping notice.

check.note: The Greek resumes with a bare “that”, with no “and remember”. The supplement is reasonable but it is added.
check.decided: Declined: “and remember” stays. The Greek “that” hangs on “remember” many lines above and the English sentence cannot be followed without the repeat; the note records that the two words are supplied.

check.greek: τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα;
check.note: The English is word for word and leaves the reader asking “otherwise than what?”; it can even be heard as “what is hard about changing these things”. The likelier sense is “what is there to resent if these things are not as you would have them”, which the next sentence answers.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “But what is hard in it, if these things are otherwise?”, which can no longer be heard as a question about changing them. “Hard” is kept because “easy” answers it in the next sentence, and “than you would wish” stays in the note because the Greek does not say it.

check.greek: τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν
check.note: The Greek “for you” is dropped: “what there is for you that is according to your own nature”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature”, restoring “for you”. “According to nature” is kept as the one phrase for κατὰ φύσιν in this passage.

check.note: The Greek word is allowance or pardon available, not a forgiveness already granted. “Is forgiven” implies a fault committed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.” This no longer implies a fault already committed, and it keeps “everyone”, which “anyone” would weaken.

passages.casaubon: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our power to wipe them off. Remembering moreover, that this care and circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his own good and happiness.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.russian: Прожить жизнь наилучшим образом — эта сила есть в душе, если человек безразличен к безразличному. А безразличным он будет, если станет рассматривать каждую из этих вещей и по частям, и в целом, и помнить, что ни одна из них не вкладывает в нас суждения о себе и не приходит к нам, но вещи стоят на месте, а это мы порождаем приговоры о них и как бы записываем их в себе, хотя в нашей власти их не записывать, а если какой-то из них и ускользнёт от нашего внимания, в нашей власти тотчас его стереть; и помнить, что такое внимание понадобится ненадолго, а потом жизнь кончится. Но что трудного в том, что эти вещи обстоят иначе? Ведь если они согласны с природой, радуйся им, и пусть они будут тебе легки. А если противны природе, ищи, что для тебя согласно с твоей собственной природой, и спеши к этому, даже если это не приносит славы. Ведь каждому, кто ищет своего блага, есть прощение.

passages.greek: Μὴ τιμήσῃς ποτὲ ὡς συμφέρον σεαυτοῦ, ὃ ἀναγκάσει σέ ποτε τὴν πίστιν παραβῆναι, τὴν αἰδῶ ἐγκαταλιπεῖν, μισῆσαί τινα, ὑποπτεῦσαι, καταράσασθαι, ὑποκρίνασθαι, ἐπιθυμῆσαί τινος τοίχων καὶ παραπετασμάτων δεομένου. ὁ γὰρ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ νοῦν καὶ δαίμονα καὶ τὰ ὄργια τῆς τούτου ἀρετῆς προελόμενος τραγῳδίαν οὐ ποιεῖ, οὐ στενάζει, οὐκ ἐρημίας, οὐ πολυπληθείας δεήσεται· τὸ μέγιστον, ζήσει μήτε διώκων μήτε φεύγων, πότερον δὲ ἐπὶ πλέον διάστημα χρόνου τῷ σώματι περιεχομένῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἢ ἐπ’ ἔλασσον χρήσεται, οὐδ᾽ ὁτιοῦν αὐτῷ μέλει· κἂν γὰρ ἤδη ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι δέῃ, οὕτως εὐλύτως ἄπεισιν, ὡς ἄλλο τι τῶν αἰδημόνως καὶ κοσμίως ἐνεργεῖσθαι δυναμένων ἐνεργήσων, τοῦτο μόνον παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον εὐλαβούμενος, τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι.
passages.english: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains. For whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue, does not make a tragedy of things, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing. Whether they will have the use of the soul, enclosed in the body, for a longer stretch of time or a shorter one matters to them not at all. For even if they have to depart this moment, they will go as free of ties as if they were about to do anything else that can be done with self-respect and in good order, on their guard through their whole life against this one thing only: that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic.

notes.note: τὸ συμφέρον with a genitive, “an advantage of your own”. The English reads “a benefit to yourself” and not the glossary’s “good for”, so that the word answers the objection that closes 3.6, the chapter before this one in the book: “the better is what benefits”.
notes.other_reading: as good for yourself

notes.note: πίστις is trust, good faith, a pledge given. “Break faith” covers both breaking a promise and betraying a trust.
notes.other_reading: to break your word

notes.note: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy of them. The English reads “self-respect” and keeps the same word for the adverb αἰδημόνως later in the passage.
notes.other_reading: to abandon your sense of shame

notes.note: The word for acting on a stage, and so for pretending.
notes.other_reading: to be a hypocrite

notes.note: προαιρέομαι is to choose one thing in preference to others. The Greek does not say “before everything”.
notes.other_reading: has chosen first

notes.note: ὄργια are the secret rites of a mystery cult; the person is pictured as the worshipper of the spirit within. τούτου, “of this one”, is taken as the spirit. ἀρετή is “virtue” or “excellence”.
notes.other_reading: the worship of its excellence

notes.note: Literally “does not compose a tragedy”: does not turn their life into a stage lament. The English keeps the word “tragedy” and supplies “of things”.
notes.other_reading: does not play the tragic actor

notes.note: The Greek moves from the present (“does not make a tragedy, does not groan”) to the future here and in what follows; the English keeps the shift.
notes.other_reading: needs neither solitude nor a crowd

notes.note: εὐλύτως is “in a way easily loosed”, like something untied without trouble; “free of ties” keeps that picture.
notes.other_reading: they will go as easily

notes.note: τροπή is a turning or change of direction; literally the thought “comes to be in a turn” that is foreign to such a being. The verb εὐλαβούμενος already means “guarding against”, so the Greek has no “not”.
notes.other_reading: that their thought should fall into any condition foreign to

notes.note: νοερός is “of mind” by the glossary, matching νοῦς, “mind”, earlier in the passage, so the English reads “that has mind”. πολιτικός is “civic”, as in 3.6: made for life among fellow citizens.
notes.other_reading: a thinking creature and a citizen

check.note: 3.6 ends on the same word, there “what benefits”, and 3.7 opens by picking it up, but here it became “good for”, and “good” is also the word for ἀγαθόν in 3.6. The link between the two chapters is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Never value as a benefit to yourself”. The word now matches “what benefits” at the end of 3.6, which this chapter takes up, and the note says why the glossary’s “good for” is not used here.

check.note: The verb is “choose, prefer”; “before everything” presses the prefix harder than the Greek does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit”. The verb is to choose one thing over others, and “before everything” said more than that.

check.note: “Makes no tragedy” is not an English idiom; the sense is striking no tragic pose, making no drama.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “does not make a tragedy of things”, which is an English idiom and keeps the Greek’s own word. “Drama” would lose the stage tragedy that the Greek names.

check.note: The adverb is “easily loosed, unencumbered”, the image of something that comes untied without trouble; “easily” keeps only half of it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “they will go as free of ties”. That gives the untying in the Greek word in one phrase; “as lightly” beside it would make two words out of one.

check.note: The same verb twice in the Greek, two verbs in the English (“carry out”, “done”).
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “do any other of the things that can be done”, one verb for the one Greek verb.

check.greek: ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι
check.note: “Come into any turn” is not English, and the double “that … that” is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic”. “Take any turn” and “foreign to” are adopted; “a living being that has mind” is kept, because “mind” has to answer the same word earlier in the passage.

passages.casaubon: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action, which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long, this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
passages.russian: Никогда не считай для себя полезным то, что однажды заставит тебя нарушить верность, отказаться от самоуважения, кого-то возненавидеть, заподозрить, проклясть, играть роль, пожелать чего-то, что нуждается в стенах и занавесях. Ведь тот, кто предпочёл свой ум и дух и обряды его добродетели, не делает из происходящего трагедии, не стонет, не будет нуждаться ни в уединении, ни в толпе. И главное — он будет жить, ни за чем не гонясь и ни от чего не убегая. Будет ли он пользоваться душой, заключённой в теле, больший срок или меньший — ему совершенно всё равно. Ведь даже если ему придётся уйти сию минуту, он уйдёт таким же свободным от уз, как если бы собирался заняться любым другим делом, какое можно делать с самоуважением и в должном порядке, всю жизнь остерегаясь только одного: чтобы его мысль не приняла какого-либо оборота, чуждого живому существу, гражданскому и наделённому умом.

passages.greek: Σωτηρία βίου ἕκαστον δι’ ὅλου αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾶν, τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες· ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τἀληθῆ λέγειν. τί λοιπὸν ἢ ἀπολαύειν τοῦ ζῆν συνάπτοντα ἄλλο ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ἀγαθόν, ὥστε μηδὲ τὸ βραχύτατον διάστημα ἀπολείπειν;
passages.english: What keeps a life safe: to see each thing through and through, what it is in itself, what in it is the material and what the cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to say what is true. What is left but to enjoy living, joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap?

notes.note: Two words with no verb: “safety of life” or “the saving of a life”. The English turns them into a clause.
notes.other_reading: The salvation of life is this

notes.note: With the preposition before it the phrase is “through the whole”: either seeing the whole of each thing or seeing it thoroughly. αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν is “what it is itself”.
notes.other_reading: to see what each thing is in itself, as a whole

notes.greek: τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες
notes.note: The two Stoic principles: the matter a thing is made of and the cause that shapes and moves it. Marcus uses the pair often.
notes.other_reading: what its matter is and what its causal part

notes.note: The same words as in 3.6, where the English has “with your whole soul” because a command is addressed to “you”. Here the Greek is impersonal throughout and the article is kept.
notes.other_reading: with your whole soul

notes.note: “Fastening one good onto another”, like links in a chain. ἀγαθόν is neuter, “a good thing”; in context it is probably a good act.
notes.other_reading: linking one good deed to the next

notes.note: An interval, here of time left empty between one good and the next.
notes.other_reading: the briefest interval

check.note: The same phrase is “with your whole soul” in 3.6. Nothing is wrong in the passage itself; only the two should match.
check.decided: Declined: “with the whole soul” stays. The Greek has “the whole soul” in both places and no “your”; in 3.6 “your” comes from the command addressed to “you”, while this passage is impersonal from start to finish. A note now records the match.

passages.casaubon: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Что сохраняет жизнь невредимой: видеть каждую вещь насквозь — какова она сама по себе, что в ней материя и что причина; всей душой делать справедливое и говорить истинное. Что остаётся, как не наслаждаться жизнью, присоединяя одно благо к другому так, чтобы не оставалось даже малейшего промежутка?

passages.greek: Παρατήρει τί σου ἡ φύσις ἐπιζητεῖ ὡς ὑπὸ φύσεως μόνον διοικουμένου· εἶτα ποίει αὐτὸ καὶ προσίεσο, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις. ἑξῆς δὲ παρατηρητέον τί ἐπιζητεῖ σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις, καὶ πᾶν τοῦτο παραληπτέον, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαι ἡ ὡς ζῴου λογικοῦ φύσις· ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν. τούτοις δὴ κανόσι χρώμενος μηδὲν περιεργάζου.
passages.english: Watch what your nature asks for, taking yourself as something governed by nature only. Then do it and accept it, unless your nature as an animal is going to be put in a worse state. Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and take up all of this, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state. And what is rational is by that very fact also civic. Using these rules, then, do not busy yourself with anything further.

notes.note: φύσις here has its narrow Stoic sense: the power of growth and nourishment that governs plants, below the soul that governs animals. So the first step is what you need simply as a growing body. ὡς with the participle means “regarded as”, not a statement that this is all you are.
notes.other_reading: as one governed only by the nature of a growing thing

notes.note: προσίεσο is “let it come to you, admit it”.
notes.other_reading: do it and allow it

notes.note: ζῷον is a being with soul and sensation, one step above a thing that only grows. The English reads “animal” here so that the three steps stay apart: a growing thing, an animal, a rational animal. In other passages of this section, where no such ladder is in play, the word is “living being”.
notes.other_reading: your nature as a living being

notes.note: Literally “is going to be disposed worse”.
notes.other_reading: is going to be the worse for it

notes.greek: ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν
notes.note: εὐθύς is “straight away, immediately”: being rational brings being civic with it at once. πολιτικός is “civic” as in 3.6.
notes.other_reading: and the rational is at once also made for a city

notes.note: περιεργάζομαι is to do more than is needed, to fuss, or to meddle in what is not one’s business. The English takes the prefix as “beyond what these rules ask”.
notes.other_reading: do not fuss over anything

check.note: The Greek is “as (the nature) of something governed only by nature”, that is, taking yourself for the moment as a thing that merely grows. “Insofar as you are” states it as a fact, and the reader has no sign that “nature” here is the narrow sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “taking yourself as something governed by nature only”. The Greek asks for this way of regarding yourself at the first step and does not state it as a fact; the note explains the narrow sense of “nature”.

check.note: The passage climbs three steps: a growing thing, an animal, a rational animal. A growing thing is a living being too, so “living being” does not mark the second step off from the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “your nature as an animal” and “your nature as a rational animal”. A growing thing is alive too, so “living being” did not mark the second step off from the first.

check.greek: εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις
check.note: “By it” is supplied, here and in the next sentence. Harmless.
check.decided: Accepted: “by it” is removed in both sentences. The Greek does not have it and the condition is clear without it.

check.note: The verb is to fuss, meddle, be over-curious. “Anything further” is one way to take the prefix; the other is simply “do not fuss over anything”.
check.decided: Declined: “do not busy yourself with anything further” stays. The verb is to be busy beyond what is needed, and “further” gives that prefix; “do not fuss over anything” is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature, doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Наблюдай, чего просит твоя природа, рассматривая себя как нечто, управляемое одной лишь природой. Затем делай это и принимай, если только твоя природа как живого существа не окажется от этого в худшем состоянии. Далее тебе нужно наблюдать, чего просит твоя природа как живого существа, и принимать всё это, если только твоя природа как разумного живого существа не окажется в худшем состоянии. А разумное тем самым есть и гражданское. Пользуясь этими правилами, больше ни о чём не хлопочи.

passages.greek: Τούτων ἀεὶ δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι, τίς ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ τίς ἡ ἐμὴ καὶ πῶς αὕτη πρὸς ἐκείνην ἔχουσα καὶ ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς ὁ κωλύων τὰ ἀκόλουθα τῇ φύσει, ἧς μέρος εἶ, πράσσειν τε ἀεὶ καὶ λέγειν.
passages.english: These things must always be remembered: what the nature of the whole is, and what mine is, and how this one stands to that one, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

notes.note: Glossary rendering. The Greek is plural, “of all things together”.
notes.other_reading: the nature of all things

notes.greek: ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα
notes.note: Literally “being what sort of part of what sort of whole”.
notes.other_reading: what sort of part it is, and of what sort of whole

notes.note: The Greek moves from “mine” to “you are”, and the English keeps the shift. “You” after “prevents” is supplied from this clause.
notes.other_reading: of which I am a part

notes.note: Literally “the things that follow nature”, as a companion follows: what is consistent with it, not what is deduced from it.
notes.other_reading: what follows from the nature

check.note: The Greek word with this case is “in keeping with, consistent with”; “follows from” suggests a logical deduction.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part”. The Greek word means following as a companion does, not following as a conclusion does.

passages.casaubon: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Всегда нужно помнить вот что: какова природа целого, и какова моя, и как эта относится к той, и какая это часть какого целого; и что нет никого, кто мешал бы тебе всегда делать и говорить то, что сообразно с природой, которой ты часть.

passages.greek: Συντιθέναι δεῖ τὸν βίον κατὰ μίαν πρᾶξιν καὶ εἰ ἑκάστη τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχει ὡς οἷόν τε, ἀρκεῖσθαι· ἵνα δὲ τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχῃ, οὐδὲ εἷς σε κωλῦσαι δύναται.—ἀλλʼ ἐνστήσεταί τι ἔξωθεν.—οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως, ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται, ἀλλὰ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει καὶ τῇ ἐπὶ τὸ διδόμενον εὐγνώμονι μεταβάσει εὐθὺς ἄλλη πρᾶξις ἀντικαθίσταται ἐναρμόσουσα εἰς τὴν σύνθεσιν, περὶ ἧς ὁ λόγος.
passages.english: You must put your life together one action at a time, and if each action does its own part as far as it can, be content. And no one at all can prevent you from making sure that it does its own part. “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented; but through being well pleased with the very thing that prevents it, and through moving over with good grace to what is given, another action at once takes its place, one that will fit into the putting together of which we are speaking.

notes.note: The verb and the noun σύνθεσιν at the end are one word; the English reads “put together” and “the putting together” so the link shows.
notes.other_reading: You must compose your life

notes.note: “By one action”, that is, action by single action.
notes.other_reading: action by action

notes.note: Literally “supplies what is its own”, with the noun left unsaid. The English reads “does its own part”; the words can also mean that the action reaches its own end.
notes.other_reading: achieves its own end

notes.note: The edition marks a change of speaker with dashes. The English uses quotation marks for the objection and none for the reply.
notes.other_reading: “But some outside thing will block it.”

notes.greek: οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως
notes.note: There is no verb: “nothing, at least for the justly and self-controlledly and reasonably”. The English supplies “acting”. εὐλογίστως is “with sound reckoning”.
notes.other_reading: Nothing, at least, that stops you being just, self-controlled and reasonable

notes.note: “Something else of an active kind”: some outward doing, as against the manner of acting just named.
notes.other_reading: but perhaps some other exercise of your activity

notes.note: κώλυμα is the noun of the verb “prevent” used twice before it in the passage: the thing that prevents. The English writes it out as “the very thing that prevents it” so that the three can be heard together.
notes.other_reading: the obstacle itself

notes.note: A noun in the dative, “by a being well pleased”, not a verb. “Well pleased” is used for this word family here and in 10.6, to keep it apart from ἀρκεῖσθαι, “be content”.
notes.other_reading: by accepting the obstacle itself gladly

notes.note: εὐγνώμων is fair-minded, sensible, good-tempered; μετάβασις is a stepping across.
notes.other_reading: by a sensible change over to what is given

check.note: “Delivers what is its own” is literal and unclear to a reader; the sense is that each action yields what belongs to it, does its own part.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “does its own part”, here and in the next sentence. The literal “supplies what is its own” is kept in the note.

check.greek: ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται
check.note: One hedge in the Greek with a plain future, two in the English (“may perhaps”).
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented”, one hedge and a plain future as in the Greek.

check.greek: τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει
check.note: Three words of one family in the Greek became “prevent”, “prevented” and then “obstacle”, so the point that the very thing that hinders becomes the material is less visible.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the three words are now one family in English, “prevent”, “prevented” and “the very thing that prevents it”. “Prevent” is kept and not “hinder”, because it is the word for this verb in 3.12, 2.9 and 6.58.

passages.casaubon: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be, instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Ты должен складывать свою жизнь действие за действием, и если каждое действие исполняет своё, насколько возможно, — будь доволен. А помешать тебе добиться, чтобы оно исполняло своё, не может вообще никто. «Но что-нибудь извне встанет на пути». Ничто не встанет — во всяком случае, на пути к тому, чтобы действовать справедливо, с самообладанием и благоразумно. Какой-то другой деятельности, может быть, и помешают; но если ты будешь вполне доволен самим тем, что мешает, и охотно перейдёшь к тому, что дано, тотчас на её место встанет другое действие, которое впишется в то складывание, о котором мы говорим.

passages.greek: ʽὈλίγα πρῆσσε, φησίν, εἰ μέλλεις εὐθυμήσειν.ʼ μήποτε ἄμεινον τἀναγκαῖα πράσσειν καὶ ὅσα ὁ τοῦ φύσει πολιτικοῦ ζῴου λόγος αἱρεῖ καὶ ὡς αἱρεῖ; τοῦτο γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καλῶς πράσσειν εὐθυμίαν φέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀλίγα πράσσειν. τὰ πλεῖστα γὰρ ὧν λέγομεν καὶ πράσσομεν οὐκ ἀναγκαῖα ὄντα ἐάν τις περιέλῃ, εὐσχολώτερος καὶ ἀταρακτότερος ἔσται. ὅθεν δεῖ καὶ παῤ ἕκαστα ἑαυτὸν ὑπομιμνῄσκειν· μήτι τοῦτο τῶν οὐκ ἀναγκαίων; δεῖ δὲ μὴ μόνον πράξεις τὰς μὴ ἀναγκαίας περιαιρεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ φαντασίας· οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲ πράξεις παρέλκουσαι ἐπακολουθήσουσιν.
passages.english: “Do few things,” he says, “if you mean to be cheerful.” Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the cheerfulness that comes from doing things well, but also the cheerfulness that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled. So on each occasion one must also remind oneself: “Is this perhaps one of the things that are not necessary?” And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too, for then superfluous actions will not follow after them either.

notes.note: The quotation is in Ionic dialect (πρῆσσε for πρᾶσσε), and “he says” names no one. From memory, unchecked: it is a saying of Democritus.
notes.other_reading: “Do little,” it is said

notes.note: εὐθυμία is good spirits, a settled and contented mind and not a passing mood. “Cheerful” and “cheerfulness” are kept for the verb and the noun.
notes.other_reading: if you mean to be of good heart

notes.note: In later Greek this opens a cautious suggestion, “perhaps”. The edition prints the sentence as a question.
notes.other_reading: Perhaps it is better

notes.note: ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ is a set phrase, “reason proves, reason dictates”; literally reason “takes” or “chooses”.
notes.other_reading: chooses, and as it chooses

notes.note: πράσσειν is “do” throughout the passage, so “doing things well” is kept; the sense is acting rightly, not prospering.
notes.other_reading: from acting rightly

notes.note: Two comparatives: “more at leisure and more undisturbed”.
notes.other_reading: will have more free time and more calm

notes.note: The Greek does not repeat “not necessary” with the impressions and has no article. The words are most naturally carried over from the actions, and the English leaves them to be carried over in the same way.
notes.other_reading: but unnecessary impressions too

notes.note: Literally “dragging alongside”: trailing after to no purpose, superfluous.
notes.other_reading: idle actions

check.note: The Greek word is settled good spirits, contentment of mind; “cheerful” and “cheerfulness” are lighter and more a matter of mood.
check.decided: Declined: “cheerful” and “cheerfulness” stay. The Greek word is literally good spirits, “cheerful” is the plain word of today for that, and the note records the fuller sense of a settled mind.

check.note: “At each thing” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “on each occasion”, which is what the Greek phrase means. “At every step” would bring in a picture the Greek does not have.

check.note: There is no article in the Greek, and “not necessary” carries over from the actions: unnecessary impressions. “The impressions” reads as all impressions.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the article is dropped and the English reads “but impressions too”. “Unnecessary” is not written in, because the Greek leaves it to be carried over from the actions and the English sentence does the same; a note says so.

check.note: The participle is “superfluous, redundant”. “Idle actions” suggests doing nothing, and there is no article.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “superfluous actions”, without the article. “Idle” could be heard as doing nothing.

passages.casaubon: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble, and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: «Делай немногое, — говорит он, — если хочешь сохранять бодрость духа». Не лучше ли делать необходимое — и то, чего требует разум живого существа, гражданского по природе, и так, как он требует? Ведь это приносит не только бодрость духа от того, что делаешь хорошо, но и бодрость духа от того, что делаешь немногое. Большая часть того, что мы говорим и делаем, не необходима, и если человек это отбросит, у него будет больше досуга и меньше тревог. Поэтому в каждом случае надо и напоминать себе: «А может быть, это из того, что не необходимо?» И отбрасывать надо не только действия, совершаемые без необходимости, но и представления: тогда и лишние действия не последуют за ними.

passages.greek: Εἴτε ἄτομοι εἴτε φύσις, πρῶτον κείσθω ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ τοῦ ὅλου ὑπὸ φύσεως διοικουμένου· ἔπειτα, ὅτι ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη. τούτων γὰρ μεμνημένος, καθότι μὲν μέρος εἰμί, οὐδενὶ δυσαρεστήσω τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ἀπονεμομένων· οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει. οὐ γὰρ ἔχει τι τὸ ὅλον ὃ μὴ συμφέρει ἑαυτῷ, πασῶν μὲν φύσεων κοινὸν ἐχουσῶν τοῦτο, τῆς δὲ τοῦ κόσμου προσειληφυίας τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι βλαβερόν τι ἑαυτῇ γεννᾶν. κατὰ μὲν δὴ τὸ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ ὅλου τοῦ τοιούτου, εὐαρεστήσω παντὶ τῷ ἀποβαίνοντι, καθόσον δὲ ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη, οὐδὲν πράξω ἀκοινώνητον, μᾶλλον δὲ στοχάσομαι τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ πρὸς τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἄξω καὶ ἀπὸ τοὐναντίου ἀπάξω. τούτων δὲ οὕτως περαινομένων ἀνάγκη τὸν βίον εὐροεῖν, ὡς ἂν καὶ πολίτου βίον εὔρουν ἐπινοήσειας προιόντος διὰ πράξεων τοῖς πολίταις λυσιτελῶν καὶ ὅπερ ἂν ἡ πόλις ἀπονέμῃ, τοῦτο ἀσπαζομένου.
passages.english: Whether it is atoms or nature, let this first be laid down: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I have a certain kinship with the parts that are of the same kind as I am. For if I remember these things, then insofar as I am a part, I will not be displeased with anything that is allotted from the whole. For nothing that is good for the whole is harmful to the part. For the whole has nothing that is not good for itself. All natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this in addition, that it is not even forced by any cause from outside to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of a whole of this kind, I will be well pleased with everything that comes about. And insofar as I have a certain kinship with the parts of the same kind, I will do nothing unsocial. Rather I will make those of my own kind my aim, and I will lead my every impulse towards what is good for all in common and lead it away from the opposite. When these things are carried through in this way, life must flow well, just as you would think that a citizen’s life flows well when that citizen goes forward through actions that profit the citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots.

notes.note: The Epicurean account (atoms moving at random) against the Stoic one (an ordering nature). The Greek has no verb. The next clause already says the whole is “governed by nature”, which sits oddly with leaving the question open; it is translated as it stands.
notes.other_reading: Whether there are atoms or a nature

notes.note: οἰκείως ἔχειν is to be related to something as to what belongs to one’s own household. πως, “in some way”, softens it.
notes.other_reading: to be in some way closely bound to

notes.note: “The parts of the same kind”, or of the same birth. The words “as I am” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: the kindred parts

notes.note: δυσαρεστεῖν and εὐαρεστεῖν later in the passage are a matched pair; the English reads “displeased” and “well pleased”.
notes.other_reading: to resent nothing

notes.greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει
notes.note: Word order in the Greek: “for nothing is harmful to the part which is good for the whole”. The English turns it round so the relative clause is not misread as describing the part. συμφέρει is “is good for” by the glossary; in τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον below, “what is good for all in common”, the words “for all” are supplied.
notes.other_reading: for nothing harms the part that benefits the whole

notes.note: The negative of κοινωνικός, “social”: an act that takes no share in the common life. The Greek answers it at once with κοινῇ, “in common”, an echo the English does not keep.
notes.other_reading: nothing that breaks the common bond

notes.note: στοχάζομαι is to aim at a target, and so to have something in view; the English keeps the picture of aiming without the sound of an attack. The genitive may be masculine (those of the same kind) or neuter (the parts of the same kind), and the possessive is supplied.
notes.other_reading: to have regard for the parts of the same kind

notes.note: Glossary rendering, “carried through”.
notes.other_reading: When this is accomplished in this way

notes.note: “To flow well”. From memory, unchecked: “a good flow of life” is an early Stoic description of happiness. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: life must go smoothly

notes.note: The passage is in the first person, but this verb is second person, “you would think”, and is kept so. The citizen is masculine in the Greek but stands for any citizen, so the English avoids “he”.
notes.other_reading: just as one would think

check.note: The word is “good for” throughout this passage but “what benefits” in 3.6, and “good” is the word for ἀγαθόν elsewhere in the section.
check.decided: Declined: “is good for” stays. It is the rendering this translation has settled for συμφέρει, and this passage does not use the word “good” for anything else, so nothing runs together here; 3.6 and 3.7 have “benefits” for a reason given in their notes.

check.greek: τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι
check.note: The Greek has “not even”: other natures can at least be forced from outside, this one not even that. The “even” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “that it is not even forced by any cause from outside”. The Greek has “not even”, and the point is that other natures can at least be forced.

check.note: The Greek word is answered at once by “in common”; the echo is lost in “unsocial … in common”.
check.decided: Declined: “nothing unsocial” stays. “Social” is the settled word for κοινωνικός and this is its negative, while “the common bond” would bring in a picture the Greek does not have. The note now points out the echo with “in common”.

check.note: “Aim at” people sounds hostile in English; the sense is to keep them in view as the target of what one does.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now makes “those of my own kind” the aim, in the words “make those of my own kind my aim”. This removes the hostile sound of “aim at” and keeps the Greek picture of aiming at a target, which “keep in view” would lose.

check.note: “Other” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “actions that profit the citizens”. “Other” is not in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred. For of these, if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is, that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that should tend to her own hurt and prejudice. As then I bear in mind that I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto, as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.
passages.russian: Атомы ли, природа ли — прежде всего пусть будет установлено: я — часть целого, которым управляет природа. Затем: я состою в некотором родстве с частями, однородными со мной. Ведь если я буду помнить это, то, поскольку я часть, я не буду недоволен ничем из того, что уделяет мне целое. Ничто из того, что хорошо для целого, не вредно части. Ведь у целого нет ничего, что не было бы хорошо для него самого. Это общее у всех природ, но у природы мироздания есть сверх того ещё и то, что её даже никакая внешняя причина не вынуждает производить что-либо вредное для неё самой. Итак, помня, что я часть такого целого, я буду доволен всем, что происходит. А поскольку я состою в некотором родстве с однородными частями, я не сделаю ничего необщественного; напротив, моей целью будут сородичи, и всякое своё побуждение я буду направлять к тому, что хорошо для всех сообща, и отводить от противоположного. Когда всё это так исполняется, жизнь непременно течёт хорошо — так же как ты считал бы, что хорошо течёт жизнь гражданина, когда он идёт вперёд, совершая дела, полезные гражданам, и приветствует всё, что уделяет ему город.

passages.greek: Δύνασαι ἀεὶ εὐροεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ εὐοδεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ ὁδῷ ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ πράσσειν. δύο ταῦτα κοινὰ τῇ τε τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ παντὸς λογικοῦ ζῴου ψυχῇ· τὸ μὴ ἐμποδίζεσθαι ὑπ’ ἄλλου καὶ τὸ ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει ἔχειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὄρεξιν ἀπολήγειν.
passages.english: You can always have your life flow well, if indeed you can also travel a good road, if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road. These two things are common to the soul of god, and of a human being, and of every rational living being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there.

notes.note: The Greek says simply “you can always flow well”. “Have your life” is supplied because 10.6 uses the same verb of a life and English does not say that a person flows.
notes.other_reading: You can always flow well

notes.note: A chain of sound and sense: εὐροεῖν (flow well), εὐοδεῖν (have a good road), ὁδῷ (by a road). ὁδῷ is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”; the English gives the sense as “step by step”, as in 6.26, and adds “as along a road” so that the play can be followed.
notes.other_reading: if you can also go on your way well, if you can also judge and act methodically

notes.note: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary: to form a judgment about things.
notes.other_reading: to think

notes.note: “The god” with the article, which in Marcus is god in general or the god of the universe. Lower case by the glossary.
notes.other_reading: the soul of the god

notes.note: ἄλλου can be masculine, “by another person”, or neuter, “by anything else”. The English takes the wider sense, which includes the other.
notes.other_reading: not to be hindered by another

notes.greek: ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει
notes.note: δικαικῇ is a rare adjective, “of justice”, read here as the edition’s δικαϊκῇ. It governs both nouns, so “just” is repeated.
notes.other_reading: in the disposition and action that belong to justice

notes.note: ὄρεξιν is taken as the subject of the infinitive, “desire coming to a stop there”. It can also be the object, “to bring desire to a stop there”.
notes.other_reading: and to end its desire there

check.note: “Your life” is supplied; the Greek is the bare verb, “you can always flow well”. Reasonable beside 10.6, but added.
check.decided: Declined: “have your life flow well” stays. English does not say of a person that they flow, the same verb is said of a life in 10.6, and the note records that “your life” is supplied.

check.note: ὁδῷ is the set phrase “by a road”, that is, in order, methodically; in 6.26 the same word is “step by step”. “As one who keeps to a road” saves the play but is obscure and does not match.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “judge and act step by step, as along a road”. “Step by step” now matches the same word in 6.26, and the road is kept beside it so that the play with “a good road” can still be heard.

check.note: The Greek word can be neuter, “by anything else”. “By another” limits it to a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “not to be hindered by anything else”. The Greek word can be a person or a thing, and the wider wording covers both; the note records “by another”.

check.note: Found while settling: “keep to a good road” suggests staying on course by effort, but εὐοδεῖν is to have a good road, an easy passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “travel a good road”, which says that the going is good and not that the traveler holds the line.

passages.casaubon: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Ты всегда можешь сделать так, чтобы твоя жизнь текла хорошо, если только ты можешь и идти хорошей дорогой, если только можешь и судить, и действовать шаг за шагом, как по дороге. Две вещи общи душе бога, и человека, и всякого разумного живого существа: не встречать помех ни от чего другого; и иметь своё благо в справедливом расположении и справедливом действии, и на этом останавливать своё желание.

passages.greek: Ἐπὶ τὴν σύντομον ἀεὶ τρέχε· σύντομος δὲ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν. ἀπαλλάσσει γὰρ ἡ τοιαύτη πρόθεσις κόπων καὶ στραγγείας καὶ πάσης οἰκονομίας καὶ κομψείας.
passages.english: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.

notes.note: The noun is left out, as Greek does with “road”: “the short [road]”. ἐπί with the accusative is “to” or “for”: make for the short road and take it.
notes.other_reading: Always run by the short road.

notes.greek: ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν
notes.note: ὥστε with the infinitive gives the result. ὑγιέστατον is “healthiest”, and so soundest. No subject is expressed; “you” comes from the command before.
notes.other_reading: so as to say and do everything in the healthiest way

notes.note: πρόθεσις is a purpose set before oneself. The verb has no object; “you” is supplied from the command that opens the passage.
notes.other_reading: For such a resolve sets a person free

notes.note: A rare word, “loitering, hanging back, delay”, translated as given. From memory, unchecked: the word is an editor’s correction, and the manuscripts have στρατείας, “campaigning, warfare”.
notes.other_reading: from toils and campaigning

notes.note: οἰκονομία is managing a household and so, in speech and conduct, arranging things for effect; κομψεία is smartness, refinement put on for show. Both are meant in a bad sense.
notes.other_reading: from all management and cleverness

check.note: The preposition with this case is “to, onto”: make for the short road. “By” is close but not the same picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “Always run to the short road.” The preposition is “to” or “onto”, not “by”.

check.note: There is no object in the Greek; the passage is addressed to “you”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “frees you”. The Greek has no object, and the passage opens with a command to “you”.

check.note: The English fits the word as given. From memory, this word is an editor’s correction of the transmitted word for “campaigning”, so the point may want a note.
check.decided: Accepted: “hanging back” stays as the sense of the word given, and the note now says, from memory and unchecked, that the word is an editor’s correction of “campaigning”.

check.note: The word here is calculated arrangement, contriving how to present things. “Managing” does not convey that and is unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “all contriving”. The word here is arranging things for effect, which “managing” did not convey.

check.note: The word is affected refinement, showy elegance; “cleverness” misses the affectation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “affectation”, which says that the refinement is put on. “Showing off” would narrow it to display in front of others.

passages.casaubon: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Всегда беги кратким путём. А краткий путь — согласный с природой, чтобы ты говорил и делал всё самым здравым образом. Ведь такое намерение избавляет от тяжких трудов и от промедления, от всяких ухищрений и рисовки.

passages.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως βιοῦν σε οὐδεὶς κωλύσει· παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως οὐδέν σοι συμβήσεται.
passages.english: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature. Nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the common nature.

notes.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως
notes.note: λόγος is “reason” by the glossary; it could also be heard as the principle or law of your nature. The Greek puts the two prepositional phrases first, in sharp parallel: “according to … contrary to …”.
notes.other_reading: according to the principle of your own nature

notes.note: “The common nature” is the nature shared by all things, the nature of the whole.
notes.other_reading: of universal nature

passages.casaubon: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Жить по разуму твоей собственной природы тебе никто не помешает. Ничто не случится с тобой вопреки разуму общей природы.

passages.greek: Ἐάν τίς σοι προβάλῃ πῶς γράφεται τὸ Ἀντωνίνου ὄνομα, μήτι κατεντεινόμενος προοίσῃ ἕκαστον τῶν στοιχείων; τί οὖν ἐὰν ὀργίζωνται, μήτι ἀντοργιῇ; μήτι οὐκ ἐξαριθμήσῃ πρᾴως προιὼν ἕκαστον τῶν γραμμάτων; οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε μέμνησο ὅτι πᾶν καθῆκον ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τινῶν συμπληροῦται. τούτους δεῖ τηροῦντα καὶ μὴ θορυβούμενον μηδὲ τοῖς δυσχεραίνουσιν ἀντιδυσχεραίνοντα περαίνειν ὁδῷ τὸ προκείμενον.
passages.english: If someone sets you the question how the name Antoninus is written, surely you will not strain as you bring out each of its letters? What then if they get angry: surely you will not get angry back? Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters? So here too, remember that every duty is made complete out of certain counted parts. These you must keep to, and, without being thrown into confusion and without being annoyed in turn at those who are annoyed, carry through step by step what lies before you.

notes.note: Antoninus is Marcus’s own name as emperor, so the example is spelling his own name.
notes.other_reading: the name of Antoninus

notes.note: μήτι expects the answer no, so the English reads “surely you will not”. κατεντεινόμενος is “straining hard”, whether of the voice or of effort in general; προφέρω is to utter aloud.
notes.other_reading: surely you will not shout out each letter at full stretch?

notes.note: στοιχεῖα here and γραμμάτων below both mean the letters of the name; the first is strictly the elements or sounds, the second the written characters. The English has “letters” for both.
notes.other_reading: each of its elements

notes.note: The Greek moves from “someone” to an unnamed plural “they”.
notes.other_reading: if people get angry

notes.note: πρᾴως, “gently”, stands between “count off” and “going on” and can go with either. The English puts it before both.
notes.other_reading: Will you not go on gently and count off each of the letters?

notes.note: καθῆκον is the Stoic term for an act that it falls to one to do, a fitting or appropriate act. “Duty” is the plain word nearest to it.
notes.other_reading: every fitting act

notes.note: ἀριθμοί, “numbers”, are the counted items that make a thing complete, picking up ἐξαριθμήσῃ, “count off”, just before. The English reads “counted parts” so the link shows; “parts” is supplied. From memory, unchecked: Stoics spoke of a right act as having all its “numbers”.
notes.other_reading: is made complete out of certain numbers

notes.note: περαίνειν is “carry through” by the glossary. ὁδῷ, literally “by a road”, is the idiom for “methodically, in order”; it is “step by step” here and in 5.34, where the road itself is also kept.
notes.other_reading: carry through, keeping to the road, what lies before you

check.note: μήτι expects the answer no: “surely you will not …?”. The plain “will you” loses that, and the same holds for “will you get angry back?”.
check.decided: Accepted: both questions now read “surely you will not”, since the Greek word that opens them expects the answer no.

check.note: “Voice” is not in the Greek: the word is straining, exerting oneself hard. Shouting is one way to picture it, not the only one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “strain as you bring out each of its letters”. “Voice” is not in the Greek.

check.note: Two Greek words, στοιχεῖα and γράμματα, are both “letters”. Little is lost, but the point should be known.
check.decided: Declined: both Greek words stay “letters”. In the spelling of a name they are the same things, and “elements” for the first would puzzle a reader; the note records the two words.

check.note: The adverb more naturally goes with the main verb: “count off calmly, going through each letter”. The English ties “gently” to the going on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?”, so that “gently” covers the counting as well as the going on. “Gently” is kept and not “calmly”, because the Greek word is the opposite of the anger just mentioned.

check.note: “Certain numbers” is obscure. The Greek “numbers” are the counted items that make a thing up, and the word answers “count off” just before.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English reads “is made complete out of certain counted parts”. “Counted” keeps the link with “count off”; “steps” is not used because “step by step” is needed for another word at the end of the passage.

passages.casaubon: if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again, or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were, to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would quarrel and fall out with thee.

nearest.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

passages.russian: Если тебя спросят, как пишется имя Антонин, неужели ты станешь напрягаться, выговаривая каждую его букву? А если рассердятся — неужели и ты рассердишься в ответ? Не станешь ли ты спокойно перечислять по порядку каждую из букв? Так и здесь помни, что всякий долг складывается из неких сочтённых частей. Их ты и должен держаться и, не приходя в смятение и не раздражаясь в ответ на тех, кто раздражён, шаг за шагом доводить до конца то, что перед тобой.

passages.greek: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιζητοῦντας· ποῦ γὰρ ἰδὼν τοὺς θεοὺς ἢ πόθεν κατειληφὼς ὅτι εἰσὶν οὕτως σέβεις; πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ὄψει ὁρατοί εἰσιν· ἔπειτα μέντοι οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἑώρακα καὶ ὅμως τιμῶ· οὕτως οὖν καὶ τοὺς θεούς, ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι, ἐκ τούτων ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι.
passages.english: To those who ask: “Well, where have you seen the gods, or from what have you grasped that they exist, that you revere them as you do?” First, they are visible even to the eye. Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it. So with the gods too: from what I experience of their power on every occasion, from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.

notes.note: A heading with no verb. The prefix of the verb can mean asking further or asking insistently, or it may add nothing; the English reads the plain “ask”, since no earlier question stands in the passage for “further” to follow.
notes.other_reading: To those who go on to ask; To those who press the question

notes.note: The particle γὰρ in a question marks it as a challenge and is not “for” here; “Well,” stands for it. The question is the questioners’ own words, so it is set in quotation marks, which the Greek does not have.
notes.other_reading: Why, where have you seen

notes.note: The Stoic school’s word for a sure grasp of a fact (katalepsis). The same verb comes back at the end (καταλαμβάνω), so the English reads “grasp” both times.
notes.other_reading: from what have you made sure that they exist

notes.note: Literally “you revere in this way”, with “them” supplied; “so” can point to the manner or to the degree, and “as you do” keeps both. The verb also covers acts of worship. “Revere” is used so that the noun of the same root in 4.16 (σεβασμὸν) can be “reverence”.
notes.other_reading: that you worship them so devoutly

notes.note: Literally “they are visible even to sight”. The small word καὶ can be “even” or “also” (visible to sight as well as known in other ways); the English reads “even”. The Greek does not say which gods: the sun, moon and stars, which were counted as gods, are probably meant, but nothing is added.
notes.other_reading: they are visible to the eye as well

notes.greek: ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι
notes.note: The verb means to make trial of or to have experience of something. The adverb ἑκάστοτε is “each time” or “on every occasion”, and so can also be “constantly”.
notes.other_reading: from the proofs of their power that are met with again and again

notes.note: A third verb, after “revere” (σέβεις) and “honour” (τιμῶ): it means respect mixed with shame or awe before someone. Three English verbs are kept for the three Greek ones.
notes.other_reading: and respect them

check.note: The Greek word answers “first” and gives the second of two numbered replies. “But then” is heard as “but then again”, so the count of two answers is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either”. The Greek word picks up “first” and brings in the second of two replies, which “But then” hid.

check.greek: ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι
check.note: The Greek ties the two verbs together with “both … and” under “from that”: the same experience is the ground of knowing that the gods exist and of revering them. The comma and the fresh “I” cut the second verb loose.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them”. The Greek joins the two verbs under “from that”, so the one experience is the ground of both.

check.note: “Each time” has nothing to refer to in the English. The Greek word is “on every occasion”, “again and again”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “on every occasion”, the plain sense of the Greek word. “At every turn” is not taken because it brings in a figure of speech that the Greek does not have.

check.note: The verb is to ask further, to go on to inquire. “Press the question” adds a note of insistence that the verb does not have to carry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “press the question” is dropped, since the verb need not carry insistence, and the English now reads “To those who ask”. “Go on to ask” is not taken because no earlier question stands in the passage for it to follow; the note records both.

check.note: The particle γὰρ in the question is dropped. It gives the question its challenging tone.
check.decided: Accepted: the question now begins “Well, where have you seen the gods”, so that the challenge the particle carries is heard.

check.note: The small word καὶ can be “even” or “also”, and the Greek states a fact (“they are visible”) where the English states a possibility (“can be seen”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now states a fact, “they are visible even to the eye”, as the Greek does. “Even” is kept, since the questioners asked where the gods had been seen and the reply meets that word; “also” is recorded in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: “worship” here and “reverence” in 4.16 stood for one Greek root (σέβεις, σεβασμὸν), while “revere” at the end of this passage stood for a different verb (αἰδοῦμαι).
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “revere” for σέβεις and “stand in awe of” for αἰδοῦμαι. “Revere” and “reverence” now answer to the one root in the two passages, and the three verbs of this passage stay distinct.

passages.casaubon: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore worship them.
passages.russian: Тем, кто спрашивает: «Где же ты видел богов или откуда понял, что они существуют, раз так их чтишь?» Во-первых, они видимы даже глазу. Во-вторых, я ведь и собственной души не видел, а всё же почитаю её. Так и с богами: из того, что я всякий раз испытываю их силу, — из этого я и понимаю, что они существуют, и благоговею перед ними.

passages.greek: ʽΣυζῆν θεοῖς.ʼ συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ἀρεσκομένην μὲν τοῖς ἀπονεμομένοις, ποιοῦσαν δὲ ὅσα βούλεται ὁ δαίμων, ὃν ἑκάστῳ προστάτην καὶ ἡγεμόνα ὁ Ζεὺς ἔδωκεν, ἀπόσπασμα ἑαυτοῦ. οὗτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς καὶ λόγος.
passages.english: “To live with the gods.” And the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself. And this spirit is each person’s mind and reason.

notes.note: A bare infinitive, which the edition sets in quotation marks as a saying. It can be a heading or a command; the English keeps the infinitive, and the next sentence then says who does live so.
notes.other_reading: “Live with the gods.”

notes.greek: συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς
notes.note: Literally “and he lives with the gods who constantly shows them”. The English turns this into “the one who … is the one who …” so that the long description does not trail far from its subject.
notes.other_reading: And a person lives with the gods who constantly shows them

notes.note: The Greek is “his own soul”: the soul of the person, not of the gods. “Their own” is written to avoid “he” for a subject not singled out as a man, so “them” is the gods and “their” is the person’s.
notes.other_reading: shows them his own soul

notes.note: Two participles say what the soul is shown to be: content, and doing. The Greek can equally be put as a clause with “that”.
notes.other_reading: constantly shows them that their own soul is content with what is allotted and does all that the spirit wants

notes.note: Literally “the things being dealt out”. The Greek does not say by whom or to whom, and the English adds neither.
notes.other_reading: pleased with what is assigned to it

notes.note: The daimon: a divine being that attends each person. The English reads “the spirit”, since the passage itself goes on to call it a protector and to say what it is. The word is repeated twice (“the spirit that Zeus”, “this spirit”) where the Greek has a relative pronoun and a “this”.
notes.other_reading: the guardian spirit; the divinity

notes.note: The first word is one who stands in front: a protector, guardian, patron or chief. The second is a leader, one who gives the lead and is followed; it is the root of the Stoic term “the ruling part” (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν), so “ruler” is also possible, and “guide” is its milder sense.
notes.other_reading: as guardian and guide; as chief and ruler

notes.note: The noun is from a verb meaning to tear or pull away, and names a detached portion of something. “Fragment” is the plain word for it; the more literal rendering spells out the root.
notes.other_reading: a piece torn off from himself

notes.note: Two nouns for one thing; both are kept, with this translation’s usual words for them. They may be meant as a single idea.
notes.other_reading: each person’s reasoning mind

check.note: The Greek is definite: “his own soul”. “A soul of their own” sounds like one soul among several, and is awkward after the singular “a person”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “their own soul”, definite as in the Greek. “Their” is the person’s, as the note says.

check.note: The Greek is an infinitive, which can be a heading or quoted phrase as well as a command. The English had made it a command, and the next sentence suits the heading at least as well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To live with the gods.”, keeping the Greek infinitive, which can be a heading or a command. The command is recorded in the note.

check.greek: συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς
check.note: The relative clause is stranded far from “a person”, which makes the sentence hard to follow. The Greek is a plain definition of the one who lives with the gods.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now reads “the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them …”, so the description is no longer stranded from its subject. The Greek is a plain statement of who lives with the gods.

check.note: “To it” is added and fixes the receiver as the soul. The Greek says only “the things that are allotted”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what is allotted”. The Greek names no receiver.

check.note: The second Greek word is a leader or commander, one who gives the lead and is obeyed. “Guide” is milder and loses the note of authority.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “protector and leader”. “Leader” keeps the authority of the second Greek word; “protector” stays for the first, which means one who stands in front of another, and “guardian” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The noun is by origin something pulled off, but in use it is simply a detached portion. “Torn off” spells out the root and adds a violence the plain noun need not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a fragment of himself”. The Greek noun names a detached portion, and its root, to pull away, is kept in the note.

check.note: “Spirit” alone is vague in today’s English and stands here beside “soul”. The Greek word names a personal divinity given to each person, and the English repeats “spirit” twice more, so the word carries the whole passage; “the guardian spirit” is proposed for the first mention.
check.decided: Declined: “the spirit” stays, because “guardian” is not in the Greek word itself: the next words call the spirit a protector, and the last sentence says what it is, so “guardian spirit” would say one thing twice. The note records “the guardian spirit” as the other reading.

passages.casaubon: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
passages.russian: «Жить вместе с богами». А живёт вместе с богами тот, кто постоянно являет им свою душу — довольную тем, что ей уделено, и делающую всё, чего хочет дух, тот дух, которого Зевс дал каждому как хранителя и вожатого, — частицу самого себя. А этот дух есть ум и разум каждого.

passages.greek: Ἐντὸς δέκα ἡμερῶν θεὸς αὐτοῖς τούτοις δόξεις οἷς νῦν θηρίον καὶ πίθηκος, ἐὰν ἀνακάμψῃς ἐπὶ τὰ δόγματα καὶ τὸν σεβασμὸν τοῦ λόγου.
passages.english: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason.

notes.note: Literally “within ten days”. It may be a round figure for “very soon”; the number is kept.
notes.other_reading: In a few days

notes.note: There is no verb in this clause; “you seem” is carried over from the main verb. The first noun is a wild animal.
notes.other_reading: to whom you are now a wild animal and a monkey

notes.note: The verb is to bend back or turn back on one’s course, so it implies a return to something left behind.
notes.other_reading: if you return

notes.note: The Greek has only the article, “the principles”, and the English keeps it. Since the verb speaks of turning back, the article may stand for “your”: the principles once held and since left.
notes.other_reading: to your principles

notes.note: The genitive is taken as the thing revered: reverence for reason. The Greek does not say whether this is a person’s own reason or the reason that runs through everything, and “reason” without an article keeps both. The noun is from the same root as “revere” (σέβεις) in 12.28.
notes.other_reading: the worship of reason

check.note: “Your” is supplied; the Greek has only the article, “the principles”. The article can stand for a possessive, so this is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the principles”, since the Greek has only the article. “Your principles” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The genitive is taken as the thing revered, which is the natural reading. Whether a person’s own reason or the reason that runs through everything is meant is left open, and “reason” without an article keeps both, so nothing needs changing.
check.decided: Accepted: “reverence for reason” stays, as the point itself proposes. The note now says that the Greek leaves open whose reason is meant.

passages.casaubon: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.
passages.russian: Не пройдёт и десяти дней, как ты покажешься богом тем самым людям, которым сейчас кажешься зверем и обезьяной, если вернёшься к принципам и к почитанию разума.

passages.greek: Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι· ἕωθεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀφορᾶν, ἵν’ ὑπομιμνῃσκώμεθα τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος· οὐδὲν γὰρ προκάλυμμα ἄστρου.
passages.english: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way, and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.

notes.note: A nominative with no verb, like a heading, followed by an infinitive that gives their instruction. The English keeps it as a jotting and does not supply “say” or “tell us”.
notes.other_reading: The Pythagoreans tell us to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn

notes.note: Literally “from dawn”. It is used both for “at dawn” and more loosely for “early in the morning”.
notes.other_reading: early in the morning

notes.note: The verb is to look away from other things and fix the eyes on one; the Greek names no direction. “Our” is supplied from the “we” of the next verb.
notes.other_reading: to look up at the sky

notes.greek: τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων
notes.note: The participle can be masculine (“those who”) or neuter (“the things that”); the last clause shows the stars are meant, so the English reads “those that”.
notes.other_reading: the beings who for ever complete their own task

notes.note: A set pair for what never varies (a phrase of Plato’s, from memory, unchecked). The first half is literally “according to the same things”; “along the same lines” is the English for it.
notes.other_reading: in the same respects and in like manner

notes.note: The verb is to bring to completion, and is also used of finishing a journey, which suits the stars’ courses. The English reads “complete”.
notes.other_reading: carry out; accomplish

notes.greek: καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος
notes.note: Three more things to be reminded of. The Greek has only the article, “the order, the purity, the nakedness”; “their” is supplied, since the last clause gives a star as the reason. The three can also be read as things named in themselves.
notes.other_reading: and of order, purity and nakedness

notes.note: Literally “for there is no covering of a star”, with no verb. The noun is anything hung in front to hide: a curtain, a veil.
notes.other_reading: for nothing covers a star

check.note: “On the same terms” suggests the conditions of an agreement. The Greek is “in the same respects”, “along the same lines”: the point is unchanging regularity.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “along the same lines and in the same way”. The Greek phrase is about what never varies, and “terms” suggested the conditions of an agreement.

check.note: The verb is to bring to an end, to complete, often of a course or journey. “Carry out” keeps the doing but loses the completing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “complete their own work”. The Greek verb is to bring to completion, as of a course or a journey.

check.greek: τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος
check.note: “Their” is supplied three times; the Greek has only the article. The three qualities can belong to the heavenly bodies, which the last clause supports, or can be named as things in themselves.
check.decided: Declined: “their order, their purity and their nakedness” stays. The Greek has the article with each noun, which points to a particular order, purity and nakedness, and the last clause gives a star as the reason; the note records the reading without “their”.

check.note: “Up” is supplied. The verb is to look away from other things and fix the eyes on one; the English gives a direction and loses the turning away.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn”, without “up”. “Our” is written and not “one’s” because the next verb is “we”.
