notes.greek: ἡ τοῦ περικεχυμένου τούτου πνεύματος τοιάδε τις δυσκρασία καὶ τροπή
notes.note: πνεῦμα is “breath” or “air”, and the Greek says “poured around” without saying around whom. δυσκρασία is a bad mixture, the medical word for an unhealthy state, here of the air; τροπή is a turn or change. From memory, unchecked, there was a real epidemic in Marcus’s reign.
notes.other_reading: some such distemper and alteration of this surrounding breath

notes.note: αὕτη points to the nearer thing, the plague of the air, and ἐκείνη to the farther, the corruption of the mind. “The latter” and “the former” keep the pointing without adding words.
notes.other_reading: For the plague of the air is a plague of animals as animals; the plague of the mind is a plague of human beings as human beings

check.note: κορεσθέντα is sated to the point of surfeit. “Had one’s fill” can be read as having enjoyed plenty of these things, where the point is dying disgusted with them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “having at least grown sick of these things”. The Greek word is “glutted”, and the second-best death is that of someone who has had too much of lying and luxury, not someone who has enjoyed a good share of them.

check.note: A proverb, literally “the second sailing”: the next best way when the best is closed. “The second-best voyage” reads as if a real voyage were being ranked.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the next best course”. The proverb’s literal picture does no work in the argument, so the sense is given, with “course” keeping a trace of the sailing and the note giving the literal words.

check.greek: πάσης ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τρυφῆς καὶ τύφου
check.note: πάσης (“all”) may run on from pretence to luxury, and in sense to the rest of the list. The English confines it to pretence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity”. “Any” is used and not “all” because the phrase is negative, and it stands once before the three nouns, so that its reach is as open as in the Greek.

check.note: The ordinary medical word for an unhealthy mixture or condition, here of the air. “Bad blending” is literal but not clear to a reader of today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “unhealthy mixture and change”. “Mixture” keeps the picture in the Greek word, which “unwholesome state” would lose, and “unhealthy” gives its medical sense plainly.

check.note: “Us” is not in the Greek, which says only “this air poured around”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “us” is removed and the English reads “this air that is poured around”. “Poured” is kept, where “surrounding” would drop it, because the Greek participle is an image of something poured.

passages.casaubon: It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood, dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are men or reasonable.
passages.russian: Признаком лучшего человека было бы уйти из среды людей, не вкусив ни лжи, ни какого-либо притворства, ни роскоши, ни тщеславия. Но, во всяком случае, испустить дух, хотя бы пресытившись всем этим до отвращения, — второй по достоинству путь. Или ты предпочёл и дальше сидеть рядом с пороком, и даже опыт ещё не убеждает тебя бежать от этой чумы? Ведь порча ума — чума, причём гораздо в большей мере, чем какое-нибудь подобное нездоровое смешение и изменение этого разлитого вокруг воздуха. Последнее — чума для живых существ, поскольку они живые существа; а первое — чума для людей, поскольку они люди.

passages.greek: ἐξεδύσατο τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἐννοήσας ὅτι ὅσον οὐδέπω πάντα ταῦτα καταλιπεῖν ἀπιόντα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων δεήσει, ἀνῆκεν ὅλον ἑαυτὸν δικαιοσύνῃ μὲν εἰς τὰ ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐνεργούμενα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμβαίνουσι τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει. τί δ’ ἐρεῖ τις ἢ ὑπολήψεται περὶ αὐτοῦ ἢ πράξει κατ’ αὐτοῦ, οὐδ’ εἰς νοῦν βάλλεται, δύο τούτοις ἀρκούμενος, εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον καὶ φιλεῖ τὸ νῦν ἀπονεμόμενον ἑαυτῷ· ἀσχολίας δὲ πάσας καὶ σπουδὰς ἀφῆκε καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο βούλεται ἢ εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καὶ εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ.
passages.english: Such a person has stripped off the body and, having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people, has given their whole self over: to justice in what they do themselves, and to the nature of the whole in the other things, those that happen. What anyone will say or think about them, or do against them, they do not even let into their mind, being content with these two things: if they themselves act justly in what is being done now, and if they love what is being allotted to them now. They have let go of all busyness and all eager pursuits, and want nothing else than to keep a straight course right through, by way of the law, and to follow god, who keeps a straight course right through.

notes.note: The passage starts in mid-chapter and the verb has no stated subject. “Such a person” is supplied: it points back to the chapter’s first sentence, not in this passage, which is about training in the study of how all things change into one another. “They” is used because the Greek names no one and its masculine forms are the general ones; the image is of taking off a garment.
notes.other_reading: He has stripped off the body

notes.note: An idiom, literally “all but now”: very soon, at any moment.
notes.other_reading: any moment now

notes.note: ἀνίημι is “let go, hand over, dedicate”, and ὅλον ἑαυτόν is “the whole of himself”, here “their whole self”. The past forms here and below (ἐξεδύσατο, ἀφῆκε) are put as English perfects, because the present verbs beside them describe the resulting state.
notes.other_reading: gave himself up wholly

notes.note: The verb belonging to ὑπόληψις, for which the glossary gives “judgment”. Here it is another person’s opinion of the one described, and “judge about” is not natural English, so “think”. περὶ αὐτοῦ (“about them”) goes with both “say” and “think”.
notes.other_reading: or what judgment anyone will form of them

notes.note: Literally “does not even cast it into the mind”. “Mind” is kept for νοῦς.
notes.other_reading: does not even give it a thought

notes.greek: εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον
notes.note: After “content with these two things” the Greek has “if”, not “that”, and the English keeps it. The second “if” repeats the one εἰ, which governs both verbs.
notes.other_reading: that they themselves act justly in what is being done now

notes.note: ἀσχολία is being occupied, having no leisure; σπουδή is eager effort or a thing pursued in earnest. πάσας (“all”) stands once in the Greek and is taken with both nouns.
notes.other_reading: all occupations and strivings

notes.note: εὐθεῖαν is “a straight [road]”, with the noun left out, and περαίνειν is to carry a thing through to its finish. The glossary’s “carried through” does not sit with “course” in English, so “keep … right through” stands for it, in the same words both times. διὰ τοῦ νόμου could be “through” or “by means of” the law.
notes.other_reading: to travel a straight road to its finish through the law

notes.note: περαίνοντι is dative and agrees with τῷ θεῷ, so it is god who keeps the straight course and the person who follows. From memory, unchecked, this echoes Plato’s Laws, book 4, where god goes straight to his goal and justice follows.
notes.other_reading: to follow god as he travels a straight road to its finish

check.note: The Greek as given begins at the verb, with no subject. A subject has to be supplied, but “Such” points back to a description the reader has not been given.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Such a person” stays, because the verb does point back to someone the chapter’s first sentence has in view, and “he” would single out a man where the Greek masculine is the general one. The note now marks the words as supplied and says what they point back to.

check.note: A participle subordinate to “leave”: all these things must be left behind on going. The English makes it a second thing that will have to be done.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people”. The Greek has one thing that must be done, the leaving behind, and the going is its occasion.

check.note: τοῖς ἄλλοις is “the other things”, “the rest”. “Everything” is slightly stronger than the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the other things, those that happen”. The Greek has no “all” here, only “the others”, set against what the person does.

check.note: The verb is to suppose, to form an opinion, not to pass judgment, and “judge about” is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What anyone will say or think about them, or do against them”. The Greek has “about them” once, serving both verbs, and the verb is forming an opinion; the note records its tie to the glossary’s “judgment”.

check.note: “They do not even take into their mind” is word for word but stiff. The idiom is “does not even give it a thought”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they do not even let into their mind”. This is ordinary English and still keeps “mind” for νοῦς, the glossary’s word, which “give it a thought” would drop.

check.greek: εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καὶ εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ
check.note: The repetition is rightly kept, but “carry a straight course through” is heavy and unclear. The verb is to go through to the end, and εὐθεῖαν is “a straight (road)”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to keep a straight course right through, by way of the law, and to follow god, who keeps a straight course right through”. The repetition stands and the phrase is plainer; “to the end” is not used because in a passage about leaving life it would be heard as “until death”, which the Greek verb does not say.

check.note: The Greek is masculine singular throughout. The singular “they” gives “has given themselves” and, next to “people”, makes “they” briefly unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “has given their whole self over”, which removes “has given themselves” and is closer to the Greek “the whole of himself”. “He” is not used, because the Greek masculine here is the general form and names no man.

part.left_out: Πῶς εἰς ἄλληλα πάντα μεταβάλλει, θεωρητικὴν μέθοδον κτῆσαι καὶ διηνεκῶς πρόσεχε καὶ συγγυμνάσθητι περὶ τοῦτο τὸ μέρος· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν.
part.why: The 1634 translation makes the chapter's first sentence its section 10.11 and begins its section 10.12 here.

passages.casaubon: He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell, and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things that should happen unto him. And contenting himself with these two things, to do all things justly, and whatsoever God doth send to like well of it: what others shall either say or think of him, or shall do against him, he doth not so much as trouble his thoughts with it. To go on straight, whither right and reason directed him, and by so doing to follow God, was the only thing that he did mind, that, his only business and occupation.
passages.russian: Такой человек сбросил с себя тело и, поняв, что очень скоро, уходя от людей, ему придётся всё это оставить, всего себя отдал: справедливости — в том, что делает сам, и природе целого — в прочем, в том, что случается. Что кто о нём скажет или подумает, или что сделает против него, он даже не впускает в ум, довольствуясь двумя вещами: если он сам поступает справедливо в том, что делается сейчас, и если любит то, что уделяется ему сейчас. Он оставил всякую суету и всякое рвение и не хочет ничего иного, как идти прямо, не сворачивая, путём закона и следовать за богом, который идёт прямо, не сворачивая.

passages.greek: Ἤδη τεθνήξῃ καὶ οὔπω οὔτε ἁπλοῦς οὔτε ἀτάραχος οὔτε ἀνύποπτος τοῦ βλαβῆναι ἃν ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἵλεως πρὸς πάντας οὔτε τὸ φρονεῖν ἐν μόνῳ τῷ δικαιοπραγεῖν τιθέμενος.
passages.english: Any moment now you will be dead, and you are not yet simple, nor untroubled, nor free of the suspicion that you could be harmed from outside, nor gracious towards everyone, nor someone who places wisdom only in acting justly.

notes.note: A future perfect, “you will be dead”, with ἤδη (“already, presently”): the state is almost here.
notes.other_reading: Soon you will have died

notes.note: The Greek has no verb after “and not yet”; “you are” is supplied. ἁπλοῦς is “simple, single”, without doubleness.
notes.other_reading: and not yet straightforward

notes.note: ἃν is a slip in the digitised text for ἂν, the particle that goes with βλαβῆναι. Literally “unsuspecting of possibly being harmed from outside”: free of the idea that outside things could do harm.
notes.other_reading: without the expectation that you might be harmed from outside

notes.note: A word used of gods who are favourable, and of people who are kindly and mild.
notes.other_reading: kindly

notes.greek: τὸ φρονεῖν ἐν μόνῳ τῷ δικαιοπραγεῖν τιθέμενος
notes.note: τὸ φρονεῖν is “being wise, having good sense”. μόνῳ (“only”) goes with acting justly: wisdom lies in that and nowhere else.
notes.other_reading: counting acting justly as the only good sense

check.note: μόνῳ limits “acting justly”: in nothing but acting justly. With “alone” at the end the English can be read as “acting justly by yourself”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “someone who places wisdom only in acting justly”. “Only” before the phrase can be taken one way, as the Greek word can.

check.note: A slip in the digitised text for ἂν, the particle that goes with “be harmed”. The English reads it correctly and needs no change.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands as “could be harmed”, which is what the particle with this verb says. The note records the slip.

passages.casaubon: Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to be just in all his actions.
passages.russian: Вот-вот ты умрёшь, а всё ещё не стал ни простым, ни невозмутимым, ни свободным от подозрения, что тебе могут повредить извне, ни благосклонным ко всем, ни тем, кто полагает мудрость только в том, чтобы поступать справедливо.

passages.greek: Οὐδὲν ἂν ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ τοῦ κεκολασμένου καὶ ἐκκεκαθαρμένου πυῶδες οὐδὲ μὴν μεμολυσμένον οὐδὲ ὕπουλον εὕροις· οὐδὲ ἀσυντελῆ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἡ πεπρωμένη καταλαμβάνει, ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι τὸν τραγῳδὸν πρὸ τοῦ τελέσαι καὶ διαδραματίσαι ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι· ἔτι δὲ οὐδὲν δοῦλον οὐδὲ κομψὸν οὐδὲ προσδεδεμένον οὐδὲ ἀπεσχισμένον οὐδὲ ὑπεύθυνον οὐδὲ ἐμφωλεῦον.
passages.english: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus, nor indeed anything stained, nor anything festering under the skin. Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the drama through. And further, nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole.

notes.note: “Mind” for διάνοια, as the glossary allows where the faculty is meant.
notes.other_reading: in the thought

notes.note: κολάζω is “check, correct, chastise”, and is also used of cutting plants back. ἐκκαθαίρω is “clean out”, also a medical word for purging, which fits the pus and the wound that follow. The Greek names no one, so “someone … their”.
notes.other_reading: of the one who has been chastened and purged

notes.note: Said of a wound that has closed over on top but is unsound beneath.
notes.other_reading: sore beneath a scar

notes.greek: ἀσυντελῆ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἡ πεπρωμένη καταλαμβάνει
notes.note: ἀσυντελής is “incomplete”, taken up by τελέσαι (“finishing”) just after; the word can also mean “contributing nothing”, which is not the sense taken here. ἡ πεπρωμένη is “the fated [share or day]”.
notes.other_reading: nor does the appointed hour catch their life incomplete

notes.greek: τὸν τραγῳδὸν πρὸ τοῦ τελέσαι καὶ διαδραματίσαι ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι
notes.note: τραγῳδός is a performer in tragedy. διαδραματίσαι is a rare word, “to play the drama through”. The Greek construction (“that the actor leaves”) is turned into “who leaves”.
notes.other_reading: that the actor in a tragedy goes off before he has completed and acted out the piece

notes.greek: ἔτι δὲ οὐδὲν δοῦλον οὐδὲ κομψὸν
notes.note: The list has no verb of its own and hangs on “you would find” at the start; the English leaves it without one. κομψόν is “smart, clever, elegant”, here in a bad sense.
notes.other_reading: And further you would find nothing servile and nothing showy

notes.note: “Bound to” and “split off from”, and the Greek does not say to or from what: presumably other people or outside things. “To anything” is added only because English cannot leave “tied to” bare.
notes.other_reading: nothing dependent, nothing cut off

notes.note: ὑπεύθυνος is the word for an official who is liable to have his accounts examined, so “liable to be called to account”. ἐμφωλεύω is said of an animal lying hidden in its den.
notes.other_reading: nothing that must answer for itself, nothing hiding away

check.note: The participle is “bound to” something, that is, dependent or clinging, and is paired with “cut off”. “Tied on” suggests an object fastened onto the person and is not clear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nothing tied to anything, nothing split off”. “Tied to anything” gives the Greek “bound to”; “split off” is kept for the second word, whose root is splitting, not cutting.

check.note: The civic word for being liable to audit, open to being called to account. “Must answer for itself” is close but a little odd in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nothing liable to be called to account”. This keeps the word’s civic sense and leaves the liability with the thing in the mind, as the Greek adjective does, where the suggestion would move it to the mind itself.

check.note: “Nor yet” is slightly archaic.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor indeed anything stained”. μήν adds stress to the “nor”, which “indeed” gives in English of today.

passages.casaubon: In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered: nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man might speak.
passages.russian: В уме человека, прошедшего выучку и до конца очищенного, ты не найдёшь ничего гнойного, ни даже чего-то запятнанного, ни чего-то нарывающего под кожей. И рок не застигает его жизнь незавершённой, как можно было бы сказать о трагическом актёре, который уходит, не закончив и не доиграв пьесу до конца. И ещё: ничего рабского, ничего напускного, ничего привязанного к чему-либо, ничего отколовшегося, ничего такого, за что пришлось бы держать ответ, ничего, что прячется в норе.

passages.greek: Ἤτοι ἐνταῦθα ζῇς καὶ ἤδη εἴθικας· ἢ ἔξω ὑπάγεις καὶ τοῦτο ἤθελες· ἢ ἀποθνῄσκεις καὶ ἀπελειτούργησας. παρὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐδέν. οὐκοῦν εὐθύμει.
passages.english: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be cheerful.

notes.note: The form is the active perfect of ἐθίζω, which usually means “you have accustomed [someone]”. With no object given it is taken as “you have got used to it”.
notes.other_reading: and by now you have made it your habit

notes.note: Literally “you are going off outside”: ἔξω answers “here”, and “from here” is added to bring that out. The Greek does not say where “here” or “outside” is. It is not death, which is the third case.
notes.other_reading: you are withdrawing elsewhere

notes.note: An imperfect: “this is what you were wanting”.
notes.other_reading: and that was your own wish

notes.note: From λειτουργία, a public service a citizen carried out for his city. The verb is “to finish one’s service, to be discharged”.
notes.other_reading: your duty is done

notes.note: “Be in good spirits, be cheerful.”
notes.other_reading: be of good heart

check.note: ἔξω answers ἐνταῦθα: here, or out of here. “Going away” keeps the sense but drops the “out”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you are going out from here”. “Out” is restored and set against “here” as in the Greek; “elsewhere” is not used because the Greek names no other place.

passages.casaubon: Either thou dost Continue in this kind of life and that is it, which so long thou hast been used unto and therefore tolerable: or thou doest retire, or leave the world, and that of thine own accord, and then thou hast thy mind: or thy life is cut off; and then mayst thou rejoice that thou hast ended thy charge. One of these must needs be. Be therefore of good comfort.
passages.russian: Либо ты живёшь здесь и уже привык; либо уходишь отсюда, и этого ты и хотел; либо умираешь, и ты отслужил своё. Кроме этого нет ничего. Так будь весел.

passages.greek: Ὀλίγον ἐστὶ τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦτο. ζῆσον ὡς ἐν ὄρει· οὐδὲν γὰρ διαφέρει ἐκεῖ ἢ ὧδε, ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ. ἰδέτωσαν, ἱστορησάτωσαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἄνθρωπον ἀληθινὸν κατὰ φύσιν ζῶντα. εἰ μὴ φέρουσιν, ἀποκτεινάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γὰρ ἢ οὕτως ζῆν.
passages.english: What is left now is little. Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city. Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature. If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.

notes.note: Literally “this that is left”: of life, which the Greek does not say. “Now” stands for “this”.
notes.other_reading: The time you have left is short

notes.note: Translated as it stands. The Greek does not say whether the mountain stands for living apart or for living in full view; the next sentences fit the second, “there or here” fits the first.
notes.other_reading: as if you were away in the hills

notes.greek: ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ
notes.note: The clause has no verb in the Greek as given. “Lives” is supplied from “live” just before; whether a word has dropped out or the verb is simply understood cannot be told from this text. πανταχοῦ (“everywhere”) is taken apart, as “wherever they are”, and τῷ κόσμῳ shares the “in” of “in a city”: the universe treated as one’s city.
notes.other_reading: if a person lives everywhere in the universe as in a city

notes.note: “Inquire into, examine, get to know by looking.”
notes.other_reading: let them look closely at

notes.note: The same word stands twice side by side, so “human beings” and “human being”. ἀληθινός is “true, real, genuine”.
notes.other_reading: let people see a real person

notes.note: Neither verb has an object in the Greek. “It” and “that person” are supplied; “him” is avoided, since ἄνθρωπον does not single out a man.
notes.other_reading: If they do not bear him, let them kill him

notes.note: “Better than to live so.” “So” is open: living as those people live, or living on in the way they would allow. “That way” keeps it open while pointing away from the life according to nature just described.
notes.other_reading: for that is better than living as they do

check.greek: ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ
check.note: The clause has no verb in the Greek as given, and the English supplies “lives”. It cannot be told from the input whether a word has dropped out or the verb is simply understood.
check.decided: Accepted: “lives” is kept, since English needs a verb and “live” has just been said, and the note records that it is supplied and that the Greek as given has none.

check.greek: πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ
check.note: The English reads as “everywhere in the universe”. In the Greek “everywhere” stands apart, and “the universe” shares the “in” of “in a city”: wherever one is, one lives in it as in a city.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city”. This is what makes “there or here” indifferent; “the universe” is kept for κόσμος, as in the glossary.

check.note: οὕτως is “in that way”: most naturally as those people live, or as they would have the true human being live. “Like this” can be taken as that person’s own present life, which reverses the point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “than to live that way”. “That way” points away from the life just described, and the note records that the Greek word is open.

check.note: The Greek is four words with no object and no “can”: if they do not bear him, let them kill him. “Such a person … that person” is heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “If they do not bear it, let them kill that person”. “Cannot” is gone and one of the two supplied objects is lightened; “him” is not used, because the Greek word is “human being” and does not single out a man.

check.note: “This that remains is little” is stiff word order in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “What is left now is little”. “Now” stands for the Greek “this”, as the note says.

passages.casaubon: So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here, or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for the place. Let them behold and see a man, that is a man indeed, living according to the true nature of man. If they cannot bear with me, let them kill me. For better were it to die, than so to live as they would have thee.
passages.russian: Остаётся теперь немного. Живи как на горе. Ведь нет никакой разницы, там или здесь, если человек, где бы он ни был, живёт в мироздании как в городе. Пусть люди увидят, пусть изучат истинного человека, живущего согласно природе. Если они его не выносят, пусть убьют. Ведь это лучше, чем так жить.

passages.greek: Τοῦτο ἔχει ἡ τελειότης τοῦ ἤθους, τὸ πᾶσαν ἡμέραν ὡς τελευταίαν διεξάγειν καὶ μήτε σφύζειν μήτε ναρκᾶν μήτε ὑποκρίνεσθαι.
passages.english: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb nor to play a part.

notes.greek: Τοῦτο ἔχει ἡ τελειότης τοῦ ἤθους
notes.note: Literally “perfection of character has this”, that is, this belongs to it. τελειότης (“perfection, completeness”) and τελευταίαν (“last”) share one root; the English does not show it.
notes.other_reading: Perfection of character consists in this

notes.note: Literally “to throb”, as a pulse does in a fever: feverish agitation, set against numbness.
notes.other_reading: to throb

notes.note: “To grow numb or torpid.”
notes.other_reading: to be sluggish

notes.note: The verb for acting a part on the stage, and so for pretending. It is the verb of ὑπόκρισις, “pretence”, in 9.2.
notes.other_reading: to pretend

check.note: Literally the throbbing of a pulse, here feverish agitation, set against torpor. “Neither to throb” is not clear English for a state of mind.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “neither to be feverish nor to go numb nor to play a part”. “Feverish” is clear and still a picture from the body; the three matching “neither … nor” of the Greek are kept, where the suggestion would make two and one.

passages.casaubon: Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day: never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
passages.russian: Совершенство нрава в том, чтобы проживать каждый день как последний, не впадать в лихорадку, не цепенеть и не играть роли.

passages.greek: Οὔτε τραγῳδὸς οὔτε πόρνη. Ὡς ἐξελθὼν ζῆν διανοῇ, οὕτως ἐνταῦθα ζῆν ἔξεστιν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐπιτρέπωσι, τότε καὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἔξιθι, οὕτως μέντοι ὡς μηδὲν κακὸν πάσχων. καπνὸς καὶ ἀπέρχομαι· τί αὐτὸ πρᾶγμα δοκεῖς; μέχρι δέ με τοιοῦτον οὐδὲν ἐξάγει, μένω ἐλεύθερος καὶ οὐδείς με κωλύσει ποιεῖν ἃ θέλω· θέλω δὲ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ ζῴου.
passages.english:
Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute.

As you have in mind to live once you have gone out, so you can live here. But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well, yet as one who is suffering nothing bad. There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much? But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want. And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living being.

notes.note: The last words of chapter 28, with no verb. The part of the chapter not given ends by saying that a person can be shown their fault without anger, so the words seem to set aside two manners, the stage performer’s and the prostitute’s. They are translated word for word, since the Greek does not say whether “be” or “there is need of” is to be understood.
notes.other_reading: Be neither a ranter nor a flatterer

notes.note: διανοῇ is “you have in mind, you intend”. ἐξελθών is “having gone out”, and the Greek does not say out of what. It is taken as leaving this place, because “go out of life as well” follows.
notes.other_reading: As you intend to live when you have departed

notes.note: “They” are not named: the people around him.
notes.other_reading: but if people will not let you

notes.note: The same “go out” as ἐξελθών above, and ἐξάγει below is “leads out”; “out” is kept in all three. ἐξαγωγή, “leading out”, is the Stoic word for a reasoned leaving of life.
notes.other_reading: then depart from life too

notes.note: Literally “smoke, and I go away”: the Greek leaves “there is” to be understood. From memory, unchecked, this is the image of the smoky room found in Epictetus: if the room smokes too much, one leaves it.
notes.other_reading: The room is full of smoke and I leave it

notes.note: πρᾶγμα here is “a matter of weight, a trouble”, which “anything much” gives. The words could also be read as a question about what the thing is.
notes.other_reading: What do you think the thing itself is?

notes.note: μένω answers “leads me out”, so “I stay”, with “free” added to it. It could also be read as one phrase, “I remain free”.
notes.other_reading: I remain free

notes.greek: θέλω δὲ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ ζῴου
notes.note: The Greek repeats “I want” and gives it no object: “and I want in accordance with the nature of the rational and social living being”. “What accords with” supplies the object.
notes.other_reading: and my wanting follows the nature of a rational and social animal

check.note: The Greek repeats the verb: “and I want what accords with the nature …”. The English turns a statement of what the speaker wills into a claim about his wants, and the repeated verb is the hinge.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living creature”. The Greek says “I want” twice running, and the second now answers the first in the same words.

check.note: Can be “I stay, and am free” or simply “I remain free”. The comma chooses the first, and “man” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “I stay, free”. “Man” is not in the Greek; “stay” is kept because the verb answers “leads me out”, and the note gives the other reading.

check.note: The verb here is to take or drive out, as the smoke does. “Leads” suggests guidance.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek verb is literally “leads out”, the verb behind the Stoic term for a reasoned leaving of life, and it is the third “out” in a row with “gone out” and “go out”. “Drives” would say more force than the Greek has.

check.note: “Great” is not in the Greek; the noun on its own carries “a thing of consequence”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Why do you think it anything much?”. This gives the idiom without an adjective the Greek does not have.

check.note: “Smoke, and I go away” is as bare as the Greek, but a reader may not see that it is a picture: the room is smoky, so I leave.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “There is smoke, and I leave”. Greek regularly leaves “there is” unsaid, so the words are a translation and not an addition, and the picture is easier to see.

part.left_out: Τῷ γράσωνι μήτι ὀργίζῃ, μήτι τῷ ὀζοστόμῳ ὀργίζῃ; τί σοι ποιήσει; τοιοῦτον στόμα ἔχει, τοιαύτας μάλας ἔχει, ἀνάγκη τοιαύτην ἀποφορὰν ἀπὸ τοιούτων γίνεσθαι. —ἀλλ’ ὁ ἄνθρωπος λόγον ἔχει, φησί, καὶ δύναται συννοεῖν ἐφιστάνων τί πλημμελεῖ.—εὖ σοι γένοιτο· τοιγαροῦν καὶ σὺ λόγον ἔχεις, κίνησον λογικῇ διαθέσει λογικὴν διάθεσιν, δεῖξον, ὑπόμνησον· εἰ γὰρ ἐπαίει, θεραπεύσεις καὶ οὐ χρεία ὀργῆς.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 5.22 before the last four words of chapter 5.28 and opens its section 5.23 with them, joined to chapter 5.29.

passages.casaubon: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged. Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable creature, regulated and directed.
passages.russian:
Ни трагический актёр, ни проститутка.

Как ты собираешься жить, когда уйдёшь, так можешь жить и здесь. А если не дают, тогда уходи и из жизни, но так, как тот, кто не претерпевает ничего дурного. Дым — и я ухожу. Почему ты считаешь это чем-то значительным? Но пока ничто подобное меня не выводит, я остаюсь, свободный, и никто не помешает мне делать то, чего я хочу. А хочу я того, что согласно с природой разумного и общественного живого существа.

passages.greek: Μὴ διαφέρου πότερον ῥιγῶν ἢ θαλπόμενος τὸ πρέπον ποιεῖς, καὶ πότερον νυστάζων ἢ ἱκανῶς ὕπνου ἔχων, καὶ πότερον κακῶς ἀκούων ἢ εὐφημούμενος, καὶ πότερον ἀποθνῄσκων ἢ πράττων τι ἀλλοῖον· μία γὰρ τῶν βιωτικῶν πράξεων καὶ αὕτη ἐστί, καθ’ ἣν ἀποθνῄσκομεν· ἀρκεῖ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτης τὸ παρὸν εὖ θέσθαι.
passages.english: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting while shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act. For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die. So in this too it is enough to manage well what is at hand.

notes.note: The middle form: “do not let it make a difference to you”.
notes.other_reading: Do not care

notes.note: τὸ πρέπον is “what is fitting, what is proper”. “You do” is the one verb for all four pairs, so the English puts it first and lets the later pairs lean on it.
notes.other_reading: whether you are shivering or warm when you do your duty

notes.note: The idiom is literally “hearing badly”, that is, being ill spoken of. εὐφημούμενος is “being spoken well of”.
notes.other_reading: whether you are blamed or well spoken of

notes.note: Literally “doing something of another kind”. “Act” is put in because the next clause takes the verb up with πράξεων, “acts”, and the reason given depends on that link.
notes.other_reading: doing something else

notes.greek: μία γὰρ τῶν βιωτικῶν πράξεων καὶ αὕτη ἐστί, καθ’ ἣν ἀποθνῄσκομεν
notes.note: βιωτικαὶ πράξεις are the acts that belong to living. Dying is counted as one of them, and the verb turns from the second person to the first person plural.
notes.other_reading: for the act by which we die is itself one of the tasks of life

notes.note: Literally “to place well what is present”, an idiom for handling a thing well. τὸ παρόν can be the present moment or the thing in front of you.
notes.other_reading: to make good use of the present

check.note: “You do what is fitting” is the one main verb for all four pairs. Placed after the first pair, the English ties it to shivering or warm only, and the later pairs read as loose states.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whether you do what is fitting shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act”. The verb comes first and every pair hangs on it, with the repeated “and whether” of the Greek kept.

check.note: “Doing” is picked up by “acts” in the next clause, and the reason given depends on it: dying is itself one of the acts of life. “Doing something else” and “acts” lose the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “dying or doing some other kind of act. For this too is one of the acts of life”. “Act” now stands in both clauses, so the reason can be seen to follow.

passages.casaubon: Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties and actions of our lives.
passages.russian: Пусть тебе будет всё равно, делаешь ли ты должное, дрожа или в тепле, сонным или выспавшись, когда о тебе говорят дурно или когда хвалят, умирая или совершая какое-то другое действие. Ведь и это одно из действий жизни — то, в котором мы умираем. Значит, и здесь довольно того, чтобы хорошо распорядиться тем, что под рукой.

passages.greek: Φαντάζου πάντα τὸν ἐφ’ ᾡτινιοῦν λυπούμενον ἢ δυσαρεστοῦντα ὅμοιον τῷ θυομένῳ χοιριδίῳ καὶ ἀπολακτίζοντι καὶ κεκραγότι· ὅμοιος καὶ ὁ οἰμώζων ἐπὶ τοῦ κλινιδίου μόνος σιωπῇ. τὴν ἔνδεσιν ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι μόνῳ τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ δέδοται τὸ ἑκουσίως ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γινομένοις, τὸ δὲ ἕπεσθαι ψιλὸν πᾶσιν ἀναγκαῖον.
passages.english: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence. Picture also how we are bound, and that to the rational living being alone it has been given to follow willingly what happens, while simply to follow is a necessity for all.

notes.note: The verb of φαντασία, “impression”: “form the impression of, picture to yourself”.
notes.other_reading: Form an impression of

notes.note: λυπούμενον is “pained, grieved”; δυσαρεστοῦντα is “displeased, discontented”.
notes.other_reading: grieved or discontented

notes.greek: ὁ οἰμώζων ἐπὶ τοῦ κλινιδίου μόνος σιωπῇ
notes.note: οἰμώζω is to cry out in grief, to lament, yet σιωπῇ is “in silence”: a lament kept inside, set beside the squealing of the piglet. “Laments” lets both words stand. κλινίδιον is a small bed or couch, a diminutive like χοιρίδιον, “piglet”.
notes.other_reading: the one who wails on a couch, alone and without a sound

notes.note: An accusative with no verb in the Greek as given, so the sentence does not construe as it stands. “Picture also” is supplied, carried over from the opening, and “how we are bound” stands for the noun ἔνδεσις, a binding or fastening-in: being tied to what happens. If the full stop before these words were taken away, they could be the object of “laments”.
notes.other_reading: Like it too is the one who, on a little bed, alone, in silence, laments our binding

notes.greek: μόνῳ τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ δέδοται τὸ ἑκουσίως ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γινομένοις
notes.note: ἕπεσθαι is “to follow”, the same word as “to follow god” in 10.11, and ἑκουσίως (“willingly”) goes with it. τοῖς γινομένοις is “the things that come about”.
notes.other_reading: only the rational animal has been granted to go along with events of its own will

notes.note: ψιλόν is “bare”: following by itself, without the willingness.
notes.other_reading: but bare following

check.note: The accusative has no verb in the Greek as given: after the full stop the sentence starts with “our binding, and that …”. “Picture also” is supplied, and the English should not smooth this over silently.
check.decided: Accepted: “Picture also” is kept, since the accusative needs a verb and “picture” is the verb the passage opens with, and the note now says that the Greek as given does not construe and that the words are supplied. The note also gives the reading that opens up if the full stop is removed.

check.note: With “alone, in silence” the verb is lamenting, not crying aloud. “Wails … in silence” contradicts itself in English, where the Greek contrasts the squealing piglet with the silent mourner.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence”. “Laments” can be silent, so the clash is gone; it is kept in place of “grieves” because the Greek verb is a word for a cry of grief, not for the feeling alone.

check.note: “Willingly” goes with “follow”. In the English it can attach to “happens”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to follow willingly what happens”. The adverb stands next to its verb, as in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: As a pig that cries and flings when his throat is cut, fancy to thyself every one to be, that grieves for any worldly thing and takes on. Such a one is he also, who upon his bed alone, doth bewail the miseries of this our mortal life. And remember this, that Unto reasonable creatures only it is granted that they may willingly and freely submit unto Providence: but absolutely to submit, is a necessity imposed upon all creatures equally.
passages.russian: Представляй себе всякого, кто огорчается или недоволен чем бы то ни было, подобным поросёнку, которого приносят в жертву, а он брыкается и визжит. Подобен ему и тот, кто плачется на своей постельке, один, молча. Представляй себе и то, как мы связаны, и что одному лишь разумному живому существу дано добровольно следовать за происходящим, а просто следовать — необходимость для всех.

passages.greek: Ἡλίκην ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἄνθρωπος μὴ ποιεῖν ἄλλο ἢ ὅπερ μέλλει ὁ θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν, καὶ δέχεσθαι πᾶν ὃν νέμῃ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός.
passages.english: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise, and to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is.

notes.note: An exclamation. ἐξουσία is the power to do a thing in the sense that it lies with one to do it, and ranges over freedom to act and authority. The English reads “power”, as in “it is in a person’s power”.
notes.other_reading: What freedom a human being has

notes.note: No article: any human being. The English reads “a human being” and “them” so as not to single out a man.
notes.other_reading: a man … to him

notes.note: μέλλει with the infinitive is “is going to” or “is sure to”, and ἐπαινεῖν is “praise” and also “approve”. The English keeps the plainer future and “praise”.
notes.other_reading: what god will approve

notes.note: The verb is “receive” or “accept”, and can be as warm as “welcome”. The English reads “accept”, as for δέχομαι in 8.23 in this section.
notes.other_reading: to welcome

notes.note: As given, ὃν (“whom”) does not construe with the neuter πᾶν or with the subjunctive. It is read as a slip of the digitised copy for ὃ ἂν νέμῃ, “whatever he assigns” (from memory, unchecked, that the edition prints ὃ ἂν). “Whatever it is” gives the indefinite force of that reading.
notes.other_reading: everything that god assigns to them

check.note: As given, ὃν cannot agree with the neuter πᾶν and the subjunctive has no ἄν; the sense requires ὃ ἂν νέμῃ. “That god assigns” is flatter than the indefinite “whatever god may assign”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is”. The Greek, read as ὃ ἂν νέμῃ, is an indefinite “whatever”, and the added words give that force without dropping “everything”.

check.note: ἐξουσία is the liberty or authority to do something, not strength or capability, and “power” can be read as ability. “How great a freedom” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “power” stands. ἐξουσία with an infinitive is the power to do a thing in the sense that it lies with one to do it, which English also calls power (“it is in your power”). “Freedom” narrows the word to one side of its range and is given in the note.

check.note: μέλλει can be a plain future or “is likely to”, and ἐπαινεῖν can be “approve” as well as “praise”. The English is defensible; the other reading is “what god will approve”.
check.decided: Declined: “is going to praise” stands. It gives the first sense of both Greek words, and the other reading is recorded in the note.

part.left_out: τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ φύσει.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 12.8 before the chapter's last three words and begins its section 12.9 with them.

passages.casaubon: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
passages.russian: Какая великая власть у человека: не делать ничего иного, кроме того, что похвалит бог, и принимать всё, что бог ему уделит, каково бы оно ни было.

passages.greek: Ἆρόν με καὶ βάλε, ὅπου θέλεις. κἀκεῖ γὰρ ἕξω τὸν ἐμὸν δαίμονα ἵλεων, τουτέστιν, ἀρκούμενον, εἰ ἔχοι καὶ ἐνεργοίη κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ.
passages.english: Pick me up and throw me wherever you want. For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious, that is, content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up.

notes.note: The Greek does not say who is addressed (fortune, a god, anyone at all). “You” is left unexplained.
notes.other_reading: Lift me up and cast me

notes.note: δαίμων is the divine being that each person has within, which Marcus elsewhere treats as one’s own mind and reason. The Greek has only the possessive, “the daimon that is mine”. The English reads “the divinity within me” because “spirit” with a possessive would be heard today as a mood.
notes.other_reading: the daimon that is mine; the guardian spirit that is mine

notes.note: ἵλεως is the word for a god who is favourable, and of a person it means kindly or cheerful. The English reads “gracious”, the word used of a god. Marcus glosses it himself in the next words.
notes.other_reading: well disposed; cheerful; serene

notes.note: The clause with εἰ can state what the divinity is content with (content if it is and acts so), or a condition on the whole promise (it will be gracious, provided it is and acts so). The English takes the first and so leaves out the comma that the edition has before εἰ.
notes.other_reading: that is, content, provided that the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up

notes.note: ἔχοι is read as intransitive, “is in a certain state”, sharing the phrase κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς with ἐνεργοίη. “The state it is in” and “the way it acts” stand for the two Greek verbs. ἔχοι could also be taken as “holds” with an object left unsaid.
notes.other_reading: if it holds its ground and acts

notes.greek: κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ
notes.note: Literally “according to what comes next in order after its own make-up”, that is, what follows from the way it is made. κατασκευή is the make or build of a thing.
notes.other_reading: in keeping with its own constitution

check.note: δαίμων here is the divinity lodged in the person, not a mood, and “spirit well disposed” reads today as being in good spirits. “Own” also adds a little to the plain possessive.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the divinity within me”. The Greek word names a divine being that a person has within, and “within me” carries the plain possessive without “own”.

check.note: ἵλεως is the word for a god who is gracious or propitious, and also “cheerful, serene”. “Well disposed” leaves open towards what.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “gracious”, the word English uses of a god who is favourable, which suits “the divinity within me”. The gloss that Marcus adds, “that is, content”, follows at once and gives the other side of the word.

check.greek: εἰ ἔχοι καὶ ἐνεργοίη κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ
check.note: The sense is right, but “in the state, and acts in the way, that follows from” is hard to read, and “the state” and “the way” are supplied nouns. “If its condition and its activity are in keeping with the way it is built” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause now reads “content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up”, one plain clause without the double insertion. “Follow from” is kept because the Greek says “what comes next in order after”, which “in keeping with” would flatten. The two nouns still stand for the two Greek verbs, as the note says.

check.note: κατασκευή is how a thing is made or equipped. “Constitution” is correct but bookish and can be misheard as a political word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “its own make-up”, the plain word for the way a thing is built.

part.left_out: Ἆρα τοῦτο ἄξιον, ἵνα δι’ αὐτὸ κακῶς μοι ἔχῃ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ χείρων ἑαυτῆς ᾖ, ταπεινουμένη, ὀρεγομένη, συνδυομένη, πτυρομένη; καὶ τί εὑρήσεις τούτου ἄξιον;
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.43 here and makes the rest of the chapter its section 8.44.

passages.casaubon: Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.
passages.russian: Возьми меня и брось куда хочешь. Ведь и там божество во мне будет благосклонным, то есть довольным, если его состояние и то, как оно действует, следуют из его собственного устройства.

passages.greek: Ἀρκεῖ ἡ παροῦσα ὑπόληψις καταληπτικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα πρᾶξις κοινωνικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα διάθεσις εὐαρεστικὴ πρὸς πᾶν τὸ παρὰ τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας συμβαῖνον.
passages.english: It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there, that the present action should be social, and that the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause.

notes.note: The Greek has no “that” or “if”: three nouns, each with an adjective as predicate, are the subject of “is enough”. “That … should” is used so as neither to assert that the three are already so nor to add a bare “if”.
notes.other_reading: It is enough if the present judgment has a firm grasp of what is there, the present action is social, and the present disposition is well pleased

notes.note: Said three times: the one that is here now. “The present” is kept each time, and “your”, which the Greek does not have, is not added.
notes.other_reading: your judgment at this moment

notes.note: A Stoic term, from the word for a grasp: said of an impression or judgment that takes hold of the thing as it really is, and so is sure. “Firm” gives the sureness, and “of what is there” is added to complete the English.
notes.other_reading: a present judgment that is certain; a present judgment that grasps its object

notes.note: κοινωνικός is “social” throughout this translation: directed to the community of human beings, done for the common good. It does not mean sociable.
notes.other_reading: the present action be for the common good

notes.note: An adjective for a settled readiness to be pleased with something. The English must choose how warm it is, and reads “well pleased with”.
notes.other_reading: content with; ready to accept

notes.note: Singular with the article: the one cause that lies outside, as against what one causes oneself. It is kept singular, and “you” is not added.
notes.other_reading: from external causes; from a cause outside you

check.note: κοινωνικός means directed to the community, done for the common good. “Social” today suggests sociable, so “the present action be social” is unclear.
check.decided: Declined: “social” stands. It is the one English word this translation uses for κοινωνικός wherever it occurs, so that a reader can follow the term from passage to passage, and nothing in this passage’s argument needs another. A note now says what the word means.

check.note: The Stoic term says the judgment takes hold securely of what is really there. “Grasp its object” supplies “its object” and drops the note of certainty.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “should have a firm grasp of what is there”. “Firm” gives the sureness that the term carries, and “what is there” replaces the bookish “its object”. A verb is kept so that the three clauses run alike.

check.note: “The cause outside” is not natural English and leaves the reader asking outside what. The Greek is the external cause, the cause outside oneself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the external cause”, still singular and with “the”, as in the Greek.

check.note: Across the section, συμβαίνω is “comes about” here but “is happening” in 8.23, where “comes about” is used for γινόμενα. A reader comparing the two loses which Greek word is which.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “everything that happens from the external cause”. In this section “happens” is now always συμβαίνω and “comes about” always γίνομαι.

passages.casaubon: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
passages.russian: Достаточно того, чтобы нынешнее суждение твёрдо схватывало то, что есть, нынешнее действие было общественным, а нынешнее расположение было вполне довольно всем, что происходит от внешней причины.

passages.greek: Τῇ πάντα διδούσῃ καὶ ἀπολαμβανούσῃ φύσει ὁ πεπαιδευμένος καὶ αἰδήμων λέγει· δὸς ὃ θέλεις· ἀπόλαβε ὃ θέλεις. λέγει δὲ τοῦτο οὐ καταθρασυνόμενος, ἀλλὰ πειθαρχῶν μόνον καὶ εὐνοῶν αὐτῇ.
passages.english: To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back, the person who is educated and modest says: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.” And that person says this not in bold defiance, but only in obedience to it and good will towards it.

notes.note: One article, so one person with both qualities. πεπαιδευμένος is the ordinary word for “educated”, and also “trained”. αἰδήμων is having a sense of shame and respect; “modest” is taken because the next sentence sets this person against over-boldness.
notes.other_reading: the person who has been trained and is respectful

notes.note: ἀπολαμβάνω is to take back or receive back what one is owed, as a lender does. The same verb returns in ἀπόλαβε, so “take back” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: which gives all things and receives them again

notes.note: θέλεις is “want”, “wish” or “will”. “Want” is kept, as for ὅπου θέλεις in 8.45a in this section.
notes.other_reading: Give what you will; take back what you will

notes.note: A rare verb built on the word for over-boldness, with a prefix that means “against”: making oneself bold against someone. It can be resistance or mere show. The English reads “bold defiance”, which the sentence sets against obeying; no object is expressed.
notes.other_reading: not out of bravado; not as a show of boldness

notes.note: μόνον stands after “obeying” and can limit that word alone or both participles, or mean “simply”. The English keeps “only” and puts it before both.
notes.other_reading: but simply obeying it, and with good will towards it

notes.note: εὐνοέω is to be well disposed or loyal to someone. αὐτῇ is nature, a feminine noun in Greek, and goes with both participles. “It” is written because “her” would add a personification the grammar alone does not require, though nature is here spoken to as “you”.
notes.other_reading: obeying her and loyal to her

check.note: εὐνοέω is to be well disposed, loyal, of good will towards someone. “Wishing it well” says something slightly different, as if nature needed good wishes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “good will toward it”. The Greek verb is about the speaker’s attitude to nature, not a wish for nature’s welfare.

check.note: The verb is built on θράσος: being over-bold, putting on a show of boldness against someone. “Defiance” takes it as resistance; the other reading is bravado.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not in bold defiance”. “Bold” brings in the over-boldness the verb is built on, and “defiance” is kept because the verb’s prefix means “against” and the sentence sets it against obeying. “Bravado” is given in the note.

check.note: αἰδήμων is having a sense of shame, respect, reverence. “Modest” today suggests unassuming; “respectful” is the other reading and fits the second sentence better.
check.decided: Declined: “modest” stands. αἰδώς, the quality the word names, is in Greek the standing opposite of the over-boldness that the next sentence denies, and “modest” keeps that contrast. “Respectful” is given in the note.

check.note: The perfect participle is “one who has been trained, formed”, here by philosophy. “Educated” today suggests schooling or degrees.
check.decided: Declined: “educated” stands. πεπαιδευμένος is the ordinary Greek word for an educated person and does not itself say by what, and “properly taught” would add “properly”, which the Greek does not have. “Trained” is given in the note.

check.note: μόνον stands after πειθαρχῶν and may limit that word alone or both participles. “But only obeying it” can also be misread as “obeying nothing but it”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “but only in obedience to it and good will toward it”. “Only” is kept, since the Greek has it, and the new wording cannot be heard as “obeying nothing but it”. “Simply” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but in mere love, and humble submission.
passages.russian: Природе, которая всё даёт и всё забирает обратно, образованный и скромный человек говорит: «Дай, что хочешь. Забери, что хочешь». И говорит он это не с дерзким вызовом, а лишь из послушания ей и доброй воли к ней.

passages.greek: Πράσσω τι; πράσσω ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπων εὐποιίαν ἀναφέρων. συμβαίνει τί μοι; δέχομαι ἐπὶ τοὺς θεοὺς ἀναφέρων καὶ τὴν πάντων πηγήν, ἀφ’ ἧς πάντα τὰ γινόμενα συμμηρύεται.
passages.english: Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings. Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.

notes.note: εὐποιία is the doing of good, a kindness done, with ἀνθρώπων as those to whom the good is done. The English keeps the stress on the doing.
notes.other_reading: the benefit of human beings

notes.note: Used twice: first of carrying an action to its aim, then of carrying an event back to its origin. “Referring it to” is kept in both places so that the pairing shows.
notes.other_reading: with the doing of good to human beings as the aim … tracing it back to the gods

notes.note: τί has an accent only because the enclitic μοι follows; it is the indefinite “something”, parallel to Πράσσω τι. Read as the interrogative it would be a different question.
notes.other_reading: What happens to me?

notes.note: πηγή is a spring of water, and the English keeps the picture. πάντων can be “of all things” or “of all”; and the καί before it may add a second thing to the gods or explain them.
notes.other_reading: the gods, that is, the source of everything

notes.note: A rare verb from μηρύομαι, to wind thread or yarn; with συν-, “wound together”. The picture is of all events as thread drawn from one place and wound into one. The bare verb is kept, with no “like thread” added, and “spun” is not used because spinning is another word in Greek.
notes.other_reading: from which everything that comes about is spun out together

check.note: εὐποιία is the act of doing good, not the good received. “The benefit of human beings” shifts from what one does to what they get.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “referring it to the doing of good to human beings”, which keeps the stress on the doing, as the Greek word does.

check.note: πηγή is a spring of water. “Source” is right but loses the picture.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the spring of all things”. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a spring of water, and the image is kept as an image.

check.note: μηρύομαι is to draw out or wind thread, and with “from which” the picture is of events drawn out together from one source. “Wound from” does not quite work in English; “spun out together” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “is wound together” stands. The Greek verb is of winding yarn, not of spinning, for which Greek has another word, so “spun” would change the picture. The note explains the image.

passages.casaubon: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
passages.russian: Делаю ли я что-нибудь? Делаю, относя это к тому, чтобы делать людям добро. Случается ли что-нибудь со мной? Принимаю, относя это к богам и к источнику всего, из которого сплетается всё происходящее.

passages.greek: ὁπουδήποτε καταληφθείς, εὔμοιρος ἄνθρωπος· τὸ δὲ εὔμοιρος, ἀγαθὴν μοῖραν σεαυτῷ ἀπονείμας· ἀγαθαὶ δὲ μοῖραι ἀγαθαὶ τροπαὶ ψυχῆς, ἀγαθαὶ ὁρμαί, ἀγαθαὶ πράξεις.
passages.english: … wherever caught, a person whose lot is good. And “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot; and good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions.

notes.note: The passage begins in the middle of a sentence and has no finite verb: the 1634 division puts the opening words of the sentence, “Once I was”, at the end of the section before. Nothing is supplied here, and the three dots mark the cut. καταληφθείς is “caught”, “overtaken” or “found”, and the Greek does not say by what.
notes.other_reading: wherever overtaken; in whatever place found

notes.note: εὔμοιρος ordinarily means “fortunate”, but it is built on μοῖρα, a share or lot, and the next two clauses argue from that. The English reads “whose lot is good” so that “lot” can be repeated.
notes.other_reading: a fortunate person

notes.note: The article quotes the word just used and there is no verb; “means” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: And “fortunate” is: having assigned a good fortune to yourself

notes.note: Second person: “to yourself”, with the participle in the nominative. ἀπονέμω is “assign” or “deal out” and is not formed from μοῖρα, so the English does not echo “lot” in it.
notes.other_reading: having dealt yourself a good portion

notes.note: τροπαί are turns or changes of direction, and ψυχῆς has no article. “Turnings” is written because “good turns” in English means favours.
notes.other_reading: good dispositions of the soul; good changes of the soul

notes.note: ὁρμή, “impulse”: the movement of the soul towards an action, the Stoic term.
notes.other_reading: good strivings

check.note: The Greek as given has no verb because the cut falls in mid-sentence, and the English is a verbless fragment too. A reader cannot tell who is spoken of or in what tense; the fragment should be marked as the end of a sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins with three dots and a small letter, “… wherever caught, a person whose lot is good.” Nothing is supplied, and the note says where the opening words of the sentence stand.

check.note: καταλαμβάνω in the passive is “caught, come upon, overtaken” by events. “Wherever overtaken” with no agent is unclear and might be read as “left behind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wherever caught”, the plainest sense of the verb, with the agent left unsaid as in the Greek.

check.note: “Allotted yourself a good lot” makes a word-echo that is not in the Greek: the echo there is εὔμοιρος, μοῖραν, μοῖραι only, and ἀπονέμω is a different word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “having assigned yourself a good lot”, so that only the three Greek words that share a root share “lot”. It also matches “assigns” for the simple verb in 12.11a.

check.note: τροπαί are turns: changes of direction, hence inclinations or movements of the soul. “Turnings” is literal and odd; “good turns of the soul” is suggested, and the Greek has no article.
check.decided: Declined: “good turnings of the soul” stands. τροπαί are changes of direction, which “turnings” says, while “good turns” is heard in English as favours done. The missing article is recorded in the note.

part.left_out: Μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς τῇ φαντασίᾳ συναρπάζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ βοηθεῖν μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα ἐλαττῶνται, μὴ μέντοι βλάβην αὐτὸ φαντάζεσθαι· κακὸν γὰρ ἔθος. ἀλλ’ ὡς ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει, μεμνημένος ὅτι ῥόμβος, οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὧδε. ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων. ἄνθρωπε, ἐπελάθου τί ταῦτα ἦν;—ναί· ἀλλὰ τούτοις περισπούδαστα.—διὰ τοῦτ’ οὖν καὶ σὺ μωρὸς γένῃ; Ἐγενόμην ποτέ,
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 5.29 with the words 'Once I was' (Ἐγενόμην ποτέ) and begins its section 5.30 with the words that follow them.

passages.casaubon: Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless. For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
passages.russian: …где бы ни был застигнут, человек с доброй долей. А «с доброй долей» — значит назначивший себе добрую долю; а добрые доли — это добрые повороты души, добрые побуждения, добрые поступки.

passages.greek: Ὡς εὔκολον ἀπώσασθαι καὶ ἀπαλεῖψαι πᾶσαν φαντασίαν τὴν ὀχληρὰν ἢ ἀνοίκειον καὶ εὐθὺς ἐν πάσῃ γαλήνῃ εἶναι.
passages.english: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.

notes.note: To wipe out or rub out, as writing from a tablet or a mark from a surface. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: to erase

notes.note: φαντασία, “impression”: what presents itself to the mind, the Stoic term.
notes.other_reading: every thought; every appearance

notes.note: ὀχληρός is troublesome, pressing in on one. ἀνοίκειος is not one’s own, foreign, and also unfitting. “Out of place” is taken as the English that says “does not belong here”.
notes.other_reading: every impression that is disturbing or alien

notes.note: γαλήνη is the stillness of the sea, and “a calm” is meant to keep that. πάσῃ is “all”, here “complete”; it answers πᾶσαν, “every”, earlier in the sentence, an echo the English does not keep.
notes.other_reading: in all calm; in perfect stillness

check.note: ἀνοίκειος is “not one’s own, alien” as well as “unfitting”. “Out of place” takes the second sense.
check.decided: Declined: “out of place” stands. It says of an impression that it does not belong where it is, which covers both sides of the Greek word. “Alien” is given in the note.

check.note: ἀπαλείφω is to wipe out, erase, as writing from a tablet. “Wipe off” suggests cleaning a surface of dirt.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wipe out”, which is said of a mark or of writing and so suits an impression.

check.note: πᾶσαν and πάσῃ answer each other in the Greek (every impression, all calm), and “every” and “complete” lose the echo. γαλήνη is the stillness of the sea, which “a complete calm” only half keeps.
check.decided: Declined: “in a complete calm” stands. “Complete” gives the full force of πάσῃ, “in all calm” is not English as it is written today, and “a calm” is the English word for stillness at sea. The echo is recorded in the note.

passages.casaubon: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!

nearest.title: My judgment is up to me

passages.russian: Как легко оттолкнуть и стереть всякое докучное или неуместное представление — и тотчас оказаться в полном покое.

passages.greek: Ἀτύφως μὲν λαβεῖν, εὐλύτως δὲ ἀφεῖναι.
passages.english: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.

notes.note: Without τῦφος: literally smoke, and so conceit, a head puffed up. The English reads “without conceit”.
notes.other_reading: without vanity; without arrogance

notes.note: The two infinitives stand alone. They can be a maxim (“to take”) or commands to oneself. No object is expressed: what is taken and let go is left open, and λαβεῖν covers both “take” and “receive”, as “take” does in English.
notes.other_reading: Receive without conceit; let go readily.

notes.note: From a word for what is easily untied or loosened: with no knot to work at, and so without clinging. The English reads “readily”.
notes.other_reading: with ease; with a loose hand

check.note: εὔλυτος is “easily loosed”: the point is letting go readily, without clinging. “With ease” can be read as “without effort”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to let go readily”. The Greek word is about how easily the hold comes loose, not about the effort of the one who lets go.

check.note: λαβεῖν is “receive” as much as “take”. Paired with ἀφεῖναι and ἀτύφως, “receive” is the likelier sense; “take” suggests reaching for a thing.
check.decided: Declined: “take” stands. λαβεῖν covers taking and receiving alike, and English “take” does the same (one takes what is given), so the wider word matches the Greek. “Receive” is given in the note.

passages.casaubon: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.
passages.russian: Брать без самомнения и легко отпускать.

passages.greek: Τοῖς μέρεσι τοῦ ὅλου, ὅσα φύσει περιέχεται ὑπὸ τοῦ κόσμου, ἀνάγκη φθείρεσθαι· λεγέσθω δὲ τοῦτο σημαντικῶς τοῦ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι. εἰ δὲ φύσει κακόν τε καὶ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τοῦτο αὐτοῖς, οὐκ ἂν τὸ ὅλον καλῶς διεξάγοιτο τῶν μερῶν εἰς ἀλλοίωσιν ἰόντων καὶ πρὸς τὸ φθείρεσθαι διαφόρως κατεσκευασμένων. πότερον γὰρ ἐπεχείρησεν ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ τὰ ἑαυτῆς μέρη κακοῦν καὶ περιπτωτικὰ τῷ κακῷ καὶ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἔμπτωτα εἰς τὸ κακὸν ποιεῖν, ἢ ἔλαθεν αὐτὴν τοιάδε τινὰ γινόμενα; ἀμφότερα γὰρ ἀπίθανα. εἰ δέ τις καὶ ἀφέμενος τῆς φύσεως κατὰ τὸ πεφυκέναι ταῦτα ἐξηγοῖτο, καὶ ὣς γελοῖον ἅμα μὲν φάναι πεφυκέναι τὰ μέρη τοῦ ὅλου μεταβάλλειν, ἅμα δὲ ὡς ἐπί τινι τῶν παρὰ φύσιν συμβαίνοντι θαυμάζειν ἣ δυσχεραίνειν, ἄλλως τε καὶ τῆς διαλύσεως εἰς ταῦτα γινομένης, ἐξ ὧν ἕκαστον συνίσταται. ἤτοι γὰρ σκεδασμὸς στοιχείων, ἐξ ὧν συνεκρίθη, ἢ τροπὴ τοῦ μὲν στερεμνίου εἰς τὸ γεῶδες, τοῦ δὲ πνευματικοῦ εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες, ὥστε καὶ ταῦτα ἀναληφθῆναι εἰς τὸν τοῦ ὅλου λόγον, εἴτε κατὰ περίοδον ἐκπυρουμένου εἴτε ἀιδίοις ἀμοιβαῖς ἀνανεουμένου. καὶ τὸ στερέμνιον δὲ καὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν μὴ φαντάζου τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης γενέσεως· πᾶν γὰρ τοῦτο ἐχθὲς καὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν ἐκ τῶν σιτίων καὶ τοῦ ἑλκομένου ἀέρος τὴν ἐπιρροὴν ἔλαβεν· τοῦτο οὖν ὃ ἔλαβε μεταβάλλει, οὐχ ὃ ἡ μήτηρ ἔτεκεν. ὑπόθου δ’ ὅτι ἐκείνῳ σε λίαν προσπλέκει τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ, οὐδὲν ὄντι οἶμαι πρὸς τὸ νῦν λεγόμενον.
passages.english: The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”. Now if this is by nature both bad and necessary for them, the whole would not be well managed, with its parts going into alteration and built in various ways for perishing. For did nature itself set out to treat its own parts badly, and to make them both liable to fall into what is bad and bound by necessity to fall into what is bad, or did such things come about without nature noticing? For both are unbelievable. And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together. For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole, whether the whole is burned up in fire at each cycle or renewed by everlasting exchanges. And do not picture the solid and the breath-like as the ones that date from the first birth. For all of this took its inflow yesterday and the day before, from food and from the air drawn in. So what changes is what it took in, not what your mother bore. But suppose that this binds you very closely to that individually qualified thing, which, I think, has no bearing on what is being said now.

notes.greek: λεγέσθω δὲ τοῦτο σημαντικῶς τοῦ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι
notes.note: Literally “let this be said as signifying being altered”. The sentence fixes the sense of φθείρεσθαι for the rest of the chapter; the English repeats “perish” in quotation marks so that the reader sees which word is being defined.
notes.other_reading: but let this be said in a way that signifies being altered

notes.note: The adverb can mean “in different ways” or “to an outstanding degree”. The English takes the first: the parts are built for perishing in their several ways, which the chapter goes on to list (scattering, turning into earth, turning into air).
notes.other_reading: and built above all for perishing

notes.note: The verb is formed from κακόν, “bad”, which stands beside it twice in the same sentence and once in the sentence before. “Bad” and “badly” are kept throughout so that the repetition is heard; “harm” would be more natural English for the verb.
notes.other_reading: set out to harm its own parts

notes.greek: ἀφέμενος τῆς φύσεως κατὰ τὸ πεφυκέναι
notes.note: A play on φύσις (nature as the power that orders things) and πεφυκέναι (to be so by nature). The person imagined drops nature as an agent and says only that things are naturally like this. “Naturally” is used for πεφυκέναι both times it comes, because the argument ends by setting it against παρὰ φύσιν, “against nature”.
notes.other_reading: dropping the term “nature” and explaining these things by the way they are constituted

notes.note: ἣ is read as ἢ, “or” (a slip of the digitised text). θαυμάζειν covers both “be surprised” and “wonder at”; the context of complaint points to surprise.
notes.other_reading: to wonder or to be displeased

notes.greek: τοῦ δὲ πνευματικοῦ εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες
notes.note: τὸ πνευματικόν is what in a living thing is of the nature of πνεῦμα, breath, the Stoic vital breath. “The breath-like” pairs with “the solid”.
notes.other_reading: and of the part that is spirit into the airy

notes.note: λόγος here is the reason that governs the whole and from which things are generated, into which the elements are taken back; it is not “the reason for” the whole. The glossary’s “reason” is kept.
notes.other_reading: into the generative principle of the whole

notes.greek: εἴτε κατὰ περίοδον ἐκπυρουμένου εἴτε ἀιδίοις ἀμοιβαῖς ἀνανεουμένου
notes.note: The two genitive participles agree with τοῦ ὅλου, so “the whole” is supplied as their subject. The first alludes to the Stoic teaching that the universe is consumed by fire at the end of each cycle; the second is the alternative of a universe that lasts for ever by exchange.
notes.other_reading: whether it is periodically turned to fire or renewed by everlasting exchanges

notes.note: Literally “yesterday and the third day”, an idiom for “very recently”. The literal shape is kept.
notes.other_reading: only the other day

notes.greek: ἐκείνῳ σε λίαν προσπλέκει τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ
notes.note: The verb “binds” has no subject expressed in the Greek, and the text of the sentence is thought doubtful (from memory, unchecked). The English supplies “this”, the matter recently taken in, from the sentence before; the subject could also be what the mother bore. τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν is the Stoic term for the individual as marked by a quality peculiar to it, which persists while its matter changes.
notes.other_reading: But suppose that what your mother bore ties you too closely to the individually qualified thing, which has no bearing on the present argument

check.note: διαφόρως can mean “in different ways” or “to a marked degree”, and the English chooses the first without the other being ruled out.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “built in various ways for perishing”. “Differently” is the basic sense of the adverb, and the chapter goes on to name different ways of perishing (scattering, turning into earth, turning into air); the note gives “above all” as the other reading.

check.note: The γὰρ (“for”) is dropped. It ties the verdict to the two-sided question just asked.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For both are unbelievable”, since the Greek has γὰρ tying the verdict to the question just asked.

check.note: “Let nature go” is not clear English. The Greek means setting aside nature as the agent of the sentence before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “were to leave nature out of it”, with a small n as everywhere else in the passage.

check.note: The Greek has no quoted speech, and it sets φύσις, the agent, against πεφυκέναι, how things are; the English uses “nature” for both, so the speaker seems to drop nature and appeal to it in one breath.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the invented quotation is gone and the English reads “explain these things by the way they naturally are” and “are naturally such as to change”. “Naturally” is kept for πεφυκέναι instead of “made”, because the Greek word shares its root with φύσις and the sentence ends by setting it against “against nature”; with “made” that last step could not be followed.

check.note: “The reason of the whole” may be taken as “the cause of the whole”. λόγος here is the rational principle of the whole.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the reason of the whole”. The Greek has the single word λόγος, for which the glossary settles “reason”, and “principle” is the glossary’s word for δόγμα; the note now says that the governing reason is meant and not “the reason for”.
