check.greek: ὑπόθου δ’ ὅτι ἐκείνῳ σε λίαν προσπλέκει τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ
check.note: The verb has no expressed subject in the Greek as given. The English supplies “this” and adds “other”, which smooths over a text that is suspected.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “other” is removed, since the Greek has only “that”, and the English reads “suppose that this binds you very closely to that individually qualified thing”. “This” stays without brackets because an English verb needs a subject and the nearest one in the Greek is the matter just taken in; the note says that the Greek names no subject and that the text is doubted.

check.note: τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν is the Stoic term for the individually qualified thing. “Yours” is not in the Greek, and the long paraphrase turns the individual into a thing that has a quality.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that individually qualified thing”, without “yours”. The bracketed explanation suggested is left to the note, because the Greek has only the bare term.

check.note: Found while settling: “here” in “let ‘perish’ be said here” answers to nothing in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let ‘perish’ be said in the sense of ‘be altered’”.

check.greek: εἰς ταῦτα γινομένης, ἐξ ὧν ἕκαστον συνίσταται
check.note: Found while settling: “the very things” adds an emphasis; the Greek has only “those things out of which”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into the things out of which each is put together”.

passages.casaubon: All parts of the world, (all things I mean that are contained within the whole world), must of necessity at some time or other come to corruption. Alteration I should say, to speak truly and properly; but that I may be the better understood, I am content at this time to use that more common word. Now say I, if so be that this be both hurtful unto them, and yet unavoidable, would not, thinkest thou, the whole itself be in a sweet case, all the parts of it being subject to alteration, yea and by their making itself fitted for corruption, as consisting of things different and contrary? And did nature then either of herself thus project and purpose the affliction and misery of her parts, and therefore of purpose so made them, not only that haply they might, but of necessity that they should fall into evil; or did not she know what she did, when she made them? For either of these two to say, is equally absurd. But to let pass nature in general, and to reason of things particular according to their own particular natures; how absurd and ridiculous is it, first to say that all parts of the whole are, by their proper natural constitution, subject to alteration; and then when any such thing doth happen, as when one doth fall sick and dieth, to take on and wonder as though some strange thing had happened? Though this besides might move not so grievously to take on when any such thing doth happen, that whatsoever is dissolved, it is dissolved into those things, whereof it was compounded. For every dissolution is either a mere dispersion, of the elements into those elements again whereof everything did consist, or a change, of that which is more solid into earth; and of that which is pure and subtile or spiritual, into air. So that by this means nothing is lost, but all resumed again into those rational generative seeds of the universe; and this universe, either after a certain period of time to lie consumed by fire, or by continual changes to be renewed, and so for ever to endure. Now that solid and spiritual that we speak of, thou must not conceive it to be that very same, which at first was, when thou wert born. For alas! all this that now thou art in either kind, either for matter of substance, or of life, hath but two or three days ago partly from meats eaten, and partly from air breathed in, received all its influx, being the same then in no other respect, than a running river, maintained by the perpetual influx and new supply of waters, is the same. That therefore which thou hast since received, not that which came from thy mother, is that which comes to change and corruption. But suppose that that for the general substance, and more solid part of it, should still cleave unto thee never so close, yet what is that to the proper qualities and affections of it, by which persons are distinguished, which certainly are quite different?
passages.russian: Частям целого — всему, что по природе объемлется мирозданием, — необходимо погибать; но пусть «погибать» будет сказано в смысле «изменяться». Если же это для них по природе и дурно, и неизбежно, то целое было бы плохо управляемо, раз его части уходят в изменение и различными способами устроены для гибели. Неужели сама природа взялась дурно обходиться со своими частями и сделать их и подверженными падению в дурное, и по необходимости обречёнными впадать в дурное, или же такое произошло без ведома природы? Ведь и то и другое невероятно. А если бы кто, оставив природу в стороне, стал объяснять это тем, каковы эти вещи по природе, то и тогда было бы смешно говорить, что части целого по природе таковы, чтобы изменяться, и вместе с тем удивляться или досадовать, будто на что-то, происходящее против природы, — особенно когда распад идёт в то, из чего каждая вещь составлена. Ведь это либо рассеяние стихий, из которых она была сложена, либо превращение твёрдого в землистое, а подобного дыханию — в воздушное, так что и они снова принимаются в разум целого, сгорает ли целое в огне в каждом круговороте или обновляется вечными обменами. И не представляй себе, что твёрдое и подобное дыханию ведут начало от первого рождения. Ведь всё это притекло вчера и позавчера — из пищи и вдыхаемого воздуха. Так что изменяется то, что оно вобрало, а не то, что родила мать. Но предположим, что это очень тесно привязывает тебя к той вещи, что обладает своим особым качеством, — что, как я думаю, не имеет отношения к тому, что сейчас говорится.

passages.english:
Look back over what has gone before: so many changes of ruling powers. It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now. So to observe human life for forty years is equal to observing it for ten thousand. For what more will you see?

And: “What grew from earth goes back to earth, and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air, back to the vault of heaven.” Or else this is a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms, and some such scattering of elements that cannot be affected.

And: “Turning the channel aside with food and drink and spells, so as not to die.” … “But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.”

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person expressed. The English uses an imperative; the second person does appear later in the chapter (ὄψει, “you will see”).
notes.other_reading: To look back over what has gone before

notes.note: ἡγεμονία is leadership or rule, and in the plural can mean reigns, dynasties or empires. The wider “ruling powers” is kept.
notes.other_reading: so many changes of dynasties

notes.note: πάντως can strengthen the statement (“certainly, in any case”) or give its extent (“altogether”). The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: For it will be altogether of the same kind

notes.note: ῥυθμός is measured movement, and also shape or pattern. “Rhythm” is kept as the image, with “step out of” for ἐκβῆναι.
notes.other_reading: it cannot depart from the pattern of what is happening now

notes.note: The verb means to inquire into or observe as a witness. The Greek says that the one observing “is equal to” the other, and the English keeps that.
notes.other_reading: to have studied human life for forty years is the same as studying it for ten thousand

notes.note: The opening Καὶ is taken as the notebook’s own “And” introducing an excerpt, here and before the next verses, so it stands outside the quotation marks. It could also be the first word of the quoted lines.
notes.other_reading: “And what grew from earth goes back to earth”

notes.note: Verse, believed to be from a lost play of Euripides (from memory, unchecked). The lines as quoted have one verb, πάλιν ἦλθε, “went back”, which stands in the second half and serves both; the English puts “goes back” in the first half and lets it serve the second. ἦλθε is an aorist stating a general truth, so the English has the present.
notes.other_reading: and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air has gone back to the vault of heaven

notes.note: There is no verb. τοῦτο is taken as subject (“or else this”, that is, what the verses describe, death) with “is” understood, giving the atomist alternative to the poet’s account. It could also be read as “or this:” introducing the alternative.
notes.other_reading: Or this: a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms

notes.note: ἀπαθής can mean “not acted upon, unchangeable” (as atoms are) or “without feeling”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: of the unfeeling elements

notes.note: Verse, believed to be from Euripides’ Suppliant Women (from memory, unchecked); the quotation has only a participle and no finite verb, and the English leaves it so. ὀχετός is a channel or conduit for water, here the course that carries a life to its end, and the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: they divert the stream with food and drink and spells, so as not to die

notes.note: After these words the text as given has a row of dots, which marks a break between two separate verse quotations (or a gap). The English shows it with an ellipsis between two sets of quotation marks and supplies nothing.
notes.other_reading: the two quotations printed as one continuous passage

notes.note: οὖρος is a sailing wind, usually a fair one that blows from behind. “Sailing wind” keeps that; plain “wind” would be easier English but loses it.
notes.other_reading: But the wind that blows from the gods must be borne

notes.note: Literally “with toils unlamented”: the toils are endured and not wailed over. The English keeps one phrase and the plural.
notes.other_reading: with toil and without lament

check.note: τοσαύτας is “so many” or “so great”, and “the many” loses its note of amazement.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “so many changes of ruling powers”, which gives τοσαύτας its plain sense. “All those great changes” would add “great” to “so many”, and the Greek word means one or the other.

check.note: πάντως usually strengthens the statement (“certainly”) and does not give a degree (“altogether”).
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For it will certainly be of the same kind”, and a note records “altogether” as the other reading.

check.note: “It is all one” is an old-fashioned idiom. The Greek says simply that the two are equal.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to observe human life for forty years is equal to observing it for ten thousand”. This removes the old idiom and keeps the Greek word “equal” and the Greek shape of the sentence.

check.note: Καὶ is taken as the notebook’s own linking word and set outside the quotation, though it may belong to the verse. The verb “goes back” in the first half is supplied from the second half.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “And:” stays outside the quotation marks, as it does before the next verses, where the same Καὶ introduces a second excerpt; a note records the other reading. The verb is no longer supplied: the one Greek verb, “goes back”, now stands in the first half and serves the second.

check.note: “Returns again” says “back” twice for the one πάλιν, and the aorist is turned into a present.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has the single verb “goes back” for πάλιν ἦλθε. The present is kept because the aorist here states a general truth, as the note says.

check.note: ἀπαθής can mean “not acted upon” or “without feeling”. As worded, “that nothing can affect” can also be misread as describing the scattering.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “scattering of elements that cannot be affected”, so that the words attach to the elements. The note keeps “unfeeling” as the other reading.

check.note: οὖρος is a sailing wind, normally a following wind, not wind in general.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the sailing wind that blows from the gods”. “Breeze” would suggest a light wind, which the Greek word does not say; a note explains the word.

check.note: ἀνοδύρτοις is an adjective on καμάτοις. The English splits one phrase into two and makes the plural singular.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in toils without lament”, one phrase with the plural kept.

passages.casaubon: To look back upon things of former ages, as upon the manifold changes and conversions of several monarchies and commonwealths. We may also foresee things future, for they shall all be of the same kind; neither is it possible that they should leave the tune, or break the concert that is now begun, as it were, by these things that are now done and brought to pass in the world. It comes all to one therefore, whether a man be a spectator of the things of this life but forty years, or whether he see them ten thousand years together: for what shall he see more? 'And as for those parts that came from the earth, they shall return unto the earth again; and those that came from heaven, they also shall return unto those heavenly places.' Whether it be a mere dissolution and unbinding of the manifold intricacies and entanglements of the confused atoms; or some such dispersion of the simple and incorruptible elements... 'With meats and drinks and divers charms, they seek to divert the channel, that they might not die. Yet must we needs endure that blast of wind that cometh from above, though we toil and labour never so much.'
passages.russian:
Оглянись на прошедшее: столько смен владычества. Можно предвидеть и будущее. Ведь оно непременно будет того же рода и не сможет выйти из ритма того, что происходит сейчас. Поэтому наблюдать человеческую жизнь сорок лет — всё равно что наблюдать её десять тысяч лет. Ведь что ты увидишь сверх этого?

И ещё: «Что выросло из земли, уходит в землю, а что проросло из семени верхнего воздуха — обратно к небесному своду». Или же это распад сцеплений между атомами и подобное рассеяние стихий, не способных ничего претерпевать.

И ещё: «Отводя русло пищей, питьём и заговорами, чтобы не умереть». … «А попутный ветер, что дует от богов, нужно сносить, в трудах, без стенаний».

passages.greek: Τὰ μὲν σπεύδει γίνεσθαι, τὰ δὲ σπεύδει γεγονέναι, καὶ τοῦ γινομένου δὲ ἤδη τι ἀπέσβη· ῥύσεις καὶ ἀλλοιώσεις ἀνανεοῦσι τὸν κόσμον διηνεκῶς, ὥσπερ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἡ τοῦ χρόνου ἀδιάλειπτος φορὰ νέον ἀεὶ παρέχεται. ἐν δὴ τούτῳ τῷ ποταμῷ τί ἄν τις τούτων τῶν παραθεόντων ἐκτιμήσειεν, ἐφ’ οὗ στῆναι οὐκ ἔξεστιν; ὥσπερ εἴ τίς τι τῶν παραπετομένων στρουθαρίων φιλεῖν ἄρχοιτο, τὸ δ’ ἤδη ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν ἀπελήλυθεν. τοιοῦτον δή τι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ζωὴ ἑκάστου, οἷον ἡ ἀφ’ αἵματος ἀναθυμίασις καὶ ἡ ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἀνάπνευσις· ὁποῖον γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἅπαξ ἑλκύσαι τὸν ἀέρα καὶ ἀποδοῦναι, ὅπερ παρέκαστον ποιοῦμεν, τοιοῦτόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ τὴν πᾶσαν ἀναπνευστικὴν δύναμιν, ἣν χθὲς καὶ πρῴην ἀποτεχθεὶς ἐκτήσω, ἀποδοῦναι ἐκεῖ ὅθεν τὸ πρῶτον ἔσπασας.
passages.english: Some things are hurrying to come to be, others are hurrying to have come to be, and of what is coming to be some part has already been quenched. Flows and alterations renew the universe continually, just as the unbroken movement of time keeps boundless eternity always new. In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on? It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight. Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air. For drawing in the air once and giving it back, which we do every moment, is the same kind of thing as giving back the whole power of breathing, which you acquired yesterday and the day before when you were born, to the place from which you first drew it.

notes.note: The perfect infinitive of the same verb as “to come to be”: these things hurry to have done their coming to be, that is, to be over. “To have come to be” keeps the one verb heard three times in the sentence.
notes.other_reading: others are hurrying to be over and done

notes.note: The verb is used of a flame going out. “Quenched” keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: some part has already gone out

notes.note: αἰών is time in its whole endless extent, here set beside χρόνος, time as it passes. “Eternity” is used for αἰών and “time” for χρόνος throughout this section.
notes.other_reading: keeps the boundless age always new

notes.note: The relative ἐφ’ οὗ (“on which”) may refer to the thing one might prize, on which no footing can be had, or back to the river, in which one cannot stand still. The English takes the nearer reference, the thing.
notes.other_reading: In this river, then, in which there is no standing still, which of these things running past would anyone prize?

notes.note: A diminutive of στρουθός, a sparrow or any small bird.
notes.other_reading: one of the little birds flying past

notes.greek: τοιοῦτον δή τι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ζωὴ ἑκάστου
notes.note: τοιοῦτον may look back to the things running past or forward to the comparison that follows (“such a thing as vapour”). “Something of the kind” followed by a colon leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: Each person’s life itself is just such a thing as the vapour that rises from blood

notes.note: A rising vapour or exhalation. The Stoics held that the soul is fed by an exhalation from the blood, and the sentence alludes to that; the plain image is kept.
notes.other_reading: the exhalation from blood

notes.note: “At each moment” or “each time”; one word here for παρ’ ἕκαστον.
notes.other_reading: time after time

notes.note: Literally “yesterday and the day before”, an idiom for “very recently”. It is kept literal, to match the similar phrase in 10.7.
notes.other_reading: only the other day

check.note: The same verb comes three times (γίνεσθαι, γεγονέναι, γινομένου). “To have been” breaks the chain and reads as “to have existed”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “others are hurrying to have come to be”, so that the one Greek verb is one English verb all three times.

check.note: ἀπέσβη is a flame image, “was quenched”. “Gone out” is pale and collides with “gone out of sight” two sentences later, which translates a different verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “some part has already been quenched”, which keeps the flame and leaves “gone out of sight” for the different verb two sentences later.

check.note: This is a relative clause, “on which one cannot stand”, which may go with the river or with the thing prized. “When” turns it into a reason and “it” is unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on?”, a relative clause again and without “when”. It is attached to the thing prized, because ἐφ’ οὗ means “upon which” and the nearer word is the thing; the note gives the reading that attaches it to the river.

check.note: καὶ (“too”) is dropped, and “the very life” is weaker than “life itself”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind”.

check.note: “For as it is to … so it is too to …” is hard to follow in today’s English. The Greek says the one act is the same sort of thing as the other.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “drawing in the air once and giving it back … is the same kind of thing as giving back the whole power of breathing”. The Greek order is kept, single breath first and last breath second, where the suggestion turned it round.

check.note: The Greek has “and”, not “or”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yesterday and the day before”.

passages.casaubon: Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished. Perpetual fluxes and alterations renew the world, as the perpetual course of time doth make the age of the world (of itself infinite) to appear always fresh and new. In such a flux and course of all things, what of these things that hasten so fast away should any man regard, since among all there is not any that a man may fasten and fix upon? as if a man would settle his affection upon some ordinary sparrow living by him, who is no sooner seen, than out of sight. For we must not think otherwise of our lives, than as a mere exhalation of blood, or of an ordinary respiration of air. For what in our common apprehension is, to breathe in the air and to breathe it out again, which we do daily: so much is it and no more, at once to breathe out all thy respirative faculty into that common air from whence but lately (as being but from yesterday, and to-day), thou didst first breathe it in, and with it, life.
passages.russian: Одно спешит возникнуть, другое спешит оказаться уже возникшим, и из того, что возникает, какая-то часть уже угасла. Течения и изменения постоянно обновляют мироздание, так же как непрерывное движение времени делает беспредельную вечность всегда новой. Что же в этой реке из того, что бежит мимо, стал бы кто-нибудь ценить — то, на чём невозможно устоять? Это как если бы кто-то начал любить одного из пролетающих мимо воробушков, а он уже скрылся из глаз. И сама жизнь каждого — нечто в этом роде: как испарение, поднимающееся от крови, и дыхание, вбираемое из воздуха. Ведь один раз вобрать воздух и отдать его обратно, что мы делаем каждый миг, — то же самое, что отдать всю силу дыхания, которую ты приобрёл вчера и позавчера, когда родился, туда, откуда ты впервые её вобрал.

passages.greek:
Πᾶν ἐφήμερον, καὶ τὸ μνημονεῦον καὶ τὸ μνημονευόμενον.

Θεώρει διηνεκῶς πάντα κατὰ μεταβολὴν γινόμενα καὶ ἐθίζου ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι οὐδὲν οὕτως φιλεῖ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ὡς τὸ τὰ ὄντα μεταβάλλειν καὶ ποιεῖν νέα ὅμοια. σπέρμα γὰρ τρόπον τινὰ πᾶν τὸ ὃν τοῦ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐσομένου, σὺ δὲ μόνα σπέρματα φαντάζῃ τὰ εἰς γῆν ἣ μήτραν καταβαλλόμενα, τοῦτο δὲ λίαν ἰδιωτικόν.
passages.english:
Everything lasts a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

Observe continually that all things come about by change, and accustom yourself to the thought that the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.

notes.note: Literally “of a day”, lasting one day. The day is kept in the English.
notes.other_reading: Everything is short-lived

notes.note: γινόμενα can be “coming to be” or “happening”; κατὰ μεταβολήν is “by way of change”. The English takes it as all things coming about through change.
notes.other_reading: Observe continually all things as they come to be through change

notes.note: Literally “new like [things]”: new things of the same sort as the old.
notes.other_reading: and make new ones of the same kind

notes.note: ὃν is read as ὂν, “being” (a slip of the digitised text): “everything that is”. The English says “exists”, here and for τὰ ὄντα just before, to avoid “is is”.
notes.other_reading: everything that is

notes.note: The verb is from the same root as φαντασία, “impression”: to form a picture of something. “Picture” is used here and in the other passages of this section.
notes.other_reading: But you imagine that the only seeds are those

notes.note: ἣ is read as ἢ, “or” (a slip of the digitised text).
notes.other_reading: into the ground or the womb

notes.note: ἰδιωτικός is what belongs to the private person without training, here the person without philosophy. It can be heard as “unphilosophical” or more sharply as “crude”; “view” is supplied for the bare adjective.
notes.other_reading: and that is very unphilosophical

check.note: Found while settling: “everything that is is” stumbles in English, and the same Greek word comes in the sentence before as “the things that are”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the things that exist” and “everything that exists”, one word for the one Greek word.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence; all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves, incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.
passages.russian:
Всё однодневно — и то, что помнит, и то, что помнят.

Постоянно наблюдай, что всё возникает через изменение, и приучай себя к мысли, что природа целого ничего так не любит, как изменять существующее и создавать новое, подобное ему. Ведь всё существующее — в некотором роде семя того, что из него произойдёт. А ты представляешь себе семенами только то, что бросают в землю или в утробу, и это взгляд весьма дилетантский.

passages.greek:
Τοῦ ὅλου αἰῶνος καὶ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας συνεχῶς φαντασία καὶ ὅτι πάντα τὰ κατὰ μέρος, ὡς μὲν πρὸς οὐσίαν, κεγχραμίς, ὡς δὲ πρὸς χρόνον, τρυπάνου περιστροφή.

Εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐφιστάντα ἐπινοεῖν αὐτὸ ἤδη διαλυόμενον καὶ ἐν μεταβολῇ καὶ οἷον σήψει ἢ σκεδάσει γινόμενον ἢ καθότι ἕκαστον πέφυκεν ὥσπερ θνῄσκειν.
passages.english:
An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.

Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change, and as it were in the course of rotting or scattering, or in whatever way it is the nature of each thing, so to speak, to die.

notes.note: The sentence has no verb: it is a note to self, “[have] constantly an impression of”. The English leaves it verbless. φαντασία is the Stoic term, “impression”.
notes.other_reading: Keep constantly before you the picture of the whole of eternity

notes.note: οὐσία is the stuff of which everything is made, “substance” or “being” or “matter”. “Substance” is used throughout this section.
notes.other_reading: and the whole of matter

notes.note: The tiny seed inside a fig. The image is of something almost too small to see.
notes.other_reading: a grain

notes.note: A twist of a borer or drill: an instant of motion.
notes.other_reading: the twist of a gimlet

notes.note: Literally “the things that lie under”: either the things presented to one, the things at hand, or more generally existing things. “Object” is meant to cover both.
notes.other_reading: each of the things in front of you

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with an accusative participle and no person expressed (“for one who attends to each thing, to think”). The English uses an imperative. ἐφιστάναι is to bring the attention to rest on something.
notes.other_reading: One should stop at each thing and think of it

notes.note: ὥσπερ softens “to die”, since it is said of things as well as living beings: “to die, as it were”. Earlier οἷον does the same for the rotting and scattering.
notes.other_reading: or as each thing is by nature made to die, as it were

check.note: “One” is added; the Greek has simply “a turn of a drill”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a turn of a drill”, since the Greek has no “one”.

check.note: ἐφιστάναι here is to fix one’s attention on a thing. “Stopping at” reads as physically halting.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Fixing attention on each object”. “Your” is left out because the Greek participle names no person.

check.note: τὰ ὑποκείμενα may be the things before one or existing things in general. “In front of you” narrows it to the first.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “each object”, which leaves both senses open and drops the “you” that the Greek does not have. “You meet” is not taken, for the same reason.

check.note: Found while settling: “is by nature made … to die” brings in a making that πέφυκεν, “is by nature”, does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in whatever way it is the nature of each thing, so to speak, to die”.

passages.casaubon: Ever to represent unto thyself; and to set before thee, both the general age and time of the world, and the whole substance of it. And how all things particular in respect of these are for their substance, as one of the least seeds that is: and for their duration, as the turning of the pestle in the mortar once about. Then to fix thy mind upon every particular object of the world, and to conceive it, (as it is indeed,) as already being in the state of dissolution, and of change; tending to some kind of either putrefaction or dispersion; or whatsoever else it is, that is the death as it were of everything in his own kind.
passages.russian:
Постоянное представление обо всей вечности и всей сущности, и о том, что всё отдельное в сравнении с сущностью — фиговое семечко, а в сравнении со временем — оборот сверла.

Сосредоточивая внимание на каждом предмете, думай о нём как об уже распадающемся и изменяющемся, как бы гниющем или рассеивающемся, или тем образом, каким каждой вещи, так сказать, по природе положено умирать.

passages.greek:
τῷ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον περιειληφέναι τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τὸν ἀίδιον αἰῶνα περινοεῖν καὶ τὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἑκάστου πράγματος ταχεῖαν μεταβολὴν ἐπινοεῖν, ὡς βραχὺ μὲν τὸ ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι διαλύσεως, ἀχανὲς δὲ τὸ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως, ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον.

Πάντα ὅσα ὁρᾷς τάχιστα φθαρήσεται καὶ οἱ φθειρόμενα αὐτὰ ἐπιδόντες τάχιστα καὶ αὐτοὶ φθαρήσονται καὶ ὁ ἐσχατόγηρως ἀποθανὼν εἰς ἴσον καταστήσεται τῷ προώρῳ.
passages.english:
By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing: how short is the stretch from coming to be to dissolution, and how gaping the time before the coming to be, just as the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless.

Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.

notes.note: The passage begins in mid-sentence with a dative infinitive, “by having encompassed”, which depends on a main clause that is not given. It is left as a fragment and nothing is supplied; only the capital letter is added. No “you” is expressed in the fragment.
notes.other_reading: by having embraced the whole universe

notes.note: γνώμη is the mind as it judges and forms a view. The glossary keeps “thought” for διάνοια and “mind” for νοῦς, neither of which occurs here; “thought” is used as the plainest fit.
notes.other_reading: in your mind

notes.note: Literally “to think around”, with the same prefix as περιειληφέναι, “to have encompassed”. “Surveying” gives the looking all round in ordinary English, at the cost of the word “think”.
notes.other_reading: and by thinking round everlasting eternity

notes.note: “Yawning, gaping”: a gulf with no visible far side. The image is kept, as with the same word in 12.32.
notes.other_reading: how vast the time before the coming to be

notes.greek: ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον
notes.note: The second ὡς may be a comparative “just as” or another “how”. With καὶ and ὁμοίως (“likewise”) beside it, the English takes it as “just as”.
notes.other_reading: and how the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless

notes.note: The verb can mean simply to look on, or to live to see something. The English takes the plainer sense.
notes.other_reading: and those who have lived to see it perish

notes.note: “The untimely one”, the one who dies before the due season. Greek uses the masculine as the general form; the English has “whoever” and “their”.
notes.other_reading: will be made equal to the one who died young

check.note: περιειληφέναι is to have encompassed or embraced. “Taken into thought” loses the image of the mind going round the whole, which the next verb repeats.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “By having encompassed the whole universe in thought”, which restores the image. “In your mind” is not taken, because the fragment has no “your” and “mind” is this translation’s word for νοῦς.

check.note: “Thinking round eternity” is not natural English and may be read as “thinking in circles”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by surveying everlasting eternity”. “Surveying” keeps the sense of looking all round that the prefix περι gives, where “taking in” would lose it; the note gives the literal “think around”.

check.note: “Gaping” is odd of a stretch of time in today’s English.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “how gaping”. ἀχανές is an image, a mouth or gulf standing wide open, and the translator’s brief requires images to be kept; “vast” would drop it, and the note gives “vast” as the plainer reading.

check.greek: ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον
check.note: With καὶ and ὁμοίως the second ὡς is more naturally the comparative “just as” than a third “how”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how gaping the time before the coming to be, just as the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless”. The Greek compares the time before with the time after and does not make a third exclamation.

part.left_out: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.30 in the middle of chapter 9.32, at 'thou shalt have room enough', and begins its 9.31 with the rest of that chapter, joined to chapter 9.33.

passages.casaubon: To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object. How short the time is from the generation of anything, unto the dissolution of the same; but how immense and infinite both that which was before the generation, and that which after the generation of it shall be. All things that thou seest, will soon be perished, and they that see their corruptions, will soon vanish away themselves. He that dieth a hundred years old, and he that dieth young, shall come all to one.
passages.russian:
Охватив мыслью всё мироздание, обозревая нескончаемую вечность и думая о быстрой перемене каждой отдельной вещи: как короток промежуток от возникновения до распада и какое зияющее время лежит до возникновения, так же как беспредельно и время после распада.

Всё, что ты видишь, очень скоро погибнет, и те, кто смотрел, как оно гибнет, очень скоро погибнут сами, и тот, кто умрёт в глубокой старости, окажется вровень с тем, кто умер раньше срока.

passages.greek:
Ἤδη πάντας ἡμᾶς γῆ καλύψει, ἔπειτα καὶ αὐτὴ μεταβαλεῖ κἀκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον μεταβαλεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἐκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον. τὰς γὰρ ἐπικυματώσεις τῶν μεταβολῶν καὶ ἀλλοιώσεων ἐνθυμούμενός τις καὶ τὸ τάχος παντὸς θνητοῦ καταφρονήσει.

Χειμάρρους ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία· πάντα φέρει.
passages.english:
Any moment now earth will cover us all. Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end. For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.

The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.

notes.note: “Already”, with a future verb: at any moment, very soon.
notes.other_reading: Soon

notes.note: “Those things” has no stated referent in the Greek; it must mean what the earth changes into. The English leaves it as bare as the Greek. εἰς ἄπειρον is “to infinity”.
notes.other_reading: and what it changes into will change without end, and that in turn without end

notes.note: A rare word: waves coming on top of waves. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: the surging waves of changes and alterations

notes.note: “The speed” is taken as a second object of “reflects on”, the speed of the changes. The following genitive παντὸς θνητοῦ then goes with “will look down on”.
notes.other_reading: who reflects on the waves of change and on the speed of everything mortal will feel contempt

notes.note: “Will think down on”: hold as of little account. It need not carry scorn.
notes.other_reading: will think little of everything mortal

notes.note: A winter torrent, a stream swollen by storm that sweeps things away.
notes.other_reading: a river in flood

notes.note: “The substance of the whole”, on the pattern of the glossary’s “the nature of the whole”. Some editors are believed to read αἰτία, “cause”, here in place of οὐσία (from memory, unchecked); the English translates the text as given.
notes.other_reading: The cause of the whole is a torrent

notes.note: φέρει is “carries”, of a current bearing things away. The same verb can mean “brings”.
notes.other_reading: it sweeps all things away

check.note: The Greek says only “and those things too”, with no stated antecedent. “What it changes into” is an explanation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and those things too will change without end, and those again without end”, as bare as the Greek, and the explanation has moved to the note.

check.note: The English follows the Greek as given. The edition may read αἰτία (“cause”) where this copy has οὐσία.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “The substance of the whole”, because the Greek as given reads οὐσία and that is the text to be translated. The note records the reading αἰτία, “cause”, as known from memory and unchecked.

part.left_out: Ταὐτά ἐστι τὰ τοῦ κόσμου ἐγκύκλια, ἄνω κάτω, ἐξ αἰῶνος εἰς αἰῶνα. καὶ ἤτοι ἐφ’ ἕκαστον ὁρμᾷ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου διάνοια· ὅπερ εἰ ἔστιν, ἀποδέχου τὸ ἐκείνης ὁρμητόν· ἢ ἅπαξ ὥρμησε, τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ τί ἐντείνῃ; τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ. τὸ δ’ ὅλον, εἴτε θεός, εὖ ἔχει πάντα· εἴτε τὸ εἰκῇ, μὴ καὶ σὺ εἰκῇ. … ὡς εὐτελῆ δὲ καὶ τὰ πολιτικὰ ταῦτα καί, ὡς οἴεται, φιλοσόφως πρακτικὰ ἀνθρώπια· μυξῶν μεστά.—ἄνθρωπε, τί ποτε; ποίησον ὃ νῦν ἡ φύσις ἀπαιτεῖ, ὅρμησον, ἐὰν διδῶται, καὶ μὴ περιβλέπου εἴ τις εἴσεται. μὴ τὴν Πλάτωνος πολιτείαν ἔλπιζε, ἀλλὰ ἀρκοῦ, εἰ τὸ βραχύτατον πρόεισι, καὶ τούτου αὐτοῦ τὴν ἔκβασιν ὡς μικρόν τί ἐστι διανοοῦ. δόγμα γὰρ αὐτῶν τίς μεταβαλεῖ; χωρὶς δὲ δογμάτων μεταβολῆς τί ἄλλο ἢ δουλεία στενόντων καὶ πείθεσθαι προσποιουμένων; ὕπαγε νῦν καὶ Ἀλέξανδρον καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Δημήτριον τὸν Φαληρέα μοι λέγε. ὄψονται, εἰ εἶδον, τί ἡ κοινὴ φύσις ἤθελε, καὶ ἑαυτοὺς ἐπαιδαγώγησαν· εἰ δὲ ἐτραγῴδησαν, οὐδείς με κατακέκρικε μιμεῖσθαι. ἁπλοῦν ἐστι καὶ αἰδῆμον τὸ φιλοσοφίας ἔργον· μή με ἄπαγε ἐπὶ σεμνοτυφίαν.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.26 in the middle of chapter 9.28 and begins its 9.27 here; it closes 9.27 with the first sentence of chapter 9.29, the torrent, and begins its 9.28 with the rest of that chapter.

passages.casaubon: Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself shall have her change. And then the course will be, from one period of eternity unto another, and so a perpetual eternity. Now can any man that shall consider with himself in his mind the several rollings or successions of so many changes and alterations, and the swiftness of all these rulings; can he otherwise but contemn in his heart and despise all worldly things? The cause of the universe is as it were a strong torrent, it carrieth all away.
passages.russian:
Вот-вот земля покроет всех нас. Потом изменится и сама земля, и то тоже будет меняться без конца, и это опять без конца. Ведь кто размышляет о волнах перемен и изменений, набегающих одна за другой, и об их быстроте, тот будет смотреть свысока на всё смертное.

Вещество целого — поток: оно несёт всё.

passages.greek: Πάντα ἐν μεταβολῇ· καὶ αὐτὸς σὺ ἐν διηνεκεῖ ἀλλοιώσει καὶ κατά τι φθορᾷ, καὶ ὁ κόσμος δὲ ὅλος.
passages.english: All things are in change. You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.

notes.note: κατά τι limits the claim: “in some respect” or “in part”. The English takes “in a certain respect”, since elsewhere in the notebook perishing is treated as a kind of alteration (10.7). φθορά is the noun of “perish” in the neighbouring passages, so “perishing” is kept.
notes.other_reading: and in part in decay

notes.note: ἀλλοίωσις is “becoming other”, alteration; “alteration” is kept for it and “change” for μεταβολή across the section.
notes.other_reading: in unbroken transformation

check.note: Found while settling: the καὶ (“too”) before “you yourself” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “You yourself too are in continual alteration”.

passages.casaubon: All things that are in the world, are always in the estate of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
passages.russian: Всё в перемене. И ты сам — в непрерывном изменении и в некотором отношении в гибели, и всё мироздание тоже.

passages.greek: Πῶς πάντα ταχέως ἐναφανίζεται, τῷ μὲν κόσμῳ αὐτὰ τὰ σώματα, τῷ δὲ αἰῶνι αἱ μνῆμαι αὐτῶν. οἶά ἐστι τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα καὶ μάλιστα τὰ ἡδονῇ δελεάζοντα ἢ τῷ πόνῳ φοβοῦντα ἢ τῷ τύφῳ διαβεβοημένα· πῶς εὐτελῆ καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητα καὶ ῥυπαρὰ καὶ εὔφθαρτα καὶ νεκρά,
passages.english: How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity. What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.

notes.note: The “how” and “what” clauses are indirect questions that depend on a verb later in the chapter, which is not part of this passage. The English leaves them all standing on their own, as headings for thought, and supplies no governing verb.
notes.other_reading: [To consider] how quickly all things vanish

notes.note: The datives go with the verb, “vanish in” or “into”: bodies are lost in the universe, memories in eternity. They could also be heard as “for the universe”, “for eternity”.
notes.other_reading: the bodies themselves in the universe, the memories of them in time

notes.note: πόνος is both “pain” and “toil, hardship”. Set against pleasure, “pain” is the nearer sense.
notes.other_reading: or frighten with hardship

notes.note: τῦφος is literally smoke: vanity, delusion, puffed-up pride. διαβεβοημένα is “shouted abroad”, made famous. The things meant are those celebrated only through people’s vanity.
notes.other_reading: or are noised abroad by empty pride

notes.note: The Greek as given stops at a comma, in mid-sentence. The English closes with a full stop so that the passage can stand on its own; nothing has been supplied.
notes.other_reading: and quick to perish and dead,

check.note: “Cried up” is dated English and may not be understood.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “are loudly celebrated through vanity”. This removes “cried up” and keeps the loudness that is in the Greek verb, which “made much of” would lose.

check.note: The Greek breaks off at a comma. The English mixes an exclamation with an indirect question that has no main verb, and closes with a full stop.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the colon after “vanish” is now a comma, so that all the clauses read alike as “how” and “what” questions awaiting a verb. The full stop stays, because a passage cut from a chapter has to stand on its own with the smallest addition, and the note says that the Greek sentence runs on.

check.greek: πῶς εὐτελῆ καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητα καὶ ῥυπαρὰ
check.note: Found while settling: “how” is said five times where the Greek has one πῶς and joins the five words with “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead”.

part.left_out: νοερᾶς δυνάμεως ἐφιστάναι. τί εἰσιν οὗτοι, ὧν αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι. τί ἐστι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ ὅτι, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ μόνον ἴδῃ καὶ τῷ μερισμῷ τῆς ἐννοίας διαλύσῃ τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ, οὐκέτι ἄλλο τι ὑπολήψεται αὐτὸ εἶναι ἢ φύσεως ἔργον· φύσεως δὲ ἔργον εἴ τις φοβεῖται, παιδίον ἐστί· τοῦτο μέντοι οὐ μόνον φύσεως ἔργον ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφέρον αὐτῇ. πῶς ἅπτεται θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος καὶ κατὰ τί ἑαυτοῦ μέρος καὶ ὅταν πῶς ἔχῃ διακέηται τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦτο μόριον.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 2.9 here; its 2.10 holds the middle of the chapter and its 2.11 begins with the chapter's last sentence.

passages.casaubon: Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world. Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things; of those especially, which either ensnare by pleasure, or for their irksomeness are dreadful, or for their outward lustre and show are in great esteem and request, how vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of all true life and being they are.
passages.russian: Как быстро всё исчезает: сами тела — в мироздании, память о них — в вечности. Каково всё воспринимаемое чувствами, и особенно то, что приманивает наслаждением, или пугает болью, или громко прославляется из тщеславия: как оно дёшево, и презренно, и грязно, и скоротечно, и мертво.

passages.greek: Πόστον μέρος τοῦ ἀπείρου καὶ ἀχανοῦς αἰῶνος ἀπομεμέρισται ἑκάστῳ· τάχιστα γὰρ ἐναφανίζεται τῷ ἀιδίῳ· πόστον δὲ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας· πόστον δὲ τῆς ὅλης ψυχῆς· ἐν πόστῳ δὲ βωλαρίῳ τῆς ὅλης γῆς ἕρπεις. πάντα ταῦτα ἐνθυμούμενος μηδὲν μέγα φαντάζου ἢ τό, ὡς μὲν ἡ σὴ φύσις ἄγει ποιεῖν, πάσχειν δὲ ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει.
passages.english: How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul. And on how small a clod of the whole earth you crawl. Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.

notes.note: πόστος asks “which in a series”, so “what fraction”. The force is “how tiny a fraction”. “How small a part” is used each of the four times the word comes.
notes.other_reading: What fraction of boundless, gaping eternity

notes.note: “Yawning, gaping”: a gulf with no visible far side. The image is kept, as with the same word in 9.32.
notes.other_reading: of boundless and vast eternity

notes.note: “To each”, with nothing added in the Greek; the second person comes only with “you crawl”.
notes.other_reading: to each person

notes.note: “The whole soul”: the soul of the universe, of which each soul is a part, as each body is a part of the whole substance.
notes.other_reading: of the universal soul

notes.note: A diminutive: a little clod or lump of earth. Literally “on what fraction of a clod of the whole earth”.
notes.other_reading: on how tiny a lump of the whole earth you creep

notes.note: The verb is from the root of φαντασία, “impression”: do not form the impression that anything is great. “Picture” is used, as elsewhere in this section.
notes.other_reading: imagine nothing to be great

notes.greek: ὡς μὲν ἡ σὴ φύσις ἄγει ποιεῖν, πάσχειν δὲ ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει
notes.note: ποιεῖν and πάσχειν are the standing pair “to do” and “to have done to one”; πάσχειν need not mean suffering. ἄγει (“leads”) and φέρει (“brings, carries”) are also a pair, kept as “leads” and “brings”. Both halves have ὡς, “as”; “things” and “them” are added because English “undergo” and “brings” need an object.
notes.other_reading: to do as your own nature leads, and to bear what the common nature brings

check.greek: πάσχειν δὲ ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει
check.note: ὡς is “as”, parallel with the first ὡς (“as your nature leads”). “What” makes it the content and not the manner.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to undergo things as the common nature brings them”, so that both halves have “as”. “Things” and “them” are added because the English verbs cannot stand without an object, and the note says so.

passages.casaubon: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl. After thou shalt rightly have considered these things with thyself; fancy not anything else in the world any more to be of any weight and moment but this, to do that only which thine own nature doth require; and to conform thyself to that which the common nature doth afford.
passages.russian: Какая малая часть безграничной, зияющей вечности отмерена каждому: ведь она очень быстро исчезает в вечном. И какая малая часть всей сущности, и какая малая часть всей души. И на каком малом комке всей земли ты ползаешь. Размышляя обо всём этом, не представляй себе великим ничего, кроме одного: поступать так, как ведёт твоя природа, и претерпевать так, как приносит общая природа.

passages.greek:
Ὁ τὰ νῦν ἰδὼν πάντα ἑώρακεν, ὅσα τε ἐξ ἀιδίου ἐγένετο καὶ ὅσα εἰς τὸ ἄπειρον ἔσται· πάντα γὰρ ὁμογενῆ καὶ ὁμοειδῆ.

Πολλάκις ἐνθυμοῦ τὴν ἐπισύνδεσιν πάντων τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ σχέσιν πρὸς ἄλληλα. τρόπον γάρ τινα πάντα ἀλλήλοις ἐπιπέπλεκται καὶ πάντα κατὰ τοῦτο φίλα ἀλλήλοις ἐστί· καὶ γὰρ ἄλλῳ ἑξῆς ἐστι τοῦτο διὰ τὴν τονικὴν κίνησιν καὶ σύμπνοιαν καὶ τὴν ἕνωσιν τῆς οὐσίας.
passages.english:
Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.

Reflect often on the linking together of all things in the universe and their relation to one another. For in a way all things are interwoven with one another, and all are on that account dear to one another. For this thing is next in order to another, through the movement of tension, the breathing together and the unity of substance.

notes.note: “From the everlasting”, that is, from all time past; “past” is added to make that plain. It is paired with εἰς τὸ ἄπειρον, “into the boundless”, given as “without end”.
notes.other_reading: all that has been from eternity and all that will be to infinity

notes.note: Two near-synonyms: “of the same birth or family” and “of the same form or kind”. “Of the same kind” is kept for ὁμοειδής, as in 7.49 and 9.35.
notes.other_reading: akin and alike in form

notes.note: A binding of one thing onto another, a chain of connection. The word is rare.
notes.other_reading: the bond that joins all things in the universe

notes.note: “Dear” or “friendly”: things are on good terms with one another because they are woven together. The word can also mean simply “akin”.
notes.other_reading: and all are on that account friendly to one another

notes.note: Literally “this is next in order to another”. As given, “this” has nothing to point to, and the phrase is thought to be damaged or emended by editors (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps it as it stands; the sense must be that each thing comes in sequence after another.
notes.other_reading: for one thing follows in order on another

notes.note: A Stoic technical term: the movement of tension (τόνος) in the breath that pervades and holds together all substance. No plain English word exists for it, so the two Greek words are given literally.
notes.other_reading: through the tensile movement

notes.note: Literally “breathing together”: the shared breath, and so the agreement, of all parts of the universe. The literal image is kept because the Stoic breath is in view.
notes.other_reading: the common accord

check.note: “From everlasting” is an archaic, biblical phrase.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “from the everlasting past”. “Everlasting” is kept because it is this section’s word for ἀίδιος; “time without beginning” would say more than the Greek word does.

check.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἄλλῳ ἑξῆς ἐστι τοῦτο
check.note: As given, the Greek says “for this is next in order to another” and does not construe smoothly. The English turns it into a general statement without showing the difficulty.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For this thing is next in order to another”, as close to the Greek as given as English allows. The note says that “this” has nothing to point to and that the text is doubted.

check.note: This is a technical Stoic phrase that a reader of today will not understand as it stands.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the movement of tension”. The Greek is a two-word technical term with no everyday equivalent, and the bracketed gloss suggested would put into the text words the Greek does not have; the note explains the term.

passages.casaubon: He that seeth the things that are now, hath Seen all that either was ever, or ever shall be, for all things are of one kind; and all like one unto another. Meditate often upon the connection of all things in the world; and upon the mutual relation that they have one unto another. For all things are after a sort folded and involved one within another, and by these means all agree well together. For one thing is consequent unto another, by local motion, by natural conspiration and agreement, and by substantial union, or, reduction of all substances into one.
passages.russian:
Кто видел то, что есть сейчас, видел всё: всё, что возникло из вечного прошлого, и всё, что будет без конца. Ведь всё одного происхождения и одного рода.

Часто размышляй о сцеплении всего в мироздании и о соотношении всего друг с другом. Ведь в некотором смысле всё сплетено друг с другом и потому всё друг другу дорого. Одно следует по порядку за другим — благодаря движению напряжения, совместному дыханию и единству вещества.

passages.greek:
Οὐδέν ἐστι κακὸν τοῖς ἐν μεταβολῇ γινομένοις, ὡς οὐδὲ ἀγαθὸν τοῖς ἐκ μεταβολῆς ὑφισταμένοις.

Ποταμός τίς ἐστι τῶν γινομένων καὶ ῥεῦμα βίαιον ὁ αἰών· ἅμα τε γὰρ ὤφθη ἕκαστον, καὶ παρενήνεκται καὶ ἄλλο παραφέρεται, τὸ δὲ ἐνεχθήσεται.
passages.english:
There is nothing bad for things that are in the course of change, just as there is nothing good for things that come to exist out of change.

Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.

notes.note: Literally “for the things coming to be in change”. It may mean things that are undergoing change, or things that come about in the process of change. The English takes the first; the thought is that being changed is no harm to them.
notes.other_reading: Nothing is bad for things that come about in the course of change

notes.note: ὑφίστασθαι is to come into existence or to subsist. The things meant are those that exist as the result of a change. The clause denies them a good as the first denies the others a harm.
notes.other_reading: just as it is no good either for things that subsist as a result of change

notes.note: αἰών is the whole endless extent of time. “Eternity” is kept so that the word is the same as in the other passages of this section, where it stands beside χρόνος, “time”; here it means endless time in its flow, not timelessness.
notes.other_reading: Time is a kind of river of things that come to be

notes.note: An aorist: “was seen”, that is, no sooner has each thing appeared than it is gone.
notes.other_reading: no sooner is each thing seen than it has been swept past

notes.note: Literally “and the other will be carried”. τὸ δέ after ἄλλο marks a further thing, so that three things stand in three tenses: carried past, being carried past, to be carried. It could also be taken of the thing just mentioned.
notes.other_reading: and that one too will be carried off

check.note: τὸ δὲ marks a further thing, not the one just mentioned, and “off” is not in the plain verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along”. After ἄλλο, “another”, the words τὸ δὲ bring in a new subject, and the three verbs run past, present, future.

check.note: “Eternity” may suggest timelessness to a reader of today, which fits badly with a river and a current. The other choice is “time”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “Eternity”. αἰών is rendered “eternity” in every passage of this section so that it stays distinct from χρόνος, “time”, which stands beside it in 6.15 and 10.17; the note gives “Time” as the other reading and says that endless time is meant.

passages.casaubon: To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
passages.russian:
Нет ничего дурного для того, что находится в изменении, как нет ничего хорошего для того, что возникает из изменения.

Вечность — своего рода река возникающего и бурный поток. Ведь едва каждую вещь увидели, как её уже пронесло мимо, и проносится другая, и понесёт ещё другую.

passages.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις τοῦτο ἔργον ἔχει, τὰ ὧδε ὄντα ἐκεῖ μετατιθέναι, μεταβάλλειν, αἴρειν ἔνθεν καὶ ἐκεῖ φέρειν. πάντα τροπαί, οὐχ ὥστε φοβηθῆναι, μή τι καινόν· πάντα συνήθη· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἴσαι αἱ ἀπονεμήσεις.
passages.english: The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there. All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar, and what is more, the allotments are equal.

notes.note: Two verbs with the same prefix, “to place elsewhere” and “to change”. English cannot keep the echo; the plain sense of each is given.
notes.other_reading: to transpose what is here to there, to transform it

notes.note: τροπή is a turning, and so a change from one state into another. “Transformations” is used here because “turnings” with nothing after it is not clear English; in 10.7, where the word has “into” after it, it is “a turning”.
notes.other_reading: All things are turnings

notes.note: Literally “not so as to fear lest something new”: the verb is left out. It is taken as fear that something new and strange may come about.
notes.other_reading: so there is no need to fear anything unheard of

notes.note: “The distributions are equal.” It may mean that what is given out is the same for everyone, or that what is taken from one place is matched by what is given to another, or that the shares are fair. The bare statement is kept.
notes.other_reading: the portions are dealt out fairly

check.note: “Turnings” is not clear English here. τροπαί are changes, things turning into other things.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “All things are transformations”. The plural and “all things” are kept as in the Greek, and “change” is left for the different verb just before.

check.note: “But” and “there is reason” are added. The Greek is “not so that one should fear”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not so that one need fear something new”, without “but” and “there is reason”.

passages.casaubon: That which the nature of the universe doth busy herself about, is; that which is here, to transfer it thither, to change it, and thence again to take it away, and to carry it to another place. So that thou needest not fear any new thing. For all things are usual and ordinary; and all things are disposed by equality.
passages.russian: Дело природы целого вот в чём: то, что здесь, переносить туда, изменять, поднимать отсюда и нести туда. Всё — превращения, но не так, чтобы надо было бояться чего-то нового. Всё привычно, и более того — доли равны.

passages.greek: Ἡ ἀποβολὴ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ μεταβολή. τούτῳ δὲ χαίρει ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, καθ’ ἢν πάντα καλῶς γίνεται καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ὁμοειδῶς ἐγίνετο καὶ εἰς ἄπειρον τοιαῦθ̓ ἕτερα ἔσται. τί οὖν λέγεις ὅτι ἐγίνετό τε πάντα κακῶς καὶ πάντα ἀεὶ κακῶς ἔσται καὶ οὐδεμία ἄρα δύναμις ἐν τοσούτοις θεοῖς ἐξευρέθη ποτὲ ἡ διορθώσουσα ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ κατακέκριται ὁ κόσμος ἐν ἀδιαλείπτοις κακοῖς συνέχεσθαι;
passages.english: Loss is nothing other than change. And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them. Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly, and that among so many gods no power, it seems, has ever been found to set these things right, but the universe has been condemned to be held fast in bad things without a break?

notes.greek: Ἡ ἀποβολὴ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ μεταβολή
notes.note: A play on two words from the same verb: ἀποβολή, a throwing away or loss, and μεταβολή, a throwing over or change. The English words do not echo each other.
notes.other_reading: A casting off is nothing but a casting over into something else

notes.note: τούτῳ is neuter, “this”, and so points to the fact or process of change in general, not to the feminine noun μεταβολή.
notes.other_reading: And change is what the nature of the whole delights in

notes.note: “In the same form”: the adverb of ὁμοειδής, rendered “of the same kind” in 7.49 and 6.37.
notes.other_reading: and from eternity came about in just the same way

notes.note: Either “why then do you say that” or “what then are you saying: that”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: What then are you saying? That all things have come about badly

notes.note: “Among so many gods”; ἄρα in the same clause marks the inference as one the speaker would be forced to, given as “it seems”.
notes.other_reading: and so, with all those gods, no power was ever found

notes.note: κακοῖς is the plural noun that goes with the adverb κακῶς, “badly”, just before, and both answer καλῶς, “well”. “Bad things” keeps the family together. συνέχεσθαι is to be held fast or gripped.
notes.other_reading: to be gripped by unceasing evils

check.note: κακῶς, κακῶς, κακοῖς are one word-family answering καλῶς. “Evils” breaks it and is heavier than the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to be held fast in bad things without a break”, so that “badly” and “bad” are heard together against “well”.

check.note: “Will always be badly” is not idiomatic English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all things will always go badly”.

check.note: τί may be “why” or “what”. The other reading is “What are you saying, then? That all things …”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “Why then do you say that”. With ὅτι, “that”, following at once, the words run most simply as one question, and the note gives the other reading.

passages.casaubon: Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is well done. For that was the estate of worldly things from the beginning, and so shall it ever be. Or wouldest thou rather say, that all things in the world have gone ill from the beginning for so many ages, and shall ever go ill? And then among so many deities, could no divine power be found all this while, that could rectify the things of the world? Or is the world, to incessant woes and miseries, for ever condemned?
passages.russian: Утрата — не что иное, как перемена. А этому радуется природа целого — природа, по которой всё происходит хорошо, и от века происходило одинаковым образом, и без конца будут другие, подобные этому. Почему же ты говоришь, что всё происходило дурно и всё всегда будет идти дурно и что среди стольких богов так и не нашлось, видно, никакой силы, чтобы это исправить, а мироздание осуждено без перерыва быть скованным дурным?

passages.greek: Ἔξω τοῦ κόσμου τὸ ἀποθανὸν οὐ πίπτει. εἰ ὧδε μένει καὶ μεταβάλλει ὧδε καὶ διαλύεται εἰς τὰ ἴδια, ἃ στοιχεῖά ἐστι τοῦ κόσμου καὶ σά. καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ μεταβάλλει καὶ οὐ γογγύζει.
passages.english: What has died does not fall outside the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into the things that are its own, which are the elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.

notes.note: Neuter: “the thing that has died”, not “the person who has died”.
notes.other_reading: That which dies

notes.greek: εἰ ὧδε μένει καὶ μεταβάλλει ὧδε
notes.note: The division between the “if” clause and its conclusion is not marked. καί is taken as “also”, beginning the conclusion: if it stays here, then here is where it changes. The whole could also be one long “if” clause with nothing after it.
notes.other_reading: If it stays here and changes here and is dissolved into what is its own

notes.note: “Into its own things”: its own proper constituents. No noun such as “parts” or “elements” is added, since “elements” comes in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: into its own constituents

notes.note: “And yours”: the elements belong to the universe and to you alike.
notes.other_reading: which are elements of the universe and yours too

notes.note: A homely word for muttering in complaint. The elements are said not to do it.
notes.other_reading: and do not complain

check.greek: εἰ ὧδε μένει καὶ μεταβάλλει ὧδε
check.note: The English begins the main clause at καὶ (“it also changes”). The Greek could also be one long “if” clause, which would leave no main clause.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “If it stays here, it also changes here”. Read this way the Greek gives a complete sentence, with καὶ as “also” and the second “here” answering the first; the note records the reading that leaves the “if” unfinished.

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why shouldest thou?
passages.russian: Умершее не выпадает за пределы мироздания. Если оно остаётся здесь, то здесь же и меняется и распадается на то, что ему принадлежит, — на стихии мироздания и твои. И они тоже меняются и не ропщут.

passages.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ νῦν μὲν ἱππάριον ἔπλασε, συγχέασα δὲ τοῦτο εἰς δενδρύφιον συνεχρήσατο τῇ ὕλῃ αὐτοῦ· εἶτα εἰς ἀνθρωπάριον· εἶτα εἰς ἄλλο τι· ἕκαστον δὲ τούτων πρὸς ὀλίγιστον ὑπέστη. δεινὸν δὲ οὐδὲν τὸ διαλυθῆναι τῷ κιβωτίῳ, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ συμπαγῆναι ἀγαθόν.
passages.english: The nature of the whole, out of the whole of substance as if out of wax, at one moment shaped a little horse; then it melted that down and used its material for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else. Each of these existed for the briefest time. But there is nothing terrible for a little box in being taken apart, just as there is nothing good in its being put together.

notes.greek: ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ
notes.note: οὐσία is the stuff of which everything is made; “substance” is used for it here and in the neighbouring passages. ὅλης may mean “the whole of” or “universal”.
notes.other_reading: out of the universal substance, as out of wax

notes.note: A diminutive, like δενδρύφιον, ἀνθρωπάριον and κιβωτίῳ after it. It may suggest a wax figurine or simply belittle the thing; “little” is kept all four times.
notes.other_reading: a toy horse (then a toy tree, a toy man, a toy box)

notes.note: The tense is a simple past. It is read as narrative with νῦν μὲν (“at one moment”), but it could be the past tense that Greek uses for what always happens.
notes.other_reading: now shapes a little horse, then melts it down and uses its material

notes.note: Literally “having poured together”, that is, having blurred or destroyed the shape. With wax the English narrows this to “melted that down”; the Greek does not say whether the wax is melted or squashed.
notes.other_reading: having broken it up

notes.note: ὑπέστη is “came to exist” or “subsisted”; the superlative ὀλίγιστον is “for the very least time”.
notes.other_reading: each of these came into existence for a moment only

notes.note: The image shifts without warning from wax to a small box or chest, and the two verbs are joinery words (taken apart, fitted together). The dative is taken with “terrible”: nothing terrible for the box.
notes.other_reading: it is nothing terrible that the little chest should be broken up

notes.note: Neither half of this sentence has a verb in the Greek, so the tense is supplied. “Is” is used in both halves, since both are general statements.
notes.other_reading: just as there was nothing good in its being put together

check.note: The Greek word is a diminutive, “little box”, like the little horse, little tree and little human before it. The draft keeps those three diminutives and drops this one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for a little box”. The Greek word is a diminutive like the three before it, so the box should sound like one more of the small made things.

check.note: The Greek clause has no verb and so no tense. “Was” against the earlier “is” sets a past event against a present one, which the Greek does not do.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “just as there is nothing good in its being put together”. Neither half of the Greek sentence has a verb, so both are general statements and take the same tense.

check.note: The verb means to pour together, blur or break up a shape. “Melted” is drawn from the wax image; wax is as easily squashed as melted and the Greek does not say which.
check.decided: Declined: “melted that down” stands. The verb is literally “poured together”, which for wax is nearer to melting than to breaking up, and the suggested “again” has no word in the Greek. The note records that the Greek does not say how the shape is destroyed.

passages.casaubon: The nature of the universe, of the common substance of all things as it were of so much wax hath now perchance formed a horse; and then, destroying that figure, hath new tempered and fashioned the matter of it into the form and substance of a tree: then that again into the form and substance of a man: and then that again into some other. Now every one of these doth subsist but for a very little while. As for dissolution, if it be no grievous thing to the chest or trunk, to be joined together; why should it be more grievous to be put asunder?
passages.russian: Природа целого из всего вещества, словно из воска, в какой-то миг вылепила лошадку; потом расплавила её и употребила материал на деревце, потом на человечка, потом на что-то ещё. Каждое из них просуществовало кратчайшее время. Но для ящичка нет ничего страшного в том, что его разбирают, как нет ничего хорошего в том, что его собирают.

passages.greek:
Πάντα τὰ ὑποκείμενα τάχιστα μεταβαλεῖ καὶ ἤτοι ἐκθυμιαθήσεται, εἴπερ ἥνωται ἡ οὐσία, ἢ σκεδασθήσεται.

Ὁ διοικῶν λόγος οἶδε πῶς διακείμενος καὶ τί ποιεῖ καὶ ἐπὶ τίνος ὕλης.
passages.english:
All existing things will very quickly change, and either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered.

The reason that governs knows in what condition it acts, what it does, and on what material.

notes.note: Literally “the things lying under”: the things that are there, the objects that impressions are about, or the underlying material things. “Existing things” takes the widest sense and brings in no observer.
notes.other_reading: all underlying things; all material objects

notes.note: The verb is from burning incense: to be turned into fumes. The image is kept as “go up in vapour”.
notes.other_reading: will be burnt off as smoke

notes.greek: εἴπερ ἥνωται ἡ οὐσία, ἢ σκεδασθήσεται
notes.note: Two pictures of the world are set side by side: substance as one continuous thing, or a scattering (of atoms, though Marcus does not say so). εἴπερ can be a real “if” or nearly “since”; the English keeps it conditional.
notes.other_reading: since substance is unified; otherwise they will be dispersed

notes.note: λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary. διοικῶν is “managing, administering”; the Greek does not say what is governed, and the English does not supply it.
notes.other_reading: the reason that administers the universe

notes.note: Literally “being how disposed”: a participle with no verb of its own. It is taken with ποιεῖ, the one verb that serves all three questions, and “acts” is supplied from that verb. It could instead stand alone as a first thing known, the state reason itself is in.
notes.other_reading: knows what state it is in, what it is doing, and on what material

notes.note: ποιεῖ is both “does” and “makes”. “Does” is kept because the phrase that follows says “on what material”, not “out of”; “makes” is possible.
notes.other_reading: what it is making

check.note: The word means the things that underlie or exist: objects, the stuff of the world. The draft’s phrase brings in an observer and narrows the claim to what is seen.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “All existing things will very quickly change”. The Greek word means the things that are there and has no observer in it; the draft’s phrase brought one in and narrowed the claim.

check.note: The draft makes three separate things known: state, action, material. The participle can equally hang on the verb (“in what state it does what it does”), and the verb can also mean “makes”, which suits the “material” that follows.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “knows in what condition it acts, what it does, and on what material”. The participle has no verb of its own, so it is hung on the one verb in the sentence. “Does” and “on” are kept, since the Greek preposition means “on” and not “out of”; “makes” is recorded in a note.

passages.casaubon: All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be scattered and dispersed. As for that Rational Essence by which all things are governed, as it best understandeth itself, both its own disposition, and what it doth, and what matter it hath to do with and accordingly doth all things; so we that do not, no wonder, if we wonder at many things, the reasons whereof we cannot comprehend.

nearest.title: The reason that governs the whole

passages.russian:
Всё существующее очень скоро изменится и либо испарится, если вещество и впрямь едино, либо рассеется.

Управляющий разум знает, в каком состоянии он действует, что он делает и над каким материалом.

passages.greek: Ἐξ αἰτιώδους καὶ ὑλικοῦ συνέστηκα, οὐδέτερον δὲ τούτων εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθαρήσεται, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος ὑπέστη. οὐκοῦν καταταχθήσεται πᾶν μέρος ἐμὸν κατὰ μεταβολὴν εἰς μέρος τι τοῦ κόσμου καὶ πάλιν ἐκεῖνο εἰς ἕτερον μέρος τι τοῦ κόσμου μεταβαλεῖ καὶ ἤδη εἰς ἄπειρον. κατὰ τοιαύτην δὲ μεταβολὴν κἀγὼ ὑπέστην καὶ οἱ ἐμὲ γεννήσαντες καὶ ἐπανιόντι εἰς ἄλλο ἄπειρον. οὐδὲν γὰρ κωλύει οὕτως φάναι, κἂν κατὰ περιόδους πεπερασμένας ὁ κόσμος διοικῆται.
passages.english: I am made up of what is causal and what is material, and neither of these will perish into what is not, just as neither came to be out of what is not. So every part of me will be assigned, through change, to some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity. It was through a change of this kind that I too came to be, and my parents; and for anyone who goes back, the line runs on into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.

notes.note: Two neuter adjectives: “the causal” and “the material”, the Stoic pair of what acts or forms and what is acted on. They are kept as plain adjectives and not glossed as form and matter.
notes.other_reading: of a cause and of matter; of a formal and a material element

notes.note: τὸ μὴ ὂν is “what is not”. The plain phrase is kept and used again for ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος so that the symmetry shows.
notes.other_reading: will be destroyed into nothing

notes.note: “Came to exist, subsisted.” The same verb returns as ὑπέστην below; “came to be” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: arose; had its existence

notes.note: A word of ordering and posting: to be assigned to a place in a rank. “Assigned” keeps that.
notes.other_reading: will be distributed into; will be reduced to

notes.note: ἄπειρον is “the unlimited”, and the last sentence answers it with πεπερασμένας, “limited”, from the same root. “Infinity” here and “finite” there let the English show the link.
notes.other_reading: and so on without limit

notes.note: Literally “those who produced me”, from the verb used of a father or a mother having a child. In the plural it is an ordinary Greek way of saying “parents”, and the English uses that noun.
notes.other_reading: and those who brought me into being

notes.note: The dative participle means “for someone going back up”, that is, tracing the line of ancestors backwards. The Greek then says only “into another unlimited”, with no noun and no verb; the English supplies “the line runs on” so that the clause can stand, and “another infinity” adds no noun.
notes.other_reading: and so, tracing the line upwards, into another series without limit

notes.note: περίοδος is a circuit or recurring period, and the preposition is “in” or “by”: the governing goes cycle by cycle. This is taken as the Stoic teaching of world cycles, each with an end (from memory, unchecked). διοικῆται is the same verb of governing as in 6.5.
notes.other_reading: even if the universe is administered by periods that have a limit

check.note: The Greek says only “into another infinity”. “On” and “stretch” are added, and “on” suggests going forward when the direction is backward through the ancestors.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and, for one who goes back, into another infinity”. “On” and “stretch” are gone, but “series” is not taken, since it too would add a noun the Greek does not have. To keep one English word for the repeated Greek word, the earlier phrase now reads “and so on to infinity”.

check.note: The noun is the one for the recurring cycles of the world, and the preposition means “by” or “according to”. “Governed in limited periods” can be heard as “governed only for limited spells”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “governed in finite cycles”. “Cycles” removes the risk of hearing “only for limited spells”. “In” is kept because “governed by cycles” would make the cycles the governor, and “finite” answers “infinity” as the Greek word answers its opposite.

check.note: The draft’s verb is archaic and in English is said of a father only. The Greek plural covers both parents.
