check.decided: Accepted: the English now names both parents with the ordinary noun in place of the draft’s verb. The Greek plural is the usual phrase for a father and mother together, and the draft’s verb is archaic and said of a father only.

passages.casaubon: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature. Every part of mine then will by mutation be disposed into a certain part of the whole world, and that in time into another part; and so _in infinitum;_ by which kind of mutation, I also became what I am, and so did they that begot me, and they before them, and so upwards _in infinitum_. For so we may be allowed to speak, though the age and government of the world, be to some certain periods of time limited, and confined.
passages.russian: Я состою из причинного и вещественного, и ни то ни другое не погибнет, уйдя в небытие, точно так же как ни то ни другое не возникло из небытия. Поэтому всякая моя часть путём изменения будет отведена в какую-нибудь часть мироздания, а та, в свою очередь, изменится в другую часть мироздания, и так до бесконечности. Через подобное изменение возник и я, и мои родители; и для всякого, кто пойдёт назад, ряд тянется дальше, в другую бесконечность. Ведь ничто не мешает так говорить, даже если мироздание управляется конечными круговоротами.

passages.greek: Πᾶν τὸ ἔνυλον ἐναφανίζεται τάχιστα τῇ τῶν ὅλων οὐσίᾳ καὶ πᾶν αἴτιον εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων λόγον τάχιστα ἀναλαμβάνεται καὶ παντὸς μνήμη τάχιστα ἐγκαταχώννυται τῷ αἰῶνι.
passages.english: Everything material very quickly vanishes into the substance of the whole, and every cause is very quickly taken back up into the reason of the whole, and the memory of everything is very quickly buried in eternity.

notes.note: Literally “what is in matter”. It is taken as simply “material”.
notes.other_reading: everything embodied in matter

notes.note: “Disappears into”: the prefix ἐν gives the “into”. The same verb is used of the person in 4.14, and “vanish into” serves in both. τάχιστα comes three times and is “very quickly” each time.
notes.other_reading: is lost in

notes.note: “Every cause”, set against the material: the active, forming element in each thing. The bare word “cause” is kept.
notes.other_reading: everything causal; every formative principle

notes.note: “Is taken up” or “taken back”. “Taken back up” matches the rendering of ἀναληφθήσῃ in 4.14. τῶν ὅλων is plural (“of all things”) and is “the whole” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: is resumed into the reason of all things

notes.note: παντὸς can be neuter (“of everything”) or masculine (“of everyone”). After two neuters “everything” is kept.
notes.other_reading: the memory of everyone

notes.note: The verb is to bury under heaped earth, and “buried” keeps it. αἰών is the whole of time, “eternity” or “the ages”.
notes.other_reading: is covered over by the ages; is entombed in time

passages.casaubon: Whatsoever is material, doth soon vanish away into the common substance of the whole; and whatsoever is formal, or, whatsoever doth animate that which is material, is soon resumed into the common reason of the whole; and the fame and memory of anything, is soon swallowed up by the general age and duration of the whole.
passages.russian: Всё материальное очень быстро исчезает в веществе целого, и всякая причина очень быстро вбирается обратно в разум целого, и память обо всём очень быстро погребается в вечности.

passages.greek:
Ἐνυπέστης ὡς μέρος. ἐναφανισθήσῃ τῷ γεννήσαντι· μᾶλλον δὲ ἀναληφθήσῃ εἰς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ τὸν σπερματικὸν κατὰ μεταβολήν.

Πολλὰ λιβανωτοῦ βωλάρια ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ βωμοῦ· τὸ μὲν προκατέπεσεν, τὸ δʼ ὕστερον, διαφέρει δʼ οὐδέν.
passages.english:
You came to exist as a part within something. You will vanish into what gave birth to you; or rather, you will be taken back up into its seminal reason, through change.

Many little lumps of incense on the same altar: one fell earlier, another later, but it makes no difference.

notes.note: The verb is “you came to exist in (something)”, and the Greek does not name the something. “Within something” renders the prefix ἐν and no more; the next sentence says what the something is.
notes.other_reading: You have subsisted as a part.

notes.note: The participle can be masculine or neuter: “the one who gave birth to you” or “that which gave birth to you”. The English takes the neuter with “what”. The verb is the ordinary one for a father or a mother having a child.
notes.other_reading: into the one who gave birth to you; into the one who fathered you

notes.note: μᾶλλον δὲ corrects what was just said: not vanishing but being taken back. “Taken back up” is the same rendering as for this verb in 7.10.
notes.other_reading: or rather you will be received back into its generative reason by a change

notes.note: The Stoic term λόγος σπερματικός: reason as the seed from which things grow. “Seminal” is meant in its literal sense, “of seed”, so that λόγος stays “reason” and the seed stays in a single adjective. αὐτοῦ is “its” or “his”, following the choice made for τῷ γεννήσαντι.
notes.other_reading: into its generative reason; into his seminal reason

notes.note: A diminutive of βῶλος, a lump or clod: small lumps or grains of frankincense.
notes.other_reading: grains of incense

notes.note: “Fell down before”: either dropped onto the altar earlier, or collapsed (burnt down) sooner. The bare “fell earlier” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: one has burnt down sooner, another later

check.note: “Of a whole” is not in the Greek. The prefix of the verb says “within something”, and the next sentence names it; the addition explains the thought before Marcus does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “You came to exist as a part within something.” “Of a whole” named what the Greek leaves unnamed; “within something” gives the verb’s prefix and no more.

check.note: The participle can be masculine or neuter: “the one who produced you” or “that which produced you”. The English chooses the impersonal reading, and its verb is archaic.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what gave birth to you”, which removes the archaic verb. The choice of “what” over “the one who” was already recorded in a note and stays there, with the other reading given.

check.note: The Greek has a single adjective, “of seed” or “generative”. “The one that works as” is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “its seminal reason”, a single adjective as in the Greek, with no explanation folded in. “Seminal” is preferred to “generative” because it keeps the seed that the Greek adjective names; a note says it is meant literally. “Through change” also returns to the end of the sentence, where the Greek has it.

check.note: The particle after “one earlier, another later” marks a turn: “but”. “And” flattens the small contrast on which the sentence closes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but it makes no difference”. The Greek particle marks a small turn against “earlier” and “later”.

passages.casaubon: As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
passages.russian:
Ты возник как часть внутри чего-то. Ты исчезнешь в том, что тебя породило; вернее, через изменение ты будешь взят обратно в его семенной разум.

Много крупинок ладана на одном алтаре: одна упала раньше, другая позже, но разницы никакой.

passages.greek: Ὁ θάνατος τοιοῦτον, οἷον γένεσις, φύσεως μυστήριον· σύγκρισις ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν στοιχείων, εἰς ταὐτὰ λύσις. ὅλως δὲ οὐκ ἐφʼ ᾧ ἄν τις αἰσχυνθείη· οὐ γὰρ παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῷ νοερῷ ζῴῳ οὐδὲ παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κατασκευῆς.
passages.english: Death is the same kind of thing as birth, a mystery of nature: a combining out of the same elements, a dissolving into the same. And in short, it is not a thing anyone would be ashamed of: for it is not contrary to what follows in sequence for a living being with mind, nor contrary to the reason on which it is built.

notes.note: γένεσις is both “birth” and “coming to be” in general. Set beside death, it is taken as “birth”.
notes.other_reading: such a thing as coming into being

notes.note: μυστήριον is a secret rite, as in the mystery cults, not just a puzzle. “Mystery” is kept and the religious sense is left to this note.
notes.other_reading: one of nature’s secret rites

notes.greek: σύγκρισις ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν στοιχείων, εἰς ταὐτὰ λύσις
notes.note: It is open whether both nouns describe both events, or the combining is birth and the dissolving is death. The two phrases are left side by side as the Greek has them. From memory, unchecked: the wording of this clause is disputed and part of it may be an editor’s repair; the English translates what is printed.
notes.other_reading: the one a combining out of certain elements, the other a dissolving into those same elements

notes.note: A phrase that sums up: “in general”, “on the whole”, “in short”. With the “not” that follows it could also be heard as “not at all”.
notes.other_reading: and on the whole; and it is not at all a thing anyone would be ashamed of

notes.note: “Would be ashamed.” It is not obvious why death should be a matter of shame, and one might expect “distressed”. The English translates the word that stands.
notes.other_reading: not a thing to be embarrassed by

notes.greek: παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῷ νοερῷ ζῴῳ
notes.note: τὸ ἑξῆς is “what follows in sequence”: death is the next step in the series for such a being. The dative could also depend on ἑξῆς itself, giving “what follows from being such a creature”. νοερός is “of mind” in the glossary; “with mind” makes an English phrase.
notes.other_reading: not at odds with what follows from being a creature of mind

notes.note: λόγος is kept as “reason”, as in the glossary, though here it is close to “plan” or “rationale”; “principle” is avoided because this translation keeps that word for δόγμα. κατασκευή is the way a thing is constructed, and “it” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: the plan of its makeup; the principle of its construction

check.greek: παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῷ νοερῷ ζῴῳ
check.note: “In order for a living being” reads at first as the start of a purpose clause, and the reader has to go back. The sense is that death is not out of the due sequence for such a creature.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it is not contrary to what follows in sequence for a living being with mind”. The misleading “in order for” is gone. “Contrary to” is kept rather than “out of sequence” because the Greek repeats the same preposition in the next phrase and the English repeats it too.

check.note: Here the word means the principle or plan on which the creature is built. “The reason of its constitution” is not clear English and may be heard as “the reason for”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the reason on which it is built”. The clearer shape of the suggestion is taken, but the Greek word stays “reason” as in the glossary, where “principle” is the word for a different Greek term.

check.note: “Altogether” at the head of a sentence is stiff and a little unclear today. The Greek means “in general” or “in short”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And in short”. The Greek phrase sums up, and “altogether” at the head of a sentence is not clear English today.

passages.casaubon: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.
passages.russian: Смерть — того же рода, что и рождение, тайна природы: соединение из тех же стихий, распад на те же самые. И вообще, это не то, чего кто-нибудь стал бы стыдиться: ведь это не противоречит тому, что следует по порядку для живого существа, наделённого умом, и не противоречит разуму, на котором оно построено.

passages.greek: Πορεύομαι διὰ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν, μέχρι πεσὼν ἀναπαύσομαι ἐναποπνεύσας μὲν τούτῳ, ἐξ οὖ καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀναπνέω, πεσὼν δὲ ἐπὶ τούτῳ, ἐξ οὗ καὶ τὸ σπερμάτιον ὁ πατήρ μου συνέλεξε καὶ τὸ αἱμάτιον ἡ μήτηρ καὶ τὸ γαλάκτιον ἡ τροφός· ἐξ οὗ καθ’ ἡμέραν τοσούτοις ἔτεσι βόσκομαι καὶ ἀρδεύομαι· ὃ φέρει με πατοῦντα καὶ εἰς τοσαῦτα ἀποχρώμενον αὐτῷ.
passages.english: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest, breathing my last into that from which I draw breath every day, and falling on that from which my father gathered the bit of seed, my mother the bit of blood and my nurse the bit of milk; from which every day, for so many years, I have been fed and watered; which bears me as I tread on it and make free use of it for so many purposes.

notes.note: “Through the things according to nature”: these may be the events, the acts or the stages of a natural life. The vague “things” is kept.
notes.other_reading: travelling by the road that accords with nature

notes.note: “Having breathed out into this”, with the sense of breathing one’s last. It plays against ἀναπνέω, “breathe in”, rendered “draw breath”. The “this” is the air, which the Greek does not name; the English leaves it unnamed.
notes.other_reading: giving back the last breath to the air

notes.note: A slip in the digitised text for ἐξ οὗ, “from which”, as twice below. It is read so.
The second “this” is the earth, again unnamed, and left so. πεσὼν repeats the earlier πεσὼν, so “fall” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: and falling upon the earth

notes.note: A diminutive, like αἱμάτιον and γαλάκτιον after it: a little seed, a little blood, a little milk. “The bit of” serves for all three; the article could also be possessive (“his”, “her”).
notes.other_reading: his drop of seed, her drop of blood, her drop of milk

notes.note: One verb, “gathered”, serves father, mother and nurse. The thought is that each drew the seed, blood and milk from the earth.
notes.other_reading: collected

notes.note: Words used of livestock and of fields: “pastured and irrigated”. “Fed and watered” keeps a trace of that. The Greek present with “for so many years” covers the whole span up to now, which English says with “have been”.
notes.other_reading: have grazed and been watered

notes.note: The verb is “tread, walk on” and also “trample”. “Tread on” is kept. With the harsher sense of the next verb as well, the clause would say that the earth bears the speaker although he tramples on it and misuses it.
notes.other_reading: which bears one who tramples on it and misuses it for so many purposes

notes.note: The verb ranges from “use to the full” to “misuse, abuse”. “Make free use of” leans to the first, which suits “for so many purposes”, but leaves a hint of the second.
notes.other_reading: and misuse it in so many ways

check.note: The verb can mean “use to the full” but also “misuse” or “abuse”. Beside the word for treading or trampling, the clause may say that the earth bears the speaker although he tramples on it and abuses it; the English takes the mild sense of both words.
check.decided: Declined: “tread on it and make free use of it” stands. The verb’s first sense is “use to the full”, and “for so many purposes” fits use better than abuse, in a sentence that has been listing what is taken from the earth. The harsher reading of both words is recorded in the notes, one of them new.

check.note: A Greek present with a span of time (“for so many years”) is an English perfect. The present tense with that phrase is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have been fed and watered”. A Greek present with a span of time covers the whole span up to now, which English says with the perfect.

passages.casaubon: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink. And lastly, which beareth me that tread upon it, and beareth with me that so many ways do abuse it, or so freely make use of it, so many ways to so many ends.
passages.russian: Я иду через то, что согласно с природой, пока не упаду и не отдохну, испустив последний вздох в то, чем дышу каждый день, и упав на то, из чего мой отец собрал толику семени, мать — толику крови, кормилица — толику молока; из чего каждый день, столько лет, меня кормят и поят; что носит меня, когда я ступаю по нему и вволю пользуюсь им для стольких целей.

passages.greek: Ἡ φύσις ἐστόχασται ἑκάστου οὐδέν τι ἔλασσον τῆς ἀπολήξεως ἢ τῆς ἀρχῆς τε καὶ διεξαγωγῆς,
passages.english: Nature has aimed at the ending of each thing no less than at its beginning and its course.

notes.note: Perfect of a verb from archery, “to aim at a target”, with its objects in the genitive. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: has had regard to; has had in view

notes.note: Masculine or neuter: “of each thing” or “of each person”. The wider “each thing” is taken.
notes.other_reading: the ending of each person

notes.note: “Ceasing, leaving off”: the point where a thing stops.
notes.other_reading: its cessation

notes.note: “A carrying through”: the passage between beginning and end. It can also mean the conduct of a life.
notes.other_reading: its continuance; the way its life is passed

notes.note: The Greek as given stops at a comma, in the middle of a sentence, because the section is cut here; the chapter goes on with a comparison. The English closes with a full stop and supplies nothing of what follows.
notes.other_reading: than at its beginning and its course,

part.left_out: ὡς ὁ ἀναβάλλων τὴν σφαῖραν· τί οὖν ἀγαθὸν τῷ σφαιρίῳ ἀναφερομένῳ ἢ κακὸν καταφερομένῳ ἢ καὶ πεπτωκότι; τί δὲ ἀγαθὸν τῇ πομφόλυγι συνεστώσῃ ἢ κακὸν διαλυθείσῃ; τὰ ὅμοια δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ λύχνου.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.18 after the chapter's first clause and begins its 8.19 with the ball-thrower and the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
passages.russian: Природа нацелилась на окончание каждой вещи не меньше, чем на её начало и течение.

passages.greek: Ἐννοεῖν συνεχῶς πόσοι μὲν ἰατροὶ ἀποτεθνήκασι, πολλάκις τὰς ὀφρῦς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀρρώστων συσπάσαντες· πόσοι δὲ μαθηματικοί, ἄλλων θανάτους ὥς τι μέγα προειπόντες· πόσοι δὲ φιλόσοφοι, περὶ θανάτου ἢ ἀθανασίας μυρία διατεινάμενοι· πόσοι δὲ ἀριστεῖς, πολλοὺς ἀποκτείναντες· πόσοι δὲ τύραννοι, ἐξουσίᾳ ψυχῶν μετὰ δεινοῦ φρυάγματος ὡς ἀθάνατοι κεχρημένοι· πόσαι δὲ πόλεις ὅλαι, ἵν’ οὕτως εἴπω, τεθνήκασιν, Ἑλίκη καὶ Πομπήιοι καὶ Ἡρκλᾶνον καὶ ἄλλαι ἀναρίθμητοι. ἔπιθι δὲ καὶ ὅσους οἶδας, ἄλλον ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ· ὁ μὲν τοῦτον κηδεύσας εἶτα ἐξετάθη, ὁ δὲ ἐκεῖνον, πάντα δὲ ἐν βραχεῖ. τὸ γὰρ ὅλον, κατιδεῖν ἀεὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα ὡς ἐφήμερα καὶ εὐτελῆ καὶ ἐχθὲς μὲν μυξάριον, αὔριον δὲ τάριχος ἢ τέφρα. τὸ ἀκαριαῖον οὖν τοῦτο τοῦ χρόνου κατὰ φύσιν διελθεῖν καὶ ἵλεων καταλῦσαι, ὡς ἂν εἰ ἐλαία πέπειρος γενομένη ἔπιπτεν, εὐφημοῦσα τὴν ἐνεγκοῦσαν καὶ χάριν εἰδυῖα τῷ φύσαντι δένδρῳ.
passages.english: Keep in mind continually how many doctors have died, after knitting their brows time and again over the sick; how many astrologers, after foretelling other people’s deaths as if that were something great; how many philosophers, after insisting on countless things about death or immortality; how many champions, after killing many; how many tyrants, after using their power over lives with terrible arrogance, as if they were immortal; and how many whole cities have, so to speak, died: Helice and Pompeii and Herculaneum and countless others. Go over as well all those you know, one after another. One buried this person and was then laid out, another buried that one, and all of it in a short time. For the sum of it is this: always see human things as lasting a day and cheap, yesterday a little slime, tomorrow a mummy or ash. So pass through this instant of time in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace, as an olive might fall when it has grown ripe, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it.

notes.note: The verb is an infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. The English uses the bare command, which names no “you” either; the same holds for the later infinitives in the passage.
notes.other_reading: To keep in mind continually

notes.note: At this date the word commonly means astrologers, and foretelling deaths fits that. It can also mean mathematicians or men of learning.
notes.other_reading: mathematicians

notes.note: The verb is to maintain a thing with all one’s force, from a root meaning “stretch”. The Greek says only “countless things”, with no word for arguments, and the English takes the verb as vehement assertion.
notes.other_reading: after straining over countless arguments about death or immortality

notes.note: The word names those who win the prize for valour, the best fighters. The killing that follows shows that the field is war.
notes.other_reading: the bravest fighters

notes.note: ψυχῶν can be “lives” or “souls”. The English takes the power of life and death.
notes.other_reading: their authority over souls

notes.note: φρύαγμα is first the snorting of a spirited horse, then insolent pride. The English gives the sense and loses the horse.
notes.other_reading: with a terrible snorting

notes.note: Literally “was stretched out”, that is, laid out as a corpse.
notes.other_reading: was then stretched out

notes.note: The Greek sets “this one” against “that one” and leaves the verb to be carried over. “That one” may be a different dead person, as the English has it, or the first burier, which makes a chain of burials.
notes.other_reading: and another buried him

notes.note: Here the phrase is adverbial, “on the whole, in sum”, not “the whole” of the glossary.
notes.other_reading: For, in a word,

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for mucus or slime. It points to the seed a human being starts from; the English keeps the plain image.
notes.other_reading: a drop of mucus

notes.note: The word means fish or meat preserved in salt, and is also used of an embalmed body. Beside “ash” the English takes the body, as “a mummy”, and loses the kitchen sense with its contempt.
notes.other_reading: a piece of salt fish

notes.note: καταλῦσαι is to unyoke at the end of a day’s journey, to put up for the night, and so to end life. ἵλεων ranges from “gracious, kindly” to “cheerful”; “with good grace” is meant to hold the willing, ungrudging mood.
notes.other_reading: and come to your lodging cheerful

notes.note: Literally “her who bore it”, with no noun. The phrase is a common way of naming the land that bore one, so “the earth” is supplied; “nature” is also possible.
notes.other_reading: speaking well of her who bore it

check.note: The Greek is one word, “champions” or “the bravest fighters”. “In war” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many champions, after killing many”. The Greek has the one word, and the killing that follows already shows the field.

check.note: The verb means to insist, to maintain something with all one’s force, not to labour through arguments. “Arguments” is supplied: the Greek has only “countless things”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “after insisting on countless things about death or immortality”. The verb is one of forceful assertion and the Greek has no word for arguments; the earlier rendering is kept in a note.

check.note: The verb has present sense, “all those you know”. “Have known” narrows it to acquaintances who are gone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all those you know”. The Greek verb has present meaning and does not say whether the people are known in person or only known of.

check.note: “In turn” is not in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and was then laid out”. The Greek has only “then”.

check.note: The pronoun can point back to the first burier, which makes a chain: one buried this person and was laid out, and another buried him. “That one” reads as an unrelated person.
check.decided: Declined: “another buried that one” stands. The Greek sets “this one” against “that one” after “one” and “another”, the ordinary way of naming two separate cases, and the English keeps the same two words. The chain reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: The word means something preserved in salt: salt fish, or a mummy. The English chooses the embalmed body and drops the contemptuous kitchen sense that goes with “a little slime”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a mummy”, one blunt word in place of “an embalmed corpse”. Set beside “ash”, the word names one of the two ends of a body, so the body is kept in the text and the kitchen sense is given in the note.

check.note: The adjective describes the person’s mood: cheerful, serene, in good humour. “Graciously” suggests good manners, and “journey” is only implied by the verb, which means to unyoke, to stop and rest.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “come to rest with good grace”. “Journey” is dropped because the verb only says to unyoke and stop. “With good grace” gives the willing, ungrudging mood, which suits the olive that blesses and thanks as it falls; “cheerful” stays in the note.

check.note: The Greek says only “her who bore it”, a feminine participle with no noun. “The earth” is supplied; nature is also possible.
check.decided: Declined: “the earth that bore it” stands. The feminine participle without a noun is a set Greek way of naming the land that bore someone, and a bare “her” would leave an English reader with no one to refer it to. The note says that “the earth” is supplied and gives the literal wording.

passages.casaubon: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after that in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable are dead and gone. Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time. For herein lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile, and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes. Thus must thou according to truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.
passages.russian: Постоянно держи в мыслях, сколько умерло врачей, много раз хмуривших брови над больными; сколько астрологов, предсказывавших чужую смерть, словно это нечто великое; сколько философов, твердивших бесчисленное множество вещей о смерти или бессмертии; сколько бойцов-победителей, убивших многих; сколько тиранов, с ужасным высокомерием пользовавшихся властью над жизнями, словно сами они бессмертны; и сколько целых городов, так сказать, умерло: Гелика, Помпеи, Геркуланум и бесчисленные другие. Перебери ещё и всех, кого знаешь, одного за другим. Один похоронил этого и потом сам лёг мёртвым, другой похоронил того — и всё это за короткое время. Ведь суть в том, чтобы всегда смотреть на человеческое как на однодневное и дешёвое: вчера — капля слизи, завтра — мумия или пепел. Так пройди это мгновение времени согласно с природой и обрети покой с лёгким сердцем, как упала бы созревшая олива, с добрым словом о земле, что её родила, и с благодарностью дереву, что её взрастило.

passages.greek: Ἐννόει συνεχῶς παντοίους ἀνθρώπους καὶ παντοίων μὲν ἐπιτηδευμάτων, παντοδαπῶν δὲ ἐθνῶν τεθνεῶτας, ὥστε κατιέναι τοῦτο μέχρι Φιλιστίωνος καὶ Φοίβου καὶ Ὀριγανίωνος. μέτιθι νῦν ἐπὶ τὰ ἄλλα φῦλα· ἐκεῖ δὴ μεταβαλεῖν ἡμᾶς δεῖ ὅπου τοσοῦτοι μὲν δεινοὶ ῥήτορες, τοσοῦτοι δὲ σεμνοὶ φιλόσοφοι, Ἡράκλειτος, Πυθαγόρας, Σωκράτης, τοσοῦτοι δὲ ἥρωες πρότερον, τοσοῦτοι δὲ ὕστερον στρατηγοί, τύραννοι· ἐπὶ τούτοις δὲ Εὔδοξος, Ἵππαρχος, Ἀρχιμήδης, ἄλλαι φύσεις ὀξεῖαι, μεγαλόφρονες, φιλόπονοι, πανοῦργοι, αὐθάδεις, αὐτῆς τῆς ἐπικήρου καὶ ἐφημέρου τῶν ἀνθρώπων ζωῆς χλευασταί, οἷον Μένιππος καὶ ὅσοι τοιοῦτοι. περὶ πάντων τούτων ἐννόει ὅτι πάλαι κεῖνται· τί οὖν τοῦτο δεινὸν αὐτοῖς; τί δαὶ τοῖς μηδ’ ὀνομαζομένοις ὅλως; ἓν ὧδε πολλοῦ ἄξιον, τὸ μετ’ ἀληθείας καὶ δικαιοσύνης εὐμενῆ τοῖς ψεύσταις καὶ ἀδίκοις διαβιοῦν.
passages.english: Keep in mind continually that people of every kind, of every kind of occupation and from every sort of nation, are dead, so that this thought comes down as far as Philistion and Phoebus and Origanion. Now pass on to the other classes. That is the place we must move to, where there are so many formidable orators, so many grave philosophers, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates, so many heroes earlier, so many generals and tyrants later; and besides these Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, other natures that were sharp, great-minded, hard-working, unscrupulous, self-willed, mockers of human life itself, which is perishable and lasts a day, such as Menippus and all of his kind. About all of these, keep in mind that they have long been lying dead. What, then, is terrible in this for them? And what for those who are not even named at all? One thing here is worth a great deal: to live life through with truth and justice, kindly towards the liars and the unjust.

notes.note: The construction is loose. “This” is taken as the subject, and “thought” is supplied to say what comes down: the review of the dead reaches these three names. It can also be “so as to go down in this as far as”.
notes.other_reading: so as to come down in this as far as Philistion

notes.note: Three people who cannot be identified here, presumably recently dead and of no standing, so that the review reaches down to the present and to the obscure (from memory, unchecked).
φῦλα is “tribes, races”. Here it is used of kinds of people (orators, philosophers, heroes, generals) and not of nations, so the English says “classes”.
notes.other_reading: the other tribes

notes.note: The verb is the one for “change” used in other passages; here it is a change of place. It can mean that everyone must in the end go where these dead are, or only that the review must now move on to them; “move to” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: must change over to that place

notes.note: δεινός of a speaker is “clever, formidable”. The same word comes back below as “terrible” (τί οὖν τοῦτο δεινὸν), and the echo may be meant; English cannot hold both with one word.
notes.other_reading: so many clever speakers

notes.note: Only “sharp” is marked as feminine and so tied to “natures”. The adjectives after it have one form for masculine and feminine and may instead name further kinds of people.
notes.other_reading: other sharp natures, and the great-minded, the hard-working, the unscrupulous, the self-willed

notes.note: Literally “ready to do anything”. It is usually a word of blame (unscrupulous, knavish), which the English follows, and sometimes a word for clever resource.
notes.other_reading: ready for anything

notes.note: Menippus was a Cynic writer known for mockery (from memory, unchecked). The genitive before it makes human life itself the thing mocked.
notes.other_reading: scoffers at this very life of human beings, perishable and short as it is, such as Menippus

notes.note: The verb is simply “lie”, the regular word for the dead lying in the ground. “Dead” is added in the English to make that plain.
notes.other_reading: they have long been lying there

check.note: The same imperative opens the chapter as “Keep thinking of” and returns here as “keep in mind”. The opening also loses the adverb “continually”.
check.decided: Accepted: the opening now reads “Keep in mind continually that people of every kind”, and so on to “are dead”, so that the one Greek verb is “keep in mind” both times and “continually” is restored. The Greek participle “dead” after this verb is given as a that-clause.

check.note: A reader cannot tell what “goes down”. The sense is that the list comes right down to recent or lesser people.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “so that this thought comes down as far as”. The Greek has only “this”, which points to what is being kept in mind, so “thought” is supplied in place of “the list”, and the note says so.

check.note: After “every sort of nation” a reader takes “tribes” as more peoples. Here the word means classes or kinds of people: orators, philosophers, heroes, generals.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Now pass on to the other classes”. What follows is a list of callings, not of peoples; “tribes” is kept in the note.

check.greek: ἐκεῖ δὴ μεταβαλεῖν ἡμᾶς δεῖ ὅπου
check.note: “Change over to” is unclear English. The verb means to shift one’s place, and it can mean that the living must go where the dead are or only that the thought must move on to them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is now “move to” and the clause begins “That is the place”. “Too” is not added because the Greek has no word for it. “Move to” leaves open, as the Greek does, whether dying or only the next step of the review is meant, and the note sets out both.

check.note: The word is a term of blame: unscrupulous, crafty, a rogue. “Ready for anything” sounds like praise.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unscrupulous”. The word is ordinarily one of blame and stands next to “self-willed”, another word of blame; the literal sense is kept in the note.

check.greek: αὐτῆς τῆς ἐπικήρου καὶ ἐφημέρου τῶν ἀνθρώπων ζωῆς
check.note: The pronoun means “itself”: mockers of human life itself. “This very” points at something, which the Greek does not.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “mockers of human life itself, perishable and lasting a day”.

check.note: The Greek says only that they have long been lying, that is, in the ground. “Dead” is supplied.
check.decided: Declined: “they have long been lying dead” stands. The Greek verb “lie” is the regular word for the dead, which English “lie” alone does not convey, and “in the ground” would be a supplement of the same size. The note records that “dead” is added.

passages.casaubon: Let the several deaths of men of all sorts, and of all sorts of professions, and of all sort of nations, be a perpetual object of thy thoughts,... so that thou mayst even come down to Philistio, Phœbus, and Origanion. Pass now to other generations. Thither shall we after many changes, where so many brave orators are; where so many grave philosophers; Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates. Where so many heroes of the old times; and then so many brave captains of the latter times; and so many kings. After all these, where Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes; where so many other sharp, generous, industrious, subtile, peremptory dispositions; and among others, even they, that have been the greatest scoffers and deriders of the frailty and brevity of this our human life; as Menippus, and others, as many as there have been such as he. Of all these consider, that they long since are all dead, and gone. And what do they suffer by it! Nay they that have not so much as a name remaining, what are they the worse for it? One thing there is, and that only, which is worth our while in this world, and ought by us much to be esteemed; and that is, according to truth and righteousness, meekly and lovingly to converse with false, and unrighteous men.
passages.russian: Постоянно держи в уме, что умерли люди всякого рода, всяких занятий и из всевозможных народов, так что эта мысль доходит вплоть до Филистиона, Феба и Ориганиона. Теперь перейди к другим разрядам. Туда нам предстоит переселиться, где столько грозных ораторов, столько важных философов — Гераклит, Пифагор, Сократ, — столько героев прежде, столько полководцев и тиранов после; а кроме них Евдокс, Гиппарх, Архимед, другие натуры — острые, высокого ума, трудолюбивые, бессовестные, своевольные, насмешники над самой человеческой жизнью, тленной и однодневной, такие как Менипп и все ему подобные. Обо всех них помни, что они давно лежат мёртвыми. Что же в этом страшного для них? А для тех, кого даже не называют вовсе? Одно здесь стоит многого: прожить жизнь в истине и справедливости, благожелательно к лжецам и несправедливым.

passages.greek:
Αἱ πάλαι συνήθεις λέξεις νῦν γλωσσήματα· οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν πάλαι πολυυμνήτων νῦν τρόπον τινὰ γλωσσήματά ἐστι, Κάμιλλος, Καίσων, Οὐόλεσος, Δέντατος, κατ’ ὀλίγον δὲ καὶ Σκιπίων καὶ Κάτων, εἶτα καὶ Αὔγουστος, εἶτα καὶ Ἁδριανὸς καὶ Ἁντωνῖνος· ἐξίτηλα γὰρ πάντα καὶ μυθώδη ταχὺ γίνεται, ταχὺ δὲ καὶ παντελὴς λήθη κατέχωσεν. καὶ ταῦτα λέγω ἐπὶ τῶν θαυμαστῶς πως λαμψάντων· οἱ γὰρ λοιποὶ ἅμα τῷ ἐκπνεῦσαι ʽἄιστοι, ἄπυστοιʼ. τί δὲ καὶ ἔστιν ὅλως τὸ ἀείμνηστον; ὅλον κενόν. τί οὖν ἐστι περὶ ὃ δεῖ σπουδὴν εἰσφέρεσθαι; ἓν τοῦτο, διάνοια δικαία καὶ πράξεις κοινωνικαὶ καὶ λόγος, οἷος μήποτε διαψεύσασθαι, καὶ διάθεσις ἀσπαζομένη πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον ὡς ἀναγκαῖον, ὡς γνώριμον, ὡς ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς τοιαύτης καὶ πηγῆς ῥέον.

Ἑκὼν σεαυτὸν τῇ Κλωθοῖ συνεπιδίδου παρέχων συννῆσαι, οἷστισί ποτε πράγμασι βούλεται.
passages.english:
Expressions that were once in ordinary use are now obsolete words. So too the names of those who were once much sung are now, in a way, obsolete words: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Dentatus, and little by little Scipio and Cato too, then Augustus too, then Hadrian and Antoninus too. For all things quickly fade and turn into tales, and quickly too complete forgetting buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way; for the rest, the moment they have breathed their last, are “unseen, unheard of”. And what is everlasting remembrance at all? All of it empty. What then is there that one should put serious effort into? This one thing: thought that is just, actions that are social, speech such as never to lie, and a disposition that welcomes everything that happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from an origin and spring of that kind.

Willingly join in giving yourself over to Clotho, and let her spin you together with whatever events she wishes.

notes.note: A grammarian’s term: obsolete or rare words that need a gloss. “Obsolete words” is used both times; the need for a gloss is not carried over.
notes.other_reading: old words that need explaining

notes.note: “Little by little” or “after a little”: the later names are sliding the same way as the early ones.
notes.other_reading: and soon Scipio and Cato too

notes.note: An aorist, which can state a general truth (“buries”) or a completed fact. The English takes the general truth, in line with the present tense before it.
notes.other_reading: complete forgetting has buried them

notes.note: Two Homeric words, marked as a quotation in the edition; they appear to come from the Odyssey, said of the lost Odysseus (from memory, unchecked). The second is “not heard of, of whom there is no news”.
notes.other_reading: “out of sight, out of hearing”

notes.note: Either “the whole of it is empty” or “wholly empty”. The English says “All of it” so that the answer picks up “at all” in the question, as the Greek ὅλον picks up ὅλως.
notes.other_reading: Wholly empty.

notes.note: “Social” is the settled word for κοινωνικός in this translation. It means directed to the community and its good, not sociable.
notes.other_reading: actions for the common good

notes.note: λόγος here is speech, not the faculty of reason, as the verb shows. The verb is middle, “to lie, to deceive”; it could be stretched to “to be mistaken”.
notes.other_reading: and reason such as never to be deceived

notes.note: Literally “from such a beginning and spring”. “Such” may mean of the same kind as the event itself (necessary, familiar), or may point to an origin already known to the writer.
notes.other_reading: as flowing from an origin and spring of the same kind as itself

notes.note: The prefix adds “together with”: to join in the giving, that is, to work with Clotho and not merely submit. It can also be heard as only strengthening the verb.
notes.other_reading: Willingly give yourself over to Clotho

notes.note: Clotho is one of the three Fates; her name means the Spinner. The verb is “to spin together with”: a person’s thread is spun in with the events.
notes.other_reading: offering yourself to be woven into whatever events she wishes

check.note: One Greek word, meaning an obsolete word that needs a gloss, is given as a five-word definition, twice. The explanation is folded into the text.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “obsolete words” in both places. The one Greek word is given by a short phrase and the explanation moves to the note.

check.note: The related noun is “tale” in two other passages of this section; here the adjective becomes “legend”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “quickly fade and turn into tales”, so that the word matches “tale” for the related noun elsewhere in the section.

check.note: The aorist states a general truth. “Has buried them” reads as one past event.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and quickly too complete forgetting buries them”. This past form is regularly used in Greek for a general truth, and it stands beside a present; the other reading is in the note.

check.greek: τί δὲ καὶ ἔστιν ὅλως τὸ ἀείμνηστον; ὅλον κενόν
check.note: The adverb means “at all”, not “in any case”, and the answer echoes it. The echo is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And what is everlasting remembrance at all? All of it empty.” The Greek answer repeats the root of the adverb in the question, and “at all” with “All of it” lets that be heard.

check.note: “Social” now reads as sociable. The Greek means acts done for the community, for the common good.
check.decided: Declined: “actions that are social” stands. “Social” is the rendering settled for this Greek word across the translation, and nothing in this passage’s argument calls for another. A note now says that it means directed to the community.

check.note: The Greek says “such an origin and spring”. “The same kind” makes the reader ask the same as what, and the first noun is an origin or beginning, not a second word for a spring.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as flowing from an origin and spring of that kind”. The first noun is a beginning, not a second spring, and the Greek says “such”, not “the same”.

check.note: The prefix says “join in giving”, that is, co-operate with her. The English drops it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Willingly join in giving yourself over to Clotho”. The prefix is given its weight, and a note records the reading without it.

passages.casaubon: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is vanity. What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou thyself and all things are. Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.
passages.russian:
Выражения, некогда обиходные, теперь — устаревшие слова. Так и имена тех, кого когда-то много воспевали, теперь в некотором роде устаревшие слова: Камилл, Цезон, Волез, Дентат, а понемногу и Сципион, и Катон, затем и Август, затем и Адриан, и Антонин. Ведь всё быстро выцветает и превращается в сказку, и быстро же его погребает полное забвение. И это я говорю о тех, кто сиял каким-то удивительным образом; а остальные, едва испустив дух, — «незримы, безвестны». Да и что такое вообще вечная память? Всё это пусто. Так к чему же стоит прилагать серьёзные усилия? Лишь к одному: к справедливой мысли, общественным действиям, речи, которая никогда не солжёт, и расположению, которое приветствует всё происходящее как необходимое, как знакомое, как текущее из такого начала и источника.

Добровольно участвуй в том, чтобы отдать себя Клото, и пусть она спрядёт тебя с какими ей угодно событиями.

passages.greek: Σατυρίωνα ἰδὼν Σωκρατικὸν φαντάζου ἢ Εὐτύχην ἢ Ὑμένα, καὶ Εὐφράτην ἰδὼν Εὐτυχίωνα ἢ Σιλουανὸν φαντάζου, καὶ Ἀλκίφρονα Τροπαιοφόρον φαντάζου, καὶ Σευῆρον ἰδὼν Κρίτωνα ἢ Ξενοφῶντα φαντάζου, καὶ εἰς σεαυτὸν ἀπιδὼν τῶν Καισάρων τινὰ φαντάζου, καὶ ἐφ’ ἑκάστου τὸ ἀνάλογον. εἶτα συμπροσπιπτέτω σοι· ποῦ οὖν ἐκεῖνοι; οὐδαμοῦ ἢ ὁπουδή. οὕτως γὰρ συνεχῶς θεάσῃ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα καπνὸν καὶ τὸ μηδέν, μάλιστα ἐὰν συμμνημονεύσῃς ὅτι τὸ ἅπαξ μεταβαλὸν οὐκέτι ἔσται ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ χρόνῳ. τί οὖν ἐντείνῃ; τί δ’ οὐκ ἀρκεῖ σοι τὸ βραχὺ τοῦτο κοσμίως διαπερᾶσαι;
passages.english: When you see Satyrion, picture Socraticus or Eutyches or Hymen; and when you see Euphrates, picture Eutychion or Silvanus; and with Alciphron picture Tropaeophorus; and when you see Severus, picture Crito or Xenophon; and when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars; and with each person the one who corresponds. Then let this come to you along with it: where, then, are those people? Nowhere, or wherever it may be. For in this way you will continually look on human things as smoke and nothing, especially if you remember along with it that what has once changed will not exist any more in boundless time. Why then do you strain? Why is it not enough for you to get across this short stretch in good order?

notes.greek: Σωκρατικὸν φαντάζου ἢ Εὐτύχην ἢ Ὑμένα
notes.note: Σωκρατικὸν can be a man’s name, Socraticus, or “a Socratic” (a follower of Socrates). The English takes it as a name and the two “or” as a list of three, like the pairs of plain names that follow. The words can also be read as a Socratic who is then named as one of two men.
notes.other_reading: picture a Socratic, either Eutyches or Hymen

notes.note: The verb belongs with φαντασία, “impression”: form the impression of, call up the image of. “Picture” is used throughout.
notes.other_reading: call up the impression of

notes.note: Here the Greek leaves out “when you see”; the English marks that with the shorter “with”. Most of the people named in this passage cannot be identified here; Crito and Xenophon were followers of Socrates.
notes.other_reading: and Alciphron, picture Tropaeophorus

notes.note: The second word is “wherever, no matter where”: either nowhere, or somewhere that does not matter.
notes.other_reading: Nowhere, or who knows where.

notes.greek: οὐκέτι ἔσται ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ χρόνῳ
notes.note: οὐκέτι is “no longer”. The boundless time is the endless time still to come.
notes.other_reading: will never be again in all the endless time

notes.note: As given, “why do you strain yourself?”. Other editions are recalled as printing a different text at this point (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands here.
notes.other_reading: Why then are you so tense?

notes.note: The verb is “to cross over, to get to the other side”, so the short thing is a stretch to be crossed; “stretch” is supplied. κοσμίως is “in good order, decently, with composure”.
notes.other_reading: to pass through this short time decently

check.greek: Σωκρατικὸν φαντάζου ἢ Εὐτύχην ἢ Ὑμένα
check.note: The English makes Eutyches and Hymen two Socratics. The Greek can as well be three alternatives, like the pairs of plain names in the clauses that follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “picture Socraticus or Eutyches or Hymen”. The Greek has the first name, then the verb, then “or” twice, which reads most simply as three alternatives like the plain pairs that follow. “A Socratic” is kept in the note.

check.note: The particle is “then”, an inference. There is no “now” in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “where, then, are those people?”. The Greek has “then” and no word for “now”.

check.note: “The boundless time” is not English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in boundless time”. The article is dropped to make it English, and “all of” is not added because the Greek has no such word.

check.note: Of conduct the adverb means decently, with composure. “In an orderly way” sounds like tidiness.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in good order”. This is an ordinary English phrase for making a crossing properly and with composure, and it keeps the link with the Greek word for order that the adverb comes from. “Decently” is in the note.

part.left_out: Οἵαν ὕλην καὶ ὑπόθεσιν φεύγεις· τί γάρ ἐστι πάντα ταῦτα ἄλλο πλὴν γυμνάσματα λόγου ἑωρακότος ἀκριβῶς καὶ φυσιολόγως τὰ ἐν τῷ βίῳ; μένε οὖν, μέχρι ἐξοικειώσῃς σεαυτῷ καὶ ταῦτα, ὡς ὁ ἐρρωμένος στόμαχος πάντα ἐξοικειοῖ, ὡς τὸ λαμπρὸν πῦρ, ὅ τι ἂν ἐμβάλῃς, φλόγα ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐγὴν ποιεῖ.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 10.31 here and makes the rest of the chapter its section 10.32.

passages.casaubon: When thou seest Satyro, think of Socraticus and Eutyches, or Hymen, and when Euphrates, think of Eutychio, and Sylvanus, when Alciphron, of Tropaeophorus, when Xenophon, of Crito, or Severus. And when thou doest look upon thyself, fancy unto thyself some one or other of the Cæsars; and so for every one, some one or other that hath been for estate and profession answerable unto him. Then let this come to thy mind at the same time; and where now are they all? Nowhere or anywhere? For so shalt thou at all time be able to perceive how all worldly things are but as the smoke, that vanisheth away: or, indeed, mere nothing. Especially when thou shalt call to mind this also, that whatsoever is once changed, shall never be again as long as the world endureth. And thou then, how long shalt thou endure? And why doth it not suffice thee, if virtuously, and as becometh thee, thou mayest pass that portion of time, how little soever it be, that is allotted unto thee?
passages.russian: Видя Сатириона, представляй себе Сократика, или Евтиха, или Гимена; видя Евфрата — Евтихиона или Сильвана; при Алкифроне — Тропеофора; видя Севера — Критона или Ксенофонта; глядя на себя — кого-нибудь из Цезарей; и при каждом — того, кто ему соответствует. Затем пусть вместе с этим придёт тебе на ум: где же они теперь? Нигде — или где бы то ни было. Ведь так ты постоянно будешь смотреть на человеческое как на дым и ничто, особенно если вспомнишь вместе с тем, что изменившееся однажды больше не будет существовать в беспредельном времени. Зачем же ты напрягаешься? Почему тебе не довольно пройти этот короткий отрезок в должном порядке?

passages.greek: Τῷ δεδευμένῳ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀληθῶν δογμάτων ἀρκεῖ καὶ τὸ βραχύτατον καὶ ἐν μέσῳ κείμενον εἰς ὑπόμνησιν ἀλυπίας καὶ ἀφοβίας, οἷον· ʽφύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει· ὣς ἀνδρῶν γενεή.ʼ φυλλάρια δὲ καὶ τὰ τεκνία σου, φυλλάρια δὲ καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ἐπιβοῶντα ἀξιοπίστως καὶ ἐπευφημοῦντα ἢ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων καταρώμενα ἢ ἡσυχῇ ψέγοντα καὶ χλευάζοντα, φυλλάρια δὲ ὁμοίως καὶ τὰ διαδεξόμενα τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν. πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ʽἔαρος ἐπιγίγνεται ὥρῃʼ. εἶτα ἄνεμος καταβέβληκεν· ἔπειθ’ ὕλη ἕτερα ἀντὶ τούτων φύει. τὸ δὲ ὀλιγοχρόνιον κοινὸν πᾶσιν, ἀλλὰ σὺ πάντα ὡς αἰώνια ἐσόμενα φεύγεις καὶ διώκεις. μικρὸν καὶ καταμύσεις, τὸν δὲ ἐξενεγκόντα σε ἤδη ἄλλος θρηνήσει.
passages.english: For someone who has been steeped in the true principles, even the shortest saying, one that lies open to everybody, is enough as a reminder of freedom from grief and fear. For example: “Leaves, some the wind pours to the ground: so the generation of men.” Your little children are little leaves too; little leaves too are these that shout convincingly and applaud, or on the contrary curse, or quietly find fault and mock; and little leaves in the same way are those who will receive in succession the fame that comes after death. For all these “come on in the season of spring”. Then the wind has thrown them down; then the forest grows others in their place. Shortness of life is common to all, but you run from all things and chase all things as if they were going to last for ever. A little while and you will close your eyes, and already someone else will be mourning the one who carried you out.

notes.note: As given, the perfect participle of “to wet, to soak”, so “steeped”. Other editions are recalled as printing a word meaning “bitten” here (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands.
notes.other_reading: For someone who has been bitten by the true principles

notes.note: Literally “lying in the middle”, an idiom for what is common property, within everyone’s reach. “Saying” is supplied: the Greek has only “the shortest thing”.
notes.other_reading: the most ordinary saying

notes.greek: φύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει· ὣς ἀνδρῶν γενεή
notes.note: Homer, from the leaves speech in the Iliad (book 6, from memory, unchecked), with the lines between left out. The two phrases quoted further on are from the same lines. The English keeps the broken grammar of the abridged quotation.
notes.other_reading: “The wind scatters some leaves on the ground: such is the race of men.”

notes.note: A diminutive of “leaves”, set beside the diminutive for “children”. “Little” is kept each time it recurs.
notes.other_reading: mere leaves

notes.note: “In a way that wins belief”. It may be meant straight (they sound sincere) or with an edge (they only sound it).
notes.other_reading: with every appearance of sincerity

notes.note: Literally “those who will receive in succession the after-fame”: the later people who will each in turn hold what is said of a person once dead. The Greek does not say whose fame; in context it is the fame of the one addressed.
notes.other_reading: those who will take over your fame after you

notes.note: In Homer the season is the subject (“the season of spring comes on”). As given here it is dative, “in the season of spring”, with “all these” as subject.
notes.other_reading: “the season of spring comes on”

notes.note: The standard pair for avoiding and pursuing. The English keeps the literal running and chasing, and repeats “all things” for both verbs where the Greek has it once.
notes.other_reading: you avoid and pursue everything

notes.note: “Already, presently”: the mourner’s own turn follows at once. “Carried you out” is the regular Greek expression for carrying a body out to burial.
notes.other_reading: and the one who carried you out to burial will soon be mourned by someone else

check.note: The English follows the Greek as given, “soaked, steeped”. Some editions are recalled as printing a different participle, “bitten”; no change is needed for the text as it stands.
check.decided: Accepted: “steeped” stands for the text as given, and the note records that other editions are recalled as printing “bitten” (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “So” is added. The adverb means “in a way that earns belief”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “these that shout convincingly and applaud”. “So” is removed. “As if they deserved belief” is not taken because the Greek does not say whether the belief is deserved, and the note keeps that open.

check.note: The Greek is “those who will receive in succession the fame after death”. “Take over your fame” reads as taking the fame for themselves, and “your” is supplied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “those who will receive in succession the fame that comes after death”. The verb is one of receiving in a line of succession, so “hand on” is not added, and “your” is dropped because the Greek does not have it.

check.greek: τὸν δὲ ἐξενεγκόντα σε ἤδη ἄλλος θρηνήσει
check.note: The adverb is “already, presently”, stronger than “soon”. “To burial” is an explanation added to “carried you out”, and the Greek is active: another will mourn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and already someone else will be mourning the one who carried you out”. The sentence is active as in the Greek, “already” replaces “soon”, and “to burial” moves to the note.

passages.casaubon: As he that is bitten by a mad dog, is afraid of everything almost that he seeth: so unto him, whom the dogmata have once bitten, or in whom true knowledge hath made an impression, everything almost that he sees or reads be it never so short or ordinary, doth afford a good memento; to put him out of all grief and fear, as that of the poet, 'The winds blow upon the trees, and their leaves fall upon the ground. Then do the trees begin to bud again, and by the spring-time they put forth new branches. So is the generation of men; some come into the world, and others go out of it.' Of these leaves then thy children are. And they also that applaud thee so gravely, or, that applaud thy speeches, with that their usual acclamation, ἀξιοπίστως, O wisely spoken I and speak well of thee, as on the other side, they that stick not to curse thee, they that privately and secretly dispraise and deride thee, they also are but leaves. And they also that shall follow, in whose memories the names of men famous after death, is preserved, they are but leaves neither. For even so is it of all these worldly things. Their spring comes, and they are put forth. Then blows the wind, and they go down. And then in lieu of them grow others out of the wood or common matter of all things, like unto them. But, to endure but for a while, is common unto all. Why then shouldest thou so earnestly either seek after these things, or fly from them, as though they should endure for ever? Yet a little while, and thine eyes will be closed up, and for him that carries thee to thy grave shall another mourn within a while after.
passages.russian: Тому, кто пропитался истинными принципами, даже самого краткого изречения, доступного всем, достаточно, чтобы напомнить о свободе от печали и страха. Например: «Листья — одни ветер наземь сыплет: таков и род людской». И детки твои — листочки; листочки и те, кто убедительно кричит и рукоплещет, или, напротив, проклинает, или втихомолку порицает и насмехается; листочки точно так же и те, кто, сменяя друг друга, примет посмертную славу. Ведь все они «приходят весенней порою». Потом ветер их сбросил; потом лес растит на их месте другие. Краткость жизни — общая для всех, а ты бежишь от всего и гонишься за всем так, будто это будет вечно. Ещё немного — и ты закроешь глаза, а того, кто тебя вынес, уже будет оплакивать другой.

passages.greek: Ἐπινόησον λόγου χάριν τοὺς ἐπὶ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ καιρούς, ὄψει τὰ αὐτὰ πάντα γαμοῦντας, παιδοτροφοῦντας, νοσοῦντας, ἀποθνῄσκοντας, πολεμοῦντας, ἑορτάζοντας, ἐμπορευομένους, γεωργοῦντας, κολακεύοντας, αὐθαδιζομένους, ὑποπτεύοντας, ἐπιβουλεύοντας, ἀποθανεῖν τινας εὐχομένους, γογγύζοντας ἐπὶ τοῖς παροῦσιν, ἐρῶντας, θησαυρίζοντας, ὑπατείας, βασιλείας ἐπιθυμοῦντας· οὐκοῦν ἐκεῖνος μὲν ὁ τούτων βίος οὐκέτι οὐδαμοῦ. πάλιν ἐπὶ τοὺς καιροὺς τοὺς Τραιανοῦ μετάβηθι· πάλιν τὰ αὐτὰ πάντα· τέθνηκε κἀκεῖνος ὁ βίος. ὁμοίως καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἐπιγραφὰς χρόνων καὶ ὅλων ἐθνῶν ἐπιθεώρει καὶ βλέπε, πόσοι κατενταθέντες μετὰ μικρὸν ἔπεσον καὶ ἀνελύθησαν εἰς τὰ στοιχεῖα· μάλιστα δὲ ἀναπολητέον ἐκείνους, οὓς αὐτὸς ἔγνως κενὰ σπωμένους, ἀφέντας ποιεῖν τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν καὶ τούτου ἀπρὶξ ἔχεσθαι καὶ τούτῳ ἀρκεῖσθαι. ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ὧδε τὸ μεμνῆσθαι, ὅτι καὶ ἡ ἐπιστροφὴ καθ’ ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν ἰδίαν ἀξίαν ἔχει καὶ συμμετρίαν· οὕτως γὰρ οὐκ ἀποδυσπετήσεις, ἐὰν μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον, ἢ προσῆκε, περὶ τὰ ἐλάσσω καταγίνῃ.
passages.english: Think, for example, of the times of Vespasian, and you will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling ill, dying, making war, keeping festivals, trading, farming, flattering, insisting on their own way, suspecting, plotting, praying for certain people to die, grumbling at how things are, falling in love, hoarding treasure, wanting consulships, wanting kingships. Well then, that life of theirs is no longer anywhere. Pass on again to the times of Trajan: again all the same things. That life too is dead. In the same way look over the other inscriptions of times and of whole nations, and see how many people strained with all their strength and a little later fell and were broken up into the elements. But above all one should go back over those whom you yourself knew, who were dragged after empty things and neglected to do what fits their own constitution, to hold on tight to that and to be content with that. And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to each action also has its own worth and proportion. For in this way you will not give up in frustration, if you do not occupy yourself with the lesser things more than is fitting.

notes.note: “Behaving in a self-willed, overbearing way.” The English makes it an action like the rest of the list; the same word-family is “self-willed” in another passage of this section.
notes.other_reading: throwing their weight about

notes.note: “Kingships”, which in a Roman setting is also the word for the emperor’s rule.
notes.other_reading: wanting to be consul, wanting to be emperor

notes.note: ἐπιγραφή is an inscription, a title or a heading. The English keeps “inscriptions”, as of what is written over the dead; it may instead be the headings under which periods are entered, like “the times of Vespasian”.
notes.other_reading: the other headings of periods and of whole nations

notes.note: “Having strained hard”, a word of the stretched string or sinew. The same family comes back in other passages of this section, and “strain” is kept for it.
notes.other_reading: after straining every nerve

notes.note: σπάω is “to pull, to drag, to wrench”. The form can be passive (dragged) or middle (pulling at, grasping for). κενά, “empty things”, is in the object case, which does not make them the ones doing the dragging.
notes.other_reading: grasping at empty things

notes.note: An impersonal form, “one must turn over again”, followed at once by the second person “you yourself knew”. The English keeps both as they stand.
notes.other_reading: you must think back over

notes.note: “Constitution, make-up”: how a thing is built and so what it is built for.
notes.other_reading: what fits the way they themselves are made

notes.note: “The turning towards”, that is, attention or care given to a thing. “Given to” renders καθ’ ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν, “for each action”.
notes.other_reading: the care spent on each action

notes.note: The verb is to give up out of impatience or discouragement. The Greek does not say at what; the next clause gives the condition.
notes.other_reading: you will not lose heart

check.note: Every other item in the list is an action; “being self-willed” is a state and is clumsy. The verb means acting stubbornly or arrogantly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “insisting on their own way”. This is an action like the other items and keeps the sense of self-will in the Greek verb. “Throwing their weight about” brings in an image the Greek does not have and is kept in the note.

check.note: The Greek is “at present circumstances”, wider than possessions.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “grumbling at how things are”. The Greek is “at present things”, which is wider than what a person has.

check.note: The word is “inscriptions” or “titles, headings”. “Records” loses the image of inscriptions over times and nations.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the other inscriptions of times and of whole nations”. “Inscriptions” is the first sense of the Greek word; the reading “headings” is kept in the note.

check.note: Hard to read. The sense is dragged this way and that by, or after, empty things.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “being dragged after empty things”. “After” is kept and “by” is not used because the Greek puts “empty things” in the object case, not as the agent. The note records the other reading, “grasping at empty things”.

check.note: The verb is to lose heart, to give up out of impatience or discouragement. “Disgust” is stronger and different in colour.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you will not give up in frustration”. “Disgust” is removed, but the verb’s prefix says “give up”, which “lose heart” alone would drop.

check.note: The Greek is “more, further”, not only longer in time.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if you do not occupy yourself with the lesser things more than is fitting”. The Greek says “more”, not only longer in time.

check.note: The imperfect of this verb is the ordinary Greek idiom for “than is fitting”. “Was” points to a past occasion.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “than is fitting”. The past form of this verb is the ordinary Greek way of saying what is fitting and does not point to a past occasion.

passages.casaubon: Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian: thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that their age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of Trajan. There likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that age also is now over and ended. In the like manner consider other periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after they had with all their might and main intended and prosecuted some one worldly thing or other did soon after drop away, and were resolved into the elements. But especially thou must call to mind them, whom thou thyself in thy lifetime hast known much distracted about vain things, and in the meantime neglecting to do that, and closely and unseparably (as fully satisfied with it) to adhere unto it, which their own proper constitution did require. And here thou must remember, that thy carriage in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired out and vexed, if thou shalt not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.
passages.russian: Представь себе для примера времена Веспасиана, и ты увидишь всё то же самое: люди женятся, растят детей, болеют, умирают, воюют, празднуют, торгуют, пашут, льстят, стоят на своём, подозревают, строят козни, молятся о смерти кое-кого, ворчат на то, как всё устроено, влюбляются, копят сокровища, жаждут консульств, жаждут царской власти. И вот той их жизни больше нигде нет. Перейди опять ко временам Траяна: опять всё то же самое. И та жизнь мертва. Так же оглядывай и прочие надписи времён и целых народов и смотри, сколько людей напрягались изо всех сил, а немного погодя пали и распались на стихии. Но прежде всего надо перебрать тех, кого ты сам знал, кого тащило за пустым и кто пренебрегал тем, чтобы делать то, что подобает их собственному устройству, крепко держаться за это и этим довольствоваться. И здесь необходимо помнить, что и внимание, уделяемое каждому действию, имеет свою ценность и соразмерность. Ведь так ты не опустишь рук в досаде, если не станешь заниматься меньшим больше, чем подобает.

passages.greek: Συνεχῶς ἀναπολεῖν τοὺς ἐπί τινι λίαν ἀγανακτήσαντας, τοὺς ἐν μεγίσταις δόξαις ἢ συμφοραῖς ἢ ἔχθραις ἢ ὁποιαισοῦν τύχαις ἀκμάσαντας· εἶτα ἐφιστάνειν· ποῦ νῦν πάντα ἐκεῖνα; καπνὸς καὶ σποδὸς καὶ μῦθος ἢ οὐδὲ μῦθος. συμπροσπιπτέτω δὲ καὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο πᾶν, οἷον· Φάβιος Κατουλλῖνος ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ καὶ Λούσιος Δοῦπος ἐν τοῖς κήποις καὶ Στερτίνιος ἐν Βαίαις καὶ Τιβέριος ἐν Καπρίαις καὶ Οὐήλιος Ῥοῦφος καὶ ὅλως ἡ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν μετ’ οἰήσεως διαφορά· καὶ ὡς εὐτελὲς πᾶν τὸ κατεντεινόμενον καὶ ὅσῳ φιλοσοφώτερον τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς δοθείσης ὕλης ἑαυτὸν δίκαιον, σώφρονα, θεοῖς ἑπόμενον ἀφελῶς παρέχειν· ὁ γὰρ ὑπὸ ἀτυφίᾳ τῦφος τυφόμενος πάντων χαλεπώτατος.
passages.english: Go back continually over those who were exceedingly indignant at something, those who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters or enmities or fortunes of whatever kind. Then stop and consider: where is all that now? Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale. And let everything of this kind come to you along with it, for example: Fabius Catullinus in the country, and Lusius Lupus in the gardens, and Stertinius at Baiae, and Tiberius on Capri, and Velius Rufus, and in general setting store by anything whatever, together with self-importance; and how cheap everything is that people strain after, and how much more philosophical it is, in the material one has been given, to show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods, without affectation. For the vanity that smoulders under a cover of having none is the most troublesome of all.

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person; so are the verbs that follow. The English uses the bare command.
notes.other_reading: To go back continually over

notes.note: “Who were at their height, who flourished”, used here of misfortunes and enmities as well as of fame.
notes.other_reading: those who stood at the peak of the greatest fame or disasters

notes.note: “To halt and fix the attention.” The question follows without a verb of asking.
notes.other_reading: then put the question:

notes.note: As given, the second name is “Dupus”, which is taken to be a slip of the copy for Λοῦπος, Lupus, and is corrected in the English. Apart from Tiberius, the emperor who withdrew to Capri, these men cannot be identified here.
notes.other_reading: Lusius Dupus

notes.note: The list has no verb: a name and a place each time, and for Velius Rufus a name only. The English leaves it so. “In the country” can also be “on his estate”.
notes.other_reading: Fabius Catullinus on his country estate

notes.greek: ἡ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν μετ’ οἰήσεως διαφορά
notes.note: διαφορά ranges over difference, distinction and disagreement. With πρός, “towards”, the English reads it as the opposite of indifference, treating a thing as making a difference, which suits the men just named at their country places. οἴησις is a high opinion of oneself.
notes.other_reading: and in general distinction in anything whatever, or a quarrel over anything whatever, joined with conceit

notes.note: A neuter participle, “what is strained after” or “the straining”. “People” is added in the English.
notes.other_reading: how cheap all straining is

notes.note: ὕλη is “material, stuff to work on”: the circumstances handed to a person, as timber is handed to a carpenter.
notes.other_reading: on the material that has been given

notes.note: “Simply, plainly, without affectation”. It stands just before the verb and may go with the whole of “show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods”, or only with the last item.
notes.other_reading: following the gods simply

notes.greek: ὁ γὰρ ὑπὸ ἀτυφίᾳ τῦφος τυφόμενος
notes.note: A play on one root three times: τῦφος is smoke, and so vanity; ἀτυφία is being without it; τυφόμενος is “smouldering”. The Greek says only “under freedom from vanity”, and “a cover of” is added to make the image plain. χαλεπώτατος is “hardest”, to bear or to deal with.
notes.other_reading: For the pride that prides itself on having no pride is the most insufferable of all.

check.note: The adverb is “too much, exceedingly”; “greatly” is weaker.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “exceedingly indignant”. This gives the adverb its full force without the added colour of “furiously”.

check.note: “At the peak of disasters or enmities” is odd English. The Greek is “who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters or enmities or fortunes of whatever kind”, which follows the Greek construction.

check.note: The Greek as given reads a name beginning with delta. The English reads it as Lupus, which is surely right but is a correction.
check.decided: Accepted: “Lupus” stands, and the note says that the copy reads “Dupus” and that this is taken as a misprinted letter.

check.note: The noun ordinarily means difference, disagreement or distinction, and “keen pursuit” is not its usual sense. Other readings are a quarrel over anything whatever, or distinction in anything whatever, joined with conceit.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the setting store by anything whatever, together with self-importance”. With the preposition “towards”, the noun is read as the opposite of indifference, treating a thing as making a difference, which fits the men just listed at their retreats. “Quarrel” and “distinction” are recorded in the note.

check.note: The adverb may go only with the last item, “following the gods simply”, or with the whole. The English chooses the whole and makes it a separate clause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods, without affectation”. The adverb comes last, as in the Greek, without a clause of its own, and a note says it may go with the last item only.

check.note: Hard to follow. The Greek plays three times on one root (smoke, conceit): conceit smouldering under cover of having none.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the vanity that smoulders under a cover of having none”. “Having none” is taken as suggested. “A cover” is used in place of “a show” because it stays with the Greek image of something smouldering underneath, and the note explains the threefold play.

check.note: “To bear” is added. The adjective is “hardest, most troublesome”, which could as well mean hardest to deal with or to cure.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is the most troublesome of all”. “To bear” is removed, and “most troublesome” stays nearer than “worst” to the Greek word, which means hard or difficult.

passages.casaubon: Let thy thoughts ever run upon them, who once for some one thing or other, were moved with extraordinary indignation; who were once in the highest pitch of either honour, or calamity; or mutual hatred and enmity; or of any other fortune or condition whatsoever. Then consider what's now become of all those things. All is turned to smoke; all to ashes, and a mere fable; and perchance not so much as a fable. As also whatsoever is of this nature, as Fabius Catulinus in the field; Lucius Lupus, and Stertinius, at Baiæ Tiberius at Capreæ and Velius Rufus, and all such examples of vehement prosecution in worldly matters; let these also run in thy mind at the same time; and how vile every object of such earnest and vehement prosecution is; and how much more agreeable to true philosophy it is, for a man to carry himself in every matter that offers itself; justly, and moderately, as one that followeth the Gods with all simplicity. For, for a man to be proud and high conceited, that he is not proud and high conceited, is of all kind of pride and presumption, the most intolerable.
passages.russian: Постоянно перебирай в памяти тех, кто крайне негодовал на что-нибудь, тех, кто был на вершине величайшей славы, или бедствий, или вражды, или какой угодно судьбы. Потом остановись и подумай: где всё это теперь? Дым, пепел и предание, а то и не предание. И пусть вместе с этим придёт тебе на ум всё подобное, например: Фабий Катуллин в деревне, Лусий Луп в садах, Стертиний в Байях, Тиберий на Капри, Велий Руф и вообще то, что придают цену чему бы то ни было, вместе с чванством; и как дёшево всё, к чему люди рвутся, и насколько философичнее на доставшемся материале показывать себя справедливым, владеющим собой, следующим богам, без рисовки. Ведь тщеславие, тлеющее под покровом мнимого его отсутствия, тягостнее всего.

passages.greek: Λούκιλλα Οὐῆρον, εἶτα Λούκιλλα· Σέκουνδα Μάξιμον, εἶτα Σέκουνδα· Ἐπιτύγχανος Διότιμον, εἶτα Ἐπιτύγχανος· Φαυστῖναν Ἀντωνῖνος, εἶτα Ἀντωνῖνος. τοιαῦτα πάντα· Κέλερ Ἁδριανόν, εἶτα Κέλερ. οἱ δὲ δριμεῖς ἐκεῖνοι ἢ προγνωστικοὶ ἢ τετυφωμένοι ποῦ; οἷον, δριμεῖς μὲν Χάραξ καὶ Δημήτριος ὁ Πλατωνικὸς καὶ Εὐδαίμων καὶ εἴ τις τοιοῦτος. πάντα ἐφήμερα, τεθνηκότα πάλαι· ἔνιοι μὲν οὐδὲ ἐπ’ ὀλίγον μνημονευθέντες, οἱ δὲ εἰς μύθους μεταβαλόντες, οἱ δὲ ἤδη καὶ ἐκ μύθων ἐξίτηλοι. τούτων οὖν μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι δεήσει ἤτοι σκεδασθῆναι τὸ συγκριμάτιόν σου ἢ σβεσθῆναι τὸ πνευμάτιον ἢ μεταστῆναι καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ καταταχθῆναι.
passages.english: Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla. Secunda buried Maximus, then Secunda. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, then Epitynchanus. Antoninus buried Faustina, then Antoninus. It is all like this. Celer buried Hadrian, then Celer. And those shrewd ones, or the ones who foretold things, or the ones puffed up with vanity, where are they? The shrewd ones, for example: Charax and Demetrius the Platonist and Eudaemon and anyone else of that kind. All of it lasting a day, long dead: some not remembered even for a short while, some changed into tales, and some by now faded even out of the tales. So remember these things: that either your little compound will have to be scattered, or your little breath be put out, or else move away and be posted somewhere else.

notes.note: The Greek has no verb at all: a name in the nominative, a name in the accusative, “then” and the first name again. “Buried” is supplied in each pair and the second half is left bare. Which Lucilla and Verus are meant is not certain: probably the writer’s mother and father (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Lucilla, Verus; then Lucilla.

notes.note: Here alone the accusative comes first; the English puts the pair in the same order as the others. Antoninus is presumably the emperor Antoninus Pius and Faustina his wife (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Faustina was buried by Antoninus, then Antoninus.

notes.note: “Sharp, keen, piercing”, of wits or of temper.
