notes.other_reading: those sharp-witted ones

notes.note: “Able to know beforehand”: said of forecasters of any kind, astrologers or doctors giving a prognosis.
notes.other_reading: the ones with foresight

notes.note: Literally “filled with smoke”, the ordinary word for being puffed up with vanity. It is from the same root as the word given as “vanity” in another passage of this section.
notes.other_reading: the conceited ones

notes.note: Neuter: “all things of a day”, though the next clauses go back to the masculine people. “Lasting a day” is kept for this word across the section.
notes.other_reading: All creatures of a day

notes.note: Literally “so remember these things, that”. The plural may point back to the people and things just listed or forward to the clause; “these things” followed by a colon leaves both open. The verb is an infinitive used as an instruction.
notes.other_reading: So remember these people, and that

notes.note: A diminutive of “compound”: the thing put together that makes up a person. So also “little breath” (πνευμάτιον), the breath of life.
notes.other_reading: the little compound that you are

notes.note: The subject is not restated; it is taken to be the little breath. The second verb is a military one, “to be assigned a post”.
notes.other_reading: or change its place and be stationed elsewhere

check.note: The Greek has no verb in any of the five pairs: “Lucilla, Verus; then Lucilla”. “Buried” is supplied five times; it is a fair supplement but it is the translator’s word.
check.decided: Accepted: “buried” stays in each pair as a recorded supplement, on the model of the same thought written out in full in another passage of this section. The note says that the Greek has no verb and gives the bare wording.

check.note: The pronoun is plural, “these things”, and can point back at the list of the dead just given. The English singular makes it point only forward.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So remember these things: that either”. The plural is kept, and the colon lets it point back to the dead just listed as well as forward.

check.note: The Greek is “your little compound”, parallel to “your little breath” just after. “That you are” is an interpretation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “your little compound”, parallel to “your little breath”.

passages.casaubon: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself. So Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself. So Antoninus Pius, Faustina his wife; then Antoninus himself. This is the course of the world. First Celer, Adrianus; then Adrianus himself. And those austere ones; those that foretold other men's deaths; those that were so proud and stately, where are they now? Those austere ones I mean, such as were Charax, and Demetrius the Platonic, and Eudaemon, and others like unto those. They were all but for one day; all dead and gone long since. Some of them no sooner dead, than forgotten. Others soon turned into fables. Of others, even that which was fabulous, is now long since forgotten. This thereafter thou must remember, that whatsoever thou art compounded of, shall soon be dispersed, and that thy life and breath, or thy soul, shall either be no more or shall ranslated (sp.), and appointed to some certain place and station.
passages.russian: Луцилла похоронила Вера, потом — Луциллу. Секунда похоронила Максима, потом — Секунду. Эпитинхан похоронил Диотима, потом — Эпитинхана. Антонин похоронил Фаустину, потом — Антонина. Всё вот так. Целер похоронил Адриана, потом — Целера. А те проницательные, или те, кто предсказывал будущее, или те, кто был раздут тщеславием, — где они? Проницательные, например: Харакс, и Деметрий-платоник, и Эвдемон, и всякий другой такого рода. Всё однодневно, всё давно мертво: одних не помнили даже недолго, другие превратились в сказания, а третьи уже стёрлись даже из сказаний. Так помни вот что: либо твоему составчику придётся рассеяться, либо твоему дыханьицу — погаснуть, либо же переселиться и занять пост где-то в другом месте.

passages.greek:
ὡς ὁ ἀναβάλλων τὴν σφαῖραν· τί οὖν ἀγαθὸν τῷ σφαιρίῳ ἀναφερομένῳ ἢ κακὸν καταφερομένῳ ἢ καὶ πεπτωκότι; τί δὲ ἀγαθὸν τῇ πομφόλυγι συνεστώσῃ ἢ κακὸν διαλυθείσῃ; τὰ ὅμοια δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ λύχνου.

Ἔκστρεψον καὶ θέασαι οἷόν ἐστι, γηρᾶσαν δὲ οἷον γίνεται, νοσῆσαν δέ, πορνεῦσαν. Βραχύβιον καὶ ὁ ἐπαινῶν καὶ ὁ ἐπαινούμενος καὶ ὁ μνημονεύων καὶ ὁ μνημονευόμενος. προσέτι δὲ καὶ ἐν γωνίᾳ τούτου τοῦ κλίματος καὶ οὐδὲ ἐνταῦθα πάντες συμφωνοῦσι καὶ οὐδὲ αὐτός τις ἑαυτῷ· καὶ ὅλη δὲ ἡ γῆ στιγμή.
passages.english:
like someone throwing a ball up. So what good is it to the little ball to be carried upward, or what harm to be carried downward, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to the bubble to hold together, or what harm to have burst? And the same holds for a lamp.

Turn it inside out and look at what it is like, and what it becomes when it has grown old, when it has been ill, when it has prostituted itself. Short-lived is the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered. And besides, in a corner of this region, and not even here do all agree, nor does any one person even agree with themselves; and the whole earth is a point.

notes.note: The passage as given begins in mid-sentence, with the second half of a comparison whose first half is not here. The English leaves it as a fragment and does not supply what is compared.
notes.other_reading: as the one who throws the ball up does

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for “ball” just used.
notes.other_reading: to the ball

notes.note: “Dissolved, come apart”, the opposite of the “holding together” before it.
notes.other_reading: or what harm when it has come apart

notes.note: “Turn inside out”, as one turns a garment. The Greek names no object; the neuter participles that follow suggest the body, not the lamp of the sentence before, which belongs to the previous chapter. The English leaves it as “it”.
notes.other_reading: Turn the body inside out

notes.note: As given, “when it has prostituted itself”. The word is abrupt after old age and illness, and editors are recalled as having doubted it (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands.
notes.other_reading: when it has given itself to debauchery

notes.note: The clause has no subject or verb in the Greek and is left without them in the English. κλίμα is a zone or region of the earth.
notes.other_reading: And besides, all this happens in a corner of this part of the world

notes.note: Literally “nor even a person himself with himself”; the verb “agree” is carried over.
notes.other_reading: and no one agrees even with himself

notes.note: A point in the geometer’s sense, a mere dot.
notes.other_reading: and the whole earth is a dot

check.note: The Greek names no object; the neuter participles that follow point to the body. Coming straight after the lamp, the English “it” will be read as the lamp, so the supplement should be marked.
check.decided: Declined: “Turn it inside out” stands without a bracketed supplement. The Greek names no object, so the English supplies none; the new paragraph separates the sentence from the lamp, and the note says that the body is probably meant.

check.note: Accurate, but “whored” as a verb is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when it has prostituted itself”, which gives the same sense in current English.

check.greek: προσέτι δὲ καὶ ἐν γωνίᾳ τούτου τοῦ κλίματος
check.note: “All this” is supplied to make a sentence; the Greek is just “and besides, in a corner of this region”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And besides, in a corner of this region”. The Greek clause has no subject or verb, the English leaves it so, and the note says so.

part.left_out: Ἡ φύσις ἐστόχασται ἑκάστου οὐδέν τι ἔλασσον τῆς ἀπολήξεως ἢ τῆς ἀρχῆς τε καὶ διεξαγωγῆς,
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first clause of chapter 8.20 in its section 8.18 and begins its 8.19 here with the ball-thrower, running on through chapter 8.21.

passages.casaubon: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground? So for the bubble; if it continue, what it the better? and if it dissolve, what is it the worse And so is it of a candle too. And so must thou reason with thyself, both in matter of fame, and in matter of death. For as for the body itself, (the subject of death) wouldest thou know the vileness of it? Turn it about that thou mayest behold it the worst sides upwards as well, as in its more ordinary pleasant shape; how doth it look, when it is old and withered? when sick and pained? when in the act of lust, and fornication? And as for fame. This life is short. Both he that praiseth, and he that is praised; he that remembers, and he that is remembered, will soon be dust and ashes. Besides, it is but in one corner of this part of the world that thou art praised; and yet in this corner, thou hast not the joint praises of all men; no nor scarce of any one constantly. And yet the whole earth itself, what is it but as one point, in regard of the whole world?
passages.russian:
как тот, кто подбрасывает мяч. Так что хорошего мячику в том, что он несётся вверх, или какой вред в том, что он несётся вниз или даже упал? И что хорошего пузырю в том, что он держится, или какой вред в том, что он лопнул? То же и со светильником.

Выверни это наизнанку и посмотри, каково оно и чем оно становится, когда состарилось, когда переболело, когда торговало собой. Недолговечен и тот, кто хвалит, и тот, кого хвалят, и тот, кто помнит, и тот, кого помнят. И к тому же — в уголке этой области, и даже здесь не все согласны друг с другом, да и ни один человек не согласен даже сам с собой; а вся земля — точка.

passages.greek: Συνεχῶς ἐπινοεῖν πῶς πάντα τοιαῦτα, ὁποῖα νῦν γίνεται, καὶ πρόσθεν ἐγίνετο, καὶ ἐπινοεῖν γενησόμενα· καὶ ὅλα δράματα καὶ σκηνὰς ὁμοειδεῖς, ὅσα ἐκ πείρας τῆς σῆς ἢ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας ἱστορίας ἔγνως, πρὸ ὀμμάτων τίθεσθαι, οἷον αὐλὴν ὅλην Ἁδριανοῦ καὶ αὐλὴν ὅλην Ἀντωνίνου καὶ αὐλὴν ὅλην Φιλίππου, Ἀλεξάνδρου, Κροίσου· πάντα γὰρ ἐκεῖνα τοιαῦτα ἦν, μόνον δι’ ἑτέρων.
passages.english: Think continually how all things of the kind that happen now happened before as well, and think of them as going to happen. And set before your eyes whole plays and scenes of the same kind, all that you have come to know from your own experience or from older history: for example the whole court of Hadrian, and the whole court of Antoninus, and the whole court of Philip, of Alexander, of Croesus. For all of those were of this kind, only with other people.

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person, though “your own experience” and “you have come to know” follow in the second person. The English uses the bare command.
notes.other_reading: To think continually

notes.note: τοιαῦτα, “of such a kind”, opens the chapter and returns in its last clause. The English reads “of the kind” and “of this kind” so that the echo can be heard. “Of the same kind” in between stands for a different Greek word (ὁμοειδεῖς, “alike in form”) that carries the same thought.
notes.other_reading: all things such as happen now … all of those were just the same

notes.note: Literally “and to think [them] going to happen”: things of the same kind will happen again.
notes.other_reading: and think that they will happen

notes.note: σκηνή is the stage, and so a scene or stage setting. “Of the same kind” may go with the scenes only or with both nouns.
notes.other_reading: whole dramas and their stages, all alike

notes.note: Presumably the emperor Antoninus Pius, the writer’s predecessor. Philip and Alexander are the kings of Macedon, Croesus the king of Lydia.
notes.other_reading: the whole court of Antoninus Pius

notes.note: Literally “only through others”: carried out by other people. After “plays and scenes” this can be heard as a change of cast, but the Greek has no word for actors and the English adds none.
notes.other_reading: only with other actors

check.note: The same Greek word opens the chapter, where the draft had “such as”. “The same” at the end says a little more than “of this kind”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the last clause now reads “For all of those were of this kind”, and the opening reads “all things of the kind that happen now”, so the repeated Greek word is heard in both places. “Just like this” was not used because “just” is not in the Greek.

check.note: Literally “through others”. After “plays and scenes” it can mean “with other actors”, and the English drops the stage image.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “only with other people”, with “other” for the Greek word in place of “different”. “Actors” is not added, since the Greek says only “others” and the stage image already stands in “plays and scenes”. The note gives “with other actors” as the other reading.

passages.casaubon: Ever to mind and consider with thyself; how all things that now are, have been heretofore much after the same sort, and after the same fashion that now they are: and so to think of those things which shall be hereafter also. Moreover, whole dramata, and uniform scenes, or scenes that comprehend the lives and actions of men of one calling and profession, as many as either in thine own experience thou hast known, or by reading of ancient histories; (as the whole court of Adrianus, the whole court of Antoninus Pius, the whole court of Philippus, that of Alexander, that of Crœsus): to set them all before thine eyes. For thou shalt find that they are all but after one sort and fashion: only that the actors were others.
passages.russian: Постоянно думай о том, как всё такого рода, что происходит теперь, происходило и прежде, и думай о том, что оно будет происходить и впредь. И ставь перед глазами целые пьесы и сцены одного рода — всё, что ты знаешь по собственному опыту или из более древней истории: например, весь двор Адриана, и весь двор Антонина, и весь двор Филиппа, Александра, Креза. Ведь всё то было такого же рода, только люди другие.

passages.greek: Ἱπποκράτης πολλὰς νόσους ἰασάμενος αὐτὸς νοσήσας ἀπέθανεν. οἱ Χαλδαῖοι πολλῶν θανάτους προηγόρευσαν, εἶτα καὶ αὐτοὺς τὸ πεπρωμένον κατέλαβεν. Ἀλέξανδρος καὶ Πομπήιος καὶ Γάιος Καῖσαρ, ὅλας πόλεις ἄρδην τοσαυτάκις ἀνελόντες καὶ ἐν παρατάξει πολλὰς μυριάδας ἱππέων καὶ πεζῶν κατακόψαντες, καὶ αὐτοί ποτε ἐξῆλθον τοῦ βίου. Ἡράκλειτος περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ἐκπυρώσεως τοσαῦτα φυσιολογήσας, ὕδατος τὰ ἐντὸς πληρωθείς, βολβίτῳ κατακεχρισμένος ἀπέθανε. Δημόκριτον δὲ οἱ φθεῖρες, Σωκράτην δὲ ἄλλοι φθεῖρες ἀπέκτειναν. τί ταῦτα; ἐνέβης, ἔπλευσας, κατήχθης· ἔκβηθι. εἰ μὲν ἐφ’ ἕτερον βίον, οὐδὲν θεῶν κενὸν οὐδὲ ἐκεῖ· εἰ δὲ ἐν ἀναισθησίᾳ, παύσῃ πόνων καὶ ἡδονῶν ἀνεχόμενος καὶ λατρεύων τοσούτῳ χείρονι τῷ ἀγγείῳ ἤπερ ἐστὶ τὸ ὑπηρετοῦν· τὸ μὲν γὰρ νοῦς καὶ δαίμων, τὸ δὲ γῆ καὶ λύθρος.
passages.english: Hippocrates, after curing many illnesses, fell ill himself and died. The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many, and then what was fated caught up with them too. Alexander and Pompey and Gaius Caesar, after so often wiping out whole cities completely and cutting down in battle many tens of thousands of horsemen and foot soldiers, one day went out of life themselves as well. Heraclitus, after saying so much as a student of nature about the burning up of the universe, was filled inside with water and died smeared with cow dung. Lice killed Democritus, and other lice killed Socrates. What of this? You went on board, you sailed, you came to harbour: get off. If to another life, nothing is empty of gods there either. And if in a state without sensation, you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures and being a slave to a vessel that is so much worse than the thing that serves it: for the one that serves is mind and divine spirit, the other earth and gore.

notes.note: The Chaldaeans of Babylon, the name by which astrologers in general were known.
notes.other_reading: The astrologers

notes.note: Julius Caesar, here called by his first name and the name Caesar.
notes.other_reading: Julius Caesar

notes.greek: περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ἐκπυρώσεως τοσαῦτα φυσιολογήσας
notes.note: φυσιολογεῖν is to give a natural philosopher’s account of things, and the English reads “saying so much as a student of nature”. ἐκπύρωσις is the turning of the universe into fire.
notes.other_reading: after so much speculation on the conflagration of the universe

notes.note: Literally “filled with water as to his insides”, that is, dropsy. The water is kept because of the contrast with the fire he wrote about.
notes.other_reading: swollen with dropsy

notes.note: “Other lice”: the men who brought Socrates to his death are called vermin. The image is kept and nothing is added to explain it.
notes.other_reading: and vermin of another sort killed Socrates

notes.note: Two words, “what [are] these things?”: what do they come to, why list them.
notes.other_reading: Why these things?

notes.note: “You were brought in to land”, the regular word for a ship putting in.
notes.other_reading: you have come to shore

notes.note: Neither branch has a verb: “if to another life”, “if in absence of sensation”. The first has “to” (ἐφ’) and this one “in”. The English keeps both prepositions and supplies no verb.
notes.other_reading: If you go on to another life … and if into unconsciousness

notes.note: λατρεύειν is to be in service or in bondage to something. The English reads “being a slave to” so that it is not taken for the different verb behind “the thing that serves it” (τὸ ὑπηρετοῦν) just after.
notes.other_reading: and serving a vessel

notes.note: As given, “than is that which serves”: the vessel (the body) is so much worse than what serves it (the mind). The clause is tight, and editors have altered it (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: a vessel as much worse as the thing that serves it is better

notes.greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ νοῦς καὶ δαίμων
notes.note: The Greek has only “the one … the other”, and the first is the thing that serves, just named. “That serves” is added to “the one” so that the sentence cannot be read with the vessel as mind.
notes.other_reading: for the one is mind and divine spirit, the other earth and gore

notes.note: The daimon: the divine spirit assigned to each person, here set beside mind as the same thing. “Divine” is added to keep it from sounding like a ghost.
notes.other_reading: mind and the god within

notes.note: Blood mixed with dirt, the filth of a battlefield. “Gore” is used here and in 8.37.
notes.other_reading: earth and filthy blood

check.greek: περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ἐκπυρώσεως τοσαῦτα φυσιολογήσας
check.note: Two prepositions stacked (“about nature on the burning up”) make the phrase hard to read, and “speculation” tilts a verb that means to give a natural philosopher’s account.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “after saying so much as a student of nature about the burning up of the universe”, with one preposition and without “speculation”. “So many accounts” was not taken because the Greek has only “so much”.

check.note: The Greek is the bare “What of all this?” or “Why all this?”. “What does this mean?” is more specific.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What of this?”, which stays as bare as the two Greek words. “All” was not added because the Greek does not have it.

check.note: The preposition is “in”, not “into”. It differs from the “to another life” of the first alternative.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And if in a state without sensation”, with “in” for the Greek preposition. The first branch is put in the same bare form, “If to another life”, so that the two different prepositions can be heard.

check.greek: τὸ μὲν γὰρ νοῦς καὶ δαίμων, τὸ δὲ γῆ καὶ λύθρος
check.note: In the English order “the one” is naturally the vessel, named first, so the sentence can be read backwards. In the Greek the first member is the thing that serves, just named.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for the one that serves is mind and divine spirit, the other earth and gore”. Naming the first member is enough to fix the order, and the Greek pair “the one … the other” is kept.

check.note: Found while settling: “lice of another kind” added an explanation where the Greek has only “other lice”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and other lice killed Socrates”, and the note explains who is meant.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “serving” for this verb and “the thing that serves” for a different Greek verb just after, and it repeated “stop” where the Greek has it once.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures and being a slave to a vessel”, with “stop” once and “serves” kept for the second verb only.

check.note: Found while settling: “filled up inside with water” can be read as something Heraclitus did, while the Greek form is passive.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “was filled inside with water”.

passages.casaubon: Hippocrates having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologians having foretold the deaths of divers, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates. Alexander and Pompeius, and Caius Cæsar, having destroyed so many towns, and cut off in the field so many thousands both of horse and foot, yet they themselves at last were fain to part with their own lives. Heraclitus having written so many natural tracts concerning the last and general conflagration of the world, died afterwards all filled with water within, and all bedaubed with dirt and dung without. Lice killed Democritus; and Socrates, another sort of vermin, wicked ungodly men. How then stands the case? Thou hast taken ship, thou hast sailed, thou art come to land, go out, if to another life, there also shalt thou find gods, who are everywhere. If all life and sense shall cease, then shalt thou cease also to be subject to either pains or pleasures; and to serve and tend this vile cottage; so much the viler, by how much that which ministers unto it doth excel; the one being a rational substance, and a spirit, the other nothing but earth and blood.
passages.russian: Гиппократ, вылечив множество болезней, сам заболел и умер. Халдеи предсказали смерть многим, а потом и их настигло то, что было суждено. Александр, Помпей и Гай Цезарь, столько раз дотла уничтожив целые города и изрубив в сражениях многие десятки тысяч всадников и пехотинцев, однажды и сами ушли из жизни. Гераклит, столько рассуждавший как исследователь природы о сгорании мироздания, наполнился изнутри водой и умер, обмазанный коровьим навозом. Демокрита убили вши, а Сократа — другие вши. Что из этого? Ты взошёл на корабль, ты плыл, ты пристал к гавани: сходи. Если в другую жизнь — и там ничто не лишено богов. А если в состояние без ощущений — ты перестанешь терпеть боли и наслаждения и быть рабом сосуда, который настолько хуже того, что ему служит: ведь одно — ум и божественный дух, а другое — земля и кровь.

passages.greek: Ταῦτα οὕτως ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων πέφυκε γίνεσθαι ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ὁ δὲ τοῦτο μὴ θέλων θέλει τὴν συκῆν ὀπὸν μὴ ἔχειν. ὅλως δὲ ἐκείνου μέμνησο, ὅτι ἐντὸς ὀλιγίστου χρόνου καὶ σὺ καὶ οὗτος τεθνήξεσθε, μετὰ βραχὺ δὲ οὐδὲ ὄνομα ὑμῶν ὑπολειφθήσεται.
passages.english: It is the nature of these things to be done in this way by people of this kind, of necessity; and whoever does not want this wants the fig tree to have no sap. But in general remember this: that within a very short time both you and this man will be dead, and a little later not even your names will be left.

notes.note: The passage does not say what things or which people: some conduct of a certain kind of person is in view. τοιούτων can be masculine (such people) or neuter (such things). People is taken, because of “this man” below, and the preposition then marks them as the doers.
notes.other_reading: These things naturally come about in this way from such causes

notes.note: The milky, acrid juice of the fig tree.
notes.other_reading: wants the fig tree to have no juice

notes.note: “This one”, masculine: the particular person whose behaviour started the thought.
notes.other_reading: both you and he

notes.note: Singular in the Greek, “not even a name of you two”. English wants the plural.
notes.other_reading: not even a name of yours will remain

check.note: The preposition marks the doer: these things are done by such people. “From” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to be done in this way by people of this kind”, since the Greek preposition marks the people as the doers.

passages.casaubon: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.
passages.russian: Такова природа этих вещей: такие люди по необходимости делают их так; а кто этого не хочет, тот хочет, чтобы у смоковницы не было сока. Но вообще помни вот что: в самое короткое время и ты, и этот человек умрёте, а немного спустя не останется даже ваших имён.

passages.greek: Μήτι νῦν παρακάθηται τῇ Οὐήρου σορῷ Πάνθεια ἢ Πέργαμος; τί δέ, τῇ Ἁδριανοῦ Χαβρίας ἢ Διότιμος; γελοῖον. τί δέ, εἰ παρεκάθηντο, ἔμελλον αἰσθάνεσθαι; τί δέ, εἰ ᾐσθάνοντο, ἔμελλον ἡσθήσεσθαι; τί δέ, εἰ ἥδοντο, ἔμελλον οὗτοι ἀθάνατοι εἶναι; οὐχὶ καὶ τούτους πρῶτον μὲν γραίας καὶ γέροντας γενέσθαι οὕτως εἵμαρτο, εἶτα ἀποθανεῖν; τί οὖν ὕστερον ἔμελλον ἐκεῖνοι ποιεῖν τούτων ἀποθανόντων; γράσος πᾶν τοῦτο καὶ λύθρος ἐν θυλάκῳ.
passages.english: Surely Pantheia or Pergamus is not sitting by Verus’s coffin now? Or Chabrias or Diotimus by Hadrian’s? Ridiculous. And if they were sitting there, would the dead be aware of it? And if they were aware, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would these who sit by them be immortal? Was it not so fated for these too, first to become old women and old men, and then to die? So what were those others going to do afterwards, once these had died? All this is a rank smell and gore in a bag.

notes.note: A question word that expects the answer no. “Surely … not” carries that.
notes.other_reading: Is Pantheia or Pergamus sitting by Verus’s coffin now?

notes.note: A vessel for the remains of the dead: a coffin or an urn for ashes. The word does not decide between them, and it names the vessel, not the building that holds it.
notes.other_reading: by the urn of Verus

notes.note: People of the household of Verus, as Chabrias and Diotimus were of Hadrian’s. Pantheia is recalled as the mistress of Lucius Verus (from memory, unchecked).
The verb has no stated subject. The sense requires the dead men, since “these” two questions later marks the sitters off from them. “The dead” is supplied in the English.
notes.other_reading: would they have noticed?

notes.note: “To be pleased”. It chimes in sound with the verb for “be aware” just before, a play English cannot keep.
notes.other_reading: would it give them pleasure?

notes.note: “These”, the ones sitting by the coffin, against “those” (ἐκεῖνοι), the dead, two sentences on. The Greek has only the two pronouns. “Who sit by them” and later “others” are added to keep the two groups apart.
notes.other_reading: would the mourners be immortal?

notes.greek: γράσος πᾶν τοῦτο καὶ λύθρος ἐν θυλάκῳ
notes.note: γράσος is the rank smell of a goat or of sweat, λύθρος is blood mixed with dirt, θύλακος is a sack. “All this” is not defined: the body, or the whole business.
notes.other_reading: The whole thing is stench and filthy blood in a sack.

check.note: The word is said to cover urn, coffin and tomb. For an emperor’s remains “coffin” is a choice, and “tomb” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “coffin”. The Greek word names the vessel that holds the remains, a coffin or an urn, and not the tomb around it. The note gives “urn” as the other reading.

check.note: The Greek leaves the subject unstated: “would they be aware?”. “The dead” is supplied, rightly by sense, and should be kept as a known supplement.
check.decided: Accepted: “the dead” stays, as the finding suggests, and the note says that it is supplied because the Greek leaves the subject unstated.

check.note: A reader cannot tell who “these people” are. They are the ones sitting by the tomb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “would these who sit by them be immortal?”, which says who is meant. “These” is kept in place of “the mourners” because the Greek sets “these” against “those” through the next two sentences.

check.note: The adverb “so, in this way” is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Was it not so fated for these too”, with the adverb restored.

passages.casaubon: What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus? O foolery! For what if they did, would their masters be sensible of It? or if sensible, would they be glad of it? or if glad, were these immortal? Was not it appointed unto them also (both men and women,) to become old in time, and then to die? And these once dead, what would become of these former? And when all is done, what is all this for, but for a mere bag of blood and corruption?
passages.russian: Неужели Пантея или Пергам сидят сейчас у гроба Вера? Или Хабрий или Диотим — у гроба Адриана? Смешно. А если бы и сидели, почувствовали бы это умершие? А если бы почувствовали, обрадовались бы? А если бы обрадовались, разве были бы бессмертны эти, что сидят возле них? Разве не было суждено и им сначала стать старухами и стариками, а потом умереть? Что же стали бы потом делать те, другие, когда эти умерли бы? Всё это смрад и кровь в мешке.

passages.greek: Ἀεὶ τοῦ Ἡρακλειτείου μεμνῆσθαι, ὅτι γῆς θάνατος ὕδωρ γενέσθαι καὶ ὕδατος θάνατος ἀέρα γενέσθαι καὶ ἀέρος πῦρ καὶ ἔμπαλιν. μεμνῆσθαι δὲ καὶ τοῦ ἐπιλανθανομένου, ᾗ ἡ ὁδὸς ἄγει· καὶ ὅτι, ᾧ μάλιστα διηνεκῶς ὁμιλοῦσι, λόγῳ τῷ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦντι, τούτῳ διαφέρονται· καὶ οἷς καθ’ ἡμέραν ἐγκυροῦσι, ταῦτα αὐτοῖς ξένα φαίνεται· καὶ ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ὥσπερ καθεύδοντας ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν, καὶ γὰρ καὶ τότε δοκοῦμεν ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν· καὶ ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ὡς παῖδας τοκεώνων, τουτέστι κατὰ ψιλόν, καθότι παρειλήφαμεν.
passages.english: Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, and the death of water is to become air, and of air, fire, and back again. And remember too the one who forgets where the road leads; and that people are at odds with the very thing they keep company with most constantly, the reason that governs the whole; and that the things they run into every day seem foreign to them; and that we must not act and speak like people asleep, for then too we think we are acting and speaking; and that we must not act and speak like children of their parents, that is, simply as we have had it handed down.

notes.note: Literally “the Heraclitean [thing]”, the saying of Heraclitus. The rest of the passage strings together further sayings of his (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: what Heraclitus said

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. The English uses the bare command.
notes.other_reading: Always to remember

notes.note: “The one who forgets”: a figure from a saying, not a particular person.
notes.other_reading: the man who forgets where the road leads

notes.note: The verbs here are third person plural with no subject, and “people” is supplied. The verb is “to keep company with, to have dealings with”. The one rendered “are at odds with” (διαφέρονται) is literally “are carried apart from”.
notes.other_reading: that they differ from that with which they have most continual dealings

notes.note: λόγος here is the governing principle, “reason” by the glossary. In Heraclitus’s own usage it also carries “account”. τὰ ὅλα is a plural, “all things taken together”, given as “the whole” as elsewhere in this translation.
notes.other_reading: the account that orders all things

notes.note: The verb can be “seem” or “think”. With an infinitive it is said of what people believe they are doing, which suits sleepers, and the English reads “think”.
notes.other_reading: for then too we seem to act and speak

notes.note: Literally “like children of parents”, with an old poetic form of “parents” and no verb. “Act and speak” is carried over from the clause before, and “their” is supplied. The phrase is hard and its text has been doubted (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: must not be like children of their parents

notes.note: This is the writer’s own gloss on the phrase before. κατὰ ψιλόν is “barely, with nothing added”. The last words say “according as” the thing has been received, with the verb in the first person plural.
notes.other_reading: that is, on bare trust, just as it has been received

check.note: The verb is “seem” or “think”, and the English chooses “think”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “think”. With an infinitive the Greek verb is said of what people believe they are doing, and a sleeper believes rather than appears to act and speak. A note now gives “seem” as the other reading.

check.note: The Greek has no verb here, and “act and speak” from the clause before carries over more naturally than “be”. “Their” is also supplied. The form is odd and the text is doubted (from memory only).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause now carries over “act and speak” from the clause before in place of “be”. “Their” stays, since English needs a possessive there and one of the first person would be supplied just as much. The note says what is supplied.

check.note: Found while settling: “going simply by” and the quotation marks around the last words were additions. The Greek has only “barely” and “as” the thing has been received.
check.decided: Accepted: the gloss now reads as a plain clause beginning “that is, simply as”, with “going by” and the quotation marks removed.

check.note: Found while settling: “the whole of things” departs from the glossary, which gives “the whole” for the same Greek word in “the nature of the whole”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the reason that governs the whole”, and the note records that the Greek is a plural.

passages.casaubon: Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being the thing by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which daily happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and that we should not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep, by opinion and bare imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example; for best reason alleging their bare καθότι παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.
passages.russian: Всегда помни изречение Гераклита: смерть земли — стать водой, смерть воды — стать воздухом, воздуха — огнём, и обратно. Помни и о том, кто забывает, куда ведёт дорога; и о том, что люди не в ладах с тем самым, с чем они постояннее всего общаются, — с разумом, управляющим целым; и что то, на что они натыкаются каждый день, кажется им чужим; и что не следует действовать и говорить, как спящие, — ведь и тогда нам кажется, что мы действуем и говорим; и что не следует действовать и говорить, как дети своих родителей, то есть просто так, как нам было передано.

passages.greek: Φοβεῖταί τις μεταβολήν; τί γὰρ δύναται χωρὶς μεταβολῆς γενέσθαι, τί δὲ φίλτερον ἢ οἰκειότερον τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει; σὺ δὲ αὐτὸς λούσασθαι δύνασαι, ἐὰν μὴ τὰ ξύλα μεταβάλῃ; τραφῆναι δὲ δύνασαι, ἐὰν μὴ τὰ ἐδώδιμα μεταβάλῃ; ἄλλο δέ τι τῶν χρησίμων δύναται συντελεσθῆναι χωρὶς μεταβολῆς; οὐχ ὁρᾷς οὖν ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ σὲ μεταβαλεῖν ὅμοιόν ἐστι καὶ ὁμοίως ἀναγκαῖον τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει;
passages.english: Is someone afraid of change? Why, what can come about without change? And what is dearer to the nature of the whole, or more its own? Can you yourself take a bath unless the firewood changes? Can you be fed unless the food changes? Can anything else that is useful be accomplished without change? Do you not see, then, that your own changing too is the same kind of thing, and in the same way necessary to the nature of the whole?

notes.note: The particle gives the ground for surprise at the fear: “[how so,] for what can …?”. The English uses “Why,” for it.
notes.other_reading: But what can come about without change?

notes.note: “Come to be, come about, happen”: the word covers being born as well as happening.
notes.other_reading: what can come into being without change?

notes.note: “More one’s own, more akin, more at home with.” Change belongs to the nature of the whole more than anything else does, and the English reads “more its own”.
notes.other_reading: dearer or closer to the nature of the whole

notes.note: Literally “the wood”: the logs burned to heat the bath.
notes.other_reading: unless the wood changes

notes.note: Literally “the very fact of you changing”. The verb is the one used of the firewood and the food. The change meant is death, but the Greek does not say so and neither does the English.
notes.other_reading: that for you too to be changed

notes.note: “Is alike, and alike necessary.” The dative “to the nature of the whole” goes most naturally with “necessary”.
notes.other_reading: is just the same, and equally needed by the nature of the whole

check.note: “More its own to the nature of the whole” is awkward English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “And what is dearer to the nature of the whole, or more its own?”. The word order is eased as suggested, but “its own” is kept because the Greek word says that change belongs to the nature of the whole, which “at home in it” would turn around.

passages.casaubon: Is any man so foolish as to fear change, to which all things that once were not owe their being? And what is it, that is more pleasing and more familiar to the nature of the universe? How couldst thou thyself use thy ordinary hot baths, should not the wood that heateth them first be changed? How couldst thou receive any nourishment from those things that thou hast eaten, if they should not be changed? Can anything else almost (that is useful and profitable) be brought to pass without change? How then dost not thou perceive, that for thee also, by death, to come to change, is a thing of the very same nature, and as necessary for the nature of the universe?
passages.russian: Боится ли кто-то изменения? Да что же может возникнуть без изменения? И что милее природе целого или свойственнее ей? Разве ты сам можешь вымыться в бане, если дрова не изменятся? Можешь ли ты питаться, если пища не изменится? Может ли что-либо другое полезное совершиться без изменения? Так разве ты не видишь, что и твоё собственное изменение — того же рода и точно так же необходимо природе целого?

passages.greek:
Καταφιλοῦντα τὸ παιδίον δεῖ, ἔλεγεν ὁ Ἐπίκτητος, ἔνδον ἐπιφθέγγεσθαι· αὔριον ἴσως ἀποθανῇ.—δύσφημα ταῦτα.—οὐδὲν δύσφημον, ἔφη, φυσικοῦ τινος ἔργου σημαντικόν· ἢ καὶ τὸ τοὺς στάχυας θερισθῆναι δύσφημον.

Ὄμφαξ, σταφυλή, σταφίς, πάντα μεταβολαί, οὐκ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὄν, ἀλλὰ εἰς τὸ νῦν μὴ ὄν.
passages.english:
A person kissing their small child, Epictetus used to say, should add inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” “Those are words of ill omen.” “Nothing is of ill omen,” he said, “that points to some work of nature. Otherwise reaping the ears of grain is of ill omen too.”

Unripe grape, ripe grape, raisin: all changes, not into what is not, but into what is not now.

notes.note: Impersonal: “[one] kissing the child”, with a diminutive for “child”. The English uses “a person … their”. The saying is from the Discourses of Epictetus (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: When you kiss your little child

notes.note: The verb is “to utter over or in addition”, as one adds a word over an act. ἔνδον is “within”, that is, not aloud.
notes.other_reading: should whisper within

notes.note: As accented, second person future, “you will die”, spoken to the child. With the accent moved it would be a third person subjunctive, which does not construe here.
notes.other_reading: “Tomorrow, perhaps, it will die.”

notes.note: The edition marks the objection off with dashes, and the English uses quotation marks for the change of speaker. δύσφημος is “of ill omen”, said of words one should not utter for fear of bringing the thing on.
notes.other_reading: “That is unlucky talk.”

notes.note: “That signifies, that is a sign of.” The sentence is “nothing [is] ill-omened [that is] significant of some natural work”.
notes.other_reading: that names some process of nature

notes.greek: ἢ καὶ τὸ τοὺς στάχυας θερισθῆναι δύσφημον
notes.note: Literally “or else the ears of grain being reaped [is] ill-omened too”. It can be read as a statement that follows from the objection, as here, or as a question.
notes.other_reading: Or is it also ill-omened for the ears of grain to be reaped?

notes.note: Three single nouns: the unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the dried grape. English has no three matching single words.
notes.other_reading: Green grape, cluster, raisin

check.note: One Greek adverb, “within”, is given twice (“silently, inside”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “should add inwardly”, with one word for the one Greek adverb. “Add” is kept for the verb because it is plainer than “say over it” and still shows that the words come on top of the kiss.

passages.casaubon: 'As often as a father kisseth his child, he should say secretly with himself' (said Epictetus,) 'tomorrow perchance shall he die.' But these words be ominous. No words ominous (said he) that signify anything that is natural: in very truth and deed not more ominous than this, 'to cut down grapes when they are ripe.' Green grapes, ripe grapes, dried grapes, or raisins: so many changes and mutations of one thing, not into that which was not absolutely, but rather so many several changes and mutations, not into that which hath no being at all, but into that which is not yet in being.
passages.russian:
Целуя своего малыша, говорил Эпиктет, нужно мысленно прибавлять: «Завтра ты, может быть, умрёшь». — «Это зловещие слова». — «Ничто не зловеще, — сказал он, — если указывает на какое-то дело природы. Иначе зловеще и жать колосья».

Незрелый виноград, спелый виноград, изюм: всё это перемены — не в то, чего нет, а в то, чего нет сейчас.

passages.greek: Αὐλὴ Αὐγούστου, γυνή, θυγάτηρ, ἔγγονοι, πρόγονοι, ἀδελφή, Ἀγρίππας, συγγενεῖς, οἰκεῖοι, φίλοι, Ἄρειος, Μαικήνας, ἰατροί, θύται· ὅλης αὐλῆς θάνατος. εἶτα ἔπιθι τὰς ἄλλας . . . μὴ καθ’ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου θάνατον, οἷον Πομπηίων. κἀκεῖνο δὲ τὸ ἐπιγραφόμενον τοῖς μνήμασιν· ἔσχατος τοῦ ἰδίου γένους, ἐπιλογίζεσθαι πόσα ἐσπάσθησαν οἱ πρὸ αὐτῶν, ἵνα διάδοχόν τινα καταλίπωσιν, εἶτα ἀνάγκη ἔσχατόν τινα γενέσθαι· πάλιν ὧδε ὅλου γένους θάνατον.
passages.english: The court of Augustus: wife, daughter, grandchildren, stepsons, sister, Agrippa, relatives, intimates, friends, Areius, Maecenas, doctors, sacrificers. The death of a whole court. Then go on to the others . . . not the death of a single person: as, for example, that of the Pompeys. And that line written on tombs, “the last of his own family”: reckon up how much those before them were racked so as to leave some successor, and then someone has to be the last. Here again the death of a whole family.

notes.note: ἔγγονοι is “grandchildren” or “descendants”. πρόγονοι is usually “ancestors”, but also “children of an earlier marriage”, that is, stepchildren. The list is of people at court who died, so the English reads “stepsons”.
notes.other_reading: descendants, ancestors

notes.note: “Those of the house”: close kin, intimates, or the people of the household. Coming between “relatives” and “friends” it is taken as those close to him.
notes.other_reading: household

notes.note: Areius, a philosopher attached to Augustus (from memory, unchecked). Agrippa was his general and son-in-law, Maecenas his friend and adviser.
notes.other_reading: Arius

notes.note: “Sacrificers”: the priests who perform the sacrifice and read the signs from it.
notes.other_reading: diviners

notes.note: The edition marks a gap after these words, and the sentence does not construe across it. “The others” is feminine plural, which would suit “courts”. The two sides of the gap are translated as they stand and nothing is supplied.
notes.other_reading: Then go on to the other courts . . .

notes.note: These words stand just after the gap with no verb to govern them, and the preposition καθ’ cannot be placed with certainty. The English gives only “not the death of a single person”.
notes.other_reading: not one person’s death at a time

notes.note: A genitive plural: “as [that] of the Pompeii”. It is taken as the family of Pompey, a whole line that died out, set against the death of a single person. The same form is the name of the city of Pompeii, which is named in 4.48 (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: as, for example, that of Pompeii

notes.note: Given as the wording of an epitaph. γένος is “family, line, stock”, and “family” is kept for it to the end of the passage.
notes.other_reading: “the last of his line”

notes.note: The verb is “were pulled, wrenched, convulsed”, and “racked” keeps the bodily image. The verb of reckoning before it is an infinitive used as an instruction. “Those before them” is plural although the epitaph is singular.
notes.other_reading: how much anguish those before them went through

notes.note: An accusative with no verb of its own. It hangs on the earlier “reckon up” or “go on to”, and the English leaves it as a bare phrase.
notes.other_reading: here again, consider the death of a whole family

check.note: The ordinary meaning of the word is “ancestors”. “Stepsons” is a rarer sense, which suits Augustus’s household but is the translator’s choice.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “stepsons”. The Greek word also means children of an earlier marriage, and it stands in a list of the living members of a court who then died, where ancestors have no place. The note records “ancestors” as the usual meaning.

check.note: The word means those close to him: intimates, or kin. After “relatives” it is more likely intimates than servants.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “intimates”. Between “relatives” and “friends” the word points to those close to him, and “household” suggested servants.

check.note: The same form is the name of the city of Pompeii, as in 4.48. As the English stood, the example hung on “the death of a single person”, when it must illustrate the opposite. The Greek has a gap here and does not construe.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not the death of a single person: as, for example, that of the Pompeys”, so that the example no longer hangs on “a single person”. Nothing is supplied in brackets, because the Greek is broken at the gap and the notes say so. “The Pompeys” is kept as a defensible reading, with the city given in the note.

check.note: “Pulled about” is unclear. The verb here means racked, torn with strain and worry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “how much those before them were racked”. “Pulled about” was unclear, but “anguish … went through” would lose the image of the Greek verb, which is of being wrenched or convulsed.

check.note: “It is necessary that someone be the last” is stiff English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and then someone has to be the last”, which keeps the necessity in plainer words.

passages.casaubon: Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together. Proceed now on to the rest that have been since that of Augustus. Hath death dwelt with them otherwise, though so many and so stately whilst they lived, than it doth use to deal with any one particular man? Consider now the death of a whole kindred and family, as of that of the Pompeys, as that also that useth to be written upon some monuments, HE WAS THE LAST OF HIS OWN KINDRED. O what care did his predecessors take, that they might leave a successor, yet behold at last one or other must of necessity be THE LAST. Here again therefore consider the death of a whole kindred.
passages.russian: Двор Августа: жена, дочь, внуки, пасынки, сестра, Агриппа, родственники, близкие, друзья, Арей, Меценат, врачи, жертвоприносители. Смерть целого двора. Затем переходи к другим . . . не смерть одного человека: как, например, смерть Помпеев. И та строчка, что пишут на гробницах: «последний в своём роду», — подсчитай, сколько мучились те, кто был до них, чтобы оставить какого-нибудь преемника, а потом кто-то должен оказаться последним. Здесь опять смерть целого рода.

passages.greek: Οὐχὶ τοῦτο μόνον δεῖ λογίζεσθαι, ὅτι καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἀπαναλίσκεται ὁ βίος καὶ μέρος ἔλαττον αὐτοῦ καταλείπεται, ἀλλὰ κἀκεῖνο λογιστέον, ὅτι, εἰ ἐπὶ πλέον βιῴη τις, ἐκεῖνό γε ἄδηλον, εἰ ἐξαρκέσει ὁμοία αὖθις ἡ διάνοια πρὸς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς θεωρίας τῆς συντεινούσης εἰς τὴν ἐμπειρίαν τῶν τε θείων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων. ἐὰν γὰρ παραληρεῖν ἄρξηται, τὸ μὲν διαπνεῖσθαι καὶ τρέφεσθαι καὶ φαντάζεσθαι καὶ ὁρμᾶν καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τοιαῦτα, οὐκ ἐνδεήσει· τὸ δὲ ἑαυτῷ χρῆσθαι καὶ τοὺς τοῦ καθήκοντος ἀριθμοὺς ἀκριβοῦν καὶ τὰ προφαινόμενα διαρθροῦν καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ εἰ ἤδη ἐξακτέον αὑτὸν ἐφιστάνειν καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα λογισμοῦ συγγεγυμνασμένου πάνυ χρῄζει, προαποσβέννυται. χρὴ οὖν ἐπείγεσθαι οὐ μόνον τῷ ἐγγυτέρω τοῦ θανάτου ἑκάστοτε γίνεσθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὸ τὴν ἐννόησιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τὴν παρακολούθησιν προαπολήγειν.
passages.english: It is not only this that has to be reckoned with, that life is being used up day by day and a smaller part of it is left. This too has to be reckoned with: if a person were to live longer, it is at least unclear whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things and of the study that is directed towards close acquaintance with divine and human things. For if a person begins to lose their wits, there will be no lack of breathing, of taking nourishment, of having impressions and impulses, and of everything else of that kind. But making use of oneself, getting every point of duty exact, setting out clearly what appears before one, stopping to consider this very question, whether it is now time to lead oneself out of life, and everything of that kind that needs thoroughly trained reasoning: this is extinguished first. So one must hurry, not only because one comes nearer to death at every moment, but also because the grasp of things and the power to follow them give out first.

notes.note: λογίζεσθαι, then λογιστέον, and further on the noun λογισμοῦ are one family of words (to reckon, to reason). The English reads “reckoned with” for the two verbs and “reasoning” for the noun, so the link is only half kept.
notes.other_reading: It is not only this that one must reason about

notes.note: αὖθις is “later on” or “again”, and ὁμοία is “the same, alike”, said of the mind. The English reads “later on” and “unchanged”.
notes.other_reading: whether their mind will again be equal to it in the same way

notes.note: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια and allows “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that may fail with age, so the English reads “mind”.
notes.other_reading: whether their thought will later on be equal

notes.greek: πρὸς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς θεωρίας
notes.note: τῆς θεωρίας is in the genitive, so as the Greek stands it depends on σύνεσιν together with τῶν πραγμάτων: understanding of things and of the study. An accusative would make the study a second thing the mind must be equal to, and editors have doubted the case (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps the genitive as given.
notes.other_reading: equal to understanding things and to the study that is directed towards close acquaintance with divine and human things

notes.note: ἐμπειρία is familiarity won by experience and practice, not knowledge in the abstract. The English reads “close acquaintance”.
notes.other_reading: towards experience of divine and human things

notes.note: παραληρεῖν is to talk beside the point, as in delirium or senility; the English gives the sense, “lose their wits”. The subject is not stated: it can be the person, as the English has it, or the mind, the nearest noun.
notes.other_reading: For if it begins to wander

notes.note: Literally “to be breathed through”. It can mean plain breathing or the wider passing of air and vapour through the body and its skin. The English keeps the plain word.
notes.other_reading: transpiring

notes.note: Literally “to make exact the numbers of duty”. In Stoic speech a duty (τὸ καθῆκον, what is fitting to do) has “numbers”, the separate points that must all be met for the act to be complete. The English reads “every point” for “the numbers”.
notes.other_reading: getting the numbers of duty exact

notes.note: διαρθροῦν is to divide by joints, to set out part by part. τὰ προφαινόμενα is “the things that show themselves”, which can be what comes into view in general or first appearances in particular.
notes.other_reading: analysing first appearances part by part

notes.note: Literally “one must lead oneself out”, the Stoic expression for leaving life by one’s own act. “Of life” is added so that the English says what is meant, and “must now” is turned into “it is now time to”.
notes.other_reading: whether one must now lead oneself out

notes.note: πάνυ, “very”, stands between the participle and the verb and can go with either. The English takes it with the participle: “thoroughly trained”.
notes.other_reading: that very much needs trained reasoning

notes.note: The image is of a flame going out beforehand. “First” stands for the prefix προ-, before the other functions or before death; the Greek does not say which. προαπολήγειν in the last sentence has the same prefix and reads “first” there too.
notes.other_reading: is extinguished beforehand

check.note: αὖθις is “later on, afterwards”, not “still”, and “as before” is not in the Greek: ὁμοία is simply “the same, unchanged”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things”. “Later on” stands for αὖθις and “unchanged” for ὁμοία, with nothing added; the suggested “in the same way” is not used because ὁμοία describes the mind itself.

check.note: The genitive τῆς θεωρίας hangs on σύνεσιν, giving “the understanding of things and of the study”, which is odd, since the study looks like a second thing the mind must be equal to. Editors have doubted the case (from memory).
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “the understanding of things and of the study”, as the point itself advises, because that is what the Greek as given says. The note now records that the phrase is awkward, that an accusative would give “and to the study”, and that the case has been doubted (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: ἐμπειρία is acquaintance won by experience, practised familiarity, not knowledge in general.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “close acquaintance with” in place of “knowledge of”, since the Greek word means familiarity got by practice. “Experience of” is given in the note.

check.greek: τῶν τε θείων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων
check.note: “Things divine and human”, with the adjectives after the noun, is an old-fashioned English turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “divine and human things”.

check.note: The subject of ἄρξηται is not stated: it can be the person as well as the mind, and παραληρεῖν is more naturally said of a person. “Ramble” is also weaker than the Greek, which means losing one’s wits.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For if a person begins to lose their wits”. The verb is used of people who talk nonsense in delirium or old age, and the list that follows (breathing, taking nourishment) is of the person’s functions; the note gives the reading with the mind as subject.

check.note: διαπνεῖσθαι is “to be breathed through, to transpire”, a wider bodily process than respiration, and “breathing” narrows it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the point holds that the Greek word is wider than breathing with the lungs, but “breathing” is kept as the plain word, which the point allows. The note now says what the wider sense is and gives “transpiring” as the other reading.

check.note: “The numbers of duty” is word for word but means nothing to a reader of today; the ἀριθμοί are the items or points that make up a duty in full.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “getting every point of duty exact”. “Numbers” here is a set Stoic expression for the points that make an act complete, not a picture the argument uses, so the sense is given and the note keeps the literal “numbers”; “what duty requires” is not used because the Greek has only “of duty”.

check.note: “Of life” is not in the Greek, which says only “lead oneself out”; it is a needed gloss but an addition.
check.decided: Accepted: “to lead oneself out of life” stands, as the point advises, since “lead oneself out” alone would not be understood. The note says that “of life” is added.

check.note: πάνυ stands between the participle and the verb and can go with either, but the English renders it twice, as “badly” and as “well”, and adds “power of”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that needs thoroughly trained reasoning”, with πάνυ rendered once and “power of” removed. A new note gives the other reading, “very much needs”.

check.note: “Put out” is ambiguous in English (annoyed, set outside); the image is of a flame going out before the rest does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “this is extinguished first”, which can only be heard of a flame.

passages.casaubon: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend. For if once he shall begin to dote, his respiration, nutrition, his imaginative, and appetitive, and other natural faculties, may still continue the same: he shall find no want of them. But how to make that right use of himself that he should, how to observe exactly in all things that which is right and just, how to redress and rectify all wrong, or sudden apprehensions and imaginations, and even of this particular, whether he should live any longer or no, to consider duly; for all such things, wherein the best strength and vigour of the mind is most requisite; his power and ability will be past and gone. Thou must hasten therefore; not only because thou art every day nearer unto death than other, but also because that intellective faculty in thee, whereby thou art enabled to know the true nature of things, and to order all thy actions by that knowledge, doth daily waste and decay: or, may fail thee before thou die.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Нужно принимать в расчёт не только то, что жизнь день за днём расходуется и остающаяся её часть всё меньше. Нужно принять в расчёт и это: если бы человек прожил дольше, то по крайней мере неясно, будет ли его ум и потом так же, без перемен, способен к пониманию вещей и к тому изучению, что направлено на близкое знакомство с божественным и человеческим. Ведь если человек начнёт выживать из ума, у него не будет недостатка ни в дыхании, ни в питании, ни в представлениях и побуждениях, ни во всём прочем подобном. Но распоряжаться собой, точно выверять каждый пункт долга, ясно раскладывать то, что предстаёт перед тобой, задерживаться на самом вопросе, не пора ли уже вывести себя из жизни, и всё подобное, что требует основательно упражнённого рассуждения, — это гаснет первым. Поэтому нужно спешить — не только потому, что с каждым мгновением приближаешься к смерти, но и потому, что постижение вещей и способность следовать за ними иссякают раньше.

passages.greek: Κἂν τρὶς χίλια ἔτη βιώσεσθαι μέλλῃς, κἂν τοσαυτάκις μύρια, ὅμως μέμνησο ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἄλλον ἀποβάλλει βίον ἢ τοῦτον ὃν ζῇ, οὐδὲ ἄλλον ζῇ ἢ ὃν ἀποβάλλει. εἰς ταὐτὸν οὖν καθίσταται τὸ μήκιστον τῷ βραχυτάτῳ. τὸ γὰρ παρὸν πᾶσιν ἴσον καὶ τὸ ἀπολλύμενον οὖν ἴσον καὶ τὸ ἀποβαλλόμενον οὕτως ἀκαριαῖον ἀναφαίνεται. οὔτε γὰρ τὸ παρῳχηκὸς οὔτε τὸ μέλλον ἀποβάλοι ἄν τις· ὃ γὰρ οὐκ ἔχει, πῶς ἄν τις τοῦτο αὐτοῦ ἀφέλοιτο; τούτων οὖν τῶν δύο δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι· ἑνὸς μέν, ὅτι πάντα ἐξ ἀιδίου ὁμοειδῆ καὶ ἀνακυκλούμενα καὶ οὐδὲν διαφέρει, πότερον ἐν ἑκατὸν ἔτεσιν ἢ ἐν διακοσίοις ἢ ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ τὰ αὐτά τις ὄψεται· ἑτέρου δέ, ὅτι καὶ ὁ πολυχρονιώτατος καὶ ὁ τάχιστα τεθνηξόμενος τὸ ἴσον ἀποβάλλει. τὸ γὰρ παρόν ἐστι μόνον, οὗ στερίσκεσθαι μέλλει, εἴπερ γε ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο μόνον καὶ ὃ μὴ ἔχει τις οὐκ ἀποβάλλει.
passages.english: Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or even three times ten thousand, still remember that no one loses any life other than this one they are living, and no one lives any life other than the one they are losing. So the longest comes to the same thing as the shortest. For the present is equal for everyone, so what perishes is equal too, and in this way what is lost shows itself to be an instant. For no one could lose either the past or the future: how could anyone take from a person what that person does not have? So these two things must be remembered. One is that all things from eternity are of the same kind and come round in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person will see the same things for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit. The other is that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal amount. For the present is the only thing a person is going to be deprived of, if indeed this is the only thing they have, and a person does not lose what they do not have.

notes.note: Literally “so many times ten thousand”, where “so many times” picks up the “three times” of three thousand. The English says “three times ten thousand” outright.
notes.other_reading: or even that many times ten thousand

notes.note: ἀποβάλλειν, literally to throw off or let drop, is the word the argument turns on and comes six times. The English reads “lose” every time.
notes.other_reading: no one throws away any life other than

notes.note: This is a different verb from ἀποβάλλειν: ἀπόλλυσθαι, to perish or be lost. The English reads “perishes” to keep it apart from “lose”, though it could be heard as one more word for the same loss. ἴσον is “equal” throughout the passage.
notes.other_reading: so what is being lost is equal too

notes.note: The word means of the shortest possible length, of a hair’s breadth of time. The English gives the noun “an instant” for the adjective.
notes.other_reading: shows itself to be momentary

notes.note: Literally “being wheeled round again”. The English keeps the circle.
notes.other_reading: and recur in cycles

notes.note: Literally “in the unlimited”, with “time” understood after the hundred and two hundred years. ἐν with a number of years means over that span, so the English reads “for”; “in a hundred years” would be heard as “a hundred years from now”.
notes.other_reading: or for ever

notes.greek: εἴπερ γε ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο μόνον
notes.note: εἴπερ γε can state a condition (“if indeed”) or a ground taken as agreed (“since”). The English keeps “if indeed”. The subject is unstated and is taken to be the same impersonal “a person” as in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: since this is in fact the only thing they have

check.note: The second “even if” (κἂν) is flattened to “or”, and “that many times ten thousand” is hard to follow; it means three times ten thousand.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or even three times ten thousand”. “Even” restores the second κἂν, and the number is said outright; the note gives the literal “so many times”.

check.note: The γάρ that makes this question the reason for the sentence before is replaced by a colon.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for how could anyone take from a person what that person does not have?”, with the “for” of the Greek restored.

check.greek: ἐν ἑκατὸν ἔτεσιν ἢ ἐν διακοσίοις ἢ ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ
check.note: “Will see the same things in a hundred years” reads in English as “a hundred years from now”; the Greek means over a span of a hundred years, two hundred, or without end.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit”, since ἐν with a number of years means during that span.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek says “this one that they are living”, and the draft’s “the one they are living” left “this” out.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “any life other than this one they are living”.

passages.casaubon: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being, is equal unto all men. And that being it which we part with whensoever we die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he hath not? These two things therefore thou must remember. First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with, is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present, is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Даже если тебе предстоит прожить три тысячи лет или даже трижды десять тысяч, всё же помни, что никто не теряет никакой иной жизни, кроме той, которой живёт, и не живёт никакой иной, кроме той, которую теряет. Поэтому самая долгая сводится к тому же, что и самая короткая. Ведь настоящее у всех равно, а значит, равно и то, что гибнет, и так теряемое оказывается мгновением. Ни прошлого, ни будущего никто потерять не может: как можно отнять у человека то, чего у него нет? Итак, нужно помнить две вещи. Первая — что всё от века одного рода и движется по кругу и что нет разницы, увидит ли человек одно и то же за сто лет, или за двести, или за бесконечное время. Вторая — что проживший дольше всех и тот, кто умрёт скорее всех, теряют поровну. Ведь настоящее — единственное, чего человек может лишиться, если только это единственное, что у него есть, а чего у человека нет, того он не теряет.

passages.greek: Ἰδιωτικὸν μέν, ὅμως δὲ ἀνυστικὸν βοήθημα πρὸς θανάτου καταφρόνησιν ἡ ἀναπόλησις τῶν γλίσχρως ἐνδιατριψάντων τῷ ζῆν. τί οὖν αὐτοῖς πλέον ἢ τοῖς ἀώροις; πάντως πού ποτε κεῖνται, Καδικιανός, Φάβιος, Ἰουλιανός, Λέπιδος ἢ εἴ τις τοιοῦτος, οἳ πολλοὺς ἐξήνεγκαν, εἶτα ἐξηνέχθησαν· ὅλον, μικρόν ἐστι τὸ διάστημα καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ; μὴ οὖν ὡς πρᾶγμα. βλέπε γὰρ ὀπίσω τὸ ἀχανὲς τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ τὸ πρόσω ἄλλο ἄπειρον. ἐν δὴ τούτῳ τί διαφέρει ὁ τριήμερος τοῦ τριγερηνίου;
passages.english: A layman’s help towards contempt of death, but an effective one all the same, is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. What more do they have, then, than those who died before their time? In any case they lie somewhere or other, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus or anyone else of that kind, who carried many out to burial and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the interval is small, and even this is drained out through how many things, in what company and in what a little body! So do not treat it as something that matters. For look behind at the yawning expanse of eternity, and ahead at another that has no limit. In this, then, what difference is there between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations?

notes.note: ἰδιωτικός is what belongs to a private person or a non-expert, here as against a philosopher’s argument. It can carry a slight of “crude” or “vulgar”.
notes.other_reading: An unphilosophical help

notes.note: γλίσχρως is “stickily”, used of clinging and of stinginess. Literally “those who spent their time stickily in living”; the English gives the adverb as “clung on”. ἀναπόλησις before it is a going over again in the mind, here “call back to mind”.
notes.other_reading: those who hung on greedily to being alive

notes.note: πού ποτε can be “somewhere or other” or “somewhere, at some time”, and πάντως can be “in any case” or “surely”. κεῖνται, “they lie”, is the ordinary word for the dead lying in their graves.
notes.other_reading: Surely they lie somewhere at last

notes.note: The name is transliterated as it is given. From memory, unchecked: other editions print Καιδικιανός, Caedicianus. The four men are not explained in the text; the context makes them people known for living long.
notes.other_reading: Caedicianus

notes.note: ἐκφέρειν, “to carry out”, is the set word for carrying a body out to its funeral. “To burial” is added once so that the sense is clear.
notes.other_reading: who carried out many, then were carried out

notes.note: With the comma as given, ὅλον is an adverb, “on the whole, in sum”. Without it the words would say “the whole interval is small”.
notes.other_reading: The whole interval is small

notes.greek: καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ;
notes.note: The Greek as given ends this sentence with a question mark, but its words (“through how many”, “with what sort”, “in what a”) are those of an exclamation, not of a question. There is also no finite verb after “and even this”, only a participle. The English makes it an exclamation and supplies “is”.
notes.other_reading: Altogether, is the interval not small, and even this drained out through how many things, in what company and in what a little body?

notes.note: The image is of baling or draining water out to the last, used for toiling through something. “Through how many” and “with what sort” do not say whether things or people are meant: the English reads the first as things, most likely troubles, and the second as people, “in what company”. σωματίῳ is a diminutive that belittles the body.
notes.other_reading: and even this is toiled through amid how many troubles, with what sort of things and in what a poor little body

notes.note: There is no verb: literally “not, then, as a matter”, with πρᾶγμα in the sense of something that counts. The English supplies “treat it” and gives πρᾶγμα as “something that matters”.
notes.other_reading: So, not as though it were something

notes.note: τὸ ἀχανές is “the yawning”, an adjective used as a noun, so English must supply a noun: “expanse”. αἰών is the whole of time, given as “eternity”.
notes.other_reading: the gaping gulf of time

notes.note: ἄπειρον can be taken with an understood “expanse” (another, without limit, ahead) or as a noun (what lies ahead is another infinity). The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: and what lies ahead, another infinity

notes.note: A made-up word that plays on “Gerenian”, Homer’s standing name for Nestor, the old king who outlived three generations, and on γέρων, “old man”: one who is three times a Nestor. The English names Nestor and gives the three as generations. τριήμερος before it is “of three days”, taken as a child three days old.
notes.other_reading: between the one who lives three days and the one who lives three generations

check.note: ἀναπόλησις is going over something again in the mind; “to go back over those” is not clear English when the object is people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life”. “Back” keeps the “again” of the Greek word.

check.note: ποτε (“at some point, at last”) is not rendered, and πάντως is more “assuredly, one way or another” than “in any case”.
check.decided: Declined: “somewhere or other” already renders πού ποτε, where ποτε is taken as the word that makes “somewhere” indefinite, and “in any case” is an ordinary sense of πάντως. The other way of taking the words, “surely” and “at last”, is recorded in the note.

check.note: ἢ is “or”, not “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or anyone else of that kind”.

check.greek: καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ;
check.note: The Greek is an exclamation built on “how many, what sort”, and as an English question it is unclear. δι’ ὅσων is plural, “through how many things”, that is troubles, and “poor” is added to the diminutive σωματίῳ.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and even this, through how many things, in what company and in what a little body it is drained out!”, an exclamation, with “poor” removed. “Things” is kept and not “troubles”, because the Greek does not name them, and “drained out” is kept; a note records that the Greek as given ends in a question mark.

check.note: “Great” is not in the Greek, which says only “not, then, as a thing (that matters)”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So do not treat it as something that matters”. The verb still has to be supplied, as the note says.

check.note: αἰών is the whole of time, eternity, not time in general, and “gaping gulf” gives two words for the one word ἀχανές.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the yawning expanse of eternity”. “Yawning” is the Greek adjective and “expanse” the plain noun English needs to carry it.

check.note: “Another without limit” is awkward English; the Greek is “another infinity ahead”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and ahead at another that has no limit”, with “expanse” understood. “Another infinity” is given in the note.

check.note: τριγερηνίου is a play on Nestor “the Gerenian”, who outlived three generations, and the allusion is dropped. τριήμερος is a child three days old.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations”, so the name the Greek points to is in the text. The note explains the made-up word.

passages.casaubon: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that which liveth three ages?
passages.russian: Дилетантское, но всё же действенное средство для презрения к смерти — вспоминать тех, кто цеплялся за жизнь и задерживался в ней. Что же у них больше, чем у тех, кто умер безвременно? Так или иначе лежат они где-то — Кадициан, Фабий, Юлиан, Лепид или кто-то ещё в этом роде, — многих вынесшие хоронить, а потом и сами вынесенные. В целом промежуток мал, да и он истощается через сколько всего, в каком обществе и в каком маленьком теле! Так не считай его чем-то важным. Посмотри назад — на зияющую ширь вечности, и вперёд — на другую, не имеющую предела. В ней же какая разница между трёхдневным младенцем и Нестором трёх поколений?

passages.greek: Μέμνησο ἐκ πόσου ταῦτα ἀναβάλλῃ καὶ ὁποσάκις προθεσμίας λαβὼν παρὰ τῶν θεῶν οὐ χρᾷ αὐταῖς. δεῖ δὲ ἤδη ποτὲ αἰσθέσθαι τίνος κόσμου μέρος εἶ καὶ τίνος διοικοῦντος τὸν κόσμον ἀπόρροια ὑπέστης καὶ ὅτι ὅρος ἐστί σοι περιγεγραμμένος τοῦ χρόνου, ᾧ ἐὰν εἰς τὸ ἀπαιθριάσαι μὴ χρήσῃ, οἰχήσεται οἰχήσῃ καὶ αὖθις οὐκ ἐξέσται.
passages.english: Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and have made no use of it. Now at last you must perceive what universe you are a part of, and from what governor of the universe you came into being as an outflow, and that a limit of time has been marked out for you. If you do not use it to clear away the clouds, it will be gone, you will be gone, and it will not be possible again.

notes.note: A legal word: the day fixed in advance by which something must be done, or the period allowed. The Greek is plural, one term after another being granted; the English reads “a set time” in the singular after “how many times”.
notes.other_reading: how many times you have been given deadlines by the gods and make no use of them

notes.note: τίνος asks “which” or “what”, and in such a phrase can lean towards “what kind of”.
notes.other_reading: what kind of universe you are a part of

notes.note: ἀπόρροια is a flowing off, a stream that runs out from a source. ὑπέστης is “you came to exist”. Literally “of what governor of the universe you came to exist as an outflow”.
notes.other_reading: and from what governor of the universe you exist as an emanation

notes.note: The verb is made from the word for a cloudless sky: to bring fair weather, to drive off the clouds. No object is given, and the weather stands for clearing one’s own mind; the English keeps the image and does not add “your mind”. The verb can also be taken as “to become clear”.
notes.other_reading: if you do not use it to become clear, as the sky does

notes.note: The two verbs stand side by side with no connecting word in the Greek as given: “it will be gone” (the time) and “you will be gone”. From memory, unchecked: editions print a καὶ between them, and its absence may be a slip of the digitised copy. The English keeps the two without “and”.
