notes.other_reading: it will be gone and you will be gone

notes.note: Literally “it will not be allowed (or possible) again”, with nothing said about what: the chance to use the time.
notes.other_reading: and there will be no second chance

check.note: προθεσμία is an appointed day, a deadline or period of grace; “fixed terms” is unclear to a reader of today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a set time”, not “a deadline” or “a set date”. The Greek goes on to say that the times are not used, and a time can be used where a date cannot.

check.note: After “you have received”, “and do not use them” jars; the Greek is a participle and a present, “having received them, you make no use of them”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and make no use of it”.

check.greek: τίνος διοικοῦντος τὸν κόσμον ἀπόρροια ὑπέστης
check.note: The content is right but the trailing “from as an outflow” is clumsy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and from what governor of the universe you came into being as an outflow”.

check.note: The image of clearing the sky is kept, but nothing tells the reader it is the sky of his own mind, so the phrase puzzles. The verb can also be taken as “to become clear”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to clear away the clouds”. The verb is made from the word for a cloudless sky and means to bring fair weather, so the image is the same, and English speaks of clouds in this way when it means the mind; “to become clear” is in the note.

check.note: The two verbs stand side by side with no connective in the Greek as given; from memory the editions print καὶ between them, so this looks like a slip in the digitised text. The English is right either way.
check.decided: Accepted: “it will be gone, you will be gone” stands, as the point advises, following the Greek as given. The note says that a καὶ may have dropped out (from memory, unchecked).

passages.casaubon: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it. It is high time for thee to understand the true nature both of the world, whereof thou art a part; and of that Lord and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, thou thyself didst flow: and that there is but a certain limit of time appointed unto thee, which if thou shalt not make use of to calm and allay the many distempers of thy soul, it will pass away and thou with it, and never after return.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Вспомни, как давно ты это откладываешь и сколько раз боги назначали тебе срок, а ты им не пользовался. Теперь наконец ты должен осознать, какого мироздания ты часть и от какого правителя мироздания произошёл как истечение, и что тебе отмерен предел времени. Если ты не употребишь его на то, чтобы развеять тучи, оно уйдёт, и ты уйдёшь, и возможности больше не будет.

passages.greek: Μὴ ὡς μύρια μέλλων ἔτη ζῆν. τὸ χρεὼν ἐπήρτηται· ἕως ζῇς, ἕως ἔξεστιν, ἀγαθὸς γενοῦ.
passages.english: Not as though you were going to live ten thousand years. What must come hangs over you. While you live, while it is possible, become good.

notes.greek: Μὴ ὡς μύρια μέλλων ἔτη ζῆν
notes.note: The sentence has no main verb: “Not as one who is going to live ten thousand years”. A verb such as “live” or “act” is left to be understood, and the English leaves it out as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: Do not live as though you were going to live ten thousand years

notes.note: τὸ χρεών is “what must be”, fate, with a sense of a debt that falls due: here death. ἐπήρτηται is “has been hung over”. The Greek does not say over whom; “you” is added.
notes.other_reading: Fate hangs overhead

notes.note: γενοῦ is “become”, which can also stand for a plain “be” in a command.
notes.other_reading: be good

passages.casaubon: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Не так, будто тебе предстоит жить десять тысяч лет. То, что должно прийти, нависло над тобой. Пока живёшь, пока можно, стань хорошим.

passages.greek: Μηκέτι πλανῶ· οὔτε γὰρ τὰ ὑπομνημάτιά σου μέλλεις ἀναγινώσκειν οὔτε τὰς τῶν ἀρχαίων Ῥωμαίων καὶ Ἑλλήνων πράξεις καὶ τὰς ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἐκλογάς, ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο. σπεῦδε οὖν εἰς τέλος καὶ τὰς κενὰς ἐλπίδας ἀφεὶς σαυτῷ βοήθει, εἴ τί σοι μέλει σαυτοῦ, ἕως ἔξεστιν.
passages.english: Stop wandering. For you are not going to read either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for your own old age. So hurry to the end, and letting go of empty hopes, come to your own rescue, if you care at all about yourself, while it is possible.

notes.note: πλανᾶσθαι is to wander, to stray, and so to be led off the point or be mistaken. Literally “wander no more”.
notes.other_reading: Stop going astray

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for notes or memoranda. It may mean notebooks like this one or other notes he kept; the Greek does not say.
notes.other_reading: your own little notes

notes.note: “Deeds”, as something to be read, so written accounts of them. It may be a collection he had made himself; the English keeps the plain word.
notes.other_reading: the histories of the ancient Romans and Greeks

notes.note: συγγράμματα are written works, treatises. The Greek says only “the writings” and does not say whose; the authors he read are the likely sense.
notes.other_reading: the selections from their books

notes.greek: ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο
notes.note: The relative ἃς is feminine plural: what was being put away is the extracts, or the deeds and the extracts together, not the writings, which are neuter. The English “which” after the comma is to be heard the same way.
notes.other_reading: all of which you were putting away for your old age

notes.note: τέλος is both “end” and “goal, the aim of life”, and εἰς τέλος can also mean “to completion”. The English reads “the end”, which can be heard as the finish or as the aim.
notes.other_reading: So hurry on to your goal

notes.note: Literally “help yourself”, the verb for running to someone’s aid. “Help yourself” is avoided because in English it is heard as “take what you like”.
notes.other_reading: rescue yourself

check.note: The inverted order of “Wander no longer” is old-fashioned English, and πλανῶ is also “go astray”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Stop wandering”. “Going astray” is given in the note.

check.greek: καὶ τὰς ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἐκλογάς, ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο
check.note: ἃς is feminine plural, so what was being put away is the extracts (and possibly the deeds too), not the writings, which are neuter; in the English “that” attaches to “the writings”. The Greek also joins deeds and extracts with “and” under one “nor”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for yourself for old age”. The comma and “which” take the clause back to the extracts, or to the deeds and extracts together, as the Greek allows, and “and” joins the two as in the Greek.

check.note: τέλος can be the end or the goal, and εἰς τέλος can also mean “to completion”; “the end” in English is heard as death, which settles the question silently.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the end” is kept, as the point allows, because like τέλος it can mean both the finish and the aim, where “goal” would shut out the first. The note now gives all three senses, and “hasten” becomes the plainer “hurry”.

check.note: “Come to your own help” is not an English phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “come to your own rescue”.

passages.casaubon: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Перестань блуждать. Ведь ты не прочтёшь ни своих записных книжечек, ни деяний древних римлян и греков, ни выписок из сочинений, которые ты откладывал себе на старость. Так спеши к концу и, отбросив пустые надежды, приди сам себе на помощь, если хоть сколько-нибудь заботишься о себе, пока это возможно.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ εἴ τίς σοι θεῶν εἶπεν, ὅτι αὔριον τεθνήξῃ ἢ πάντως γε εἰς τρίτην, οὐκέτ’ ἂν παρὰ μέγα ἐποιοῦ τὸ εἰς τρίτην μᾶλλον ἢ αὔριον, εἴ γε μὴ ἐσχάτως ἀγεννὴς εἶ· πόσον γάρ ἐστι τὸ μεταξύ; οὕτως καὶ τὸ εἰς πολλοστὸν ἔτος μᾶλλον ἢ αὔριον μηδὲν μέγα εἶναι νόμιζε.
passages.english: Just as, if one of the gods told you that you will die tomorrow or at any rate the day after, you would no longer count it a great thing that it should be the day after rather than tomorrow, unless you are utterly abject (for how much lies between?), so too think it nothing great that it should be many years from now rather than tomorrow.

notes.note: Literally “on the third (day)”. Greek counts today as the first, so this is the day after tomorrow.
notes.other_reading: or at any rate on the third day

notes.note: An idiom: to reckon something as making a great difference.
notes.other_reading: you would no longer make much of the day after as against tomorrow

notes.note: ἀγεννής is “low-born” and so “ignoble, without spirit, cowardly”. English must pick one; “abject” keeps both the lowness and the want of spirit.
notes.other_reading: unless you are a coward to the last degree

notes.note: “How much” is asked expecting the answer “very little”. The question is kept as it stands and set in brackets, so that the sentence can run on to “so too” as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: for how small is the difference!

notes.note: Literally “in the many-eth year”, an ordinal made from “many”: in a year a long way down the count.
notes.other_reading: that it should be in some far-off year rather than tomorrow

check.note: ἀγεννής is ignoble, abject, cowardly. “Mean-spirited” today means unkind or petty, which misleads, and “in the last degree” is dated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unless you are utterly abject”.

check.note: The English runs the “Just as” clause, the condition and this question into one sentence that ends in a question mark though its main clause is a statement, and “So too” then starts a new sentence. It is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the question now stands in brackets and the sentence runs on to “so too”, as in the Greek. It is kept as a question, “for how much is the gap between?”, and not turned into the exclamation “how small”, because the Greek asks “how much”.

passages.casaubon: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Подобно тому как, если бы кто-нибудь из богов сказал тебе, что ты умрёшь завтра или, во всяком случае, послезавтра, ты уже не счёл бы чем-то великим, что это будет послезавтра, а не завтра, если только ты не жалок до крайности (ведь велик ли промежуток?), — так и не считай чем-то великим, что это будет через много лет, а не завтра.

passages.greek: Μήτι δυσχεραίνεις ὅτι τοσῶνδέ τινων λιτρῶν εἶ καὶ οὐ τριακοσίων; οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὅτι μέχρι τοσῶνδε ἐτῶν βιωτέον σοι καὶ οὐ μέχρι πλείονος· ὥσπερ γὰρ τῆς οὐσίας ὅσον ἀφώρισταί σοι στέργεις, οὕτως καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ χρόνου.
passages.english: You are not upset, are you, that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred? So too, then, with having to live to so many years and no more. For just as you are content with the amount of matter that has been marked off for you, so too with time.

notes.note: μήτι opens a question that expects the answer no. δυσχεραίνειν is to take something hard, to be annoyed or put out.
notes.other_reading: Surely you do not resent

notes.note: Literally “you are of so many pounds”; the English reads “weigh”. The λίτρα is the Roman pound. From memory, unchecked: about 327 grams, so three hundred of them is a little under a hundred kilograms.
notes.other_reading: that you are of such and such a number of pounds

notes.note: The second sentence has no verb of its own: “so too, then, that you must live to so many years”. The verb “be upset” is carried over from the question, and the English leaves it unstated too.
notes.other_reading: Then do not be upset either that you must live to so many years and no more

notes.note: οὐσία is “substance”, the stuff a thing is made of, here the matter of the body, which fits the pounds just mentioned. The same word is also the ordinary Greek for a person’s property.
notes.other_reading: the amount of property that has been marked off for you

notes.note: στέργειν is to be content with, to put up with gladly, and also to feel affection for. The English takes the cooler sense.
notes.other_reading: you accept with affection

check.greek: μέχρι τοσῶνδε ἐτῶν βιωτέον σοι καὶ οὐ μέχρι πλείονος
check.note: “Live up to” is an English idiom with another meaning (to match expectations), and “no further” is spatial where the Greek is “not up to more”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with having to live to so many years and no more”.

check.note: “Substance” for οὐσία is a technical term; here it is simply the bodily matter allotted to you, which is what the weight comparison is about.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the amount of matter that has been marked off for you”. The note keeps “substance” as the literal sense of the word.

passages.casaubon: Dost thou grieve that thou dost weigh but so many pounds, and not three hundred rather? Just as much reason hast thou to grieve that thou must live but so many years, and not longer. For as for bulk and substance thou dost content thyself with that proportion of it that is allotted unto thee, so shouldst thou for time.

nearest.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

passages.russian: Ты ведь не огорчаешься, что весишь столько-то фунтов, а не триста? Так же, значит, и с тем, что жить тебе столько-то лет, и не больше. Ведь как ты доволен тем количеством материи, которое тебе отмерено, так и со временем.

passages.greek: Μὴ καταφρόνει θανάτου, ἀλλὰ εὐαρέστει αὐτῷ, ὡς καὶ τούτου ἑνὸς ὄντος ὧν ἡ φύσις ἐθέλει. οἷον γάρ ἐστι τὸ νεάσαι καὶ τὸ γηρᾶσαι, καὶ τὸ αὐξῆσαι καὶ τὸ ἀκμάσαι, καὶ ὀδόντας καὶ γένειον καὶ πολιὰς ἐνεγκεῖν, καὶ σπεῖραι καὶ κυοφορῆσαι καὶ ἀποκυῆσαι, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα φυσικὰ ἐνεργήματα ὅσα αἱ τοῦ βίου ὧραι φέρουσι, τοιοῦτο καὶ τὸ διαλυθῆναι. τοῦτο μὲν οὖν κατὰ ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι λελογισμένον, μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς μηδὲ ὠστικῶς μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνως πρὸς τὸν θάνατον ἔχειν ἀλλὰ περιμένειν ὡς μίαν τῶν φυσικῶν ἐνεργειῶν, καὶ ὡς νῦν περιμένεις πότε ἔμβρυον ἐκ τῆς γαστρὸς τῆς γυναικός σου ἐξέλθῃ, οὕτως ἐκδέχεσθαι τὴν ὥραν ἐν ᾗ τὸ ψυχάριόν σου τοῦ ἐλύτρου τούτου ἐκπεσεῖται. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδιωτικὸν παράπηγμα ἁψικάρδιον θέλεις, μάλιστά σε εὔκολον πρὸς τὸν θάνατον ποιήσει ἡ ἐπίστασις ἡ ἐπὶ τὰ ὑποκείμενα, ὧν μέλλεις ἀφίστασθαι, καὶ μεθ’ ἠθῶν οὐκέτι ἔσται ἡ . . . ἐμπεφυρμένη. προσκόπτεσθαι μὲν γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἥκιστα δεῖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ κήδεσθαι καὶ πρᾴως φέρειν, μεμνῆσθαι μέντοι ὅτι οὐκ ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπων ὁμοδογματούντων σοι ἡ ἀπαλλαγὴ ἔσται. τοῦτο γὰρ μόνον, εἴπερ ἄρα, ἀνθεῖλκεν ἂν καὶ κατεῖχεν ἐν τῷ ζῆν, εἰ συζῆν ἐφεῖτο τοῖς τὰ αὐτὰ δόγματα περιπεποιημένοις· νῦν δ’ ὁρᾷς ὅσος ὁ κόπος ἐν τῇ διαφωνίᾳ τῆς συμβιώσεως, ὥστε εἰπεῖν· θᾶττον ἔλθοις, ὦ θάνατε, μή που καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπιλάθωμαι ἐμαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Do not despise death, but be well pleased with it, since this too is one of the things nature wills. For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved. This, then, is what fits a human being who has reasoned it out: not to be offhand towards death, nor violent, nor disdainful, but to wait for it as one of the natural activities; and, as you now wait for the time when the unborn child will come out of your wife’s womb, in the same way to await the hour in which your little soul will drop out of this husk. But if you also want a layman’s rule that touches the heart, what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave, and [at what kind of] characters [your soul] will no longer be mixed up with. For there must be no taking offence at them at all; rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently, yet remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you. For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own. But as it is, you see how much weariness there is in the discord of living together, so that one says: “Come sooner, death, in case I too should perhaps forget myself.”

notes.note: καταφρονεῖν runs from “despise” to “think little of, make light of”. In 12.34 the same attitude is spoken of with approval, so “despise” is used in both places and the tension is left visible.
notes.other_reading: Do not make light of death

notes.note: λελογισμένον can agree with ἄνθρωπον (“a human being who has reasoned”) or be neuter with τοῦτο (“this is a thing reasoned out”). The English takes it with the human being; “it” is added.
notes.other_reading: This, then, is the considered course that fits a human being

notes.greek: μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς μηδὲ ὠστικῶς μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνως
notes.note: Three adverbs with a range. ὁλοσχερῶς is “in the gross, summarily”, so carelessly; ὠστικῶς is “in a pushing way”, which could mean pushing towards death or shoving it away, and “violent” leaves that open; ὑπερηφάνως is “haughtily”.
notes.other_reading: not carelessly, nor impatiently, nor arrogantly

notes.greek: πότε ἔμβρυον ἐκ τῆς γαστρὸς τῆς γυναικός σου ἐξέλθῃ
notes.note: γυνή is “woman” or “wife”; with σου the English reads “your wife”. The words “as you now wait” read like a real circumstance of the writer, but they could be a general illustration.
notes.other_reading: when the child will come out of your woman’s belly

notes.note: ἔλυτρον is any case or covering (a pod, a shell, a sheath). After the comparison with birth it may suggest the membrane round an unborn child; the English reads “husk”. ψυχάριον just before is a diminutive, kept as “little soul”.
notes.other_reading: out of this sheath

notes.note: παράπηγμα is literally a peg-board calendar or table, and so a rule to steer by. ἰδιωτικόν is “of the layman”, that is, not a philosopher’s argument. ἁψικάρδιον is “that takes hold of the heart”.
notes.other_reading: an unphilosophical maxim that grips the heart

notes.greek: ἡ ἐπίστασις ἡ ἐπὶ τὰ ὑποκείμενα
notes.note: ἐπίστασις is a stopping to attend. τὰ ὑποκείμενα is “the things lying before you”, the objects or circumstances of your life; whether this covers only things or people as well is open, and the English keeps it general.
notes.other_reading: close attention to the objects before you

notes.note: The Greek as given does not construe: the edition marks a gap after ἡ where a feminine noun is missing, and there is no relative word before ἠθῶν. The words in square brackets are supplied; from memory, unchecked, editors read a relative (“what kind of”) here and supply “soul”. ἐμπεφυρμένη is “kneaded in with” and can imply being soiled.
notes.other_reading: and with characters the … will no longer be mixed up

notes.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ κήδεσθαι καὶ πρᾴως φέρειν
notes.note: καί before κήδεσθαι is read as “even”. It can also be the first half of “both … and” with the καί that follows. δεῖ (“must”) governs the whole sentence.
notes.other_reading: but both care for them and bear with them gently

notes.note: A hedge: “if anything at all (would)”. The two verbs that follow have no object in the Greek; the impersonal “one” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: For this alone, if indeed anything, could have drawn you back and kept you in life

notes.note: διαφωνία is literally being out of tune, discord. It answers ὁμοδογματούντων, people whose principles sound together with yours, so the musical word is kept. συμβίωσις is “living together”, echoing συζῆν in the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: in the disagreement of those you live with

notes.greek: μή που καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπιλάθωμαι ἐμαυτοῦ
notes.note: To forget oneself here is to lose hold of what one is and of one’s principles. καὶ αὐτός (“too”) implies that the others have already done so, and που adds “perhaps”.
notes.other_reading: before I too lose sight of what I am

check.greek: καὶ μεθ’ ἠθῶν οὐκέτι ἔσται ἡ . . . ἐμπεφυρμένη
check.note: The Greek as given has a gap after ἡ and no relative word before ἠθῶν, so it does not construe. The English fills the gap with “[soul]”, adds “your” and supplies a relative, and only the first of these is marked.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and [at what kind of] characters [your soul] will no longer be mixed up with”, so that every supplied word stands in square brackets. The Greek as given has neither a relative word nor the noun, and the note says so.

check.note: The English takes λελογισμένον with the human being (“who has reasoned it out”). It can also be neuter with “this”: “this is the reasoned course, in keeping with a human being”.
check.decided: Declined: “what fits a human being who has reasoned it out” stands. The participle stands beside ἄνθρωπον and agrees with it in form, and the neuter reading is recorded in the note.

check.note: ὠστικῶς is “in a pushing, violent way”. “Impatient” narrows it to eagerness for death to come, which is one possible reading but not what the word itself says.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nor violent”. The word says only that the manner is pushing or forcible, not which way the push goes, and “impatient” chose one direction.

check.note: “To look for the hour” can be read today as “search for”. The Greek means “await, expect”, parallel to the verb “wait for” just before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to await the hour”. The verb means to wait for and expect, and “look for” could be heard as “search for”.

check.note: “Make you easy toward death” is not natural English and the sense is unclear. εὔκολος is “content, untroubled, good-tempered”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what will most put you at ease about death”. εὔκολος is content and untroubled, and “at ease” keeps the root that returns as “easily” for the same word in 10.36.

check.note: καί (“even”, “also”) is dropped. Marcus says one should go as far as caring for them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently”. “Must” is repeated in place of “should”, because one δεῖ governs the whole sentence, and a note records that the καί can also be the first half of “both … and”.

check.note: συμβιώσεως picks up συζῆν (“live together”) in the sentence before. “A shared life” loses the echo, and the indefinite article makes general what the Greek says of his actual company.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in the discord of living together”, so that the noun echoes “live together” in the sentence before. “This” is not added: the Greek has only the article, and “as it is you see” already ties the words to his actual company.

check.note: που (“perhaps”) is not rendered. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: “should perhaps” is added to the closing words, so that που is rendered.

check.greek: οἷον γάρ ἐστι τὸ νεάσαι καὶ τὸ γηρᾶσαι
check.note: Found while settling: “For as being young and growing old are, … such also is being dissolved” was hard to follow as English.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now runs “For as it is with being young and growing old, … so it is with being dissolved”. The order and every item of the Greek are kept; only the frame of the comparison is made plain.

passages.casaubon: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed. For what thou dost conceive of these, of a boy to become a young man, to wax old, to grow, to ripen, to get teeth, or a beard, or grey hairs to beget, to bear, or to be delivered; or what other action soever it be, that is natural unto man according to the several seasons of his life; such a thing is it also to be dissolved. It is therefore the part of a wise man, in matter of death, not in any wise to carry himself either violently, or proudly but patiently to wait for it, as one of nature's operations: that with the same mind as now thou dost expect when that which yet is but an embryo in thy wife's belly shall come forth, thou mayst expect also when thy soul shall fall off from that outward coat or skin: wherein as a child in the belly it lieth involved and shut up. But thou desirest a more popular, and though not so direct and philosophical, yet a very powerful and penetrative recipe against the fear of death, nothing can make they more willing to part with thy life, than if thou shalt consider, both what the subjects themselves are that thou shalt part with, and what manner of disposition thou shalt no more have to do with. True it is, that, offended with them thou must not be by no means, but take care of them, and meekly bear with them However, this thou mayst remember, that whensoever it happens that thou depart, it shall not be from men that held the same opinions that thou dost. For that indeed, (if it were so) is the only thing that might make thee averse from death, and willing to continue here, if it were thy hap to live with men that had obtained the same belief that thou hast. But now, what a toil it is for thee to live with men of different opinions, thou seest: so that thou hast rather occasion to say, Hasten, I thee pray, O Death; lest I also in time forget myself.
passages.russian: Не презирай смерть, а будь вполне доволен ею, раз и она — одно из того, чего хочет природа. Ведь как обстоит дело с юностью и старением, с ростом и расцветом, с появлением зубов, бороды и седины, с зачатием, вынашиванием и родами и со всеми прочими природными действиями, которые приносит каждая пора жизни, так обстоит и с распадом. Вот что, стало быть, подобает человеку, который всё обдумал: не относиться к смерти ни небрежно, ни неистово, ни высокомерно, а ждать её как одного из природных действий; и, как ты сейчас ждёшь, когда ещё не рождённое дитя выйдет из чрева твоей жены, так же ожидать часа, в который твоя маленькая душа выпадет из этой шелухи. А если хочешь ещё и житейского правила, которое трогает сердце, то лучше всего успокоит тебя насчёт смерти, если ты остановишься и посмотришь на то, что собираешься оставить, и [на то, с какими] характерами [твоей душе] больше не придётся смешиваться. Ведь обижаться на них вовсе нельзя; напротив, нужно даже заботиться о них и мягко их терпеть, но всё же помнить, что освобождение будет не от людей, держащихся тех же принципов, что и ты. Если что и могло бы тянуть назад и удерживать в жизни, то лишь одно: если бы было позволено жить вместе с теми, кто сделал те же принципы своими. А теперь ты видишь, сколько усталости в разладе совместной жизни, так что скажешь: «Приходи скорее, смерть, как бы и я, чего доброго, не забылся».

passages.greek:
Πρὸς θανάτου καταφρόνησιν ἐγερτικώτατον ὅτι καὶ οἱ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸν πόνον κακὸν κρίνοντες ὅμως τούτου κατεφρόνησαν.

Ὧι τὸ εὔκαιρον μόνον ἀγαθὸν καὶ ᾧ τὸ πλείους κατὰ λόγον ὀρθὸν πράξεις ἀποδοῦναι τῷ ὀλιγωτέρας ἐν ἴσῳ ἐστὶ καὶ ᾧ τὸν κόσμον θεωρῆσαι πλείονι ἢ ἐλάσσονι χρόνῳ οὐ διαφέρει, τούτῳ οὐδὲ ὁ θάνατος φοβερόν.

Ἄνθρωπε, ἐπολιτεύσω ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ ταύτῃ πόλει· τί σοι διαφέρει, εἰ πέντε ἔτεσιν ἢ τρισί; τὸ γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς νόμους ἴσον ἑκάστῳ. τί οὖν δεινόν, εἰ τῆς πόλεως ἀποπέμπει σε οὐ τύραννος οὐδὲ δικαστὴς ἄδικος, ἀλλ’ ἡ φύσις ἡ εἰσαγαγοῦσα, οἷον εἰ κωμῳδὸν ἀπολύοι τῆς σκηνῆς ὁ παραλαβὼν στρατηγός;—ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἶπον τὰ πέντε μέρη, ἀλλὰ τὰ τρία.—καλῶς εἶπας· ἐν μέντοι τῷ βίῳ τὰ τρία ὅλον τὸ δρᾶμά ἐστι. τὸ γὰρ τέλειον ἐκεῖνος ὁρίζει ὁ τότε μὲν τῆς συγκρίσεως. νῦν δὲ τῆς διαλύσεως αἴτιος· σὺ δὲ ἀναίτιος ἀμφοτέρων. ἄπιθι οὖν ἵλεως· καὶ γὰρ ὁ ἀπολύων ἵλεως.
passages.english:
What most rouses one to despise death is that even those who judge pleasure good and pain bad have despised it all the same.

A person for whom only what comes at the right time is good, for whom performing more actions in line with right reason is equal to performing fewer, and to whom it makes no difference whether they look on the universe for a longer or a shorter time: to that person not even death is a thing to fear.

Man, you have been a citizen in this great city. What difference does it make to you whether for five years or for three? For what accords with the laws is equal for each. So what is terrible if you are sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in, just as if the magistrate who engaged a comic actor were to dismiss him from the stage? “But I have spoken not the five acts but the three.” Well said; in life, however, the three are the whole play. For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither. So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.

notes.note: ἐγερτικώτατον is “most rousing, most awakening”. καταφρόνησις is the noun of the verb in 9.3, where Marcus tells himself not to despise death; “despise” is kept in both places so that the tension can be seen.
notes.other_reading: The strongest incentive to think little of death

notes.greek: οἱ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸν πόνον κακὸν κρίνοντες
notes.note: The Epicureans are meant, though not named. πόνος is “pain” or “toil”; against pleasure the English reads “pain”.
notes.other_reading: those who judge pleasure a good and toil an evil

notes.note: εὔκαιρον is “well-timed, in season”. “What comes at the right time” matches καιρός in 12.23. μόνον could also be heard as “simply”.
notes.other_reading: for whom the good is simply what is in season

notes.note: οὐδέ can be “not even” or “not … either”. φοβερόν is neuter, “a fearful thing”.
notes.other_reading: to that person death is not a fearful thing either

notes.note: The address is “human being”, not specifically a male, and it is blunt. “Man” is used as the nearest natural English form of address.
notes.other_reading: Human being,

notes.note: Translated as given. From memory, unchecked: the words “or for three” are not secure in the transmission, and other editors print a different number (“or a hundred”). “Three” here prepares the three acts below.
notes.other_reading: whether for five years or for a hundred

notes.greek: τὸ γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς νόμους ἴσον ἑκάστῳ
notes.note: ἴσον is “equal” or “fair”. “Equal” is kept because the previous chapter uses ἐν ἴσῳ (“is equal to”).
notes.other_reading: For what follows the laws is fair to everyone.

notes.note: στρατηγός is literally “general” and is also the standard Greek for the Roman praetor, the magistrate who put on public shows; the English says “magistrate”. παραλαβών is “who took him on”.
notes.other_reading: the general who took him on

notes.note: μέρη is “parts”, here the acts of a play. εἶπον is the verb “say, speak”, and the answer καλῶς εἶπας (“you have said well”, that is, “you are right”) picks it up; the English has “spoken” and “Well said”.
notes.other_reading: But I have not played the five parts, but the three.

notes.greek: ὁ τότε μὲν τῆς συγκρίσεως. νῦν δὲ τῆς διαλύσεως αἴτιος
notes.note: The full stop after συγκρίσεως in the text as given breaks one phrase and is read as a comma. ἐκεῖνος is masculine, so it is not grammatically “nature” (feminine): it is god, or the magistrate of the image. αἴτιος and ἀναίτιος are both rendered with “responsible”; the Greek does not say whose putting together is meant, and the English leaves it unsaid too.
notes.other_reading: the one who was then the cause of your being combined and is now the cause of your being dissolved; you are the cause of neither

notes.note: ἵλεως is used of gods (“propitious”) and of people (“cheerful, kindly”). The same word is used of the one leaving and of the one dismissing, so one English word is kept, “gracious”, as also in 10.36.
notes.other_reading: So go in good cheer, for the one who releases you is kindly too.

check.note: “Praetor” is a Roman technical term that a reader of today may not know. The Greek word is the ordinary one for a general or magistrate, so the identification is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the magistrate who engaged a comic actor”. The Greek word is an ordinary one for a general or magistrate, and the point that the Roman praetor is meant is moved to the note.

check.greek: ὁ τότε μὲν τῆς συγκρίσεως. νῦν δὲ τῆς διαλύσεως αἴτιος
check.note: The full stop after συγκρίσεως in the Greek as given cuts the pairing of “then” and “now” and must be a comma; the English rightly reads straight through. “Your” is added twice.
check.decided: Accepted: the full stop is read as a comma, as the pairing of “then” and “now” requires, and the note says so. The two added “your” are removed as well, so the English now reads “for the putting together” and “for the dissolving”.

check.note: In English of today “well spoken” describes a manner of speech. The Greek is “you have said well”, that is, “you are right”, and it picks up the verb in the actor’s protest.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Well said”. This is the plain way to say “you are right” and still answers “spoken” in the protest.

check.note: “Only” is added. The Greek is “not the five parts but the three”.
check.decided: Accepted: “only” is removed, and the actor’s protest now ends “not the five acts but the three”, as the Greek does.

check.note: “Delivering actions” is odd English. ἀποδοῦναι is “to render, perform (what is due)”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “performing more actions … is equal to performing fewer”. The verb means to render or perform what is due, and “delivering” was not natural with “actions”.

check.note: “Go away gracious” is awkward as English. Whatever word is chosen must be the same for the person leaving and for the one who dismisses, as the Greek repeats it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.” One word is kept for both, and “go away” stays for ἄπιθι as in 10.36.

check.note: Found while settling: “The strongest spur” brings in an image. The Greek word is simply “most rousing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “What most rouses one to despise death is that”. The image of a spur is not in the Greek.

passages.casaubon: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any. And can death be terrible to him, to whom that only seems good, which in the ordinary course of nature is seasonable? to him, to whom, whether his actions be many or few, so they be all good, is all one; and who whether he behold the things of the world being always the same either for many years, or for few years only, is altogether indifferent? O man! as a citizen thou hast lived, and conversed in this great city the world. Whether just for so many years, or no, what is it unto thee? Thou hast lived (thou mayest be sure) as long as the laws and orders of the city required; which may be the common comfort of all. Why then should it be grievous unto thee, if (not a tyrant, nor an unjust judge, but) the same nature that brought thee in, doth now send thee out of the world? As if the praetor should fairly dismiss him from the stage, whom he had taken in to act a while. Oh, but the play is not yet at an end, there are but three acts yet acted of it? Thou hast well said: for in matter of life, three acts is the whole play. Now to set a certain time to every man's acting, belongs unto him only, who as first he was of thy composition, so is now the cause of thy dissolution. As for thyself; thou hast to do with neither. Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that dismisseth thee.
passages.russian:
Сильнее всего подталкивает к презрению смерти то, что даже те, кто считает наслаждение благом, а боль — злом, всё же её презирали.

Тот, для кого благо лишь то, что приходит вовремя, для кого совершить больше действий согласно правому разуму — то же, что совершить меньше, и кому безразлично, дольше или короче смотреть на мироздание, — для того даже смерть не страшна.

Человек, ты был гражданином этого великого города. Какая тебе разница — пять лет или три? Ведь то, что согласно с законами, равно для каждого. Так что же страшного, если тебя высылает из города не тиран и не неправедный судья, а природа, которая тебя и ввела, — как если бы магистрат, нанявший комического актёра, отпускал его со сцены? «Но я сказал не пять актов, а три». Хорошо сказано; однако в жизни три акта — это вся пьеса. Ведь завершённость определяет тот, кто тогда был в ответе за соединение, а теперь в ответе за распад; ты же не в ответе ни за то, ни за другое. Так уходи милостиво: ведь милостив и тот, кто тебя отпускает.

passages.greek: Οὐδείς ἐστιν οὕτως εὔποτμος ᾧ ἀποθνῄσκοντι οὐ παρεστήξονταί τινες ἀσπαζόμενοι τὸ συμβαῖνον κακόν. σπουδαῖος καὶ σοφὸς ἦν· μὴ τὸ πανύστατον ἔσται τις ὁ καθ’ αὑτὸν λέγων· ἀναπνεύσομέν ποτε ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ; χαλεπὸς μὲν οὐδενὶ ἡμῶν ἦν, ἀλλὰ ᾐσθανόμην ὅτι ἡσυχῇ καταγινώσκει ἡμῶν. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τοῦ σπουδαίου, ἐφ’ ἡμῶν δὲ πόσα ἄλλα ἐστί, δι’ ἃ πολὺς ὁ ἀπαλλακτιῶν ἡμῶν. τοῦτο οὖν ἐννοήσεις ἀποθνῄσκων καὶ εὐκολώτερον ἐξελεύσῃ, λογιζόμενος· ἐκ τοιούτου βίου ἀπέρχομαι, ἐν ᾧ αὐτοὶ οἱ κοινωνοί, ὑπὲρ ὧν τὰ τοσαῦτα ἠγωνισάμην, ηὐξάμην, ἐφρόντισα, αὐτοὶ ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσί με ὑπάγειν, ἄλλην τινὰ τυχὸν ἐκ τούτου ῥᾳστώνην ἐλπίζοντες. τί ἂν οὖν τις ἀντέχοιτο τῆς ἐνταῦθα μακροτέρας διατριβῆς; μὴ μέντοι διὰ τοῦτο ἔλαττον εὐμενὴς αὐτοῖς ἄπιθι, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἴδιον ἔθος διασῴζων, φίλος καὶ εὔνους καὶ ἵλεως· καὶ μὴ πάλιν ὡς ἀποσπώμενος, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ εὐθανατοῦντος εὐκόλως τὸ ψυχάριον ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος ἐξειλεῖται, τοιαύτην καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τούτων ἀποχώρησιν δεῖ γίνεσθαι· καὶ γὰρ τούτοις ἡ φύσις συνῆψε καὶ συνέκρινεν, ἀλλὰ νῦν διαλύει. διαλύομαι ὡς ἀπὸ οἰκείων μέν, οὐ μὴν ἀνθελκόμενος ἀλλʼ ἀβιάστως· ἓν γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο τῶν κατὰ φύσιν.
passages.english: No one is so fortunate that, as they die, there will not be some people standing by who welcome the bad thing that is happening. Say the person was good and wise: might there not, at the very last, be someone who says this to themselves? “Shall we at last get a breathing space from this minder? He was not hard on any of us, but I could feel that he was quietly condemning us.” That, then, in the case of the good person. But in our case how many other things there are that make many a person long to be rid of us! So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, cared, those very people want me to go, hoping perhaps to get some other relief out of it. Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?” Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly towards them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious. And, on the other hand, not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, so too must the withdrawal from these people take place. For nature tied you to these people too and put you together with them, but now it unties. I am being untied, as from my own people, it is true, yet not pulled back but without force; for this too is one of the things that accord with nature.

notes.note: ἀσπάζεσθαι is “to greet gladly, to welcome”. κακόν, “bad thing”, is said from the ordinary point of view, not as Marcus’s own verdict on death.
notes.other_reading: who are glad of the misfortune that is befalling him

notes.note: The Greek before this is a bare statement (“was good and wise”) used as a supposition; “Say the person” is added. A question with μή is hesitant and often expects the answer no, but the argument needs such a person to exist, so it is read as a tentative “might there not be”. σπουδαῖος is the Stoic word for the good, serious person.
notes.other_reading: The person was earnest and wise. Surely at the very end there will not be someone who says to themselves …?

notes.greek: ἀναπνεύσομέν ποτε ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ
notes.note: The edition punctuates this as a question; it could be an exclamation. A παιδαγωγός was the slave who escorted, supervised and corrected a boy, not a teacher, and “minder” gives that status. The verb is literally “breathe again from”.
notes.other_reading: At last there will be room to breathe, away from this tutor!

notes.note: ἀπαλλακτιάω is “to long to be rid of”. ἡμῶν is a first-person plural: Marcus means himself and people like him as against the truly good person, and the plural is kept.
notes.other_reading: many a one wants to be rid of me

notes.note: κοινωνοί are sharers or partners, from the same root as κοινωνικός (“social” in this project). The possessive is supplied.
notes.other_reading: the very companions

notes.greek: ἄλλην τινὰ τυχὸν ἐκ τούτου ῥᾳστώνην ἐλπίζοντες
notes.note: ἄλλην τινά is “some other” relief, perhaps “some further”. ἐκ τούτου is “from this”, that is, from the departure, or possibly “after this”.
notes.other_reading: hoping perhaps for some further relief after this

notes.greek: τί ἂν οὖν τις ἀντέχοιτο τῆς ἐνταῦθα μακροτέρας διατριβῆς
notes.note: It is open whether this question still belongs to the dying person’s reasoning or is Marcus’s own comment. It is kept inside the quotation, because it draws the conclusion of that reasoning and the next sentence turns back to “you”.
notes.other_reading: (outside the quotation) Why, then, would anyone cling to a longer stay here?

notes.note: πάλιν here is “on the other hand, conversely”: not unkindly, but not clinging either. It could also be heard as “again”.
notes.other_reading: And, again, not as one being torn away

notes.note: Literally “is unrolled, unwound out of”. The English reads “slips out”; the image is of something coming free without a tug.
notes.other_reading: is unwound from the body

notes.greek: τούτοις ἡ φύσις συνῆψε καὶ συνέκρινεν, ἀλλὰ νῦν διαλύει
notes.note: The verbs have no object; “you” is supplied, though the next word is first person and the object may be the speaker. καί before τούτοις is “too”, looking back to the soul and the body. διαλύειν is also the usual word for the dissolving of a person at death (as in 9.3 and 12.36), so “untie” loses a second sense, while “put together” matches 12.36.
notes.other_reading: For nature bound me to these people too and combined me with them, but now she dissolves the bond. I am being dissolved

notes.note: The form is passive (“pulled back”) or middle (“pulling back, resisting”). The passive is taken, parallel to “torn away” above and to “pull one back” for the same verb in 9.3.
notes.other_reading: yet not pulling back

check.note: The English gives a question that confidently expects “yes”, as if the Greek had οὐ. With μή the question is tentative: “may there not perhaps be someone”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “may there not, at the very last, be someone”. With μή the question is hesitant, not a confident “will there not”, and the note explains why it is not read as expecting the answer no.

check.note: A παιδαγωγός is the attendant who minds and corrects a boy, not a teacher in a school. “Schoolmaster” is also a dated word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “minder”. The word names the attendant who supervised and corrected a boy, which “schoolmaster” did not.

check.note: The Greek is simply “breathe again from”. “Freely” and “rid of” are expansions, and “rid” returns a few lines later for a different Greek word, making an echo the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the onlooker’s question now asks for “a breathing space from this minder”. “Freely” and “rid of” are gone, so “rid” is heard only where the Greek has ἀπαλλακτιῶν; “a breathing space from” is preferred to the suggested wording because the Greek verb with ἀπό means to have respite from something.

check.greek: ἄλλην τινὰ τυχὸν ἐκ τούτου ῥᾳστώνην
check.note: “Some other ease from it” is hard to follow. The sense is some further relief as a result of the departure.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “hoping perhaps to get some other relief out of it”. “Relief” replaces “ease”; “other” stays because ἄλλην is “other”, and “it” stays because the Greek has only “this”, with the reference explained in the note.

check.greek: τί ἂν οὖν τις ἀντέχοιτο τῆς ἐνταῦθα μακροτέρας διατριβῆς
check.note: The English puts this question inside the dying person’s own reasoning. The Greek has no marks, and the reasoning may end one sentence earlier, leaving this as Marcus’s comment.
check.decided: Declined: the question stays inside the dying person’s reasoning. Its οὖν (“then”) draws the conclusion from what was just reasoned, and the turn back to “you” comes only with the next sentence; the other placing is recorded in the note.

check.note: πάλιν here is “on the other hand, conversely”: do not leave unkindly, but do not cling either. “Again” reads as “once more”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And, on the other hand, not as one being torn away”. The word sets the second warning against the first and does not mean “once more”.

check.note: καὶ τούτοις is most naturally “to these too”, as the soul was joined to the body in the comparison just made. The English drops “too” and adds an emphasis the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For nature tied you to these people too”. “Too” is restored, pointing back to the soul and the body, and the added emphasis “it was … that” is gone.

check.note: The Greek has no object. The English supplies “you” twice, but the next sentence is in the first person, so the speaker is at least as likely.
check.decided: Partly accepted: English needs an object, and it stays “you”. The Greek addresses “you” up to this point and turns to the first person only with the next verb; the note now says that the object is supplied and that the speaker may be meant.

check.note: These verbs are the same pair as the nouns in 12.36 (“put together”, “dissolved”) and the verb in 9.3 (“being dissolved”). As “joined” and “unties” they lose the link between parting from people and the dissolution of the body.
check.decided: Partly accepted: συνέκρινεν now reads “put you together with them”, matching “the putting together” in 12.36. διαλύει and διαλύομαι stay “unties” and “being untied”: with ἀπό the verb is the ordinary one for parting from people, and “dissolved from” people would not be plain English. The note records the lost link.

check.note: The English takes the participle as middle (“resisting”). It can also be passive, parallel to “torn away”: “not being dragged against one’s will”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “yet not pulled back”, the passive. This matches the passive “torn away” above and “pull one back” for the same verb in 9.3; the middle reading goes to the note.

check.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τοῦ σπουδαίου
check.note: Found while settling: “Say he was good and wise” and “the good man” single out a man where the Greek speaks of a good person in general.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Say the person was good and wise” and “the good person”. “He” remains only inside the onlooker’s speech, where one particular person is spoken of.

passages.casaubon: There is not any man that is so happy in his death, but that some of those that are by him when he dies, will be ready to rejoice at his supposed calamity. Is it one that was virtuous and wise indeed? will there not some one or other be found, who thus will say to himself; 'Well now at last shall I be at rest from this pedagogue. He did not indeed otherwise trouble us much: but I know well enough that in his heart, he did much condemn us.' Thus will they speak of the virtuous. But as for us, alas I how many things be there, for which there be many that glad would be to be rid of us. This therefore if thou shalt think of whensoever thou diest, thou shalt die the more willingly, when thou shalt think with thyself; I am now to depart from that world, wherein those that have been my nearest friends and acquaintances, they whom I have so much suffered for, so often prayed for, and for whom I have taken such care, even they would have me die, hoping that after my death they shall live happier, than they did before. What then should any man desire to continue here any longer? Nevertheless, whensoever thou diest, thou must not be less kind and loving unto them for it; but as before, see them, continue to be their friend, to wish them well, and meekly, and gently to carry thyself towards them, but yet so that on the other side, it make thee not the more unwilling to die. But as it fareth with them that die an easy quick death, whose soul is soon separated from their bodies, so must thy separation from them be. To these had nature joined and annexed me: now she parts us; I am ready to depart, as from friends and kinsmen, but yet without either reluctancy or compulsion. For this also is according to Nature.
passages.russian: Нет никого столь удачливого, чтобы, когда он умирает, рядом не стояли какие-нибудь люди, которые рады происходящему злу. Допустим, человек был хорошим и мудрым: разве не найдётся под самый конец кто-то, кто скажет про себя: «Отдохнём ли мы наконец от этого надзирателя? Ни к кому из нас он не был суров, но я чувствовал, что он молча нас осуждает»? Это — в случае хорошего человека. А в нашем случае сколько есть ещё другого, из-за чего многие жаждут от нас избавиться! Так вот, ты будешь думать об этом, умирая, и уйдёшь легче, рассуждая: «Я ухожу из такой жизни, в которой сами мои товарищи, ради которых я столько боролся, молился, заботился, — сами эти люди хотят, чтобы я ушёл, надеясь, может быть, получить от этого какое-то иное облегчение. Зачем же кому-то держаться за более долгое пребывание здесь?» Однако не уходи из-за этого менее благосклонным к ним, а, сохраняя свой обычный нрав, — дружелюбным, доброжелательным и милостивым. И, с другой стороны, не как тот, кого отрывают; напротив, как у человека, умирающего лёгкой смертью, маленькая душа легко выскальзывает из тела, так же должно происходить и отделение от этих людей. Ведь природа связала и соединила тебя и с ними, но теперь развязывает. Я развязываюсь — правда, как от своих, но не так, будто меня тянут назад, а без насилия; ведь и это одно из того, что согласно с природой.

passages.greek: νοερᾶς δυνάμεως ἐφιστάναι. τί εἰσιν οὗτοι, ὧν αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι. τί ἐστι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ ὅτι, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ μόνον ἴδῃ καὶ τῷ μερισμῷ τῆς ἐννοίας διαλύσῃ τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ, οὐκέτι ἄλλο τι ὑπολήψεται αὐτὸ εἶναι ἢ φύσεως ἔργον· φύσεως δὲ ἔργον εἴ τις φοβεῖται, παιδίον ἐστί· τοῦτο μέντοι οὐ μόνον φύσεως ἔργον ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφέρον αὐτῇ.
passages.english: To attend [to these things] belongs to the power of mind. What these people are, whose judgments and voices give a good name. What dying is, and that, if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child. This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.

notes.note: The passage begins in mid-sentence. The infinitive has no object in the Greek given, because what is to be attended to stands in the part of the chapter before the cut; “to these things” is added in square brackets. The questions that follow (“what these people are”, “what dying is”) may also depend on this verb.
notes.other_reading: … is for the power of mind to attend to.

notes.greek: αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι
notes.note: ὑπόληψις is the Stoic term rendered “judgment” here; the verb ὑπολήψεται below is the same word, so it is “judge” there. φωναί is “voices” or “words”; εὐδοξία is good repute.
notes.other_reading: whose opinions and words confer fame

notes.note: Either “by dividing the notion” (taking the idea of death apart) or “by the division that thought performs”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: by taking it apart in thought

notes.note: The verb belongs to the family of φαντασία (“impression”): the things that show themselves in it, or are imagined into it. αὐτῷ is taken as “in it”, meaning death.
notes.other_reading: the impressions that attach themselves to it

notes.note: αὐτῇ is nature; the noun is repeated, because “good for it” would be unclear in English. συμφέρον is rendered “good for”, as in the glossary; in 12.23, where it stands beside ἀγαθόν, it is “benefits”.
notes.other_reading: but also to nature’s advantage

check.note: “These things” is not in the Greek as given: the object of the verb lies in the part not supplied, so the addition should be marked. The clauses that follow may also depend on this verb, whereas the English sets them out as sentences of their own.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To attend [to these things] belongs to the power of mind.” The object lies in the part of the chapter not given, so the supplied words stand in square brackets; the clauses that follow keep the full stops of the Greek, and the note says they may depend on the same verb.

check.note: “Bestow” is ornate for a plain verb meaning “provide, give”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “give a good name”. The Greek verb is a plain one.

check.note: The English takes the genitive as the thing divided (the notion of death). It can also be the thing that does the dividing: “by analysis in thought”.
check.decided: Declined: “by dividing up the notion” stands. The genitive is most simply the thing divided, the notion of death, which is then cleared of what is imagined into it; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: συμφέρον is “of benefit, useful”, not the Greek word for “good”. Nothing clashes here, but in 12.23 the same rendering sits beside “a good thing” and blurs the argument, so the two passages should be settled together.
check.decided: Declined: “something good for nature” stands, as in the glossary. Here συμφέρον has no ἀγαθόν beside it, so nothing is blurred; in 12.23, where the two words meet, the English changes to “benefits” and the notes in both passages say so.

part.left_out: Πῶς πάντα ταχέως ἐναφανίζεται, τῷ μὲν κόσμῳ αὐτὰ τὰ σώματα, τῷ δὲ αἰῶνι αἱ μνῆμαι αὐτῶν. οἶά ἐστι τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα καὶ μάλιστα τὰ ἡδονῇ δελεάζοντα ἢ τῷ πόνῳ φοβοῦντα ἢ τῷ τύφῳ διαβεβοημένα· πῶς εὐτελῆ καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητα καὶ ῥυπαρὰ καὶ εὔφθαρτα καὶ νεκρά, … πῶς ἅπτεται θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος καὶ κατὰ τί ἑαυτοῦ μέρος καὶ ὅταν πῶς ἔχῃ διακέηται τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦτο μόριον.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first part of the chapter in its section 2.9, begins its 2.10 here, and carries the chapter's last sentence over to open its 2.11.

passages.casaubon: It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty, to consider what they themselves are in very deed, from whose bare conceits and voices, honour and credit do proceed: as also what it is to die, and how if a man shall consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate from it in his mind all those things which with it usually represent themselves unto us, he can conceive of it no otherwise, than as of a work of nature, and he that fears any work of nature, is a very child. Now death, it is not only a work of nature, but also conducing to nature.
passages.russian: Вникать [в это] — дело силы ума. Что за люди те, чьи суждения и голоса создают доброе имя. Что такое умирать, и то, что, если человек рассмотрит это само по себе и, расчленив понятие, разложит то, что вкладывает в него воображение, он уже не сочтёт это ничем иным, кроме дела природы; а кто боится дела природы — тот ребёнок. Это же не только дело природы, но и благо для природы.

passages.greek: Μία καὶ ἡτισοῦν ἐνέργεια κατὰ καιρὸν παυσαμένη οὐδὲν κακὸν πάσχει, καθὸ πέπαυται· οὐδὲ ὁ πράξας τὴν πρᾶξιν ταύτην κατ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καθὸ πέπαυται, κακόν τι πέπονθεν. ὁμοίως οὖν τὸ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πράξεων σύστημα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ βίος, ἐὰν ἐν καιρῷ παύσηται, οὐδὲν κακὸν πάσχει κατ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο, καθὸ πέπαυται· οὐδὲ ὁ καταπαύσας ἐν καιρῷ τὸν εἱρμὸν τοῦτον κακῶς διετέθη. τὸν δὲ καιρὸν καὶ τὸν ὅρον δίδωσιν ἡ φύσις, ποτὲ μὲν καὶ ἡ ἰδία, ὅταν ἐν γήρᾳ, πάντως δὲ ἡ τῶν ὅλων, ἧς τῶν μερῶν μεταβαλλόντων νεαρὸς ἀεὶ καὶ ἀκμαῖος ὁ σύμπας κόσμος διαμένει. καλὸν δὲ ἀεὶ πᾶν καὶ ὡραῖον τὸ συμφέρον τῷ ὅλῳ. ἡ οὖν κατάπαυσις τοῦ βίου ἑκάστῳ οὐ κακὸν μὲν ὅτι οὐδὲ αἰσχρόν, εἴπερ καὶ ἀπροαίρετον καὶ οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον· ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἴπερ τῷ ὅλῳ καίριον καὶ συμφέρον καὶ συμφερόμενον. οὕτως γὰρ καὶ θεοφόρητος ὁ φερόμενος κατὰ ταὐτὰ θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ ταὐτὰ τῇ γνώμῃ φερόμενος.
passages.english: Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped; nor has the one who did this action suffered anything bad just in this respect, that it has stopped. In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped; nor has the one who brought this chain to a stop at the right time been put in a bad state. The right time and the limit are given by nature: sometimes by one’s own nature too, when the stopping comes in old age, but in every case by the nature of the whole, with the changing of whose parts the entire universe stays always young and in its prime. And everything that benefits the whole is always fine and in season. So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole. For in this way a person is also carried by god: the one who is carried in the same way as god and is carried, in their purpose, towards the same things.

notes.greek: Μία καὶ ἡτισοῦν ἐνέργεια κατὰ καιρὸν παυσαμένη
notes.note: Marcus says ἐνέργεια (“activity”) and then πρᾶξις (“action”) for the same thing; two English words are kept. καιρός is the right moment, “the right time” throughout, including for καίριον near the end. The whole chain on παύομαι is kept as “stop”.
notes.other_reading: Any one activity whatever, ceasing in due season

notes.greek: τὸ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πράξεων σύστημα
notes.note: σύστημα is a composite whole. “Sum” keeps “the whole” free for τὸ ὅλον later in the passage.
notes.other_reading: the system composed of all one’s actions

notes.greek: ὁ καταπαύσας ἐν καιρῷ τὸν εἱρμὸν τοῦτον κακῶς διετέθη
notes.note: The one who “brought the chain to a stop” is, by the parallel with “the one who did this action”, the person whose life it is, though it could be heard as whoever ends it. κακῶς διετέθη is a past passive, literally “was put into a bad condition”.
notes.other_reading: nor has the one who ended this series at the right time been badly dealt with

notes.note: There is no verb and no subject. The English supplies “the stopping comes”.
notes.other_reading: when one is old

notes.note: A genitive absolute inside a relative clause, which can give the means (“through the changing of whose parts”) or only the accompanying circumstance. “With” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: through the changing of whose parts

notes.greek: καλὸν δὲ ἀεὶ πᾶν καὶ ὡραῖον
notes.note: καλόν is “fine, beautiful, noble”. ὡραῖον is “in season, in bloom”, which picks up both the theme of timing and “young and in its prime” just before.
notes.other_reading: always beautiful and in bloom

notes.greek: εἴπερ καὶ ἀπροαίρετον καὶ οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον
notes.note: ἀπροαίρετον is “not within one’s choice” (προαίρεσις). οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον is “not unsocial”, that is, not against the common interest. The step “not bad, since not shameful” rests on the Stoic view that only the shameful is bad.
notes.other_reading: since it is not chosen and does not go against the community

notes.note: A play on φέρω, “carry”: συμφέρον (literally “bearing together”), συμφερόμενον (“carried along with”), θεοφόρητος (“god-carried”, normally “inspired”) and φερόμενος twice; “carried” is kept for all but the first. συμφέρον is “benefits” here, not the glossary’s “is good for”, so that it is not confused with ἀγαθόν (“a good thing”) in the same sentence. “The whole” is repeated three times where the Greek has it once.
notes.other_reading: is good for it and in step with it. For in this way a person is inspired by god

notes.note: γνώμη is “judgment, mind, intention”. The English reads “purpose”, which fits being carried towards something and keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις and “mind” for νοῦς in this project. κατὰ ταὐτά just before is “in the same way” or “along the same lines”.
notes.other_reading: carried in judgment towards the same things

check.greek: ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἴπερ τῷ ὅλῳ καίριον καὶ συμφέρον καὶ συμφερόμενον
check.note: Two different Greek words, ἀγαθόν and συμφέρον, are both given as “good”, so the sentence reads as “it is good if it is good for the whole”. The Greek argues from benefit to the whole, to fine, to good; the same rendering stands in the sentence before.
check.decided: Accepted: the two places now read “everything that benefits the whole” and “benefits the whole”, so that συμφέρον is no longer the same English word as ἀγαθόν (“a good thing”). The step from what benefits the whole to what is good can be heard again, and the note records the departure from the glossary.

check.note: The Greek is a relative clause attached to the nature of the whole. The English starts a new clause, “its” reads as the universe’s, and “as” makes merely simultaneous what the Greek presents as the means.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by the nature of the whole, with the changing of whose parts the entire universe stays always young and in its prime”. The clause is attached to the nature of the whole again; “with” is used and not “through”, because the Greek construction does not itself say whether the changing is the means or the accompaniment.

check.note: The Greek is elliptical: “when [it happens] in old age”. In the English “it” seems to refer to one’s own nature being in old age, which is unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “when the stopping comes in old age”. The unclear “it” is gone; “the stopping” is used in place of “the end” so that the passage keeps its one word for παύομαι.

check.note: The verb is a past passive, “was put in a bad state”, parallel to “has suffered anything bad” earlier. “Is badly off” turns it into a present condition.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor has the one who brought this chain to a stop at the right time been put in a bad state”. The verb is past and passive, as the point says; “put in a bad state” is closer to it than “badly treated” and keeps “bad” for the Greek root.

check.greek: κατὰ ταὐτὰ θεῷ καὶ ἐπὶ ταὐτὰ τῇ γνώμῃ φερόμενος
check.note: “Path” is an image added to “in the same way as god”. “Own” is added, and “purpose” is narrower than γνώμη, which is “judgment, mind”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “carried in the same way as god and is carried, in their purpose, toward the same things”. “Path” and “own” are removed. “Purpose” stays for γνώμη: it is one of the word’s senses and fits being carried toward something, “judgment” is kept in this project for ὑπόληψις, and the note gives the other rendering.

check.greek: ἡ οὖν κατάπαυσις τοῦ βίου ἑκάστῳ
check.note: Found while settling: “for anyone” stands for ἑκάστῳ, which is “for each”, and “outside our choice” has a possessive the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing” and “outside one’s choice”. “Each” is kept as the Greek has it, and no first-person possessive is added.

passages.casaubon: No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end. Neither can he that is the author of that operation; for this very respect, because his operation is at an end, be said to suffer any evil. Likewise then, neither can the whole body of all our actions (which is our life) if in time it cease, be said to suffer any evil for this very reason, because it is at an end; nor he truly be said to have been ill affected, that did put a period to this series of actions. Now this time or certain period, depends of the determination of nature: sometimes of particular nature, as when a man dieth old; but of nature in general, however; the parts whereof thus changing one after another, the whole world still continues fresh and new. Now that is ever best and most seasonable, which is for the good of the whole. Thus it appears that death of itself can neither be hurtful to any in particular, because it is not a shameful thing (for neither is it a thing that depends of our own will, nor of itself contrary to the common good) and generally, as it is both expedient and seasonable to the whole, that in that respect it must needs be good. It is that also, which is brought unto us by the order and appointment of the Divine Providence; so that he whose will and mind in these things runs along with the Divine ordinance, and by this concurrence of his will and mind with the Divine Providence, is led and driven along, as it were by God Himself; may truly be termed and esteemed the θεοφόρητος, or divinely led and inspired.
passages.russian: Любое отдельное действие, какое бы оно ни было, прекратившись вовремя, не претерпевает ничего дурного оттого, что прекратилось; и тот, кто совершил это действие, не претерпел ничего дурного именно в том, что оно прекратилось. Точно так же и совокупность всех действий, то есть жизнь, если она прекращается вовремя, не претерпевает ничего дурного именно в том, что прекратилась; и тот, кто вовремя прекратил эту цепь, не оказался в дурном положении. Надлежащее время и предел даёт природа: иногда и собственная природа, когда прекращение приходит в старости, но всякий раз — природа целого, благодаря смене частей которой всё мироздание остаётся всегда молодым и цветущим. А всё, что полезно целому, всегда прекрасно и своевременно. Итак, для каждого прекращение жизни — не дурное, раз оно и не позорное, если только оно и вне выбора, и не противно общественному; а хорошее, если только оно своевременно для целого, полезно целому и несётся вместе с целым. Ведь так человека несёт и бог — того, кто несётся тем же путём, что и бог, и в своём намерении несётся к тому же.

passages.greek: Ἐνεργείας ἀπόληξις, ὁρμῆς, ὑπολήψεως παῦλα καὶ οἷον θάνατος· οὐδὲν κακόν. μέτιθι νῦν ἐπὶ ἡλικίαν, οἷον τὴν παιδικήν, τὴν τοῦ μειρακίου, τὴν νεότητα, τὸ γῆρας· καὶ γὰρ τούτων πᾶσα μεταβολή, θάνατος· μήτι δεινόν; μέτιθι νῦν ἐπὶ βίον τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πάππῳ, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῇ μητρί, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πατρί, καὶ ἄλλας δὲ πολλὰς διαφθορὰς καὶ μεταβολὰς καὶ ἀπολήξεις εὑρίσκων ἐπερώτα σεαυτόν· μήτι δεινόν; οὕτως τοίνυν οὐδὲ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου σου βίου λῆξις καὶ παῦλα καὶ μεταβολή.
passages.english: The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad. Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible? Now pass on to your life under your grandfather, then your life under your mother, then your life under your father; and as you find many other things perishing and changing and ending, ask yourself: “Surely that is nothing terrible?” In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.

notes.greek: ὁρμῆς, ὑπολήψεως παῦλα καὶ οἷον θάνατος
notes.note: How the genitives divide is open. The English follows the word order, in which each noun comes after its genitives: “ending” with the activity, “stopping and, as it were, death” with impulse and judgment. All three genitives could instead be the subject and “a stopping and a kind of death” the predicate.
notes.other_reading: The ending of an activity, of an impulse, of a judgment is a stopping and, as it were, a death

notes.note: Literally “the age of the lad” (the teens) and “youth” (young adulthood). English has no fixed pair for these; the English reads “adolescence, youth”.
notes.other_reading: boyhood, young manhood

notes.note: A question that expects the answer no, which “surely” gives. “That is” is added in English.
notes.other_reading: Is that anything terrible?

notes.greek: τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πάππῳ, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῇ μητρί, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πατρί
notes.note: The Greek has only articles; “your” is supplied each time. These are stages of Marcus’s own upbringing; the “father” is probably his adoptive father Antoninus (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the life under the grandfather, then the one under the mother, then the one under the father

notes.note: Three plural nouns, turned into “things perishing and changing and ending” because the first has no natural English plural. “Changing” and “ending” still echo “change” and “ending” elsewhere in the passage.
notes.other_reading: many other destructions and changes and endings

notes.greek: οὐδὲ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου σου βίου λῆξις καὶ παῦλα καὶ μεταβολή
notes.note: There is no predicate: “terrible” is understood from the questions before, and the English is left as short as the Greek. λῆξις is from the same root as ἀπόληξις above, so both are “ending”.
notes.other_reading: So then neither is the close, the pause and the change of your whole life anything terrible.

check.greek: Ἐνεργείας ἀπόληξις, ὁρμῆς, ὑπολήψεως παῦλα καὶ οἷον θάνατος
check.note: The three genitives and three nouns can be shared out in more than one way. The English gives “ending” to activity alone and “stopping and death” to impulse and judgment; equally possible is “the ending of an activity, of an impulse, of a judgment is a stopping and, as it were, a death”.
check.decided: Declined: the draft’s division stands. In the Greek each noun follows its own genitive or genitives (“of activity ending, of impulse, of judgment stopping and as it were death”), and the English keeps that grouping; the other division is recorded in the note.

check.note: μήτι marks a question that expects the answer no. The English question is neutral, in both places.
check.decided: Accepted: both questions now read “Surely that is nothing terrible?”, which expects the answer no as μήτι does. “That is” is kept so that the last sentence (“neither is …”) still has something to lean on.

check.note: The plural “destructions” is unnatural English. The word here means things perishing or passing away.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “many other things perishing and changing and ending”. The Greek “and … and” is kept, and a note gives the literal nouns.

passages.casaubon: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it. In all this there is no hurt. Apply this now to a man's age, as first, a child; then a youth, then a young man, then an old man; every change from one age to another is a kind of death And all this while here no matter of grief yet. Pass now unto that life first, that which thou livedst under thy grandfather, then under thy mother, then under thy father. And thus when through the whole course of thy life hitherto thou hast found and observed many alterations, many changes, many kinds of endings and cessations, put this question to thyself What matter of grief or sorrow dost thou find in any of these? Or what doest thou suffer through any of these? If in none of these, then neither in the ending and consummation of thy whole life, which is also but a cessation and change.
passages.russian: Прекращение деятельности, остановка и как бы смерть побуждения, суждения — ничего плохого. Теперь перейди к возрастам: например, детство, отрочество, молодость, старость. Ведь и всякая их перемена — смерть. Разве это что-то страшное? Теперь перейди к своей жизни при деде, затем к жизни при матери, затем к жизни при отце; и, находя многое другое, что гибнет, меняется и прекращается, спрашивай себя: «Разве это что-то страшное?» Значит, точно так же не страшно и прекращение, остановка и перемена всей твоей жизни.

passages.greek: Ὁ τὸν θάνατον φοβούμενος ἤτοι ἀναισθησίαν φοβεῖται ἢ αἴσθησιν ἑτεροίαν. ἀλλ’ εἴτε οὐκέτι αἴσθησιν, οὐδὲ κακοῦ τινος αἰσθήσῃ· εἴτε ἀλλοιοτέραν αἴσθησιν κτήσῃ, ἀλλοῖον ζῷον ἔσῃ καὶ τοῦ ζῆν οὐ παύσῃ.
passages.english: Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.

notes.note: αἴσθησις is “sensation, perception, feeling”. “Sensation” is kept for every form, including the verb αἰσθήσῃ (“you will have no sensation of”), so that the argument can be followed.
notes.other_reading: fears either not feeling or feeling in a different way

notes.note: The clause as given has no verb: the accusative needs “you have”, understood from κτήσῃ in the next clause (from memory, unchecked, editors supply a verb here). The Greek also moves here from “whoever” to “you”, which is kept.
notes.other_reading: if it is sensation no longer

notes.greek: ἀλλοιοτέραν αἴσθησιν κτήσῃ, ἀλλοῖον ζῷον ἔσῃ
notes.note: ἀλλοιοτέραν is a comparative, “rather different” or “more different”. ζῷον (“living thing”, also “animal”) is echoed by ζῆν (“living”), and the echo is kept.
notes.other_reading: if you get an altered sensation, you will be an altered creature

check.note: The clause as given has no verb: the accusative has nothing to govern it unless the verb of the next clause is understood. The English supplies “have”, which is the natural sense, and the meaning is not affected.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, and the note now says plainly that the clause as given has no verb and that “have” is supplied from the next clause.

passages.casaubon: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
passages.russian: Кто боится смерти, тот боится либо отсутствия ощущения, либо ощущения иного рода. Но если ощущения у тебя больше не будет, ты не будешь ощущать и ничего плохого; а если приобретёшь ощущение несколько иного рода, ты станешь живым существом иного рода и не перестанешь жить.

passages.greek: Θάνατος ἀνάπαυλα αἰσθητικῆς ἀντιτυπίας καὶ ὁρμητικῆς νευροσπαστίας καὶ διανοητικῆς διεξόδου καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὴν σάρκα λειτουργίας.
passages.english: Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.

notes.note: The word is “rest, respite from” something, and can also be simply “cessation”. “Rest” keeps the sense of relief.
notes.other_reading: Death is the ceasing of

notes.note: ἀντιτυπία is the resistance or striking back of something hard. Here it is either the blows that things deal the senses or the senses’ own answering reaction. “Impacts” is used, and “impression” is avoided, since this project keeps it for φαντασία.
notes.other_reading: the imprinting of the senses

notes.note: νευροσπαστία is the working of a puppet by its strings. The adjective says the pulling is done by impulse (ὁρμή).
notes.other_reading: being jerked about like a puppet by impulse

notes.note: διέξοδος is a way through, a course followed step by step, used of thought working its way through a matter. “Step-by-step” spells out the prefix; the Greek does not say that the course is laborious.
notes.other_reading: the discursive working of thought

notes.note: λειτουργία is a public service that a citizen is obliged to perform. The English says only “service”; the sense of a duty imposed is not carried by a separate English word.
notes.other_reading: the duty of waiting upon the flesh

check.note: διέξοδος is a “going through”, the step-by-step course of discursive thinking. “Windings” adds the idea of meandering, which is not in the word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the step-by-step course of thought”. “Windings” is gone; “course” is used in place of “workings” because the Greek word is built on the word for a road.

check.note: “Owed” is added. The Greek says only “the service to the flesh”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from service to the flesh”. “Owed” is removed, and the note explains the sense of obligation in the Greek word.

check.note: ἀντιτυπία is “striking back, resistance, repercussion”. The English takes it as things striking the senses; it may also be the senses’ own answering reaction.
check.decided: Declined: “the impacts on the senses” stands. ἀντιτυπία is a striking against, which “impacts” gives; “impressions” would collide with the word this project keeps for φαντασία, and the other reading is in the note.

passages.casaubon: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
passages.russian: Смерть — отдых от толчков, приходящих через чувства, от того, как побуждение дёргает за кукольные нити, от движения мысли шаг за шагом и от служения плоти.

passages.greek:
Εἰς μὲν τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα μία ψυχὴ διῄρηται, εἰς δὲ τὰ λογικὰ μία νοερὰ ψυχὴ μεμέρισται, ὥσπερ καὶ μία γῆ ἐστιν ἁπάντων τῶν γεωδῶν καὶ ἑνὶ φωτὶ ὁρῶμεν καὶ ἕνα ἀέρα ἀναπνέομεν, ὅσα ὁρατικὰ καὶ ἔμψυχα.
