Πάντα ὅσα κοινοῦ τινος μετέχει πρὸς τὸ ὁμογενὲς σπεύδει. τὸ γεῶδες πᾶν ῥέπει ἐπὶ γῆν· τὸ ὑγρὸν πᾶν σύρρουν· τὸ ἀερῶδες ὁμοίως, ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας· τὸ πῦρ ἀνωφερὲς μὲν διὰ τὸ στοιχειῶδες πῦρ, παντὶ δὲ πυρὶ ἐνταῦθα πρὸς τὸ συνεξάπτεσθαι ἕτοιμον οὕτως, ὥστε καὶ πᾶν τὸ ὑλικὸν τὸ ὀλίγῳ ξηρότερον εὐέξαπτον εἶναι διὰ τὸ ἔλαττον ἐγκεκρᾶσθαι αὐτῷ τὸ κωλυτικὸν πρὸς ἔξαψιν. καὶ τοίνυν πᾶν τὸ κοινῆς νοερᾶς φύσεως μέτοχον πρὸς τὸ συγγενὲς ὁμοίως σπεύδει ἢ καὶ μᾶλλον· ὅσῳ γάρ ἐστι κρεῖττον παρὰ τὰ ἄλλα, τοσούτῳ καὶ πρὸς τὸ συγκιρνᾶσθαι τῷ οἰκείῳ καὶ συγχεῖσθαι ἑτοιμότερον. εὐθὺς γοῦν ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ἀλόγων εὑρέθη σμήνη καὶ ἀγέλαι καὶ νεοσσοτροφίαι καὶ οἷον ἔρωτες· ψυχαὶ γὰρ ἤδη ἦσαν ἐνταῦθα καὶ τὸ συναγωγὸν ἐν τῷ κρείττονι ἐπιτεινόμενον εὑρίσκετο, οἷον οὔτε ἐπὶ φυτῶν ἦν οὔτε ἐπὶ λίθων ἢ ξύλων. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν λογικῶν ζῴων πολιτεῖαι καὶ φιλίαι καὶ οἶκοι καὶ σύλλογοι καὶ ἐν πολέμοις συνθῆκαι καὶ ἀνοχαί. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἔτι κρειττόνων καὶ ἐκ διεστηκότων τρόπον τινὰ ἕνωσις ὑπέστη οἵα ἐπὶ τῶν ἄστρων· οὕτως ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον ἐπανάβασις συμπάθειαν καὶ ἐν διεστῶσιν ἐργάσασθαι ἐδύνατο. ὅρα οὖν τὸ νῦν γινόμενον· μόνα γὰρ τὰ νοερὰ νῦν ἐπιλέλησται τῆς πρὸς ἄλληλα σπουδῆς καὶ συννεύσεως καὶ τὸ σύρρουν ὧδε μόνον οὐ βλέπεται. ἀλλ’ ὅμως καίτοι φεύγοντες περικαταλαμβάνονται· κρατεῖ γὰρ ἡ φύσις. ὄψει δὲ ὃ λέγω παραφυλάσσων· θᾶσσον γοῦν εὕροι τις ἂν γεῶδές τι μηδενὸς γεώδους προσαπτόμενον ἤπερ ἄνθρωπον ἀνθρώπου ἀπεσχισμένον.
passages.english:
One soul has been divided among the animals without reason, and one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones, just as there is one earth for all earthy things, and we see by one light and breathe one air, all of us that have sight and a soul.

All things that share in something common hurry towards what is of their own kind. Everything earthy tends towards earth. Everything wet flows together. What is airy does the same, so that there is need of things to hold them apart, and of force. Fire is carried upward because of the elemental fire, yet it is so ready to be kindled together with every fire here that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle, because less of what hinders kindling is mixed into it. So too, then, everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries towards its kin in the same way, or even more. For the better it is compared with the rest, the readier it is to mix with what is its own and to be poured together with it. At any rate, right from the start, among the animals without reason there were found swarms and herds and the rearing of nestlings and what one might call loves; for here there were already souls, and the thing that draws together was found growing stronger in what is better, of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber. Among the rational animals there were states and friendships and households and gatherings, and in wars treaties and truces. Among those better still, even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union, such as there is among the stars. In this way the climb towards the better was able to produce a shared feeling even in things that stand apart. See, then, what is happening now. For only the beings that have mind have now forgotten their hurrying towards one another and their leaning together, and only here is the flowing together not to be seen. And yet, though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch closely. At any rate, one would sooner find something earthy touching nothing earthy than a human being split off from a human being.

notes.note: νοερός is “of mind, able to think”. “Mind” is kept as the one word for it through the passage (“one soul that has mind”, “a common nature of mind”, “the beings that have mind”) so the chain can be followed. The verb differs from “divided” in the first clause and has a different English verb.
notes.other_reading: one thinking soul has been shared out

notes.note: A neuter plural (“whatever things can see and have soul in them”) attached to verbs in “we”. ἔμψυχα is literally “ensouled”, in ordinary Greek simply “alive”; “soul” is kept because the sentence is about soul.
notes.other_reading: all of us creatures that can see and are alive

notes.note: σπεύδω is “hurry, press eagerly towards”, and also “strive”. “Hurry” is used for the verb both times and “hurrying” for the noun σπουδή near the end, since the argument turns on the repetition.
notes.other_reading: strive towards what is of their own kind

notes.note: The word for a scale pan going down: to incline, to tend. “Tends” is used so that “leaning” can be kept for a different word near the end.
notes.other_reading: Everything earthy sinks towards earth

notes.greek: ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας
notes.note: The Greek has no subject: “so that there is need of things that keep apart, and of force”. The clause may cover the wet as well as the airy.
notes.other_reading: so that barriers and force are needed

notes.note: Literally “because of the elemental fire”. It is taken as the pure fire of the upper region, towards which fire down here rises; the words could also name the fiery element within the flame itself.
notes.other_reading: because of the element of fire in it

notes.note: Three words in this sentence are made from one verb for setting alight. “Kindle” is used for all three.
notes.other_reading: to catch light together

notes.note: ὑλικός is “material, made of matter”, but ὕλη is also the ordinary word for wood and fuel, and that sense is close to the surface here. “Even” is taken with the whole phrase: not only fire itself but anything material.
notes.other_reading: even all fuel that is a little drier

notes.greek: ὅσῳ γάρ ἐστι κρεῖττον παρὰ τὰ ἄλλα
notes.note: κρείττων is “better”, also “stronger” or “superior”. The word returns four times as the rungs of a ladder; “better” is kept each time and not “higher”, since the Greek has no image of height until the “climb” later on.
notes.other_reading: For the higher it stands above the rest

notes.note: εὐθύς is “straight away” and can mark the first moment in time or the first case in a list; the past tenses that follow tell the ladder of beings as if it were a history. “Right from the start” leaves both senses possible. γοῦν, “at any rate”, brings in the evidence, as it does again in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: To begin with, at any rate,

notes.note: A school term: wholes made of members that stand physically apart, as opposed to one continuous body. The same word comes back as διεστῶσιν in the next sentence; “things that stand apart” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: even out of separated things

notes.note: “In a way” stands between “things that stand apart” and “union” and could soften either. It is taken with the union.
notes.other_reading: even out of things that in a way stand apart there came to be a union

notes.note: A Stoic term for parts of the universe being affected together, as if by one feeling. The English word “sympathy” now means pity, so the English reads “a shared feeling”.
notes.other_reading: sympathy

notes.greek: τὸ σύρρουν ὧδε μόνον οὐ βλέπεται
notes.note: μόνον is taken with ὧδε: “here alone it is not seen”. μόνον οὐ can also be an idiom for “all but”, but “is all but seen” gives no sense here. “The flowing together” repeats the word used of water above.
notes.other_reading: and in this one case the running together is not seen

notes.note: The participle turns masculine: the neuter “beings that have mind” have become people. The verb is one word, “overtake and surround”; the English needs two.
notes.other_reading: though they flee, they are caught all the same

check.greek: ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας
check.note: The Greek has no subject (“there is need of things that keep apart, and of force”). “They need” has no clear referent and can be read as if the elements wanted to be held apart.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “so that it takes things to hold them apart, and force”. The Greek clause has no subject, and the point is that it takes something outside them, and force, to stop them joining.

check.note: The word is the tilt of a scale: inclines, tends. “Sinks” adds a downward fall and loses the idea of a tendency, which the argument goes on to generalise.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “tends toward earth”. The word names a tendency, not a fall; “leans” is not used because “leaning together” is kept for a different Greek word later in the passage.

check.greek: ὥστε καὶ πᾶν τὸ ὑλικὸν τὸ ὀλίγῳ ξηρότερον
check.note: “Even” goes with “any material thing” (not only fire itself), not with “a little”. “Every material” is also unclear English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle”. “Even” belongs with the whole phrase, and “everything” keeps the Greek “all”.

check.note: “At any rate” (γοῦν) is dropped here though it is given in the last sentence. εὐθύς may mean “straight away, at the very first step” and not merely open a list.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “At any rate, right from the start”. “At any rate” is restored, as in the last sentence; “right from the start” is used and not “already”, because “already” comes as a separate Greek word in the next clause.

check.note: The word is made from “nestling, chick”. The three examples are bees, herd animals and birds, and “young” in general loses the third picture.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the rearing of nestlings”. The Greek word names nestlings, so the picture of birds is kept.

check.note: “For” is dropped. The sentence gives the reason for “See what is happening now”.
check.decided: Accepted: The sentence now begins “For only the beings that have mind”. The Greek marks it as the ground for the sentence before.

check.note: The verb is “prevails, has the mastery”. There is no comparison in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for nature prevails”. The Greek verb makes no comparison, so “stronger” said more than it does.

check.note: The compound is “overtaken and hemmed in on every side”. “Caught” keeps the result but drops the picture of being surrounded.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same”. The one Greek verb says both that they are caught up with and that they are surrounded.

check.note: “In a way” stands between “things that stand apart” and “union” and could soften either. The English chose the union without any sign.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union”, which follows the Greek order. “In a way” is still taken with the union, since the stars stand apart without qualification; a note gives the other reading.

check.note: The verb is to hurry, to press eagerly toward; “strive” suggests effort against resistance. The chain of three is rightly kept in one word; only the word chosen is a shade off.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “hurry toward” and “hurries toward”. For the noun it reads “their hurrying toward one another” and not “eagerness”, so that the one Greek word keeps one English word through the passage.

check.greek: οἷον οὔτε ἐπὶ φυτῶν ἦν οὔτε ἐπὶ λίθων ἢ ξύλων
check.note: “Such as it was not in plants or in stones or in timber” is accurate but stiff, and a reader has to stop to parse it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber”. “Did not exist” is used and not “not found”, because the Greek has a plain “was” here and “found” in the clause before.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning” and ἄλογος as “unreasoning”, where the renderings settled for this translation have “rational” for λογικός and “reason” for λόγος.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the rational ones”, “the rational animals” and “the animals without reason”. “Without reason” keeps the pair audible beside “rational”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave νοερός as “thinking” three times, where this translation uses “mind, of mind” for the word, as the draft itself did in 4.4 and 8.54.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “one soul that has mind”, “a common nature of mind” and “the beings that have mind”. “Mind” is the constant word, so the chain can still be followed.

check.note: Found while settling: three words in one sentence are made from the same Greek verb for setting alight, and the draft gave them as “catch light”, “set alight” and “kindling”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to be kindled together”, “easy to kindle” and “what hinders kindling”, one English word for the one Greek root.

passages.casaubon: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all. As of all earthly things there is but one earth, and but one light that we see by; and but one air that we breathe in, as many as either breathe or see. Now whatsoever partakes of some common thing, naturally affects and inclines unto that whereof it is part, being of one kind and nature with it. Whatsoever is earthly, presseth downwards to the common earth. Whatsoever is liquid, would flow together. And whatsoever is airy, would be together likewise. So that without some obstacle, and some kind of violence, they cannot well be kept asunder. Whatsoever is fiery, doth not only by reason of the elementary fire tend upwards; but here also is so ready to join, and to burn together, that whatsoever doth want sufficient moisture to make resistance, is easily set on fire. Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind. For by how much in its own nature it excels all other things, by so much more is it desirous to be joined and united unto that, which is of its own nature. As for unreasonable creatures then, they had not long been, but presently begun among them swarms, and flocks, and broods of young ones, and a kind of mutual love and affection. For though but unreasonable, yet a kind of soul these had, and therefore was that natural desire of union more strong and intense in them, as in creatures of a more excellent nature, than either in plants, or stones, or trees. But among reasonable creatures, begun commonwealths, friendships, families, public meetings, and even in their wars, conventions, and truces. Now among them that were yet of a more excellent nature, as the stars and planets, though by their nature far distant one from another, yet even among them began some mutual correspondency and unity. So proper is it to excellency in a high degree to affect unity, as that even in things so far distant, it could operate unto a mutual sympathy. But now behold, what is now come to pass. Those creatures that are reasonable, are now the only creatures that have forgotten their natural affection and inclination of one towards another. Among them alone of all other things that are of one kind, there is not to be found a general disposition to flow together. But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended. Do they what they can, nature doth prevail. And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it. For sooner mayst thou find a thing earthly, where no earthly thing is, than find a man that naturally can live by himself alone.
passages.russian:
Одна душа разделена между неразумными животными, и одна душа, наделённая умом, распределена между разумными, так же как одна земля для всего земного и мы видим при одном свете и дышим одним воздухом — все мы, у кого есть зрение и душа.

Всё, что причастно чему-то общему, спешит к своему роду. Всё земное тянется к земле. Всё влажное стекается вместе. С воздушным то же самое, так что нужны вещи, которые держали бы его порознь, и нужна сила. Огонь несётся вверх из-за стихийного огня, но он так готов воспламеняться вместе со всяким здешним огнём, что даже всякая материя, чуть более сухая, легко воспламеняется, потому что в неё меньше примешано того, что мешает воспламенению. Значит, и всё, что причастно общей природе ума, точно так же спешит к родному или даже сильнее. Ведь чем оно лучше по сравнению с остальным, тем охотнее смешивается со своим и сливается с ним. Во всяком случае, уже с самого начала у неразумных животных обнаружились рои, и стада, и выкармливание птенцов, и то, что можно назвать любовью; ведь здесь уже были души, и то, что стягивает вместе, обнаруживалось в лучшем более сильным — такого рода, какого не было ни в растениях, ни в камнях или брёвнах. У разумных животных были государства, и дружбы, и семьи, и собрания, а в войнах — договоры и перемирия. У ещё лучших даже из того, что отстоит друг от друга, возникло в некотором роде единство, как у звёзд. Так восхождение к лучшему смогло породить общее чувство даже в том, что отстоит друг от друга. Посмотри же, что происходит теперь. Ведь только существа, наделённые умом, теперь забыли, как спешить друг к другу и склоняться друг к другу, и только здесь не видно, чтобы что-то стекалось вместе. И всё же, хоть они и убегают, их всё равно настигают и теснят: природа одолевает. Ты увидишь, о чём я, если будешь внимательно наблюдать. Во всяком случае, скорее найдёшь что-нибудь земное, не касающееся ничего земного, чем человека, отколотого от человека.

passages.greek: Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς, τοιαύτη σοι ἔσται ἡ διάνοια· βάπτεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τῶν φαντασιῶν ἡ ψυχή. βάπτε οὐν αὐτὴν τῇ συνεχείᾳ τῶν τοιούτων φαντασιῶν· οἷον, ὅτι ὅπου ζῆν ἐστιν, ἐκεῖ καὶ εὖ ζῆν· ἐν αὐλῇ δὲ ζῆν ἐστιν· ἔστιν ἄρα καὶ εὖ ζῆν ἐν αὐλῇ. καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι οὗπερ ἕνεκεν ἕκαστον κατεσκεύασται, πρὸς τοῦτο φέρεται· πρὸς ὃ φέρεται δέ, ἐν τούτῳ τὸ τέλος αὐτοῦ· ὅπου δὲ τὸ τέλος, ἐκεῖ καὶ τὸ συμφέρον καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἑκάστου· τὸ ἄρα ἀγαθὸν τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κοινωνία. ὅτι γὰρ πρὸς κοινωνίαν γεγόναμεν, πάλαι δέδεικται· ἢ οὐκ ἦν ἐναργὲς ὅτι τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, τὰ δὲ κρείττω ἀλλήλων; κρείττω δὲ τῶν μὲν ἀψύχων τὰ ἔμψυχα, τῶν δὲ ἐμψύχων τὰ λογικά.
passages.english: Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind; for the soul is dyed by its impressions. So dye it with an unbroken run of impressions such as these. For example: where it is possible to live, there it is also possible to live well; but it is possible to live at court; therefore it is also possible to live well at court. And again: each thing is carried towards that for the sake of which it was built; and what it is carried towards, in that lies its goal; and where its goal is, there also is the benefit and the good of each thing; therefore the good of a rational animal is community. For it has long since been shown that we were born for community. Or was it not plain that the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.

notes.note: The verb is the one from which φαντασία (“impression”) is made: “whatever sort of things you often have appear to you”. The English reads “impressions you often form” so that verb and noun stay one word.
notes.other_reading: Whatever kind of things you often picture to yourself

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought, understanding”, and also the mind as the thing that thinks. “Thought” is used, as elsewhere in this translation.
notes.other_reading: your mind will be of that kind

notes.note: Literally “is dipped”, the dyer’s word; the same verb is the command in the next sentence, and “dye” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: is steeped

notes.note: Literally “by the continuity of such impressions”, made concrete as “an unbroken run”.
notes.other_reading: by having such impressions continually

notes.note: αὐλή is a courtyard and then a ruler’s court: his household and the life lived around him. Marcus means his own. The building is not the point.
notes.other_reading: in a palace

notes.note: The form can be passive (“is carried”) or middle (“moves, tends”). “Is carried” is kept both times; it need not imply an outside force.
notes.other_reading: each thing tends towards that for the sake of which it was built

notes.note: “What is good for a thing”, built on the same verb as “is carried” just before; the echo cannot be kept in English. “Benefit” is used here because “the good” follows at once as a separate word.
notes.other_reading: what is good for each thing

notes.note: The word covers “sharing, partnership, fellowship, community”. “Community” is used here and in the next sentence. It is the noun behind the adjective given as “social” elsewhere in this translation.
notes.other_reading: fellowship

notes.note: “Has been shown long ago”: the Greek does not say whether earlier in his own notes or in the teaching of his school is meant. The English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: was proved long ago

notes.note: Plain comparatives, “worse” and “better”; they can also be heard as “lower” and “higher” in a scale of beings.
notes.other_reading: the lower exist for the sake of the higher

notes.note: Taken as a comparison, in parallel with the clause before: rational things are better than things that have a soul and no more. The words can also be read as picking the rational ones out from among things with a soul.
notes.other_reading: and among things with a soul the rational ones are better

check.note: The word is the court, the ruler’s household and its way of life, not the building. Marcus is speaking of his own life at court; “in a palace” makes it any grand house.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “at court” both times. The word names the ruler’s court and the life lived there, which is Marcus’s own, and not a building.

check.note: The parallel clause before is a comparison (“better than things without a soul”), so this one is most naturally “and rational things better than those with a soul”. The English made it “among things with a soul”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and rational things better than things with a soul”. The Greek sets the two clauses in exact parallel, so the same comparison is read in both; a note gives the other reading.

check.note: The form can be passive (“is carried”) or middle (“moves, tends”). “Is carried” suggests an outside force; “tends toward” is equally possible.
check.decided: Declined: “Is carried toward” stands in both places. The Greek form allows either sense and “carry” is the plain meaning of the verb, on which the passage plays again in its word for “benefit”; a note now records “tends toward”.

check.greek: Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς, τοιαύτη σοι ἔσται ἡ διάνοια
check.note: Found while settling: the draft began “Your mind will be of the same kind as the impressions you often form”, which reversed the Greek order (first the impressions, then what follows from them) and gave διάνοια as “mind”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind”. The order of thought follows the Greek, and “thought” is the word used for διάνοια elsewhere in this translation.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a rational animal” and, in the last sentence, “rational things”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave τὸ συμφέρον as “the advantage”, where this translation uses “is good for” or “benefits” for the verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the benefit and the good of each thing”. “What is good for” is not used here because “the good” follows at once as a separate Greek word and the two would run together.

passages.casaubon: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations. As for example. Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy. But thou mayest live at the Court, there then also mayest thou live well and happy. Again, that which everything is made for, he is also made unto that, and cannot but naturally incline unto it. That which anything doth naturally incline unto, therein is his end. Wherein the end of everything doth consist, therein also doth his good and benefit consist. Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature. For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated. Or can any man make any question of this, that whatsoever is naturally worse and inferior, is ordinarily subordinated to that which is better? and that those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Какие представления ты часто себе составляешь, такой будет и твоя мысль: ведь душа окрашивается представлениями. Так окрашивай её непрерывной чередой таких представлений. Например: где можно жить, там можно и жить хорошо; но можно жить при дворе; значит, можно и жить хорошо при дворе. И ещё: каждая вещь несётся к тому, ради чего она устроена; и в том, к чему она несётся, — её цель; а где её цель, там и польза, и благо каждой вещи; следовательно, благо разумного живого существа — общность. Ведь давно показано, что мы рождены для общности. Или не было ясно, что худшее существует ради лучшего, а лучшее — друг ради друга? А одушевлённое лучше неодушевлённого, и разумное лучше одушевлённого.

passages.greek: Εἴ ποτε εἶδες χεῖρα ἀποκεκομμένην ἢ πόδα ἢ κεφαλὴν ἀποτετμημένην, χωρίς πού ποτε ἀπὸ τοῦ λοιποῦ σώματος κειμένην· τοιοῦτον ἑαυτὸν ποιεῖ, ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ, ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸ συμβαῖνον καὶ ἀποσχίζων ἑαυτὸν ἢ ὁ ἀκοινώνητόν τι πράσσων. ἀπέρριψαί πού ποτε ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἑνώσεως· ἐπεφύκεις γὰρ μέρος· νῦν δὲ σεαυτὸν ἀπέκοψας. ἀλλ’ ὧδε κομψὸν ἐκεῖνο, ὅτι ἔξεστί σοι πάλιν ἑνῶσαι σεαυτόν. τοῦτο ἄλλῳ μέρει οὐδενὶ θεὸς ἐπέτρεψεν, χωρισθέντι καὶ διακοπέντι πάλιν συνελθεῖν, ἀλλὰ σκέψαι τὴν χρηστότητα ᾗ τετίμηκε τὸν ἄνθρωπον· καὶ γὰρ ἵνα τὴν ἀρχὴν μὴ ἀπορραγῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὅλου ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἐποίησε, καὶ ἀπορραγέντι πάλιν ἐπανελθεῖν καὶ συμφῦναι καὶ τὴν τοῦ μέρους τάξιν ἀπολαβεῖν ἐποίησεν.
passages.english: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens and split themselves off, or when they do something unsocial. You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature; for you were by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off. But here is the neat thing: you are allowed to unite yourself again. To no other part has god granted this, to come together again once it has been separated and cut through. But consider the kindness with which he has honoured the human being: for he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place, and, for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together and take up again the place of a part.

notes.note: The “if” clause never gets a main clause; the sentence breaks off and starts again with “that is what”. The break is kept with a colon.
notes.other_reading: Have you ever seen a hand cut off? That is what

notes.note: The head has a different verb from the hand: “cut away”. “Severed” keeps the two apart.
notes.other_reading: a head cut away

notes.note: πού ποτε (“somewhere, at some time”) is repeated in the next sentence of you yourself, so the thrown-away self lies where the hand lay. “Somewhere or other” is used both times; the “at some time” is only faintly there.
notes.other_reading: lying at some time, in some place, apart

notes.note: “As far as rests with oneself.” The same phrase comes back at the end, of what god has made to rest with the human being; “power” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: as far as it lies with them

notes.note: “What happens”, with the sense “what happens to them”. The Greek has no “to them”.
notes.other_reading: what befalls them

notes.note: The adjective negates the word for community: “something that has no share in community”. “Unsocial” is used as the negative of “social”, the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation; it does not here mean keeping to oneself.
notes.other_reading: something that goes against community

notes.note: The form is either passive (“you have been thrown away, you lie thrown away”) or reflexive (“you have thrown yourself away”). The passive is taken, because the next clause adds an express “yourself” and this one does not, and because it matches the severed limb “lying” somewhere.
notes.other_reading: You have thrown yourself somewhere or other away from the union

notes.note: A past form of the verb “grow”, the verb behind φύσις (“nature”) just before and “grow together” at the end: “you had grown as, you were by nature, a part”.
notes.other_reading: for you grew as a part

notes.note: κομψός is “neat, elegant, clever”, said of a nice touch or a pretty arrangement.
notes.other_reading: But here is the fine thing

notes.note: No article: “god”, “a god”, or the one god of the next sentence, who honoured the human being. Lower-case “god” is used, as throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: no god has granted this to any other part

notes.note: τὴν ἀρχήν is the adverbial idiom “at all, in the first place”, not “the beginning”. The verb is “be broken or torn off”, stronger than the “cut” words above.
notes.other_reading: so as not to be torn away at all

notes.note: τάξις is a post or rank in a formation: “the station of the part”.
notes.other_reading: its post as a part

check.note: The form can be “you have been cast away”, “you lie cast off” or “you have cast yourself away”. The next clause marks self-action with an express “yourself” and this one does not, so the passive is at least as likely and matches the limb “lying” somewhere.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature”. The form allows both, but only the next clause has an express “yourself”, and the passive answers the limb “lying” somewhere; a note gives the reflexive reading.

check.note: The form means “you were by nature a part”. “Grew as a part” describes a process, not what he was by nature.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for you were by nature a part”. The form states what he was by nature, and “by nature” keeps the link with “the union that accords with nature” just before.

check.note: Keeping the two Greek verbs apart is right, but “a head cut away” is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a severed head”. The two Greek verbs are still kept apart, “cut off” for the hand and “severed” for the head.

check.note: The word negates the word for community. “Unsocial” today suggests keeping to oneself and hides the link.
check.decided: Declined: “Something unsocial” stands. κοινωνικός is “social” throughout this translation and this word is its negative, so “unsocial” keeps one English word for the family; a note now says that it does not mean keeping to oneself and gives the suggested wording.

check.note: The word is neat, clever, elegant: the neat twist in the arrangement. “Fine” is vaguer.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “But here is the neat thing”. The word is said of a clever touch in an arrangement.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “himself”, “him” and “he” for the person who splits off and for the human being at the end, where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a person makes of themselves … when they do not want what happens” and, at the end, “the human being’s power” and “for one who has been broken off”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “God” with a capital, where this translation uses lower-case “god”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “To no other part has god granted this”. The word order keeps “god” away from the start of the sentence, so that the lower case can be seen.

check.note: Found while settling: the same Greek phrase, “resting with oneself”, stands near the start and near the end. The draft gave it as “as far as it lies with him” and “in the person’s own power”, and added “own”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “as far as it is in their power” and “he put it in the human being’s power”, so that the echo can be heard.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft left out the “for” that makes the last sentence the ground for “consider the kindness”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “for he put it in the human being’s power”.

passages.casaubon: If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body, such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened, (whatsoever it be) and as it were divides himself from it: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men: or, he that, commits any act of uncharitableness. Whosoever thou art, thou art such, thou art cast forth I know not whither out of the general unity, which is according to nature. Thou went born indeed a part, but now thou hast cut thyself off. However, herein is matter of joy and exultation, that thou mayst be united again. God hath not granted it unto any other part, that once separated and cut off, it might be reunited, and come together again. But, behold, that GOODNESS how great and immense it is! which hath so much esteemed MAN. As at first he was so made, that he needed not, except he would himself, have divided himself from the whole; so once divided and cut off, IT hath so provided and ordered it, that if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again, and be admitted into its former rank and place of a part, as he was before.
passages.russian: Если ты когда-нибудь видел отрубленную руку, или ногу, или отсечённую голову, лежащую где-то в стороне от остального тела, — вот что делает из себя человек, насколько это в его силах, когда не хочет того, что происходит, и откалывает себя, или когда совершает что-то необщественное. Ты лежишь где-то там, отброшенный от единства, согласного с природой; ведь ты по природе был частью, а теперь сам себя отсёк. Но вот что тут изящно: тебе позволено снова соединить себя. Ни одной другой части бог не даровал этого — снова сойтись, когда она уже отделена и рассечена. Но посмотри, с какой добротой он почтил человека: он дал человеку власть вовсе не отрываться от целого, а тому, кто оторвался, дал возможность снова вернуться, срастись и вновь занять место части.

passages.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ἐν ἡνωμένοις τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος, τοῦτον ἔχει τὸν λόγον ἐν διεστῶσι τὰ λογικά, πρὸς μίαν τινὰ συνεργίαν κατεσκευασμένα. μᾶλλον δέ σοι ἡ τούτου νόησις προσπεσεῖται, ἐὰν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν πολλάκις λέγῃς, ὅτι μέλος εἰμὶ τοῦ ἐκ τῶν λογικῶν συστήματος. ἐὰν δὲ διὰ τοῦ ῥῶ στοιχείου μέρος εἶναι ἑαυτὸν λέγῃς, οὔπω ἀπὸ καρδίας φιλεῖς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους· οὔπω σε καταληκτικῶς εὐφραίνει τὸ εὐεργετεῖν· ἔτι ὡς πρέπον αὐτὸ ψιλὸν ποιεῖς, οὔπω ὡς ἑαυτὸν εὖ ποιῶν.
passages.english: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart, being built to do a single task together. The thought of this will strike you more if you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.” But if, by using the letter rho, you say that you are a part [meros], you do not yet love people from the heart; doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself.

notes.note: A school distinction (from memory, unchecked): bodies that are one continuous whole, such as an animal, against wholes made of members that stand apart, such as an army or a chorus. The second term is ἐν διεστῶσι in the next clause. “United” is used because the Greek word is made from “one”, like “union” in the neighbouring passages.
notes.other_reading: in bodies that are all of one piece

notes.note: λόγος here is “relation, proportion”, not “reason”, though it is the word from which λογικά (“rational beings”) is made, and the echo may be intended.
notes.other_reading: the same account holds for

notes.note: μέλος is a limb or bodily member. “Limb” is used because the passage goes on to set it against “part”.
notes.other_reading: the members of the body

notes.note: Literally “for some one working-together”: the activity of working together, not a thing produced.
notes.other_reading: for a certain single cooperation

notes.note: Literally “will fall upon you”: the thought will hit you, come home to you.
notes.other_reading: will come home to you more

notes.note: σύστημα is a whole put together out of members: a body of people, an organised group. It is a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον). Its English descendant, “system”, sounds mechanical today.
notes.other_reading: the system made up of rational beings

notes.note: The point is a play on two Greek words one letter apart: μέλος (limb) and μέρος (part), with rho (r) in place of lambda (l). Since the passage is talking about the words themselves, both are added in square brackets; the brackets and what is in them are not in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: by changing the l to an r

notes.note: A rare adverb and a doubted reading (from memory, unchecked). As it stands it comes from the verb “to come to an end, to stop”, and is taken as “to the end, fully”; it could also mean “as the point at which one stops”. Editors have proposed καταληπτικῶς, a Stoic term for a firm grasp (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: doing good does not yet delight you as an end in itself; or, with the proposed reading, with full conviction

notes.note: Literally “as a bare fitting thing”: what is proper and nothing more. “Duty” is avoided, since that is a different Stoic word.
notes.other_reading: simply as a bare duty

check.note: A rare adverb from the verb “to come to an end”: roughly “finally, conclusively, completely”. “As an end in itself” is a confident philosophical phrase that says more than the word does, and some editors print a different word here (from memory).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “doing good does not yet delight you fully”. The adverb is rare and comes from a verb meaning “to come to an end”, and “as an end in itself” made a settled philosophical claim out of it. The note marks the reading as doubted and gives the other senses.

check.note: The transliterations “(melos)” and “(meros)” are not in the Greek. They are needed for the play on one letter, but as printed they sit inside Marcus’s sentence as if his.
check.decided: Accepted: The two Greek words now stand in square brackets, “[melos]” and “[meros]”, and a note says that the brackets and their contents are not in the Greek. They are kept because the play on one letter cannot be followed without them.

check.note: The word for “a certain” is dropped, and the noun is the activity of working together, not a work produced.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “being built to do some one work together”. “Some” restores the dropped word and “to do … together” makes it an activity; “as one” is not used because the Greek says one work, not one worker.

check.note: “System” sounds technical or mechanical in today’s English. The word is a whole composed of members, which is what makes “limb” fit.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the whole made up of rational beings”. The Greek word is a whole composed of members; a note says that it is a different word from the one given elsewhere as “the whole”.

check.note: “In things that are unified … in things that stand apart” is literal and accurate but hard to picture. The contrast is between a body that is one continuous thing and one made of separate individuals.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “in things that are united”, a plainer word than “unified” and one that links with “union” in the neighbouring passages. “Things that stand apart” is kept, because the same Greek word is so given in 9.8–9 and the Greek says “things”, not “bodies” or “members”; the note explains the contrast.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικός as “reasoning beings”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “rational beings” both times.

passages.casaubon: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common operation. And this thou shalt apprehend the better, if thou shalt use thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and body of reasonable substances. But if thou shalt say I am μέρος, or a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart. The joy that thou takest in the exercise of bounty, is not yet grounded upon a due ratiocination and right apprehension of the nature of things. Thou dost exercise it as yet upon this ground barely, as a thing convenient and fitting; not, as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others.
passages.russian: Какое отношение имеют части тела в том, что едино, такое же отношение имеют разумные существа в том, что существует раздельно, ведь они устроены, чтобы вместе исполнять одну задачу. Мысль об этом будет сильнее поражать тебя, если ты будешь часто говорить себе: «Я — часть тела [мелос] того целого, что составлено из разумных существ». Если же, употребив букву ро, ты скажешь, что ты часть [мерос], то ты ещё не любишь людей от сердца; делать добро ещё не радует тебя вполне; ты ещё делаешь это лишь как подобающее, а не как добро, которое делаешь самому себе.

passages.greek: Εἰ τὸ νοερὸν ἡμῖν κοινόν, καὶ ὁ λόγος, καθʼ ὃν λογικοί ἐσμεν, κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, καὶ ὁ νόμος κοινός· εἰ τοῦτο, πολῖταί ἐσμεν· εἰ τοῦτο, πολιτεύματός τινος μετέχομεν· εἰ τοῦτο, ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις ἐστί· τίνος γὰρ ἄλλου φήσει τις τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πᾶν γένος κοινοῦ πολιτεύματος μετέχειν; ἐκεῖθεν δέ, ἐκ τῆς κοινῆς ταύτης πόλεως, καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ νοερὸν καὶ λογικὸν καὶ νομικὸν ἡμῖν ἢ πόθεν; ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ γεῶδές μοι ἀπό τινος γῆς ἀπομεμέρισται καὶ τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀφʼ ἑτέρου στοιχείου καὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀπὸ πηγῆς τινος καὶ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ πυρῶδες ἔκ τινος ἰδίας πηγῆς (οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἔρχεται, ὥσπερ μηδʼ εἰς τὸ οὐκ ὂν ἀπέρχεται), οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸ νοερὸν ἥκει ποθέν.
passages.english: If mind is common to us, then reason too, by which we are rational, is common. If that is so, then the reason that commands what is to be done or not done is also common. If that is so, law too is common. If that is so, we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city. For in what other common civic body will anyone say that the whole race of human beings shares? And it is from there, from this common city, that our very mind and reason and sense of law come; or from where else? For just as what is earthy in me has been portioned off from some earth, and what is wet from another element, and what is breath from some source, and what is warm and fiery from some source of its own (for nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing goes away into what is not), so too mind has come from somewhere.

notes.note: Literally “the thing of mind”, the part of us that thinks. “Mind” is used for it throughout this passage.
notes.other_reading: If the power to think is common to us

notes.note: The adjective made from λόγος, “reason”: “having reason”. “Rational” is used, as throughout this translation; the Greek link with “reason” is closer than the English shows.
notes.other_reading: by which we are reasoning beings

notes.greek: ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος
notes.note: “The reason that gives orders about things to be done or not”: this reads as a school definition of law, which is why “law” follows at once. The Greek leaves “to be done” to be supplied after “or not”.
notes.other_reading: the reason that prescribes what we must do and what we must not

notes.note: πολίτευμα is made from the word for citizen and can mean a constitution, a government, a state, or the body of citizens. “Civic body” is used and kept in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: we share in some kind of state

notes.note: κόσμος is the ordered whole of things, “the universe” throughout this translation. ὡσανεί softens the claim: “as if, so to speak”.
notes.other_reading: the world is like a city

notes.note: Three adjectives under one article, answering to mind, reason and law in the chain above: “the thing in us that is of mind, of reason and of law”. νομικόν is literally “having to do with law”; “sense of law” marks that it is the capacity in us, not law itself, which was an earlier step.
notes.other_reading: the very thing in us that thinks, reasons and keeps law

notes.note: πνευματικόν is “what is of breath or wind”. “From some source” is oddly vague beside “from some source of its own” in the following phrase, and the words have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what stands.
notes.other_reading: the airy part from some spring

notes.note: ἥκω is a present with perfect sense: “has come, is here”.
notes.other_reading: comes from somewhere

check.greek: καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ νοερὸν καὶ λογικὸν καὶ νομικὸν ἡμῖν
check.note: The Greek has “to us” once, and the English gave it twice (“in us” and “to us”).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “that our very mind and reason and sense of law come”. “Our” gives the one Greek “to us” once.

check.note: The three words are adjectives used as nouns: the thinking, the reasoning and the law-observing element in us. Law itself was an earlier step of the chain; here it is the capacity for law.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “sense of law”. The word names what in us has to do with law, not law itself.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κόσμος as “the world”, where this translation uses “the universe” unless the inhabited earth is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the universe is, as it were, a city”. The whole ordered sum of things is meant, since mind, earth, water, breath and fire are all drawn from it.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave λογικοί as “reasoning beings”, where this translation uses “rational”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by which we are rational”. A note says that the Greek word is made from the word for “reason”.

passages.casaubon: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath proceeded.
passages.russian: Если ум у нас общий, то и разум, благодаря которому мы разумны, общий. Если так, то общий и разум, повелевающий, что делать и чего не делать. Если так, то и закон общий. Если так, мы граждане. Если так, мы участвуем в некоем гражданском сообществе. Если так, мироздание — как бы город. Ведь о каком ещё общем гражданском сообществе можно сказать, что в нём участвует весь род человеческий? И именно оттуда, из этого общего города, приходят и сам наш ум, и разум, и чувство закона; или откуда же ещё? Ведь как земляное во мне отделено от какой-то земли, влажное — от другой стихии, дыхание — из некоего источника, а тёплое и огненное — из своего собственного источника (ведь ничто не возникает из ничего, как и ничто не уходит в несуществующее), так и ум откуда-то пришёл.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ αὐτὸς σὺ πολιτικοῦ συστήματος συμπληρωτικὸς εἶ, οὕτως καὶ πᾶσα πρᾶξίς σου συμπληρωτικὴ ἔστω ζωῆς πολιτικῆς. ἥτις ἐὰν οὖν πρᾶξίς σου μὴ ἔχῃ τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἴτε προσεχῶς εἴτε πόρρωθεν, ἐπὶ τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος, αὕτη διασπᾷ τὸν βίον καὶ οὐκ ἐᾷ ἕνα εἶναι καὶ στασιώδης ἐστίν, ὥσπερ ἐν δήμῳ ὁ τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸν μέρος διιστάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης συμφωνίας.
passages.english: Just as you yourself help to complete a civic whole, so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life. So any action of yours that does not look, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one, and it is seditious, like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony.

notes.note: πολιτικός is “of citizens, of the city”; “civic” is used for both occurrences. σύστημα is an organised whole made of members, a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον).
notes.other_reading: a civic system

notes.note: An adjective: “such as to fill up together”, said of a member without which the whole is not complete. “Help to complete” gives the “together” of the Greek prefix; the Greek has no noun such as “part” here.
notes.other_reading: you yourself go to make up a civic whole

notes.note: Two words for life in this passage: ζωή here (being alive, life as lived) and βίος in the next sentence (a life as a course or career). English has one word for both.
notes.other_reading: a life lived as a citizen

notes.note: “Reference”, a carrying-back of the act to what it is for.
notes.other_reading: that is not directed

notes.note: Literally “whether next in line or from afar”: directly or through other steps.
notes.other_reading: whether closely or from far off

notes.note: κοινωνικός, “social”, is the adjective of κοινωνία, community. τέλος is “end” in the sense of what a thing is for; “goal” avoids the other sense of “end”.
notes.other_reading: to the end that is community

notes.note: The Greek has “the life” with no possessive. “Your” is supplied because the action is yours; it could be read more generally.
notes.other_reading: tears life apart

notes.note: The adjective of στάσις, faction or civil strife inside a city: “of the nature of civil strife”.
notes.other_reading: and it is a kind of civil strife

notes.note: δῆμος is the people as a political body; it can also mean the popular assembly or a democracy.
notes.other_reading: in a popular assembly

notes.note: “Their own part” is taken as adverbial (“as far as they are concerned”) and the verb as “stands apart”. It could also be taken as “withdrawing their own share (or party)”. The verb is the one used elsewhere for things that “stand apart”.
notes.other_reading: who pulls their own party away from such harmony

notes.note: Literally “sounding together”, a musical word also used for agreement.
notes.other_reading: agreement

check.note: The Greek is one adjective, “completing, going to make up”. “A part” is not in the Greek, and “part” is a marked word in these passages that occurs in this very sentence in another sense; “helps to” also softens it. The same holds for the second occurrence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “you yourself help to complete a civic whole” and “help to complete a civic life”. “A part” is removed, since the Greek has no such noun; “help to” is kept because the Greek prefix says that the completing is done together with others. The same wording is used in 11.8a.

check.note: “In a people” is not clear English. The word here is the citizen body, the people as a political community or assembly.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “in a citizen body”. The word is the people as a political community.

check.note: “Factious” is rare today and easily misread. The Greek is the adjective of the word for civil strife.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “and it is seditious”. An adjective is kept, and not “a kind of civil strife”, because the Greek goes on to compare the action with a person; the note gives the root sense.

check.note: The word is a sounding together: harmony, concord. “Agreement” flattens the image and can sound like a contract.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “from such harmony”. The Greek word is a musical one, and “agreement” lost the image.

check.note: Taken adverbially (“as far as he is concerned”), which is the likelier reading. It can also be heard as closer to an object (“who sets his own share apart”), and the choice was made without sign.
check.decided: Declined: “For their own part” stands. It is the likelier reading, as the point itself says, and it keeps the word “part” in view; the other reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: The first word is “immediately, directly” (next in line), set against “at a distance”. “Closely” is not the natural opposite and suggests a degree of attention.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “whether directly or at a distance”. The Greek sets what is next in line against what is far off.

check.note: As in 7.13, “system” sounds technical; the word is a whole made up of members.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a civic whole”, in line with 7.13.

check.note: The Greek has one word for life here and another in the next sentence, and both become “life”. The reader may take them as the same thing.
check.decided: Declined: “A civic life” stands. The Greek repeats one adjective for the whole and for the life, so “civic” is repeated; the suggested wording would still give both Greek words as “life”, and the note records the two words.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κοινωνικός as “communal”, where this translation uses “social”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to the social goal”. The note says that the word is the adjective of the word for community.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “the man … his own part”, where the Greek does not single out a man. It also left out the “too” in “so too”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart” and, in the first sentence, “so too let every action of yours”.

passages.casaubon: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable. What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action; yea it is seditious; as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself.
passages.russian: Как ты сам помогаешь восполнить гражданское целое, так пусть и всякое твоё действие помогает восполнить гражданскую жизнь. Поэтому всякое твоё действие, которое ни прямо, ни издалека не обращено к общественной цели, разрывает твою жизнь и не даёт ей быть единой, и оно мятежно, как тот, кто среди граждан со своей стороны отстраняется от такого согласия.

passages.greek: Ἓν φῶς ἡλίου, κἂν διείργηται τοίχοις, ὄρεσιν, ἄλλοις μυρίοις. μία οὐσία κοινή, κἂν διείργηται ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις. μία ψυχή, κἂν φύσεσι διείργηται μυρίαις καὶ ἰδίαις περιγραφαῖς. μία νοερὰ ψυχή, κἂν διακεκρίσθαι δοκῇ. τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων, οἷον πνεύματα καὶ ὑποκείμενα, ἀναίσθητα καὶ ἀνοικείωτα ἀλλήλοις· καίτοι κἀκεῖνα τὸ ἑνοῦν συνέχει καὶ τὸ ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτὰ βρῖθον. διάνοια δὲ ἰδίως ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμόφυλον τείνεται καὶ συνίσταται καὶ οὐ διείργεται τὸ κοινωνικὸν πάθος.
passages.english: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains, by countless other things. One common substance, even if it is divided by countless bodies, each with its own quality. One soul, even if it is divided by countless natures and individual outlines. One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated. Now the other parts of the things just named, such as breaths and the matter that underlies things, are without sensation and have no attachment to one another; and yet even those are held together by what makes them one and by the weight that bears towards the same place. But thought, in a way of its own, stretches towards what is of the same kind and joins with it, and the social feeling is not divided.

notes.note: The first four sentences have no verb “is”, and are left so. The verb διείργω (“keep apart, bar off”) comes four times in the passage; “divided” is used every time, including the last sentence, where the repetition makes the point.
notes.other_reading: There is one light of the sun, even if it is shut off by walls

notes.note: ἰδίως ποιόν is a Stoic term for an individual thing marked off by a quality that is its own. The dative is read as in the first sentence, “by”: the one thing is divided by the many. It could also be heard as “among”.
notes.other_reading: even if it is shared out among countless individually qualified bodies

notes.note: περιγραφή is a line drawn around something: an outline or limit. ἰδίαις is “own, individual”; “countless” may cover the outlines as well as the natures.
notes.other_reading: by countless natures and their own boundaries

notes.note: νοερά is “of mind, able to think”; “that has mind” keeps “mind” for this word, as in the other passages. διάνοια in the last sentence is a different word and is given as “thought”.
notes.other_reading: One thinking soul

notes.note: A different verb from “divided”: “to be separated out, distinguished”. The change is marked with “separated”.
notes.other_reading: even if it seems to have been split up

notes.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων
notes.note: “The other parts of the things said” is loose in the Greek too. It is taken as the portions of the things just listed other than the soul that has mind. It could also mean the remaining constituents of the bodies and natures just mentioned.
notes.other_reading: the remaining parts of the wholes just mentioned

notes.note: πνεῦμα is breath or wind, and in Stoic physics the breath that holds a body together; ὑποκείμενα are “things that underlie”, the material a thing is made of. Both are kept literal, and the plural “breaths” is kept because separate portions are meant.
notes.other_reading: such as currents of air and material things

notes.note: “Without perception or feeling.” “Sensation” is used so that “feeling” can be kept for a different word in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: without feeling

notes.note: A negative made from the Stoic word for treating something as one’s own (οἰκείωσις): “not made one another’s own, with no sense of belonging to one another”.
notes.other_reading: and have no kinship with one another

notes.note: “That which makes one”, from the word “one” that opens each of the first four sentences. This is a correction, and the manuscripts have τὸ νοοῦν, “that which thinks” (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text given.
notes.other_reading: by what thinks

notes.note: Literally “that which weighs down towards the same things”: a pull like weight towards a common point.
notes.other_reading: and by what presses towards the same things

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought, understanding, mind”. ἰδίως, “in a way peculiar to itself”, picks up the words given above as “its own quality” and “individual outlines”, used there of what divides.
notes.other_reading: But mind, in a special way,

notes.note: “Combines, joins, holds together” with its own kind; the parts of the word are “stand” and “together”.
notes.other_reading: and stands together with it

notes.note: “The social feeling” is taken as the subject. It could instead be an accusative of respect, with thought still the subject. πάθος is something undergone, a feeling; κοινωνικόν, “social”, is the adjective of the word for community.
notes.other_reading: and is not divided in its social feeling

check.greek: κἂν διείργηται ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις
check.note: The datives in the second and third sentences are the same construction as “by walls, by mountains” in the first, yet the English switches from “by” to “among”. The Greek picture is the same each time: the one thing is shut off by the many.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “divided by countless bodies” and “divided by countless natures”. The construction is the same as with the walls and mountains, so the same “by” is used; “among” made the one thing something shared out.

check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by countless natures and individual outlines”. The Greek does not tie the outlines to the natures; “individual” is used because the Greek word is “own, individual”.

check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “without sensation”. “Feeling” is not used because it is kept for a different Greek word in the last sentence.

check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “have no attachment to one another”. The word says that they do not treat one another as their own, not that they differ in kind.

check.note: The verb is to combine, to cohere, to join with. “Stands together” copies the parts of the Greek word and not its meaning.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “joins with it”.

check.decided: Partly accepted: The chain word is changed throughout, but to “divided”, so that the last clause reads “and the social feeling is not divided” and plainly answers the walls and mountains. “Shut off” is not used because the Greek verb is “keep apart”, and a substance “shut off by countless bodies” gives the wrong picture.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave νοερά as “thinking” and διάνοια as “mind”, where this translation uses “mind” for the first word and “thought” for the second.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “One soul that has mind” and “But thought, in a way of its own”. The two Greek words stay two English words.

check.note: Found while settling: with “divided” now used for the repeated verb, this different verb needs a different English word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “even if it seems to be separated”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft gave κοινωνικόν as “of community”, where this translation uses “social”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the social feeling”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek word is “that which makes one”, built on the “one” that opens each of the first four sentences. “What unites them” lost that echo.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “held together by what makes them one”.

check.note: Found while settling: “in a way of its own … of its own kind” gave two “own” words in a row where the Greek has two different words.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “stretches toward what is of the same kind”. The Greek word is “of the same stock”.

passages.casaubon: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects. There is but one common substance of the whole world, though it be concluded and restrained into several different bodies, in number infinite. There is but one common soul, though divided into innumerable particular essences and natures. So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided. And as for all other parts of those generals which we have mentioned, as either sensitive souls or subjects, these of themselves (as naturally irrational) have no common mutual reference one unto another, though many of them contain a mind, or reasonable faculty in them, whereby they are ruled and governed. But of every reasonable mind, this the particular nature, that it hath reference to whatsoever is of her own kind, and desireth to be united: neither can this common affection, or mutual unity and correspondency, be here intercepted or divided, or confined to particulars as those other common things are.
passages.russian: Один свет солнца, хотя он и разделён стенами, горами, бесчисленным другим. Одна общая сущность, хотя она и разделена бесчисленными телами, каждое со своим качеством. Одна душа, хотя она и разделена бесчисленными природами и отдельными очертаниями. Одна душа, обладающая умом, хотя и кажется, что она разъединена. Прочие же части названного, такие как дыхания и лежащая в основе вещей материя, лишены ощущения и не привязаны друг к другу; и всё же даже их держит вместе то, что делает их единым, и тяжесть, влекущая к одному месту. А мысль на свой лад тянется к однородному и соединяется с ним, и общественное чувство не разделяется.

passages.greek: ʽὯι μὴ εἶς καὶ ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν ἀεὶ τοῦ βίου σκοπός, οὗτος εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς δι’ ὅλου τοῦ βίου εἶναι οὐ δύναται.ʼ οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τὸ εἰρημένον, ἐὰν μὴ κἀκεῖνο προσθῇς, ὁποῖον εἶναι δεῖ τοῦτον τὸν σκοπόν. ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐχ ἡ πάντων τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν ὑπόληψις ὁμοία ἐστίν, ἀλλ’ ἡ τῶν τοιῶνδέ τινων, τουτέστι τῶν κοινῶν, οὕτω καὶ τὸν σκοπὸν δεῖ τὸν κοινωνικὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν ὑποστήσασθαι. ὁ γὰρ εἰς τοῦτον πάσας τὰς ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ἀπευθύνων πάσας τὰς πράξεις ὁμοίας ἀποδώσει καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἔσται.
passages.english: “A person who does not always have one and the same aim in life cannot be one and the same through the whole of life.” The saying is not enough unless you also add what kind of aim this must be. For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind, that is, the common goods, so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one. For whoever directs all their private impulses towards this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same.

notes.note: The edition marks the first sentence as a quotation; the source is not named. The Greek has simply “he for whom” and “this one”, and “a person” is supplied. “One and the same” is said first of the aim and then of the person, and the same English is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: that man cannot be one and the same through his whole life

notes.note: σκοπός is the mark an archer aims at. “Aim” is used for it throughout.
notes.other_reading: target in life

notes.note: Literally “what has been said”.
notes.other_reading: What has been said is not enough

notes.greek: τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν
notes.note: ὁπωσοῦν (“in whatever way”) is taken with “seem good”. οἱ πλείονες is “the majority, most people”.
notes.other_reading: all the things most people somehow or other think good

notes.note: ὑπόληψις is a judgment taken up about something. “Alike” is understood as the same from one person to the next, and is kept for the same adjective in the last sentence. The Greek does not repeat “is alike” after “but”; it is repeated for clarity.
notes.other_reading: people do not judge alike about all the things

notes.note: “The common ones”: goods that are shared, or that concern everyone; the Greek does not say which more exactly. “Goods” is supplied from the clause before, so that “common” is not heard as “ordinary”.
notes.other_reading: that is, the shared ones

notes.note: Two adjectives, “social” and “of citizens (of the city)”. In Greek the first is made from the word “common” just used, a link that “social” does not show; “social” is kept because it is the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation.
notes.other_reading: the communal and civic one

notes.note: “To set under oneself”: to lay down as a basis.
notes.other_reading: must be laid down as one’s foundation

notes.note: ἴδιος is “one’s own”, and also “private” as against “common” above; “private” is used so that the contrast can be heard. ὁρμή is the Stoic “impulse”, the movement towards an action.
notes.other_reading: all their own impulses

notes.note: “In accordance with this”: either “in this way, by this means” or “in this respect”. The first is taken, as the result of aiming everything at one mark.
notes.other_reading: and in this respect will always be the same

check.note: The phrase can be “in this respect” or “by this, in this way”. “In this respect” reads as a limit, whereas the argument wants a result, and the choice was made without sign.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and in this way will always be the same”. The phrase allows either, and the sentence states what follows from aiming everything at one mark; the note gives “in this respect”.

check.note: “The opinion held is not alike about” is accurate in its parts but hard to follow. The Greek says that people’s judgment is not the same about all such things, only about some.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind”. The noun “judgment” is kept, since it is the set word for ὑπόληψις in this translation, and “people” and “only” are not added because the Greek does not have them.

check.note: “Common” alone can be read as “ordinary”. The word is the root of the word for “communal” just after and means the goods that are shared.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “that is, the common goods”. The noun is supplied from the clause before so that “common” cannot be heard as “ordinary”; “common” itself is kept because it is the word used for κοινός in the other passages.

check.note: The word is set against “common” and “communal”: private, individual impulses directed at the common aim. “His own” reads as a mere possessive and the contrast is lost.
