check.decided: Accepted: “practical” is removed and the English reads “except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter”. The note records that the word can also mean a larger ordering of things.

check.greek: πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν
check.note: The Greek as given does not construe cleanly: the adverb is attached to the command and the last word hangs loose. The English smooths this, and the sentence should carry a mark of doubt.
check.decided: Accepted: the adverb is no longer turned into a description of the topic, and the English reads “For leave aside now, out of season, the gift of nature, which from here on belongs to some other discussion”, close to the words as they stand. The note says that the Greek does not construe cleanly and that the text is doubted.

check.note: The words can also mean “hanging on someone else’s word”, which would tie the sentence to praise. The English has chosen “another discussion” without a sign.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “belongs to some other discussion”, the ordinary sense of the Greek phrase, and a new note records the second reading, “hangs on someone else’s word”.

check.note: The Greek adjective is also “fine” or “noble”. “Beautiful” suits the emerald and the flower but narrows the word where the examples are law, truth, goodwill and shame.
check.decided: Accepted: “beautiful” is kept throughout so that one English word serves the one Greek word, and the note on the first words of the chapter says that it is a choice and gives “fine”.

check.note: The Greek “for” is dropped: the question about the emerald is offered as the ground for the one before it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For does a little emerald become worse than itself”, which restores the Greek “for”.

passages.casaubon: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?
passages.russian:
Тот, кого волнует посмертная слава, не представляет себе, что каждый из тех, кто его помнит, и сам очень скоро умрёт; затем, в свою очередь, и тот, кто примет память от него, пока не угаснет и вся память, переходя через тех, кто зажигается и гаснет. Но допусти даже, что помнящие бессмертны и память бессмертна, — что тогда тебе до этого? И я уж не говорю, что для мёртвого это ничто; но для живого — что такое похвала, разве что ради устройства какого-то дела? Оставь же теперь, не ко времени, дар природы: отныне это дело какого-то другого рассуждения.

Всё, что хоть как-то прекрасно, прекрасно само по себе и завершается в себе, и похвала не составляет его части. Во всяком случае, то, что хвалят, не становится от этого ни хуже, ни лучше. Я говорю это и о том, что называют прекрасным в более обыденном смысле, например о вещественном и о сделанном искусством (а истинно прекрасное — в чём оно нуждается? Не больше, чем закон, не больше, чем истина, не больше, чем доброжелательность или чувство стыда). Что из этого прекрасно оттого, что его хвалят, или портится, когда его порицают? Разве изумрудик становится хуже, чем был, если его не хвалят? А что сказать о золоте, слоновой кости, пурпуре, лире, ножичке, цветочке, деревце?

passages.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ὃ ποιοῦσι. τοὺς μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ χρόνου καὶ μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν ζῶντας ἀνθρώπους εὐφημεῖν οὐ θέλουσιν, αὐτοὶ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν μεταγενεστέρων εὐφημηθῆναι, οὓς οὔτε εἶδόν ποτε οὔτε ὄψονται, περὶ πολλοῦ ποιοῦνται. τοῦτο δὲ ἐγγύς ἐστι τῷ λυπηθῆναι ἄν, ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ λόγους εὐφήμους ἐποιοῦντο.
passages.english: What a thing they do. They are unwilling to speak well of the people who live at the same time as them and alongside them, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see. This is almost as if you were pained that those who came before did not also speak well of you.

notes.note: Literally “what sort of thing it is that they do”, an exclamation of surprise. “They” are not named.
notes.other_reading: How strange is what they do.

notes.note: The same word comes three times, as a verb active and passive and then in the phrase “well-speaking words”. “Speak well of” is kept each time.
notes.other_reading: to praise

notes.note: Literally “with themselves”: in their own company.
notes.other_reading: and in their own company

notes.note: The particle makes the infinitive hypothetical: it is close to how it would be if one were pained. The Greek does not say who is pained; the English says “you”, since the one pained is the “you” spoken of in the same clause.
notes.other_reading: This is close to being pained

notes.greek: οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ
notes.note: The passage turns to “you” here, after “they” throughout. The Greek “also” goes with those who came before: they as well as those who come after.
notes.other_reading: that the earlier generations as well did not speak well of you

check.note: The English idiom is “set great store by”, not “on”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “set great store by”, which is the English idiom.

check.note: The Greek particle makes the case a supposed one: it is like what it would be to grieve. The English states it flatly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This is close to what it would be to be pained that”. The Greek particle makes the case a supposed one.

check.note: The Greek “also” belongs with “those who came before”: they as well as those who come after. “Of you too” reads as “you as well as someone else”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “did not also speak well of you”, with “also” moved so that it goes with those who came before. The suggested “either” is not taken, because it would say that those who come after do not speak well of you, which the Greek does not say.

passages.casaubon: Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived before him.
passages.russian: Что же они делают! Они не хотят хвалить тех, кто живёт в одно время с ними и рядом с ними, а сами придают большое значение тому, чтобы их хвалили потомки, которых они никогда не видели и не увидят. Это почти как если бы ты огорчался, что и предшественники не хвалили тебя.

passages.greek:
Ὁ μὲν μὴ εἰδὼς ὅ τι ἐστὶ κόσμος, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅπου ἐστίν. ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅστις ἐστὶν οὐδὲ τί ἐστι κόσμος. ὁ δὲ ἕν τι τούτων ἀπολιπὼν οὐδὲ πρὸς ὅ τι αὐτὸς πέφυκεν εἴποι. τίς οὖν φαίνεταί σοι ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων, οἳ οὔθ’ ὅπου εἰσὶν οὔτε οἵτινές εἰσι γινώσκουσιν;

Ἐπαινεῖσθαι θέλεις ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου τρὶς τῆς ὥρας ἑαυτῷ καταρωμένου; ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ ὁ μετανοῶν ἐφ’ ἅπασι σχεδὸν οἷς πράσσει;
passages.english:
Whoever does not know what the universe is does not know where they are. Whoever does not know what it is by nature for does not know who they are, nor what the universe is. And whoever is missing any one of these could not even say what they themselves are by nature for. What, then, does a person seem to you to be who runs from or chases the praise of those who clap, people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves? Is a person pleased with themselves who regrets nearly everything they do?

notes.note: The noun has no article here or below: “what a universe is”. The word also means order. The English keeps the glossary’s “the universe”.
notes.other_reading: what a universe is

notes.greek: ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν
notes.note: The subject of the last verb is not stated. It can be the universe just named or the person. The English takes the universe, because the next sentence adds an emphatic “they themselves” to the same verb, which reads as a contrast with a different subject here.
notes.other_reading: Whoever does not know what they are by nature for

notes.note: Literally “has grown” or “is by nature”, with a preposition of aim: what a thing’s nature fits it for. No maker is named.
notes.other_reading: what it has come to be for

notes.note: The participle can mean having left out, or falling short in. “These” are the points of knowledge just listed.
notes.other_reading: whoever has left out any one of these

notes.note: An optative with no particle, where “could say” would normally have one. The English reads it as “could say”.
notes.other_reading: may they not even say what they themselves are by nature for

notes.greek: ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων
notes.note: Literally “the one fleeing or pursuing the praise of the clappers”. The verb for clapping is used of applause and of any rattling noise. Running from praise is odd beside chasing it, but that is what the Greek as given says; from memory, unchecked: the words have been suspected, with blame as the thing fled.
notes.other_reading: who runs from the blame of those who clap, or chases their praise

notes.note: Literally “three times in the hour”. The noun can also mean a season or a moment.
notes.other_reading: three times every hour

notes.greek: ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ
notes.note: One verb, “please”, three times: please a person who does not please themselves. English “please oneself” means to do as one likes, so the English reads “is pleased with themselves” and keeps the root.
notes.other_reading: Do you want to please a person who does not satisfy themselves?

notes.note: To change one’s mind afterwards, to regret.
notes.other_reading: who repents of nearly everything they do

check.greek: ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν
check.note: The verb has no stated subject and can be the universe just named; the emphatic “they themselves” in the next sentence supports that. The English takes the person without a sign, and “made” brings in a maker the Greek does not name.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whoever does not know what it is by nature for”, with the universe as subject, and “made” is gone from both sentences. The emphatic “they themselves” in the next sentence reads as a contrast with a different subject here; the note gives the reading with the person.

check.note: “Left out” sounds like an item omitted from a list. The sense is of someone who falls short in, or lacks, one of these pieces of knowledge.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whoever is missing any one of these”, since what is meant is a piece of knowledge the person lacks, not an item dropped from a list.

check.note: The Greek as given has the optative without the particle that “could” needs. The English reads “could”, which the sense requires; no change is asked for.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, “could not even say”, and the note on the verb records that the Greek as given lacks the particle that “could” would normally have.

check.note: The English follows the Greek as given. Running from praise is odd beside chasing it, and from memory the words have been suspected; the doubt should be noted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged and follows the Greek as given. The note now records the doubt about the words, marked as from memory and unchecked.

passages.casaubon: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world. Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything that he doth?
passages.russian:
Кто не знает, что такое мироздание, тот не знает, где он. Кто не знает, для чего оно по природе, тот не знает ни кто он, ни что такое мироздание. А кому недостаёт хоть чего-то одного из этого, тот не мог бы даже сказать, для чего по природе он сам. Каким же тебе кажется человек, который бежит от похвалы хлопающих или гонится за ней, — людей, которые не знают ни где они, ни кто они?

Хочешь ли ты, чтобы тебя хвалил человек, который трижды в час проклинает себя? Хочешь ли нравиться человеку, который сам себе не нравится? Нравится ли сам себе тот, кто раскаивается почти во всём, что делает?

passages.greek: Οἷοί εἰσιν ἐσθίοντες, καθεύδοντες, ὀχεύοντες, ἀποπατοῦντες, τὰ ἄλλα· εἶτα οἷοι ἀνδρονομούμενοι καὶ γαυρούμενοι ἢ χαλεπαίνοντες καὶ ἐξ ὑπεροχῆς ἐπιπλήττοντες, πρὸ ὀλίγου δὲ ἐδούλευον πόσοις καὶ δι’ οἷα· καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον ἐν τοιούτοις ἔσονται.
passages.english: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest. Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.

notes.note: A word used of male animals covering females. Applied to people it is blunt.
notes.other_reading: coupling

notes.note: Literally “stepping aside”, the ordinary word for relieving the bowels.
notes.other_reading: relieving themselves

notes.note: A very rare word of uncertain sense, built from “man” and a root for managing or ruling, and middle or passive in form. “Lording it” is a guess from its parts and from the context of pride, and should not be read as certain. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the word and have proposed others.
notes.other_reading: when playing the man

notes.note: To prance or plume oneself, used of a proud horse.
notes.other_reading: and strutting

notes.note: Literally “rebuking from superiority”: from a higher position.
notes.other_reading: and scolding from above

notes.note: The verb is to be a slave. It is probably meant of serving and courting others, not of legal slavery, but the image is kept. “To how many, and for what” is an exclamation inside the sentence.
notes.other_reading: they were dancing attendance on how many, and for what ends

notes.note: Literally “they will be in such things”. The English takes it as pointing back to the slavery just mentioned; it can also point to the bodily state of the opening, or forward to death.
notes.other_reading: they will be in such a state

check.note: The word is known from nowhere else and the Greek is suspect. “Lording it over people” is a guess from its parts that does not explain the middle or passive form, and should not read as certain.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “lording it”, without “over people”, since the form is middle or passive and an object is not supported. The rendering stays a guess from the word’s parts, and the note marks the word as doubtful.

check.note: The Greek is plural, “in such things”, and can point back to the slavery or forward to death. “Such a state” gives the reader nothing to attach it to.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they will be in the same sort of case”, pointing back to the slavery just mentioned. The suggested “again” is not added, because the Greek does not have it; the note keeps the other readings.

check.note: “From on high” suggests heaven. The Greek is from a position of superiority.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “scolding from a position of superiority”, which is what the Greek says and does not suggest heaven.

passages.casaubon: Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives: as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust. Again, when they either are in their greatest exultation; and in the middle of all their pomp and glory; or being angry and displeased, in great state and majesty, as from an higher place, they chide and rebuke. How base and slavish, but a little while ago, they were fain to be, that they might come to this; and within a very little while what will be their estate, when death hath once seized upon them.
passages.russian: Каковы они, когда едят, спят, совокупляются, испражняются и прочее. Затем каковы они, когда властвуют и важничают или гневаются и бранятся свысока. А ведь совсем недавно они были рабами — скольких и ради каких вещей. И вскоре они окажутся в таком же положении.

passages.greek: Πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα πῶς ἑαυτὸν μὲν ἕκαστος μᾶλλον πάντων φιλεῖ, τὴν δὲ ἑαυτοῦ περὶ αὑτοῦ ὑπόληψιν ἐν ἐλάττονι λόγῳ τίθεται ἢ τὴν τῶν ἄλλων. ἐὰν γοῦν τινα θεὸς ἐπιστὰς ἢ διδάσκαλος ἔμφρων κελεύσῃ μηδὲν καθ’ ἑαυτὸν ἐνθυμεῖσθαι καὶ διανοεῖσθαι ὃ μὴ ἄμα καὶ γεγωνίσκων ἐξοίσει, οὐδὲ πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν τοῦτο ὑπομενεῖ. οὕτως τοὺς πέλας μᾶλλον αἰδούμεθα, τί ποτε περὶ ἡμῶν φρονήσουσιν, ἢ ἑαυτούς.
passages.english: I have often wondered how it is that each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others. At any rate, if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them to turn over nothing in their mind and think nothing to themselves that they will not at the same moment bring out, crying it aloud, they will not put up with this for even one day. So it is that we feel more shame before those near us, at what they will think of us, than before ourselves.

notes.note: Literally “more than all”, which can be all people or all things. The English takes people, since the sentence goes on to set each person against “the others”.
notes.other_reading: more than everything

notes.note: The judgment or opinion one holds; “judgment” follows the glossary.
notes.other_reading: their own opinion of themselves

notes.note: An idiom: to put in a lesser account. λόγος here is “account” or “reckoning”, not reason.
notes.other_reading: holds in less account

notes.note: The participle is used of a god or a dream figure appearing and standing by a person.
notes.other_reading: if a god stood over someone

notes.note: Two verbs for inward thinking, the second from the word the glossary gives as “thought”. “By oneself” means privately, inside.
notes.other_reading: to have no idea and no thought in private

notes.note: Literally “will bring out, shouting it”: the verb is to cry out so as to be heard.
notes.other_reading: that they will not at once shout out loud

notes.note: To feel shame before someone, to stand in awe of them or respect them.
notes.other_reading: So much more do we respect our neighbours

notes.note: Literally “those nearby”, the usual phrase for other people.
notes.other_reading: our neighbours

check.note: The Greek “all” can be “all people” or “all things”. The English has chosen people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “more than everyone else”, since the sentence goes on to set each person against “the others”, and the note records “more than everything”.

check.note: The participle is of someone appearing at one’s side; “stood over” adds menace. The English tenses also clash, where the Greek is a plain condition about the future.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them”. The participle is of one who comes and stands by, without menace, and the present tenses now fit the Greek condition about the future.

check.note: The verb is to cry out so as to be heard, to proclaim. “Saying it aloud” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “crying it aloud”. The Greek verb is to cry out so as to be heard, which “saying” was too weak for.

check.note: As in 8.44, ὑπόληψις is an opinion, and “judgment” runs into “judges” in 9.18. “Their own opinion about themselves” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: ὑπόληψις is the school’s word for the view a mind takes up of a thing, and the glossary settles it as “judgment” so that it stays one English word across the book. The “judges” of 9.18 stand in another passage, and the note here gives “opinion”.

passages.casaubon: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own. For if any God or grave master standing by, should command any of us to think nothing by himself but what he should presently speak out; no man were able to endure it, though but for one day. Thus do we fear more what our neighbours will think of us, than what we ourselves.
passages.russian: Я часто удивлялся, как это каждый любит себя больше всех остальных, но ценит собственное суждение о себе меньше, чем суждение других. Во всяком случае, если рядом с кем-нибудь появится бог или благоразумный учитель и велит ему ничего не перебирать в уме и ничего не думать про себя такого, чего он тут же не вынес бы наружу, выкрикивая вслух, — он не выдержит этого и одного дня. Вот так мы больше стыдимся ближних — того, что они о нас подумают, — чем самих себя.

passages.greek: Τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν διάβλεπε καὶ τοὺς φρονίμους, οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν.
passages.english: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.

notes.note: “Their”: the people are not named, and the line has no context. It is presumably people in general.
notes.other_reading: Look closely into people’s ruling parts

notes.note: To look straight at or see through. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, its object, is “the ruling part”.
notes.other_reading: See right through

notes.note: “The wise” stands in the same case as “ruling parts”, a second thing to look at, and its point is open. It can mean “even the wise”, with contempt, or “and look at the wise” as the contrast and model; “as well” leaves both possible. From memory, unchecked: the words have been doubted.
notes.other_reading: and even at the wise

notes.greek: οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν
notes.note: The subject can be the wise alone or everyone whose ruling part is being looked at. The verbs are “flee” and “pursue”, the same pair as in 8.52.
notes.other_reading: what sort of things they avoid and what sort they pursue

check.note: The small word can be “even”: look into their ruling minds, even those of the sensible among them, one group and not two. The English makes the wise a second group and leaves “they” unclear; from memory the words have been doubted.
check.decided: Declined: the Greek sets “the wise” in the same case as “ruling parts”, as a second thing to look at, where “those of the wise” would need another case. “And at the wise as well” keeps that and leaves open, as the Greek does, whether they are a further target or a model; the note gives “even the wise” and records the doubt about the words.

passages.casaubon: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
passages.russian: Вглядись в их ведущие начала, и в мудрых тоже: от чего они бегут и за чем гонятся.

passages.greek: Δίελθε ἔσω ἔσω εἰς τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν καὶ ὄψει τίνας κριτὰς φοβῇ, οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς.
passages.english: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.

notes.note: “Inside” is written twice. The English takes the doubling as emphasis; it could also be a copying slip for a single word.
notes.other_reading: Pass inside

notes.note: “What judges”, with the sense of what kind. The verb is present: you fear them now.
notes.other_reading: what kind of judges you fear

notes.greek: οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς
notes.note: Literally “being what sort of judges about themselves too”. The pronoun as printed is reflexive. The small word given as “as well” can also be “even”.
notes.other_reading: and what poor judges they are even of themselves

check.note: The meaning is right and the doubled word is kept, but “go through” followed by “to” is clumsy and hides the plain sense of passing inside.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts”. The clumsy “go through” is gone, but “pass” keeps the verb’s sense of going through, and “inside” is still said twice, as in the Greek, which the suggested “deep inside” would not do.

passages.casaubon: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.
passages.russian: Войди внутрь, в самую глубь, в их ведущие начала, и ты увидишь, каких судей ты боишься и какие они судьи самим себе.

passages.greek: Ἀλλήλων καταφρονοῦντες ἀλλήλοις ἀρεσκεύονται καὶ ἀλλήλων ὑπερέχειν θέλοντες ἀλλήλοις ὑποκατακλίνονται.
passages.english: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.

notes.note: From the word for an over-eager pleaser: to play up to someone, to fawn. It has the same root as “please” in 6.59 and 8.53 but is a harsher verb.
notes.other_reading: they try to please one another

notes.note: Literally “to hold oneself over”, to be superior. The spatial sense is kept because the next verb answers it with “under”.
notes.other_reading: wanting to outdo one another

notes.note: Literally “to lie down beneath”, used of taking the lower place on a dining couch and so of giving way to someone.
notes.other_reading: they give way to one another

check.note: This is the verb of the fawner, harsher than the plain “please” of 6.59 and 8.53. “Try” is added and the contempt is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they fawn on one another”. It is the verb of the over-eager pleaser, a different and harsher word than “please”, and “try” was not in the Greek.

check.note: The Greek has a picture: lying down in the lower place, giving way. The English keeps the above and beneath but not the gesture.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they take the lower place beneath one another”, which gives the picture of the lower place at table. The suggested “bow down” is not taken: it is a different gesture, and it loses the “above” and “beneath” that the two Greek verbs set against each other.

passages.casaubon: They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another: and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better part one to another.
passages.russian: Презирая друг друга, они друг перед другом заискивают; и, желая быть выше друг друга, становятся ниже друг друга.

passages.greek: Ὁ μὲν φιλόδοξος ἀλλοτρίαν ἐνέργειαν ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ὑπολαμβάνει, ὁ δὲ φιλήδονος ἰδίαν πεῖσιν, ὁ δὲ νοῦν ἔχων ἰδίαν πρᾶξιν.
passages.english: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.

notes.note: Literally a lover of δόξα, which is reputation and also other people’s opinion.
notes.other_reading: The lover of reputation

notes.note: The line turns on “another’s” against “one’s own”, the second word coming three times. Another’s activity is the praising that other people do. The Greek names the activity first; the English puts “their own good” first so that “their” is clearly the lover of fame.
notes.other_reading: takes another person’s activity to be their own good

notes.note: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: judges

notes.note: Literally “their own being acted on”: what is passively felt, set against activity and action.
notes.other_reading: what they themselves undergo

notes.note: The everyday idiom for being sensible, literally “having mind”. The glossary gives “mind” for the noun; the English reads “sense” because the idiom is the point.
notes.other_reading: the person who has mind

notes.note: A different noun from the “activity” of the first clause: a deed, something one does.
notes.other_reading: what they themselves do

check.note: After “another person’s”, “their own good” can be read as that other person’s good. The Greek is the fame-lover’s own good.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “takes their own good to be another person’s activity”, with “their own good” set next to the lover of fame so that it cannot be read as the other person’s good.

check.note: The sentence turns on “own” three times against “another’s”. The English breaks the middle one into a clause; “their own experience” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “own” now comes three times, as in the Greek, and the English reads “their own feeling”. “Feeling” stands in place of the suggested “experience” because the Greek noun is what is passively felt, and “experience” in English also covers what a person does.

passages.casaubon: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.
passages.russian: Любитель славы считает своим благом чужую деятельность; любитель наслаждений — собственное чувство; человек здравомыслящий — собственное действие.

passages.greek: Ἀράχνιον μυῖαν θηρᾶσαν μέγα φρονεῖ, ἄλλος δὲ λαγίδιον, ἄλλος δὲ ὑποχῇ ἀφύην, ἄλλος δὲ συίδια, ἄλλος δὲ ἄρκτους, ἄλλος Σαρμάτας. οὗτοι γὰρ οὐ λῃσταί, ἐὰν τὰ δόγματα ἐξετάζῃς;
passages.english: A little spider thinks a great deal of itself for having hunted down a fly; someone else for a little hare, another for a sprat in a hand net, another for little boars, another for bears, another for Sarmatians. For are these not robbers, if you examine their principles?

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for spider; the same form can also mean a spider’s web.
notes.other_reading: A spider

notes.note: Literally “thinks big”: is proud.
notes.other_reading: is proud

notes.note: “Another” is masculine, so a person and not another spider, which is why the English reads “someone else” the first time. The participle “having hunted” is carried over from the first clause. The hare is a diminutive.
notes.other_reading: another man when he has caught a leveret

notes.note: The first word is a kind of fishing net held under the catch; the second is small fry, a named tiny fish such as a sprat or an anchovy.
notes.other_reading: an anchovy in a scoop net

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for pig or boar. Among things hunted it is presumably wild boar.
notes.other_reading: piglets

notes.note: A people beyond the Danube against whom Marcus himself fought as emperor, so the last hunter is himself.
There is no verb, and the particle “for” opens the question. The noun covers robbers, bandits and pirates.
notes.other_reading: Why, are these not bandits

notes.note: “The principles”, the Stoic word for the settled beliefs a person acts on. The Greek has “the”; the English reads “their”.
notes.other_reading: if you examine the beliefs behind it

check.note: The Greek names a particular tiny fish, small fry such as a sprat or anchovy, as every other item in the list is a named creature. “A small fish” is less.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a sprat in a hand net”. The Greek names a particular tiny fish, as every other item in the list is a named creature.

passages.casaubon: As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud, and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or northern nations lately defeated. For these also, these famous soldiers and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what do they for the most part but hunt after prey?
passages.russian: Паучок много о себе мнит оттого, что изловил муху; другой — зайчонка, другой — кильку в сачок, другой — кабанчиков, другой — медведей, другой — сарматов. А разве это не разбойники, если исследовать их принципы?

passages.greek:
Γενικῶς μὲν ἡ κακία οὐδὲν βλάπτει τὸν κόσμον, ἡ δὲ κατὰ μέρος οὐδὲν βλάπτει τὸν ἕτερον, μόνῳ δὲ βλαβερά ἐστι τούτῳ ᾧ ἐπιτέτραπται καὶ ἀπηλλάχθαι αὐτῆς, ὁπόταν πρῶτον οὕτως θελήσῃ.

Τῷ ἐμῷ προαιρετικῷ τὸ τοῦ πλησίον προαιρετικὸν ἐπίσης ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν, ὡς καὶ τὸ πνευμάτιον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ σαρκίδιον. καὶ γὰρ εἰ ὅτι μάλιστα ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν γεγόναμεν, ὅμως τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ ἡμῶν ἕκαστον τὴν ἰδίαν κυρίαν ἔχει· ἐπεί τοι ἔμελλεν ἡ τοῦ πλησίον κακία ἐμοῦ κακὸν εἶναι, ὅπερ οὐκ ἔδοξε τῷ θεῷ, ἵνα μὴ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ᾖ τὸ ἐμὲ ἀτυχεῖν.
passages.english:
Wickedness in general does no harm to the universe, and wickedness in the particular case does no harm to the other person. It is harmful only to the one who has also been given the power to be rid of it, as soon as they wish to.

To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority. Otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be an evil for me, which god decided against, so that my being unfortunate should not depend on someone else.

notes.note: The adverb means “as a kind” or “taken generally” and is set against κατὰ μέρος, “in the particular case”. The English takes the first as wickedness taken all together and the second as one person’s particular wickedness.
notes.other_reading: Generically, wickedness does no harm to the universe

notes.note: Literally “the other one” of a pair: the person on the receiving end of a particular piece of wickedness. The English keeps it as “the other person”.
notes.other_reading: does no harm to anyone else

notes.note: The verb is “it has been entrusted” or “it has been permitted”, for which the English has the slightly fuller “has been given the power”. καὶ is “also”: the one person wickedness harms is the same person who can also be free of it. The perfect infinitive suggests being rid of it once and for all.
notes.other_reading: to whom it has also been left to be quit of it

notes.note: τὸ προαιρετικόν is the part of a person that chooses, a term at home in Epictetus (from memory, unchecked). The glossary has no entry; “faculty of choice” is used for both occurrences.
notes.other_reading: To my will

notes.note: ἀδιάφορον is the Stoic technical term for what is neither good nor bad. The English reads “a matter of indifference”, which keeps the term without suggesting that the neighbour’s faculty of choice does not care. ἐπίσης with the following ὡς καὶ gives “just as much … as”.
notes.other_reading: is equally a thing neither good nor bad for it

notes.greek: τὸ πνευμάτιον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ σαρκίδιον
notes.note: Both nouns are belittling diminutives of “breath” and “flesh”, kept with “bit of”. The Greek pronoun is masculine singular for the neighbour; the English has “their”.
notes.other_reading: his poor breath and his poor flesh

notes.note: κυρίαν here is a noun, “authority” or “mastery”. The subject is plural (“our ruling parts”) with “each” and a singular verb, rendered “has its own authority”.
notes.other_reading: each is its own master

notes.greek: ἐπεί τοι ἔμελλεν ἡ τοῦ πλησίον κακία ἐμοῦ κακὸν εἶναι
notes.note: ἐπεί τοι is “since otherwise”, and the past tense ἔμελλεν says what would have followed if each ruling part did not have its own authority. κακία (“wickedness”) and κακόν (“an evil”) share one root, an echo the English does not carry because “wickedness” is kept for κακία throughout. ἐμοῦ is literally “of mine”; “for me” takes it as an evil that falls on the speaker, as the closing words suggest.
notes.other_reading: For otherwise my neighbour’s badness would be something bad of mine

notes.note: Literally “which did not seem good to the god”, the ordinary Greek phrase for a decision. The English reads “which god decided against”, since the purpose clause that follows suits a decision that it should not be so. “god” is lower case, as the glossary asks, although the Greek has the article.
notes.other_reading: which was not what god decided

notes.note: Literally “my being unlucky”; the verb ranges from “to meet misfortune” to “to fail” or “to be unhappy”. The English keeps “being unfortunate”. ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ is “in another’s power”, rendered “depend on someone else”.
notes.other_reading: so that my unhappiness should not be in another’s power

check.note: “Indifferent” said of a thing reads today as “uncaring”, so the sentence can be taken to say that the neighbour’s faculty of choice does not care. The Greek says that it is neither good nor bad for one’s own.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is just as much a matter of indifference as”, which cannot be heard as “does not care”. The word “indifference” is kept because ἀδιάφορον is the Stoic term for what is neither good nor bad, and the note explains it.

check.greek: ἡ τοῦ πλησίον κακία ἐμοῦ κακὸν εἶναι
check.note: κακία and κακόν share a root that “wickedness” and “evil” hide. “An evil of mine” can also be heard as a wrong the speaker commits, where the Greek means a bad thing that falls on the speaker.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “would be an evil for me”, so it can no longer be heard as a wrong the speaker commits. “Wickedness” is kept for κακία, as in chapter 55 and in 7.1, and the note says that the two Greek words share one root.

check.note: “Did not see fit” is left hanging in English, since it normally needs “to do something”. The Greek is a plain statement of what god did not decide.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which god decided against”. The Greek phrase is the ordinary one for a decision, and the purpose clause that follows suits a decision that it should not be so.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s note on this clause held only the word “placeholder” in both of its fields.
check.decided: Accepted: the note is now written out. It explains “for otherwise … would be”, the shared root of κακία and κακόν, and the genitive ἐμοῦ behind “for me”.

passages.casaubon: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it. Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will, whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent. For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction. For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy: which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.
passages.russian:
Порочность, взятая в целом, не вредит мирозданию, а порочность в отдельном случае не вредит другому. Она вредна только тому, кому дано и избавиться от неё, как только он захочет.

Для моей способности выбора способность выбора моего ближнего так же безразлична, как его толика дыхания и его толика плоти. Ведь как бы верно ни было, что мы возникли ради друг друга, всё же ведущее начало каждого из нас имеет свою собственную власть. Иначе порочность ближнего была бы для меня злом, а бог решил, что этому не быть, чтобы моё несчастье не зависело от другого.

passages.greek:
Ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει· ὁ ἀδικῶν ἑαυτὸν ἀδικεῖ, ἑαυτὸν, ἑαυτὸν κακὸν ποιῶν.

Ἀδικεῖ πολλάκις ὁ μὴ ποιῶν τι, οὐ μόνον ὁ ποιῶν τι.
passages.english:
Whoever does wrong does wrong at their own cost. Whoever acts unjustly does injustice to themselves, making themselves bad.

Often the one who does not do something acts unjustly, not only the one who does something.

notes.note: The dative can mean “for themselves, to their own cost” or “against themselves”. The English takes the first, the more natural force of a bare dative, which also keeps this clause apart from the next, where the Greek has the accusative and the person is the one wronged.
notes.other_reading: Whoever does wrong does wrong against themselves

notes.note: A different verb from the first clause: ἁμαρτάνω is “do wrong, go wrong”, ἀδικέω is “act unjustly, do injustice to”. The two are kept apart in English, here and in chapter 5.
notes.other_reading: Whoever wrongs another wrongs themselves

notes.note: The Greek as given has ἑαυτὸν twice with a comma between. The first has a grave accent directly before the comma, where this copy otherwise has an acute before a stop, so it is read as an accidental doubling and translated once. From memory, unchecked: editions print the word once here, and some read a verb “makes bad” instead of “making bad”.
notes.other_reading: does injustice to themselves, themselves, by making themselves bad

notes.note: τι can be “something” (a particular thing left undone) or, after the negative, “anything”. The parallel with ὁ ποιῶν τι, “the one who does something”, decides for “something”.
notes.other_reading: the one who does nothing

check.note: The Greek as given has the word for “themselves” twice with a comma between, and the English gives it once. It is either a doubled word in the digitised copy or an emphatic repetition.
check.decided: Declined: the English gives the word once and the note says so. The first ἑαυτὸν has a grave accent directly before a comma, where this copy otherwise has an acute before every stop, which marks it as an accidental doubling and not an emphatic repetition. The printed edition could not be consulted.

check.note: The first clause has the dative (to their own cost) and the second the accusative (the person is the one wronged). “To themselves” for both flattens the step from one to the other.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the first clause now reads “does wrong at their own cost”, so the dative is heard apart from the accusative of the second clause. The second clause keeps “does injustice to themselves”, because ἀδικεῖ repeats ἀδικῶν and returns in chapter 5, and “wrongs” would blur it with “does wrong” for the other verb.

passages.casaubon: He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes unjust.
passages.russian:
Кто поступает дурно, поступает дурно себе же в ущерб. Кто поступает несправедливо, поступает несправедливо с самим собой, делая себя плохим.

Часто несправедливо поступает тот, кто чего-то не делает, а не только тот, кто что-то делает.

passages.greek: Φιλοσόφως ὁ Θεόφραστος ἐν τῇ συγκρίσει τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, ὡς ἄν τις κοινότερον τὰ τοιαῦτα συγκρίνειε, φησὶ βαρύτερα εἶναι τὰ κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν πλημμελούμενα τῶν κατὰ θυμόν. ὁ γὰρ θυμούμενος μετά τινος λύπης καὶ λεληθυίας συστολῆς φαίνεται τὸν λόγον ἀποστρεφόμενος· ὁ δὲ κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν ἁμαρτάνων, ὑφ’ ἡδονῆς ἡττώμενος ἀκολαστότερός πως φαίνεται καὶ θηλύτερος ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις. ὀρθῶς οὖν καὶ φιλοσοφίας ἀξίως ἔφη μείζονος ἐγκλήματος ἔχεσθαι τὸ μεθ’ ἡδονῆς ἁμαρτανόμενον ἤπερ τὸ μετὰ λύπης· ὅλως τε ὁ μὲν προηδικημένῳ μᾶλλον ἔοικε καὶ διὰ λύπης ἠναγκασμένῳ θυμωθῆναι· ὁ δὲ αὐτόθεν πρὸς τὸ ἀδικεῖν ὥρμηται, φερόμενος ἐπὶ τὸ πρᾶξαί τι κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν.
passages.english: Theophrastus speaks as a philosopher when, in his comparison of wrongdoings (as one might compare such things in a more everyday way), he says that offences committed from desire are more serious than those committed from anger. For the one who is angry is seen to turn away from reason with a certain pain and a shrinking inside that goes unnoticed; but the one who does wrong from desire, overcome by pleasure, is seen to be somehow more unrestrained and more womanish in their wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.

notes.note: An adverb, “philosophically”, going with “says”. The English turns it into “speaks as a philosopher when … he says”, which adds the verb “speaks”.
notes.other_reading: It is philosophically that Theophrastus says

notes.greek: ὡς ἄν τις κοινότερον τὰ τοιαῦτα συγκρίνειε
notes.note: A qualification: “as one might compare such things in a more common way”. It is taken to concede that comparing wrongdoings at all is a looser, everyday way of talking, since strict Stoic teaching held all wrongdoings equal (from memory, unchecked). κοινότερον could also mean “by more widely shared notions”.
notes.other_reading: so far as one may compare such things by the standards people commonly share

notes.note: Literally “heavier”, the ordinary Greek word for a grave offence. The English has “more serious”.
notes.other_reading: heavier

notes.note: A different verb from ἁμαρτάνω: literally “to strike a false note”, then “to offend”. The English has “offences” here and keeps “wrongdoing” and “do wrong” for ἁμαρτάνω and its nouns in the rest of the passage.
notes.other_reading: the false steps made from desire

notes.note: θυμός is “anger” but also the spirited temper more broadly, and the Greek word for desire, ἐπιθυμία, is built on it, so the pair sounds alike in Greek. The English has “from anger” and “from desire”; the κατά is literally “in accordance with”.
notes.other_reading: than those committed in a fit of temper

notes.note: συστολή is the Stoic term for the drawing in of the soul in distress, usually put as “contraction”. The English keeps the image as “a shrinking” and adds “inside” so that a reader can tell what shrinks. λεληθυίας is “that escapes notice”, without saying whose notice: most likely the angry person’s own.
notes.other_reading: an unnoticed contraction

notes.note: φαίνεται with a participle normally means “is plainly, is seen to be” and not merely “seems”. The same verb stands in the next clause with adjectives only, where it could be the weaker “appears”. The English has “is seen to” in both places so that the one verb is heard of both people.
notes.other_reading: seems to turn away from reason … appears somehow more unrestrained

notes.note: The word is the opposite of self-control: “more undisciplined, more licentious”. The English has “more unrestrained”.
notes.other_reading: more self-indulgent

notes.note: Literally “more female”, a reproach meaning soft. The image is kept as it stands. The subject is a generic masculine, rendered “the one who … their”.
notes.other_reading: softer

notes.note: Literally “is held by a greater accusation”, a legal turn of phrase. The English has “is open to a greater charge”.
notes.other_reading: deserves heavier blame

notes.note: From here the Greek moves from reported speech to plain statements. This may be Marcus adding his own point, or still a summary of Theophrastus. The English leaves it as plain statement, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: And in general, he said, the one is more like

notes.note: ὥρμηται is the verb of ὁρμή, “impulse” in the glossary, so “impulse” is brought into the English. αὐτόθεν is taken as “from themselves, of their own accord”, but it can also mean “straight off, at once”, that is, without being provoked first.
notes.other_reading: the other has set out straight away to do injustice

check.note: “Heavier offences” is over-literal; English of today says “more serious” or “graver”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “more serious”. “Heavier” is the literal sense and is given in a note.

check.note: The Greek is an indefinite “in a more common, everyday manner”. “The more ordinary way” with the definite article suggests one known method of comparing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as one might compare such things in a more everyday way”. The Greek has no article and names a looser manner of speaking, not one known method.

check.note: “Contraction” on its own is opaque to a reader of today. The word is the shrinking or tightening of the soul that goes with pain, and the participle says it is not noticed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a shrinking inside that goes unnoticed”. “Shrinking” keeps the image of the Greek noun, “inside” is a small addition named in the note, and “goes unnoticed” leaves open whose notice it escapes, as the Greek does.

check.note: φαίνεται is used of both people. The English has “is seen to” for the angry one and “appears” for the other, so the parallel is lost and the second judgment sounds weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “is seen to” for φαίνεται in both places, “is seen to turn away” and “is seen to be somehow more unrestrained”, so that the same verb is heard of both people.

passages.casaubon: Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust, than those which are committed through anger. For he that is angry seems with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn away from reason; but he that sins through lust, being overcome by pleasure, doth in his very sin bewray a more impotent, and unmanlike disposition. Well then and like a philosopher doth he say, that he of the two is the more to be condemned, that sins with pleasure, than he that sins with grief. For indeed this latter may seem first to have been wronged, and so in some manner through grief thereof to have been forced to be angry, whereas he who through lust doth commit anything, did of himself merely resolve upon that action.
passages.russian: Феофраст рассуждает как философ, когда, сравнивая дурные поступки (как можно сравнивать такие вещи на более житейский лад), говорит, что проступки, совершённые из вожделения, тяжелее совершённых из гнева. Ведь гневающийся, как видно, отворачивается от разума с некоторой болью и незаметным внутренним сжатием; а тот, кто поступает дурно из вожделения, побеждённый наслаждением, оказывается как-то более распущенным и более женоподобным в своём дурном поступке. Верно, значит, и достойно философии он сказал, что дурной поступок, совершённый с наслаждением, заслуживает большего обвинения, чем совершённый с болью. И вообще первый больше похож на человека, с которым сперва поступили несправедливо и которого боль вынудила к гневу; второй же движется к несправедливости собственным побуждением, увлекаемый вожделением к тому, чтобы что-то сделать.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἄλλου ἁμάρτημα ἐκεῖ δεῖ καταλιπεῖν.
passages.english: Another person’s wrongdoing must be left there.

notes.note: Literally “there”: in the place where it arose, that is, with the person who did it. The English keeps “there”, the same word as in 9.38 (“the evil is there”), so that the two sayings answer each other.
notes.other_reading: Another person’s wrongdoing must be left where it is.

notes.note: The word covers anything from a mistake to a moral fault. The English keeps “wrongdoing”, as for the same family of words in the neighbouring passages.
notes.other_reading: Another person’s error

notes.note: Impersonal: “it is necessary to leave”. The English uses a passive (“must be left”) so as not to supply “you”.
notes.other_reading: one must leave it there

check.note: ἐκεῖ is simply “there”, with the person who did it. “Left where it is” leans towards “let it be”, and the same word is “there” in 9.38, so the two sayings should match.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “must be left there”. ἐκεῖ is plainly “there”, with the one who did it, and the same word is “there” in 9.38.

passages.casaubon: it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
passages.russian: Чужой дурной поступок нужно оставить там.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν ἥμαρτεν, ἐκεῖ τὸ κακόν. τάχα δ’ οὐχ ἥμαρτεν.
passages.english: If the person did wrong, the evil is there. But perhaps they did not do wrong.

notes.note: The verb has no expressed subject: “he, she or someone did wrong”. The English supplies “the person” and then “they”, since the Greek does not single out a man.
notes.other_reading: If he did wrong

notes.note: Literally “there the bad”: the bad thing lies there, with the one who did it, and not with you. No verb is expressed, and “is” is supplied. τὸ κακόν could be “the harm” as well as “the evil”; ἐκεῖ is “there”, as in 9.20.
notes.other_reading: the harm is theirs

passages.casaubon: If he have sinned, his is the harm, not mine. But perchance he hath not.
passages.russian: Если человек поступил дурно, зло — там. Но, может быть, он и не поступил дурно.

passages.greek: Ἡ μετάνοιά ἐστιν ἐπίληψίς τις ἑαυτοῦ ὡς χρήσιμόν τι παρεικότος· τὸ δὲ χρήσιμον ἀγαθόν τι δεῖ εἶναι καὶ ἐπιμελητέον αὐτοῦ τῷ καλῷ καὶ ἀγαθῷ ἀνδρί· οὐδεὶς δ’ ἂν καλὸς καὶ ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ μετανοήσειεν ἐπὶ τῷ ἡδονήν τινα παρεικέναι· οὔτε ἄρα ·χρήσιμον οὔτε ἀγαθὸν ἡδονή.
passages.english: Regret is a kind of reproach against oneself for having let something useful go by. But what is useful must be something good, and the honourable and good man must attend to it. And no honourable and good man would regret having let a pleasure go by. So pleasure is neither useful nor good.

notes.note: The word is a change of mind after the fact. “Regret” is used for the noun and its verb throughout, since the argument depends on the repetition.
notes.other_reading: Repentance

notes.note: ἐπίληψις is literally a laying hold of, and so a censure. The genitive is the object: oneself is what is laid hold of.
notes.other_reading: a kind of catching oneself out

notes.note: From a verb meaning “to let pass, to neglect”. It returns below as παρεικέναι, and one English phrase, “let go by”, is kept for both, because the argument turns on it.
notes.other_reading: for having neglected something useful

notes.greek: τὸ δὲ χρήσιμον ἀγαθόν τι δεῖ εἶναι
notes.note: The English follows the order of the Greek as given: the useful must be something good. From this premise “not useful” follows, but the closing “nor good” does not strictly follow; it would if the premise ran the other way. The reverse order may be what the printed edition has (from memory, unchecked), though the accents in this copy fit the order as given.
notes.other_reading: But what is good must be something useful

notes.note: “Must be something good” or “must be a good”, in the sense of a real good. The same word “good” then recurs in the phrase for the good man and in the conclusion, so “good” is kept each time.
notes.other_reading: must be a good of some kind

notes.note: A set Greek phrase for the thoroughly decent man, literally “the fine and good man”. The Greek has ἀνήρ, a man, so “man” is kept. The verbal adjective before it, ἐπιμελητέον, says that the useful thing is his to look after, rendered “must attend to it”.
notes.other_reading: the true gentleman must make it his care

notes.note: The raised dot before χρήσιμον is a stray mark in the copy and is ignored. There is no verb; “is” is understood.
notes.other_reading: Pleasure, then, is neither a useful thing nor a good

check.greek: τὸ δὲ χρήσιμον ἀγαθόν τι δεῖ εἶναι
check.note: The English renders the Greek as given, but the conclusion “nor good” only follows if the premise is “the good must be something useful”. The two words may be transposed in this copy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “what is useful must be something good”, because that is the order of the Greek as given and its accents fit that order, so nothing in the copy itself shows a slip. A note now says that “nor good” does not strictly follow from this premise and gives the reverse order as the other reading, from memory, unchecked.

check.note: A stray raised dot stands directly before this word in the Greek as given. It is a digitising slip with no effect on the sense, and the English is right to ignore it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, as suggested. The raised dot is a stray mark in the copy, and the note on the closing words records it.

check.note: The Greek form means active attention: something the man must look after. “Care about” is only a feeling and is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the honourable and good man must attend to it”. The Greek form says that the thing is to be looked after, which is more than a feeling.

passages.casaubon: Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure: no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
passages.russian: Раскаяние — это своего рода упрёк самому себе за то, что упустил что-то полезное. Но полезное должно быть чем-то хорошим, и достойный и хороший человек должен о нём заботиться. А ни один достойный и хороший человек не стал бы раскаиваться в том, что упустил наслаждение. Значит, наслаждение не полезно и не хорошо.

passages.greek: Τί ἐστι κακία; τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ὃ πολλάκις εἶδες. καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς δὲ τοῦ συμβαίνοντος πρόχειρον ἔχε ὅτι τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ πολλάκις εἶδες. ὅλως ἄνω κάτω τὰ αὐτὰ εὑρήσεις, ὧν μεσταὶ αἱ ἱστορίαι αἱ παλαιαί, αἱ μέσαι, αἱ ὑπόγυιοι· ὧν νῦν μεσταὶ αἱ πόλεις καὶ αἱ οἰκίαι. οὐδὲν καινόν· πάντα καὶ συνήθη καὶ ὀλιγοχρόνια.
passages.english: What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen. In general, high and low, you will find the same things. The histories are full of them, the ancient ones, those in between and the recent ones; cities and households are full of them now. Nothing is new. Everything is both familiar and short-lived.

notes.note: κακία is badness of character. The glossary has no entry; “wickedness” is used here as in 8.55 and 8.56.
notes.other_reading: What is vice?

notes.note: The same formula comes twice, and the English is the same both times: “This is what you have often seen”. The verb is a simple past, “you often saw”, which English puts more naturally as “you have often seen”.
notes.other_reading: what you saw many times

notes.note: Literally “have ready to hand”, Marcus’s usual phrase for a thought to be kept ready for use.
notes.other_reading: have this thought ready

notes.note: An idiom, literally “up, down”. It can mean “high and low, wherever you look”, or “round and round, over and over”. The English takes the first, which suits the histories, cities and households that follow.
notes.other_reading: over and over you will find the same things

notes.greek: αἱ ἱστορίαι αἱ παλαιαί, αἱ μέσαι, αἱ ὑπόγυιοι
notes.note: ἱστορίαι are written histories or records. αἱ μέσαι is literally “the middle ones”, the histories of the period between ancient and recent, rendered “those in between”. ὑπόγυιοι is literally “under the hand”, that is, close to the present.
notes.other_reading: the histories of ancient times, of the times between and of our own day

notes.note: The Greek hangs two relative clauses (“of which … are full”) on “the same things”. The English makes them a separate sentence with “them”; nothing is dropped.
notes.other_reading: the same things, of which the histories are full … and of which cities and households are now full

notes.note: οἰκίαι is “houses” or “households”. It is taken as households, the private scale set beside the public one.
notes.other_reading: the cities and the houses

notes.note: Literally “of little time”, rendered “short-lived”.
notes.other_reading: lasting only a little while

check.note: The same formula comes twice in the Greek and the repetition is the point. The English has “It is what” the first time and “this is what” the second.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This is what you have often seen” both times, so the answer about wickedness is heard again word for word for everything that happens.

check.note: “Up and down” set off by commas is literal and not clear in English. The Greek means high and low, everywhere you look.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “In general, high and low, you will find the same things”. “High and low” is an English idiom that keeps the two directions of the Greek. “In general” stays for ὅλως, which does not mean “in short”, and “look” is not added.

check.note: “The middle ones” is awkward and unclear. The Greek means the histories of the times between the ancient and the recent.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the ancient ones, those in between and the recent ones”. This is clearer than “the middle ones” and adds no noun such as “times” that the Greek does not have.

passages.casaubon: What is wickedness? It is that which many time and often thou hast already seen and known in the world. And so oft as anything doth happen that might otherwise trouble thee, let this memento presently come to thy mind, that it is that which thou hast already often Seen and known. Generally, above and below, thou shalt find but the same things. The very same things whereof ancient stories, middle age stories, and fresh stories are full whereof towns are full, and houses full. There is nothing that is new. All things that are, are both usual and of little continuance.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Что такое порочность? Это то, что ты часто видел. И при всём, что случается, держи под рукой: это то, что ты часто видел. Вообще, вверху и внизу ты найдёшь одно и то же. Этим полны истории — древние, средние и недавние; этим полны сейчас города и дома. Ничего нового нет. Всё и привычно, и недолговечно.

passages.greek: Τῷ ἀναρριφέντι λίθῳ οὐδὲν κακὸν τὸ κατενεχθῆναι οὐδὲ ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἀνενεχθῆναι.
passages.english: For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.

notes.note: The two infinitives are passive forms of one verb (φέρω, “carry”) with opposite prefixes, down and up. The passive is also the ordinary Greek for a thing moving down or up, with no carrier in view. “Be carried” is kept for both so that the pairing shows and the stone, which was thrown, stays passive in both directions.
notes.other_reading: to come down … to go up; or: to fall … to rise

notes.note: Literally “nothing bad”, with “nor good” following and no second “nothing”; “nothing” is repeated in the second half for the English. κακόν and ἀγαθόν are the ordinary words for bad and good, and can also be heard as nouns, “an evil” and “a good”.
notes.other_reading: it is no evil to be carried down, nor a good to be carried up

notes.note: A dative of the one concerned, with the article used generically, and a participle of completed action: the stone has already been thrown when its coming down is judged. The English reads “a stone” and “upward”, since “thrown up” has another sense in English.
notes.other_reading: For the stone that has been thrown up

notes.note: The Greek names the coming down first and the going up second, though the stone goes up first; the Greek order is kept. The aorist infinitive marks the event, not a past time, so the English does not read “to have been carried up”.
notes.other_reading: nor good to have been carried up

check.note: The passive of this verb, said of a thing in the air, simply means to come down or fall, and “carried down” makes a reader look for someone carrying. The second reader calls this a matter of taste, not of sense, and suggests “to come down … to go up” or “to fall … to rise”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “to be carried down” and “to be carried up”. Both are passive forms of one Greek verb, “carry”, that differ only in the prefix, and the stone has been thrown, so it is moved in both directions and does not move itself. The note gives “to come down … to go up” and “to fall … to rise”.

check.note: The participle is aorist, a stone that has been thrown up, so the rise is already behind it when the fall is called no harm. “That has been thrown up” would keep the sequence better than “thrown upward”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For a stone that has been thrown upward”, so that the throw is already over when the coming down is judged. “Upward” stays in place of “up”, because “thrown up” has another sense in English.

passages.casaubon: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
passages.russian: Для камня, брошенного вверх, нет ничего плохого в том, чтобы нестись вниз, и ничего хорошего — в том, чтобы нестись вверх.

passages.greek: Ὀρθός, μὴ ὀρθούμενος.
passages.english: Upright, not held upright.

notes.note: The Greek has no verb: a bare masculine nominative, “upright” (also “straight”, “right”), and the English is left without a verb too. It is probably meant as a rule, with “be” or “one must be” understood. The negative μή would show that in older Greek, but in the Greek of Marcus’s time it is also the usual negative with a participle, so it does not settle the question alone.
notes.other_reading: Be upright, not held upright.

notes.note: A present participle of ὀρθόω, “set upright, straighten, put right”, from the same root as ὀρθός, taken as passive: kept upright by someone or something else. The present tense marks a state that goes on, so the English reads “held upright”, and “upright” is repeated so that the play on the one root shows.
notes.other_reading: Upright, not set upright. Or: Straight, not straightened.

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to read ἢ (“or”) here, and μή (“not”) is an editor’s correction supported by the similar sentence in 3.5. The English follows the text as given, so the “not” is uncertain.
notes.other_reading: Upright, or held upright.

check.note: The negative is μή, not οὐ, so the two words are a precept with “be” or “one must be” understood, not a description. The English, with no verb, can be read as a description of someone.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English stays without a verb, as the Greek has none, and the note now says that the two words are probably a rule and gives “Be upright” as the other reading. In the Greek of Marcus’s time μή is also the usual negative with a participle, so the negative alone does not prove a command.

check.note: The participle is present passive or middle: being kept or held upright as a continuing state, while “set upright” reads as a single finished act. The verb also means to set straight, so “straight, not straightened” is the other reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Upright, not held upright”, since the present participle describes a state that goes on and not one finished act. “Straight, not straightened” is recorded in the note.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, the manuscripts read ἢ here (“upright, or set upright”) and μή is a correction made on the strength of the parallel in 3.5. The English rightly follows the Greek as given, but the word should be marked as doubtful.
check.decided: Accepted: “not” is kept, following the Greek as given, and the note marks the word as uncertain, from memory and unchecked.

passages.casaubon: Straight of itself, not made straight.
passages.russian: Прямой, а не выпрямляемый.

passages.greek: Τὸ τῷ σμήνει μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῇ μελίσσῃ συμφέρει.
passages.english: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.

notes.note: σμῆνος means both the beehive and the swarm of bees that lives in it. The contrast is between the community of bees and the single bee. The English reads “hive”, which also names the colony and not only its box, while “swarm” in English suggests bees on the move.
notes.other_reading: What is not good for the swarm

notes.greek: μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῇ μελίσσῃ συμφέρει
notes.note: The same verb, συμφέρω, “be to the advantage of, benefit”, stands on both sides, first as a participle and then as a finite verb, and “is good for” renders it both times, as elsewhere in this translation. It is not ἀγαθόν, the word for “good” in 9.17.
notes.other_reading: What does not benefit the hive does not benefit the bee either.

notes.note: οὐδέ can be “not … either” or the stronger “not even”. The weaker sense is taken, since the sentence moves from the group to its member.
notes.other_reading: is not good even for the bee

check.note: The Greek word is “what benefits, what is to the advantage of”, not ἀγαθόν. Since 9.17 in the same section uses “good” for ἀγαθόν, one English word covers two Greek words that Marcus keeps apart; “benefit” would separate them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “is good for”, the rendering of συμφέρει settled for this whole translation, and 9.17 is a separate chapter from another book with no argument running between the two. The note now says that the Greek word here is “be to the advantage of” and not the “good” of 9.17, and gives “benefit” as the other reading.

check.note: The word means both the hive and the swarm, the colony of bees itself. “Hive” is defensible and reads naturally, but the point is about the community, which “swarm” says more directly.
check.decided: Declined: “hive” stays. The Greek word names the hive and the bees in it at once, and English “hive” does the same, while “swarm” in English suggests bees in flight away from their home; the note gives “swarm”.

passages.casaubon: That which is not good for the bee-hive, cannot be good for the bee.
passages.russian: Что не на пользу улью, то не на пользу и пчеле.

passages.greek: Ἄριστος τρόπος τοῦ ἀμύνεσθαι τὸ μὴ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι.
passages.english: The best way to fight back is to not become like them.

notes.note: The middle of ἀμύνω covers both “defend oneself, ward off” and “pay back, take revenge on”. “Fight back” is chosen because it can be heard either way. The Greek is impersonal and names no “you”.
notes.other_reading: The best way to defend oneself. Or: The best way to retaliate.

notes.note: The verb means “to be made like” or “to make oneself like” and has no object here: the Greek does not say like whom. “Them” is supplied as the smallest word English allows, and stands for whoever is being fought, one person or many. The negative belongs to the infinitive, “the not becoming like”, which “is to not become” makes plain.
notes.other_reading: is to not become like the one who did the wrong. Or, as a passive: is to not be made like them.

notes.note: τρόπος is “way, manner”, and also “character”. The plain sense “way” is what the genitive that follows needs.
notes.other_reading: The best manner of fighting back

check.note: The middle verb means both to defend oneself, to ward off, and to pay someone back. “Retaliate” picks the second and narrows it to hitting back; a word that holds both would be safer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “The best way to fight back”, which can be heard both as warding off and as paying back, as the Greek verb can. “Defend yourself” was not used because it keeps only one of the two senses and adds a “you” that the Greek does not have.

check.note: The Greek has no object: “not to become like”. English needs one, but “them” is supplied and the plural is a choice, since nothing says whether one wrongdoer or many is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “them” stays as the smallest object English can supply, and in today’s English it stands for one person or many, so it does not decide the number. The note says the word is supplied and gives a singular reading.

check.note: “Is not to become” can be read for a moment as “is not, to become like them”. Putting the negative with the infinitive removes the stumble.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is to not become like them”, which puts the negative with the infinitive, where the Greek has it, and removes the reading “is not the best way”.

passages.casaubon: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
passages.russian: Лучший способ дать отпор — не стать таким, как они.

passages.greek: ὅταν γένηται ʽσφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃʼ.
passages.english: once it has become a “rounded sphere, in stillness”.

notes.note: This is a subordinate clause only, and the English begins in lower case to show it. Its main clause stands in the part of 8.41 that is not given, which says that nothing at all touches the mind; “it” is the mind. ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive is “once” or “whenever”.
notes.other_reading: whenever it becomes

notes.note: A quotation of verse, from memory, unchecked, a line of Empedocles that goes on with a word meaning “rejoicing”, which governs the dative μονίῃ. Marcus stops before that word, so the dative is left hanging. The English gives it as “in stillness” and adds nothing from the rest of the line.
notes.other_reading: a “rounded sphere”, in stillness (with the dative outside the quotation); or, with the rest of the line supplied, “a rounded sphere rejoicing in its stillness”

notes.note: A rare poetic noun that can be derived from μένω, “stay”, giving “rest, stillness, steadfastness”, or from μόνος, “alone”, giving “solitude”. The English takes the first. From memory, unchecked, scholars are divided on which the poet meant.
notes.other_reading: in solitude

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to end here with μένει, “it stays”, which gives the clause a verb of its own, and μονίῃ is an editor’s restoration from the same verse quoted at greater length in 12.3. The English follows the text as given.
notes.other_reading: once it has become a rounded sphere, it stays so

notes.note: A masculine form of the usual feminine σφαῖρα, “ball, sphere”, the poet’s name for his perfectly round whole. Marcus applies it to the mind as an image, so the English has no capital. κυκλοτερής, “rounded, circular”, repeats the idea of roundness, and both words are kept.
notes.other_reading: a well-rounded Sphere; or: a round ball

check.note: The noun is disputed: from μένω it is rest, stillness, staying put; from μόνος it is solitude, being alone. The English chooses stillness; the other reading is “in its solitude”, and the other sense should at least be noted.
check.decided: Accepted: “stillness” is kept and the note sets out both derivations and gives “in solitude” as the other reading.

check.note: As given the Greek does not fully construe: the dative has nothing to depend on, because the line of verse is cut off before the word that governs it. The English turns the bare dative into a phrase with “in” and adds “its”, and the reader is not told that the quotation breaks off.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “its” is removed and the English now reads “in stillness”, the barest English for a dative. No mark of a break is put into the English, since the Greek has none, and the note says that the quotation stops before the word that governs the dative.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, the manuscripts end here with μένει (“once it has become a rounded sphere, it stays so”), which gives the clause its main verb, and μονίῃ is an editor’s restoration from the verse quoted in full at 12.3. The English rightly follows the Greek as given, but the last word should be marked.
check.decided: Accepted: the English follows the Greek as given, and a new note says, from memory and unchecked, that the last word is an editor’s restoration and that the manuscripts are said to read “it stays”.

check.note: The clause is subordinate and hangs on the sentence before it, which is not given, so with a capital and a full stop it reads as a broken sentence. The supplied “it” is correct, and “once” would give ὅταν with the aorist more exactly than “when”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins in lower case and reads “once it has become”, so that it shows as the end of a sentence whose beginning is not given. “It” stays: the words just before, which are not part of the passage, show that the subject is the mind.

check.note: The adjective is “round, circular”, an epic word, and the noun is the masculine σφαῖρος, the poet’s name for the cosmic Sphere, not the ordinary σφαῖρα. “Rounded sphere” is acceptable, but a capital would show that it is a proper name in the verse.
check.decided: Declined: “rounded sphere” stays without a capital. The Greek as given has no capital, and Marcus uses the poet’s words as an image for the mind, not as a name; the note on σφαῖρος says that it is the poet’s name for his round whole.

part.left_out: Ἐμποδισμὸς αἰσθήσεως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἐμποδισμὸς ὁρμῆς ὁμοίως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἔστι δέ τι ἄλλο ὁμοίως ἐμποδιστικὸν καὶ κακὸν τῆς φυτικῆς κατασκευῆς. οὕτως τοίνυν ἐμποδισμὸς νοῦ κακὸν νοερᾶς φύσεως. πάντα δὴ ταῦτα ἐπὶ σεαυτὸν μετάφερε. πόνος, ἡδονὴ ἅπτεταί σου; ὄψεται ἡ αἴσθησις. ὁρμήσαντι ἔνστημα ἐγένετο; εἰ μὲν ἀνυπεξαιρέτως ὥρμας, ἤδη ὡς λογικοῦ κακόν, εἰ δὲ τὸ κοινὸν λαμβάνεις, οὔπω βέβλαψαι οὐδὲ ἐμπεπόδισαι. τὰ μέντοι τοῦ νοῦ ἴδια οὐδεὶς ἄλλος εἴωθεν ἐμποδίζειν· τούτου γὰρ οὐ πῦρ, οὐ σίδηρος, οὐ τύραννος, οὐ βλασφημία, οὐχ ὁτιοῦν ἅπτεται,
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 8.39 just before the closing image of the rounded sphere and makes that image its whole section 8.40.

passages.casaubon: If once round and solid, there is no fear that ever it will change.
