passages.russian: как только он стал «округлым шаром, в покое».

passages.greek: Πάντα ταῦτα συνήθη μὲν τῇ πείρᾳ, ἐφήμερα δὲ τῷ χρόνῳ, ῥυπαρὰ δὲ τῇ ὕλῃ· πάντα νῦν οἷα ἐπ’ ἐκείνων οὓς κατεθάψαμεν.
passages.english: All these things are familiar in experience, lasting a day in time, and filthy in their matter. Everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried.

notes.note: The chapter does not say what “all these things” are. The English leaves it as open as the Greek.
notes.other_reading: All of this

notes.note: Literally “customary by experience”: things known from having been met again and again. The dative could also be heard as “to experience”, that is, to the person who has had it.
notes.other_reading: well known by experience

notes.note: Literally “lasting a day”. The English keeps the image of the single day, although “in time” follows it.
notes.other_reading: short-lived in time

notes.note: The adjective means dirty or grimy, and by extension mean or sordid. The physical sense is kept because the dative names the material the things are made of.
notes.other_reading: sordid in their material

notes.note: The preposition before this phrase can mean “in the time of” or “in the case of”. The English takes it as time. The verb is a plain past, which English gives as a perfect.
notes.other_reading: Everything now is just as it was with those we buried.

check.note: “Short-lived” gives the sense of the Greek word but loses its image, which is literally “lasting a day”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “lasting a day in time”. The Greek word carries the image of a single day, and the brief asks for images to be kept.

passages.casaubon: All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary; for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are they now also, and no otherwise.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Всё это знакомо по опыту, однодневно по времени и грязно по материи. Всё теперь так же, как было при тех, кого мы похоронили.

passages.greek: Τὸ σαπρὸν τῆς ἑκάστῳ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης· ὕδωρ, κόνις, ὀστάρια, γράσος, ἢ πάλιν· πῶροι γῆς τὰ μάρμαρα καὶ ὑποστάθμαι ὁ χρυσός, ὁ ἄργυρος, καὶ τριχία ἡ ἐσθὴς καὶ αἷμα ἡ πορφύρα, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα τοιαῦτα. καὶ τὸ πνευμάτιον δὲ ἄλλο τοιοῦτον καὶ ἐκ τούτων εἰς ταῦτα μεταβάλλον.
passages.english: The rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing: water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek. Or again: marble is the earth’s callus, gold and silver are sediment, clothing is little hairs, and purple dye is blood, and all the rest is of this kind. And the little breath too is another thing of this kind, changing out of these things and into these.

notes.note: A neuter adjective used as a noun, “the rotten (side)”, with no verb: a heading followed by a list. The English keeps it verbless.
notes.other_reading: How rotten is the matter that underlies each thing

notes.note: The dative “each” can be neuter (each thing) or masculine (each person). The English reads “each thing”, because the list goes on to marble, gold and clothing.
notes.other_reading: of the matter that underlies each person

notes.note: The word names the smell of a goat and is used of the rank smell of the unwashed body. The English keeps the goat.
notes.other_reading: the rank smell of sweat

notes.note: As punctuated, “or again” closes the first list and opens a second. It could also be run on into the next clause.
notes.other_reading: or, to take it another way,

notes.note: The noun means a porous stone (tufa) and also a callus or hard lump formed in the body. The English takes the bodily sense, which keeps the image in one word. As with “sediment” below, the Greek plural is taken as a mass noun.
notes.other_reading: marble is hardened lumps of earth

notes.note: What settles at the bottom of a liquid: sediment, dregs. The plural is kept as a mass noun in English.
notes.other_reading: gold and silver are dregs

notes.note: The noun is the purple dye, or cloth dyed with it, and not the colour, so the English says “purple dye”. The blood is that of the shellfish the dye came from, which the Greek does not mention and the English does not add.
notes.other_reading: the purple robe is blood

notes.note: The diminutive of pneuma, the breath that for the Stoics is the stuff of life and soul. The English keeps the diminutive and the image of breath, as in 9.24 of this section.
notes.other_reading: the little soul; the bit of breath that is our life

notes.note: Literally “changing out of these into these”, the same pronoun twice. It may mean out of such things and into such things again, or from some of these materials into others. The English repeats “these” as the Greek does and leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: changing from one of these things into another

check.note: The form for “each” can be masculine or neuter, so the matter may underlie each thing or each person. The English chooses “each thing”.
check.decided: Declined: “each thing” stands. The form allows “each person” as well, but the list runs on from water and bones to marble, gold and clothing, which only “each thing” covers, and the other reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: The word is specific: the rank, goat-like smell of the body. “Stench” is general and loses the bodily reference that goes with the bones.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a goatish reek”. The word names the smell of a goat, used of the unwashed body, so the bodily reference is restored, but “sweat” is not in the Greek and is not added.

check.note: The noun means a hard concretion, a stone or a callus in the body. “Hardened lumps” paraphrases it in two words and loses the possible bodily sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “marble is calluses of the earth”. The noun is one word for a hard growth, in stone or in the body, and “calluses” keeps it as one image; the plainer “hardened lumps” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The Greek word is the purple dye or purple cloth, not the colour. Bare “purple” reads as the colour.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “purple dye is blood”. The Greek noun is the dye or the dyed cloth and not the colour.

check.note: “From these into these” is word for word but hard to follow in English. The idiom is taken to mean from some of these things into others of them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “changing out of these things and into these”, which is easier to follow than the bare pronouns. The Greek uses the same pronoun twice and may mean out of such things and back into them, so the narrower “from one of these into another” goes in the note as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek uses one word, “such”, for all the rest and again for the little breath, and the draft had “of the same kind” and then “of this kind”.
check.decided: Accepted: both now read “of this kind”, so the repetition can be heard.

check.note: Found while settling: the word is a diminutive, “little hairs”, like “little bones” before it and “little breath” after it, and the draft had “bits of hair”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “clothing is little hairs”, so the three belittling forms in the chapter are given in the same way.

passages.casaubon: How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted. And again those other things that are so much prized and admired, as marble stones, what are they, but as it were the kernels of the earth? gold and silver, what are they, but as the more gross faeces of the earth? Thy most royal apparel, for matter, it is but as it were the hair of a silly sheep, and for colour, the very blood of a shell-fish; of this nature are all other things. Thy life itself, is some such thing too; a mere exhalation of blood: and it also, apt to be changed into some other common thing.
passages.russian: Гниль вещества, лежащего в основе каждой вещи: вода, пыль, косточки, козлиный смрад. Или ещё: мрамор — мозоль земли, золото и серебро — осадок, одежда — волоски, пурпурная краска — кровь, и всё прочее такого же рода. И дыханьице — ещё одно из того же рода: оно меняется, выходя из этого и переходя в это.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ προσίσταταί σοι τὰ ἐν τῷ ἀμφιθεάτρῳ καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις χωρίοις ὡς ἀεὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ὁρώμενα, καὶ τὸ ὁμοειδὲς προσκορῆ τὴν θέαν ποιεῖ, τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ ὅλου τοῦ βίου πάσχειν· πάντα γὰρ ἄνω κάτω τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν. μέχρι τίνος οὖν;
passages.english: Just as what goes on in the amphitheatre and places of that kind repels you, since the same things are always being seen, and the sameness makes the spectacle cloying, feel this way about the whole of life too. For all things, up and down, are the same and from the same. How long, then?

notes.note: Literally “stands against you”. It is used of food that turns the stomach and so of anything that offends or wearies. The English uses a verb of physical distaste.
notes.other_reading: wearies you; turns your stomach

notes.note: Literally “as being always the same things seen”. The Greek is passive and names no viewer, and the English keeps it so.
notes.other_reading: because you always see the same things

notes.note: The word means causing surfeit, too much of one thing. “Cloying” keeps the image of being overfed.
notes.other_reading: makes one sick of the sight

notes.note: The Greek as given has a bare infinitive with no verb to govern it. The English reads it as the notebook’s infinitive of instruction, “feel”. It can also be taken as a statement of what happens, and some editors are said to alter it to an indicative in the second person (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: this is what happens to you with the whole of life too

notes.note: Literally “up down”, an idiom for “everywhere, from top to bottom” or “over and over, back and forth”. The English keeps the literal pair, which can be heard both ways.
notes.other_reading: For everything, over and over, is the same

notes.note: “Out of the same”: the same materials or the same causes. The Greek has no verb here and does not say which, and the English adds neither.
notes.other_reading: and come from the same causes

notes.note: Literally “up to what point, then?”. It may ask how long this will go on, or how long one is to go on watching.
notes.other_reading: Until when, then?

check.greek: τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ ὅλου τοῦ βίου πάσχειν
check.note: The Greek as given has an infinitive with no verb to govern it. The English makes it a command to oneself, but it could be a statement that the same thing happens to you with the whole of life.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the command “feel the same about the whole of life too” stands, because the Greek as given has an infinitive, which this notebook often uses for an instruction to oneself, and a statement would need a different form of the verb. The note now says plainly that the infinitive has nothing governing it and gives the statement as the other reading.

check.note: “All things, up and down, are the same” is literal but unclear. The idiom means high and low, back and forth, everywhere and over and over.
check.decided: Declined: “up and down” stands. “High and low” would settle the idiom as “everywhere”, while the Greek pair may as well mean back and forth, over and over, and the literal words leave both open; the note explains the idiom.

check.note: The Greek means producing surfeit, making one sick of a thing. “Cloying” is mostly used of sweetness today and sits oddly with a spectacle.
check.decided: Declined: “cloying” stands. The Greek word means causing surfeit, the image of being overfed, and “cloying” is the English word for exactly that; the suggestion would drop the image and add a viewer (“one”) that the Greek does not name.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek says only “the same and from the same”, with no verb, and the draft’s “come from the same” leaned toward causes over materials.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “are the same and from the same”, which adds nothing.

passages.casaubon: As the ordinary shows of the theatre and of other such places, when thou art presented with them, affect thee; as the same things still seen, and in the same fashion, make the sight ingrateful and tedious; so must all the things that we see all our life long affect us. For all things, above and below, are still the same, and from the same causes. When then will there be an end?

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Как тебя отталкивает то, что творится в амфитеатре и подобных местах, потому что там всегда видишь одно и то же и однообразие делает зрелище приторным, так относись и ко всей жизни. Ведь всё, и вверху и внизу, одно и то же и из одного и того же. До каких же пор?

passages.greek: Ὁποῖόν σοι φαίνεται τὸ λούεσθαι· ἔλαιον, ἱδρώς, ῥύπος, ὕδωρ γλοιῶδες, πάντα σικχαντά· τοιοῦτον πᾶν μέρος τοῦ βίου καὶ πᾶν ὑποκείμενον.
passages.english: As bathing appears to you (oil, sweat, dirt, slimy water, all of it disgusting), such is every part of life and every object.

notes.note: “Of what kind bathing appears to you” is answered later by “of that kind is every part of life”. The English keeps the pair as “As” and “such” in one sentence and puts the list between them in brackets.
notes.other_reading: What bathing looks like to you, that is what every part of life is like

notes.note: The adjective comes from the word for the mix of oil and dirt scraped off the skin at the baths, so the water is thick and sticky with that scum.
notes.other_reading: scummy, sticky water

notes.note: “All things nauseating”: this sums up the list. The adjective is rare, and its sense is that of causing loathing.
notes.other_reading: everything sickening

notes.note: Literally “everything that underlies” or “that lies before one”. In Stoic use it is the material substrate, and more loosely any object one has to do with. The English takes the looser sense; the same word is “the matter that underlies” in 9.36.
notes.other_reading: and every underlying material

check.note: The participle means what underlies or what lies before one. “Material” is added and narrows it, and the link with “underlies” in 9.36 is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “every object”. “Material” is not in the Greek and is dropped; “underlying thing” is not plain English, and the other suggestion adds a viewer the Greek does not have, so the link with 9.36 is made in the note.

check.note: The adjective means sticky or slimy, like the oily scum scraped off in the baths. “Greasy” only repeats the oil and weakens the sliminess.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “slimy water”. The adjective describes the sticky scum of oil and dirt scraped off at the baths, and “greasy” only repeated the oil.

check.note: The Greek is one sentence, “such as bathing appears, of that kind is every part of life”. The English splits it, and its opening hangs unfinished until the next sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is now one sentence, “As bathing appears to you (oil, sweat, dirt, slimy water, all of it disgusting), such is every part of life and every object”. The Greek is a single sentence built on “of what kind” and “of that kind”, and the brackets let the list sit inside it.

passages.casaubon: By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body: all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life; and every worldly object.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Каким тебе видится мытьё (масло, пот, грязь, склизкая вода, всё это отвратительно), такова и всякая часть жизни, и всякий предмет.

passages.greek:
Μέλαν ἦθος, θῆλυ ἦθος, περισκελὲς ἦθος, θηριῶδες, βοσκηματῶδες, παιδαριῶδες, βλακικόν, κίβδηλον, βωμολόχον, καπηλικόν, τυραννικόν.

Εἰ ξένος κόσμου ὁ μὴ γνωρίζων τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ ὄντα, οὐχ ἧττον ξένος καὶ ὁ μὴ γνωρίζων τὰ γινόμενα.
passages.english:
A dark character, a womanish character, a stubborn character, like a wild beast, like cattle, childish, dull, counterfeit, clownish, like a petty trader, tyrannical.

If the one who does not know the things that are in the universe is a stranger to the universe, no less a stranger too is the one who does not know the things that happen.

notes.note: Literally “black character”: dark, malignant. The English says “dark”, which the word also means, so that it is not heard as a matter of skin. The chapter is a bare list with no verb and does not say whether it describes one person or sets out kinds of character.
notes.other_reading: A black, malicious character

notes.note: Literally “a female character”, an ancient term of reproach for softness. The English keeps what the Greek says and does not swap in “soft”.
notes.other_reading: a soft, unmanly character

notes.note: The adjective means very hard, rigid, and of character obstinate or harsh.
notes.other_reading: a hard, unbending character

notes.note: “Like a grazing animal”, that is like livestock, as against the wild beast just before it.
notes.other_reading: like a herd animal

notes.note: The range runs from slack and lazy to slow-witted and stupid. “Dull” can be heard both ways.
notes.other_reading: sluggish, slack; stupid

notes.note: The first is the low jester who will say anything for a laugh. The second is the petty retailer, with a suggestion of cheating that the English leaves to this note.
notes.other_reading: a buffoon’s, a cheating shopkeeper’s

notes.note: The noun means a foreigner or stranger, someone not at home in a place. The genitive is “of the universe”, and English needs “to the universe”. The same word comes back in 12.13 and is “stranger” there too.
notes.other_reading: a foreigner in the universe

notes.note: The verb is to know in the sense of being acquainted with, or to recognise. The English uses “know” both times it occurs.
notes.other_reading: does not recognise

notes.note: “The things that come about” is set against “the things that are”. The Greek does not repeat “in it”, and the English does not supply it. The passage is only the opening of chapter 29, but this sentence is complete as given.
notes.other_reading: what comes to pass in it

check.note: The Greek means dark or malignant in character. “A black character” can be misread today as being about skin colour.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “A dark character”. The Greek word means dark as well as black, and of character it means malignant, which “dark” conveys without the risk of being heard as a matter of skin.

check.note: The Greek is simply “female”, used of character to mean soft, unmanly. “Womanish” is correct but dated.
check.decided: Declined: “womanish” stands. The Greek says “female” and uses it as a reproach, which is what “womanish” does in English; “soft” would drop the image and “effeminate” is used today of manner and not of character.

check.note: The word covers slack, lazy and sluggish as well as dull-witted. “Stupid” picks only the second sense.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “dull”. The Greek word covers both the slack and the slow-witted, and “dull” can be heard both ways, where “sluggish” would pick only the first as “stupid” picked only the second.

check.note: The Greek means of a petty trader, with the suggestion of cheating. “Huckstering” is an old word that few readers today will know.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “like a petty trader”. The cheating is only a suggestion in the Greek word, so it is left to the note, and “peddling” does not describe a character.

check.greek: καὶ ὁ μὴ γνωρίζων τὰ γινόμενα
check.note: The “also” is dropped. It marks the second person as added to the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “no less a stranger too is the one who does not know the things that happen”. The Greek has an “also” that adds the second person to the first.

check.note: The same Greek word is “world” in 6.56 and “universe” here. One word throughout may be wanted.
check.decided: Declined: “universe” stands here, as the glossary has it. The rest of the chapter speaks of the nature common to all things, so the whole ordered universe is meant, while 6.56 keeps “came into the world” as the plain English for being born, with a note.

part.left_out: φυγὰς ὁ φεύγων τὸν πολιτικὸν λόγον· τυφλὸς ὁ καταμύων τῷ νοερῷ ὄμματι· πτωχὸς ὁ ἐνδεὴς ἑτέρου καὶ μὴ πάντα ἔχων παρ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὰ εἰς τὸν βίον χρήσιμα· ἀπόστημα κόσμου ὁ ἀφιστάμενος καὶ χωρίζων ἑαυτὸν τοῦ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως λόγου διὰ τοῦ δυσαρεστεῖν τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν· ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν· ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης.
part.why: The 1634 translation joins the opening sentence of chapter 29, on the stranger in the world, to the list of characters in its section 4.23 and begins its 4.24 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world, that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well, that wonders at the things that are done in it?

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian:
Тёмный нрав, женоподобный нрав, упрямый нрав, звероподобный, скотский, ребяческий, тупой, фальшивый, шутовской, торгашеский, тиранический.

Если тот, кто не знает того, что есть в мироздании, чужд мирозданию, то не менее чужд и тот, кто не знает того, что происходит.

passages.greek: Παιδίων ὀργαὶ καὶ παίγνια, καὶ ʽπνευμάτια νεκροὺς βαστάζονταʼ, ὥστε ἐναργέστερον προσπεσεῖν τὸ τῆς Νεκυίας.
passages.english: Children’s tantrums and toys, and “little breaths carrying corpses”, so that the scene of the Calling Up of the Dead strikes home more vividly.

notes.note: There is no verb, and the Greek does not say what is being called this. The first noun is fits of anger. The second is first of all playthings, and can also be games or play; the English takes the objects.
notes.other_reading: Children’s fits of anger and children’s games

notes.note: The edition marks this as a quotation. It seems to echo a saying of Epictetus that Marcus cites at 4.41, “you are a little soul carrying a corpse”, here in the plural and with “little breath” for the soul (from memory, unchecked). “Little breaths” matches 9.36.
notes.other_reading: “little souls carrying dead bodies”

notes.note: A result clause with an infinitive: “so as to strike more vividly”. The Greek does not say whom it strikes, and “strikes home” lets the English name no one either.
notes.other_reading: so that it comes home to you more clearly

notes.note: Literally “the (matter) of the Nekyia”; “the scene” fills in the bare article. Nekyia, a calling up of the dead, is the traditional title of book 11 of the Odyssey, where Odysseus meets the shades. The English translates the title and does not add Homer, since other works bore the name (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: so that what is in the Nekyia strikes home more vividly

check.note: The word means playthings but also games or play. Beside “tantrums”, an activity, “games” is at least as likely as the objects.
check.decided: Declined: “toys” stands. The first sense of the Greek word is the plaything, the object, and “games” is possible but no more certain; the note records it as the other reading.

check.note: “Nekyia” is left as a Greek title that a reader of today will not know. The Greek phrase is also looser than “what is in”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the scene of the Calling Up of the Dead”. Nekyia is a Greek title that the passage is not discussing as a word, so it is translated, and the note gives the title and says that “the scene” fills in a bare article.

check.note: The Greek has no object. “One” is supplied and is a little stiff for plain English of today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “strikes home more vividly”. The Greek names no one who is struck, so “one” is dropped and no “you” is put in its place, and “strikes” keeps the verb’s image.

passages.casaubon: Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that common dirge song.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Детские капризы и игрушки, и «дыханьица, носящие трупы», — так что сцена «Вызывания мёртвых» доходит до тебя ещё живее.

passages.greek: Πῶς γελοῖος καὶ ξένος ὁ θαυμάζων ὁτιοῦν τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ γινομένων.
passages.english: How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is the person who is surprised at anything at all that happens in life.

notes.note: An exclamatory “how”, covering both adjectives. The edition ends the sentence with a full stop and the English does the same.
notes.other_reading: How ridiculous and how much a stranger

notes.note: A foreigner or stranger, as in 4.29, where the one who does not know what happens is a stranger to the universe. The word can also mean “strange”, but the link with 4.29 favours “stranger”.
notes.other_reading: How ridiculous and strange is the person

notes.note: The verb covers being surprised, wondering and marvelling. “Surprised” is used, since the point is being caught unprepared.
notes.other_reading: who wonders at; who is astonished at

notes.note: “Anything whatever”. The English keeps the full force with “anything at all”.
notes.other_reading: at any one of the things that happen in life

passages.casaubon: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Как смешон тот, кто удивляется чему бы то ни было, что происходит в жизни, и какой же он чужак!

passages.greek: Ἴσον τὸ ἑκατὸν ἔτεσι καὶ τὸ τρισὶ ταῦτα ἱστορῆσαι.
passages.english: To have observed these things for a hundred years or for three comes to the same.

notes.note: “Equal”, with no verb: the hundred years and the three are declared equal. It stands at the end of the English sentence as “comes to the same”, and the Greek “and” between the two spans becomes “or”.
notes.other_reading: It is equal, to have observed these things for a hundred years and for three.

notes.note: A dative of time, which in Greek of this period can express duration. The English takes it as “for a hundred years”. It could be pressed as “in” or “over” a hundred years.
notes.other_reading: over a hundred years or over three

notes.note: “These things” points back to the earlier part of the chapter, which is not in this passage and which speaks of looking at the cause and the matter of things. Nothing is supplied.
notes.other_reading: all this

notes.note: The verb is to inquire into, and also to observe, to come to know by seeing. The English takes it as observing, since the earlier part of the chapter twice says “look at it”. The aorist views the looking as a whole, hence “to have observed”.
notes.other_reading: To look into these things; to have been a witness of these things

check.note: The verb can mean to inquire into, but also to observe, to see for oneself. “Look into” suggests an investigation, and the aorist suggests a completed view.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To have observed these things for a hundred years or for three comes to the same”. The verb can mean simply seeing for oneself, and the earlier part of the chapter, not in this passage, twice says “look at it”, which favours observing over investigating.

part.left_out: Ἅλις τοῦ ἀθλίου βίου καὶ γογγυσμοῦ καὶ πιθηκισμοῦ.—τί ταράσσῃ; τί τούτων καινόν; τί σε ἐξίστησι; τὸ αἴτιον; ἴδε αὐτό. ἀλλ’ ἡ ὕλη; ἴδε αὐτήν. ἔξω δὲ τούτων οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἤδη ποτὲ ἁπλούστερος καὶ χρηστότερος γενοῦ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter up to the sentence about the gods in its section 9.35 and makes the closing sentence its whole section 9.36.

passages.casaubon: It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together or but for three years.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Наблюдать это сто лет или три — одно и то же.

passages.greek: Σῦκον χειμῶνος ζητεῖν μαινομένου· τοιοῦτος ὁ τὸ παιδίον ζητῶν, ὅτε οὐκέτι δίδοται.
passages.english: To ask for a fig in winter is the act of someone mad. Such is the person who asks for their child when it is no longer given.

notes.note: The saying appears to come from Epictetus, Discourses 3.24, as do the neighbouring chapters of book 11 (from memory, unchecked). Only what stands here is translated.
notes.other_reading: A fig in wintertime

notes.note: A genitive with no verb: “(it is the part) of one who is mad”. The participle is masculine but general, so the English says “someone”.
notes.other_reading: is a madman’s act

notes.note: The verb is to seek or look for, and also to ask for or want. It is used of the fig and of the child, so one English verb serves both. “Ask for” is used because “look for a child” would be heard as searching for one who is lost.
notes.other_reading: To look for a fig in winter; the person who looks for their child

notes.note: Literally “the little child”. The article can stand for a possessive, and the English takes it so.
notes.other_reading: the one who asks for the child

notes.note: A present passive: “when it is no longer given” or “granted”. The Greek does not say by whom, and the English keeps the passive.
notes.other_reading: when it is no longer granted to them

check.note: “Looks for their child” reads as searching for a missing child. The Greek means wanting or asking for a child when it is no longer granted, parallel to the fig in winter.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To ask for a fig in winter” and “the person who asks for their child”. The Greek verb means to ask for and want as well as to search, one English verb still serves both halves, and “asks for” answers “is no longer given”.

passages.casaubon: As they that long after figs in winter when they cannot be had; so are they that long after children, before they be granted them.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Просить смокву зимой — дело безумца. Таков и тот, кто просит своего ребёнка, когда это уже не дано.

passages.greek:
Ἐμὸν δ’ ἐγέλασσε φίλον κῆρ.

Μέμψονται δ’ ἀρετὴν χαλεποῖς βάζοντες ἔπεσσιν.
passages.english:
And my own heart laughed.

And they will find fault with virtue, speaking harsh words.

notes.note: The possessive belongs to the speaker of the verse and not necessarily to Marcus. The chapter is a bare line of poetry with no comment. The particle after it can be “and” or “but”.
notes.other_reading: But my heart laughed.

notes.note: A line-end from Homer, probably Odyssey 9.413, Odysseus after tricking the Cyclops (from memory, unchecked). The epic adjective, literally “dear”, usually means little more than “one’s own”, and is taken so.
notes.other_reading: and my dear heart laughed

notes.note: A future with no stated subject, hence “they”. The verb is to blame or find fault with.
notes.other_reading: They will blame virtue

notes.note: The line appears to be Hesiod, Works and Days 186, where the transmitted text has two small words at this point (“then” and “them”) and no mention of virtue (from memory, unchecked). The wording here may be Marcus’s own adaptation or a copying change. The English translates the line as it stands here.
notes.other_reading: And they will find fault with them, speaking harsh words.

notes.note: Literally “speaking with harsh words”. The line does not say whether the words are aimed at virtue or are simply the way these people talk.
notes.other_reading: railing at it in harsh words

check.note: This is a line of Hesiod, whose own text is recalled as having two small words here and no “virtue”. The English translates the Greek as given correctly, and no change is suggested.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is kept as it is and translates the Greek as given, with “virtue”. The note records that the line in Hesiod has other words at this point (from memory, unchecked).

passages.casaubon: 'My heart smiled within me.' 'They will accuse even virtue herself; with heinous and opprobrious words.'
passages.russian:
И моё сердце рассмеялось.

И станут они порицать добродетель, говоря резкие слова.

passages.greek: Τὸν μῦν τὸν ὀρεινὸν καὶ τὸν κατοικίδιον καὶ τὴν πτοίαν τούτου καὶ διασόβησιν.
passages.english: The mountain mouse and the house mouse, and this one’s fright and its being scared away.

notes.greek: Τὸν μῦν τὸν ὀρεινὸν καὶ τὸν κατοικίδιον
notes.note: The Greek as given does not construe on its own: everything is in the accusative with no verb, as if after an unspoken “think of” or “remember”. The English leaves a bare phrase and supplies no verb. The reference is taken to be the fable of the country mouse and the town mouse.
notes.other_reading: Think of the mountain mouse and the house mouse

notes.note: Literally “of the mountains” or hill country, the mouse that lives in the wild. English tradition says “country mouse”. The English keeps the Greek’s word.
notes.other_reading: the country mouse

notes.note: “Of this one”, pointing to the nearer of the two, the house mouse. The English keeps “this one” and does not name it.
notes.other_reading: the fright of the house mouse

notes.note: A fluttering fear, a state of alarm or agitation.
notes.other_reading: this one’s panic

notes.note: A rare noun from a verb meaning to scare off or throw into confusion. It may be the mouse’s being scared away, or its own agitated running about. The English takes the first, which is what the verb says.
notes.other_reading: and its scurrying in alarm

check.note: The whole chapter is in the accusative with no verb, so the Greek as given does not construe on its own. A bare list is fair, but the reader cannot tell that the mice are the object of a missing verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stays a bare list, the first of the two courses suggested, and supplies no verb. The note now says that the Greek as given is a string of accusatives with nothing to govern them.

check.note: The noun comes from a verb meaning to scare away and means being scared off. “Scurrying” adds a picture of movement the word does not give, and “in alarm” partly repeats “fright”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “its being scared away”. The noun comes from a verb for scaring off, and “scurrying” added a movement the word does not give, while “in alarm” repeated the fright.

check.note: The Greek is “of this one”. The house mouse is the natural reference, but “the latter” decides it and is rather formal.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “this one’s fright”. The Greek says “of this one” and leaves the reader to take the nearer mouse, and the English now does the same.

passages.casaubon: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse, and the great fright and terror that this was put into.

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Горная мышь и домашняя мышь, и испуг этой, и то, как её спугнули.

passages.greek: Πόσοι, μεθ’ ὧν εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸν κόσμον, ἤδη ἀπεληλύθασιν.
passages.english: How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone away.

notes.note: “How many” can be a question or an exclamation. The edition prints a full stop, so the English takes it as an exclamation and keeps the full stop.
notes.other_reading: How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone away?

notes.note: The form can be first person singular or third person plural. Only the first makes sense with “with whom”, so the speaker is the one who came in.
notes.other_reading: with whom they came into the world

notes.note: The glossary prefers “the universe” for this word. “The world” is used because the sense is being born among people, and “came into the world” is the plain English for that.
notes.other_reading: with whom I entered the universe

notes.note: A perfect, “have gone away”, built on the same verb as “came in”. It means they have died, but the Greek keeps the image of leaving, and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: have already departed; have already left it

check.note: The Greek pairs “came in” with “have gone away”, both compounds of the same verb. “Gone” alone slightly weakens the pair.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “have already gone away”. “Away” gives the Greek prefix and keeps the pair of coming and going, while “left it” would add an “it” the Greek does not have.

passages.casaubon: How many of them who came into the world at the same time when I did, are already gone out of it?

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Сколько из тех, с кем я вместе пришёл в мир, уже ушли.

passages.greek: Τὰ ἴδια τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς· ἑαυτὴν ὁρᾷ, ἑαυτὴν διαρθροῖ, ἑαυτὴν ὁποίαν ἂν βούληται ποιεῖ, τὸν καρπὸν ὃν φέρει αὐτὴ καρποῦται (τοὺς γὰρ τῶν φυτῶν καρποὺς καὶ τὸ ἀνάλογον ἐπὶ τῶν ζῴων ἄλλοι καρποῦνται), τοῦ ἰδίου τέλους τυγχάνει, ὅπου ἂν τὸ τοῦ βίου πέρας ἐπιστῇ, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ ὀρχήσεως καὶ ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἀτελὴς γίνεται ἡ ὅλη πρᾶξις, ἐάν τι ἐγκόψῃ, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ παντὸς μέρους καὶ ὅπου ἂν καταληφθῇ, πλῆρες καὶ ἀπροσδεὲς ἑαυτῇ τὸ προτεθὲν ποιεῖ, ὥστε εἰπεῖν· ἐγὼ ἀπέχω τὰ ἐμά. ἔτι δὲ περιέρχεται τὸν ὅλον κόσμον καὶ τὸ περὶ αὐτὸν κενὸν καὶ τὸ σχῆμα αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀπειρίαν τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκτείνεται καὶ τὴν περιοδικὴν παλιγγενεσίαν τῶν ὅλων ἐμπεριλαμβάνει καὶ περινοεῖ καὶ θεωρεῖ ὅτι οὐδὲν νεώτερον ὄψονται οἱ μεθ’ ἡμᾶς οὐδὲ περιττότερον εἶδον οἱ πρὸ ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ ὁ τεσσαρακοντούτης, ἐὰν νοῦν ὁποσονοῦν ἔχῃ, πάντα τὰ γεγονότα καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἑώρακε κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές. ἴδιον δὲ λογικῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τὸ φιλεῖν τοὺς πλησίον καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ αἰδὼς καὶ τὸ μηδὲν ἑαυτῆς προτιμᾶν, ὅπερ ἴδιον καὶ νόμου· οὕτως ἄρ’ οὐδὲν διήνεγκε λόγος ὀρθὸς καὶ λόγος δικαιοσύνης.
passages.english: What is the rational soul’s own: it sees itself, it analyses itself, it makes itself whatever it wishes, it gathers for itself the fruit it bears (for the fruits of plants, and what corresponds to them in animals, are gathered by others), and it reaches its own end wherever the limit of life comes upon it. It is not as with dancing and acting and things of that kind, where the whole action falls short of its end if something cuts in, but at every part, and wherever it is overtaken, it makes what was set before it full and in need of nothing more, for itself, so that it can say: “I have what is mine in full.” Further, it goes round the whole universe and the void around it and its shape, and it stretches out into the boundlessness of time, and it takes in the periodic rebirth of the whole and considers it from every side, and it observes that those after us will see nothing newer and that those before us saw nothing more remarkable, but that in a way a person of forty, if they have any mind at all, has seen all that has been and all that will be, in that it is all of one kind. The rational soul’s own are also love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame, and valuing nothing above itself, which is law’s own too. In this way, then, right reason and the reason of justice turn out not to differ at all.

notes.note: ἴδιος runs through the passage (τὰ ἴδια, τοῦ ἰδίου τέλους, ἴδιον twice), and the last step, that what is the soul’s own is also law’s own, depends on it. The English keeps “own” in all four places.
notes.other_reading: The properties of the rational soul

notes.note: διαρθρόω is literally to give something its joints, and so either to set out distinctly, to analyse, or to shape in detail. The English takes the first, since making itself what it wishes follows as a separate item.
notes.other_reading: it gives itself its articulate shape

notes.note: ἀτελής (incomplete) answers τέλους (end) just before: the soul reaches its end wherever it stops, while a dance cut short is left without one. “End” is kept in both places to show the link.
notes.other_reading: the whole action becomes incomplete

notes.note: The dative ἑαυτῇ, “for itself”, is taken with the main statement: the soul makes its task full for itself. It could also go with the participle, giving “what it set before itself”. The participle is passive: what was set before it, what was proposed.
notes.other_reading: it makes what it set before itself full and in need of nothing more

notes.note: ἀπέχω is the word for acknowledging payment in full, as on a receipt. The English adds “in full” to carry that sense.
notes.other_reading: have received

notes.note: This is the Stoic teaching that the universe is destroyed and born again in cycles. τῶν ὅλων is plural, “of all things together”; the English follows the glossary’s “the whole”.
notes.other_reading: the cyclical regeneration of all things

notes.note: περινοεῖ is taken with the rebirth, as a second verb beside “takes in”: both are compounds of περί, like “goes round” before them. Only θεωρεῖ is taken with the clause that follows. Both verbs can instead govern that clause.
notes.other_reading: and it takes in the periodic rebirth of the whole, and it grasps and observes that

notes.note: περιττός is what goes beyond the ordinary: either “more remarkable” or simply “more”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: saw nothing more

notes.note: Literally “in accordance with the sameness of kind”. It may give the ground (everything is of one kind) or limit the claim (has seen it all, as far as its kind goes). “In that” leans to the first.
notes.other_reading: has seen, as far as their kind goes, all that has been and all that will be

notes.note: αἰδώς covers shame, modesty and respect for others. The English has “a sense of shame”.
notes.other_reading: modesty

notes.note: ἑαυτῆς is taken as a genitive of comparison with προτιμᾶν: to rank nothing above itself.
notes.other_reading: to prefer nothing to itself

notes.note: λόγος is “reason” in both phrases, as in the glossary; the second could also be “the principle of justice”. The verb διήνεγκε is an aorist, taken as stating a result (“turn out not to differ”), not a past event.
notes.other_reading: In this way, then, right reason did not differ at all from the principle of justice.

check.note: The verb means to give something joints or articulate structure. It can be the soul analysing itself, or the soul giving itself articulate form, which would lead into the next clause.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “it analyses itself”. The verb is also used of setting a thing out distinctly, the next clause already says that the soul makes itself what it wishes, and the note records the other reading.

check.note: The Greek is one contrast: not as with dancing and acting, but at every part. The draft broke the sentence and dropped the “but”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the two halves are one sentence again, joined by “but at every part, and wherever it is overtaken”. The plain “but” of the Greek is used instead of the suggested “No:”.

check.note: The dative “for itself” most naturally goes with “makes” or with “lacking nothing”, and the participle is passive. The draft folded the dative into “set before itself”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it makes what was set before it full and in need of nothing more, for itself”, so that “for itself” belongs to the main statement and the participle is passive. “Set before” is kept for the Greek verb instead of “set out to do”, and a note records the other way of taking the dative.

check.note: The two verbs may both govern the “that” clause. The draft gave the first verb an added object, the rebirth, and attached only the second to what follows.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the first verb is still taken with the rebirth, since it stands beside “takes in” and shares its prefix, but a note now gives the other construction. The second verb now reads “observes”, to keep it apart from the plain verbs of seeing in the same sentence.

check.note: The word can mean “more out of the ordinary” or simply “more”. Beside “nothing newer” the plainer sense is possible.
check.decided: Accepted: the suggestion allows keeping the word with the choice noted, and that is what stands. The English reads “nothing more remarkable” and the note gives “nothing more” as the other reading.

check.note: One Greek word opens the chapter, returns in “its own end” and comes twice more at the close. With “properties” and “own” the English no longer shows that it is one idea.
check.decided: Accepted: the passage now opens “What is the rational soul’s own”, keeps “its own end”, and closes with “the rational soul’s own” and “law’s own”. The last step of the argument rests on the repeated word, so one English word is used for it.

check.note: The Greek says “in this way, then”. “So, then” reads as a bare “therefore”.
check.decided: Accepted: the last sentence now begins “In this way, then”. The Greek word points to the way just shown, not to a bare “therefore”.

check.note: Found while settling: “to love those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame” could be read as loving truthfulness and shame. In the Greek, truthfulness and the sense of shame stand beside the loving as further things that are the soul’s own.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now reads “Also the rational soul’s own are love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame, and valuing nothing above itself”, a list of four.

passages.casaubon: The natural properties, and privileges of a reasonable soul are: That she seeth herself; that she can order, and compose herself: that she makes herself as she will herself: that she reaps her own fruits whatsoever, whereas plants, trees, unreasonable creatures, what fruit soever (be it either fruit properly, or analogically only) they bear, they bear them unto others, and not to themselves. Again; whensoever, and wheresoever, sooner or later, her life doth end, she hath her own end nevertheless. For it is not with her, as with dancers and players, who if they be interrupted in any part of their action, the whole action must needs be imperfect: but she in what part of time or action soever she be surprised, can make that which she hath in her hand whatsoever it be, complete and full, so that she may depart with that comfort, 'I have lived; neither want I anything of that which properly did belong unto me.' Again, she compasseth the whole world, and penetrateth into the vanity, and mere outside (wanting substance and solidity) of it, and stretcheth herself unto the infiniteness of eternity; and the revolution or restoration of all things after a certain period of time, to the same state and place as before, she fetcheth about, and doth comprehend in herself; and considers withal, and sees clearly this, that neither they that shall follow us, shall see any new thing, that we have not seen, nor they that went before, anything more than we: but that he that is once come to forty (if he have any wit at all) can in a manner (for that they are all of one kind) see all things, both past and future. As proper is it, and natural to the soul of man to love her neighbour, to be true and modest; and to regard nothing so much as herself: which is also the property of the law: whereby by the way it appears, that sound reason and justice comes all to one, and therefore that justice is the chief thing, that reasonable creatures ought to propose unto themselves as their end.
passages.russian: Что свойственно разумной душе: она видит себя, разбирает себя, делает себя такой, какой хочет, собирает для себя плод, который приносит (ведь плоды растений и то, что им соответствует у животных, собирают другие), и достигает своей цели, где бы ни застиг её предел жизни. Не так, как в пляске, игре на сцене и тому подобном, где всё действие не достигает своей цели, если что-то его прервёт, — но в любой части и где бы её ни застигли, она делает то, что было ей предложено, полным и ни в чём больше не нуждающимся — для себя, так что может сказать: «Я имею своё сполна». Далее, она обходит всё мироздание, и пустоту вокруг него, и его форму, и простирается в беспредельность времени, и охватывает периодическое возрождение целого, и рассматривает его со всех сторон, и замечает, что те, кто после нас, не увидят ничего нового и те, кто до нас, не видели ничего более удивительного, но что в некотором роде сорокалетний, если у него есть хоть сколько-нибудь ума, видел всё, что было, и всё, что будет, поскольку всё это одного рода. Свойственны разумной душе также любовь к тем, кто рядом, и правдивость, и чувство стыда, и то, чтобы ничего не ценить выше себя, — что свойственно и закону. Так что правый разум и разум справедливости, оказывается, ничем не различаются.

passages.greek: Ὑβρίζει ἑαυτὴν ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ μάλιστα μέν, ὅταν ἀπόστημα καὶ οἷον φῦμα τοῦ κόσμου, ὅσον ἐφ̓ ἑαυτῇ, γένηται· τὸ γὰρ δυσχεραίνειν τινὶ τῶν γινομένων ἀπόστασίς ἐστι τῆς φύσεως, ἧς ἐν μέρει αἱ ἑκάστου τῶν λοιπῶν φύσεις περιέχονται. ἔπειτα δέ, ὅταν ἄνθρωπόν τινα ἀποστραφῇ ἢ καὶ ἐναντία φέρηται ὡς βλάψουσα, οἷαί εἰσιν αἱ τῶν ὀργιζομένων. τρίτον ὑβρίζει ἑαυτήν, ὅταν ἡσσᾶται ἡδονῆς ἢ πόνου. τέταρτον, ὅταν ὑποκρίνηται καὶ ἐπιπλάστως καὶ ἀναλήθως τι ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ. πέμπτον, ὅταν πρᾶξίν τινα ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὁρμὴν ἐπ’ οὐδένα σκοπὸν ἀφιῇ, ἀλλ’ εἰκῇ καὶ ἀπαρακολουθήτως ὁτιοῦν ἐνεργῇ, δέον καὶ τὰ μικρότατα κατὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος ἀναφορὰν γίνεσθαι· τέλος δὲ λογικῶν ζῴων τὸ ἕπεσθαι τῷ τῆς πόλεως καὶ πολιτείας τῆς πρεσβυτάτης λόγῳ καὶ θεσμῷ.
passages.english: The human soul does violence to itself most of all when it becomes, so far as it lies with it, an abscess, a thing standing apart, and a kind of growth on the universe. For to be vexed at anything that happens is a standing apart from nature, in some part of which the nature of each of the other things is contained. Next, when it turns away from some person, or even moves against them with the aim of doing harm, as the souls of angry people do. Third, it does violence to itself when it is beaten by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it plays a part and does or says something in a feigned and untrue way. Fifth, when it lets some action or impulse of its own fly at no target, but does anything whatever at random and without attention, though even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end. And the end of rational living beings is to follow the reason and law of the oldest city and constitution.

notes.note: ὑβρίζειν is to treat with insolence or outrage, to maltreat wantonly. The English reads “does violence to”, here and in 2.6, where the same verb is set against τιμῆσαι, “to honour”.
notes.other_reading: The human soul dishonours itself

notes.greek: ἀπόστημα καὶ οἷον φῦμα τοῦ κόσμου
notes.note: ἀπόστημα, the medical word for an abscess, is literally “a thing that has stood apart”, and the next clause explains it with ἀπόστασις, a standing apart or defection. The English gives the one Greek word twice, as “an abscess” and as “a thing standing apart”, so that the reason can be followed. These are not two items in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: an abscess and a kind of growth on the universe

notes.greek: ἧς ἐν μέρει αἱ ἑκάστου τῶν λοιπῶν φύσεις περιέχονται
notes.note: ἐν μέρει with the genitive is taken literally, “in a part of which”: each thing’s nature lies within its own portion of nature as a whole. It can also be read as “as a part”.
notes.other_reading: in which the nature of each of the other things is contained as a part

notes.note: πόνος is toil or pain. Set against pleasure, it is taken as pain.
notes.other_reading: by pleasure or by hardship

notes.note: The verb of the stage actor: to play a part, and so to pretend. “Plays a part” is kept, as in 9.39b.
notes.other_reading: when it pretends

notes.note: σκοπός is a target and ἀφιέναι is to let fly, as with an arrow or a spear. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: directs some action or impulse of its own to no aim

notes.note: Literally “without following along”: without keeping track of what one is doing, or without connection to anything. The English takes the first and reads “without attention”.
notes.other_reading: inconsequently

notes.greek: τῆς πόλεως καὶ πολιτείας τῆς πρεσβυτάτης
notes.note: The universe thought of as a city. πρεσβυτάτης is “oldest” and also “most revered”; πολιτεία is the constitution or the community of citizens. The English takes the plain sense of age, and “constitution”, which goes with the “law” that follows.
notes.other_reading: the most venerable city and commonwealth

notes.note: λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary; θεσμός is an old, solemn word for a law laid down.
notes.other_reading: the principle and ordinance

check.note: The verb is strong: to outrage, abuse, do violence to. “Dishonours” is pale beside it, and the choice should match 2.6.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “does violence to itself”, here, in the third item and in 2.6. The Greek verb is one of insolent ill treatment, which “dishonours” did not reach.

check.note: The word for “abscess” and the word here are from one root, and the “for” depends on that link. With “abscess” and “standing apart” the reader cannot see why the second sentence explains the first.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the first sentence now reads “an abscess, a thing standing apart, and a kind of growth on the universe”, and the second keeps “a standing apart from nature”, so the “for” can be followed. “Abscess” is not replaced by “something broken away”, because the Greek word is the medical one and stands beside a second medical word. The note says that one Greek word is given twice.

check.note: The Greek can also be taken as “in a part of which”: each of the other natures is held within its own portion of the nature of the whole.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in some part of which the nature of each of the other things is contained”, which follows the Greek construction. “Some” is used so that each nature is heard as lying in its own part, and the note keeps “as a part” as the other reading.

check.note: “Without following what it does” is hard to understand. The word means without attention, without keeping track of what one is doing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “at random and without attention”. The note keeps the literal sense of the word.

check.note: The superlative means “oldest” but also “most venerable”, and “constitution” is narrower than the Greek, which can mean the commonwealth itself.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the oldest city and constitution”. “Oldest” is the first sense of the Greek superlative, “constitution” fits the “reason and law” that the sentence goes on to name, and the note records “most venerable” and “commonwealth”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek sets the fifth case out as a contrast, no target “but” anything at random, and the draft had “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but does anything whatever at random and without attention”.

passages.casaubon: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are. Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are the souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done, without relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures is, to follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of this great city, and ancient commonwealth.
passages.russian: Человеческая душа больше всего творит над собой насилие, когда становится, насколько это от неё зависит, нарывом, чем-то обособленным, своего рода наростом на мироздании. Ведь досадовать на что-либо происходящее — значит обособляться от природы, в какой-то части которой содержится природа каждой из прочих вещей. Затем — когда она отворачивается от какого-нибудь человека или даже идёт против него с целью навредить, как души гневающихся. В-третьих, она творит над собой насилие, когда её побеждает наслаждение или боль. В-четвёртых, когда она играет роль и делает или говорит что-то притворно и неправдиво. В-пятых, когда пускает какое-то своё действие или побуждение лететь мимо всякой мишени и делает что бы то ни было наугад и без внимания, тогда как даже самое малое надлежит делать с оглядкой на цель. А цель разумных живых существ — следовать разуму и закону древнейшего города и государственного устройства.

passages.greek: Πρὸς τί ποτε ἄρα νῦν χρῶμαι τῇ ἐμαυτοῦ ψυχῇ; παρ’ ἕκαστα τοῦτο ἐπανερωτᾶν ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἐξετάζειν τί μοί ἐστι νῦν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μορίῳ, ὃ δὴ ἡγεμονικὸν καλοῦσι, καὶ τίνος ἄρα νῦν ἔχω ψυχήν; μήτι παιδίου; μήτι μειρακίου; μήτι γυναικαρίου; μήτι τυράννου; μήτι κτήνους; μήτι θηρίου;
passages.english: “Just what, then, am I using my own soul for now?” Ask yourself this at every turn, and examine: “What do I have now in this part, the one they call the ruling part? And whose soul, then, do I have now? Not a small child’s, surely? Not a youth’s? Not a silly woman’s? Not a tyrant’s? Not a farm animal’s? Not a wild beast’s?”

notes.note: ποτε sharpens the question and ἄρα draws it as an inference. The English gives them as “Just what” and “then”.
notes.other_reading: What ever, then

notes.note: An infinitive used as an instruction, with the reflexive ἑαυτόν, which in later Greek serves for any person. The English reads “ask yourself”, since Marcus is addressing himself; the Greek does not mark the person.
notes.other_reading: To ask oneself this at every turn, and to examine

notes.note: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is the Stoic term for the governing part of the soul. “They” are those who use the term, presumably the philosophers, and δή marks the name as the familiar one.
notes.other_reading: which is called the ruling part

notes.note: μήτι introduces a question said with misgiving, hoping for the answer no, and it is repeated before each of the six nouns. The English repeats “Not” six times and adds “surely” to the first only.
notes.other_reading: Can it be a small child’s? Can it be a youth’s?

notes.note: A μειράκιον is a lad in his teens or a little older.
notes.other_reading: Not a boy’s?

notes.note: A diminutive of “woman” used with contempt. The Greek is dismissive and the English does not soften it.
notes.other_reading: Not a little woman’s?

notes.note: κτῆνος is a domestic animal, cattle or a beast of burden, set against θηρίον, a wild animal.
notes.other_reading: Not a beast of burden’s?

check.note: The particle is repeated six times, once before each kind of soul, and expects the answer no. The draft gave it once and then a bare list.
check.decided: Accepted: each of the six questions now begins with “Not”, and the first adds “surely”: “Not a small child’s, surely? Not a youth’s?” and so on. The Greek particle stands before every one of the six.

check.note: The small word that sharpens the opening question was dropped, and so was the “then” of the later question about whose soul this is.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the opening question now begins “Just what, then,” and the later question has its “then” as well. “Just what” is used for the sharpening word because “What ever” reads awkwardly in English of today.

check.note: The particle marks the name as the well known one. It is a small loss.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in this part, the one they call the ruling part”. The clause around it was also brought closer to the Greek, which has a dative of the possessor, so the question now asks what the speaker has in this part.

check.note: “Adolescent” is a clinical word beside “small child” and “silly woman”. The Greek is an ordinary word for a lad or youth.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a youth’s”. The Greek is an everyday word, and “boy” would sit too close to the small child before it.

passages.casaubon: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?
passages.russian: «Для чего же я теперь пользуюсь собственной душой?» Спрашивай себя об этом на каждом шагу и исследуй: «Что у меня сейчас в этой части, той, которую называют ведущим началом? И чья же у меня теперь душа? Уж не малого ли ребёнка? Не юноши ли? Не глупой ли женщины? Не тирана ли? Не скотины ли? Не дикого ли зверя?»

passages.greek: Οἵα ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἕτοιμος, ἐὰν ἤδη ἀπολυθῆναι δέῃ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἤτοι σβεσθῆναι ἢ σκεδασθῆναι ἢ συμμεῖναι. τὸ δὲ ἕτοιμον τοῦτο ἵνα ἀπὸ ἰδικῆς κρίσεως ἔρχηται, μὴ κατὰ ψιλὴν παράταξιν ὡς οἱ Χριστιανοί, ἀλλὰ λελογισμένως καὶ σεμνῶς καὶ ὥστε καὶ ἄλλον πεῖσαι, ἀτραγῴδως.
passages.english: What a soul it is that is ready, if it must this moment be released from the body, and either be extinguished or be scattered or hold together. But this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and so as to convince someone else too, without theatrics.

notes.greek: Οἵα ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἕτοιμος
notes.note: οἵα can be an exclamation (“what a soul!”) or a description (“of what kind is the soul”). The English takes it as an exclamation of admiration.
notes.other_reading: Of what kind is the soul that is ready

notes.note: Three possible fates of the soul at death: to go out like a flame, to be dispersed, or to stay in one piece. The images are kept; συμμεῖναι is “hold together” here and in 4.21.
notes.other_reading: to be snuffed out, to be dispersed, or to survive

notes.note: The ἵνα clause has no governing verb: literally “that this readiness may come”. It is read as an instruction and “should” is supplied. ἰδικός is “one’s own” or “particular, specific”; κρίσις is a judgment or decision, a different word from the glossary’s ὑπόληψις.
notes.other_reading: see that this readiness comes from a judgment made on the particular case

notes.note: παράταξις is a drawing up in line of battle, and so opposition or defiance; ψιλή is “bare, mere”. The English takes it as mere opposition, but it could mean a readiness that comes from mere drill, like troops standing where they have been ranked.
notes.other_reading: not by mere drill

notes.note: This is thought to be the only mention of Christians in the book, and some editors suspect that the words are a reader’s comment that entered the text; they sit loosely in the sentence (from memory, unchecked). They are translated as they stand.
notes.other_reading: not by way of bare opposition, but in a reasoned and dignified way (with the three words left out)

notes.note: A result clause: in such a way as to convince another person too. It can go with what precedes or with ἀτραγῴδως, which follows; the English attaches it to the manner as a whole.
notes.other_reading: and, if it is to convince anyone else, without theatrics

notes.note: Literally “untragically”: without the gestures of the tragic stage.
notes.other_reading: without tragic show

check.note: The adjective can mean “one’s own” but also “specific, particular”: a judgment reached on this particular matter.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “a judgment of one’s own”, as the suggestion does in substance, and the note now gives the other sense, a judgment made on the particular case.

check.note: The noun is literally a drawing up in line of battle and can mean sheer opposition or mere drill. The preposition is “by way of”, not “from” as in the clause before.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the preposition is now “by way of”, since the Greek changes preposition here. “Bare opposition” is kept for the noun and the note gives “mere drill” as the other reading.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, these words have often been suspected of being a later reader’s marginal note that entered the text, and they sit loosely in the sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: the words are translated as they stand, and the note says that they may be a reader’s comment and not from Marcus (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: In today’s English “be put out” also means to be annoyed, which distracts. The image is of a flame.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “be extinguished”. It keeps the image of a flame without the other meaning of “be put out”.

check.note: The Greek clause has no governing verb: it is a bare “that this readiness may come”. “Should” is supplied, not stated.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “should come”. The Greek has only “that this readiness may come”, so any English must supply the sense of instruction; “should” supplies less than “see that”, and the note says that it is supplied.

passages.casaubon: That soul which is ever ready, even now presently (if need be) from the body, whether by way of extinction, or dispersion, or continuation in another place and estate to be separated, how blessed and happy is it! But this readiness of it, it must proceed, not from an obstinate and peremptory resolution of the mind, violently and passionately set upon Opposition, as Christians are wont; but from a peculiar judgment; with discretion and gravity, so that others may be persuaded also and drawn to the like example, but without any noise and passionate exclamations.
passages.russian: Какова та душа, что готова, если ей уже в это мгновение нужно освободиться от тела, либо угаснуть, либо рассеяться, либо остаться целой! Но эта готовность должна исходить из собственного суждения, не из голого противостояния, как у христиан, а обдуманно и с достоинством и так, чтобы убедить и другого, без театральности.

passages.greek: Σφαῖρα ψυχῆς αὐτοειδής, ὅταν μήτε ἐκτείνηται ἐπί τι μήτε ἔσω συντρέχῃ μήτε σπειρᾶται μήτε συνιζάνῃ, ἀλλὰ φωτὶ λάμπηται ᾧ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁρᾷ τὴν πάντων καὶ τὴν ἐν αὑτῇ.
passages.english: The sphere of the soul is true to its own form when it neither stretches out towards anything nor runs together inward, neither coils up nor sinks in on itself, but shines with a light by which it sees the truth, the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

notes.note: A sentence without a verb. αὐτοειδής is a very rare word, apparently “having its own form”; it is taken as the predicate and “is true to” is supplied. The text here is thought to have been doubted and emended (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: The soul is a sphere of its own form when

notes.note: The verbs describe ways the sphere loses its shape; the first pair is outward and inward. ἐπί τι is “towards something”, which may suggest reaching after an object of desire.
notes.other_reading: reaches out after anything

notes.note: As printed this is from σπειράομαι, “to be coiled” (σπεῖρα, a coil). Another reading, σπείρηται, “is scattered”, would make an opposite to the next verb (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text as given.
notes.other_reading: nor is scattered

notes.note: To settle together, to collapse on itself; the prefix means “together”.
notes.other_reading: nor collapses

notes.note: The verb is middle: the sphere shines with a light. A passive sense, “is lit by a light”, would make the light come from outside.
notes.other_reading: is lit by a light

notes.greek: τὴν πάντων καὶ τὴν ἐν αὑτῇ
notes.note: αὑτῇ with the rough breathing is reflexive, “in itself”, that is, in the soul. “The truth” is repeated so that the two articles are clear in English.
notes.other_reading: the truth of all things and the one in it

check.note: The verb is middle: the sphere shines with a light. “Is lit by” makes the soul passive and suggests a light from outside.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but shines with a light by which it sees the truth”. The Greek does not say that the light comes from elsewhere.

check.note: The Greek has no verb, only a rare adjective. “Keeps” adds the idea of holding on to a form over time.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The sphere of the soul is true to its own form when”. The note says that the Greek has no verb and that the adjective is rare.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, the text is doubtful at this word, and a reading that means “is scattered” would give two matched pairs.
check.decided: Accepted: “coils up” is kept for the text as given, and the note flags the doubt and the other reading (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The prefix means “together”: to settle or collapse in on itself. “Sinks down” gives only the downward movement.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nor sinks in on itself”.

passages.casaubon: Then is the soul as Empedocles doth liken it, like unto a sphere or globe, when she is all of one form and figure: when she neither greedily stretcheth out herself unto anything, nor basely contracts herself, or lies flat and dejected; but shineth all with light, whereby she does see and behold the true nature, both that of the universe, and her own in particular.
passages.russian: Сфера души верна собственной форме, когда она ни простирается к чему-либо, ни сбегается внутрь, ни свёртывается, ни оседает в себя, а сияет светом, которым видит истину — истину всего и истину в себе самой.

passages.greek: Εἰ διαμένουσιν αἱ ψυχαί, πῶς αὐτὰς ἐξ ἀιδίου χωρεῖ ὁ ἀήρ; πῶς δὲ ἡ γῆ χωρεῖ τὰ τῶν ἐκ τοσούτου αἰῶνος θαπτομένων σώματα; ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐνθάδε ἡ τούτων μετὰ ποσήν τινα ἐπιδιαμονὴν μεταβολὴ καὶ διάλυσις χώραν ἄλλοις νεκροῖς ποιεῖ, οὕτως αἱ εἰς τὸν ἀέρα μεθιστάμεναι ψυχαί, ἐπὶ ποσὸν συμμείνασαι, μεταβάλλουσι καὶ χέονται καὶ ἐξάπτονται εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων σπερματικὸν λόγον ἀναλαμβανόμεναι καὶ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον χώραν ταῖς προσσυνοικιζομέναις παρέχουσι. τοῦτο δ’ ἄν τις ἀποκρίναιτο ἐφ’ ὑποθέσει τοῦ τὰς ψυχὰς διαμένειν. χρὴ δὲ μὴ μόνον ἐνθυμεῖσθαι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν θαπτομένων οὑτωσὶ σωμάτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἑκάστης ἡμέρας ἐσθιομένων ζῴων ὑφ̓ ἡμῶν τε καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων. ὅσος γὰρ ἀριθμὸς καταναλίσκεται καὶ οὑτωσί πως θάπτεται ἐν τοῖς τῶν τρεφομένων σώμασι, καὶ ὅμως δέχεται ἡ χώρα αὐτὰ διὰ τὰς ἐξαιματώσεις, διὰ τὰς εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες ἢ πυρῶδες ἀλλοιώσεις. Τίς ἐπὶ τούτου ἡ ἱστορία τῆς ἀληθείας; διαίρεσις εἰς τὸ ὑλικὸν καὶ εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες.
passages.english: If souls go on existing, how has the air had space for them from eternity? And how does the earth have space for the bodies of those who have been buried over so long an age? For just as here the change and dissolution of these bodies, after they have gone on existing for a certain time, makes space for other dead, so the souls that pass over into the air, after holding together for a while, change and are poured out and are set alight, being taken back into the generative reason of the whole, and in this way they give space to those that come to settle there after them. That is what a person might answer on the supposition that souls go on existing. But one should consider not only the multitude of bodies buried in this way, but also that of the animals eaten every day by us and by the other animals. For how great a number is consumed and, in a way, buried like this in the bodies of those that feed on them! And yet the space takes them in, through their being turned into blood, through their alteration into what is airy or fiery. What is the way to inquire into the truth in this matter? Division into what is matter and what is cause.

notes.note: διαμένειν is to last on, here to go on existing after death. Marcus does not affirm it: the answer is given “on the supposition” that they do. The noun ἐπιδιαμονή, used below of the buried bodies, is from the same verb, so “go on existing” is used there too.
notes.other_reading: If souls survive

notes.note: χωρεῖν is “to have room for”, and χώρα, “room, space”, comes three times below. “Space” is used throughout so that the thread shows. The present tense with “from eternity” is rendered “has had”.
notes.other_reading: how does the air contain them

notes.note: γάρ here introduces the answer to the two questions, not a reason for them; “for” is the nearest plain word. ἐνθάδε, “here”, means in the earth.
notes.other_reading: The answer is that, just as here in the earth

notes.note: Literally “are poured” (melt, spread out) and “are kindled”. Both images are kept.
notes.other_reading: are diffused and catch fire

notes.note: The Stoic σπερματικὸς λόγος: the reason of the whole thought of as seed, from which all things grow. “Generative” is used for plain English; the usual technical rendering is “seminal”.
notes.other_reading: the seminal reason of the whole

notes.note: A triple compound: those who are settled in besides, as additional fellow inhabitants.
notes.other_reading: to the souls that come to share the dwelling

notes.note: Literally “the space receives them”. χώρα may be the room there is or the place, the region of the earth.
notes.other_reading: And yet the place has room for them

notes.note: “Turnings into blood”: the eaten animal becomes the eater’s blood. This and the following abstract noun are turned into verbal phrases.
notes.other_reading: through the conversions into blood, through the alterations into the airy or the fiery

notes.note: ἱστορία is inquiry or investigation. The phrase is compressed and is taken as “the way of inquiring into the truth”.
notes.other_reading: What is the investigation of the truth on this point?

notes.greek: εἰς τὸ ὑλικὸν καὶ εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες
notes.note: Two adjectives used as nouns: what a thing is made of, and what acts in it as cause. The sentence has no verb and is left so.
notes.other_reading: into the material and the causal

check.note: This noun is from the same verb as the one in the opening question. The lasting of bodies and the lasting of souls are being compared, so one English word would show the parallel.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “after they have gone on existing for a certain time”. The Greek noun is from the verb of the opening question, and the note says so.

check.note: The English is faithful and keeps the chain with “makes space” and “give space”, but it is a little hard to follow on first reading.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the space takes them in”, which gives the Greek verb and noun as they stand and keeps “space” for the word used twice before. The suggested wording adds “the same”, which the Greek does not have.

check.note: Found while settling: “from all eternity” had an “all” that the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from eternity”.

passages.casaubon: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed: and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto bodies, now begin to subsist single. This, upon a supposition that the souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.
passages.russian: Если души продолжают существовать, как в воздухе от века хватало для них места? И как находится место в земле для тел тех, кого хоронят уже столько веков? Ведь как здесь изменение и распад этих тел, после того как они просуществуют какое-то время, освобождают место для других мёртвых, так и души, переселившиеся в воздух, продержавшись какое-то время в целости, изменяются, разливаются и воспламеняются, принимаемые обратно в порождающий разум целого, и таким образом дают место тем, кто поселяется там после них. Вот что можно было бы ответить, исходя из предположения, что души продолжают существовать. Но следует учитывать не только множество тел, похороненных таким образом, но и множество животных, которых каждый день съедаем мы и другие животные. Ведь какое великое число их поглощается и в некотором роде хоронится так в телах тех, кто ими питается! И всё же место их вмещает — через их обращение в кровь, через их превращение в воздушное или огненное. Каков путь к исследованию истины в этом вопросе? Разделение на то, что есть материя, и то, что есть причина.

passages.greek: Ψυχάριον εἶ βαστάζον νεκρόν, ὡς Ἐπίκτητος ἔλεγεν.
passages.english: You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.

notes.note: A diminutive of ψυχή, belittling or pitying.
notes.other_reading: a poor soul

notes.note: βαστάζειν is to carry a load; νεκρός is a dead body, here the living body seen as already a corpse.
notes.other_reading: lugging a dead body about

notes.note: The imperfect can mean “used to say” or simply “said”. The saying is thought not to be in the surviving books of Epictetus (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: as Epictetus said

passages.casaubon: What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?
passages.russian: Ты — маленькая душа, несущая труп, как говаривал Эпиктет.

passages.greek: Διὰ τί συγχέουσιν ἄτεχνοι καὶ ἀμαθεῖς ψυχαὶ ἔντεχνον καὶ ἐπιστήμονα; τίς οὖν ψυχὴ ἔντεχνος καὶ ἐπιστήμων; ἡ εἰδυῖα ἀρχὴν καὶ τέλος καὶ τὸν δι’ ὅλης τῆς οὐσίας διήκοντα λόγον καὶ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος κατὰ περιόδους τεταγμένας οἰκονομοῦντα τὸ πᾶν.
passages.english: Why do unskilled and ignorant souls throw into confusion one that has skill and understanding? Which soul, then, has skill and understanding? The one that knows beginning and end, and the reason that runs through the whole of substance and, through all of time, manages the sum of things in appointed periods.

notes.note: Literally “pour together”: to confound, upset, throw into confusion.
