notes.other_reading: trouble

notes.note: Without τέχνη (art, skill) and without learning, answered by ἔντεχνος and ἐπιστήμων, having skill and having expert knowledge. The feminine adjectives that follow agree with an understood “soul”, supplied in English as “one”. “Understanding” is used for ἐπιστήμων so that “knows” is left for the different verb in the answer.
notes.other_reading: souls without art and without learning … one that has art and knowledge

notes.note: ἀρχή is beginning or first principle; τέλος is end or goal. The plainer pair is kept.
notes.other_reading: origin and purpose

notes.note: οὐσία is the Stoic name for the stuff of which everything is made, which reason runs through and shapes. “Substance” is kept as the one word for it.
notes.other_reading: through the whole of what exists

notes.note: Fixed, ordered cycles; the same thought as the periodic rebirth in 11.1, so “periods” is kept.
notes.other_reading: in ordained cycles

notes.note: οἰκονομεῖν is to manage a household. τὸ πᾶν, “the all”, is another name for the universe; “the sum of things” keeps it apart from “the whole” (τὸ ὅλον) and “the universe” (κόσμος).
notes.other_reading: administers the universe

check.greek: καὶ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος κατὰ περιόδους τεταγμένας οἰκονομοῦντα τὸ πᾶν
check.note: The Greek has two participles joined by “and”, both describing the reason that the soul knows. In the draft “manages” read as a new main verb, and “through all of time” was attached to “runs”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the answer now reads “and the reason that runs through the whole of substance and, through all of time, manages the sum of things in appointed periods”, so both verbs describe the reason that the soul knows. “The sum of things” and “periods” are kept, the first to stay apart from the glossary’s “the whole” for another Greek word, the second to match 11.1.

check.note: Two different Greek words are both given as “know”, the adjective in the question and the participle in the answer. In English the answer looks circular, which it is not in Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the question now asks which soul “has skill and understanding”, and “knows” is left for the verb of the answer. Two different Greek words no longer share one English word.

check.note: “Substance” is a term from philosophy books that a reader of today may not follow. The word means all that there is, the stuff of things.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the whole of substance”. In Stoic use the Greek word names the stuff that reason runs through and shapes, and “what exists” would take in reason itself; the note explains the term.

check.note: “Unlearned” is slightly archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “ignorant”.

passages.casaubon: Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it were this universe by certain periods of time.
passages.russian: Отчего неискусные и невежественные души приводят в смятение душу искусную и понимающую? Какая же душа искусна и понимает? Та, что знает начало и конец и разум, который проходит через всё вещество и на протяжении всего времени управляет совокупностью всего по установленным периодам.

passages.greek: τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ λέγεις· τέθνηκας, ἔφθαρσαι, τεθηρίωσαι, ὑποκρίνῃ, συναγελάζῃ, βόσκῃ;
passages.english: Do you say to the ruling part: “You are dead, you are ruined, you have turned into a wild beast, you are playing a part, you are running with the herd, you are grazing”?

notes.note: This is the end of a chapter and its construction is open. With the question mark at the end, the whole is taken as one question, with the six verbs as statements made to the ruling part. They can also be read as questions put to the ruling part, and some editors are thought to change λέγεις to an imperative (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: You say to your ruling part: “Are you dead? Are you ruined? Have you turned into a wild beast? Are you playing a part, running with the herd, grazing?”

notes.note: Perfect passive of φθείρω: destroyed, spoilt, or morally corrupted. “Ruined” is used because it can be heard in each of these ways, as the Greek can.
notes.other_reading: you are corrupted

notes.note: Literally “you have been made a wild beast” (θηρίον).
notes.other_reading: you have been brutalised

notes.note: The actor’s verb: you play a part, you pretend. Same rendering as in 2.16.
notes.other_reading: you are pretending

notes.note: Both are words used of animals: to gather in a herd (ἀγέλη) and to feed at pasture.
notes.other_reading: you herd together, you feed

check.note: The fragment can be punctuated two ways: one question, “do you say …?”, or a statement followed by six questions put to the ruling part. The Greek also allows “your ruling part”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps one question with six statements inside it. The Greek as printed has “you say” in the form of a statement and a single question mark at the end, which this reading follows, and the note gives the other reading in full. “The ruling part” is kept because the Greek has only the article.

check.note: Said of a mind, this verb more naturally means “corrupted, ruined, gone bad” than “destroyed”, which merely repeats “you are dead”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you are ruined”. The Greek verb covers both perishing and going bad, and after the talk of atoms and scattering just before the cut either may be meant; “ruined” leaves both open and the note gives “corrupted”.

part.left_out: Ἤτοι ἀπὸ μιᾶς πηγῆς νοερᾶς πάντα ὡς ἑνὶ σώματι ἐπισυμβαίνει καὶ οὐ δεῖ τὸ μέρος τοῖς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὅλου γινομένοις μέμφεσθαι· ἢ ἄτομοι καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ κυκεὼν καὶ σκεδασμός· τί οὖν ταράσσῃ;
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.38 at the question why you are troubled and begins its 9.39 with the closing address to the ruling part.

passages.casaubon: Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as well as the body?

nearest.title: The sameness and meanness of things

passages.russian: Говоришь ли ты ведущему началу: «Ты мертво, ты погублено, ты превратилось в дикого зверя, ты играешь роль, ты бежишь со стадом, ты пасёшься»?

passages.greek:
Οὐκ ἴσασι, πόσα σημαίνει τὸ κλέπτειν, τὸ σπείρειν, τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι, τὸ ἡσυχάζειν, τὸ ὁρᾶν τὰ πρακτέα, ὃ οὐκ ὀφθαλμοῖς γίνεται ἀλλ’ ἑτέρᾳ τινὶ ὄψει.

Σῶμα, ψυχή, νοῦς· σώματος αἰσθήσεις, ψυχῆς ὁρμαί, νοῦ δόγματα.
passages.english:
They do not know how many things are meant by “stealing”, by “sowing”, by “buying”, by “being at rest”, by “seeing what must be done”, which is not done with the eyes but with a different kind of sight.

Body, soul, mind. To the body belong sensations, to the soul impulses, to the mind principles.

notes.note: “They” are not identified; presumably people in general.
notes.other_reading: People do not know

notes.note: Literally “how many things it signifies”: the ordinary words have further senses that are missed. The verb is singular, with each infinitive in turn as its subject.
notes.other_reading: how much is meant by

notes.greek: τὸ κλέπτειν, τὸ σπείρειν, τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι
notes.note: Infinitives with the article, quoted as words. The English puts them in quotation marks as verbal nouns.
notes.other_reading: to steal, to sow, to buy

notes.note: To be quiet, to be at rest, to keep still.
notes.other_reading: “keeping quiet”

notes.note: The neuter relative most naturally picks up the last item, seeing what must be done. It could reach back to the understanding of all these words.
notes.other_reading: and this is not a matter for the eyes but for another kind of sight

notes.greek: σώματος αἰσθήσεις, ψυχῆς ὁρμαί, νοῦ δόγματα
notes.note: Three genitives with no verb; “belong” is supplied. The glossary words are kept: impulse (ὁρμή), mind (νοῦς), principle (δόγμα). Only the opening of 3.16 is given, so the thought is left where the Greek stops.
notes.other_reading: Of the body, sensations; of the soul, impulses; of the mind, principles.

check.note: The Greek is plural: how many things each word signifies. “How much” can be heard as depth of meaning, where the point may be the number of senses.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how many things are meant by”. The Greek word is a plural of number.

part.left_out: τὸ μὲν τυποῦσθαι φανταστικῶς καὶ τῶν βοσκημάτων· τὸ δὲ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι ὁρμητικῶς καὶ τῶν θηρίων καὶ τῶν ἀνδρογύνων καὶ Φαλάριδος καὶ Νέρωνος· τὸ δὲ τὸν νοῦν ἡγεμόνα ἔχειν ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα καθήκοντα καὶ τῶν θεοὺς μὴ νομιζόντων καὶ τῶν τὴν πατρίδα ἐγκαταλειπόντων καὶ τῶν ποιούντων, ἐπειδὰν κλείσωσι τὰς θύρας. εἰ οὖν τὰ λοιπὰ κοινά ἐστι πρὸς τὰ εἰρημένα, λοιπὸν τὸ ἴδιόν ἐστι τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φιλεῖν μὲν καὶ ἀσπάζεσθαι τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ συγκλωθόμενα αὐτῷ, τὸν δὲ ἔνδον ἐν τῷ στήθει ἱδρυμένον δαίμονα μὴ φύρειν μηδὲ θορυβεῖν ὄχλῳ φαντασιῶν, ἀλλὰ ἵλεων διατηρεῖν, κοσμίως ἑπόμενον θεῷ, μήτε φθεγγόμενόν τι παρὰ τὰ ἀληθῆ μήτε ἐνεργοῦντα παρὰ τὰ δίκαια. εἰ δὲ ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄνθρωποι, ὅτι ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως καὶ εὐθύμως βιοῖ, οὔτε χαλεπαίνει τινὶ τούτων οὔτε παρατρέπεται τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς ἀγούσης ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος τοῦ βίου, ἐφ’ ὃ δεῖ ἐλθεῖν καθαρόν, ἡσύχιον, εὔλυτον, ἀβιάστως τῇ ἑαυτοῦ μοίρᾳ συνηρμοσμένον.
part.why: The 1634 translation joins the opening sentence of chapter 16, on body, soul and mind, to its section 3.16 and begins its 3.17 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.casaubon: To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
passages.russian:
Они не знают, сколько всего означают слова «красть», «сеять», «покупать», «быть в покое», «видеть, что надо делать», — а это делается не глазами, а зрением иного рода.

Тело, душа, ум. Телу принадлежат ощущения, душе — побуждения, уму — принципы.

passages.greek: Ἐκ σωματίου εἰμὶ καὶ ψυχῆς. τῷ μὲν οὖν σωματίῳ πάντα ἀδιάφορα· οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται διαφέρεσθαι. τῇ δὲ διανοίᾳ ἀδιάφορα ὅσα μή ἐστιν αὐτῆς ἐνεργήματα· ὅσα δέ γε αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἐνεργήματα, ταῦτα πάντα ἐπ’ αὐτῇ ἐστιν. καὶ τούτων μέντοι περὶ μόνον τὸ παρὸν πραγματεύεται· τὰ γὰρ μέλλοντα καὶ παρῳχηκότα ἐνεργήματα αὐτῆς καὶ αὐτὰ ἤδη ἀδιάφορα.
passages.english: I am made of a little body and a soul. Now to the little body all things are indifferent, for it cannot tell a difference. To the mind, whatever is not its own activity is indifferent; and whatever is its own activity, all of that is in its power. Even of these, though, it is concerned only with the present, for its future and past activities are themselves already indifferent as well.

notes.note: σωμάτιον is a diminutive, “little body”, and belittling; the soul gets no diminutive. “Little” is kept.
notes.other_reading: a body and a soul

notes.note: A play on ἀδιάφορα, the Stoic term for things “indifferent” (neither good nor bad), and διαφέρεσθαι, which can mean to make distinctions or to be affected differently. “Indifferent” and “tell a difference” keep the echo.
notes.other_reading: for nothing can make a difference to it

notes.note: After “soul” in the first sentence Marcus switches to διάνοια. The glossary prefers “thought” but allows “mind” where the faculty is meant, as it is here; the passage has no νοῦς to confuse it with.
notes.other_reading: To thought

notes.note: The products of ἐνέργεια: its acts, what it itself does. The English has the singular “activity” in the general clauses and the plural at the end.
notes.other_reading: its own acts

notes.note: The full phrase is the Stoic expression for what is “up to” someone, in their power.
notes.other_reading: all of these are up to it

notes.note: Literally “it busies itself only about the present”. τὸ παρόν may be the present activity or the present time, and the English leaves that as open as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: it is concerned only with the present one

notes.note: ἤδη is taken as logical, “already, at once”: not being present, they fall straight into the class of indifferent things. καὶ αὐτά, “they too”, puts past and future activities with external things.
notes.other_reading: are themselves indifferent as well by now

check.note: The adverb here is logical, not temporal: they are at once, already, indifferent. “By now” is odd English when said of future activities.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “are themselves already indifferent as well”. The Greek adverb marks a consequence, not a point in time, and “by now” could not be said of future activities.

check.note: The verb can mean “to distinguish” or “to be affected differently”. The opening words may be a plain “for it cannot”, without the emphasis of “not even”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for it cannot tell a difference”, without “even”, since the Greek opening is a plain “for it cannot”. “Tell a difference” is kept and the note gives the other sense, that nothing can make a difference to the body.

check.note: The Greek says “only with the present”, which may be the present activity or the present moment. “The present one” settles it as the activity.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is concerned only with the present”, which is as open as the Greek. The note gives “the present one” as the narrower reading.

check.note: Marcus begins with “soul” and then changes to a different word for the thinking faculty. Elsewhere in this set “mind” stands for another Greek word.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the mind”. The glossary allows “mind” for this word where the faculty is meant, the other Greek word for mind does not occur in this passage, and the note records the change of word after “soul”.

passages.casaubon: I consist of body and soul. Unto my body all things are indifferent, for of itself it cannot affect one thing more than another with apprehension of any difference; as for my mind, all things which are not within the verge of her own operation, are indifferent unto her, and for her own operations, those altogether depend of her; neither does she busy herself about any, but those that are present; for as for future and past operations, those also are now at this present indifferent unto her.
passages.russian: Я состою из маленького тела и души. Для маленького тела всё безразлично: ведь оно не способно различать. Для ума безразлично всё, что не есть его собственная деятельность; а всё, что есть его собственная деятельность, всё это в его власти. Но и в ней его заботит лишь настоящее: ведь его будущая и прошлая деятельность уже и сама безразлична.

passages.greek: Ὕβριζε, ὕβριζε σεαυτήν, ὦ ψυχή· τοῦ δὲ τιμῆσαι σεαυτὴν οὐκέτι καιρὸν ἕξεις· εἷς γὰρ ὁ βίος ἑκάστῳ, οὗτος δέ σοι σχεδὸν διήνυσται, μὴ αἰδουμένῃ σεαυτήν, ἀλλ’ ἐν ταῖς ἄλλων ψυχαῖς τιθεμένῃ τὴν σὴν εὐμοιρίαν.
passages.english: Do violence, do violence to yourself, soul; but you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished, while you do not respect yourself but place your good fortune in the souls of others.

notes.note: An imperative, said in bitter irony and answered by “but”; the Greek has no “go on” and no possessive with “soul”. Some are thought to read an indicative here, “you are doing violence to yourself” (from memory, unchecked). “Do violence” matches 2.16, and the verb is set against τιμῆσαι, “to honour”.
notes.other_reading: You are doing violence, violence to yourself, soul

notes.note: καιρός is the right moment or opportunity, not time in general.
notes.other_reading: you will no longer have the time

notes.note: As printed: “for each has one life”. The wording of this clause is thought to be doubted in the transmission and to rest on an editor’s repair (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what is given.
notes.other_reading: for life is a single thing for each person

notes.note: A perfect: has been all but completed, like a journey travelled to its end.
notes.other_reading: is nearly at its end

notes.note: Dative participles agreeing with σοι: literally “for you, not respecting yourself but placing”. They are made a clause with “while”; a plain relative, “you who do not respect yourself”, is also possible. αἰδεῖσθαι is to feel respect or shame before someone, the verb of αἰδώς in 11.1.
notes.other_reading: yours, who do not respect yourself but place

notes.note: Literally “your good portion”, the lot that falls to a person: good fortune, and so well-being or happiness.
notes.other_reading: your happiness

check.note: The Greek imperative is a bitter concession, answered by “but you will have no time left”, and the bare English imperative can be read as a real instruction. The verb is also stronger than “dishonour”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is now “do violence to”, as in 2.16, and the command is joined to the next clause by a semicolon and “but”, so that it is heard as a concession. “Go on” and a possessive with “soul” are not added, because the Greek has neither; the note explains the irony.

check.note: From the second reader’s memory, this clause is an editor’s repair of a doubtful text, and the opening verb of the chapter is read by some as a statement instead of a command.
check.decided: Accepted: both places are translated as given, and the notes say that the opening verb is read by some as a statement and that this clause may be an editor’s repair (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “Good fortune” suggests luck. The word is literally “having a good portion” and here means well-being or happiness.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “your good fortune”. The Greek word is built on the word for a lot or portion, which “fortune” keeps, and the note gives “happiness” as the other reading.

check.note: The participles simply describe the “you” whose life is nearly over. “While” makes the link temporal, which is one choice among several.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “while you do not respect yourself”. The Greek participles state the circumstances in which the life is running out, which “while” gives, and the note now records the plain relative as the other reading.

passages.casaubon: Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.

nearest.title: Living now as one about to die

passages.russian: Твори, твори над собой насилие, душа; но случая почтить себя у тебя уже не останется. Ведь у каждого одна жизнь, и твоя почти прошла, а ты не уважаешь себя и полагаешь своё благополучие в душах других.

passages.greek: Ἆρα τοῦτο ἄξιον, ἵνα δι’ αὐτὸ κακῶς μοι ἔχῃ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ χείρων ἑαυτῆς ᾖ, ταπεινουμένη, ὀρεγομένη, συνδυομένη, πτυρομένη; καὶ τί εὑρήσεις τούτου ἄξιον;
passages.english: Is this worth it, that because of it my soul should be in a bad way and be worse than itself: brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright? And what will you find that is worth that?

notes.note: The passage is the second part of a chapter. “This” points back to something not given here, and it is not supplied.
notes.other_reading: Is this thing worth such a price

notes.note: Literally “worse than itself”, that is, worse than it is in its right state. The literal phrase is kept.
notes.other_reading: fall below itself

notes.note: Literally “stretching out” after something, the ordinary verb for desiring. In this list of bad states it is given as “craving”; the literal sense may be meant as a pair with the next word.
notes.other_reading: reaching out

notes.note: A rare word: literally “sinking in together”, taken as shrinking into itself. The reading is thought to be doubted, and a word meaning “bound, fettered” to have been proposed (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: fettered

notes.note: Used of a horse that shies: startled, scared.
notes.other_reading: panicking

notes.note: The person changes from the first person to “you will find”, and the change is kept. τούτου, “worth this”, means worth such a cost to the soul; “that” keeps it apart from the first “this”.
notes.other_reading: And what will you find that is worth this?

check.note: In this list of bad states the verb means craving or grasping after something. “Reaching out” is neutral, even friendly, in today’s English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “craving”. The Greek verb is the ordinary one for desiring, and in a list of the soul’s bad states “reaching out” did not sound like a fault; the note keeps the literal sense.

check.note: This is a rare word. From the second reader’s memory it has been doubted, and a word meaning “tied up, bound” proposed in its place.
check.decided: Accepted: “shrinking in” is kept for the word as given, and the note flags the doubt and the proposed word (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The English is literal and a little puzzling. The sense is that the soul falls below what it is.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “worse than itself”, which is what the Greek says word for word. “Fall below itself” would bring in an image of falling that the Greek does not have, and the note explains the sense.

part.left_out: Ἆρόν με καὶ βάλε, ὅπου θέλεις. κἀκεῖ γὰρ ἕξω τὸν ἐμὸν δαίμονα ἵλεων, τουτέστιν, ἀρκούμενον, εἰ ἔχοι καὶ ἐνεργοίη κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the first half of the chapter, on being thrown anywhere, in its section 8.43 and begins its 8.44 with the question whether this is worth the soul's harm.

passages.casaubon: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
passages.russian: Стоит ли это того, чтобы из-за этого моя душа была в плохом состоянии и стала хуже самой себя: поникшей, вожделеющей, сжимающейся, пугающейся? И что ты найдёшь такого, что этого стоило бы?

passages.greek: Πῶς ἑαυτῷ χρῆται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν; ἐν γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ πᾶν ἐστι. τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἢ προαιρετικά ἐστιν ἢ ἀπροαίρετα, νεκρὰ καὶ καπνός.
passages.english: How is the ruling part using itself? For everything lies in that. As for the rest, it is either within choice or outside it: dead things and smoke.

notes.note: A question to keep asking, with no verb of asking expressed. The present can be “how does it use” or “how is it using”.
notes.other_reading: How does the ruling part use itself?

notes.greek: ἐν γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ πᾶν ἐστι
notes.note: Literally “for in this is the all”, an idiom for “everything depends on this”. τούτῳ may be the ruling part or the way it uses itself.
notes.other_reading: for everything depends on this

notes.note: προαίρεσις is choice, the Stoic term for moral purpose. The Greek states flatly that the rest is either a thing of choice or not, and then, with no connecting word, “dead things and smoke”; the English keeps that shape, with a colon. It is striking that even what falls within choice seems to be dismissed with the rest, and this is not softened.
notes.other_reading: As for the rest, whether it falls within choice or outside it, it is dead things and smoke.

notes.note: νεκρά is neuter plural: “dead things” or “corpses”.
notes.other_reading: corpses and smoke

check.note: The Greek is a flat statement followed, with no connective, by “dead things and smoke”. “Whether … or” makes explicit that both kinds are dead things and smoke, which is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “As for the rest, it is either within choice or outside it: dead things and smoke.” This keeps the flat statement of the Greek and its unlinked last words, and the note gives the “whether … or” reading.

passages.casaubon: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.

nearest.title: The reason that governs the whole

passages.russian: Как ведущее начало пользуется самим собой? Ведь всё в этом. А остальное — либо в пределах выбора, либо вне его: мёртвое и дым.

passages.greek: Ἄνω, κάτω, κύκλῳ φοραὶ τῶν στοιχείων, ἡ δὲ τῆς ἀρετῆς κίνησις ἐν οὐδεμιᾷ τούτων, ἀλλὰ θειότερόν τι καὶ ὁδῷ δυσεπινοήτῳ προιοῦσα εὐοδεῖ.
passages.english: Up, down, round in a circle: such are the motions of the elements. The movement of virtue, though, is in none of these, but is something more divine, and, going forward by a road hard to make out, it fares well on its way.

notes.note: φορά is a being carried, a course: the natural motions of the elements. There is no verb and “such are” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: Upward, downward, in a circle run the courses of the elements

notes.note: κίνησις is a different word from φοραί; the English has “motions” for the first and “movement” for this one.
notes.other_reading: the motion of virtue

notes.note: Neuter, “something more divine”. It can be a predicate (virtue’s movement is a more divine thing) or adverbial (in some more divine way). It is taken as a predicate.
notes.other_reading: but in some more divine way

notes.note: A road that is hard to form a notion of, hard to conceive. “Hard to make out” fits both a road and a thought.
notes.other_reading: by a path hard to understand

notes.note: Literally “has a good road”, echoing ὁδῷ just before; in ordinary use it means “prospers”. The road is kept.
notes.other_reading: it prospers on its way

check.note: One grasps an idea, not a road, so “a road hard to grasp” reads oddly. The word means hard to conceive or make out.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by a road hard to make out”, which can be said of a road and still carries the sense of being hard to conceive.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek joins the last clause to the denial with “but”, and the draft began a new sentence without it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is in none of these, but is something more divine”. The earlier “But” became “though”, so that the word is not used twice in one sentence.

passages.casaubon: Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
passages.russian: Вверх, вниз, по кругу — таковы движения стихий. Движение же добродетели — ни в одном из них, оно нечто более божественное и, продвигаясь по едва различимой дороге, идёт хорошо.

passages.greek: Ἄλλως βέλος, ἄλλως νοῦς φέρεται. ὁ μέντοι νοῦς καὶ ὅταν εὐλαβῆται καὶ ὅταν περὶ τὴν σκέψιν στρέφηται, φέρεται κατ’ εὐθὺ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον.
passages.english: An arrow travels in one way, the mind in another. Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it turns about in considering something, travels straight none the less, and towards what is set before it.

notes.note: βέλος is any missile, an arrow or a javelin. φέρεται, “is carried, travels”, is the same verb in both sentences, and “travels” is kept for it.
notes.other_reading: A missile is carried one way, the mind another.

notes.note: To be cautious, to take care; εὐλάβεια is the Stoic word for reasonable caution.
notes.other_reading: when it is on its guard

notes.note: Literally “turns about around the inquiry”. The turning is set against the straight line that follows, so “turns” is kept.
notes.other_reading: when it is occupied with an inquiry

notes.note: “No less”: either “none the less” (in spite of the caution and the turning) or “no less than the arrow”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: travels straight no less than the arrow does

notes.note: What lies before it: its target, or the matter in hand.
notes.other_reading: to its mark

passages.casaubon: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
passages.russian: Стрела движется одним образом, ум — другим. Но ум, и когда он проявляет осторожность, и когда поворачивается, обдумывая что-то, всё равно движется прямо и к тому, что перед ним поставлено.

passages.greek: σχολαῖόν τι καὶ ἅμα εὐκίνητόν ἐστι καὶ φαιδρὸν ἅμα καὶ συνεστηκὸς ὁ τῷ λόγῳ κατὰ πᾶν ἑπόμενος.
passages.english: Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.

notes.note: Neuter predicates with a masculine subject: such a person is “something” unhurried, and so on. σχολαῖος is leisurely, unhurried, sometimes slow.
notes.other_reading: something leisurely

notes.note: Easily moved: quick to act, nimble. It is set in deliberate contrast with “unhurried”.
notes.other_reading: ready to move

notes.note: Bright, beaming, cheerful. “Cheerful” is used because “bright”, said of a person, would be heard as “clever”.
notes.other_reading: radiant

notes.note: Literally “standing together”: firm, compact, collected.
notes.other_reading: steady

notes.greek: ὁ τῷ λόγῳ κατὰ πᾶν ἑπόμενος
notes.note: The passage is the close of a chapter. The masculine article is generic, so the English has “someone who”.
notes.other_reading: the man who follows reason in everything

check.note: Said of a person, “bright” in today’s English is likely to be read as “clever”. The word means cheerful, radiant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “cheerful”.

check.note: Calling a person “a thing” is odd English. The Greek neuter is lighter: something unhurried.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed”. The Greek has an indefinite neuter, which “something” gives.

part.left_out: Τίς ὑπονοίας χρεία παρὸν σκοπεῖν τί δεῖ πραχθῆναι, κἂν μὲν συνορᾷς, εὐμενῶς, ἀμεταστρεπτὶ ταύτῃ χωρεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ συνορᾷς, ἐπέχειν καὶ συμβούλοις τοῖς ἀρίστοις χρῆσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἕτερά τινα πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιβαίνῃ, προιέναι κατὰ τὰς παρούσας ἀφορμὰς λελογισμένως, ἐχόμενον τοῦ φαινομένου δικαίου; ἄριστον γὰρ κατατυγχάνειν τούτου, ἐπεί τοι ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter up to the sentence on missing the mark in its section 10.13 and makes the closing sentence its whole section 10.14.

passages.casaubon: What is that that is slow, and yet quick? merry, and yet grave? He that in all things doth follow reason for his guide.

nearest.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

passages.russian: Тот, кто во всём следует разуму, — это нечто одновременно неспешное и лёгкое на подъём, одновременно весёлое и собранное.

passages.greek: Τὰ πράγματα ἔξω θυρῶν ἕστηκεν αὐτὰ ἐφ’ ἑαυτῶν, μηδὲν μήτε εἰδότα περὶ αὑτῶν μήτε ἀποφαινόμενα. τί οὖν ἀποφαίνεται περὶ αὐτῶν; τὸ ἡγεμονικόν.
passages.english: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.

notes.note: πράγματα are things, affairs, the objects and events one has to deal with.
notes.other_reading: Outward things

notes.note: The image is of things standing outside the doors; the Greek does not say whose doors. The phrase that follows is literally “themselves upon themselves”, that is, on their own.
notes.other_reading: stand outside our doors, on their own

notes.note: αὑτῶν with the rough breathing is reflexive, “about themselves”, and belongs to both participles, though the English states it once. The question that follows has the plain αὐτῶν, “about them”.
notes.other_reading: having no knowledge of themselves and making no declaration about themselves

notes.note: ἀποφαίνεσθαι is to declare, to give a verdict. The same verb comes back in the question, so “pronounce” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: nor making any statement

passages.casaubon: The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors, neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on them? The understanding.
passages.russian: Вещи стоят за дверьми, сами по себе, ничего о себе не зная и ничего не высказывая. Что же тогда высказывается о них? Ведущее начало.
